# System design interview questions, beginner to advanced

## Foundations

Before anyone draws a box on a whiteboard, a design needs requirements to satisfy. This part gives you the language to work from them: what system design is, how an interview tests it, and the standard components, six broad categories of them, that designs are assembled from. It separates the behavior a system is supposed to accomplish from the overall properties, such as availability or performance, by which its operation is judged. Along the way come eight problems that recur in large-scale production systems, each with a standard remedy, and the practices that keep an architecture honest as it evolves.

### What system design is and how interviews work

System design is the process of defining the architecture, interfaces and data of a system so that it satisfies specific requirements. This chapter introduces the field, the interview built around it, and the vocabulary of requirements and architecture that the rest of the course leans on. A functional requirement says what a system is supposed to accomplish, a non-functional one says how it should operate, and software architecture is the set of structures needed to reason about both. The interview that tests all of this has no single expected answer.

- **System design: choices that are hard to undo**

  The choices a team makes earliest are the ones it is least able to take back. System design is the process of defining the architecture, interfaces and data of a system so that it satisfies specific requirements. It is one of the earliest decisions made when building a system, and high-level design decisions are very difficult to correct later. That is why it is essential to think from a high level early on. The goal is a system that is scalable, reliable and efficient, and that meets the needs of a business or organization through a systematic approach to building it. Good design means thinking about everything, from the infrastructure all the way down to the data and how it is stored. The study of it is the study of a system's component parts and how they interact with one another. The scope is wide. It starts with the requirements a system must meet, covered in Functional requirements: what the system must do and Non-functional requirements: how the system must be. It runs through the choice of data store, the ways of scaling up and out, and the passing of messages between parts. It ends with watching a running system and automating how it is built, tested and deployed. A clear design pays off again later, because it makes architectural changes easier to reason about and manage as the system evolves.

  <!-- sysd-found-130 -->

- **System design interview: no single right answer**

  There is no answer key for a system design interview. It evaluates a candidate's ability to produce technical solutions to abstract problems, so it is not designed for one specific answer. The questions are vague or abstract by nature, and the topic is very extensive. The interview is also unusual, because it runs both ways between the candidate and the interviewer. Expectations differ at each engineering level, since an experienced engineer approaches the problem differently from someone new, which is why no single strategy keeps every candidate organized. One practical tip comes from Singh: read the engineering blog of the company you are interviewing with, to learn its technology stack and which problems matter to it. The subject being tested is system design itself, covered in System design: choices that are hard to undo.

  <!-- sysd-found-131 -->

- **System design building blocks: six categories**

  Large systems look different from one another, yet they are assembled from the same standard pieces. The building blocks of system design are those components, grouped into six broad categories. Distributed computing comes first. Its blocks are a queue of messages that lets services communicate asynchronously and stay decoupled. Next come a cache spread across machines, which keeps frequently accessed data in memory, and a task scheduler that coordinates running tasks. Scaling and performance is the second category. It holds scaling services that adjust capacity to demand and CDNs that serve content from geographically closer locations. It also holds a hashing scheme that minimizes key remapping when nodes join or leave, covered in Consistent hashing: adding a server without reshuffling everything. Service management is the way services find and talk to each other without hard-coded network locations, covered in Service discovery: finding services that keep moving. Networking and communication brings DNS, which maps domain names to network addresses. It also brings a load balancer that spreads incoming traffic across servers, and a single entry point for a group of services, covered in API gateway: one entry point to many services. Data storage and management covers stores for structured data and storage for images, videos and documents. It also covers sharding, which partitions data across nodes, and copying data to multiple nodes, which scales the store. The sixth category, observing the system and keeping it resilient, means gaining insight into its internal state through metrics, logging and tracing.

  *Figure: Each of the six categories groups the standard components named in its row.*

  | Category | Blocks |
  |---|---|
  | Distributed computing | Message queues, distributed caching, task scheduler |
  | Scalability and performance | Scaling services, CDNs, consistent hashing |
  | Service management | Service discovery |
  | Networking and communication | DNS, load balancer, API gateway |
  | Data storage and management | Databases, object storage, sharding, replication |
  | Observability and resiliency | Metrics, logging, tracing |

- **Functional requirements: what the system must do**

  Every system begins as a list of things it must do. A functional requirement defines a function of a system or component as behavior between inputs and outputs, a statement of what the system is supposed to accomplish. It is usually written 'system shall do <requirement>', for one individual action or part of the system. Functional requirements drive the application architecture, and they are planned in the system design, covered in System design: choices that are hard to undo. A good specification gives each one a unique name and number, a brief summary, a rationale, the required behavior and references to related use cases.

  <!-- sysd-found-207 -->

- **Non-functional requirements: how the system must be**

  A system can do everything on its list and still fail. A system's overall properties commonly mark the difference between a development project succeeding or failing. A non-functional requirement specifies criteria for judging how a system operates, an overall property such as availability or performance, rather than a specific behavior. Where a functional requirement says what the system shall do, a non-functional one says what it shall be. Each should be stated in a specific and measurable way. These requirements go by many names, including quality attributes, qualities, constraints and, informally, the 'ilities'. Execution qualities such as safety, security and usability show at run time. Evolution qualities such as testability, maintainability and extensibility live in the static structure of the system. In an interview they sound like a demand that every request be processed with the minimum delay, or that the system be highly available.

  <!-- sysd-found-139 -->

- **Software architecture: the blueprint behind a system**

  A blueprint is cheap to change on paper and costly to change once the building stands. Software architecture works the same way. It is the set of structures needed to reason about a software system, and the discipline of creating them. Each structure comprises software elements, the relations among them, and properties of both. The architecture is about fundamental structural choices that are costly to change once implemented. It shapes the infrastructure in which the functionality runs, so that the system's non-functional requirements are met. Two fundamental laws of software architecture are that everything is a trade-off and that why is more important than how. As an abstraction a team can grasp, it lets people analyse a system's behavior before it is built, saving cost and risk. Architectures fall into two main types, monolith and distributed, and tend to become more complex over time.

- **Common scaling problems and their standard fixes**

  Large systems tend to break in the same few places, and each place has a standard remedy. Eight problems recur in production. A read-heavy system is helped by a cache, covered in Caching: answering from a copy instead of the source. High write traffic goes to async workers that process the writes, or to data stores powered by LSM-trees. A part whose failure would stop the whole system is removed with redundant copies of critical components, such as the data store. A mechanism that switches over when one copy fails completes the fix. To keep a service available, a load balancer sends requests only to healthy server instances. Copying the data store to other machines improves availability and protects the data from loss. A long delay before a response arrives is reduced with a CDN, covered in Content delivery networks: serving users from nearby. Large files and complex data go to block and object stores, covered in Block storage: raw blocks owned by one server and Object storage: flat, huge and cheap. Watching a system and raising alerts relies on a centralized logging system, for example the ELK stack. Slow queries are fixed with proper indexes and by sharding to scale the data store horizontally.

  <!-- sysd-found-137 -->

  *Figure: Each row pairs a recurring problem with its standard remedy.*

  | Problem | Standard fix |
  |---|---|
  | Read-heavy system | Caching |
  | High write traffic | Async workers, or LSM-tree databases |
  | Single point of failure | Redundancy and failover |
  | High availability | Load balancing and database replication |
  | High latency | Content delivery network |
  | Large files and complex data | Block storage and object storage |
  | Monitoring and alerting | Centralized logging, such as the ELK stack |
  | Slower database queries | Indexes and sharding |

- **Architecture decision records: writing the why down**

  A decision nobody wrote down tends to be argued again and again. Forgotten, undocumented or misunderstood decisions, often those communicated by email, cause repeated discussions without resolution. Architecture decision records are the remedy: single, accessible records that capture each architectural decision with its technical and business justification. Architects usually record both, often about cost, user satisfaction and time to market, in one record kept in an accessible repository such as a wiki. That gives a single, updated source of truth. The records also help the architect who fears choosing wrongly and delays: deciding at the 'last responsible moment', in close collaboration with the development team, avoids analysis paralysis.

  <!-- sysd-found-142 -->

- **Software architecture activities: four steps, repeated**

  Nobody finishes an architecture in one pass. Software architecture design consists of four core activities, analysis, synthesis, evaluation and evolution, carried out iteratively at different stages of development. Analysis understands the environment of a proposed system and determines its requirements. Its outputs are the architecturally significant requirements, those with a measurable impact on the architecture. Synthesis creates and improves the design from them, and evaluation determines how well the current design satisfies them, for example with the Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method. Evolution maintains and adapts an existing architecture to changing requirements. Supporting activities run throughout: knowledge management, design reasoning and documentation.

  <!-- sysd-found-141 -->

- **Software architecture erosion: when the build drifts from the plan**

  Between the architecture a team intends and the one it builds, a gap tends to open. Software architecture erosion is that gradual gap, widening over time between a system's intended and implemented architecture. Its causes are architectural violations, accumulating technical debt and knowledge vaporization, and it can decrease performance, substantially increase evolutionary costs and degrade software quality. Enforcing architectural rules, regular code reviews and automated testing help prevent it. Refactoring, redesign and documentation updates remedy it, and conformance checks and static analysis detect it early. When documentation is out of date or the architecture has eroded, architecture recovery uncovers the architecture from the implementation and documentation.

  <!-- sysd-found-143 -->

- **Requirements engineering: settling the what before the how**

  Before anyone designs a solution, someone has to settle what the system must do. Requirements engineering is the work of eliciting, analysing, specifying, validating and managing what a system must do, the 'what' that architecture answers with a 'how'. It addresses the problem space, while software architecture, covered in Software architecture: the blueprint behind a system, targets the solution space. The waterfall model makes it the first phase of development. Later methods such as the Rational Unified Process assume it continues through a system's lifetime. Required behavior impacts the solution architecture, which may introduce new requirements in turn, and the Twin Peaks model aims to exploit this relation.

  <!-- sysd-found-144 -->

- **Software design pattern: a template for a recurring problem**

  Some problems come up so often in code that their solutions have names. A software design pattern is a reusable template for solving a commonly needed behavior in software. It is a template for a type of problem, not a rigid structure to copy into source code. It works below architecture patterns, which solve broader challenges. Reusing proven patterns speeds up development and helps prevent subtle issues. Patterns are grouped as creational, structural, behavioral and concurrency patterns. Critics say a need for a pattern may signal a missing language feature. Of the 23 patterns in Design Patterns, 16 are simplified or eliminated in Lisp or Dylan.

  <!-- sysd-found-208 -->

- **Architectural patterns and styles: the vocabulary of structure**

  The vocabulary for the shape of a system is crowded, and its edges blur. A software architecture pattern is a reusable, proven solution to a recurring system-level problem about overall structure, component interactions and quality attributes. It sits at a higher level of abstraction than a software design pattern, covered in Software design pattern: a template for a recurring problem. An architecture style is a high-level structural organization. It says how components are organized, how they interact and what constrains those interactions, using a vocabulary of component and connector types. Styles are the most coarse-grained level of system organization, for example layered architecture and hexagonal architecture, besides those covered in Microservices: small services that scale on their own and Event-driven architecture: parts that announce, not command.

  <!-- sysd-found-140 -->

- **Requirements clarification: ask before you design**

  The first move with a vague interview question is to ask questions back. Requirements clarification means asking early about the exact scope of the problem and sorting what the system must do into functional, non-functional and extended requirements. Functional requirements are the basic functionalities the end user demands, all of which must be built into the system as part of the contract. Ask which features to design for and which edge cases to consider. Non-functional requirements are quality constraints, so ask about aspects such as data volume, availability and scale. For example, every request should be handled with minimum delay, and the system should be highly available. Extended requirements are nice-to-have items that may be out of scope, such as recording metrics and analytics or tracking the health and performance of the service.

  <!-- sysd-found-133 -->

- **The system design interview framework, step by step**

  A system design question is open-ended, but a good answer follows a fixed order. The order is to clarify requirements, estimate capacity, design the high-level structure, the data and the interfaces, then address scale and reliability. Start by clarifying requirements, covered in Requirements clarification: ask before you design. Ask about the core features and about aspects such as data volume, availability and scale. Estimate capacity next, meaning the number of users, traffic, storage and memory needs, and compute and networking requirements. Useful questions are the desired scale, the read/write ratio, requests per second and storage needed. Define the data model early. List the entities and the relationships between them, which shows the data flow at the core of every system. Then choose a type of data store and settle the schema. Design the APIs as a simple interface of parameters, functions, classes, types and entities, without writing code. Keep it simple and revisit it when covering extended requirements. Then break the system into components such as client apps, servers, load balancers and data stores. Draw a simple block diagram, focus on the data flow, and walk through how the system works from the client's perspective. In the detailed design, pick with the interviewer the major components to go deeper on. Examples are data partitioning, load distribution, a cache and handling a sudden traffic spike. Finish with bottlenecks and reliability. Ask whether there are enough replicas of the data and whether any part's failure would stop everything. Ask whether the data needs sharding, and how to make the system and its cache more robust.

  <!-- sysd-found-132 -->

  *Figure: The framework runs from the top down, from clarifying requirements to bottlenecks and reliability.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Clarify requirements] --> B[Estimate capacity]
  B --> C[Define the data model]
  C --> D[Design the APIs]
  D --> E[Break into components]
  E --> F[Go deeper on key parts]
  F --> G[Bottlenecks and reliability]
  ```

- **Machine learning systems design: a model inside a system**

  Recommendation engines, fraud detection and natural language processing all depend on systems built around a machine learning model. Machine learning systems design builds scalable, reliable and efficient systems that integrate machine learning models to solve real-world problems. The key components are problem definition, which covers data requirements and evaluation metrics, and a data pipeline. The others are model selection and training, deployment and serving, and watching and maintaining the running system. The design balances trade-offs between accuracy, response delay, cost and maintainability. It overlaps with MLOps, practices that unify machine learning development and operations to ease deployment and lifecycle management.

  <!-- sysd-found-135 -->

- **Conway's law: software mirrors the organization**

  Software tends to look like the organization that wrote it. Conway's law says that the structure of a system mirrors the communication structure of the organization that designs it. The reason is that the authors of a product's parts must communicate to keep them compatible, so the technical structure reflects the organization's social boundaries. Strictly, the law describes a correspondence, not a cause, and commentators differ on whether design drives the organization, the organization drives design, or both. Researchers at MIT and Harvard Business School found strong evidence for it. The product from the loosely-coupled organization was significantly more modular than the product from the tightly-coupled one.

  <!-- sysd-found-209 -->

- **Discussing trade-offs in an interview without preaching**

  A blanket claim that one kind of data store is simply better and another does not scale reflects poorly in an interview. In the detailed design stage, present different approaches with their advantages and disadvantages, and explain design decisions with examples. This is a good time to show expertise, but avoid being too opinionated about technologies. Singh advises being humble about what you know and do not know, and using existing knowledge with examples to navigate this part of the interview. The framework this stage belongs to is described in The system design interview framework, step by step.

### Latency, throughput and back-of-the-envelope numbers

Latency is the time delay between a cause and its effect in a system, such as the wait between sending a request and seeing the response. Its companions are bandwidth, the maximum rate of data transfer across a given path, and throughput, the rate at which messages are successfully delivered. Rough latencies of common operations, from cache reads taking nanoseconds to a transatlantic packet taking 100 ms, let a designer judge which steps of a system are slow. Tail latency is measured at a high percentile, such as the 95th, 99th or 99.9th, rather than as an average. This chapter also gives you the units for sizing data and the nine metrics used to judge a website's performance.

- **Latency: why every system has some delay**

  No signal travels faster than light, so any system with distance between cause and effect has some delay built in. Latency is the time delay between a cause and its effect in a system, such as the wait between sending a request and seeing the response. Physically, it is a consequence of the limited speed at which any interaction can propagate, and that speed never exceeds the speed of light. The precise definition depends on the system being observed. In communications, the lower limit of latency is set by the medium used to transfer the information. Networks with relatively small delays are called low-latency networks, and the others are high-latency networks. Delay is not only about distance. Mechanical latency is limited by physics too: a disk read waits for the arm's seek time and then for the platter's rotational latency. In multitasking computers, a process can be postponed while other processes run, and the operating system schedules when each action happens, which adds software latency. People notice. Perceptible latency strongly affects user satisfaction and usability, and for high-scale user-facing systems high latency means a big loss of revenue.

  <!-- sysd-found-087 -->

- **Bandwidth: a ceiling, not the speed you get**

  A channel rated at x bit/s may not carry data at rate x. In computing, bandwidth is the maximum rate of data transfer across a given path. Protocols, encryption and other factors add overhead, TCP's three-way handshake adds more for each transaction, and lost packets cut useful throughput further. Useful throughput is therefore less than or equal to the actual channel capacity minus implementation overhead. The word is slippery. It may be called network, data or digital bandwidth, which differs from signal bandwidth, the frequency range in hertz used in signal processing and wireless communications. In web hosting it often means the data transferred to or from a site in a period, such as gigabytes per month. The more accurate phrase is monthly data transfer. The maximum physical-layer speeds of common links are 100 Mbit/s for Fast Ethernet and 1 Gbit/s for Gigabit Ethernet. They are 10 Gbit/s for 10 Gigabit Ethernet and 100 Gbit/s for 100 Gigabit Ethernet.

  <!-- sysd-found-099 -->

- **Network latency: distance, hops and queues**

  Even at the speed of light, distance costs time. Network latency is the delay for data to cross a network, measured one way from source to destination or as the round-trip delay time. Round-trip is quoted more often, because it can be measured from a single point. Light in optical fiber travels at about two thirds of its vacuum speed, which works out to about 5.0 μs of latency per kilometer. In a vacuum light takes 3.33 μs per kilometer. Fiber rarely runs in a straight line, and amplifiers or regenerators added beyond 100 kilometers add their own latency. A packet crosses several links and gateways that each wait for the whole packet. Minimal latency is therefore the sum of each link's transmission delay plus each gateway's forwarding latency. Queuing and processing delays join in, making the profile complex and variable. A geostationary satellite adds about a quarter of a second each way, while a low Earth orbit satellite 400 km up adds about 12 ms.

  <!-- sysd-found-088 -->

- **Percentile: the value that beats a given share of the data**

  Internet providers bill burstable bandwidth at the 95th or 98th percentile, which cuts off the top 5% or 2% of peaks each month. Infrequent peaks are ignored, so the customer is charged more fairly. A percentile is a value greater than a given percentage of all the values in a sample. The 97th percentile, for instance, is above 97% of the data points. The 50th percentile is the median, and the 25th and 75th are the quartiles. A percentile is stated in the unit of the measured values, not in percent. There is no standard definition. Some methods return a score that exists in the data, as nearest rank does, and others interpolate between scores. All give similar results when the sample is very large. Engineers also use percentiles on the numbers a running system reports about itself. The 99th percentile response time over a small window, such as one minute, can give a very early signal of saturation.

  <!-- sysd-found-192 -->

- **Tail latency: when the average hides the slow requests**

  A web service with a 100 ms average latency at 1,000 requests per second may still have 1% of its requests taking 5 seconds. That gap is what tail latency names. Tail latency is the high-percentile response time of a system, usually measured at the 95th, 99th or 99.9th percentile rather than as an average. Average and median latency can mislead in software systems, because a few outliers distort them. In distributed systems, cloud computing and large-scale web services, even a small number of slow requests can make user experience and system performance much worse. The causes are often resource contention, network variability, garbage collection pauses and hardware heterogeneity. Managing it is a major design problem, because lowering average latency does not always improve worst-case performance. Common ways to lessen it are request hedging, adaptive timeouts and the techniques of Replication: keeping several copies in step and Load balancing: spreading requests across many servers. It matters most for search engines, financial systems and real-time services, where service-level objectives are often based on high-percentile latencies.

  <!-- sysd-found-089 -->

- **Latency numbers to know, from nanoseconds to 100 ms**

  A read from RAM takes about 100 ns, while a packet sent from California to the Netherlands and back takes about 100 ms. Rough figures like these let a designer judge which steps of a system are slow. They are not accurate: they come from online benchmarks, including Jeff Dean's latency numbers, plus other sources. L1 and L2 caches take 1 ns and 10 ns and are usually built onto the microprocessor chip. Unless you work with hardware directly, you probably do not need to worry about them. Sending 1K bytes over a 1 Gbps network takes about 10 μs. Reading from an SSD takes about 100 μs. An insert into a data store takes about 1 ms, since it must store the data, create the index and flush logs. The long trip to the Netherlands and back is like the delay on a long-distance Zoom call. Retry or refresh intervals, by comparison, are on the order of 1-10 s.

  | Operation | About how long |
  |---|---|
  | L1 cache read | 1 ns |
  | L2 cache read | 10 ns |
  | RAM access | 100 ns |
  | 1K bytes over a 1 Gbps network | 10 μs |
  | SSD read | 100 μs |
  | Database insert | 1 ms |
  | California to the Netherlands and back | 100 ms |

- **Design trade-offs: every choice costs something**

  There is no right or wrong system design. Everything in system design is a trade-off and a compromise, so every design is a compromise between competing goals. Important trade-offs include cost versus performance, reliability versus the ability to scale, performance versus consistency, security versus flexibility, and development speed versus quality. The same pattern repeats in smaller choices. Scaling vertically means adding resources such as CPU and RAM to an existing server, while scaling horizontally means adding more servers to the pool. Consistency promises the most recent data every time, while availability keeps the system up even when parts fail. Synchronous processing performs tasks one after another, while asynchronous tasks can run in the background and new tasks start without waiting. Collecting data and handling it all at once, as in daily billing, differs from handling it in real time, as in fraud detection.

  <!-- sysd-found-094 -->

- **Reducing latency: the standard techniques**

  For high-scale user-facing systems, high latency is a big loss of revenue, so engineers rely on a handful of techniques to reduce it. The top strategies are indexing, a load balancer, a CDN, async processing and data compression. An index speeds up data retrieval on a table, at the cost of additional writes and storage space to maintain it. A load balancer distributes tasks over resources, optimizing response time and avoiding overloading some nodes while others sit idle. A CDN is a geographically distributed network of proxies and data centers, and its edge servers sit closer to the end user than traditional servers. Async processing through a queue of messages lets producers add requests without waiting for them to be processed. Compression with gzip reduces the amount of data transferred for web objects. A cache benefits latency, throughput or both, and prefetching that guesses future reads and requests them ahead of time bypasses the latency altogether if done optimally. One limit applies to all of these: propagation time depends on distance, and more bandwidth does not reduce it, as Round-trip time: what more bandwidth cannot fix explains.

  <!-- sysd-found-095 -->

- **Round-trip time: what more bandwidth cannot fix**

  More bandwidth cannot make a signal arrive sooner than the distance allows. Round-trip time is the time it takes to send a signal plus the time for its acknowledgement to come back. One-way delay is often approximated as half the RTT. RTT is twice the network latency plus a processing delay at the destination. Propagation time depends on distance, while transmission time is message size divided by bandwidth, so more bandwidth shrinks only the second. Networks with both high bandwidth and high RTT hold large amounts of data in transit and need special protocol design, such as the TCP window scale option.

  <!-- sysd-found-194 -->

- **Website performance metrics: nine ways to judge a page**

  A web page can feel slow for nine different reasons, and each has its own metric. Website performance is judged by nine metrics. They are load time, time to first byte, request count, DOMContentLoaded, above-the-fold load time, first contentful paint, page size, round trip time and render-blocking resources. Load time is how long the browser takes to download and display the page, measured in milliseconds. Time to first byte is how long the browser waits for the first byte from the web server. It shows the server's general ability to handle traffic. Request count is the number of requests the browser must make to load the page fully, and the lower it is, the faster the site feels. DOMContentLoaded is the time for the full HTML to load, not counting CSS and other assets, and the sooner it happens, the sooner users see useful functionality. Above-the-fold content, the part of the page that fits in the browser window without scrolling, is seen first and often decides whether users keep reading. First contentful paint is when any content, text, image or background color, is first painted. Page size is the total file size of all content and assets, and the bigger the page, the longer it takes to load. Round trip time is a request going from the browser to the origin server plus the response coming back. Reducing it is a key way to improve a website's performance. Render-blocking resources stop other parts of the page from loading, so the more a page has, the greater the delay.

  <!-- sysd-found-098 -->

  *Figure: The nine metrics side by side, each with what it tells you.*

  | Metric | What it tells you |
  |---|---|
  | Load time | How long the browser takes to download and display the page |
  | Time to first byte | How long the browser waits for the first byte from the server |
  | Request count | How many requests the browser makes to load the page |
  | DOMContentLoaded | When the full HTML has loaded, without CSS and other assets |
  | Above-the-fold load time | Content in the window without scrolling |
  | First contentful paint | When any content is first painted |
  | Page size | Total file size of all content and assets |
  | Round trip time | Request to the origin server plus the response back |
  | Render-blocking resources | Resources that stop other parts of the page loading |

- **Data size units: decimal and binary prefixes**

  A kilobyte is 1,000 bytes, but the hardware often means 1,024. Data sizes are expressed as multiples of the bit and the byte, using either decimal or binary prefixes. Decimal prefixes such as kilo- are commonly used with bit and byte, but hardware sizes are usually binary. So each prefix 1000^n is customarily used for a close approximation of 1024^n. In decimal units each step up multiplies by 1,000, up to the petabyte, 1,000 terabytes. The IEC binary prefixes, such as kibi-, are accurate but not commonly used. A kibibyte is 1,024 bytes and a mebibyte is 1,024 kibibytes.

  <!-- sysd-found-100 -->

- **Network throughput: the speed actually achieved**

  A link rated at 100 Mbit/s that delivers 70 Mbit/s is running at 70% channel efficiency. Network throughput is the rate at which messages are successfully delivered over a communication channel. It is usually measured in bits per second, and sometimes in packets per second. Aggregate throughput is the sum of the data rates delivered over all channels in a network. Bandwidth is the maximum achievable speed or capacity, while throughput is the speed actually achieved, and it is always less than bandwidth. The physical medium, the processing power of system components and end-user behavior all limit it, and protocol overhead can make the useful rate much lower than the maximum. When a link with data rate R is shared by N active users, each can ideally achieve about R/N. Router and switch schedulers decide how the bandwidth is actually shared. Without fair queuing, users that send large packets get more bandwidth. Weighted fair queuing can prioritize some users when differentiated quality of service is provided.

  <!-- sysd-found-090 -->

- **Goodput: the throughput you can actually use**

  Not every bit that crosses a link is something the application wanted. Goodput is the amount of useful information delivered per second to the application layer protocol. It excludes dropped packets, retransmissions and protocol overhead, so it is lower than the maximum throughput. Maximum throughput is often an unreliable measure of effective bandwidth, because the achieved throughput is usually lower and protocol overhead eats into it. In file transmission, goodput is the file size in bits divided by the file transmission time.

  <!-- sysd-found-092 -->

- **Maximum throughput measures: four upper limits**

  A system's maximum throughput can mean four different things. The measures are maximum theoretical, asymptotic, peak measured and maximum sustained throughput. The highest data rate a system can deliver is used most often to compare systems, so comparisons must use the same definitions. Maximum theoretical throughput is the most data that could be sent under ideal circumstances. Peak measured throughput is measured on a real or simulated system over a short period, which suits burst transmission. Maximum sustained throughput is averaged over a long time and is likely the most accurate indicator for networks under constant load.

  <!-- sysd-found-091 -->

- **Latency vs throughput: two different questions**

  A passenger's trip on the London to New York air link takes the same time whether 100 or 10,000 passengers a day make it. That is the difference between latency and throughput. Latency is how long one operation takes, while throughput is how many operations complete per unit of time, and one does not determine the other. Throughput is counted in messages per second, the reciprocal of the unit for propagation delay, seconds per message. The two still interact. In reliable two-way communication, latency limits total throughput, as the bandwidth-delay product describes. When that product is larger than the TCP window, the sender must wait for acknowledgements before sending more packets, so flow control lowers throughput, as covered in Flow control: the receiver's window sets the pace. A cache can benefit latency, throughput or both. Beyond partitions, distributed systems also face a trade-off between latency and consistency, as the theorem covered in PACELC: the trade-off CAP leaves out states.

  <!-- sysd-found-093 -->

- **Back-of-the-envelope estimation: sizing a system roughly**

  A billion requests a month sounds enormous, yet it works out to 400 requests per second. Back-of-the-envelope estimation is a rough calculation built on simplified assumptions that sizes a system's users, traffic and storage before it is designed. It is more than a guess but less than an accurate calculation or proof. Physicist Enrico Fermi emphasized approximating complex problems within an order of magnitude using simple calculations, and such sample calculations are called Fermi questions. For a design, ask about the desired scale, the read/write ratio, requests per second and storage needed. A handy conversion guide says a month has about 2.5 million seconds, so 1 request per second is 2.5 million requests per month. Storage per record comes from adding up its fields. A paste has 1 KB of content, a 7-byte shortlink, a 4-byte expiration length, a 5-byte creation time and a 255-byte path, which make about 1.27 KB. The primer advises clarifying with the interviewer whether to run these calculations at all.

  <!-- sysd-found-096 -->

- **Little's law: how many are inside a system**

  A store that sees 10 arrivals an hour, with an average stay of 0.5 hour, holds 5 customers on average. Little's law says the long-term average number of customers in a stable system equals the average arrival rate times the average time a customer spends there. It holds whatever the arrival process, the service distribution or the service order. It applies to any system and to systems within systems: in a bank branch it holds for the customer line, for each teller and for the whole branch. If the mean number in the system and the mean throughput are known, mean response time is their ratio. An average of ten jobs in the system at 50 per second gives 0.2 seconds. A system is stable when arrivals match exits. If arrivals exceed exits, the waiting grows without bound, and a system with limited space rejects the overflow, so its effective arrival rate is below the arrival rate.

  <!-- sysd-found-193 -->

### How computers talk: IP, TCP and UDP

A client asks and a server answers, but between them the data passes down a stack of layers, and this chapter takes that stack apart. The OSI model splits network communication into seven abstract layers, and the TCP/IP model organizes the Internet's protocols into four. As data is sent, each layer nests it inside a packet with a header, a step called encapsulation. The transport layer carries it from an application on one host to an application on another: TCP offers reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery of a stream of bytes after a three-way handshake, while UDP just sends messages as datagrams to other hosts on an IP network. Underneath both, IP gives each device a numerical address so it can be found, and it relays datagrams across network boundaries.

- **The OSI model: seven layers for talking about networks**

  Network engineers share a common vocabulary, and the OSI model supplied it. It is a logical, conceptual model that splits network communication into seven abstract layers, each stacked on the last. The layers run from sending bits across a physical medium up to the highest-level representation of data in a distributed application. Each layer has well-defined functions, serves the layer above it and is served by the layer below it. A protocol lets an entity in one host interact with the matching entity at the same layer in another host. Today's TCP/IP networks, described by the The TCP/IP model: the Internet's four layers, do not implement the model directly. It still makes troubleshooting easier, and it encourages hardware makers to build products that can talk to each other. Thinking in layers also breaks a complex function into simpler parts and supports a security-first mindset.

  <!-- sysd-found-024 -->

- **The TCP/IP model: the Internet's four layers**

  Where the OSI model stacks seven layers, the TCP/IP model gets by with four: link, internet, transport and application. It sorts the Internet's protocols by scope and specifies how data is packetized, addressed, transmitted, routed and received. Its foundational protocols are TCP: reliable, ordered delivery over an unreliable network, UDP: send the datagram and hope and IP: how packets find their way across networks. The link layer covers the local network, meaning every host reachable without crossing a router. The internet layer routes data between independent networks. The The transport layer: from one application to another gives applications host-to-host data channels. The application layer holds protocols such as FTP, SMTP and DHCP, and leaves formatting and presentation to libraries and APIs. An application sends its data down through the layers, and each level encapsulates it further.

  <!-- sysd-found-029 -->

- **Clients ask, servers answer**

  In online banking, the browser asks a web server, and that web server acts as a client of the server that stores the data. An application server applies the business logic, and the web server returns the result. This is the client-server model: it splits the work of a distributed application between servers, which provide a resource or service, and clients, which request it. Clients start the conversation and servers wait for incoming requests. Whether a machine is a client, a server or both depends on the application. They exchange messages in a request-response pattern defined by an application-layer protocol, so the client only has to understand the response. Work runs on the server when it needs data or functions the client lacks, or would be slow, unreliable or insecure on the client. A server is often a central system serving many clients, and it is scaled beyond one machine with Load balancing: spreading requests across many servers and Failover: when a standby takes over.

  <!-- sysd-found-154 -->

- **The seven OSI layers, from application to physical**

  From top to bottom, the seven layers are application, presentation, session, transport, network, data link and physical. The application layer is the only one that interacts directly with user data. It provides protocols such as HTTP: the request and response behind every web page and SMTP that browsers and email clients rely on, though the client software is not part of it. The presentation layer, also called the translation layer, handles translation, encryption and decryption, and compression of the application's data. The session layer opens and closes communication between two devices. It keeps a session open long enough to transfer all the data, synchronizes the transfer with checkpoints, then closes it promptly to avoid wasting resources. Layer 4, the The transport layer: from one application to another, is responsible for end-to-end communication between two devices. It breaks data into segments and reassembles them on the receiving device. Just below it, the The network layer: getting packets across networks moves data between two different networks. It breaks segments into packets and finds the best physical path to the destination, which is called routing. The data link layer moves data between two devices on the same network, breaking packets into smaller pieces called frames. The physical layer covers equipment such as cables and switches. It converts data into a bit stream of 1s and 0s, with both devices agreeing on a signal convention.

  <!-- sysd-found-025 -->

  *Figure: The seven OSI layers from top to bottom, each with the one job the entry gives it.* (layers; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The transport layer: from one application to another**

  The transport layer carries variable-length sequences of data from an application on a source host to an application on a destination host. Its protocols are either connection-oriented or connectionless. The layer below it imposes an MTU, a maximum packet size, so long streams are cut into segments small enough to leave room for the headers. Segmentation is optional. Connection-oriented protocols such as TCP: reliable, ordered delivery over an unreliable network segment and reassemble data, while connectionless protocols such as UDP: send the datagram and hope usually do not. The layer can also control reliability through flow control, error control and acknowledgments. Protocols that keep state about a connection track segments and retransmit those that fail delivery. Reliability is not strictly required, though. Some protocols serve applications willing to accept packet loss, reordering, errors or duplication. TCP and UDP were not developed under the OSI model, but they are commonly categorized as layer 4 protocols.

  <!-- sysd-found-030 -->

- **Encapsulation: wrapping data in headers, layer by layer**

  Every layer of the network stack wraps the data it is given. Take data sent over HTTP: the request and response behind every web page. The application layer first adds a header of its own. At the transport layer a TCP or UDP header goes on, making a TCP segment whose header holds the source port, destination port and sequence number. The next layer down wraps the segment in an IP header with the source and destination addresses. At the data link layer the IP datagram gets a MAC header with source and destination MAC addresses. The resulting frames travel over the physical layer as binary bits. This nesting of a data payload inside a packet with a header is called encapsulation. The receiving device reverses it, removing the headers layer by layer until it can read the data. Each unit has its own name. A segment is the TCP protocol data unit, a datagram is the IP unit and a frame is the data link unit. The design works because each layer focuses on its own responsibilities. It relies on the headers for processing instructions and never needs to know what the data from the last layer means.

  <!-- sysd-found-019 -->

  *Figure: Each layer wraps what it receives from the layer above, and the receiver strips the headers in reverse order.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Application: HTTP header added] --> B[Transport: TCP segment]
  B --> C[Network: IP datagram]
  C --> D[Data link: frame with MAC header]
  D --> E[Physical: binary bits]
  ```

- **TCP: reliable, ordered delivery over an unreliable network**

  The Web, email, remote administration, file transfer and media streaming all rely on TCP. SSL/TLS often runs on top of it as well. TCP is one of the main protocols of the Internet. It provides reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery of a stream of bytes between applications on hosts communicating over an IP network. That is a bold promise, because the layers below may lose, duplicate or reorder IP packets. TCP detects those faults and requests retransmission of lost data. It rearranges data that arrives out of order and helps reduce network congestion. Every byte received is identical to what was sent, and in the same order. Before any data flows, sender and receiver establish a connection on agreed parameters through a three-way handshake. The application sees none of this. TCP hides the networking details behind a socket interface, the subject of Sockets: where programs meet the network. It splits the data into segments that are wrapped in IP datagrams and reassembled at the receiver. Reliability has a price: handshaking, retransmission and error detection all lengthen latency. TCP is optimized for accurate rather than timely delivery, with delays on the order of seconds. It is not particularly suitable for real-time applications such as voice over IP. Those can use UDP: send the datagram and hope instead, a connectionless datagram service that prioritizes time over reliability.

  <!-- sysd-found-005 -->

- **How TCP opens and closes a connection**

  Before a client can connect, the server has to be ready. It binds to a port and listens there, which is called a passive open. The client then makes an active open with a three-way handshake. It sends a SYN, the segment that asks to open a connection, carrying a random sequence number x. The server replies with a SYN-ACK that acknowledges x + 1 and carries its own random sequence number y. The client answers with an ACK holding sequence number x + 1 and acknowledgment number y + 1. Both sides have now received acknowledgments, and full-duplex communication, with data flowing both ways, is established. The cost is one round trip of latency before any data can be sent, which matters a lot for short flows. Closing takes a four-way handshake. An endpoint that wants to stop its half sends a FIN, and the other end acknowledges it with an ACK. A typical tear-down needs a FIN and ACK from each side. The side that sent the first FIN then waits out a timeout with the port unavailable, commonly 30 seconds, 1 minute or 2 minutes. That wait lets it resend the final ACK if it was lost. A host that closes a connection while unread incoming data remains sends an RST instead of a FIN. The received data is lost, and the RST tells the application so.

  <!-- sysd-found-006 -->

  *Figure: The three-way handshake opens a connection, and a FIN and an ACK from each side close it.*

  | Step | Who sends | What it carries |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 | Client: SYN | random sequence number x |
  | 2 | Server: SYN-ACK | acknowledges x + 1, own random number y |
  | 3 | Client: ACK | sequence x + 1, acknowledgment y + 1 |
  | 4 | Either side: FIN | wants to stop its own half |
  | 5 | Other side: ACK | acknowledges the FIN; each side needs both |

- **Common application-layer protocols and what each is for**

  Above the transport layer, protocols are standard methods of transferring data between two computers. The Web runs on a client-server protocol for fetching resources such as HTML documents, described in HTTP: the request and response behind every web page. Its encrypted extension is HTTPS: ordinary HTTP inside an encrypted tunnel. Servers can push real-time updates over WebSocket: one persistent channel, open both ways, which gives full-duplex communication over TCP, while REST: the architectural style behind most web APIs always pulls. SMTP moves email from one user to another, and FTP moves files between client and server. Many of these build on TCP. HTTP/3 and QUIC: leaving TCP behind describes a version whose transport relies on UDP instead, for faster page responsiveness.

  <!-- sysd-found-020 -->

- **IP: how packets find their way across networks**

  The Internet Protocol essentially establishes the Internet, because its routing function is what enables internetworking. IP is the network-layer protocol that relays datagrams across network boundaries. It delivers packets from the source host to the destination host based solely on the addresses in the packet headers. To do that, it defines packet structures that encapsulate the data to be delivered. It also defines addressing methods that label each datagram with source and destination information. Each datagram has a header, with the addresses and other metadata needed to route it, and a payload, which is the data being transported. The address space is divided into subnets by designating network prefixes, and addresses are assigned to host interfaces. All hosts and routers perform IP routing. A router's main function is to carry packets across network boundaries, and routers exchange routes with each other through routing protocols. IPv4, the first major version, is the dominant protocol of the Internet. Its successor, IPv6, has been in increasing deployment on the public Internet since around 2006.

  <!-- sysd-found-001 -->

- **IP addresses: labels that let devices be found**

  The Internet needs some way to tell computers, routers and websites apart, and the answer is the IP address. It is a numerical label assigned to a device on a network that uses the Internet Protocol, so that the device can be found and addressed. It does two jobs: identifying a network interface and giving that interface a location. An IPv4 address is 32 bits, which limits the address space to 4294967296 addresses. Some are reserved for special purposes such as private networks. People usually write one in dot-decimal notation: four decimal numbers from 0 to 255, each an 8-bit octet, separated by dots, as in 192.0.2.1. IANA and the five regional Internet registries manage the address space globally. They hand blocks on to local registries such as ISPs and large institutions. A host can even deduce the geographic position of a peer by looking its address up in geolocation data.

  <!-- sysd-found-021 -->

- **UDP: send the datagram and hope**

  UDP makes almost no promises, and that is its whole design. It is a core Internet protocol that sends messages, carried as datagrams in packets, to other hosts on an IP network. It is connectionless: there is no handshake or shared connection, and a host is not expected to keep track of what it has sent. A datagram is a header of four 2-byte fields (source port, destination port, length and checksum) followed by the payload. UDP does not guarantee delivery, indicate the original ordering or detect duplication, and it gives the sender no feedback. A program that wants reliability must build it, for example by adding its own confirmation that a message was received. The 16-bit length field sets a theoretical limit of 65,535 bytes for a datagram, and the actual limit for data over IPv4 is 65,507 bytes. Being connectionless, UDP can also broadcast to all devices on the subnet and support multicast, where one datagram is routed to a group of subscribers.

  <!-- sysd-found-015 -->

- **Port numbers: telling services apart on one address**

  One IP address can serve many services at once, and the port number is how traffic finds the right one. TCP uses 16-bit port numbers, so each port has 65,536 possible values. A connection is identified by a four-tuple: source address, source port, destination address and destination port. Well-known ports, 0 through 1023, are assigned by IANA to system-level processes. They include FTP (20 and 21), SSH (22), Telnet (23), SMTP (25), plain web traffic (80) and web traffic over SSL/TLS (443). On Unix-like systems, using one requires superuser permission. Registered ports run from 1024 to 49151. Dynamic or private ports (49152-65535) are commonly used as ephemeral ports for temporary client connections. On its public side, NAT: how a private network shares one public address typically uses dynamic port numbers to tell apart traffic for many private hosts that share a single public address. Because a TCP connection's identity depends on addresses, it breaks if an endpoint's address changes.

  <!-- sysd-found-011 -->

- **Sockets: where programs meet the network**

  A socket address works like a phone number plus an extension. In TCP and UDP it is an IP address plus a port number. Internet sockets use it to deliver incoming packets to the right application process. A network socket is the software endpoint in a network node that sends and receives data, identified externally by its protocol, IP address and port number. It exists only for the lifetime of the application process, which gets a socket descriptor from the networking API. Stream sockets, usually TCP, give a reliable, ordered flow of data. Datagram sockets, using UDP, address and route each packet individually, with no guarantee of order or delivery. A server creates a socket in the listening state and waits for clients. A TCP server makes a dedicated socket for each client connection. Many of these can share one local address and port, because each socket pair has a unique 4-tuple. A UDP server socket has no established state and handles datagrams from every client.

  <!-- sysd-found-152 -->

- **IPv4 versus IPv6: running out of addresses**

  IPv4 is running out of room. Its 32-bit addresses, written as four dotted decimal numbers such as 192.168.0.12, allow approximately 4.3 billion unique addresses. The rapid exhaustion of that space led the IETF to redesign the Internet Protocol as IPv6. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons. That gives up to approximately 3.403×10^38 addresses, deemed sufficient for the foreseeable future. The header changed too. IPv4's is more complex, with fields such as header length, header checksum and options. IPv6's is a simpler fixed 40 bytes, with rare fields in optional extension headers, which speeds packet processing. The two versions are in simultaneous use today. Dual stack runs both at once on the same devices, using whichever fits the destination address. One guide calls it one of the best approaches for a smooth transition.

  <!-- sysd-found-018 -->

  *Figure: IPv6 widens the address and simplifies the header.*

  | Feature | IPv4 | IPv6 |
  |---|---|---|
  | Address size | 32 bits | 128 bits |
  | Written as | four dotted decimal numbers | eight groups of four hexadecimal digits |
  | Addresses | about 4.3 billion | about 3.403×10^38 |
  | Header | more complex, with options | simpler, a fixed 40 bytes |

- **TCP versus UDP: reliable but heavy, light but unreliable**

  TCP and UDP make opposite bets. TCP needs a handshake first: three packets set up a socket connection before any user data is sent, after which data may flow in both directions. It is reliable, managing acknowledgment, retransmission and timeouts. Either nothing is missing or, after multiple timeouts, the connection is dropped. It is also ordered, buffering out-of-order data until it can be delivered in sequence, though it is a byte stream with no signals marking message boundaries. All of that, plus congestion control, makes it heavyweight. UDP sends information in one direction without checking the receiver's readiness or state, and the sender cannot know whether a message arrives. There is no acknowledgment, retransmission or timeout. In return it is lightweight, sending packets individually with definite message boundaries, so one read at the receiver yields a whole message as it was sent. UDP does not avoid congestion itself, so the application or the network must handle that.

  <!-- sysd-found-016 -->

  *Figure: TCP and UDP compared on the same five properties, as the entry describes them.*

  | Property | TCP | UDP |
  |---|---|---|
  | Connection | handshake first | connectionless |
  | Delivery | acknowledged, retransmitted | no acknowledgment or retransmission |
  | Order | ordered byte stream | order not guaranteed |
  | Message boundaries | none | definite |
  | Weight | heavyweight | lightweight |

- **When UDP wins: voice, video, games and lookups**

  In a live voice or video stream, a late packet is worse than a lost one. That is why time-sensitive applications often use UDP: dropping packets is preferable to waiting for ones delayed by retransmission. Media streaming, real-time multiplayer games and VoIP are typical UDP applications. Loss of packets is not usually fatal, and in VoIP latency and jitter are the primary concerns. Video and audio protocols are designed to handle the occasional lost packet, so quality degrades slightly instead of suffering the large delays that retransmission would cause. DNS queries typically use UDP for its fast, lightweight nature, though DNS can also use TCP for large responses. Because UDP is stateless, it suits very large numbers of clients, as in IPTV streaming. Low-latency trading uses it to deliver market information to many recipients at once. One reliable and secure transport is built on UDP: QUIC: a faster transport built on UDP. Web traffic carried over it needs a single handshake instead of the separate ones that TCP and TLS need.

  <!-- sysd-found-017 -->

- **Best-effort delivery: IP promises nothing**

  IP never promises that a packet will arrive. It provides only best-effort delivery: it is connectionless and unreliable, and the end hosts and upper-layer protocols must repair any faults. The Internet follows the end-to-end principle, which treats the network as unreliable at any single element or link and puts the intelligence in the end nodes. Data corruption, packet loss and duplication may all occur, and the end nodes must detect and compensate for each. Routing is dynamic and every packet is treated independently, so packets to the same destination may take different paths and arrive out of order. Upper-layer protocols resolve these reliability issues, for example when a host buffers network data so it reaches the application in the correct order. IPv4 does add one safeguard for the header. A routing node discards packets that fail the header checksum test, and it is not required to tell either end node. IPv6 has no header checksum.

  <!-- sysd-found-002 -->

- **How TCP notices lost data and resends it**

  TCP builds reliability on top of Best-effort delivery: IP promises nothing by numbering bytes and demanding receipts. A sequence number identifies each byte, so data can be rebuilt in order however it arrives. Receivers use the numbers to discard duplicates and reorder packets, and acknowledgments tell senders when to retransmit. An ACK says that data has arrived up to a specified byte. It does not mean the data reached the application, only that delivering it is now the receiver's responsibility. The sender keeps a timer for each packet and retransmits if it expires before an acknowledgment arrives. That timeout is one of two main ways TCP identifies loss. The other is duplicate cumulative acknowledgments: a lost segment makes the receiver repeat the acknowledgment for the last in-order packet. After three duplicates, the sender retransmits the last unacknowledged packet. The threshold is three because the network may reorder segments. After a timeout the sender retransmits and doubles the timeout, a pattern called Exponential backoff: waiting twice as long each time.

  <!-- sysd-found-007 -->

- **Flow control: the receiver's window sets the pace**

  A fast sender can drown a slow receiver, such as a PC sending to a smartphone that processes data slowly. Flow control prevents that by keeping a TCP sender from sending data faster than the receiver can receive and process it reliably. TCP uses a sliding window. Each segment carries a receive window field that states how many more bytes the receiver will buffer. The sender may send only that much before it waits for an acknowledgment and a window update. When the receiver advertises a window of 0, the sender stops and starts a persist timer, which protects against deadlock if the window update is lost. A receiver that handles data in small increments may keep advertising a small window, a pattern called Silly window syndrome: the tiny-window trap. The 16-bit window field is limited to 65,535 bytes, so the window scale option raises the maximum to 1 gigabyte for high-bandwidth networks. The option is sent only in the SYN segments during the handshake, with a value from 0 (no shift) to 14.

  <!-- sysd-found-009 -->

- **Unicast, broadcast, multicast and anycast: who receives a packet**

  How many machines should one message reach? IP has four principal addressing methods, unicast, broadcast, multicast and Anycast: one address, many servers, and they differ in how many receivers a message reaches. Unicast delivers a message to one specific node, because each destination address uniquely identifies a single receiver endpoint. It carries traffic such as HTTP: the request and response behind every web page, FTP and SMTP. Broadcast delivers a message to all nodes in the network. One datagram from one sender is routed to every endpoint tied to the broadcast address, generally across an entire subnet. ARP, DHCP and NTP use it, though a broadcast does not mean every receiver gets the message. Multicast delivers a message to a group of nodes that have expressed interest. Its destination address designates a subset, not necessarily all, of the accessible nodes, and IPTV and video conferences use it. Sending the same data to several unicast addresses means sending it once per recipient. With multicast the sender sends a single datagram to the group address, and the routers copy it to all interested receivers. The fourth method delivers a message to any one node out of a group that share the same destination address, typically the nearest. The routing algorithm picks it by some distance or cost measure, and DNS querying and CDNs use it. Sources differ a little here. One describes it as reaching a single device or a specific group, with the other hosts in the group also expected to receive the message.

  <!-- sysd-found-003 -->

  *Figure: The four addressing methods differ in how many receivers a message reaches.*

  | Method | Reaches | Used by |
  |---|---|---|
  | Unicast | one specific node | HTTP, FTP, SMTP |
  | Broadcast | all nodes, generally a whole subnet | ARP, DHCP, NTP |
  | Multicast | a group that asked to receive | IPTV, video conferencing |
  | Anycast | one node of a group, typically the nearest | DNS querying, CDNs |

- **MTU and fragmentation: when a packet is too big**

  Across Ethernet, no packet may exceed 1500 bytes. That limit is the maximum transmission unit (MTU), the largest packet a link can carry. IPv4 automatically fragments a datagram into smaller units when it exceeds the link's MTU. IPv6 does not fragment in network elements, so end hosts must avoid exceeding the path MTU, which Path MTU Discovery: finding the smallest hop can find. TCP adjusts its segment size to stay smaller than the MTU. UDP and ICMP disregard it and force IP to fragment oversized datagrams. On Ethernet the minimum TCP and IPv4 headers are 20 bytes each, so the maximum segment size is 1500 - (20 + 20), or 1460 bytes. Fragmentation has costs. The whole packet is lost if any fragment is dropped. A tunnel header that pushes packets just over the MTU forces two fragments per packet, so every router forwards twice as many packets. A larger MTU is more efficient, but large packets hold a link longer, add delay and cost more to retransmit after an error.

  <!-- sysd-found-004 -->

- **TCP congestion control: how a sender finds the right speed**

  A TCP sender has to guess how fast the network can go, using only acknowledgments and timers. Congestion control is the set of sender-side mechanisms that keep a connection from sending more than the network can carry. The sender keeps a congestion window limiting unacknowledged data in flight. The receive window protects the receiver, and the sender stays within both. Slow start begins with a window of 1, 2, 4 or 10 MSS, where an MSS is one maximum-size segment. The sender adds 1 MSS per ACK, which doubles the window each round trip. This continues until a loss, the receiver's window or the threshold ssthresh stops it. Then congestion avoidance grows the window by up to 1 MSS per round trip. After a timeout loss the sender saves half the window as ssthresh and restarts slow start. Fast retransmit resends a segment after three duplicate acknowledgments instead of waiting for the timer, and fast recovery then halves the window and skips slow start. Treating loss as congestion misfires on wireless links, where fading and interference cause losses.

  <!-- sysd-found-010 -->

- **ARP: finding the hardware address for an IP address**

  To send a packet to 192.168.0.55 on its own network, host A first has to learn that machine's hardware address, so it asks everyone. The Address Resolution Protocol (ARP) discovers the link-layer address, such as a MAC address, that goes with an internet-layer address, typically an IPv4 address. A broadcasts a request to FF:FF:FF:FF:FF:FF containing the target's IP address. Only B answers, with its MAC address, and A then sends the data packet addressed to that MAC. ARP is a request-response protocol carried directly in link-layer frames. It works only within one subnetwork and is never routed. Nodes cache IP-to-MAC mappings so they need not broadcast every time. ARP cannot authenticate replies, so a spoofer can answer for another system's address to intercept its traffic. In IPv6 networks the Neighbor Discovery Protocol does ARP's job. Sources disagree about where ARP sits. RFC 826 and RFC 1122 place it in the link layer. Other textbooks put it in the OSI data link layer, the The network layer: getting packets across networks or an intermediate layer 2.5.

  <!-- sysd-found-148 -->

- **Head-of-line blocking: waiting behind a lost packet**

  One lost packet can freeze everything queued behind it. Head-of-line blocking is the delay that occurs when data that arrived later cannot be used until earlier lost or reordered data has been retransmitted and received. TCP offers a reliable byte stream, so the application cannot access packets after a lost one until the retransmitted copy arrives. If independent messages share one TCP connection, a fully received later message must wait for an earlier one. Browsers mitigate this by opening parallel connections. That repeats the connection establishment cost, and each connection runs congestion control on its own instead of pooling information.

  <!-- sysd-found-012 -->

- **QUIC: a faster transport built on UDP**

  TCP treats any error as blocking. When several streams of HTTP/2: many requests sharing one connection share one TCP connection, a single lost packet stalls all of them. QUIC is a general-purpose transport protocol, normally layered on UDP, that carries several streams over one connection and builds TLS into its handshake. UDP has no loss recovery, so QUIC does the recovery itself. Each stream is flow-controlled separately and lost data is retransmitted at the QUIC level, so an error in one stream does not block the others. The key exchange and the list of supported protocols are part of the initial handshake, which cuts connection setup latency. Every packet carries a connection identifier, so a connection survives an IP address change, such as a phone moving from Wi-Fi to cellular. Many middleboxes, the devices that sit in a network path, rate-limit or block UDP. So Chromium starts a QUIC and a TCP connection at the same time and falls back to TCP. The IETF standardized QUIC in RFC 9000 in May 2021, using TLS 1.3: a faster protocol built by removing things. Its first application is described in HTTP/3 and QUIC: leaving TCP behind.

  <!-- sysd-found-149 -->

- **Public and private addresses: who can be reached**

  At home, every connected device shares one public address from the outside. It is the address the ISP assigns to the whole network. A public IP address is a globally routable unicast address that may be used for communication between hosts on the global Internet. A private address is reserved for use inside a private network. Private ranges are not routed on the Internet and need no coordination with an address registry. A home router hands them to devices such as computers, tablets and phones. Private networks typically reach the Internet through NAT: how a private network shares one public address, which lets them conserve public address space.

  <!-- sysd-found-022 -->

- **NAT: how a private network shares one public address**

  IPv4 can identify about 4.3 billion devices, yet one Internet-routable address on a NAT gateway can serve an entire private network. Network address translation (NAT) maps one IP address space into another by rewriting address information in packet headers as they cross a routing device. The common one-to-many form maps many private hosts to one public address. A router rewrites outbound source addresses to its public address and tracks each active connection, so replies reach the right host. For TCP and UDP it rewrites port numbers too. It keeps a table of internal address, original source port and translated port. An incoming packet whose destination port is not in the table is dropped or rejected. Outside hosts cannot initiate a connection to an internal host unless port forwarding publishes the service. NAT also breaks end-to-end connectivity. VoIP and other applications that link users directly need application-level gateways or NAT traversal: reaching a peer behind another NAT. NAT is not commonly used in IPv6, because the large address space lets every device have a unique, globally routable address.

  <!-- sysd-found-028 -->

- **Static and dynamic addresses: fixed or lent**

  Some addresses are set once and never change; others are lent for a while. A static IP address is configured persistently, so network infrastructure such as routers and mail servers typically uses static addressing. Static addresses are usually more expensive but more reliable, and they suit remote access and server hosting. A dynamic address is assigned by the network each time a host joins or restarts, most often with DHCP: how a device gets its address automatically. That spares administrators from assigning an address to each device. A DHCP address carries a lease, and an unrenewed lease may be given to another device.

  <!-- sysd-found-023 -->

- **DHCP: how a device gets its address automatically**

  A device joining a network needs an address, and nobody has to type one in. The Dynamic Host Configuration Protocol (DHCP) automatically assigns IP addresses and other communication parameters to devices on a network. A central DHCP server manages a pool of addresses and parameters such as the default gateway and name servers. DHCP is connectionless and runs over UDP. The server listens on port 67 and the client on port 68, and a joining client sends a broadcast query for its configuration. A server can allocate addresses three ways. A dynamic address is leased from a reserved range and reclaimed if unrenewed. An automatic one is permanent. A manual one is mapped by an administrator from a client ID or MAC address. A broadcast stays on its own subnet, so relay agents on routers forward it by unicast to configured DHCP servers. Base DHCP has no way to check who is sending a message. A rogue server can hand clients false information such as a DNS server, and a client can exhaust the address pool with fresh identifiers.

  <!-- sysd-found-146 -->

- **The DHCP handshake: discover, offer, request, acknowledge**

  Getting an address from DHCP takes four exchanges: discovery, offer, request and acknowledgement. The client starts with a DHCPDISCOVER broadcast to 255.255.255.255 or the subnet broadcast address. It may ask for a particular address that the server can take into account. A server that receives it reserves an address and replies with DHCPOFFER. That message carries the offered IP address, subnet mask, lease duration and the server's own address. The client may receive several offers but accepts only one. It broadcasts a DHCPREQUEST that names the chosen server, and the other servers withdraw their offers and return those addresses to their pools. The chosen server completes the exchange with a DHCPACK that carries the lease duration and any other configuration the client asked for. Before claiming an address, the client should probe it, for example with ARP, to see whether another host already uses it. The address is a lease. The client starts renewing once half the lease interval has passed, unicasting a DHCPREQUEST to the granting server. If that server stays unreachable, the client rebinds by broadcasting the request so any server can renew the lease. When a lease expires, the client must stop using the address and restart with a DHCPDISCOVER. Its address then changes, so ongoing connections break. A client may send DHCP Release to give up its address, but the protocol does not require it, because devices are often unplugged without warning.

  <!-- sysd-found-147 -->

  *Figure: A DHCP client gets its address through four messages, alternating between client and server.*

  | Step | Message | Sent by | What it does |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | 1 | DHCPDISCOVER | Client | broadcasts to find a server |
  | 2 | DHCPOFFER | Server | offers an address, mask and lease |
  | 3 | DHCPREQUEST | Client | accepts one offer, naming that server |
  | 4 | DHCPACK | Server | confirms the lease and configuration |

- **Subnets and CIDR: where the network part ends**

  An IP address is really two addresses in one. The high-order bits are the network prefix, and the remaining bits, the host identifier, number the hosts within that network. A subnet is a part of an IP network, made by designating network prefixes within the address space. The subnet mask or CIDR notation determines where the split falls. In CIDR notation the address is followed by a slash and the number of bits of the network part. So 192.0.2.1 with mask 255.255.255.0 is written 192.0.2.1/24, because the first 24 bits indicate the network. Only IPv4 uses the term subnet mask, but both versions use CIDR.

  <!-- sysd-found-027 -->

- **The retransmission timeout: how long TCP waits before resending**

  How long should a TCP sender wait for an acknowledgment before resending? Networks vary so much that no fixed answer works, so the retransmission timeout (RTO) must be determined dynamically. It is computed by the algorithm in RFC 6298, which includes Karn's algorithm for taking samples of the Round-trip time: what more bandwidth cannot fix. Successive timeouts for the same segment back off exponentially. The backed-off value is kept until a segment with new data has been sent and acknowledged without retransmission. An endpoint must implement slow start, congestion avoidance and Exponential backoff: waiting twice as long each time of the RTO to avoid congestion collapse.
