Excessive retransmission of one segment signals a failed remote host or path. At a threshold called R1, which should be at least 3 retransmissions, TCP advises IP to start dead-gateway diagnosis. At a larger threshold, R2, which should be at least 100 seconds, it closes the connection. An application must be able to set R2 per connection. Opening a connection can fail the same way, through excessive SYN retransmissions, and R2 for a SYN must allow at least 3 minutes.

  <!-- sysd-found-162 -->

- **TCP segments and the maximum segment size**

  A program that makes one send call may see its data travel in several segments. TCP guarantees no correlation between the boundaries of segments and those of the application's read or write buffers. Segmentation is how TCP cuts the byte stream into segments, and the Maximum Segment Size (MSS) option tells the peer the largest segment it will accept. Larger segments mean fewer packets in flight, fewer interrupts and layer crossings, and less header overhead, though the benefit shrinks as segments grow. Smaller segments avoid a datagram larger than the smallest MTU on the path, which means loss or fragmentation. Some firewalls and middleboxes drop fragmented packets or the ICMP messages about them. Without an MSS option the default send MSS is 536 (576 - 40) for IPv4 or 1220 (1280 - 60) for IPv6. The effective send MSS is the smaller of two sizes. One is the peer's advertised MSS, which reflects its reassembly buffer. The other is the largest size the IP layer permits, less the TCP header and any IP options.

  <!-- sysd-found-161 -->

- **Nagle's algorithm: waiting to fill a packet**

  Waiting 200 ms is a long time when a keystroke must appear on screen. Nagle's algorithm makes TCP wait for a full packet of data before sending, grouping small messages into a single packet. By default TCP waits 200 ms for a full packet. That creates small but potentially serious delays when repeated constantly during a file transfer. In Telnet each keystroke is echoed back by the server before the user sees it, so the wait would be very annoying. Applications can set the TCP_NODELAY socket option to override the 200 ms delay and force output after writing a character or a line.

  <!-- sysd-found-014 -->

- **TCP sequence numbers: numbering every byte**

  At 100 Gbps, TCP can use up its entire sequence number space in around a third of a second. At 2 megabits per second the same job takes 4.5 hours. TCP gives every octet of data on a connection a sequence number, so the receiver can acknowledge, order and de-duplicate what it gets. Acknowledgments are cumulative: an acknowledgment of X means all octets up to but not including X have arrived. The sequence space is finite, from 0 to 2^32 - 1, so all sequence number arithmetic is done modulo 2^32. A new connection takes a 32-bit initial sequence number from a clock that typically ticks about every 4 microseconds and cycles in roughly 4.55 hours. Implementations should add a pseudorandom function of the addresses, ports and a secret key, because an attacker who could compute the number could guess sequence numbers. At high data rates the sequence space can wrap within the segment lifetime. TCP Timestamp Options and Protection Against Wrapped Sequences (PAWS) then detect and discard old duplicates.

  <!-- sysd-found-156 -->

  *Figure: The faster the link, the sooner the sequence number space is used up.*

  | Link speed | Time to use up 2^32 octets |
  |---|---|
  | 2 megabits/sec | 4.5 hours |
  | 100 megabits/sec | 5.4 minutes |
  | 1 Gbps | 34 seconds |
  | 10 Gbps | 3 seconds |
  | 100 Gbps | about a third of a second |

- **Selective acknowledgment: resend only what is missing**

  Say the second of ten equal segments, covering sequence numbers 2,000 to 2,999, is lost. With only cumulative acknowledgments, the receiver can acknowledge nothing past 2,000, so the sender may have to resend everything from there. Selective acknowledgment (SACK) is a TCP option that lets the receiver acknowledge discontinuous blocks of correctly received data. The receiver sends a cumulative ACK of 2,000 plus a SACK option with sequence numbers 3,000 and 11,000, and the sender retransmits only the second segment. All popular TCP stacks support it, though it works only if both parties do. SACK can name a maximum of three blocks.

  <!-- sysd-found-008 -->

- **Why TCP needs three messages to open a connection**

  Why three messages and not two? The principal reason is to prevent old duplicate connection initiations from causing confusion. The three-way handshake is the procedure TCP uses to establish a connection, in which the two peers exchange and acknowledge each other's initial sequence numbers. Each side sends a SYN carrying its own initial sequence number and needs it acknowledged. The acknowledgment of the first SYN and the second side's own SYN travel in one segment, which makes three messages. The handshake is needed because sequence numbers are not tied to a global clock. The receiver of a first SYN cannot know whether it is an old one, so it asks the sender to verify it. In the basic exchange the first SYN uses sequence number 100, so the reply acknowledges 101. A bare ACK takes no sequence space, because otherwise acknowledgments would themselves need acknowledging. Now suppose an old duplicate SYN reaches the passive peer. It replies normally, and the first peer sees the wrong acknowledgment and sends a RST. The passive peer returns to LISTEN, and the genuine SYN then completes the handshake. The procedure also works when both peers open at once, and an implementation must support this simultaneous open. Handshake segments may carry data, but the receiver must buffer it until the connection reaches ESTABLISHED.

  <!-- sysd-found-155 -->

- **The states a TCP connection moves through**

  A TCP connection moves through a fixed set of states during its life. They are LISTEN, SYN-SENT, SYN-RECEIVED, ESTABLISHED, FIN-WAIT-1, FIN-WAIT-2, CLOSE-WAIT, CLOSING, LAST-ACK, TIME-WAIT and the fictional CLOSED, which means no connection record exists. Incoming segments carrying SYN, ACK, RST or FIN, user calls and timeouts cause the changes. A passive OPEN means the process wants to accept incoming connection requests, and an active OPEN attempts to initiate one. Opening starts in LISTEN, which waits for a request from any remote peer. SYN-SENT has sent a request and awaits a matching one. SYN-RECEIVED has both received and sent one and awaits the acknowledgment. ESTABLISHED is the normal state for data transfer. Closing uses the other states. The FIN-WAIT states wait for the peer's termination request, and CLOSE-WAIT waits for the local user to close. CLOSING and LAST-ACK wait for acknowledgment of a termination request already sent. TIME-WAIT keeps delayed segments from earlier connections from affecting new ones.

  <!-- sysd-found-157 -->

- **SYN floods and TCP hijacking**

  A flood of bogus connection requests can swamp a server. In a SYN flood, an attacker uses a spoofed IP address and repeatedly sends crafted SYN packets. The server spends large amounts of resources tracking bogus connections. SYN cookies and cryptographic puzzles have been proposed as defenses, though SYN cookies come with their own vulnerabilities. A connection can also be hijacked. An attacker who can eavesdrop on a session and redirect packets can learn the sequence number. The attacker then forges a segment that looks like the next one in the stream. That is why the initial sequence number should be unpredictable.

  <!-- sysd-found-013 -->

- **The network layer: getting packets across networks**

  A sender only supplies the message and a destination address, and the network finds the way. That is the network layer's job: moving packets from one node to another across different networks, routing through intermediate nodes where needed. If a message is too large for the data link layer between two nodes, the network may split it into fragments. It sends them independently and reassembles them at another node. Delivery is not necessarily reliable, since a protocol may, but need not, report errors or provide reliable delivery. If the two devices are on the same network, the network layer is unnecessary.

  <!-- sysd-found-031 -->

- **ICMP: how the network reports its own errors**

  When a packet cannot get through, ICMP is how the network says so. The Internet Control Message Protocol is a supporting protocol that routers and other network devices use to send error messages and operational information about IP communication. It reports problems such as an unavailable service or an unreachable host or router. The errors go to the source IP address of the packet that caused them. Unlike TCP and UDP, ICMP does not normally carry data between systems or serve end-user applications, and an ICMP packet has no port number. Its messages travel inside IPv4 packets, and IPv6 uses a separate ICMPv6. Each forwarding router decrements the packet's TTL, explained in Time to live: giving data an expiry. At 0 the packet is discarded and an ICMP time exceeded message goes to the source. Ping uses echo request and echo reply. Traceroute sends datagrams with increasing TTL values and reads the time exceeded and destination unreachable messages to find each router on the path. Destination unreachable is also sent when a packet must be fragmented but carries the don't-fragment flag, which Path MTU Discovery: finding the smallest hop relies on.

  <!-- sysd-found-153 -->

- **Choosing TCP or UDP: completeness or speed**

  The choice comes down to one question: is late data worse than lost data? Use TCP when data must arrive complete and in order, and use UDP when the lowest latency matters more than losing some data. TCP has built-in error checking and guarantees that data is delivered in the order it was sent, which suits still images, data files and web pages. Its feedback mechanisms make it reliable but add overhead, using more of the available network bandwidth. UDP has no overhead for opening, maintaining or terminating a connection, and it sends data continuously whether or not the recipient receives it. It is faster, simpler and more efficient than TCP, but only TCP can retransmit lost packets. Typical TCP uses are web traffic, mail with SMTP and POP, and FTP. Typical UDP uses are video streaming, DNS and VoIP, and UDP is largely preferred for real-time communication such as broadcast or multicast transmission.

  <!-- sysd-found-026 -->

- **NAT traversal: reaching a peer behind another NAT**

  Two peers that both sit behind NAT devices cannot simply call each other. NAT traversal is the set of techniques, such as port forwarding and TCP hole punching, that lets them communicate. VoIP, videoconferencing and other applications that connect users directly must use them to work. STUN was specified to let a client find its external address and the type of mapping its NAT uses. TCP hole punching, the most popular TCP technique, needs the NAT to preserve ports for outgoing connections. UDP needs no such preservation, because many UDP communications can share one source port.

  <!-- sysd-found-145 -->

- **Delayed ACKs: acknowledging less often**

  A receiver does not have to acknowledge every segment. With a delayed ACK it sends fewer than one acknowledgment per data segment received, which saves effort in both the network and the hosts. A TCP endpoint should delay ACKs but never excessively: the delay must be less than 0.5 seconds. Excessive delays disturb round-trip timing and packet clocking. So out-of-order segments, segments above a gap and segments that fill a gap should be acknowledged immediately, to speed loss recovery. Combined with Nagle's algorithm: waiting to fill a packet, both on by default in common operating systems, delayed ACKs can badly hurt request-response applications. Many applications simply disable Nagle with a socket option.

  <!-- sysd-found-164 -->

- **Silly window syndrome: the tiny-window trap**

  TCP can fall into a stable pattern of small incremental window movements that leaves it performing extremely poorly. Both sender and receiver must avoid it. Nagle's algorithm curbs tiny segments from small data increments, and silly window avoidance curbs those from a window edge that advances in small steps. The receiver moves its right window edge only when the freed space reaches the smaller of a recommended half of its buffer and the effective send MSS. The sender cannot see that buffer, so it estimates it as the largest window seen. An override timeout of 0.1 - 1.0 seconds forces data out, so a wrong estimate cannot deadlock.

  <!-- sysd-found-165 -->

- **Half-close: stop sending but keep listening**

  Hanging up a TCP connection can happen in halves. Because TCP closes the two directions independently, an endpoint can stop sending while it keeps receiving. CLOSE means 'I have no more data to send', and TCP treats it as one-directional. The closing user can keep receiving until the remote peer has closed too. An endpoint that receives a FIN acknowledges it but does not send its own FIN until its user also closes. A host may instead implement a half-duplex close, in which the application cannot keep reading after CLOSE.

  <!-- sysd-found-160 -->

- **TCP keep-alive: checking an idle peer is still there**

  TCP has no built-in way to tell whether a peer is still alive. A keep-alive sends a probe on an idle connection to check. Keep-alives are optional and not universally accepted. A connection is idle when no segments have arrived for a long time and nothing new or unacknowledged is waiting to be sent. Keep-alives must default to off, with a per-connection switch. A probe goes out only after a configurable interval of silence, which must default to no less than two hours. One unanswered probe is not proof that the connection is dead, because ACK segments without data are not reliably transmitted.

  <!-- sysd-found-163 -->

- **TCP reset: telling a peer the connection does not exist**

  A host that receives a segment for a connection it knows nothing about answers with a reset. A reset (RST) segment tells a TCP peer that a segment does not belong to a live connection. The receiver then ignores it or aborts the connection. A RST is sent whenever a segment arrives that apparently is not meant for the current connection, such as a SYN that matches no existing connection. A half-open connection exists when one peer closed, aborted or lost its state without the other knowing. It is reset automatically when either side attempts to send data, because the peer with no connection answers with a reset.

  <!-- sysd-found-159 -->

- **What a TCP header carries**

  Every TCP segment starts with a header, and its fields are the protocol in miniature. The header follows the IP header and carries ports, sequence and acknowledgment numbers, flags, window and checksum. The ports are 16 bits each. The sequence number is 32 bits, and so is the acknowledgment number, which is always sent once a connection is established. The control bits, also called flags, are CWR, ECE, URG, ACK, PSH, RST, SYN and FIN. The checksum is never optional: the sender must generate it and the receiver must check it. It covers a pseudo-header of IP information, which protects the connection against misrouted segments.

  <!-- sysd-found-167 -->

- **TIME-WAIT: why a closed connection lingers**

  The endpoint that closes a TCP connection first cannot walk away at once. It must linger in TIME-WAIT for twice the Maximum Segment Lifetime (MSL), which the specification takes to be 2 minutes. This limits the rate of connection reuse. Segments from an earlier incarnation of a connection, an earlier use of the same connection, must not be confused with the new one. A host in TIME-WAIT may accept a new SYN from the remote endpoint to reopen the connection directly. A timestamp-based algorithm that shortens TIME-WAIT supports higher connection establishment rates on busy servers.

  <!-- sysd-found-158 -->

- **Zero-window probing: knocking on a closed window**

  A receiver's window can stay at zero, and the sender must keep checking. Zero-window probing is how it does that, so the reopening of the window is reliably reported. Even at zero, the sender must regularly transmit at least one octet of new data, or retransmit, to probe the window. The first probe should be sent once a zero window has lasted the retransmission timeout. The interval between probes should increase exponentially. A receiver may keep its window closed indefinitely, as in the 'printer ran out of paper' case. The sender must then keep the connection open while the receiver keeps acknowledging probes.

  <!-- sysd-found-166 -->

- **Path MTU Discovery: finding the smallest hop**

  Some connections work for small messages and stall once a host sends a large block, which is how a failed Path MTU Discovery shows itself. The path MTU is the smallest MTU of any hop between source and destination, the largest packet that crosses the path without fragmentation. To find it, the sender sets the DF (don't fragment) bit. A device with a smaller MTU drops the packet and returns an ICMP Datagram Too Big message giving its MTU. The sender lowers its estimate and repeats until packets fit. Networks that drop ICMP traffic break discovery. Packetization Layer Path MTU Discovery is more robust to ICMP filtering.

  <!-- sysd-found-150 -->

- **Reno, CUBIC and BBR: different ways to react to congestion**

  Tahoe and Reno both treat a retransmission timeout and three duplicate ACKs as loss. On duplicate ACKs, Tahoe drops the window to 1 MSS and restarts slow start, while Reno halves it and enters fast recovery. CUBIC makes the window a cubic function of time since the last congestion event, and it has been the Linux default since kernel 2.6.19. BBR (Google, 2016) is not loss-based: it builds a network model from the maximum bandwidth and round-trip time delivered. Its fairness in version 1 is disputed. Google's presentation shows it coexisting with CUBIC, while researchers found that it can take the link from a CUBIC flow.

  <!-- sysd-found-151 -->

### The Domain Name System

Computers find each other by number, but people use names, and the Domain Name System translates one into the other. It replaced HOSTS.TXT, a single central file that grew slow and unwieldy with ARPANET, and is now a hierarchical, distributed tree of labels. This chapter covers what a domain publishes in its resource records, from addresses and aliases to mail servers, and who hands out the right to use a name. It also follows the queries themselves, sent over UDP and TCP on port 53 or over encrypted transports. Time to live limits how long answers are kept, and anycast lets servers in many locations share one address.

- **DNS: the phone book of the Internet**

  Computers find each other by number, but people remember names. The Domain Name System, or DNS, translates the names people use into the numeric IP addresses that computers use. It works like the phone book of the Internet: www.example.com translates to 93.184.216.34 in IPv4 and to a much longer address in IPv6.

  No single store holds all of this. Responsibility for each domain goes to its own authoritative servers, and administrators can hand pieces of a name to other servers. The result is a distributed, fault-tolerant service designed to avoid one large central store, and it can serve billions of hosts efficiently. It also mirrors how the Internet is run: each piece of a name is a zone of administrative autonomy, delegated to a manager.

  A name server keeps the records for a domain and answers queries against them. Those records are conventionally kept in a structured text file called a zone file. Because records can be updated quickly, a service can change its network location while users keep typing the same hostname.

  Queries run on port 53 over UDP and TCP. DNS began with UDP alone; reliability, security and privacy concerns later brought TCP and other transports. DNS also stores more than addresses. It has been extended to hold signing records, which DNSSEC: signing DNS answers explains, and, as a general-purpose store, spam blocklists.

  <!-- sysd-found-101 -->

- **Anycast: one address, many servers**

  Anycast gives one IP address to servers in many locations, and traffic goes to the nearest one. Each server announces the shared address by BGP, the protocol routers use to tell each other which addresses they can reach. Routers treat the announcements as alternative routes and often pick the path with fewer hops.

  All Internet root name servers use anycast. Many commercial DNS providers switched to it for faster queries, resilience and spread-out load. An early worry was that a long-lived TCP connection could be rerouted to another server midway. In practice this was not observed, and measured failures from instance switches were below 0.017%.

  The sharp edge is failure. If a dead server keeps announcing its route, it becomes a black hole for the nearby clients, the most serious failure mode. The automation that withdraws routes can itself fail. And anyone whose announcements are accepted can hijack anycast traffic, so announcements must be filtered.

  <!-- sysd-found-201 -->

- **How DNS queries travel: UDP, TCP and encrypted transports**

  Classic DNS is startlingly plain. A client sends a clear-text request in a single UDP packet to port 53 and gets a clear-text reply in a single UDP packet. With EDNS support, answers longer than 512 bytes may use larger UDP packets. UDP suits a simple query-response protocol, and TCP's complexity can burden a server that answers simple requests from huge numbers of clients.

  Still, UDP is limited by its lack of transport-layer encryption, a way to verify who is talking and reliable delivery, and by message length. RFC 1123, in 1989, added optional TCP, which allows longer responses, reliable delivery and reuse of long-lived connections.

  Encrypted transports came later. DNS over TLS, or DoT (2016), protects the entire connection with TLS on TCP port 853. Its standard, RFC 7858, supports opportunistic and authenticated encryption but did not make it mandatory for server or client to authenticate. DoH (2018) is DNS carried over HTTPS: ordinary HTTP inside an encrypted tunnel. It tunnels queries over TCP port 443, so it looks like web traffic, though the two are easily told apart without proper padding.

  DNS over QUIC (RFC 9250, 2022) has privacy properties similar to DoT and latency similar to classic DNS over UDP. DNSCrypt (2011), developed outside the IETF, has clients encrypt query payloads with servers' public keys published in the DNS, and uses TCP or UDP port 443.

  <!-- sysd-found-114 -->

  *Figure: The encrypted transports arrived between 2011 and 2022, each on its own port or protocol.*

  | Transport | Year | Runs over |
  |---|---|---|
  | Classic DNS | TCP added 1989 | UDP and TCP, port 53 |
  | DNSCrypt | 2011 | TCP or UDP, port 443 |
  | DNS over TLS | 2016 | TCP, port 853 |
  | DNS over HTTPS | 2018 | TCP, port 443 |
  | DNS over QUIC | 2022 | QUIC |

- **Reading a domain name as a tree**

  Read a domain name from right to left and you are walking down a tree. The DNS namespace is a tree whose nodes each carry a label and zero or more records of information about that name. A full domain name is the labels from a node up to the root, joined by dots, so www.example.com is www joined to example.com. The rightmost label, here com, is the TLD, introduced in Top-level domains: the last label of every name.

  Each label names a subdivision of the domain to its right, and the tree may have up to 127 levels. A label may hold up to 63 characters, and a whole name may not exceed 253 characters in text form. Hostname labels use only letters, digits and hyphens, cannot start or end with a hyphen, and ignore case. To show other alphabets, browsers use IDNA, which maps Unicode strings into that character set with Punycode.

  The tree divides into zones beginning at the root zone, and a zone may contain as many domains as its manager chooses.

  <!-- sysd-found-102 -->

  *Figure: www.example.com is read from the root down through com and example.* (tree; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Top-level domains: the last label of every name**

  Made-up internal names can collide with real ones later. ICANN rejected .home and .corp as TLDs over conflicts with networks already using them, and local domains such as test.dev collided with the .dev TLD created in 2019.

  A top-level domain, or TLD, is the highest level of the DNS hierarchy below the root: the last label of any name, such as .com in www.example.com. TLD names are installed in the root zone. ICANN delegates management of most of them to specific organizations and operates IANA, which maintains the root zone.

  IANA sorts TLDs into infrastructure, generic, generic restricted, sponsored, country-code and internationalized country-code types. Country-code names are two letters that, with some historical exceptions, match the territory's two-letter ISO 3166 code. The IETF also reserves names such as .test, .local and .onion, which should not be used in production on the global DNS.

  <!-- sysd-found-202 -->

- **Time to live: giving data an expiry**

  Data that lives forever can cause trouble, so networks give it an expiry. A TTL is a counter or timestamp attached to data; when the count or time runs out, the data is discarded or revalidated. In IP, it is an 8-bit header field with a maximum of 255, reduced by every router. At zero the datagram is discarded, which stops packets circulating forever. IPv4 defines it in seconds, but in practice it falls by one per hop, so IPv6 renamed it the hop limit. In DNS, the authoritative server sets a TTL per record to tell resolvers how long to keep it.

  <!-- sysd-found-203 -->

- **Resource records: the entries DNS stores**

  Everything DNS knows is stored as resource records. On the wire, each has NAME, TYPE, CLASS, TTL, RDLENGTH and RDATA fields. TYPE gives the format and use of the data, and RDATA holds the type-specific part, such as an address or an MX priority and hostname. CLASS is IN for ordinary Internet records. The TTL counts the seconds the record stays valid, up to 2^31 minus 1, about 68 years. Records of the same type form a set, an RRset, which resolvers return whole.

  <!-- sysd-found-109 -->

- **Who hands out domain names: registrars and registries**

  What a buyer gets from a domain name is the right to use it. That right is delegated by registrars, which are accredited by ICANN or similar organizations, while a registry runs the master records of names for each TLD. The registrant, the person or organization that asked for the name, is a customer of the registrar, sometimes through resellers. The registry takes registration information from registrars and publishes it using the WHOIS protocol. Most gTLD registries have kept that data centrally since about 2001, a thick approach, while COM and NET use a thin one that keeps only basic data.

  <!-- sysd-found-117 -->

- **Before DNS: one file called HOSTS.TXT**

  Before DNS, the address book of an entire network was a single file. HOSTS.TXT, kept by the Network Information Center (NIC), mapped host names to the numerical addresses of ARPANET computers, and every host fetched it by FTP. The bandwidth needed to distribute each new version grew with the square of the number of hosts. Local organizations ran their own names but had to wait for the NIC to change the file. By the early 1980s the central table was slow and unwieldy. Paul Mockapetris created DNS in 1983, and RFC 1034 and RFC 1035 superseded the original specifications in November 1987.

  <!-- sysd-found-118 -->

- **DNS record types: A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, NS and friends**

  A domain publishes several kinds of information, and each kind has its own record type. An A record maps a domain name to an IPv4 address, and an AAAA record does the same for an IPv6 address. Both are essential for turning names into IP addresses. A CNAME record aliases one name to another, often pointing child names at the main domain. It forwards to the other name and does not itself provide an IP address.

  Other types point elsewhere. Records of type MX direct email to the right mail server, which also protects mail delivery against failures and spreads its load. An NS record names the authoritative DNS servers for a domain and directs queries to them for further lookups. A PTR record maps an IP address back to a domain name and is commonly used to verify the authenticity of a server.

  An SRV record specifies a host and port for services such as VoIP, voice calls over IP, and is used together with A records. A TXT record attaches human-readable text to a domain, for example verification records such as SPF for email security. The SOA, or start of authority, record stores administrative information and is among the most common types.

  <!-- sysd-found-110 -->

  *Figure: Each record type names one kind of information a domain publishes.*

  | Type | What it holds |
  |---|---|
  | A | An IPv4 address |
  | AAAA | An IPv6 address |
  | CNAME | An alias for another name |
  | MX | The mail server |
  | NS | The authoritative DNS servers |
  | PTR | The name for an IP address |
  | SRV | The host and port of a service |
  | TXT | Human-readable text |
  | SOA | Administrative information |

- **Reverse DNS lookup: from address back to name**

  Sometimes you know the address and want the name. A reverse lookup asks the DNS for the domain names tied to an IP address that is already known. The answers are PTR records under the infrastructure TLD arpa, with the address written in reverse order, so 208.80.152.2 becomes 2.152.80.208.in-addr.arpa. Without a PTR record the lookup cannot resolve, and several names may share one IP address. Email servers commonly use reverse lookups to check that a message came from a valid server, and many reject messages from servers that do not support them.

  <!-- sysd-found-111 -->

- **CNAME records: one name standing in for another**

  A resource often has several names: one canonical, or primary, name and some aliases. A CNAME record marks its owner name as an alias and names the canonical one, but provides no IP address itself. If a node has a CNAME record it should hold no other data, so an alias and its canonical name cannot differ. A server that finds a CNAME instead of the wanted record includes it in the response and restarts the query at the canonical name. Records that point at another name should use the primary name, not an alias, and software should follow CNAME chains and signal CNAME loops as an error.

  <!-- sysd-found-126 -->

- **The rarer DNS records: DNAME, SVCB, CAA, TLSA and more**

  Beyond A, AAAA, MX and NS, DNS defines many more record types for aliases, locating services, certificates, security and zone transfers. A DNAME record aliases a name and all its subnames, unlike CNAME, which aliases only the exact name. Non-standard ALIAS or ANAME records synthesize A and AAAA records from a target so the bare domain can be aliased. TXT began as human-readable text but since the early 1990s mostly carries machine-readable data such as SPF, DKIM and DMARC. SRV gives generalized service location for newer protocols, instead of protocol-specific records like MX.

  SVCB records give clients connection metadata such as supported protocols and alternative endpoints. The record type named for HTTPS: ordinary HTTP inside an encrypted tunnel is a specialized SVCB that supplies those connection details up front, enabling Encrypted Client Hello and lower first-connection latency. CAA constrains which certificate authorities may issue for a domain. TLSA associates a TLS server certificate or key with a name for DANE, and SSHFP publishes SSH host key fingerprints.

  Five types belong to signing, which DNSSEC: signing DNS answers explains. RRSIG holds signatures and DNSKEY the zone key. DS identifies a delegated zone's signing key. NSEC proves a name does not exist, and NSEC3 proves it without letting anyone list the zone's names.

  Some types serve the protocol itself. AXFR transfers a whole zone from primary to secondary, and IXFR only the differences since a serial number. ANY returns all cached records, and OPT supports EDNS. Many early types are obsolete: MX replaced MD and MF, and HINFO is now repurposed for minimal answers to ANY queries.

  <!-- sysd-found-204 -->

- **The three parts of DNS**

  DNS has three major components: the domain name space with its resource records, the name servers that hold the data, and the resolvers that extract it for clients. A name server has complete information about a subset of the space, for which it is the authority, plus pointers to other servers. A resolver answers client requests directly or follows referrals. It is typically a system routine, so no protocol is needed between it and the user program. To the user, DNS is a call to a local resolver; to a name server, it is zones to refresh from master copies while answering queries.

  <!-- sysd-found-121 -->

- **What DNS was designed to do**

  DNS aimed to give one consistent name space that is distributed and cached, useful for many applications, and independent of any one network, protocol or host type. That is the opposite of HOSTS.TXT's single central copy. Names need not contain network identifiers, addresses or routes. The data is distributed with local caches, and creating and deleting names is distributed too. Where there are trade-offs between the cost of acquiring data, update speed and cache accuracy, the data's source controls them. Every item is tagged with a type and a class, so one name space can carry different protocol families' address formats.

  <!-- sysd-found-119 -->

- **What a domain registrar does**

  Only a domain's designated registrar can change or delete its information in the central registry. A registrar is a company or office, accredited by a registry, that manages the reservation of domain names for registrants. Registering a domain creates name server records in the parent zone pointing to the domain's authoritative servers, usually at least two. It does not imply DNS hosting, which most registrars offer as an optional service. To change registrar, the owner unlocks the domain and gets a code from the old registrar that proves the request is genuine. The new registrar must also obtain the holder's express permission.

  <!-- sysd-found-206 -->

- **Subdomains: splitting a site into sections**

  In blog.example.com, blog is the subdomain, example is the primary domain and .com is the top-level domain. A subdomain is an extra part added to a main domain name, and one domain can have several. Websites commonly use them to separate logical sections, as in support.example.com and careers.example.com. Each subdomain can also be delegated to its own manager as a zone of administrative autonomy.

  <!-- sysd-found-129 -->

- **How a DNS lookup works, step by step**

  Typing google.com into a browser starts a short chain of questions. The answer comes back quickly: lookups average 20-120 milliseconds, according to YSlow.

  The browser hands the name to the resolver, the program that does the asking. The resolver asks a root server for the .com TLD server. It asks that server for the domain's authoritative server, the one that gives the actual answer, and queries it. The authoritative server returns the IP address for google.com to the resolver, which passes it back to the browser.

  Resolvers work from the rightmost label of the name toward the left. With no cached records, resolution starts at a root server. Roots usually do not answer directly but refer the resolver onward, so a query for www.wikipedia.org is referred to the org servers. The resolver repeats this, following referrals until it receives an authoritative answer. Each host is configured with hints, an initial cache of the known addresses of the root name servers.

  Starting every lookup at the root would put a large burden on the roots. There are 13 logical root name servers, with additional copies spread worldwide by anycast addressing. Caches in DNS servers keep the roots to a small fraction of all requests.

  <!-- sysd-found-105 -->

  *Figure: Each answer points the resolver one level further down, until the authoritative server gives the IP address.*

  | Step | The resolver asks | It gets back |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 | A root server | The .com TLD server |
  | 2 | The .com TLD server | The authoritative server for google.com |
  | 3 | The authoritative server | The IP address for google.com |

- **The resolver: DNS's client side**

  A resolver is the client side of DNS, which initiates and sequences the queries that end in a full resolution. It is a program that sits between user programs and name servers, on the same machine as the program it serves. Because it may consult several servers or its cache, it can take from milliseconds to several seconds.

  Applications ask the resolver in the local operating system. It answers from its cache of recent lookups if it can, and otherwise queries designated DNS servers, usually the ISP's, set up manually or through DHCP. It stores the result and hands it back to the software that asked.

  A recursive resolver is the first stop in a DNS query and a middleman between client and name servers. It answers from cache, or asks a root, then a TLD, then an authoritative server, and replies to the client. ISPs typically provide such servers. Without them, every query would start at the root zone, and each user system would need resolver software capable of recursion.

  <!-- sysd-found-106 -->

- **DNS caches and the TTL: why changes take time**

  DNS stays fast by remembering. A resolver answers from its cache whenever it can. That removes network delay and name server load from most requests, and caches shared by many users work better than unshared ones. Each stored result carries a TTL that says how long it stays valid. The authoritative server's administrator sets it, from a few seconds to several days or weeks. RFC 1912 gives 1 to 5 days as typical.

  A cached record keeps its TTL, which the server counts down every second. At zero the record is purged, and the next query must start resolution again. The price is slow change: a changed record spreads only after all caches expire and refresh. TTLs can be lowered before a change, at the cost of more network traffic.

  Even a negative answer can be cached. RFC 1034 limits it by the SOA record's MINIMUM field, though later practice also uses the SOA's own TTL. Browsers often keep their own DNS cache, typically for around one minute, which makes DNS issues harder to debug.

  <!-- sysd-found-108 -->

- **Spreading load with DNS**

  Ask DNS for the same name from two places and you may get two different answers. That is deliberate. Hostnames and IP addresses need not match one to one, so a single hostname can resolve to many addresses. That gives resilience to failures and spreads load across server instances in an enterprise or across the Internet.

  Cloud services and CDNs go further. They translate a name into the address of a server near the user, because different users can receive different answers for the same name at the same time. Assigning nearby servers through DNS is key to faster and more reliable responses, and most major Internet services use it.

  Servers may also rotate the order of a record set to balance load, and records of type MX can do the same for mail. The reverse works too. Many hostnames can map to one IP address for virtual hosting, and the Host header of a web request then tells the server which name was asked for.

  <!-- sysd-found-112 -->

- **How DNS can be attacked**

  DNS was designed without strong security, so its responses can be forged or abused. In cache poisoning, data is fed to resolvers as though it came from an authoritative server. This pollutes the cache with false information and long TTLs, so legitimate requests may be redirected to malicious hosts. The weakness is that DNS responses traditionally carry no cryptographic signature. A fix, covered in DNSSEC: signing DNS answers, adds signed responses. TSIG lets trusted peers verify each other and is commonly used to authorize zone transfers and dynamic updates.

  DNS is also often seen as innocuous and passes firewalls. It can leak from private connections, carry malware commands in TXT records, as in DNSMessenger, and be used to exfiltrate data. And lookalike names such as paypal.com and paypa1.com can be indistinguishable in some fonts, an IDN homograph attack that is occasionally exploited in phishing.

  <!-- sysd-found-115 -->

- **Recursive, iterative and non-recursive queries**

  Who does the legwork in a lookup depends on the kind of query. In a recursive query, the client asks one server, which answers completely by querying other name servers as needed, or returns an error. A simple resolver on a home router typically does this against the ISP's server.

  In an iterative query, the resolver asks a chain of servers, each referring it to the next until one can fully resolve the request. For www.example.com that means a root server, then a com server, then an example.com server. In a non-recursive query, no further rounds are needed. The server already has the answer, from its cache or as an authoritative server, or it returns a partial result.

  A single resolution may combine all three. Typically a client sends a recursive query to a recursive server that keeps a cache, which issues non-recursive queries and returns a single answer. Bits in the query headers negotiate the use of recursion. RFC 1034 requires name servers to implement the iterative approach, which suits datagram access, and allows the recursive approach as an option.

  <!-- sysd-found-107 -->

- **DNSSEC: signing DNS answers**

  The original DNS design had no security features, so nothing stopped a forged answer from looking genuine. DNSSEC is a suite of IETF extensions that secures DNS data by adding digital signatures, while keeping backward compatibility. It stops applications accepting forged or manipulated data, such as that created by cache poisoning. It proves where data came from, that a name does not exist, and that data is unaltered. It gives neither availability nor confidentiality: responses are signed, not encrypted.

  Each answer from a signed zone carries an RRSIG record, a signature checked with the public key found in a DNSKEY record. NSEC or NSEC3 records give cryptographic evidence that a record does not exist. A security-aware resolver sets the DO flag in its query. Because that flag lives in the EDNS extended flags, all DNSSEC transactions must support EDNS.

  Deployment has been slow. The standard had to stay backward compatible, scale and prevent zone enumeration, and it met disagreement over root key ownership and perceived complexity.

  <!-- sysd-found-195 -->

- **Round-robin DNS: simple load spreading**

  Round-robin DNS is easy to implement and hard to manage. The DNS holds several A records for one name, one per server hosting identical content. Each response permutes the address list, and clients normally try the first address, so successive users reach different servers.

  Caches in the DNS hierarchy and client-side address caches make it hard to manage. Some resolvers reorder the list to favor numerically closer networks, which RFC 3484 standardized for IPv6, and a Windows Vista bug on IPv4 once defeated the balancing. It only alternates the order of records and ignores transaction time, server load and congestion. So it suits many uniformly distributed connections to equal servers.

  It should not be relied on alone for availability. If a service at one listed address fails, DNS keeps handing out that address, though some desktop clients try alternates after a timeout of up to 30 seconds. Modified DNS servers can poll mirrored servers for availability and load, and temporarily remove a server from the pool until it reports being within specs again.

  <!-- sysd-found-200 -->

- **DNS cache poisoning: teaching a resolver a lie**

  A resolver that believes a lie repeats it to everyone who asks. DNS cache poisoning, also called DNS spoofing, introduces corrupt data into a resolver's cache so that it returns a wrong answer, such as an attacker's IP address. Poisoning one DNS server affects the users it serves directly and those served by its downstream servers, until the cache entry expires. Victims can land on a fake site for phishing or malware.

  In one variant, a vulnerable server caches the extra A record for the target domain's name server from an answer about the attacker's own domain. That lets the attacker resolve queries for the whole target domain.

  Many attacks are prevented by being less trusting of other servers and ignoring returned records not directly relevant to the query. Randomizing the source port and the 16-bit nonce, a one-time number, with cryptographically secure random numbers greatly reduces the chance of a successful race attack. But NAT devices may rewrite source ports and remove the randomness. DNSSEC counters the attack with digital signatures.

  <!-- sysd-found-199 -->

- **Who can read your DNS queries?**

  Anyone along the path can read a DNS query. DNS was designed as a public directory with no confidentiality controls. Unencrypted queries and responses therefore allow sniffing, hijacking, cache poisoning and tampering by someone in the middle. Defenses include VPNs, which move resolution to the VPN operator, and proxies or public DNS servers, which move it to a trusted third party. Some public servers support DoH, DoT and DNSCrypt. These fixes are argued over. Critics say that stopping the local network operator from inspecting DNS thwarts corporate security policies and Internet censorship. They also say public servers centralize control of resolution in a few large companies.

  <!-- sysd-found-116 -->

- **Root servers and TLD servers**

  The root of DNS has only thirteen server addresses, yet behind them stand about 1954 instances. The limit exists because the original DNS limits UDP packets to 512 bytes, and IPv6 addresses need more room, which the EDNS0 extension allows. Each operator runs redundant equipment in many locations using anycast addressing, for better performance and to survive failures.

  A root server answers requests for records in the root zone. Otherwise it directs the resolver to the TLD name servers for the domain's extension, such as .com, .net or .org. The root zone file, about 2 MB, lists the authoritative servers for all TLDs. A resolver bootstraps from hints, a small root.hints file of root server addresses, which breaks the circular need to know a root server's address before resolving anything.

  A TLD name server maintains information for all domain names sharing an extension, the part after the last dot. It answers with the address of the domain's authoritative server. TLD servers fall into generic TLDs such as .com and .org, and country code TLDs such as .uk and .jp.

  <!-- sysd-found-128 -->

  *Figure: Thirteen root server addresses are served by about 1954 instances.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **The stub resolver: DNS work done elsewhere**

  A stub resolver does almost nothing, on purpose. It moves the resolution work into a name server that supports recursive queries and keeps only a list of such servers. A PC that lacks the resources to resolve names gets an easy way to use DNS. The cache for a whole local network or organization can also be centralized. A simple stub resolver on a home router typically makes a recursive query to the DNS server run by the user's ISP. The drawback is that recursive requests take arbitrary time, so the stub struggles to tune retransmissions for lost UDP packets and dead servers.

  <!-- sysd-found-124 -->

- **The authoritative name server: the source of truth**

  Every domain has at least one server that speaks for it with final authority. An authoritative name server answers DNS queries only from data configured by an original source, such as the domain administrator. It does not answer from a cache of another server's answers. It publishes information about the domain and about the name servers of any domains below it. It is either primary, holding the original copies of all zone records, or secondary, keeping an identical copy through an automatic updating mechanism in the DNS protocol.

  A zone's authoritative servers are stored in the parent zone as NS records. RFC 1034 requires every zone to be available on at least two servers, so it survives host or link failure. Authoritative answers carry the Authoritative Answer (AA) bit. A server named as authoritative for a domain it has no data for causes a lame delegation.

  It is usually the resolver's last stop. It holds information specific to its domain, such as the A record, and returns NXDOMAIN if it cannot find the domain.

  <!-- sysd-found-104 -->

- **Delegation: handing a piece of the namespace to someone else**

  To find www.example.org, a resolver needs ns1.example.org. To find ns1.example.org, it needs example.org first. Delegation has to cope with that loop.

  Delegation is the mechanism that assigns responsibility for different parts of the DNS namespace to different name servers. Dividing a zone creates a new one. Authority over it goes to a designated name server, and the parent zone stops being authoritative for it. Each public domain under the TLDs is delegated through an NS record in the parent domain.

  An NS record gives a name, not an address. So the resolver must issue another request to find the address of the server it was referred to. If the delegated server is a subdomain of the domain it serves, that is the loop above. The delegating server breaks it by supplying the server's IP addresses as glue. A glue record, a name server paired with its IP address, travels in the additional section of the response. For www.example.org, the org TLD name server includes address records for ns1.example.org along with the delegation.

  <!-- sysd-found-103 -->

- **DNS zones: who is responsible for which names**

  Cut the DNS tree between any two adjacent nodes, and each connected group of names becomes a zone, authoritative for all names in that region. A zone is a distinct part of the name space delegated to a person, organization or company that maintains it. That organization can change its data unilaterally, grow new sections of the tree, delete nodes or delegate subzones, and larger ones can nest delegations to match their substructure.

  A zone's data has four parts, all written as resource records. They are authoritative data for its nodes, data for its top node, data describing delegated subzones, and data giving access to those subzones' name servers. The top node carries NS records listing every server for the zone and a single SOA record of management parameters. Because NS records give no addresses, a zone also holds glue records for servers whose names lie below the cut.

  A zone's servers need not sit inside its own domain. One name server for the UK domain is in the US, saving transatlantic bandwidth.

  <!-- sysd-found-122 -->

- **How a secondary server copies a zone**

  A change made at one server must reach every server for a zone. Changes are made at the primary, typically by editing a master file and then signalling the server to load it. The preferred way to spread them is the DNS protocol's zone transfer, not FTP or ad hoc procedures. This is how a secondary name server polls its primary and copies a changed zone, so every authoritative server for a zone serves the same data.

  Secondaries check for changes at a selectable interval by comparing the SERIAL field of the zone's SOA record. The serial must advance whenever the zone changes, so the more recent of two copies can be told apart. The check is a simple query to the primary for the SOA record. If the serial equals the secondary's own, nothing changed and the REFRESH wait restarts.

  Three SOA parameters set the rhythm of the checks. A secondary waits REFRESH seconds between checks, retries every RETRY seconds if a check cannot complete, and after EXPIRE seconds without one must discard its copy as obsolete. When the serial shows a change, the secondary sends an AXFR request. The answer is a stream of messages carrying every record of the zone, from which the secondary builds its copy. Because accuracy is essential, AXFR requests must use TCP or another reliable protocol. Secondaries may also run these operations against other secondaries, which helps when the primary is down.

  <!-- sysd-found-123 -->

  *Figure: A secondary asks for the serial, and only a changed serial triggers a full transfer.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Wait REFRESH seconds] --> B[Ask primary for SOA record]
  B --> C{Serial changed?}
  C -->|no| A
  C -->|yes| D[Send AXFR request over TCP]
  D --> E[Build copy from every record]
  ```

- **DNS chooses availability over instant consistency**

  DNS would rather give you an old answer than no answer. RFC 1034 treats access to information as more critical than instantaneous updates or consistency guarantees. So updates percolate out through the users of the system rather than reaching every copy at once. When updates are unavailable because of network or host failure, the usual course is to believe old information while continuing efforts to update it.

  The owner of the data sets how stale a copy may get. Copies are distributed with timeouts for refreshing. The distributor sets the timeout and the recipient performs the refresh. Very short intervals can be specified, and the owner can prohibit copies. Most data changes very slowly, such as mailbox bindings and host addresses, but the system must also handle subsets that change on the order of seconds or minutes.

  Each organization responsible for a set of domains provides redundant name servers. Every zone must be available on at least two servers, so it stays available despite host or link failure.

  <!-- sysd-found-120 -->

- **The DNSSEC chain of trust**

  A signature is only as good as the key behind it. An answer can be proved correct only if at least one key or DS record is known to be correct from a source other than DNS. These starting points are trust anchors, typically supplied with the operating system. A chain is a series of linked DS and DNSKEY records from a trust anchor to the domain's authoritative server. Without a complete chain, an answer cannot be securely verified.

  Each DS record in a parent zone verifies a DNSKEY record below it. To validate www.example.com, a resolver ideally starts with the DS and DNSKEY at the root. It uses the root's DS for com to verify com's DNSKEY, then example.com's DS and DNSKEY, and finally the RRSIG on the answer. DNSSEC was deployed at the root on July 15, 2010.

  A DS record in the parent with no RRSIG in the reply signals a problem. The cause may be someone in the middle stripping the DNSSEC data, a broken server along the path, or a configuration error.

  <!-- sysd-found-196 -->

  *Figure: Trust passes from the root key down, link by link, to the signature on the answer.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Root key: trust anchor] --> B[Root DS and DNSKEY]
  B -->|DS for com| C[com DNSKEY]
  C -->|DS for example.com| D[example.com DNSKEY]
  D --> E[RRSIG on the answer]
  ```

- **DNSSEC: proving that a name does not exist**

  How do you sign the answer that nothing exists? Proving a name is absent means signing the answer to every query for a non-existent name. That is hard, because DNSSEC was designed for offline signing and it is impossible to pre-generate a response to every hostname. NSEC records link each pair of names in a zone, so a query for k.example.com is answered with an NSEC saying nothing exists between a.example.com and z.example.com. That exposes real names and so allows zone enumeration. NSEC3 hashes the names instead, but GPUs and dedicated hardware let its responses be brute-forced cheaply with offline dictionary attacks.

  <!-- sysd-found-198 -->

- **DNSSEC keys: signing keys, rollovers and expiry**

  DNSSEC uses two kinds of keys. Key signing keys (KSK) sign the DNSKEY records that hold the zone signing keys (ZSK), which sign the other records. ZSKs can be switched more easily and can be shorter, which shrinks RRSIG and DNSKEY records. A new KSK needs its DS record transferred to the parent zone. DS records hold a message digest of the KSK, not the full key, which keeps them small for very large zones such as com. RRSIG records carry absolute timestamps that limit replay. So resolver clocks must be roughly in sync, and a zone must be re-signed regularly or validating resolvers will reject its signatures.

  <!-- sysd-found-197 -->

- **Split-horizon DNS: different answers for different askers**

  The same name can lead to different machines depending on who asks. Split-horizon DNS lets a DNS implementation return different sets of information for the same query, usually chosen by the source address of the request. It manages security and privacy by separating DNS information for internal access from access over an unsecure public network such as the Internet. A common case is a server with both a private LAN address and a public one. The same name resolves to either, depending on the client, so local clients reach it directly with lower latency. Done badly, it can clash with DNSSEC, which vouches for the data returned.

  <!-- sysd-found-205 -->

- **Inside a DNS message**

  Every DNS message, query or response, has the same shape: a header followed by question, answer, authority and additional sections. The header holds Identification, Flags and the counts of questions, answers, authority records and additional records, each field 16 bits long. The identification field matches responses to queries. The flags tell whether the message is a query or reply (QR) and whether the answer is authoritative (AA). They also tell whether it was truncated (TC), and whether recursion is desired (RD) or available (RA). The response code RCODE can be NOERROR (0), FORMERR (1), SERVFAIL (2) or NXDOMAIN (3, nonexistent domain).

  <!-- sysd-found-113 -->

- **DNS standard queries and inverse queries**

  Most DNS traffic is one simple question. A standard query names a domain (QNAME), a record type (QTYPE) and a class (QCLASS), and asks a name server for the matching records. Standard queries are the vast majority of DNS queries, in UDP datagrams or over TCP. A server may add helpful records: a query for the mail-exchange records of ISI.EDU also returns the mail exchangers' addresses. Inverse queries map a resource to the domain names having it, but they are mainly for debugging, are not guaranteed complete, and their results should never be cached. IN-ADDR.ARPA, not inverse queries, is the way to map addresses to host names.

  <!-- sysd-found-127 -->

- **The resolver's recipe in RFC 1034**

  RFC 1034 gives the resolver a four-step recipe. Look for the answer in local information and return it if found. Find the best servers to ask. Send them queries until one responds. Then analyze the response. An answer or name error is cached and returned. A better delegation is cached and the server search repeats. A CNAME is cached and the search restarts at the canonical name. A failed server is dropped and the next tried. Authoritative data is preferred to cached data, and the resolver should bound its work so a loop cannot start.

  <!-- sysd-found-125 -->

### HTTP, HTTPS and TLS

A browser asks and a server answers, and that exchange is the foundation of data communication for the World Wide Web. HTTP is a stateless, application-layer request-response protocol, so each request can be understood on its own. This chapter follows it from the shape of a message, through its methods and status codes, to the cookies that give it a memory. It then turns to the encryption that lets the same conversation stay private: public keys, shared secret keys and the certificates that say who owns a key.

- **HTTP: the request and response behind every web page**

  A browser asks for a page, and a server sends one back. That exchange is HTTP, the foundation of data communication for the World Wide Web. It is a stateless, application-layer request-response protocol that clients and servers use to exchange hypertext and other content.

  HTTP lives in the client-server model. The client sends a request, and the server returns a response that describes the outcome and may carry a resource such as an HTML document. A web browser is the usual client and a web server the usual server. Other user agents include voice browsers and mobile apps. A web resource is located by a URL, using the http scheme or, when encrypted, the HTTPS: ordinary HTTP inside an encrypted tunnel scheme.

  HTTP needs a reliable transport underneath. Before HTTP/3 the standard choice is TCP, typically on port 80 when unencrypted and port 443 when encrypted. Because HTTP is stateless, the server is not required to retain information about each user across multiple requests.

  Intermediaries such as web caches and proxies can improve or enable communication, and browsers also cache what they fetch to reduce network traffic. Some headers are managed hop by hop by intermediaries, while others are managed end to end, only by the source client and the target web server. RFC 9110 defines the semantics shared by all versions of HTTP, and those semantics are not versioned: methods, status codes and fields mean the same in every version.

  <!-- sysd-found-032 -->

- **Public-key cryptography: one key to lock, another to open**

  A shared secret key has an awkward first step: both sides must get the key, securely, before they can say anything private. Public-key cryptography, or asymmetric cryptography, removes that burden. It uses pairs of related keys, a public key that can be shared openly and a private key that must stay secret. Only private keys need protecting. Anyone with the public key can encrypt a message, but only the private-key holder can decrypt it. That hides the content without telling the recipient who sent it. A digital signature runs the other way. The sender signs with the private key, anyone with the public key can verify it, and a forger cannot make a valid one. The price is speed. Public-key algorithms are far more computationally intensive than symmetric ones, so Transport Layer Security: three jobs in one protocol, SSH and PGP are hybrids. A public-key exchange shares a symmetric key, and that key then encrypts the data at higher throughput. The hard part is proving a public key is authentic, because an attacker who swaps in their own key can mount a Man-in-the-middle attacks: the eavesdropper who relays everything.

  <!-- sysd-found-173 -->

- **Inside an HTTP message: start line, headers and body**

  A request begins with one line such as GET /customer/123 HTTP/1.1. Every HTTP message is a header followed by an optional body: clients send request messages, and servers answer with response messages. A request's start line holds the method name, the request URI and the protocol version. A response's start line holds the protocol version, a status code and optionally a reason phrase, as in HTTP/1.1 400 Bad Request. Below it come header fields, name-value pairs separated by a colon that carry metadata about the message. In HTTP/1.1 every request header field except Host is optional, and a field name is matched ignoring case, unlike a method name, which must match exactly. The body may hold data in any format. The format must match the Content-Type header field when the message has one, and the body can be blank. Messages in HTTP/2: many requests sharing one connection and HTTP/3 are binary, compress headers with HPACK or QPACK, and replace the request or response line with pseudo-header fields.

  <!-- sysd-found-033 -->

- **Why HTTP reuses one TCP connection for many requests**

  In the early web, every resource cost its own TCP connection. HTTP/0.9 always closed the connection after the response and HTTP/1.0 should do so, so each resource needed a new one. A persistent connection lets one TCP connection be reused for more than one HTTP request and response, and HTTP/1.1 officially introduced keep-alive to allow it. Reuse cuts latency, because the client does not repeat the TCP 3-way handshake. The connection also tends to speed up over time because of TCP's slow-start mechanism. HTTP/1.1 added HTTP pipelining: sending requests without waiting too, which lets a client send several requests before waiting for each response. It was never really safe. Some servers and many proxies mishandled it. They served only the first request, closed the connection or returned responses out of order, so it was disabled and then removed from most browsers. Under HTTP/2: many requests sharing one connection, many concurrent requests and responses are multiplexed through a single TCP/IP connection, while HTTP/3 uses QUIC over UDP instead of TCP. Either side can close a connection at any time.

  <!-- sysd-found-038 -->

- **GET, POST, PUT and the other HTTP request methods**

  The first word of an HTTP request is a verb, and it decides what the request means. The request method, informally a verb, is the primary source of request semantics: it names the action the client wants applied to the target resource.

  GET retrieves a current representation of a resource and should only read data. It is the focus of almost all performance optimizations, and its URL can be bookmarked, shared and cached. HEAD is identical to GET except that the server must not send content, so a client can read headers such as Content-Length without transferring the representation.

  POST asks the target resource to process the enclosed representation by its own semantics. That covers submitting form data, posting a message or creating a resource, which is reported with 201 (Created) and a Location header. PUT creates or replaces the target resource's state with the state in the request. Unlike POST, the client chooses the target URI, and repeating the same PUT updates the same resource. DELETE removes the association between a resource and its current functionality, like rm in UNIX. PATCH applies a partial modification, saving bandwidth compared with a full PUT.

  CONNECT asks a proxy to open a tunnel to the destination server, commonly so TLS can run through it. OPTIONS asks for a resource's communication options, and TRACE loops the request message back for testing and diagnostics. General-purpose servers must support GET and HEAD, and everything else is optional. An unrecognized method should get 501 (Not Implemented), and a known but disallowed one 405 (Method Not Allowed). Responses to GET and HEAD are cacheable. Responses to PUT and DELETE are not.

  <!-- sysd-found-034 -->

  *Figure: Each method names a different action to apply to the target resource.*

  | Method | What it asks for |
  |---|---|
  | GET | A current representation of the resource |
  | HEAD | The same as GET, without the content |
  | POST | Process the enclosed representation |
  | PUT | Create or replace the resource's state |
  | DELETE | Remove the resource's association |
  | PATCH | Apply a partial modification |
  | CONNECT | Open a tunnel to the destination |
  | OPTIONS | The resource's communication options |
  | TRACE | Loop the request back for testing |

- **Why HTTP forgets you, and how sessions fix that**

  A web server may forget you the moment it answers. HTTP is stateless, so it does not require the server to retain information or status about each user across multiple requests. The meaning of each request can be understood on its own, whatever connection it arrives on. That sounds like a handicap, yet many implementations depend on it to reuse proxied connections or to spread requests across multiple servers. A server must also not assume two requests on one connection come from the same user agent. The exception is a connection that is secured and specific to that agent. An application that must remember a user builds a session on top. It implements one with an How a cookie gives a forgetful protocol a memory, hidden variables in a web form or another mechanism. A session typically starts with an interactive login and ends with a logout, using a custom mechanism rather than HTTP authentication: the server challenges, the client answers.

  <!-- sysd-found-042 -->

- **How a cookie gives a forgetful protocol a memory**

  HTTP forgets you after every response, yet a shop remembers what is in your cart. The memory lives in a cookie: a small block of data that a web server creates and the user's browser stores and sends back. The server sets it with a Set-Cookie response header, and the browser returns it with every request. A cookie is a name and value plus attributes such as expiry, domain and flags. Browsers use the attributes to decide when to delete, block or send the cookie. A session cookie has no Expires or Max-Age and is deleted when the browser closes. A persistent cookie expires at a set date or after a set time and often keeps users logged in. Usually the cookie holds only a unique session identifier, and the server itself keeps the cart or user data. A third-party cookie belongs to a domain other than the one in the address bar. It lets advertisers build a browsing history of a user across every site carrying their content.

  <!-- sysd-found-168 -->

- **HTTP status codes: five classes of three digits**

  Three digits tell a client how its request went. An HTTP status code is a three-digit number in a response that describes the result of the request and the semantics of the response. Valid codes run from 100 to 599, and the first digit gives the class. Those are informational (100-199), success (200-299), redirection (300-399), client error (400-499) and server error (500-599). The last two digits have no categorization role.

  In plain terms, 1xx means the request was received and processing continues, and 2xx that it was accepted. A 3xx says more action is needed. A 4xx says the request is malformed or cannot be fulfilled, and a 5xx that the server failed on a valid-looking request. A single request can have zero or more interim 1xx responses followed by exactly one final response.

  Clients are built to cope with codes they do not know. A client must understand the class from the first digit. It treats an unrecognized code as the x00 code of that class, so an unrecognized 471 is handled like 400 (Bad Request). One that receives an invalid status code should treat the response as a 5xx. The reason phrase after the code is only a recommendation and human-readable, while the code is machine-readable.

  Some codes are heuristically cacheable, such as 200, 203, 204, 206, 300, 301, 308, 404, 405, 410, 414 and 501. A cache can reuse those with heuristic expiration unless the method or cache controls say otherwise.

  <!-- sysd-found-037 -->
