- **Idempotent methods: which requests are safe to retry**

  If a connection drops before the response arrives, can the client simply send the request again? For some methods it can. A request method is idempotent if the intended effect on the server of several identical requests with it is the same as the effect of one. PUT, DELETE and all Safe methods: requests that only read are idempotent. POST, CONNECT and PATCH are not necessarily, so an identical POST sent twice may modify state again or send two emails. A PUT that sets an email to the value already recorded changes nothing, and deleting an already deleted user has no further effect. A client can repeat an idempotent request automatically after a failure that happens before it reads the response. It should not automatically retry a non-idempotent one unless it knows the request is really idempotent or can detect the original was never applied. A proxy must never do so. Duplicate POSTs can also happen by accident, so it is generally up to the web application to keep a POST from being processed twice.

  <!-- sysd-found-036 -->

- **Safe methods: requests that only read**

  Search spiders can crawl the web without fear of causing harm, thanks to a rule about methods. A request method is safe if its defined semantics are essentially read-only: the client does not request or expect any state change on the origin server. RFC 9110 defines GET, HEAD, OPTIONS and TRACE as safe, the later QUERY method is also safe, and POST, PUT, DELETE, CONNECT and PATCH are not. The distinction lets spiders and caches that prefetch work without fear of causing harm. It also lets a user agent warn the user before an unsafe action. A safe method may still have side effects the client did not request and cannot be blamed for, such as appending to an access log. What it must not do is contradict its own semantics. Even if a URI such as page?do=delete suggests an unsafe action, the resource owner must disable it for safe methods. Nothing technically stops a server from changing state on a GET. It is discouraged, because caches, search engines and other automated agents may then make unintended changes.

  <!-- sysd-found-035 -->

- **Digital certificates: how a browser knows a key is real**

  Anyone can claim to be your bank, so a public key by itself proves little. A digital certificate certifies that a named subject owns a public key, and certificate authorities are trusted third parties that sign certificates so others can rely on them. A TLS server certificate holds the server name, the trusted certificate authority that vouches for it, and the server's public key. Trust is anchored in a list of certificates shipped with user agent software such as the browser. To serve a site over HTTPS: ordinary HTTP inside an encrypted tunnel, an administrator creates a certificate for the web server and has a trusted authority sign it, otherwise browsers warn users. Commercial authorities sell certificates, and a free automated service such as Let's Encrypt issues basic ones. X.509 certificates make an authority and a public key infrastructure necessary to verify the link between a certificate and its owner. That is also the weak point: if one authority cooperates or is compromised, a Man-in-the-middle attacks: the eavesdropper who relays everything becomes possible.

  <!-- sysd-found-053 -->

- **Symmetric-key encryption: one shared secret for both directions**

  Symmetric-key encryption uses the same secret key to encrypt plaintext and to decrypt ciphertext, so both parties must hold that shared secret. Needing both to have it is the main drawback compared with Public-key cryptography: one key to lock, another to open. Its strength is bulk data. Apart from the one-time pad, symmetric algorithms have smaller keys, which means less storage space and faster transmission. Modern systems therefore agree on a fresh secret key for each session using Diffie-Hellman: agreeing on a secret in public or another public-key protocol, then encrypt the bulk of the messages symmetrically. No physically secure channel is needed. Stream ciphers encrypt a message one digit or byte at a time, and block ciphers encrypt a block of bits as one unit; AES uses 128-bit blocks. Popular algorithms include AES, ChaCha20 and Twofish. Encryption does not guarantee a message stays unchanged. So a separate code that checks the message is often added, and one can be built from an AEAD cipher such as AES-GCM. Session keys come from pseudorandom key generators, and weak randomness in them has led to cryptanalytic breaks, so implementations need a high-entropy source.

  <!-- sysd-found-181 -->

- **Diffie-Hellman: agreeing on a secret in public**

  Two parties can end up holding the same secret key while an eavesdropper reads every message. Diffie-Hellman key exchange is a mathematical method of securely generating a shared symmetric key over a public channel. It replaces key exchange by courier, and the key then encrypts later traffic with a symmetric cipher. Both parties publicly agree on a prime modulus p and a base g. Each picks a secret number and sends g raised to it mod p, then raises the received value to its own secret and reaches the same shared value. Only the two secret numbers stay private. An eavesdropper must solve the discrete logarithm problem, which is hard for large groups, and primes of at least 2048 bits are recommended. By itself the method is non-authenticated, so a way to check who is on the other end must be added to prevent a Man-in-the-middle attacks: the eavesdropper who relays everything. Ephemeral keys give Forward secrecy: keeping old conversations safe from future theft: new key pairs are generated for each session and discarded afterwards. Much Internet traffic uses groups of 1024 bits or less, and the Logjam attack exploited export-grade 512-bit groups.

  <!-- sysd-found-174 -->

- **The chain of trust from a root certificate down to a site**

  A certificate is only as good as the signature on it, and that signature has a signer of its own. A chain of trust lets a certificate be validated against its parent certificates, back to a root certificate that serves as a trust anchor. A root certificate is self-signed and has no parent. Intermediate certificates only sign other certificates and must themselves be signed by a root or another intermediate. A leaf certificate cannot sign others. To validate a server certificate, the client checks that its subject matches the hostname it connects to and that a trusted certificate authority signed it. Browsers and operating systems ship lists of default-trusted authorities set by root programs. Firefox uses the Mozilla program everywhere, while Chrome, Edge and Safari mostly use the operating system's trust store. Trust bits record each root's valid purposes, so an authority can be trusted for TLS server certificates but not for code signing. A self-signed certificate is worthless for trust between unacquainted parties, so public Internet servers need certificates from a trusted public authority.

  <!-- sysd-found-175 -->

  *Figure: A root certificate anchors the chain, intermediates sign other certificates, and a leaf signs none.* (layers; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Why one bad certificate authority can break everyone's trust**

  A certificate authority is a trusted third party that stores, signs and issues digital certificates, so the whole system's security depends on it. It verifies an applicant's credentials before certifying that a public key belongs to the named entity. X.509's critical weakness is that any authority a party trusts can issue a certificate for any domain. A browser trusts dozens of them, so subverting one lets an attacker impersonate any site. An attacker who steals an authority's private keys can forge certificates without further access. Publicly trusted authorities therefore keep keys in hardware security modules and the long-term root key in an offline one, signing only shorter-lived intermediates. The CA/Browser Forum Baseline Requirements cap certificate lifetime: 60 months from 1st July 2012, 398 Days from 1 September 2020, and 47 Days from 15 March 2029. Certificate Transparency requires all TLS certificates to be logged in publicly auditable records, to detect fraudulent ones in real time. It has largely superseded HTTP Public Key Pinning, which browsers deprecated for its risk of bricking sites.

  <!-- sysd-found-178 -->

- **RSA: encrypting with a key you can publish**

  RSA is a public-key cryptosystem in which publicly revealing the encryption key does not reveal the decryption key. So anyone can encrypt for the key's owner, and the owner can sign messages. A message is enciphered with the key its intended recipient has publicly revealed, and only that recipient, who knows the decryption key, can decipher it. Anyone can verify a message signed with the privately held decryption key by using the public encryption key. Signatures cannot be forged, and a signer cannot later deny a valid one. Encryption represents the message as a number M, raises it to a publicly specified power e, and takes the remainder when divided by n. Here n is the public product of two large secret primes p and q. Decryption uses a secret power d, where e * d is congruent to 1 modulo (p - 1) * (q - 1). Security depends in part on the difficulty of factoring n. In practice RSA often exchanges the secret key for symmetric encryption, which is better for bulk data.

  <!-- sysd-found-191 -->

- **HTTP authentication: the server challenges, the client answers**

  HTTP has a built-in way to ask who is knocking: a general framework for access control with extensible challenge-response schemes. The server issues a challenge before serving the content, and the client supplies credentials. An origin server challenges a request with 401 (Unauthorized) and must include a WWW-Authenticate header listing at least one challenge. The client answers by sending its credentials in a request header. Valid credentials that are not adequate to gain access should get 403 (Forbidden), not 401. A protection space is the server's origin combined with the realm value, so realms split a server's resources into spaces, each with its own scheme.

  <!-- sysd-found-043 -->

- **HTTP client errors: the 4xx codes you meet most**

  A 404 is the error everyone has seen, and it is one of a family. The 4xx class says the client seems to have erred. The server should explain the error and whether it is temporary or permanent, and the codes apply to any method.

  400 (Bad Request) means the server will not process the request because of a perceived client error, such as malformed syntax, invalid message framing or deceptive routing. 401 (Unauthorized) means the request lacks valid credentials and must carry a WWW-Authenticate challenge. 403 (Forbidden) means the server understood the request but refuses it, even with credentials that are insufficient.

  404 (Not Found) means no current representation was found, or the server will not disclose one. It does not say whether this is permanent, and 410 (Gone) is preferred when the condition is likely permanent. 405 (Method Not Allowed) means the method is known but not supported by the target resource, and the response must list the supported methods in an Allow header. 408 (Request Timeout) means the server did not receive a complete request in time, and the client may repeat it, on a new connection if needed.

  409 (Conflict) means the request conflicts with the target resource's current state, and the user might be able to resolve it and resubmit. 412 (Precondition Failed) means a precondition in the request headers evaluated to false. 413 (Content Too Large), 414 (URI Too Long) and 415 (Unsupported Media Type) mean the content is too big, the URI too long, or the format unsupported. A temporary 413 should carry Retry-After.

  | 403 | Understood but refused |
  | 404 | No current representation found |
  | 405 | Method not supported by the resource |
  | 408 | Complete request not received in time |
  | 409 | Conflicts with the resource's current state |
  | 410 | Gone: the condition is likely permanent |
  | 412 | A precondition evaluated to false |

- **HTTP intermediaries: proxies, gateways and tunnels**

  A request rarely travels straight from browser to origin server. An HTTP intermediary is a proxy, gateway or tunnel placed between client and origin server so a request can be satisfied through a chain of connections. A message that crosses three intermediaries passes through four separate connections. A proxy is chosen by the client, usually through local configuration, and organizations use proxies for security services, annotation or shared caches. A gateway, also called a Reverse proxy: a front door for servers, acts as the origin server toward the client but translates requests and forwards them inbound. A tunnel is a blind relay between two connections that does not change messages, for example carrying TLS through a firewall proxy. An interception proxy is not chosen by the client but filters or redirects outgoing port 80 traffic. At the protocol level it is indistinguishable from an on-path attacker. Each proxy must append a Via header describing how it received the message, which helps avoid request loops. An intermediary that holds a shared cache is especially vulnerable to cache poisoning.

  <!-- sysd-found-062 -->

- **HTTP redirects: the 3xx codes and where they send you**

  Sometimes the right answer to a request is to look somewhere else. The 3xx class says the user agent must take further action to fulfill the request, usually by repeating it at a different URI.

  Most redirects point to another URI in the Location header: 301, 302, 307 and 308. Others offer a choice of representations (300), send the client to a different resource (303), or point to a stored result (304). 301 (Moved Permanently) assigns a new permanent URI that future references should use, and it is heuristically cacheable. 302 (Found) means the resource is temporarily elsewhere, so the client keeps using the original URI.

  For historical reasons a client may turn a POST into a GET after 301 or 302. 308 (Permanent Redirect) and 307 (Temporary Redirect) avoid this, and 307 forbids changing the method on automatic redirection. 303 (See Other) is mainly used to send the output of a POST to a resource that can be separately identified, bookmarked and cached. 304 (Not Modified) means a conditional GET or HEAD would have given 200 but its condition was false. The stored representation is still valid, so no content is sent.

  When following a redirect, the client replaces the target URI and drops automatically generated connection and origin-specific headers. It should consider removing headers that carry credentials or cookies for security. It should also detect and break cyclical redirection. An earlier specification advised at most five redirections, and some clients still enforce such a limit.

  | Code | Meaning |
  |---|---|
  | 300 | A choice of representations |
  | 301 | Moved permanently |
  | 302 | Found: temporarily elsewhere |
  | 303 | See other: a different resource |
  | 304 | Not modified: the stored copy is still valid |
  | 307 | Temporary redirect, method unchanged |
  | 308 | Permanent redirect, method unchanged |

- **HTTP server errors: the 5xx codes**

  When a 5xx arrives, the fault is on the server's side. The 5xx class says the server is aware it has erred or cannot perform the requested method. 500 (Internal Server Error) means the server hit an unexpected condition that prevented it from fulfilling the request. 501 (Not Implemented) means it does not support the functionality needed, for example when it does not recognize the request method. 505 (HTTP Version Not Supported) means it does not support the major HTTP version in the request. Two codes belong to servers acting as gateways or proxies. 502 (Bad Gateway) means the server received an invalid response from the inbound server. 504 (Gateway Timeout) means it did not get a timely response from an upstream server. 503 (Service Unavailable) means the server cannot currently handle the request because of temporary overload or scheduled maintenance. It may send Retry-After to say how long the service is expected to be unavailable, as an HTTP-date or a number of seconds. An overloaded server might simply refuse connections instead.

  <!-- sysd-found-073 -->

- **Four extra status codes: 428, 429, 431 and 511**

  RFC 6585 defines four optional status codes, 428, 429, 431 and 511, for common situations that less precise codes handled poorly. Clients treat an unknown code as the generic code of its class. 428 Precondition Required says the server requires a conditional request, typically to avoid the lost update problem. That is where a client GETs a resource, modifies it and PUTs it back while a third party changed it. 429 Too Many Requests says the user sent too many requests in a given time. 431 means the request headers are too large, and 511 means the client must authenticate for network access.

  <!-- sysd-found-190 -->

- **HTTP caching: answering a request without asking the server**

  The fastest request is one that never reaches the origin server. An HTTP cache is a local store of earlier responses, with the subsystem that controls their storage, retrieval and deletion. It reuses a prior response to answer a later request, which cuts response time and network bandwidth. Using a cache is optional in HTTP, but reuse is the default when nothing prevents it. So the rules focus on stopping a cache from storing a response that is not reusable or reusing a stored one inappropriately. The cache key is at least the request method and target URI. Many caches store only GET responses and so key on the URI alone, while the The Vary header: telling caches what a response depended on adds request fields to the key. Most commonly a cache stores a 200 (OK) response to a GET. On a miss a cache can collapse several incoming requests into a single forward request, reducing load on the origin server. It must write unsafe requests through to the origin before replying, and such requests may invalidate stored responses.

  <!-- sysd-found-077 -->

- **HTTP cache freshness: how long a stored response stays good**

  A cached copy has a clock. A response is fresh while its age has not exceeded its freshness lifetime, and a fresh response can be reused without contacting the origin server. Lifetime is the time between the origin generating a response and its expiration time. Age is the time since the origin generated or last successfully validated it, and a response is stale once age exceeds the lifetime. The primary mechanism is an explicit expiration time from the origin, using the Expires header or the max-age directive. A cache takes the lifetime from the first matching rule: s-maxage for a shared cache, then max-age, then the Expires value minus the Date value. When none exists, the cache may assign a heuristic one, only for heuristically cacheable status codes or explicitly cacheable responses. It should use no more than some fraction, typically 10%, of the interval since Last-Modified. The Age header carries the cache's estimate of seconds since the origin generated or validated the response.

  <!-- sysd-found-079 -->

- **Certificate revocation: cancelling trust before the expiry date**

  A stolen key stays useful to an attacker until its certificate expires, unless the certificate is revoked. A certificate can be revoked before it expires, for example because its private key was compromised, and browsers check whether that has happened. With the Online Certificate Status Protocol, the browser sends the certificate's serial number to the certificate authority, which answers whether it is still valid. The authority may also publish a certificate revocation list naming revoked certificates. The CA/Browser forum no longer requires these lists, but they are still widely used. Support for sending multiple OCSP responses arrived with TLS 1.3: a faster protocol built by removing things.

  <!-- sysd-found-054 -->

- **What happens when you type a URL**

  You type an address, press Enter, and a page appears. Behind that moment, the browser resolves the domain to an IP address, opens a TCP connection, sends an HTTP request and renders the server's response. It starts by reading the URL. The scheme, such as http://, tells the browser to connect using HTTP. The domain is the site's domain name, and the path names the requested resource on the server. Next the browser needs an address. It looks up the domain's IP address with a DNS lookup. Caches at the browser, the operating system, the local network and the ISP speed this up. If no cache has the address, the browser asks DNS servers for a recursive DNS lookup until the IP address is found. With the address in hand, the browser establishes a TCP connection and sends an HTTP request such as GET /phone HTTP/1.1 with a Host header. The server processes the request and sends back a response, with status code 200 for success. The browser then renders the HTML content.

  <!-- sysd-found-044 -->

  *Figure: The browser works through these steps in order, from the typed URL to the rendered page.*

  | Step | What the browser does |
  |---|---|
  | 1 | Reads the URL: scheme, domain and path |
  | 2 | Looks up the domain's IP address with a DNS lookup |
  | 3 | Establishes a TCP connection |
  | 4 | Sends an HTTP request such as GET /phone HTTP/1.1 with a Host header |
  | 5 | Receives the response, with status code 200 for success |
  | 6 | Renders the HTML content |

- **HTTP versions from 0.9 to 3: what changed and why**

  The protocol behind every web page has been rewritten several times. HTTP has evolved through versions 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 2 and 3, each changing how requests share connections and which transport carries them. HTTP/0.9 (1991) and HTTP/1.0 (1996) are obsolete, while HTTP/1.1 (1997), version 2 (2015) and HTTP/3 (2022) are standard. One source dates HTTP/3 to 2019. HTTP/1 and its sub-versions introduced persistent connections, pipelining and headers, all built on top of TCP. HTTP/1.0 used a separate TCP connection per resource request, while HTTP/1.1 reuses one. Version 2, the subject of HTTP/2: many requests sharing one connection, brought multiplexing, stream prioritization, server push and HPACK compression, but still ran over TCP. It sends compressed binary headers, uses one connection per server domain instead of 2 to 8, and splits traffic into bidirectional streams that almost solve head-of-line blocking. HTTP/3 uses QUIC, which is built on UDP, so it moves away from TCP. Neither of the two newer versions obsoletes the earlier major ones.

  <!-- sysd-found-039 -->

  *Figure: The five HTTP versions fall in order on a timeline, with only the last three still standard.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **HTTP/2: many requests sharing one connection**

  Loading one page used to mean opening several connections. HTTP/1.0 allowed one outstanding request per TCP connection, and pipelining in HTTP/1.1 only partly helped. HTTP/2 is a revision of HTTP that maps HTTP semantics onto binary frames multiplexed over one connection. It needs one connection per server domain instead of 2 to 8. Messages are encoded in binary and split into frames. Each request and response exchange gets its own stream, and frames from many streams are interleaved and reassembled on the other side. HTTP fields are repetitive and verbose, so HTTP/2 compresses them with HPACK, which saves bandwidth. Two features proved awkward. The priority signaling of RFC 7540 was complex and unevenly implemented, so RFC 9113 deprecates it. Server push, an optional mode, lets a server speculatively send data the client will probably need. It is hard to use well, because the server must predict requests. Over TLS the protocol is negotiated with the ALPN extension under the identifier h2, and implementations must use TLS 1.2 or higher. It does not address TCP head-of-line blocking.

- **HTTP/3 and QUIC: leaving TCP behind**

  HTTP/3 is the third major version of HTTP, specified in RFC 9114, and it runs over QUIC instead of over TCP. QUIC (RFC 9000) is a multiplexed transport built on UDP that provides reliability and does congestion control in user space. HTTP/3 keeps the semantics of earlier versions, with the same request methods, status codes and message fields. The differences lie in how they are encoded and mapped to the transport. The reason for the move is head-of-line blocking. TCP cannot see the parallel streams of HTTP/2, so one lost packet stalls every transaction. QUIC's native multiplexing makes a lost packet affect only the streams that lost data. HTTP/3 also compresses headers with QPACK instead of HPACK, which sends table updates on separate unidirectional streams to reduce head-of-line blocking among streams. In real-world use it loads faster than earlier versions, in some cases over four times faster than HTTP/1.1, though one source says over three times. As of July 2026, more than 95% of major web browsers in use and 40% of the top 10 million websites support it.

  <!-- sysd-found-041 -->

- **HTTP/2 streams: how one connection carries many conversations**

  One slow response should not freeze a whole page. That is the job of the stream. An HTTP/2 stream is an independent, bidirectional sequence of frames within one connection, and giving each request and response its own stream is how HTTP/2 multiplexes requests. One connection can hold many concurrently open streams, with either endpoint interleaving frames from different streams. Streams are largely independent, so a stalled request or response does not stop progress on the others, although TCP head-of-line blocking is not addressed. The basic unit is the frame, with a fixed 9-octet header, and HEADERS and DATA frames carry requests and responses. Stream identifiers are 31-bit integers. Clients use odd numbers and servers even, each new one must exceed all earlier ones from that endpoint, and none is reused. A long-lived connection can therefore run out, and then a client opens a new connection while a server sends a GOAWAY frame to force it to. SETTINGS_MAX_CONCURRENT_STREAMS limits the streams a peer may open. It is initially unlimited, and a value no smaller than 100 is recommended.

  <!-- sysd-found-182 -->

- **HTTP pipelining: sending requests without waiting**

  Pipelining dramatically improves page load times, especially on high-latency links such as satellite connections. HTTP pipelining is a feature of HTTP/1.1 that lets a client send several requests over one TCP connection without waiting for the matching responses. The server must answer in the order requests arrived, so the connection stays first-in-first-out and head-of-line blocking can occur. GET and HEAD requests can always be pipelined, while a POST should not be. Many legacy servers and especially proxies handle it badly, even mixing up the order of responses, so browsers disabled or removed it. HTTP/2 multiplexing superseded it, and in HTTP/3 QUIC does the multiplexing.

- **Certificate validation levels: what the issuer actually checked**

  Not every certificate proves the same thing. Validation levels describe how much a certificate authority checks before issuing one: domain control only, organization identity, or extended legal identity. A domain-validated certificate proves control of a domain name, not who the applicant is. An organization-validated one also needs the organization's existence as a legal entity, and an Extended Validation certificate needs manual human checks of legal identity. EV does not fully fix the weakness of domain validation, because an attacker could still get a domain-validated certificate for the victim domain. Until 2019 major browsers showed the legal identity for EV certificates.

  | Level | What the authority checks |
  |---|---|
  | Domain validated | Control of the domain name only |
  | Organization validated | Also the organization's existence as a legal entity |
  | Extended Validation | Manual human checks of legal identity |

  Servers use status codes that no standard defines. IETF-defined codes are documented in RFCs and maintained by IANA, while other values come from various servers. Among web servers, Nginx: a web server that also proxies and balances expands the 4xx space: 444 closes the connection with no response, and 499 reports a client that closed the request early. Cloudflare's proxy expands 5xx to signal origin problems, with 521 for refused connections and 522 for a timed-out contact. Some HTTP proxies informally use 598 for a network read timeout and 599 for a network connect timeout behind the proxy.

- **HTTP extensibility: growing without a new version**

  HTTP can gain new abilities without a new protocol version. It has generic extension points, such as methods, status codes, header fields, HTTP authentication schemes and cache directives. Because the semantics of HTTP are not versioned, these points persist and mean the same in every version. Version-specific extension points, such as transfer codings in HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 frame types, cannot override a version-independent mechanism unless that element allows it, as CONNECT does. New methods and status codes should be registered in the IANA HTTP Method and Status Code registries.

- **Informational 1xx codes: interim responses before the real one**

  Not every response is the last one. A 1xx status code is an interim response that reports connection status or request progress before the final response. It ends with the header section and has no content. 100 (Continue) says the initial part of a request was received and not rejected. A client that sends Expect: 100-continue and waits wastes no upload when the headers get the request rejected. 101 (Switching Protocols) answers an Upgrade request by naming the protocol now in effect, such as a newer HTTP version. 103 (Early Hints) returns some response headers before the final message. 102 (Processing), a WebDAV code, is deprecated.

- **Resources and representations: what HTTP really transfers**

  A resource can be anything, even the current weather. A resource is the target of an HTTP request. A representation is information reflecting the past, current or desired state of a resource in a format the protocol can carry. HTTP gives clients a uniform interface to a resource, whatever its type or implementation, by sending messages that manipulate or transfer representations. Because it communicates a representation and not the resource itself, implementation details stay hidden. One resource can have several representations, and an algorithm, usually Content negotiation: one URL, several versions, picks the selected one.

- **Content-Type, Content-Encoding and Content-Length**

  Every body needs a label saying what it is. Representation metadata describes the content of a message: Content-Type gives its media type, Content-Encoding the codings applied, such as compression, and Content-Length its size in octets. The media type defines both the data format and how the recipient should process it after any content codings are decoded. Content-Encoding exists mainly so data can be compressed without losing its media type,. When the length is unknown in advance, Content-Length is omitted. A client that takes a close as the end then cannot tell a premature close from a complete response, so chunked transfer encoding streams content reliably instead.

- **Content negotiation: one URL, several versions**

  One address can serve the same thing in different formats, languages or encodings. Content negotiation is how HTTP chooses among several representations of a resource to fit what a client can handle or prefers. In proactive negotiation, the server picks from the client's stated preferences. In reactive negotiation, the server lists options and the client chooses. In request content negotiation, the client uses the server's stated preferences. Proactive negotiation uses Accept, Accept-Charset, Accept-Encoding and Accept-Language headers, and the server also weighs hints such as the client's network address or User-Agent. It can save a round trip. But the server cannot know what is best for each user. Describing capabilities in every request is inefficient and a privacy risk, and it limits reuse of responses by shared caches. Reactive negotiation often works from a list in a 300 (Multiple Choices) or 406 (Not Acceptable) response, and it costs a second request. A q parameter weights each preference from 0 to 1, and the default is 1.

- **Success codes: 200, 201, 202, 204 and 206**

  The 2xx class says the client's request was successfully received, understood and accepted. 200 (OK) means the request succeeded. 201 (Created) means one or more new resources were created, and the primary one is identified by the Location header or, if absent, by the target URI. 202 (Accepted) means the request was accepted for processing but not completed, and it may never be acted on. HTTP has no way to send the final status of an asynchronous operation later. 204 (No Content) means the request succeeded with nothing more to send, and 206 (Partial Content) means a range request is being fulfilled.

  <!-- sysd-found-070 -->

- **HTTP/2 connection management: one long-lived connection per host**

  HTTP/2 uses one long-lived, persistent connection per host and port, reused across requests and shut down gracefully with a GOAWAY frame. Clients should not open more than one per host and port, except to replace one near exhausting stream identifiers, needing fresh TLS keys or failed. Before closing, an endpoint should send GOAWAY naming the highest stream that might have been processed. Requests on higher streams, or on a stream reset with REFUSED_STREAM, were unprocessed and are safe to retry. Idle connections can silently break because middleboxes discard connection bindings, so a client can send a PING frame to test one without sending a request.

  <!-- sysd-found-187 -->

- **HTTP/2 flow control: the receiver sets the pace**

  Streams contend for one TCP connection, and contention can block them. HTTP/2 flow control is a credit-based scheme, driven by the receiver, that keeps multiplexed streams on one connection from destructively interfering with each other. It applies to individual streams and to the connection as a whole, through WINDOW_UPDATE frames. Receivers advertise how many octets they will accept. The initial window is 65,535 octets for each new stream and for the connection, and only DATA frames count against it. Flow control works hop by hop, not end to end, and protects resource-constrained endpoints such as a proxy with a slow upstream and fast downstream.

  <!-- sysd-found-183 -->

- **HTTP/2 header compression: HPACK and shared state**

  Headers repeat themselves, request after request. HTTP/2 compresses each set of header fields into a field block (HPACK) using state shared across the connection. Repetitive fields quickly fill the initial TCP congestion window, so compressing them lets many requests fit into one packet. Compression is stateful: each endpoint keeps an encoder and decoder context with a dynamic table, whose maximum size the decoder sets, starting at 4,096 bytes. A receiver must decompress field blocks even when discarding the frames, because they change compression state. The Cookie header may be split into separate fields, because updating one pair would otherwise invalidate the stored field line and hurt compression.

  <!-- sysd-found-184 -->

- **HTTP/2 server push: answering before the question**

  Why wait to be asked? HTTP/2 server push lets a server send responses, with the promised requests that go with them, to a client before the client asks. The server synthesizes a request, sends it as a PUSH_PROMISE frame, and then answers it on a separate server-initiated stream. The aim is to remove a round trip: a request for HTML is often followed by requests for the stylesheets and scripts it references. In practice push is hard to use well, because the server must predict requests despite caches, content negotiation and user behavior, and wrong guesses waste bandwidth. Promised requests must be safe and cacheable.

  <!-- sysd-found-185 -->

- **Keeping sensitive data out of URLs**

  URIs are meant to be shared, not secured, so sensitive or personally identifiable information should not be placed in them. Many servers, proxies and user agents log or display them where third parties can see them. A GET form builds a URI from user input, so POST is often preferred for sensitive fields because it sends them in the content. That hinders reuse by caches, though, and uses an unsafe method for what would be a safe request. The Referer header can reveal a user's recent browsing history and any personal data in the referring URI.

- **POST versus PUT: who decides where the data lives**

  Same payload, different promise. The fundamental difference is intent: the target of a POST handles the representation by the resource's own semantics, whereas a PUT replaces the state of the target resource. Hence the intent of PUT is idempotent and visible to intermediaries, though only the origin server knows the exact effect. A proper PUT presumes the client knows which resource it wants. A service that selects the URI itself after receiving a state-changing request should use POST instead. A successful PUT returns 201 (Created) if it created the resource and 200 (OK) or 204 (No Content) if it modified an existing one.

  <!-- sysd-found-063 -->

- **The Vary header: telling caches what a response depended on**

  A server that picks your language needs to tell caches it did. The Vary response header names the request fields, beyond method and URI, that may have influenced which content the origin server chose. Its value is a list of selecting header field names, such as accept-encoding and accept-language, or the wildcard *. A cache may reuse a response with Vary only for a later request with the same values in the listed fields, so Vary expands the cache key. A * signals that other aspects of the request, even outside the message, played a role. A cache then cannot judge reuse without asking the origin.

  <!-- sysd-found-065 -->

- **The Cache-Control header: one line steering every cache**

  One header steers the caches along the way. The Cache-Control header lists directives that control caches along the request and response chain. Directives are unidirectional: one in a request does not imply the same directive in the response. A proxy must pass them through in forwarded messages, whether or not it implements a cache. No directive can target a specific cache. Request directives are advisory, which caches may implement but need not, while a cache must obey the response directives. Cache-Control takes precedence over the older Expires header, which is ignored when max-age or, for a shared cache, s-maxage is present.

  <!-- sysd-found-082 -->

- **Cache-Control request directives: what a client may ask of a cache**

  A client can ask a cache for fresher or staler answers, but it can only ask. Request directives are advisory, and caches need not honor them. A max-age directive asks for a response no older than the given seconds. A max-stale directive accepts a response past its freshness lifetime. A no-cache directive asks that a stored response not be used without successful validation at the origin. A no-store directive says a cache must not store any part of the request or its response. With only-if-cached the client wants a stored response only, and a cache that honors it answers with one or with 504 (Gateway Timeout).

  <!-- sysd-found-084 -->

- **Shared and private HTTP caches: whose copy is it**

  Some caches serve many people, and some serve one. A shared cache stores responses for reuse by more than one user and usually sits in an intermediary. A private cache is dedicated to one user, often inside a user agent. The private response directive stops a shared cache from storing a response meant for one user, but a private cache may store it. A shared cache needs extra permission to reuse a response to a request that carried credentials, and s-maxage applies only to shared caches. Private caches can be used to reconstruct their one user's activity.

  <!-- sysd-found-085 -->

- **HTTP cache security risks: poisoning, timing and leaks**

  Caches add an attack surface, because their contents persist after a request ends, so an attack on a cache can reveal or alter information long afterwards. In cache poisoning an attacker inserts a malicious response into a cache, which is especially effective when a shared cache distributes it to many clients. Cache timing leaks which resources were previously requested, since a fast load shows a site was visited. Adding the referring site to the cache key, called double keying, mitigates it. Deployment flaws can cache sensitive information, such as credentials, and a cacheable response with Set-Cookie can be reused for later requests.

- **Transport Layer Security: three jobs in one protocol**

  TLS does three jobs at once. Encryption hides the data from third parties. A check of identity ensures the parties are who they claim to be. An integrity check verifies the data has not been forged or tampered with. Transport Layer Security is a cryptographic protocol that provides secured communications over a computer network, giving applications privacy, integrity and authenticity.

  It is used in email and voice over IP, but securing HTTPS: ordinary HTTP inside an encrypted tunnel is its most visible use. TLS evolved from SSL: the old name that will not go away and is an IETF standard first defined in 1999. The current version is TLS 1.3: a faster protocol built by removing things, defined in August 2018. It is made of two layers, the record protocol and the handshake protocol, and runs on top of a reliable transport such as TCP.

It does so either with a separate port, 443 for secured web traffic rather than 80 for HTTP, or with a protocol-specific STARTTLS request. The handshake uses an asymmetric cipher to set the cipher parameters and a session-specific shared key, and further communication is encrypted with a symmetric cipher. That key is unique to each connection and negotiated at the start, which keeps the connection private. Public-key cryptography proves identity, required for the server and optional for the client. Each message carries a check code, so lost or altered data is detected.

  <!-- sysd-found-049 -->

- **HTTPS: ordinary HTTP inside an encrypted tunnel**

  Plain HTTP is not encrypted, so it is open to eavesdropping and to a Man-in-the-middle attacks: the eavesdropper who relays everything. Those attacks expose accounts and sensitive information or inject malware and advertisements into pages. HTTPS is designed to withstand them. It is HTTP carried over an encrypted TLS connection, so web traffic is private, authenticated and protected from tampering in transit. The main motivations are proof that the website is the one requested and protection of the privacy and integrity of exchanged data.

  HTTPS is not a separate protocol but ordinary HTTP over an encrypted SSL/TLS connection. Its URLs begin with https:// and use port 443 by default, while HTTP uses port 80. Because HTTP runs entirely on top of TLS, the URL, query parameters, headers, cookies and message data can all be encrypted.

  Usually only the server is verified, by the client examining its certificate, which a trusted third party must sign. TLS still protects the channel when only one side is verified. It typically uses long-term public and private keys to generate a short-term session key that encrypts the data flow. A hijacker of the traffic gets only binary data. For HTTPS to be effective a whole site must be served over it. Loading scripts or images over HTTP, or only a login page over HTTPS, leaves users open to attacks and surveillance. Deploying HTTPS also allows HTTP/2 and HTTP/3, which are designed to reduce page load times, size and latency.

  <!-- sysd-found-048 -->

- **Man-in-the-middle attacks: the eavesdropper who relays everything**

  The attacker does not need to break any encryption. A man-in-the-middle attack, or on-path attack, is one where an attacker secretly relays and possibly alters communication between two parties who believe they are talking directly. In active eavesdropping the attacker makes independent connections with both victims and relays messages, controlling the whole conversation. That means intercepting all relevant messages and injecting new ones, which is easy near an unencrypted Wi-Fi access point. With public keys it goes like this. Mallory replaces Bob's public key with her own, so Alice encrypts to Mallory. Mallory decrypts, reads or alters the message and re-encrypts it with Bob's key. The parties need a way to know they hold real keys. Variants include HTTPS spoofing with a fake certificate, SSL/TLS stripping that downgrades HTTPS to HTTP, evil-twin Wi-Fi and certificates signed by a fraudulent CA. The defenses are identity checks and tamper detection. TLS verifies one or both parties through a mutually trusted certificate authority, but most connections verify only the server, so these attacks can still occur.

  <!-- sysd-found-179 -->

- **Securing cookies against theft, scripts and forgery**

  Steal a user's cookies and, to most servers, you are that user. Most sites use cookies as the only identifier of a user session. An attacker who steals a victim's full set of cookies is therefore treated by the server as the victim's session. Securing cookies means protecting those identifiers from theft and misuse. Cookies sent over unencrypted HTTP can be read by anyone on the network, such as on open Wi-Fi. TLS fixes this, and the Secure attribute makes the browser send the cookie only over an encrypted channel. Attackers can also steal cookies with Cross-site scripting: when a page runs an attacker's code, by getting their JavaScript to send document.cookie to them. An HttpOnly cookie cannot be read by client-side scripts, which mitigates this. A second danger is Cross-site request forgery: abusing a site's trust in your browser, which abuses automatic cookie sending. Browsers attach a domain's cookies to any request to it, so a forged request from another page looks real to a server that trusts the cookie. SameSite=Strict sends cookies only when the target domain matches the origin, which mitigates it.

  <!-- sysd-found-169 -->

- **Datagram TLS: security for UDP applications**

  TLS runs on a reliable transport such as TCP, but some applications send datagrams instead. Datagram TLS (DTLS) is a protocol based on TLS that secures datagram-based applications against eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery. It is intended to give security guarantees similar to TLS but works with datagram protocols such as UDP, not only stream protocols. Because it preserves the semantics of the underlying transport, an application avoids the delays of stream protocols. It must handle packet reordering, datagram loss and data larger than one datagram. All modern web browsers support DTLS-SRTP for WebRTC.

  <!-- sysd-found-060 -->

- **HTTP Strict Transport Security: never again without HTTPS**

  A site can tell browsers to stop talking to it over anything but HTTPS. HTTP Strict Transport Security (HSTS) does this, protecting against man-in-the-middle attacks such as protocol downgrades and cookie hijacking. A server sets the policy with the Strict-Transport-Security response header, honored only over an HTTPS connection. Its max-age is in seconds, so max-age=31536000 keeps the policy for one non-leap year. While a policy is in effect the browser rewrites insecure links to https before contacting the server. It must end the connection, without letting the user continue, if the connection cannot be secured. This fixes SSL stripping, where an attacker silently turns an HTTPS connection into plain HTTP with no warning. Protection relies on trust on first use: the first visit, and the first request after max-age expires, are unprotected. Browsers ship a preload list of known HSTS sites so that even the first request uses HTTPS, but such a list cannot scale to cover every website. - **HTTP origins: why the browser checks the certificate matches**

For https, authority depends on the server's ability to use the private key matching a certificate the client trusts for that origin. A client must verify that the service's identity matches the URI's origin server, to prevent impersonation by an on-path attacker. If the certificate is not valid for the origin, the user agent must get user confirmation or end the connection with a bad certificate error. Ignoring the server's identity leaves the connection open to active attack.

- **SSL: the old name that will not go away**

  Most major certificate providers still call certificates SSL certificates, although SSL has been deprecated in favor of TLS. SSL, Secure Sockets Layer, is a protocol for encrypting and securing communications on the internet, first developed in 1995. Web data was originally sent in plaintext that anyone who intercepted it could read, and SSL was created to fix this and protect user privacy. By encrypting data between the user and a web server, SSL also stops certain attacks by preventing tampering with data in transit.

  <!-- sysd-found-046 -->

- **Forward secrecy: keeping old conversations safe from future theft**

  Suppose someone records your encrypted traffic today and steals the server's key later. Forward secrecy is the property that keeps a session key safe even if one of the private keys is compromised in the future. Without it, a compromised server private key exposes all future sessions that use its certificate and also any past sessions that were intercepted and stored. Having one of the long-term asymmetric keys used to establish an HTTPS session should not make it easier to derive the short-term session key. Nor should it help decrypt the conversation later. TLS can provide it by requiring ephemeral Diffie-Hellman key exchange to establish session keys, and only the DHE and ECDHE exchanges do. In TLS 1.3: a faster protocol built by removing things it is mandatory: static RSA and other key exchanges without it are dropped. Many clients and servers are not configured to require it, so without Diffie-Hellman a third party that obtains the server's private key can decrypt all recorded traffic. Session tickets and weak Diffie-Hellman parameters can weaken the forward secrecy a server aims to provide.

  <!-- sysd-found-052 -->

- **TLS versions: from 1.0 to 1.3**

  TLS has gone through versions 1.0, 1.1, 1.2 and 1.3, each defined in an RFC and each revised to address security threats. TLS 1.1 was defined in RFC 4346 in April 2006 and TLS 1.2 in RFC 5246 in August 2008. The newest, TLS 1.3: a faster protocol built by removing things, came in RFC 8446 in August 2018. It supports 1-RTT handshakes with initial 0-RTT support and mandates perfect forward secrecy through ephemeral keys in the (EC)DH key agreement. It drops insecure or obsolete features, including compression, renegotiation, non-AEAD ciphers and static RSA and static DH key exchanges,. It also encrypts all handshake messages after the ServerHello, including the server certificate.

  <!-- sysd-found-055 -->

- **The TLS handshake: from hello to a shared secret**

  A TLS connection begins with a short exchange that ends with both sides holding the same secret key. In the TLS handshake, the client and server agree on cipher parameters. The server proves its identity with a certificate, and both derive a shared session key for the secured connection.

  The client opens with a ClientHello holding the highest TLS version it supports, a random number, and its suggested cipher suites and compression methods. The server answers with a ServerHello choosing from them, ideally the highest version both support. It usually sends a digital certificate holding its name, the trusted certificate authority that vouches for it, and its public key. The client confirms the certificate is valid before proceeding.

  Then the session key is made. In older TLS and SSL the client encrypts a random PreMasterSecret with the server's public key. The server decrypts it with its private key, and both derive the session key from it. Alternatively Diffie-Hellman key exchange, or its elliptic-curve variant, generates the session key with forward secrecy. Both sides compute a master secret from the random numbers and key material. All other key data for the connection, such as the encryption key and MAC key, is derived from it.

  Each side finishes by sending a Finished message, authenticated and encrypted, containing a hash and MAC over the previous handshake messages. The other side verifies it, and if any verification fails, the handshake fails and no connection is created. Otherwise data flows over a secure bi-directional channel until the connection closes. The handshake in TLS 1.3: a faster protocol built by removing things takes one round trip instead of the two earlier versions need. The client guesses the key exchange algorithm and sends public keys for its guesses in the ClientHello.

  <!-- sysd-found-050 -->

  *Figure: The handshake runs in this order, ending with data encrypted under the session key.*

  | Step | Who | What happens |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 | Client | Sends ClientHello: highest TLS version, random number, cipher suites |
  | 2 | Server | Answers with ServerHello, choosing from them |
  | 3 | Server | Sends its certificate |
  | 4 | Client | Confirms the certificate is valid |
  | 5 | Both | Derive the shared session key |
  | 6 | Both | Send and verify Finished messages |
  | 7 | Both | Exchange data encrypted with the session key |

  A server hosting several sites must choose a certificate before it knows which site was asked for. Server Name Indication is a TLS extension in which the client names the host it wants in its ClientHello, so the server can send the right certificate. The TLS handshake happens before the application protocol starts. Without SNI, the server must choose right after the ClientHello, and co-hosted name-based virtual servers would share one certificate. Workarounds exist: a wildcard certificate when all virtual servers share a domain, or listing every virtual host name in the subjectAltName extension. SNI sends the host name before the connection is encrypted.

  <!-- sysd-found-057 -->

- **TLS cipher suites and key exchange methods**

  Before protected data flows, the two sides must agree on a key and a cipher. The client presents the cipher suites it supports, and the server picks one it also supports and tells the client. Key exchange methods include RSA, Diffie-Hellman, ephemeral Diffie-Hellman, elliptic-curve variants, anonymous Diffie-Hellman and pre-shared key. Anonymous Diffie-Hellman does not check who is on the other end and is rarely used because it is open to man-in-the-middle attacks. Only the ephemeral DHE and ECDHE methods provide forward secrecy. HMAC protects integrity for CBC mode block ciphers, while authenticated encryption such as GCM and CCM has an integrated MAC.

  <!-- sysd-found-056 -->

- **TLS 1.3: a faster protocol built by removing things**

  TLS 1.3 got better largely by losing features. It is the current version of Transport Layer Security, designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery between client and server applications. It gives a secure channel over any reliable, in-order stream. The server is always verified and the client optionally, data is visible only to the endpoints, and tampering is detected even if an attacker controls the network. TLS has two components, a handshake protocol that checks the parties, negotiates parameters and establishes keys, and a record protocol that protects traffic in independently protected records. Legacy features were pruned. Only AEAD ciphers remain, static RSA and Diffie-Hellman suites are gone so all public-key key exchange gives forward secrecy, and compression and custom DHE groups were removed. The handshake has three phases, key exchange, server parameters and proof of identity, and every handshake message after the ServerHello is now encrypted. If the client's key_share is unacceptable, the server sends a HelloRetryRequest and the client restarts with a suitable one. Key derivation was redesigned around HKDF.

The interception software terminates the incoming TLS connection, inspects the HTTP plaintext, and opens a new TLS connection to the destination. Network operators use it to scan for malware that encryption would otherwise hide. It creates risks of its own. Traffic is unencrypted at the interception point, which attracts attackers, and the operator or anyone who gains access to the system can mount man-in-the-middle attacks on users.

- **What HTTPS does not protect**

  Even over HTTPS, an eavesdropper can still see which server you contacted. HTTPS protects content in transit but leaves some information visible. That includes the server's IP address and port, sometimes the domain name, and the amount and duration of traffic. Addresses and port numbers belong to the underlying TCP/IP protocols. Traffic analysis can infer properties of encrypted traffic, because TLS changes the contents but has minimal impact on size and timing. SSL stripping turns an https link into an http link so the attacker talks in clear with the client, and HTTP Strict Transport Security is the countermeasure.

  <!-- sysd-found-058 -->

- **Starting an HTTP/2 connection: ALPN, h2 and the preface**

  An http or https URI does not say which HTTP versions the server supports. For https the client uses TLS with the ALPN extension and the identifier h2, and both sides must then send a connection preface. Support over cleartext http can only be known out of band, and the h2c Upgrade mechanism is deprecated. The client preface is the 24-octet string PRI * HTTP/2.0 followed by SETTINGS, and the server's first frame is a SETTINGS frame. HTTP/2 over TLS must use TLS 1.2 or higher with the SNI extension.

  <!-- sysd-found-186 -->

- **Mutual TLS: when the client proves itself too**

  TLS usually proves only the server's identity. Mutual TLS, or mTLS, is a mode in which both ends of a connection verify that the other holds the correct private key. The mutual mode requires the user to install a personal client certificate in the browser. In the handshake the server requests a certificate. The client sends it plus a signature made with its private key, which proves it owns the certificate. mTLS keeps traffic secure and trusted in both directions. Systems built from Microservices: small services that scale on their own commonly use it to verify each other, in a Zero trust: no one is trusted by default.

  <!-- sysd-found-047 -->

- **Types of TLS certificate: server, client, SAN and wildcard**

  Certificates differ in what they identify. A server certificate proves the server is the intended destination. A client certificate verifies the client for access control and usually names a person, though username and password is more common. A Subject Alternative Name (SAN) certificate lists several values, such as DNS names and IP addresses, in its subjectAltName field. SANs are the preferred place for DNS names. A wildcard certificate uses an asterisk so one certificate secures many subdomains, but only one level: *.example.com matches sub1.example.com, not example.com or deeper names. Other kinds include email certificates and code-signing certificates that show binaries were not tampered with.

  <!-- sysd-found-176 -->

  *Figure: Certificate types differ in what they identify.*

  | Type | What it identifies |
  |---|---|
  | Server | The server as the intended destination |
  | Client | The client, for access control |
  | SAN | Several names, such as DNS names and IP addresses |
  | Wildcard | Many subdomains, but only one level |
  | Code-signing | Binaries that were not tampered with |

- **Why HTTPS switches to symmetric keys for the data**

  HTTPS uses asymmetric encryption only to set up a session key and then switches to symmetric encryption for the data. Once client and server hold the same session key, the encrypted data travels over a secure bi-directional channel using symmetric encryption. There are two reasons for the switch. Asymmetric encryption works only one way, so data the server encrypted for the client could be decrypted by anyone holding the public key. It also adds a lot of mathematical overhead for the server, so it is not suitable for data transmission in long sessions.

  <!-- sysd-found-045 -->

- **TLS session resumption: skipping the expensive part**

  Public-key math is expensive, so TLS lets a returning client skip it. A resumed TLS session reuses the results of an earlier handshake, through a session ID, a session ticket or, in TLS 1.3, a pre-shared key (PSK). With session IDs the server maps the ID to the previously negotiated master secret, and the client sends the ID on reconnecting. With session tickets the server stores its session state in an encrypted and authenticated ticket that the client keeps and presents later. The server then stores no per-session state. Tickets can undermine forward secrecy, because long-lived ticket keys defeat the protection of forward secrecy cipher suites. TLS 1.3 replaces both with one PSK exchange. The server sends a ticket after the handshake, and the client offers it in a later ClientHello. If accepted, its key bootstraps the new connection without a full handshake. A PSK combined with (EC)DHE keeps forward secrecy, while a PSK alone loses it for application data. Servers must not set a ticket lifetime above 604800 seconds (7 days).

  <!-- sysd-found-051 -->

- **TLS 0-RTT: sending data in the first message**

  A returning client can send data in its very first flight, and that speed has a price. TLS 1.3 early data (0-RTT) lets a client that shares a pre-shared key (PSK) with the server send application data in its first flight. That saves a round trip at the cost of weaker security. The weakness is that 0-RTT data is not forward secret, being encrypted only under keys derived from the PSK, and nothing guarantees it is not replayed between connections. There are two threats: a network attacker duplicating a flight of 0-RTT data, and one exploiting client retries. The second cannot be prevented in TLS, and any application whose clients retry already needs its own anti-replay defense. Clients cannot know what protection a server has, so they must send as early data only what is safe to replay, as with Idempotent methods: which requests are safe to retry. Servers should ensure early data is accepted at most once, for example with single-use tickets deleted from the server's ticket records on use.

  <!-- sysd-found-189 -->

- **HTTP conditional requests: act only if nothing has changed**

  Two clients edit the same resource, and the second save silently erases the first. That is the lost update problem, and conditional requests prevent it. A conditional request carries header fields that set a precondition to be tested before the method is applied to the target resource. Each precondition compares validators from earlier representations with the current validators. If-Match makes a method conditional on the current entity tag matching, mostly with POST, PUT and DELETE, and a failure gets 412. If-None-Match with * stops an unsafe method such as PUT from overwriting a representation when the client believes none exists. Conditional GET is the most efficient mechanism for HTTP cache updates. There, If-None-Match is the cheap check: if a listed tag matches, the server answers 304 (Not Modified) for GET and HEAD and 412 (Precondition Failed) for other methods. If-Modified-Since makes a GET or HEAD conditional on a newer modification date, and caches build it from the cached Last-Modified value. When several preconditions are present they are evaluated in order: If-Match, If-Unmodified-Since, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since, then If-Range.

  <!-- sysd-found-067 -->

- **HTTP range requests: asking for part of a file**

  An interrupted download does not have to start over. A range request asks for only part of a representation, such as the remainder of an interrupted download, by sending a Range header on a GET. A server fulfilling it sends 206 (Partial Content). A single part needs a Content-Range header, and several parts are sent as multipart/byteranges. A server answers 416 (Range Not Satisfiable) when no requested range is satisfiable. It also does so when the client asks for an excessive number of small or overlapping ranges, a potential denial of service attack.

  <!-- sysd-found-069 -->

- **Validators and entity tags: how HTTP spots a changed resource**

  A date is a blunt way to tell whether a resource changed. A validator is resource metadata that can be used in a precondition to make a conditional request, and HTTP defines modification dates and opaque entity tags. An ETag is an opaque quoted string that identifies one representation of a resource. An entity tag can be more reliable than a modification date when one-second resolution is not enough or dates are not consistently maintained. A strong validator changes whenever the observable representation data changes. A validator such as the ETag in a 201 response describes the new representation, so later conditional requests can prevent lost updates.

  <!-- sysd-found-068 -->

- **HTTP cache validation: asking the origin whether a copy is still good**

  A stale response is not necessarily a wrong one, and a cache can find out cheaply. Validation, or revalidation, is a cache using a conditional request to ask the next server whether a stored response is still valid instead of fetching it in full. A cache validates when it holds responses for a URI but cannot serve them, for example because they are stale. The forwarded request carries preconditions built from the stored response's validators: the Last-Modified timestamp, sent in If-Modified-Since, and the ETag entity tags, sent in If-None-Match. A cache must send stored entity tags and should send the Last-Modified value as well. If-None-Match takes precedence over If-Modified-Since.

  The answer decides what happens next. A 304 (Not Modified) answer means the stored response can be updated, using the headers in the 304, and reused, so no content is transferred. A full response means no stored response was suitable, so the cache uses it for the request and may store it. If validation returns a 5xx, the cache may forward it, or act as if the server did not respond and send a stored response where allowed, or retry. A cache can also send a HEAD request to update or invalidate stored GET responses when validators are missing. Each client in a request chain may have its own cache, so an intermediary cache often receives conditional requests from other caches.

  <!-- sysd-found-080 -->

  *Figure: A stale stored response is checked with a conditional request, and the answer decides what the cache does.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Stored response is stale] --> B[Cache sends a conditional request]
  B --> C{Origin answers}
  C -->|304| D[Update and reuse the stored response]
  C -->|Full response| E[Use it and may store it]
  C -->|5xx error| F[Forward it, send a stored response, or retry]
  ```

- **Cache-Control response directives: the origin's instructions**

  Origin servers give caches their orders in a handful of directives. Response directives are instructions from the origin server that tell caches whether and for how long a response may be stored and reused. The max-age directive says the response is stale once its age exceeds the given seconds. The s-maxage directive overrides max-age and Expires for shared caches and also requires them to revalidate once stale. The no-cache directive means the response must not be used for another request without forwarding it for successful validation. The no-store directive means a cache must not store any part of the request or response. It is not a reliable or sufficient privacy mechanism, since compromised caches may ignore it and networks may be eavesdropped.

  The private directive means a shared cache must not store the response because it is for a single user, though a private cache may. It controls where a response can be stored, not the privacy of its content. The public directive explicitly marks a response as cacheable, even for a request with credentials. The must-revalidate directive means that once stale a response must not be reused until the origin validates it. This holds even when the cache is disconnected, in which case a cache should return 504 (Gateway Timeout). Servers should use it only when failing to validate could cause incorrect operation, such as a silently unexecuted financial transaction. The proxy-revalidate directive is like it but applies only to shared caches, and no-transform forbids intermediaries from transforming the content.

  <!-- sysd-found-083 -->

  *Figure: Each response directive tells caches something different about storing and reusing the response.*

  | Directive | What it tells caches |
  |---|---|
  | max-age | Stale once its age exceeds the given seconds |
  | s-maxage | Overrides max-age and Expires for shared caches |
  | no-cache | Validate before reusing the response |
  | no-store | Do not store any part of it |
  | private | Shared caches must not store it |
  | public | Explicitly cacheable |
  | must-revalidate | Once stale, do not reuse until validated |

- **HTTP cache invalidation: forgetting what a write made stale**

  Invalidation is a cache removing or marking invalid its stored responses for a URI. Unsafe methods such as PUT, POST or DELETE can change state on the origin, so intervening caches must invalidate stored responses to stay current. A cache must invalidate the target URI when it receives a non-error response, with a 2xx or 3xx status, to an unsafe method. It may also invalidate other URIs, such as those in Location and Content-Location, but never when their origin differs from the target URI's. Invalidation is not global: a state-changing request invalidates responses only in the caches it travels through.

  <!-- sysd-found-081 -->

- **Storing and reusing HTTP cached responses: the two rule sets**

  A cache follows one set of rules for what it may store and another for what it may reuse. It must not store a response unless it understands the request method, the status code is final, and the response has no no-store directive. A stored response may be reused only if the target URIs match, the stored method allows it, and the request headers nominated by Vary match. It must also be fresh, allowed to be served stale, or successfully validated. A shared cache must not reuse a response to a request with credentials unless must-revalidate, public or s-maxage allows it.

  <!-- sysd-found-078 -->

## Building blocks

Every large system is assembled from smaller parts that each do one job well. This part gathers those building blocks, and it begins with the smallest: algorithms and data structures. A hash function maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, a hash collision happens when two distinct pieces of data share one, and a Bloom filter tests whether an element is in a set, allowing false positives but never false negatives. Trees such as the quadtree, k-d tree and trie, and curves such as the Z-order and Hilbert curves, organize space and strings so they can be searched. Later chapters build on them with load balancing, proxies, caching and storage.

### Algorithms behind the systems

Behind the big boxes in a system diagram sit small ideas from computer science. A hash function maps data of arbitrary size to fixed-size values, and a hash collision is what happens when two distinct pieces of data share one. Base64 lets binary data travel over channels that carry only text, and MD5 is a widely used hash function that produces a 128-bit value. The chapter then turns to space and strings: the quadtree, the k-d tree and the trie, curves such as the Z-order and the Hilbert curve, and geohash, which encodes latitude and longitude as a short string. Along the way it meets the Bloom filter, which tests set membership with false positives but never false negatives, and similarity hashing, which shows when data is similar but not identical.

- **Hash function: any input, one fixed-size value**

  Feed a hash function a short word or a very long document and it hands back a value of the same fixed size. People call that value a hash value, hash code, digest or simply a hash. Usually it indexes a table of data, a structure with its own entry, Hash table: jumping straight to the value. Retrieval then takes small, nearly constant time. A good function does three jobs. It folds variable-length keys into fixed-length values, scrambles the bits so values spread uniformly, and maps them into the size of the table. It must be fast and deterministic, so the same input always gives the same value. That rules out anything that depends on a random number generator or the time of day. Pathological keys, a poor design or a crowded table can still push access time toward linear. A hash function is also an essential ingredient of Bloom filter: a set that answers maybe or never.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-106 -->

- **Base64: carrying binary data as plain text**

  Some channels carry only text, and a photo is not text. Base64 is the workaround: a binary-to-text encoding that represents each 6-bit segment of the data with one of 64 printable characters. Four characters stand for every three input bytes, so the encoded data is 33% larger, plus about 3% more if line breaks are inserted. When the input is not a multiple of three bytes, the last group is padded with = characters, one after two leftover bytes and two after one. The alphabet is A-Z, a-z and 0-9 for the first 62 values. Many variants add + and / for the last two, and RFC 4648 describes the most common one. Base64 embeds images in HTML, CSS and XML. It also carries e-mail attachments, because SMTP was originally designed to transport only 7-bit ASCII. Not every system follows RFC 4648: Unix crypt does not, and neither does the scheme in bcrypt: a hash that can be made slower.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-117 -->

- **Hash collision: when two inputs share one value**

  Two different inputs can end up with the same hash value. That is a hash collision, and it is not a bug but a certainty. Hash functions are many-to-one, with far more possible inputs than output values. With more objects than hash values, the pigeonhole principle guarantees a collision. The birthday paradox makes collisions likely long before the output range is used up. A birthday attack exploits this: finding any two inputs that collide is easier than matching one specific value. Cryptographic hash functions are designed so that finding a collision is computationally infeasible. Simple checks such as CRC have essentially no such resistance, so they cannot protect input an attacker can manipulate. A table indexed by hash values copes with open addressing, which probes for another empty cell, or with separate chaining, which keeps a linked list in each cell. Whether collisions hurt depends on the job: checksums try to avoid them between similar inputs, while hashes built to find similar data want them.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-107 -->

- **Bloom filter: a set that answers maybe or never**

  A Bloom filter answers "have I seen this before?" with either "definitely not" or "probably yes". It is a space-efficient probabilistic data structure that tests whether an element is in a set, allowing false positives but never false negatives. It is a bit array of m bits, all 0 at first, plus k hash functions. Adding an element sets to 1 the k positions its hashes select. To test an element, check those positions. Any 0 means it is definitely absent. All 1s mean it is present, or that other elements set those bits by chance. The false positive rate climbs as items are added, until every bit is 1 and every query answers positive. The bargain is thrifty. With an optimal number of hash functions, a 1% false positive rate takes only about 9.6 bits per element, whatever its size, because the filter stores no items. Cassandra, HBase and PostgreSQL use Bloom filters to skip disk lookups for missing rows.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-001 -->

- **Quadtree: cutting space into four, again and again**

  Measuring the distance from one point to every other point does not scale. Finding how close points are with latitude, longitude and Euclidean distance is CPU-intensive on large data sets. A quadtree avoids that work. It is a tree in which each internal node has exactly four children. It partitions two-dimensional space by recursively subdividing it into four quadrants or regions, and each child or leaf stores spatial information. Searching for points within a two-dimensional range then becomes efficient. Subdividing a node only after a size threshold saves computation, and a mapping such as Hilbert curve: a space-filling curve that keeps neighbors near can improve range query performance further. Quadtrees are the two-dimensional analog of octrees, which partition three-dimensional space. They serve spatial indexing and range queries, location-based services such as Google Maps and Uber, image processing and compression, mesh generation and sparse data storage.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-006 -->

- **MD5: a famous hash that collisions broke**

  MD5 turns a message of any length into a 128-bit hash value, typically written as 32 hexadecimal digits. It pads the message and processes it in 512-bit blocks, and the avalanche effect means a small change gives a mostly different hash. Yet in 2004 MD5 was shown not to be collision-resistant. Collisions can now be found within seconds, and the CMU Software Engineering Institute calls it cryptographically broken. It is unsuitable for SSL certificates or digital signatures. An MD5 checksum can still reveal a corrupt or incomplete download, but it cannot protect against deliberate tampering.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-110 -->

- **K-d tree: splitting space one axis at a time**

  A k-d tree finds the stored point nearest to a query without checking every one. It is a space-partitioning data structure, a binary tree whose nodes are points, for organizing points in a k-dimensional space. Each non-leaf node implicitly defines a splitting hyperplane perpendicular to one of the k axes. Points on one side go to the left subtree and points on the other side to the right. In the canonical construction the splitting axis cycles as you go down and each node takes the median point on that axis, which yields a balanced tree. Nearest-neighbor search descends as if inserting the query point, saves the leaf's point as the current best, then unwinds, updating the best at each node. At each node it asks whether a hypersphere around the query crosses the splitting plane, with the current best distance as radius. If not, that whole branch is eliminated. In low dimensions this takes O(log n) on average. In high dimensions the curse of dimensionality makes the search no better than exhaustive search.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-116 -->

- **Trie: a tree that spells out its keys**
