  Type the first letters of a word and a list of completions appears. Tries are built for that kind of lookup. A trie, also called a prefix tree or digital tree, is a search tree for storing and retrieving strings from a dictionary or set. Its nodes do not store their keys. A node's position determines its key, edges stand for single characters, every child shares a common prefix with its parent, and the root represents the empty string. Searching follows the key's characters from the root, and a null link means the key does not exist. The search takes O(m) time, where m is the length of the key. A trie needs no hash function, has no collisions and sorts keys lexicographically. The cost is memory: each node has as many links as the alphabet has characters, 128 for ASCII, and most are null. A radix tree, or compressed trie, merges any node with only one child into its parent to save space. Tries suit autocomplete, spell checking and longest-prefix matching in IP routing, because lookups follow prefixes.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-113 -->

- **Z-order curve: flattening many dimensions into one**

  How do you put points from a map into one list so that neighbors stay neighbors? The Z-order, or Morton, curve is one answer. It maps multidimensional data to one dimension while preserving locality: points close together in several dimensions usually lie close together in the order. The z-value of a point comes from interleaving the bits of its binary coordinates. Connecting the values in numerical order draws a recursively Z-shaped curve. Once the data are sorted this way, any one-dimensional structure can hold them, and a balanced tree handles dynamic data with O(log n) insertion and deletion. The order equals a depth-first traversal of a quadtree, so the points in any quadtree square form a contiguous interval. A range query cannot simply use binary search. From the z-value reached, the search computes the next z-value inside the range and skips the stretch between. Z-order is one of the few multidimensional access methods in commercial data stores. A rival with better order-preserving behavior is Hilbert curve: a space-filling curve that keeps neighbors near, while Geohash: a place as a short string is based on Z-order.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-114 -->

- **Geohash: a place as a short string**

  In a geohash, the longer two places' codes agree at the start, the closer the places are. A geohash encodes latitude and longitude into a short alphanumeric string. It is a hierarchical spatial index in a Base-32 alphabet: its first character identifies one of 32 cells, and that cell in turn contains 32 cells. The world is recursively divided into smaller cells with each additional bit until the desired precision is reached. A longer string therefore means a smaller cell and a more precise location. The codes 9q8yy9mf and 9q8yy9vx are close because they share the prefix 9q8yy9. A geohash is a plain string, so a location is easy to store in a data store column. Nearest neighbors can then be found with simple string comparisons and efficient index searches. The scheme applies the Z-order curve, and removing characters from the end gradually reduces both the code size and the precision. Depending on its length, a geohash tells only that a user is somewhere within an area, which gives a degree of anonymity.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-005 -->

- **Hilbert curve: a space-filling curve that keeps neighbors near**

  In 1891 David Hilbert first described a continuous space-filling fractal curve that now carries his name. The Hilbert curve maps between one and two dimensions while preserving locality fairly well: points that are close in one dimension stay close after folding. That property is why the curve is widely used in computer science, including to index geospatial location data. Singh's Uber design applies mapping algorithms such as the Hilbert curve to run range queries that find nearby drivers. For multidimensional data the Hilbert order has also been proposed instead of Z order, because it preserves locality better.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-115 -->

- **Similarity hashing: when similar data should collide**

  A cryptographic hash is built so that even a tiny change gives a very different value. Similarity hashing, also called fuzzy hashing, does the opposite: it produces hashes that show when data is similar but not identical. A perceptual hash fingerprints multimedia and is a type of locality-sensitive hash, so similar features give similar hashes. It is used to find online copyright infringement and in digital forensics. Hashes meant to find similar data, such as homologous DNA sequences or similar audio files, are designed to maximize collisions between similar items. Fuzzy hashing has also been used to identify malware.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-109 -->

- **String hashing: folding text into a number**

  Strings have very uneven distributions, which makes them awkward to hash. String hashing folds the characters of a variable-length string into a fixed-size hash code. A common fold multiplies a running total by a sizable prime constant, adds the next character and ignores overflow. A modulo or mask then fits the result to the table. Information can cluster in the upper or lower bits of the bytes, because ASCII codes have a top bit of 0, for example. That clustering survives into the hash and causes more collisions. Hashing only the first and last characters saves iterating over the string, but such functions can readily become linear.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-108 -->

- **Distributed unique ID generation: many machines, no clashes**

  Many machines must hand out IDs at the same moment, and no two IDs may ever match. A distributed unique ID generator produces globally unique numerical IDs that are roughly sorted by time and generated at low latency by many machines. In social media, IDs should be roughly sorted by time, numerical only, and highly scalable with low latency. Each generator has its own pros and cons.

  A UUID has 128 bits and is simple to generate without calling another service. It is not sequential, though, and it is inefficient for indexing in a data store. ID conflicts, though unlikely, are possible. The Snowflake scheme builds an ID from a timestamp, a machine ID and a serial number, with the first bit unused so IDs stay positive. It needs no network call to an ID service, so it is fast and scalable. Implementations vary: a data center ID can be added to the machine ID component to guarantee global uniqueness.

  A data store's auto-increment column uses its transaction management to handle concurrent requests and guarantees uniqueness within one table. It needs network communication, and as user IDs it may expose sensitive business data, giving competitors a rough idea of the total number of registered users. In the segment approach, ID servers fetch IDs from the data store in batches and cache them, each server handling a segment of IDs. That greatly saves I/O pressure. The store described in Redis: a cache that is also a data store can also generate unique IDs from a key-value pair, and because it keeps data in memory this performs better than the data store approach.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-008 -->

- **Universally unique identifier: 128 bits, no registry**

  A UUID is a 128-bit number that identifies information in computer systems and needs no central authority to be generated. It is usually written as 32 hexadecimal digits in the 8-4-4-4-12 hyphenated format. In software typically created by Microsoft it is called a GUID. Because no registration or coordination between generators is needed, independent parties can label information that ends up in the same data stores, with negligible probability of duplication. The probability is not zero, but it is close enough. For properly generated version-4 UUIDs, a duplicate within 103 trillion of them has a one-in-a-billion chance.

  One catch is locality. Used as a data store's key for each row, random versions 3, 4 and 5 can hurt performance. So can the field ordering of versions 1 and 2. Reordering time-based UUIDs so the timestamp comes first averts the loss, which is the rationale for versions 6 and 7.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-013 -->

- **Snowflake ID: a timestamp, a machine and a counter in one number**

  41 bits of time, 10 bits of machine, 12 bits of counter: that is the whole recipe for a Snowflake ID. It packs a timestamp, a machine ID and a sequence number into one number, a form of unique identifier used in distributed computing. Twitter created the format and uses it for tweet IDs, and Discord and Instagram have since adopted it. The timestamp counts milliseconds since a chosen epoch, the machine ID prevents clashes, and the per-machine sequence number lets several IDs be made in one millisecond. Only 63 bits vary, so the value fits in a 64-bit signed integer; the first bit is unused to keep IDs positive.

  Snowflakes sort by creation time, and that time can be calculated from the ID. Objects created before or after a given date can therefore be selected by ID. A generator needs no network call to an ID service, so Snowflake IDs are fast and scalable. Implementations vary: Instagram, for example, uses 41 timestamp bits, 13 shard ID bits and 10 sequence bits.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-012 -->

  *Figure: The three varying fields of a Snowflake ID add up to 63 bits.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **UUID versions: time, name, random and custom layouts**

  A UUID's bits can be filled in several ways. The choice decides whether the IDs sort by time, repeat from a name, or reveal when a system started. The versions fall into five families: time and node based, name hash based, random, time-ordered with random bits, and custom.

  Version 1 is time-based. It holds a 60-bit timestamp counting 100-nanosecond intervals since 15 October 1582 UTC, a 48-bit node ID, usually a MAC address, and a clock sequence. The clock sequence avoids duplicates when the clock moves backwards. Versions 3 and 5 are name-based: they hash a namespace identifier, itself a UUID, with a name, using MD5 for version 3 and SHA-1 for version 5. Systems can then derive the same UUID from a name without a registry. Version 4 is made from random or pseudorandom numbers. Six bits are fixed for variant and version, leaving 122 random bits, which gives 5.3×10^36 possible version-4, variant-1 UUIDs.

  Version 6 is field-compatible with version 1 but stores the timestamp from most to least significant byte for better locality in a data store. Systems without legacy version-1 UUIDs should use version 7 instead. Version 7 puts a 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp in the most significant bits and fills the other 74 non-version, non-variant bits with random bits. Its UUIDs are monotonically ascending and lexically sortable, so new records land at the end of the key sequence. Random version 4 keys scatter across it and hurt performance. Version 8 is for experimental or vendor-specific use, and its uniqueness must not be assumed. Versions 1, 2, 6 and 7 expose the time of generation, so UUIDs can reveal when a system went live. The RFC calls the embedded timestamp a very small attack surface.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-014 -->

  *Figure: Each version fills a UUID's bits in a different way.*

  | Version | How its bits are filled | Notable point |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 | 60-bit timestamp, 48-bit node ID, clock sequence | Exposes the time of generation |
  | 3 and 5 | Hash of a namespace and a name: MD5, SHA-1 | Same name, same UUID |
  | 4 | 122 random bits | Keys scatter across the key sequence |
  | 6 | Version 1 fields, timestamp first | Better locality in a data store |
  | 7 | 48-bit Unix millisecond timestamp, then random bits | Sortable; new records land at the end |
  | 8 | Custom: only version and variant fixed | Uniqueness must not be assumed |

- **UUID best practices: storing, sorting and trusting them**

  RFC 9562 does more than define UUIDs. It advises how to generate, store, sort and protect them. Where feasible, store a UUID as its 128-bit binary value: text needs 288 bits for the same value, while binary takes less space and may be faster. Time-ordered monotonic UUIDs sort as raw bytes and give index locality because new values sit near each other. The gap from random inserts can be one order of magnitude or more. Avoid name-based UUIDs as keys, because the name input, such as a postal code or license number, can later change. Random bits should come from a cryptographically secure pseudorandom number generator. Do not assume UUIDs are hard to guess, and do not use them as security capabilities, identifiers whose mere possession grants access. Weigh the consequences of a collision: a duplicate log entry is low impact, but where failure is unacceptable, use as much collision resistance as the context allows. Treat UUIDs as opaque and avoid parsing them.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-118 -->

- **Count-min sketch: counting events in a tiny table**

  How do you count how often each event occurs in a stream when you cannot keep a counter for every kind? A count-min sketch is a probabilistic data structure that serves as a frequency table of events in a stream of data. It uses hash functions to map events to frequencies but, unlike an ordinary hash-keyed table, takes only sub-linear space. The price is that collisions make it overcount some events. The sketch is a two-dimensional array of w columns and d rows, with a hash function for each row. To record an event, each row hashes it to a column and increments that cell. A point query returns the least value among the event's cells. It never underestimates the true count, and with probability 1 − δ it overshoots by at most εN, where N is the total number of items seen. Because the sketch is linear, summing the sketches of two streams gives the same result as sketching the concatenated streams, so it is mergeable and suits distributed settings.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-111 -->

- **Merkle tree: checking big data with one root hash**

  Download a big file from strangers and you want to know two things: is it intact, and if not, which piece is bad? A Merkle tree, or hash tree, answers both. Each leaf is labelled with the cryptographic hash of a data block, and each inner node with the hash of its children's labels. The root hash comes from a trusted source, while the tree itself can come from any untrusted peer. A tree that does not match the root hash is damaged or fake, so another source is tried. One branch can be checked at a time, even before the whole tree has arrived. A file split into small blocks then needs only the damaged blocks downloaded again. Proving that a leaf belongs to a binary hash tree takes hashes proportional to the logarithm of the leaf count. A hash list needs the leaf count itself. Hash trees are used in ZFS, Git, Bitcoin and Ethereum, and in systems such as Cassandra, Riak and Dynamo.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-112 -->

- **HyperLogLog: counting distinct items in tiny memory**

  Counting exactly how many distinct items a data set holds takes memory proportional to that number, which is impractical for very large sets. HyperLogLog solves this count-distinct problem with a single pass over the data and very little memory. It estimates cardinalities well beyond 10^9 with a typical accuracy of 2% using only 1.5 kilobytes. The idea is to hash each element into a uniformly distributed random number and note the maximum number of leading zeros in their binary forms. One estimate alone has a large variance. So the hashed values are split into many subsets, the maximum is found in each, and a harmonic mean combines the results. In practice the state is an array of m registers, and the first b bits of an element's hash pick the register to update. Merging two sets takes the maximum of each pair of registers, so the algorithm parallelizes optimally. It is biased for small cardinalities, which HyperLogLog++ fixes with an empirical bias correction and a sparse register representation.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-010 -->

- **Cache filtering with a Bloom filter: skipping one-hit wonders**

  Nearly three-quarters of the URLs accessed from a typical web cache are one-hit-wonders, requested once and never again, so storing them wastes disk resources. The fix is to cache an object only when it is requested a second time. A Bloom filter keeps track of every URL users access, so a web object is stored only if it has been accessed before. Most one-hit-wonders are then never written to disk. The disk write workload drops, cache space is saved and hit rates rise. Akamai's servers use this to keep one-hit-wonders out of their disk caches.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-004 -->

- **Counting Bloom filter: a Bloom filter that can delete**

  A plain Bloom filter cannot forget; a counting Bloom filter can. It swaps each single bit of the array for a multibit counter, so a regular Bloom filter is just a counting filter with one-bit buckets. Insert increments the counters its hashes select, lookup checks that each is non-zero, and delete decrements each one. The price is space. Counters are usually 3 or 4 bits, so the filter takes 3 to 4 times more room than a static one. They must also be large enough that overflow stays rare. The table cannot be expanded, so the maximum number of keys must be known in advance.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-002 -->

- **Bloom filter alternatives: cuckoo, quotient and xor filters**

  A classic Bloom filter uses 1.44log2(1/ε) bits per inserted key. Any structure in the same role needs only log2(1/ε), so a Bloom filter uses 44% more space than an optimal one. Cuckoo, quotient and xor filters store short fingerprints of keys instead. A cuckoo filter keeps them in a table built by cuckoo hashing, and like a quotient filter it supports deletions and has better locality. An xor filter is more memory efficient, at 1.23log2(1/ε) bits per key, and faster than both. But it is harder to create, and its set cannot be modified afterwards.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-003 -->

- **Quadtree types: regions, points, lines and curves**

  Quadtrees are classified by the kind of data they hold, such as areas, points, lines and curves. They are also classified by whether the tree's shape depends on the order data is added. A region quadtree splits a region into four equal quadrants and so on. A point quadtree adapts a binary tree to two-dimensional points, with every subdivision centered on a point. It usually runs in O(log n) time, though k-d trees have surpassed it. A point-region quadtree stores a list of points in each leaf cell. Like the point quadtree, it can grow to linear height on a bad set of points.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-011 -->

- **Limits of geohash proximity search: where neighbors look far apart**

  Geohashes that share a long prefix are close together, but the reverse is not guaranteed: two nearby points can have a short or no shared prefix. Close points on opposite sides of the 180 degree meridian, near the poles, or either side of the Equator or Greenwich meridian get very different geohashes. They lie in different halves of the world. A bounding-box search between the southwest and northeast corner geohashes retrieves every point along the Z-order curve between them, which can be far too many. Even so, geohashing has been used for proximity search in MongoDB, HBase and Accumulo.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-009 -->

- **Nearby search with a quadtree: walking down to the origin**

  A location service finds nearby businesses by walking down a tree. The quadtree is an in-memory data structure, not a data store, built on each server when it starts. The root is the whole world map, divided into 4 quadrants until no node has more than 100 businesses. To search, walk from the root to the leaf holding the origin. If it has 100 businesses, return it; otherwise add businesses from its neighbors. Building a quadtree for 200 million businesses may take a few minutes, during which the server cannot serve traffic. New releases roll out to a few servers at a time to avoid a brownout.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-007 -->

  *Figure: The quadtree is built by repeated splitting, then searched from the root down to the origin's leaf.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Root: whole world map] -->|split into 4| B[Four quadrants]
  B -->|split again| C[Leaves hold 100 or fewer]
  C --> D[Walk from root to origin's leaf]
  D --> E{Leaf has 100?}
  E -->|yes| F[Return it]
  E -->|no| G[Add neighbors' businesses]
  ```

### Load balancing

Once one server cannot carry the traffic, you add more servers, and then something has to decide who gets each request. Load balancing distributes incoming network traffic across several computing resources, sending requests only to those that are online. This chapter looks at where that decision can be made, in the DNS, in the client or in a dedicated balancer, and at the rules for making it, from taking turns to picking the least busy server. It also covers keeping a user's session together, whether a balancer reads addresses or whole requests, and what happens when a server, or the balancer itself, fails.

- **Load balancing: spreading requests across many servers**

  A busy website must serve hundreds of thousands, if not millions, of concurrent requests. The cost-effective way to meet that volume is to add more servers. Then something has to decide which server gets which request. That something is a load balancer. Load balancing distributes a set of tasks or incoming network traffic across several computing resources. It sends requests only to those that are online, so the overall work is processed more efficiently.

  A load balancer sits in front of the servers and routes each request to one that can fulfil it. It does so in a way that maximizes speed and capacity use, so no single server is overworked. It can improve response time and keeps some nodes from being overloaded while others sit idle. If a server goes down, the balancer redirects traffic to the remaining online servers. When a new server joins the group, requests start flowing to it automatically. That is what makes horizontal scaling work: add servers to the pool and the balancer spreads traffic across all of them.

  Load balancing is also widely used for HTTP requests on high-traffic sites, most commonly to provide one Internet service from many servers. Such a group is sometimes known as a server farm. A balancer's main jobs are traffic distribution, availability, SSL termination, keeping a user's session on one server, scaling and keeping track of server health. Which algorithm fits depends on the nature of the tasks, their complexity, the hardware and the error tolerance required, so a compromise must be found for each application.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-112 -->

  *Figure: The balancer sits in front of the pool and routes each request to one server.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[Clients] --> B[Load balancer]
  subgraph Server pool
  C[Server]
  D[Server]
  E[Server]
  end
  B --> C
  B --> D
  B --> E
  ```

- **DNS load balancing: spreading traffic by name lookup**

  The simplest load balancer needs no extra machine at all. DNS load balancing configures a domain in the Domain Name System so that client requests to it are spread across a group of servers. Round-robin DNS associates several IP addresses with one domain name and hands them to clients in rotation, with no dedicated software or hardware node.

  The limits are real. DNS does not check for server and network outages, so it keeps returning the same IP addresses even when servers are down or unreachable. Returning several records and letting the client choose gives little control, because records are picked randomly and each attracts roughly equal traffic.

  DNS delegation does better. A sub-domain such as www is delegated to a zone served by the website's own servers. Each answers with its own address, so a down server simply does not respond. The quickest answer nearly always comes from the closest server, which gives geo-sensitive balancing. A short TTL on the A-record diverts traffic quickly when a server fails.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-118 -->

- **Load balancing algorithms: rules for picking a server**

  How does a balancer choose? The rules it follows are called scheduling algorithms or load-balancing methods, and they decide which back-end server receives each request. The simple ones are random choice, round robin and least connections. Round robin, sticky round robin, weighted round robin and hash are static algorithms. Least connections and least response time are dynamic ones.

  Least connections sends a new request to the server with the fewest current connections to clients, factoring in each server's relative computing capacity, and it can be weighted. Least response time uses a formula that combines the fastest response time and fewest active connections. Least bandwidth picks the server carrying the least traffic in Mbps. Hashing applies a hash function to a key the operator defines, such as the client IP address or the request URL, and routes by the result. Random assignment works quite well, and a random permutation computed in advance avoids per-assignment communication and the need for a distribution master. Power of two choices picks two servers at random and chooses the better of the two.

  More sophisticated balancers may also weigh a server's reported load, response times, up or down status from regular checks, active connections, geographic location, capabilities or recently assigned traffic. One source lists least connections among the static methods, so the labels are not universal.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-114 -->

  *Figure: The facts sort these algorithms into static and dynamic, though one source lists least connections as static.* (tree; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Session persistence: keeping a user on one server**

  The next request from a user may land on a server that knows nothing about the last one. Information kept across a session, if stored on one backend server, cannot be found when later requests go to other backends. Session persistence, also called stickiness, is the fix. It sends all requests in one user session to the same backend server so that session data kept there can be found.

  Assignment can be based on username, client IP address or random choice. IP-based assignment may be unreliable because of DHCP, network address translation and web proxies. Random assignments must be remembered by the balancer, which costs storage and may be lost if it fails. The client must also keep state, which fails if a browser has disabled cookies.

  The significant downside is no automatic recovery. If the backend goes down, its per-session information becomes inaccessible and the sessions that depend on it are lost. Sophisticated balancers use several persistence techniques to avoid the shortcomings of any one.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-120 -->

- **Static and dynamic load balancing: ignoring load or watching it**

  A balancer can follow a plan made in advance, or it can watch what is happening and adapt. A load-balancing algorithm is static when it ignores the current state of the system and dynamic when it takes each node's current load into account.

  A static algorithm ignores system state such as processor load. It relies on assumptions made beforehand about arrival times, resource needs and processor speeds. Static algorithms are easy to set up and efficient for fairly regular tasks such as processing HTTP requests from a website. But statistical variance in assignment can still overload some computing units.

  Dynamic algorithms use the current load of each node and can move tasks from an overloaded node to an underloaded one for faster processing. They are much more complicated to design, but can improve performance, particularly when execution time varies greatly from one task to another. They need nodes to exchange information, and one that needs too much communication to reach its decisions risks slowing down the overall solution. A dynamic architecture can be more modular, because no specific node has to be dedicated to distributing the work.

  Either way, the more is known about the tasks when deciding, the better the optimization. Knowing the exact execution time of every task is an idealized and extremely rare situation.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-113 -->

- **Client-side load balancing: let the client pick**

  Sometimes the balancer is the client itself. In client-side random load balancing, the client receives a list of server IPs and picks one at random for each connection. The list is delivered as a DNS list without round-robin, or hardcoded. It relies on all clients generating similar loads and on the law of large numbers to give a reasonably flat distribution across servers. It has been claimed to distribute load better than round-robin DNS, because large DNS servers that remember answers skew round-robin DNS, while random client selection is unaffected. A smart client that detects a down server and connects randomly again can also ride out failures.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-119 -->

- **Master-worker load balancing: workers ask for tasks**

  One of the simplest dynamic load balancing algorithms is the master-worker scheme: a master hands out tasks to workers that ask for them. All workers start idle and report to the master, which answers with tasks and tells them to stop asking when none remain. When assignment overhead is low, the work is distributed evenly. But the scheme scales badly to many processors, because of the high amount of communication, and the master is a bottleneck. A task list shared by the processors improves it, though that is slightly harder to implement and still insufficient for very large computing centers.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-127 -->

- **Round robin load balancing: taking turns**

  Round robin is load balancing as taking turns. The first request goes to the first server, the next to the second, and so on down to the last, and then the cycle restarts. The services are usually required to be stateless. Weighted round robin lets the administrator give each server a weight, so more powerful servers handle more requests. Sticky round robin improves on it: if a user's first request goes to service A, the following requests go to A as well. When request sizes are homogeneous or unknown, lower-powered units may simply receive fewer requests than larger ones.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-115 -->

- **Session state storage: where a session can live instead**

  If session data does not live on one server, the balancer is free to pick any backend. Session state can be kept in a data store, in the client's browser, or in a table spread over many servers. A data store adds load to a system best used for less transient data. In a web browser, the data can live in a time-stamped, encrypted cookie or in rewritten URLs. Client-side storage is generally preferred, though it may not suit large session state, and URL rewriting has major security issues. Spreading named blocks of data over servers by hash is the idea behind Distributed hash tables: a lookup service with no center.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-121 -->

- **Work stealing: idle processors take work from busy ones**

  Work stealing flips the usual question: instead of a balancer pushing tasks out, idle processors pull work in. Each processor is given some tasks, and then idle processors take work from busy or overloaded ones. This overcomes scaling problems when task completion time is unknown. An idle processor asks others at random. If the target can subdivide its task it sends part of it, otherwise it returns an empty task. The method can be particularly effective but is difficult to implement, since communication must not become the processors' main occupation.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-128 -->

- **Layer 4 and layer 7 load balancing: addresses or content**

  A load balancer can look at a request from two very different heights. A layer 4 load balancer routes on transport-level information such as IP addresses and ports. A layer 7 load balancer reads whole requests and routes on their content.

  A layer 4 balancer works at the transport layer. It routes on network information such as IP addresses and TCP and UDP ports, so it cannot perform content-based routing. These balancers are often dedicated hardware devices that can operate at high speed.

  A layer 7 balancer works at the application layer, reads requests in their entirety and performs content-based routing. Load can then be managed from a full understanding of the traffic. It comes in variations. Host-based routing uses the requested hostname, path-based routing uses the entire URL, and content-based routing inspects the message, for example the value of a parameter. Routing by URL needs plain HTTP, or HTTPS that is terminated (decrypted) at the balancer. Platform-specific routing can send requests from different device types, such as mobiles and desktops, to specialized backend systems.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-116 -->

  *Figure: The two kinds differ in what they can see and so in how they route.*

  |  | Layer 4 | Layer 7 |
  |---|---|---|
  | Works at | Transport layer | Application layer |
  | Routes on | IP addresses and TCP and UDP ports | Whole requests: hostname, URL or content |
  | Content-based routing | Cannot | Can |
  | Notes | Often dedicated, fast hardware | Routing by URL needs plain or terminated HTTPS |

- **Hardware, software and cloud load balancers**

  A load balancer can be a box in a rack, a program on an ordinary machine or a managed service in the cloud. A hardware balancer is physical on-premises equipment that handles a large volume of traffic. It often costs a lot, is fairly inflexible and runs proprietary firmware that needs patches. Software balancers are usually easier to deploy, cost-effective and flexible, at the cost of more set-up work. Cloud balancers such as AWS Elastic Load Balancer are built into the provider's infrastructure.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-117 -->

- **Global server load balancing: balancing across the world**

  When a service's users are spread across the world, its balancing can be spread too. Global server load balancing distributes traffic across multiple geographical locations to improve performance at a global scale. Cross-zone load balancing distributes incoming traffic across geographic or network zones, which increases the system's resilience and its capacity for large volumes of requests. DNS-based delegation gives geo-sensitive balancing, since the quickest DNS response is nearly always from the network's closest server. For content delivery, server-load balancing uses service-based (global load balancing) or hardware-based techniques, such as layer 4-7 switches, to share traffic among several servers or web caches.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-126 -->

- **Health checks: noticing which servers are down**

  A balancer is only as useful as its picture of which servers are alive. A health check lets the load balancer tell whether a server is down or performing poorly so it can remove that server from the pool. The balancer polls servers for application-layer health and removes failed servers. It monitors components continually, for example web servers by fetching known pages. When one becomes unresponsive, the balancer stops sending it traffic, and it resumes when the server is back online. This continuous evaluation directs requests only to instances that are fully operational, which maintains performance and keeps service uninterrupted.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-122 -->

- **Load balancer failover: staying up when a server fails**

  When a server dies, the balancer is the one that notices. Load balancing is often used to keep service going after the failure of one or more components. The balancer is informed when a component fails, stops sending it traffic, and reroutes traffic to it when it returns. For this to work there must be at least one component in excess of the service's capacity, an arrangement called N+1. That is much cheaper and more flexible than pairing every live component with a standby that takes over on failure.

  The catch is that the balancer itself can become the one part whose failure stops everything. To avoid that, a second or N load balancers can run in cluster mode, and if the active one fails, a passive one takes over. Balancers are usually implemented in high-availability pairs, which may also replicate session persistence data if the application needs it. Some balancers do something special when all backend servers are unavailable, such as forwarding to a spare balancer or displaying a message about the outage.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-123 -->

- **TLS termination: decrypting at the balancer**

  TLS encryption can become a major part of a web server's CPU demand. A load balancer can terminate TLS connections itself: it decrypts the traffic and passes plain HTTP requests to the backend servers. It can then also balance or switch content based on data inside the HTTPS request. The downside is that all TLS processing is concentrated on one device, which can become a new bottleneck. Adding a few web servers may be cheaper than upgrading it. The balancer also needs the TLS certificate and private key, which widens access to unencrypted data and makes it a more valuable attack target.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-124 -->

- **Load balancer features: beyond handing out requests**

  Distributing requests is only the beginning of what balancers do. The fundamental feature is spreading incoming requests over the backend servers in the cluster according to a scheduling algorithm. Most other features are vendor specific.

  Some features manage load. Asymmetric load assigns a manual ratio so some backends get a bigger share, a simple way to reflect capacity differences. Priority activation brings standby servers online when too few servers remain or load is too high. Connection multiplexing consolidates multiple HTTP requests from multiple clients into a single TCP socket to the backends. TCP buffering spoon-feeds responses to slow clients so web server threads are freed sooner. HTTP compression cuts transferred data and helps more for larger responses and distant clients. It adds CPU demand on the balancer, though, and could be done by the web servers instead. An application-layer balancer may also cache static content to answer some requests without contacting the servers.

  Others protect and observe. Balancers can mitigate SYN flood attacks with SYN cookies and delayed binding, where backends do not see the client until it completes its TCP handshake. HTTP security features include hiding error pages, removing server identification headers and encrypting cookies so end users cannot manipulate them. Logging request and response metadata gives an audit trail or analytics data, and request tracing gives each request a unique id for logging and troubleshooting.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-125 -->

### Proxies and API gateways

A proxy server is an intermediary between a client requesting a resource and the server providing it. It can face two ways: a forward proxy sits in front of a group of client machines and speaks to the Internet for them, while a reverse proxy appears to clients to be an ordinary web server but merely forwards their requests on. Add a single entry point that enforces security and throttling policies before passing requests to backend services, and you have an API gateway. This chapter also meets caching and transparent proxies, the Backend For Frontend pattern, and two widely used tools, HAProxy and nginx.

- **Proxy server: the intermediary in the middle**

  Sometimes the best way to reach a server is not to talk to it directly. A proxy server is an intermediary between a client requesting a resource and the server providing it. The client directs the request to the proxy, which evaluates it and performs the required network transactions. That indirection controls complexity or adds benefits such as load balancing, privacy or security. A proxy may sit on the user's own computer or at any point between the user's computer and the destination servers.

  Proxies typically filter requests, log them, or transform them by adding or removing headers, encrypting or decrypting, or compressing. Proxies may add headers such as X-Forwarded-For, or the standardised Forwarded field, to pass on client information. These should not be trusted blindly, because they may be absent, modified or added by several proxies. A proxy works at layer 7 of the OSI model. Network address translation is similar but works at layer 3, so it is less resource-intensive and less flexible.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-129 -->

- **Forward proxy: a middleman for clients**

  A forward proxy is a middleman for clients: no origin server ever communicates directly with them. It is a server that sits in front of a group of client machines and communicates with Internet servers on their behalf. When the clients request sites and services on the Internet, the proxy intercepts the requests and talks to the web servers for them. It can regulate traffic by preset policies, convert and mask client IP addresses, enforce security protocols and block unknown traffic, which strengthens policy enforcement inside an internal network.

  Common uses are blocking access to certain content, reaching geo-restricted content, providing anonymity and avoiding other browsing restrictions. An anonymous proxy reveals that it is a proxy but does not disclose the client's originating IP address. Web filtering proxies cannot see inside HTTPS unless managed clients are configured to trust a root certificate whose private key the proxy knows. Proxies bring anonymity but can still track personal information, and setting one up and maintaining it can be costly.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-130 -->

- **Reverse proxy: a front door for servers**

  A reverse proxy, also called a surrogate server, appears to clients to be an ordinary web server. It merely forwards their requests to one or more ordinary web servers. It returns the original server's response as if it came from the proxy itself, so the client never learns of the original server. The web servers can be hidden behind a firewall on the internal network, with only the reverse proxy exposed to the Internet. A forward proxy serves clients; a reverse proxy protects the servers.

  By inspecting HTTP headers it can present a single IP address to the Internet while relaying requests to different internal servers by URL. It can balance load and often terminates TLS connections from clients, which centralizes certificate management, access control, logging and routing and reduces TLS work on backend servers. It can also cache static and dynamic content, greatly reducing the load on origin servers. Application firewall features can protect against denial-of-service attacks, but the proxy gives no protection against attacks on the web application itself.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-137 -->

  *Figure: Clients reach only the reverse proxy; the web servers stay hidden on the internal network.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[Clients] --> B[Reverse proxy]
  subgraph Internal network
  C[Web server]
  D[Web server]
  end
  B --> C
  B --> D
  ```

- **HAProxy: an open source balancer and proxy**

  On 64-core ARM servers, HAProxy has reached 2 million requests per second and 100 Gbit/s. It is free, open source software that provides a high-availability load balancer and proxy for TCP and HTTP-based applications, spreading requests across multiple servers. It balances at layer 4 (TCP) and layer 7 (HTTP). It also offers SSL/TLS termination, URL rewriting, simplified circuit breaking, HTTP/2 on both sides and hitless reloads. Written in C with an event-driven multithreaded architecture, it has a reputation for speed and efficiency. Servers with 6 to 8 cores generally reach 200,000 to 500,000 requests per second.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-191 -->

- **API gateway: one entry point to many services**

  Backend services built as small units typically expose fine-grained APIs, nothing like what a client needs, so clients would have to talk to several of them. An API gateway removes that burden. It is a tool for managing APIs. It sits between clients and a set of backend services as their single entry point, enforcing security and throttling policies before passing requests on.

  Its core functions are routing requests to the appropriate backend service, load balancing, and API composition, which combines several backend API requests into one frontend request. It also handles security and traffic control: identity checks, data encryption, request-rate limits and throttling, and IP whitelisting or blacklisting. Resilience and visibility features include retries, circuit breaking, stored copies of frequent responses, logging, tracing and analytics. Its advantages are a hidden internal structure, a centralized view of the API and simpler client code. The disadvantages are one component whose failure could block all traffic, a possible performance impact, a bottleneck if not scaled properly, and challenging configuration.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-133 -->

- **Caching proxy: answering from saved copies**

  The caching proxy was the first kind of proxy server, and web proxies are commonly used to keep copies of web pages from a web server. A caching proxy speeds up requests by returning content saved from an earlier request by the same or another client. Keeping local copies of frequently requested resources lets large organizations significantly cut upstream bandwidth use and costs while significantly increasing performance. Poorly implemented ones can cause problems, such as an inability to identify users. A Performance Enhancing Proxy goes after link problems instead, for example improving TCP performance under high round-trip times or packet loss.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-132 -->

- **Nginx: a web server that also proxies and balances**

  A single nginx server can hold more than 10,000 simultaneous connections, using about 2.5 MB per 10k inactive keep-alive connections. It does so by handling requests asynchronously, driven by events rather than threads, which gives predictable performance under high load. The nginx web server can also act as a reverse proxy, load balancer, mail proxy and HTTP cache. It can serve static content, act as a proxy server and serve dynamic content through FastCGI, SCGI, WSGI servers or Phusion Passenger. As a software load balancer, it offers in-band health checks.

  It supports HTTP/2, including as an upstream protocol, and experimental HTTP/3. It was written to be faster than Apache, which has offered similar performance since version 2.4. Its speed came at the cost of flexibility, such as no per-file access overrides like Apache's .htaccess. It can upgrade its executable and configuration without losing client connections, and the paid NGINX Plus adds advanced load balancing.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-190 -->

- **Transparent proxy: a proxy clients do not choose**

  A transparent proxy is one the client never chose, and may never notice. Also called an intercepting proxy, it redirects or filters client traffic without being explicitly selected by the client. It is often deployed without browser or application proxy settings and commonly redirects outgoing TCP port 80 traffic. Businesses use intercepting proxies to enforce acceptable use policies without configuring client browsers. ISPs in some countries use them to save upstream bandwidth by keeping copies of content. Interception raises problems: the original destination IP and port must reach the proxy, HTTP logins such as NTLM break, and some responses become uncacheable by a shared cache.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-131 -->

- **Reverse proxy trade-offs: a single door is a single risk**

  A reverse proxy is a single door to the servers behind it, which makes it a risk as well as a shield. Misconfiguration, a denial-of-service attack or a software fault can make every frontend service unreachable, and adding spare proxies increases complexity further. To filter, cache or compress encrypted traffic, the proxy must decrypt and re-encrypt it. That needs the TLS certificate and private key, extends the number of systems with access to unencrypted data and makes the proxy a more valuable attack target. Giving a third party's reverse proxy access to private keys places confidentiality, integrity and availability in that party's hands.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-138 -->

- **API gateway request flow: stage by stage**

  A request to an API gateway has several hurdles to clear before any service sees it. The gateway parses and validates the request's attributes and runs allow-list and deny-list checks. It then consults an outside service that knows who the caller is, the idea behind Identity provider. Next it applies rate-limit rules and rejects the request if it is over the limit. Once the basic checks pass, the gateway finds the relevant service by path matching, transforms the request into the appropriate protocol and sends it to the backend services. It can handle errors, and use circuit breaking for faults that take longer to recover.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-134 -->

  *Figure: A request passes each check in turn and is rejected if it is over the limit.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Client request] --> B[Validate request and check lists]
  B --> C[Identity check]
  C --> D{Over rate limit?}
  D -->|yes| E[Reject request]
  D -->|no| F[Match path to a service]
  F --> G[Transform and send to backend]
  ```

- **Reverse proxy vs API gateway vs load balancer**

  Reverse proxies, API gateways and load balancers all sit in front of servers. Each suits a different job, and a system can use all three together. A reverse proxy keeps servers hidden from clients and shields sensitive websites from cyber-attacks. An API gateway delivers requests to the right services and suits busy applications with many intercommunicating services. A load balancer directs traffic evenly across servers to prevent bottlenecks, and it helps when several servers do the same job. A reverse proxy helps even with one server and can also balance load, but not the other way around.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-136 -->

  *Figure: Each component suits a different job, and a system can use all three.*

  | Component | Main job | Useful when |
  |---|---|---|
  | Reverse proxy | Hides servers and shields them from attacks | Even with a single server |
  | API gateway | Delivers requests to the right services | Many services talk to each other |
  | Load balancer | Spreads traffic evenly across servers | Several servers do the same job |

- **Backend for frontend pattern: one backend per interface**

  Each frontend gets its own backend. The Backend For Frontend pattern creates a separate backend service for each specific frontend application or interface, which avoids customizing a single backend for multiple interfaces. Backend service output is often not in the exact format or filtering a front end needs. The pattern moves that reformatting logic from the frontend into an intermediate layer. Its primary function is to get the required data from the appropriate service, format it and send it to the frontend. Consider it when a shared general-purpose backend carries significant development overhead or should be optimized for one client.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-135 -->

- **API management: publishing, controlling and measuring an API**

  Publishing an API is only the start of running one. API management is the process of publishing APIs on the web, enforcing their usage policies, controlling access, supporting their users, and collecting and analyzing usage statistics and performance. Typical products combine a gateway, publishing tools, a developer portal or API store, reporting and analytics, and monetization. Publishing tools define, document, test and deploy APIs under access and usage policies. The developer portal gathers documentation, sample code, a sandbox and subscription-key management. Reporting analyzes usage and load, which helps optimize the API and set the service levels it promises.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-189 -->

### Caching

The fastest way to answer a request is to have answered it already, and that single trick runs through nearly every fast system. A cache is a hardware or software component that stores data so that future requests for it can be served faster. This chapter starts inside the processor and the operating system, then moves out to the caches between a web service and its data. It asks how often an item is found, what to discard when the cache is full and when a write reaches the data behind it.

- **Caching: answering from a copy instead of the source**

  The fastest way to answer a request is to have answered it already. A cache is a hardware or software component that stores data so that future requests for it can be served faster. The stored data is either a copy of data kept elsewhere or the result of an earlier computation. A cache attacks latency, the wait for an answer, which is the subject of Latency: why every system has some delay.

  Think of a cache as a pool of entries. Each entry holds a copy of data from a backing store, the slower place where the data really lives, plus a tag that says which data it copies. A client checks the cache first and uses the entry whose tag matches. A match is a cache hit. No match is a cache miss, and then the client must make a more expensive trip to the backing store. The data is typically copied into the cache on the way back.

  A hit is faster than recomputing the result or reading a slower data store, so the more requests the cache serves, the faster the system performs. Why not make the cache enormous? Larger capacity means greater physical distances for signals, and so propagation delays. Fast technologies such as SRAM also cost more than commodity DRAM, flash or hard disks. To be cost-effective, caches must stay relatively small. They still work well because typical applications access data with a high degree of locality, a habit explained in Locality of reference: why caches usually win.

  CPUs and storage drives often include hardware-based caches, while web browsers and web servers commonly rely on software caching.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-001 -->

  *Figure: A client checks the cache first, and only a miss sends it to the slower backing store.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Client request] --> B{Tag matches?}
  B -->|hit| C[Answer from cache]
  B -->|miss| D[(Backing store)]
  D -->|more expensive| E[Answer]
  D -.->|typically| F[Copy into cache]
  ```

- **Locality of reference: why caches usually win**

  A cache is a bet that the future will resemble the recent past, and programs usually let it win. Locality of reference is the tendency of a processor or application to access the same set of memory locations, or nearby ones, repeatedly over a short period. It comes in two basic types. Temporal locality is the reuse of specific data within a relatively small time, so a copy kept in faster memory cuts the latency of later references. Spatial locality is the use of data elements within relatively close storage locations, and sequential locality is a special case of it. Data enters a cache one cache line, a block of neighboring data, at a time, so touching one element brings a few neighbors in with it. Poor locality does the opposite and causes cache thrashing and cache pollution. Walking a matrix row by row matches how C stores it and uses the cache well. As matrices grow, non-sequential traversals cause far more cache misses and RAM accesses.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-002 -->

- **The CPU cache: tiny, costly memory beside the core**

  Main memory can be tens to hundreds of times slower than a small memory sitting next to the processor core. That small memory is the CPU cache, a hardware cache that reduces the average time or energy needed to access data from main memory. It is typically costly SRAM and holds copies of frequently used data in fixed-size cache lines, each stored with a tag naming its memory location. Larger caches hit more often but answer more slowly, so processors use levels. L1, the smallest and fastest, is checked first, then L2, and often a larger L3 shared among cores, before main memory.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-159 -->

  *Figure: A lookup tries each level in turn, from the smallest and fastest down to main memory.* (layers; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Cache hit ratio: the number that judges a cache**

  A cache is judged by two numbers. The hit ratio of a cache is how often a searched-for item is found in it, expressed as the percentage of accesses that are hits. The other number is latency, how long after a request the cache can return an item when there is a hit. The miss ratio is simply 1 minus the hit ratio.

  The ratio is not a property of the cache alone, because it varies by application. Video and audio streaming often has a hit ratio near zero, since each bit of the stream is read once, used and never read or written again. That first read is called a compulsory miss. Worse, many cache algorithms, LRU in particular, let streaming data fill the cache and push out information that will soon be used again. This is called cache pollution. LRU is covered in Least recently used: the default eviction rule. Even the replacement strategy is a compromise between hit rate and latency. Faster strategies track less usage information, and more efficient ones track more.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-003 -->

- **Eviction policies: what a full cache forgets**

  A full cache has to forget something. On a miss, some existing entry is typically removed to make room for the new data, and the heuristic that picks it is the replacement policy. Cache replacement policies, also called eviction policies, are the algorithms that decide which items a full cache discards. One policy, LRU, replaces the entry accessed less recently than any other. More sophisticated algorithms also take into account how often entries are used. LRU is covered in Least recently used: the default eviction rule. Every choice trades hit rate against latency: tracking more usage information improves the hit rate for a given cache size, while tracking less makes the policy faster. A policy may also weigh other factors, such as item size, the time needed to obtain the item and expiration. And if the cache is large enough, no discarding algorithm may be needed at all.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-005 -->

- **Cache write policies: when the backing store finds out**

  Reading from a cache is simple. Writing raises a question: when does the backing store find out? A cache's write policy governs when a write made to the cache is propagated to the backing store. A write-miss policy governs whether data is loaded into the cache on a write miss.

  There are two main write policies. Write-through performs every write synchronously to both the cache and the backing store. Write-back first writes only to the cache and postpones the write to the backing store until the modified content is about to be replaced by another cache block. That is more complex. The cache must track which locations were written over and mark them dirty, then write them back only on eviction, a process called a lazy write. A read miss in a write-back cache may need two trips to the backing store: one to write back dirty data, one to fetch the requested data.

  On a write miss, write allocate, also called fetch on write, loads the missed location into the cache and then writes. No-write allocate, or write around, writes directly to the backing store and loads data only on read misses. The usual pairings follow the logic. A write-back cache typically uses write allocate, expecting later reads or writes of the same location to hit. A write-through cache uses no-write allocate, because later writes must still go to the backing store.

  Write-through is common over unreliable networks, where the coherency protocol needed between several write-back caches is enormously complex. Whatever the policy, a cached copy can become stale, or out-of-date, when other entities change the backing store or other caches update their copies.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-004 -->

  *Figure: The two write policies differ in when the backing store is updated and in what usually happens on a write miss.*

  | Policy | A write goes to | Usual write-miss policy |
  |---|---|---|
  | Write-through | Cache and backing store, synchronously | No-write allocate: write around, load only on read misses |
  | Write-back | Cache only; the store later, on eviction | Write allocate: load the location, then write |

- **Least frequently used: when popularity outlives its use**

  An item that was popular once can outstay its welcome. Least frequently used (LFU) counts how often each item is needed and discards the items used less often first. It resembles LRU, the subject of Least recently used: the default eviction rule. The difference is that LFU stores how many times a block was accessed instead of how recently. The flaw is a long memory. An object that was accessed often and then becomes unpopular stays in an LFU cache for a long time. It blocks newer or less-popular objects from replacing it. LFU with dynamic aging (LFUDA) adds a cache-age factor to the reference count, so such objects become eligible for replacement. It also reduces the cache pollution LFU causes when a cache is small. Least frequent recently used (LFRU) combines the benefits of LFU and LRU. It splits the cache into a protected privileged partition for popular content and an unprivileged partition.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-008 -->

- **Least recently used: the default eviction rule**

  When Singh's case studies choose an eviction policy for a URL shortener, WhatsApp, Twitter, Netflix or Uber, they choose the same one each time: LRU. Least recently used (LRU) discards the least recently used items first. The idea is easy; the bookkeeping is not. LRU must track what was used and when, so it keeps age bits for cache lines and finds the least recently used line from those bits. Whenever a line is used, the age of the other lines changes.

  The cost grows with the hardware. When a CPU cache lets a line sit in any of many slots, generally more than four ways, the cost becomes prohibitive. Designers then often use pseudo-LRU, which needs only one bit per cache item. Operating systems cannot afford LRU in the critical path because of its high overhead, so they commonly use Clock, an approximation of it. LRU is also a family of algorithms that includes 2Q and LRU/K.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-007 -->

- **Cache coherence: keeping copies in agreement**

  When several caches hold copies of the same data, one copy can change while the others never find out. Cache coherence is the uniformity of shared resource data that is stored in multiple local caches. In a coherent system every cached copy of a shared memory region is the same. Changes in any cache must reach the copies in peer caches, and writes to the same location must be sequenced. Snooping broadcasts every request to all processors: faster given enough bandwidth, but not scalable. Directory-based protocols send point-to-point messages through a common directory, with longer latency but much less bandwidth, which suits larger systems.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-158 -->

- **The page cache: free memory put to work**

  The operating system quietly spends any memory that programs are not using on a cache. A page cache, or disk cache, is a transparent cache in main memory. It holds pages that originate from a secondary storage device such as a hard disk or SSD. Because that memory is easily reclaimed, there is generally no performance penalty. Disk reads and writes are slow and random accesses need expensive seeks, so more main memory means more data cached and better performance. A write goes to the cached page, which is marked dirty and flushed to disk before it is freed.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-160 -->

- **Buffer versus cache: similar parts, different jobs**

  A buffer and a cache both hold data on its way somewhere, so they are easy to confuse. A cache reduces accesses to slower underlying storage for data transferred repeatedly. A buffer reduces the number of transfers of otherwise novel data between communicating processes. It spreads the overhead of several small transfers over fewer, larger ones. It can reduce the jitter of latency even when data is written once and read once. A cache also needs a possibly distributed coherency protocol to stay consistent with where the data resides, which strict buffering does not. Caching almost always involves some buffering, but strict buffering does not necessarily involve caching.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-015 -->

- **Prefetching: fetch it before anyone asks**

  Why wait for a request that is probably coming? Prefetching loads data into a cache ahead of time, guessing that the next chunk or two will soon be required. The plain alternative, demand paging, reads only the minimum on a read miss. That might be one page of virtual memory, often 4 KB, from disk into the disk cache in RAM. Anticipatory paging also prefetches the next chunk or two. It helps most when the first chunk is slow to read but the next few arrive in much shorter times, as with disk storage and DRAM. Done optimally, prediction can bypass the latency altogether.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-013 -->

- **Caching strategies: keeping a cache and its data in sync**

  A cache and the data store behind it can drift apart. Caching strategies are the patterns for keeping them in sync, and they split by direction. For reads there are two. In the first, the application loads data into the cache itself, a pattern covered in Cache-aside: the application does the fetching. In read-through, the cache itself loads data from the store when a read misses. For writes there are three: write-through, write-around and write-back. They are often combined. For example, write-around is often used together with that first read pattern to make sure the cache is up to date.

  A write-through cache writes data to the cache and the store simultaneously. That gives fast retrieval and complete consistency between them, at the cost of higher latency for write operations. Write-around sends writes straight to permanent storage, bypassing the cache. That may reduce latency but increases cache misses, because the cache must read from the store on a miss. Applications that write and quickly re-read data pay with slower reads from back-end storage.

  A write-back cache, also called write-behind, writes only to the caching layer and confirms the write as soon as it completes there. The cache then syncs the write to the store asynchronously. This reduces latency and gives high throughput for write-intensive applications, but it risks data loss if the caching layer crashes. Having more than one replica acknowledge the write in the cache reduces that risk.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-022 -->

- **Distributed cache: memory pooled across machines**

  A cache is usually limited to the memory of one machine, unless it borrows from others. A distributed cache pools the RAM of multiple networked computers into a single in-memory data store used as a data cache to provide fast access to data. It can grow beyond the memory limits of a single computer by linking many computers together. Its hosts can be co-located or spread over different geographical regions. A global cache is one kind: a single shared cache that all application nodes use. When data is missing, the cache itself finds it in the underlying data store.

  Each cache key is assigned to a specific shard, also called a partition. A technique for spreading keys evenly across shards, even if some crash or become unavailable, is the subject of Consistent hashing: adding a server without reshuffling everything. A common example is described in Redis: a cache that is also a data store. The idea became feasible because main memory became cheap and network cards fast, with 1 Gbit standard and 10 Gbit gaining traction.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-025 -->

- **Redis: a cache that is also a data store**

  Redis starts from a bold idea: a cache can also act as a full-fledged data store. Redis (Remote Dictionary Server) is an in-memory store of key-value pairs, used as a distributed cache and as a broker for messages. It serves reads and writes from main memory with sub-millisecond latency. It also persists data to disk with snapshots (RDB) and AOF, so it can serve as fully persistent storage.

  Redis is fast for three reasons. It is RAM-based, and RAM access is at least 1000 times faster than random disk access. It uses IO multiplexing with a single-threaded execution loop. And it uses efficient lower-level data structures: strings, bitmaps, lists, sets, sorted sets, hashes and JSON. These suit counting clicks and comments per post (hash) or sorting and deduping commented users (sorted set). Top use cases are distributed caching, session storage, passing messages and a high-speed store. The price is that Redis operates as a single process, so one instance cannot run tasks in parallel.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-029 -->

- **Memcached: servers that never talk to each other**

  Memcached keeps its design simple enough that its servers never talk to each other. It is a general-purpose distributed memory-caching system. It often speeds up dynamic database-driven websites by caching data and objects in RAM, so an external data source is read less often. Servers keep a key-value associative array that clients populate and query by key. Keys can be up to 250 bytes and values at most 1 megabyte. Each client knows all the servers and hashes the key to pick one, a simple form of sharding. When memory runs out, servers discard the oldest values. Clients must therefore treat Memcached as a transitory cache and never assume stored data is still there.

  In the usual read pattern the client checks for a value under a unique key, such as userrow plus the user id. If it is absent, the client selects from the data store and adds the result to Memcached. After an update, the cached view goes out of date unless the code also sets the new value or deletes the entry.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-030 -->

- **Redis replication and clustering: copies for reads, clusters for scale**

  One Redis server can feed any number of copies of itself. Redis scales reads and protects data through master-replica copying, and scales further through a clustering mode. A replica may itself be master to another, giving a single-rooted tree. The copies help reads and data safety but not writes, and replicas can be configured to accept writes, which permits inconsistency between instances. A Redis cluster can scale up to 1,000 nodes, achieve acceptable write safety and keep operating when some nodes fail. In a cluster all single-key commands are available, but multi-key operations are restricted to keys that belong to the same node.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-032 -->

- **Memoization: remembering what a function already computed**

  A function that has already answered a question should not be asked twice. Memoization is an optimization technique that speeds up programs by storing the results of expensive function calls and returning them when the same inputs occur again. It is a type of caching. A memoized function stores its inputs together with the computed result the first time, then returns the remembered result on later calls. Only a referentially transparent function can be memoized, one whose call has exactly the same effect as its return value. Memoization is a typical space-time tradeoff: runtime falls as memory use rises.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-014 -->

- **Belady's clairvoyant algorithm: the perfect eviction rule**

  The perfect cache policy exists on paper, and nobody can run it. Bélády's optimal algorithm, also called the clairvoyant algorithm, discards the information that will not be needed for the longest time. That means it must know the future, so it is unfeasible in practice, and a general-purpose operating system cannot implement it. Its practical minimum can still be calculated after experimentation, which gives a yardstick for judging a chosen cache algorithm. Some of the best-performing policies attempt to imitate it by predicting future reuse from past access patterns.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-006 -->

- **FIFO and random eviction: choosing without a memory**

  The simplest eviction rules do not track recency or frequency at all. FIFO evicts the oldest entry, LIFO the newest, and random replacement an arbitrary one. With FIFO the cache behaves like a queue and evicts blocks in the order they were added, however often they were accessed before. With LIFO it behaves like a stack and evicts the block added most recently, again regardless of how often it was accessed. Random replacement picks an item and discards it to make space when necessary, and it needs no access history. It has been used in ARM processors because of its simplicity, and it allows efficient stochastic simulation.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-011 -->

- **Most recently used: evicting what you just touched**

  Throwing out what you just used sounds backwards, yet sometimes it wins. Most recently used (MRU) is the reverse of LRU: it discards the most recently used items first. Chou and DeWitt said that when a file is repeatedly scanned in a looping sequential reference pattern, MRU is the best replacement algorithm. For random access patterns and repeated scans over large datasets, called cyclic access patterns, MRU gets more hits than LRU because it tends to retain older data. It is most useful where the older an item is, the more likely it is to be accessed.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-009 -->

- **SIEVE and S3-FIFO: evicting the one-hit wonders**

  Two newer eviction algorithms are built on one observation: cache workloads show high one-hit-wonder ratios, meaning many objects are requested once and never again. SIEVE is designed for web caches, such as key-value caches and CDNs, a topic taken up in Content delivery networks: serving users from nearby. It keeps a single FIFO queue and quickly evicts newly inserted objects. S3-FIFO, designed in 2023, uses three FIFO queues. A small queue takes 10% of cache space, a main queue takes 90%, and a ghost queue stores only object metadata. The small queue filters out one-hit wonders, and the main queue keeps popular objects through reinsertion.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-012 -->

- **Segmented LRU: making an item earn its place**

  A cache can make an item earn its place. A segmented LRU (SLRU) cache is divided into a probationary segment and a protected segment. Data from a miss enters the probationary segment. A hit moves the line to the most-recently-accessed end of the protected segment, so protected lines have been accessed at least twice. Promoting a line can push the protected segment's LRU line back to the probationary one for another chance. Discards come from the LRU end of the probationary segment. A refinement that uses recently evicted items to resize the two segments is the subject of Adaptive replacement cache: learning from what it evicted.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-010 -->

- **Adaptive replacement cache: learning from what it evicted**

  A cache that remembers what it threw away can learn from it. The adaptive replacement cache (ARC) is a page replacement algorithm that outperforms LRU. It tracks both frequently used and recently used pages, plus a recent eviction history for both. It splits the usual single list into T1, entries seen once recently, and T2, frequent entries referenced at least twice. Each list gets a ghost list, B1 or B2, holding only the keys of entries evicted from it, never their data. A hit in B1 grows the target size of T1, and a hit in B2 shrinks it.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-161 -->

- **Caching layers: caches from browser to storage**

  Caches hide at nearly every layer of a system, from the client-facing side to the backend. Browsers cache HTTP responses, guided by directives in response headers. CDNs cache static content such as images and JavaScript closer to users, and some load balancers cache frequently requested data to answer without engaging backend servers. Services often check an in-memory cache before querying a data store, and distributed caches such as Redis hold key-value pairs across services. Even the data store caches. A bufferpool holds copies of data pages in memory, and materialized views store the results of expensive queries.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-021 -->

- **Time to live: giving every cache entry an expiry date**

  The simplest way to keep a cache fresh is to let every entry expire. Time to live (TTL) gives each cache item a specific lifespan after which it is dropped or refreshed. It is not strictly an eviction algorithm; each item is simply given a lifespan. Time-aware LRU (TLRU) is an LRU variant for caches whose contents have a valid lifetime, with a time-to-use timestamp on each item. One practical tip: avoid giving keys the same expiry time by adding a random number to the TTL. Give keys that do not exist only a short TTL.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-028 -->

- **Cache invalidation: the famously hard problem**

  Phil Karlton counted cache invalidation among the two hard things in computer science. Cache invalidation is the process by which a computer system declares cache entries out of date and replaces or removes them. Data goes stale when something other than the cache changes the backing store. It also goes stale when a client updates data in one cache while copies sit in other caches. If data is modified, it should be invalidated in the cache, or the application can behave inconsistently.

  Explicit invalidation marks what the client received as out of date, so a client that asks again is given the new version. It is hard when many objects must be invalidated, and invalidating several representations adds complexity to the application. The simplest rule is a TTL, the longest an entry may stay cached before refresh. Very low TTLs, validating on every request, or not caching volatile content also keep data fresh but raise load on the application. Protocols that keep cache managers consistent are called cache coherence protocols, and invalidation can be one of their steps.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-024 -->

- **Cache-aside: the application does the fetching**

  In cache-aside, the application, not the cache, does the work. On a read the service checks the cache and returns the cached contents if present. On a miss it reads the data from the data store and then updates the cache. A read-through cache, by contrast, loads data by itself, as Caching strategies: keeping a cache and its data in sync describes.

  Cached entries can go stale. The simplest rule is a maximum time an entry may stay in the cache before it is updated, usually called time to live (TTL). Write-around is often used together with cache-aside to make sure the cache is up to date. And because a cache has limited capacity, the query-cache design uses a least recently used approach to expire older entries.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-023 -->

  *Figure: The application, not the cache, goes to the data store when a read misses.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Application reads] --> B{In cache?}
  B -->|hit| C[Return cached contents]
  B -->|miss| D[(Data store)]
  D -->|fetch contents| E[Update cache]
  ```

- **Cache stampede: when expiry sends everyone at once**

  Suppose a page takes 3 seconds to render and traffic is 10 requests per second. The moment its cached copy expires, 30 processes are recomputing it at once. That is a cache stampede, also called dog-piling: a chain-reaction failure in which very heavy load makes many parallel processes recompute the same expired cached value at once.
