  While a page stays cached, a heavily loaded system remains responsive, because requests are served from the cached copy and the expensive rendering stays to a minimum. At expiry, many threads across the server farm may try to render it together, and none of them knows the others are doing so. Recomputing usually queries a data store or other service, so at a high request rate that shared resource is overloaded. The concurrent load can exhaust shared resources and cause congestion collapse. Every attempt to re-render times out, the cache hit rate drops to zero, and the collapse lasts as long as the load stays heavy.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-017 -->

- **Stopping a stampede: locks, early expiry and other fixes**

  Every fix for a cache stampede answers one question: who recomputes the expired value? Cache stampede mitigation, also called dogpile prevention, covers the techniques that stop many processes recomputing it at the same moment. They fall into three groups: locking, external recomputation and probabilistic early expiration.

  With locking, a process that misses on a key recomputes the value only if it acquires the key's lock. A process that fails to get the lock can return not-found or serve a stale item. Locking can prevent stampedes but doubles the writes. It is also hard to implement correctly: the lock holder may fail, the lock needs its own time-to-live, and race conditions arise.

  External recomputation moves the work to a separate process, triggered as the cached value nears expiration or on a miss. With probabilistic early expiration, each process decides whether to recompute before expiry, with a probability that rises as expiry nears. One implementation, based on an exponential distribution, was shown to be optimal. It needs extra cache memory to store the recompute time.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-018 -->

  *Figure: Each of the three approaches to stopping a stampede carries a cost.*

  | Approach | How it works | Cost |
  |---|---|---|
  | Locking | The process that wins the key's lock recomputes it | Doubles the writes; hard to get right |
  | External recomputation | A separate process recomputes near expiry or on a miss | A moving part to maintain |
  | Probabilistic early expiration | Each process may recompute early, more likely as expiry nears | Extra cache memory for the recompute time |

- **Cache penetration: requests for data that does not exist**

  Some requests can never be answered from a cache, because the answer does not exist. Cache penetration happens when the requested key exists in neither the cache nor the data store, so every such request ends up at the store. The store has nothing to return, so the application cannot populate the cache. A malicious user sending many such queries can easily overload the store. One fix is to cache a null value for missing keys, with a short TTL. Another is a Bloom filter, which tells whether an element is in a set. Queries for keys it rules out never reach the cache or the store.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-019 -->

- **Cache failure modes: four ways a cache goes wrong**

  Caches typically go wrong in four ways, and each one ends at the data store behind them. When many keys expire together, queries hit the store directly and overload it, so add a random number to the expiry times. A key that exists in neither the cache nor the store stresses both; cache a null value for it, or check a Bloom filter first. When a hot key expires, many requests hit the store; hot keys take up 80% of the queries, so they are given no expiration time. When the cache is down, all requests go to the store, and a cache cluster improves cache availability.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-020 -->

  *Figure: Each failure mode ends at the data store, and each has its own remedy.*

  | Failure | What happens | Remedy |
  |---|---|---|
  | Many keys expire together | Queries hit the store directly and overload it | Add a random number to expiry times |
  | Key exists nowhere | Stresses cache and store | Cache a null value, or check a Bloom filter |
  | Hot key expires | Many requests hit the store | Give hot keys no expiration time |
  | Cache is down | All requests go to the store | Use a cache cluster |

- **Multi-level caching: falling through the levels**

  A lookup can fall through several caches before it finds anything. Multi-level caching keeps data in a hierarchy of cache levels, labeled L1, L2, L3 and so on, with each level searched in turn. A lookup searches the tags in level one first. If the data is not there, it searches L2, then L3 and lower, until it is found and read. Most CPUs since the 1980s have used one or more caches, sometimes in cascaded levels. The same idea works in software: in two-tiered caching, an in-memory cache is the first layer and a distributed cache is the second.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-026 -->

- **When to use a cache, and when not to**

  Caches are not free, and they do not always pay. A cache pays off when data is read repeatedly, and it should be treated as transient storage rather than a permanent store. Done well, it improves performance, reduces load on the data store and network cost, and increases read throughput. It does not help when reading the cache takes as long as reading the primary store, or when requests rarely repeat. Nor does it help when data changes frequently, since the cached version gets out of sync. And because caches are almost always built on memory that is fast but volatile, they are transient.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-027 -->

- **Redis persistence: snapshots and the append-only file**

  On default settings, a complete Redis system failure loses only a few seconds of data. Redis persists its in-memory dataset to disk in two ways. Snapshotting asynchronously dumps the dataset to disk at regular intervals as a binary dump. Journaling adds a record of each modifying operation to an append-only file (AOF) in the background, and it is generally considered the safer approach. By default it writes data to a file system at least every two seconds. It forks the process that holds the data, so the parent keeps serving clients while the child writes to disk.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-031 -->

- **Memcached or Redis: the interview question and its answer**

  Memcached or Redis? It is a popular interview question, and the answer turns on the data structures, persistence and scaling each offers. On data structures, Memcached offers a distributed table of keys up to 250 bytes and values up to 1 megabyte. Redis supports strings, hashes, lists, sets, JSON and more. These suit counting clicks and comments per post (hash) and sorting and deduping commented users (sorted set). They also suit caching user behavior history and storing boolean flags, such as login or membership status, in small space.

  On persistence, Memcached discards its oldest values when memory runs out and must be treated as transitory. Redis can persist data with snapshots or an append-only file. On scaling, Memcached clients hash keys across servers that do not talk to each other. Redis offers master-replica copying and a cluster mode that scales up to 1,000 nodes. The two systems are covered in Redis: a cache that is also a data store and Memcached: servers that never talk to each other.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-033 -->

- **Purge, refresh and ban: telling a caching proxy to forget**

  Sometimes waiting for an entry to expire is too slow, and a caching proxy has to be told to forget. Purge, refresh and ban are three methods of explicitly invalidating content held in a caching proxy. Purge removes content, including all its variants, immediately. The next request fetches the data from the application and stores it again. Refresh fetches the content from the application even when a cached copy exists and replaces the stored copy. It affects only one variant. Ban adds a reference to the cached content to a ban list that requests are checked against. On a match, new content is fetched, returned and cached.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-157 -->

- **The thundering herd: many wake, one wins**

  Waking a crowd of processes to serve one of them wastes everyone else's effort. That is the thundering herd problem: many processes or threads are awakened at once but only one can use the resource. The others fail and go back to sleep. The needless awakenings consume CPU and other resources, and can slow the one process that succeeds. When it happens while accessing a cache, it is often called a cache stampede. Operating systems mitigate it by waking one waiter, as the Linux kernel, epoll's EPOLLEXCLUSIVE flag and Windows I/O completion ports do. Clients can add jitter, randomness in their retry waits, to break the synchronization.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-162 -->

- **Caching weather forecasts: one answer for a whole neighborhood**

  In 2011, smartphone weather features overloaded AccuWeather servers. Two requests from the same area generated separate requests, so the servers did the same work twice for what was, to the user, the same forecast.

  The fix lived at the edge. Edge servers truncated the GPS coordinates to fewer decimal places. Many slightly different positions then became one position, and the cached result of a nearby query could be used for the next. Locality of reference was doing the work here: requests from the same area are alike, so one stored answer can serve many.

  The result showed in the numbers. Every request answered at the edge was one the server never saw, and the number of lookups reaching the server per day dropped by half. The lesson is about the label a cache files an answer under. A cache can reuse an answer only when a new request looks identical to an old one. Loosening what counts as identical turned near misses into hits and raised the hit ratio.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-016 -->

### Content delivery networks

A content delivery network is a geographically distributed network of proxy servers and data centers that delivers content to users from locations close to them. The origin server holds the original content, and the many edge servers spread around the world cache it and serve users nearby. A request is answered from the nearest edge server's cache, or the edge fetches the content from the origin, stores a copy and delivers it. This chapter follows that idea through the ways content reaches an edge, how requests find the right server and the variants built by content owners and telecommunications providers.

- **Content delivery networks: serving users from nearby**

  A visitor in the UK opens a site hosted in the USA, and the page arrives from London. That is a content delivery network at work. A CDN is a geographically distributed network of proxy servers and data centers that delivers content to users from locations close to them. Users fetch content from a nearby CDN node instead of the origin, the server where the content actually lives. The origin's servers then do not have to handle the requests the CDN fulfills. A close edge location is also much quicker than a full request to the origin.

  CDNs arose in the late 1990s to relieve bottlenecks in the Internet's performance. They now serve a large portion of Internet content: web text, graphics and scripts, downloadable files, applications, live and on-demand streams, and social media services. Static files such as HTML, CSS and JavaScript, photos and videos are generally what a CDN serves, though it can deliver dynamic content too.

  The benefits are reduced bandwidth costs, faster page loads, higher global availability and better security, notably protection against distributed denial-of-service attacks, covered in DDoS: a flood from many sources at once. Someone pays for all this. Content owners pay CDN operators to deliver their content, and the CDN in turn pays ISPs, carriers and network operators for hosting its servers in their data centers. The drawbacks are real too. A CDN can be expensive for high-traffic services. Some organizations and countries block popular CDN domains or IPs. And an audience far from any CDN server may see data travel farther.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-069 -->

- **Peer-to-peer: when every participant is also a server**

  In a peer-to-peer network, nobody is only a customer. Peer-to-peer (P2P) is a distributed architecture in which participants share part of their own resources, such as processing power, storage or network capacity, directly with other peers. Each peer is both provider and requester, with no intermediary. The client-server model instead gives the roles to different participants.

  Unstructured networks form by random connections, so they are easy to build and cope well with churn, peers frequently joining and leaving. Structured networks impose a topology so any node can efficiently find even a rare resource, most commonly with the design described in Distributed hash tables: a lookup service with no center. Decentralization removes the weak spot of client-server systems, a central server whose failure takes the whole service down, and capacity grows as nodes arrive. For content delivery, serving capacity can rise as more users fetch the content, which keeps the distributor's cost low. The catch is the freeloader problem. P2P systems reach full potential only when many nodes contribute, yet many users take without sharing, which can in some cases make the community collapse.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-181 -->

- **DDoS: a flood from many sources at once**

  Sometimes the flood has no attacker: a link on a major site can deny service with the same effect as a DDoS attack. A distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attack makes a machine or network resource unavailable by flooding it with traffic that comes from many different sources. The sources are often thousands of malware-infected hosts in a botnet, so blocking a single source is not enough.

  Common attacks are UDP flooding, SYN flooding and DNS amplification. A SYN flood leaves half-open connections that exhaust the server's available connections, because the forged sender address never replies. In a reflected attack, forged requests carrying the victim's spoofed address go to many computers, whose replies flood the victim. An application-layer (layer 7) attack over-exercises specific functions, such as search. It needs fewer resources and can look like legitimate traffic. Defense combines attack detection, traffic classification and response tools. Upstream filtering diverts traffic through a scrubbing center that passes only legitimate traffic, since DDoS can overwhelm any hardware firewall.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-180 -->

- **Origin and edge servers: where a CDN's content lives**

  Where does a CDN's content really live? On the origin server, the primary source of content, which holds its original versions. The edge servers that cache and serve it are numerous and spread across the world. A CDN caches content in many geographic locations called edge locations, and each one holds several caching servers that deliver content to visitors in its proximity.

  Providers serve a defined set of points of presence (PoPs), chosen for the coverage wanted, such as the United States, Asia-Pacific or global. PoPs are also called edges, edge nodes or edge networks. A CDN's footprint is the geographic area where its edge servers can effectively serve clients' requests. Size varies. Some CDNs have thousands of nodes and tens of thousands of servers on many remote PoPs. Others build a global network with only a small number of PoPs. An origin shield protects the origin during heavy traffic. DNS resolves the domain name to the IP address of the nearest edge server, and a control plane configures and manages the edge servers.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-070 -->

- **Image CDN: one picture, many versions**

  One image can need many versions. An Image CDN serves multiple versions of the same image over HTTP, depending on the properties of the requesting browser. The browser or server-side logic determines those properties. It generally combines three components: a CDN for fast serving of images, image manipulation and optimization, and device detection. Manipulation can happen on the fly through URL directives, in batch mode through manual upload of images, or fully automatically. Device detection reads the properties of the requesting browser or device from the User-Agent string, HTTP Accept headers, Client-Hints or JavaScript.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-083 -->

- **Peer-to-peer CDN: delivery that improves with demand**

  The more people want a file, the better a peer-to-peer CDN can perform. In a peer-to-peer CDN, clients provide resources as well as use them. CDN offloading is the mechanism that lets clients help deliver content to each other, in addition to edge server delivery. Unlike client-server systems, such a network can perform better as more users access the content, especially with protocols such as BitTorrent that require users to share. That keeps setup and running costs very small for the original content distributor. Web3 and blockchain technologies can also incentivize peers: nodes that take part receive crypto tokens in exchange for their involvement.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-076 -->

- **Private CDN: building your own delivery network**

  Content owners unsatisfied with the options or costs of a commercial CDN can build their own. A private CDN is made of PoPs that serve content only for that owner. Its PoPs can be caching servers, reverse proxies or application delivery controllers. It can be as simple as two caching servers or large enough to serve petabytes of content. Inside a company network it is also called an enterprise CDN, or eCDN. Large CDNs may likewise build their own private network to distribute copies of content across cache locations. They fall back on public networks when that network's capacity is insufficient or reduced by a failure.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-077 -->

- **Telco CDN: the network provider becomes the CDN**

  Streaming video grew so fast that telecommunications providers began launching CDNs of their own. A telco CDN runs on the network the provider owns, to lessen demands on the network backbone and reduce infrastructure investment. Telcos own the last mile, the final stretch of network to the customer. They can cache content deep in their networks, minimizing the distance video travels over the general Internet. They also have a built-in cost advantage, because traditional CDNs must lease bandwidth from telcos and build the operator's margin into their own costs. And running the delivery infrastructure gives operators control over resource utilization and better quality of service.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-079 -->

- **Virtual CDN: caches that appear where needed**

  A virtual CDN can create a cache wherever one is needed. A virtual CDN (vCDN), also called a software-defined CDN (sd-CDN), uses virtualization to deploy CDN caches dynamically. The aim is to reduce content provider costs while increasing elasticity and decreasing service delay. The virtual caches are deployed on physical servers across the provider's coverage. The two technologies they run on are covered in Virtual machine: a whole computer made of software and Containers: an application and everything it needs, isolated. That avoids traditional CDN limits on performance, reliability and availability. Where a cache is placed depends on both the content type and the server or end-user location, so vCDNs significantly affect service delivery and network congestion.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-080 -->

- **CDN request flow: edge first, origin second**

  The first request for a file at an edge location goes all the way to the origin. Later ones do not. Here is how a single request travels. After DNS resolution, the user's device sends its content request to the CDN edge server. The edge server checks its local cache for the content and, if it finds it, serves it to the user. If the content is not in the cache, the edge server forwards the request to the origin server. After receiving the content from the origin, the edge server stores a copy in its cache and delivers it to the user.

  Once static assets are cached at a location, later requests there are served from its edge servers instead of the origin, which reduces origin load. Streaming follows a variation. The CDN receives the stream at its origin server and replicates it to many or all of its edge cache servers. Delivering it over HTTP then costs about the same as HTTP web caching.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-071 -->

  *Figure: One request, step by step, from the user's device to the edge and, on a miss, to the origin.*

  | Step | What happens |
  |---|---|
  | 1 | After DNS resolution, the device sends its request to the CDN edge server |
  | 2 | The edge checks its local cache and, on a hit, serves the content |
  | 3 | On a miss, the edge forwards the request to the origin server |
  | 4 | The edge stores a copy of what the origin returns and delivers it |

- **Push and pull CDNs: who fills the cache**

  CDNs differ in who fills the cache: the site owner or the first visitor. Push CDNs are sent new content whenever it changes. Pull CDNs fetch content from the origin when a user first requests it.

  With a push CDN, the site owner uploads content directly to the CDN and rewrites URLs to point to it. The owner also configures when content expires and when it is updated. Content is uploaded only when it is new or changed, which minimizes traffic but maximizes storage, and it is placed once instead of re-pulled at regular intervals. That suits sites with little traffic or with content that is not often updated.

  In a pull CDN the cache is updated on request. If the CDN lacks an asset, it fetches it from the origin, populates its cache and sends the asset to the user. Pull CDNs need less maintenance than push CDNs, because cache updates happen in response to client requests. They suit heavy-traffic sites, since traffic is spread more evenly and only recently requested content remains on the CDN. The same split holds for web caches in general: they are populated from user requests (pull caching) or from preloaded content disseminated by content servers (push caching).

  <!-- sysd-blocks-072 -->

  *Figure: Push and pull CDNs compared on who fills the cache and where each fits.*

  |  | Push CDN | Pull CDN |
  |---|---|---|
  | Who fills the cache | Owner uploads new or changed content | CDN fetches from the origin on first request |
  | Expiry | Owner configures it | Cache updates on request |
  | Trade-off | Minimal traffic, maximal storage | Less maintenance |
  | Suits | Little traffic or rarely updated content | Heavy-traffic sites |

- **CDN request routing: choosing which server answers**

  A CDN has many servers that could answer a request, so something must choose. Request routing directs each client request to the content source best able to serve it. That might be the service node closest to the client or the one with the most capacity. The algorithms include global server load balancing, DNS-based request routing, dynamic metafile generation, HTML rewriting and anycasting. Global server load balancing (GSLB) routes requests by factors such as geographic proximity, server load and network conditions. Anycast DNS lets multiple servers share the same IP address and helps route incoming traffic to the nearest data center. Proximity is estimated by probing, either reactive or proactive, and by watching live connections. Choosing for performance picks the fewest hops, the shortest time to the client or the highest server performance. Choosing for cost picks the cheapest locations. Edge servers near users tend to win on both. CDN providers also establish a presence at major Internet Exchange Points, so they can exchange traffic directly with ISPs and other networks.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-073 -->

- **Content networking techniques: intelligence at the edge**

  The Internet's core is deliberately simple. It follows the end-to-end principle: intelligence sits at the hosts and clients, so the core network only forwards data packets. A CDN adds intelligence as an overlay on top of that core, combining web caching, server-load balancing, request routing and content services. Web caches store popular content on servers close to the greatest demand, which reduces bandwidth requirements and server load and improves client response times. Server-load balancing shares traffic among servers or web caches, for example with a layer 4-7 switch holding one virtual IP address, adding capacity, reliability and health checks.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-074 -->

- **Edge content services: ICAP, OPES and Edge Side Includes**

  Some pages cannot simply be cached, because their content is generated. Changing catalogs and forums, or personalization, create a problem for caching systems. Content service protocols give access to content services, such as content adaptation and dynamic page assembly, distributed through a content network. ICAP, developed in the late 1990s, is an open standard for connecting application servers. The more recent OPES architecture lets service applications run on the OPES processor itself or remotely on a Callout Server. A group of companies also created Edge Side Includes (ESI), a small markup language for assembling dynamic web content at the edge.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-081 -->

- **End-user mapping: finding the client behind the resolver**

  A CDN may route a client in India to its edge server in Singapore, because that client uses a public DNS resolver in Singapore. CDNs traditionally located a client by the IP of its recursive DNS resolver. That performs poorly when the resolver is far away. End-user mapping fixes this. With the edns-client-subnet option, a CDN uses the IP address of the requesting client's subnet when resolving DNS requests. This drastically reduces round-trip latencies for clients on non-local resolvers. It has drawbacks. It reduces the effectiveness of caching resolutions at recursive resolvers, increases total DNS resolution traffic, and raises a privacy concern by exposing the client's subnet.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-075 -->

- **Multi-CDN: not trusting one network with a live event**

  High peak audiences, especially during live events, are why some content providers prefer not to rely on a single CDN. Multi-CDN means a provider combines several CDN services instead. Traffic can be split among them on the client side, on the server side at the origin, or on the cloud side between origin and audience. Selection criteria can be performance, availability and cost, and a CDN selector is the decision-making service that chooses among the CDNs. The IETF standardized a framework and request-routing interface for interconnecting CDNs, so a request can be redirected between them. Open Caching APIs let a provider use several CDNs consistently.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-078 -->

- **Edge computing: running the code near the user**

  Running an application near its users, instead of in a centralized data center, can cut latency. Edge computing is a distributed computing model that brings computation and data storage closer to the sources of data, and so to users. It is any design that pushes computation physically closer to a user. It generalizes the CDN idea. CDN nodes at the network edge prefetch and cache content and can customize it, and edge computing extends this by leveraging cloud infrastructure.

  Processing locally avoids long transfers. Recognizing speech at the edge lets a system send text to the cloud instead of audio, cutting bandwidth. A voice assistant at the edge can keep serving local users during cloud or internet outages. The costs are real. Data traveling between nodes needs its own encryption, and edge nodes may be resource-constrained. Offloading every task to the edge can even slow things down because of transfer times between device and node, so the best configuration depends on the workload.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-178 -->

- **Subresource Integrity: checking what a CDN delivers**

  What if someone tampers with the scripts a CDN serves? Subresource Integrity (SRI) is a W3C recommendation that protects website delivery. It validates assets served by a third party, such as a CDN, so they have not been compromised. The page author gives a cryptographic hash of the resource along with its location. The browser compares that hash with one computed from the fetched resource and discards the resource if they do not match. An integrity value may hold several expressions, each a hash algorithm name plus a Base64 digest, and the browser validates with the strongest recognized one. SRI works with JavaScript files and linked stylesheets.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-179 -->

- **CDN security and privacy: protection and its price**

  A CDN can shield a site, and it can also expose it. It can improve website security, especially against DDoS attacks. But CDNs serving JavaScript have been targeted to inject malicious content into pages. Subresource Integrity ensures a page loads only a script whose content matches a hash the site author references. Providers can profit from tracking data collected as their scripts load in the customer's browser origin. CDNs are therefore pointed out as potential privacy intrusions for behavioral targeting. A website using a CDN may violate the EU's GDPR: in 2021 a German court ruled that sending a visitor's IP address to a CDN violated it.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-082 -->

### Choosing a database

Sooner or later every design in this course has to say where its data lives. A database is an organized collection of data, usually managed by software that lets users define, create, maintain and control access to it. This chapter starts with the relational database, which stores data in tables of rows and columns, and with NoSQL, which stores and retrieves it differently, as key-value pairs, documents or graphs. It also meets the transaction, a unit of work that the four ACID properties are meant to protect against errors, power failures and other mishaps. By the end you will be able to match a kind of database to the workload it suits.

- **Database: an organized collection of data**

  A flight reservation system, a parts inventory and a website built from webpages all keep their data in a database. A database is an organized collection of data, usually managed by database management software that lets users and applications capture and analyze it. Organizations rely on databases for their internal operations and for their online interactions with customers and suppliers. Strictly, the database, the software that manages it and the applications around it together form a database system. People often use the word loosely for any of the three. Databases can be classified by their contents, their application area, or a technical aspect such as structure. Some live primarily in main memory, which is faster than disk and used where response time is critical. Others spread both the data and the software over several computers. Copies protect it. Replicas of database objects give simultaneous access and resilience to partial failure. Saved copies, taken occasionally or continuously, let the database be restored after corruption or erroneous updates.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-035 -->

- **Relational database: data in tables**

  The relational database replaced the hierarchical and network databases before it largely because it was easier to implement and administer. It stores data in tables of columns and rows, with a unique key identifying each row. Each table generally represents one entity type, such as customer or product. Its rows are instances of that type, and its columns hold values such as address or price. Keys and normalization keep the data correct and avoid repeating it, and the model handles many-to-many relationships and supports complex queries and transactions. Many relational systems are queried with the simple language SQL. To work accurately they must use ACID transactions, described in ACID: four guarantees for every transaction. Singh lists the costs as expensive maintenance, difficult schema evolution, performance hits from joins, and poor horizontal scaling. A popular alternative today is NoSQL: data without the table, which scales horizontally across clusters of computers.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-044 -->

- **NoSQL: data without the table**

  NoSQL stands for "not only SQL", or simply "non-relational". A NoSQL database stores and retrieves data differently from the table structure of a relational database. Instead of rows and columns, it holds information in a single data structure such as key-value pairs, wide columns, graphs or documents. With no fixed schema, it scales easily to large, often unstructured datasets. That suits big data and real-time web applications, which value its simple design, horizontal scaling across clusters and cheap commodity hardware. The price is transactions: most NoSQL systems lack full ACID support, though some, like MongoDB, include it as a key feature. Many follow the BASE model, which trades strict consistency for speed and availability. Updates reach all nodes eventually, but reads may be stale. Barriers to adoption include low-level query languages, no ad hoc joins across tables and no standardized interfaces.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-058 -->

- **Graph database: relationships as stored links**

  A social network's friends relationship is essentially unbounded, and following it through tables takes join after join. A graph database stores the links themselves. It represents data with nodes for entities, edges for the relationships between them, and properties. Edges can be labeled, directed and given properties. Most systems use index-free adjacency: each node holds direct references to its neighbors instead of consulting a global index. An adjacent lookup is typically O(1) versus O(log n) for an index, so query time tracks the part of the graph touched. A relational database needs many joins for complex relationships, while a graph database follows stored links, and its advantage grows with query depth. Relational systems still suit flat data with relationships one or two levels deep, so the graph model alone should not justify a switch without evidence of gains. As of 2021 no graph query language had been adopted as universally as SQL.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-061 -->

- **Document database: one object, one document**

  In a document database, an object in your program becomes one record in the store. It is designed to store, retrieve and manage documents, or semi-structured information, and it is one of the main categories of NoSQL databases. A document is a self-contained unit encoded in a standard format such as XML, YAML, JSON or binary BSON. A relational database splits one object across tables joined by foreign keys. A document database keeps everything about it in one document, fetched by key without multi-table lookups. Documents need no fixed schema: those in one collection may have different fields, so new information can be added to some without affecting others. Each document has a unique identifier, and most stores index it. Beyond key access, a query language can retrieve documents by content, such as all whose field matches a value. That separates it from Key-value store: lookup by key, which treats values as opaque. Singh counts the lack of a schema as both an advantage and a disadvantage.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-059 -->

- **Elasticsearch: search over large volumes of data**

  Traditional databases are sometimes not fast enough to store, search and analyze huge volumes of data in near real time, with results in milliseconds. Elasticsearch addresses that gap. It is a distributed, open search and analytics engine built on Apache Lucene, with an HTTP web interface and schema-free JSON documents. Documents are stored in indices divided into primary shards, each with zero or more replicas spread across the cluster's nodes, and routing and rebalancing are automatic. One catch: once an index has been created, its number of primary shards cannot be changed. Beyond full-text search it supports faceted search, real-time search and percolation, in which stored queries are matched against incoming documents rather than the reverse. Real-time GET requests make it usable as a NoSQL datastore, though it does not support transactions that span several nodes. In a design from the System Design Primer, the search cluster is scatter-gathered: every server is asked for matches, then results are merged, ranked, sorted and returned.

  <!-- sysd-q-025 -->

- **Key-value store: lookup by key**

  One of the simplest non-trivial data models is the dictionary, a collection of key-value pairs in which each key appears at most once. A key-value store takes that model as its whole design. Every record is stored and found through its unique key. The value is opaque to the database, which typically supports only storing, retrieving, updating and deleting it by key. A document database can interpret a record's structure, but a key-value store returns a value whole. That suits low-latency, high-throughput workloads of direct key lookups, and Singh lists session management among its strengths. It is less suited to complex queries or relationships, since values cannot be filtered and there is no indexing or scanning. Variants add structure: keys kept in lexicographic order so ranges are retrieved efficiently, composite keys, or complex values such as Redis lists. Memcached and Redis hold data in memory, while Berkeley DB, Riak and Voldemort persist it.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-060 -->

- **Database management system: the software in the middle**

  MySQL, MariaDB, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, Oracle Database and Microsoft Access are all examples of one kind of software: a database management system, or DBMS. It lets users define, create, maintain and control access to a database. It sits between the database and its users or programs, letting them capture, retrieve, update and analyze data. It also provides facilities to administer the database, such as tuning and recovery. Storage, retrieval and update are the core, but what a DBMS offers beyond that varies enormously. Codd proposed that a general-purpose DBMS also provide a metadata catalog, transactions and concurrency, recovery, remote access and constraint enforcement. The database engine is the core part, between the database and the application interface. A general-purpose DBMS offers public APIs, and a special-purpose one may use a private API tied to a single application. Client-server architecture put the application on a client and the database on a server; multitier architectures later added application and web servers.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-036 -->

- **Database transaction: a unit of work, all or nothing**

  A bank transfer needs two steps: subtract the amount from one account and add the same amount to the other. A database transaction treats them as one. It is a unit of work performed in a database management system and handled in a coherent and reliable way, independent of other transactions. Transactions serve two purposes. They are reliable units of work that allow correct recovery from failures and keep the database consistent. They also isolate programs that access the database concurrently, because without that their outcomes are possibly erroneous. A transaction must be atomic (complete or have no effect), consistent (conform to existing constraints), isolated (not affect other transactions) and durable (written to persistent storage). Together these are abbreviated ACID, and ACID: four guarantees for every transaction takes them one at a time. The programmer sets a transaction's boundaries with special commands. A transaction over data on multiple nodes, covered in Distributed transactions: one commit across many databases, enforces the same guarantees, and typically an entity coordinates the process so all parts are applied everywhere.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-039 -->

- **ACID: four guarantees for every transaction**

  A power failure in the middle of a bank transfer should leave no trace. ACID names four properties of database transactions that are intended to guarantee data validity despite errors, power failures and other mishaps. Relational databases follow it to keep data correct before and after a transaction.

  Atomicity means all or nothing. The writes in a transaction are executed all at once and cannot be broken into smaller parts, and if a fault occurs they are rolled back. Consistency means preserving database invariants: data written by a transaction must be valid under all defined rules. This differs from the consistency meant in The CAP theorem: why no store can have everything, where every read receives the most recent write or an error. The third property, covered in Isolation: how much transactions see of each other, keeps concurrent transactions from contending. The database moderates access so transactions appear to run sequentially, and the strictest form, serializability, makes each act as if it were the only one running. The fourth, covered in Durability: a commit that survives the crash, means data stays persisted after a transaction commits, written to disk even through a system failure. In a distributed system it is replicated to other nodes.

  Implementations use write-ahead logging, which writes the prospective change to a persistent log before changing the database so it can recover after a crash. The alternative is shadow paging, which applies updates to a partial copy that is activated on commit. Guaranteeing ACID across a distributed database is harder, because a network connection or another node may fail. Atomicity there comes from a protocol covered in Two-phase commit: asking everyone to vote before committing, in which a coordinator asks participants whether they are prepared before formalizing the transaction.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-055 -->

  *Figure: The four ACID properties and what each one guarantees.*

  | Property | What it guarantees |
  |---|---|
  | Atomicity | All or nothing; a fault rolls the writes back |
  | Consistency | Data stays valid under all defined rules |
  | Isolation | Concurrent transactions appear to run in sequence |
  | Durability | Committed data stays persisted, even through a failure |

- **Database models: how data is organized logically**

  Data can be organized as a table, a tree, a graph or a document, and each choice is a database model. A database model is a type of data model that determines the logical structure of a database and how its data can be stored, organized and manipulated. The most popular is the relational model, or its SQL approximation, which uses a table-based format. The list is long. Navigational, hierarchical, network, graph, relational, entity-relationship, object, document, entity-attribute-value and star schema models are all common. An object-relational database combines the object and relational structures. Others include the multidimensional, array and multivalue models. Some are specialized for particular data, such as XML, semantic and content store databases.

  Three shapes show how the models differ. The flat model puts data in a single table, one record per row and one attribute per column. It is as simple as a spreadsheet but cannot efficiently handle complex relationships between entities. The hierarchical model is a tree in which each record has one parent but can have many children. It suits clear parent-child relationships but struggles with many-to-many ones and can become complex and rigid. The network model lets each record have multiple parents and children, forming a graph, and so handles many-to-many relationships efficiently.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-037 -->

- **Isolation: how much transactions see of each other**

  Of the four ACID properties, isolation is the one most often relaxed. It determines how a transaction's changes are visible to other users and systems. At its strictest, a transaction runs as if no others were running at the same time, a form called serializability. That is hard to implement in reality, so looser settings are often adopted. A lower level lets more users access the same data at once but increases concurrency effects such as dirty reads or lost updates. A higher level reduces those effects but needs more system resources and raises the chance that one transaction blocks another. It also makes deadlock more likely. To keep the highest isolation, a DBMS usually acquires locks on data, which can cost concurrency, or implements Multiversion concurrency control: readers never wait for writers. Most transactions can be built to avoid levels such as SERIALIZABLE, which cuts locking overhead. The programmer must then analyze access code carefully, because relaxed isolation can cause bugs that are hard to find. The database usually enforces isolation, though a client-side transaction manager can also provide it.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-040 -->

- **Primary and foreign keys: identifying and linking rows**

  Every row in a table needs an identity, and the primary key supplies it. Most implementations give each row a unique primary key. A new unique value is generated when a row is written, the system uses it primarily to access the table, and performance is optimized for it. Natural attributes are sometimes good primary keys, but a surrogate key is often used instead, an artificial attribute with no intrinsic meaning, such as a student ID. Natural keys often need several columns, called a composite key, which is one reason a single integer column is usually made the primary key. A foreign key is a column that holds the primary key of a row in another table. A key that migrates to another table becomes a foreign key there, and foreign keys need not be unique. The foreign key restricts an attribute to values that exist in the referenced table, which is how tables are cross-referenced. Most designs resolve many-to-many relationships with an extra table holding the primary keys of both entity tables.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-045 -->

- **Wide-column store: rows whose columns can vary**

  A wide-column store looks like a relational table, but each row is free to choose its own columns. It uses tables, rows and columns, yet column names and formats can vary from row to row. It can be read as a two-dimensional key-value store, where each value is identified by two keys, a row identifier and a column identifier. Columns are grouped into column families stored together on disk, inside a top-level keyspace. A row can span several families, and a family is often likened to a relational table. The name once meant column-oriented relational databases such as C-Store. It came to mean systems that keep column families together and drop the relational model: Bigtable: Google's structured storage at petabyte scale, the prototypical example, and Apache Cassandra: a database with no special node. Compared with relational databases they are denormalized, with columns added dynamically. Compared with document databases, they split records into column families that the database treats as units. Singh calls them highly scalable, able to handle petabytes, and names increased write time as a disadvantage.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-062 -->

- **OLTP and OLAP: serving users versus answering analysts**

  An ATM withdrawal and a business intelligence report make opposite demands on a database. OLTP systems serve transaction-oriented applications such as order entry, retail sales, financial transactions and ATMs, and they respond to users in real time. OLAP systems answer complex analytical queries for reporting and decision support.

  OLTP applications have high throughput, are insert- or update-intensive and serve hundreds of concurrent users. Their key goals are availability, speed, concurrency and recoverability. OLAP queries are much more complex and run in smaller volumes, and the workload is generally read-only. OLTP databases hold detailed, current data in normalized schemas, usually third normal form, and favor row-oriented systems. OLAP databases store aggregated, historical data in multi-dimensional schemas, usually star schemas, and benefit from column-oriented systems, because analytics usually selects specific fields rather than whole rows. OLTP performance is measured in transactions per second. OLAP has a low rate of transactions and complex queries with aggregations, so its measure is response time.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-051 -->

  *Figure: OLTP and OLAP compared on the same five properties.*

  | Aspect | OLTP | OLAP |
  |---|---|---|
  | Purpose | Transactions in real time | Analytical queries, reporting |
  | Operations | Read, insert, update, delete | Generally read-only |
  | Data | Detailed, current, normalized | Aggregated, historical, star schemas |
  | Storage | Row-oriented | Column-oriented |
  | Measured by | Transactions per second | Response time |

- **Data warehouse: a separate copy built for analysis**

  Long analysis queries and fast transactions fight over locks in the same database. A data warehouse ends the fight by keeping a separate copy for analysis. It is a central repository of data integrated from disparate sources and organized for reporting and analysis, used by analysts and managers to make decisions. Data from operational systems such as marketing or sales is uploaded, often cleansed first, and the warehouse stores current and historical data. Operational databases keep a snapshot of the business, while warehouses keep history and favor column-oriented storage, because analytic access selects specific fields. Warehouse data is subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and nonvolatile: it spans a long horizon, up to 10 years, and is read-only once loaded unless a regulatory obligation requires change. There are two main storage approaches. The dimensional approach (Kimball) uses star schemas, and the normalized approach (Inmon) stores third-normal-form tables grouped by subject area. A data lake instead keeps large volumes of data raw and processes it at run time.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-170 -->

- **Star and snowflake schemas: shaping warehouse data**

  A star schema takes its name from its shape: a fact table at the center, referencing any number of dimension tables around it. It is the simplest data mart schema style and the most widely used for warehouses. Facts hold measurable, quantitative data such as sales price, quantity, distance or weight, while dimensions hold descriptive attributes such as product models, colors, sizes, locations and salesperson names. Fact tables record metrics for specific events as numeric values plus foreign keys to dimensions, so they accumulate many rows. Dimension tables have relatively few records but many attributes each. Star schemas are denormalized: relaxing normalization gives simpler join logic, faster read-only queries and aggregations, and fewer joins per query. An analytic query usually joins one large fact table with a handful of small dimensions, as in a sales example that joins Fact_Sales to Dim_Date, Dim_Store and Dim_Product. A snowflake schema instead normalizes the dimension hierarchies into multiple linked tables. That reduces repeated data and improves integrity but needs more joins, and Kimball advises avoiding it without clear need.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-052 -->

  *Figure: In the sales example the fact table sits at the center and references three dimension tables.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  F[Fact_Sales] --> A[Dim_Date]
  F --> B[Dim_Store]
  F --> C[Dim_Product]
  ```

- **Online analytical processing: slicing data cubes**

  It has been claimed that OLAP cubes answer complex queries in around 0.1% of the time the same question needs on OLTP relational data. Online analytical processing is an approach to quickly answering multi-dimensional analytical queries, part of business intelligence, in which users analyze data organized in cubes interactively.

  At its core is the cube: numeric facts called measures, categorized by dimensions, placed at the intersections of a hypercube and usually manipulated through a pivot-table-like interface. Its metadata is typically built from a star or snowflake schema. Three basic operations do the work. Roll-up aggregates along dimensions, such as offices up to a division. Drill-down navigates into detail, such as sales by product within a region. Slicing and dicing views a subset of the cube along other dimensions.

  Aggregations, built by coarsening granularity along dimensions, are the main reason OLAP is fast. Possible aggregations are so many that usually only a predetermined number are fully calculated, and the others are solved on demand. Choosing which is the view selection problem, which is NP-complete.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-168 -->

- **Connection pooling: reusing database connections**

  Serverless functions can flood a database with connections. AWS Lambda opens a new database connection per invocation, which under high concurrency can cause connection storms. A proxy such as Amazon RDS Proxy pools the connections to calm them. A connection pool is a cache of reusable database connections managed by the client or middleware. Pooling reduces the overhead of opening and closing connections, which improves performance. It matters for SQL databases, which typically use stateful binary protocols that keep session information such as the state of a transaction and prepared statements. DynamoDB and Cosmos DB use stateless HTTP-based protocols, which often reduces the need. Pool settings should match the database's capacity and the workload, since overprovisioned pools cause rejected connections, throttling, resource contention and higher latency. Idle pooled connections can break through NAT timeouts, dropped connections or session invalidation, and expired login tokens can invalidate them, forcing costly reconnection. Pooling is usually done on the client side, by libraries such as ADO.NET and JDBC, not by the database engine.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-176 -->

- **Database languages: four sublanguages**

  A database language is a special-purpose language for working with a database, each specific to a particular data model. Four sublanguages divide the work. Data control (DCL) handles access, data definition (DDL) handles tables and relationships, data manipulation (DML) inserts, updates and deletes, and data query (DQL) searches. SQL combines definition, manipulation and query in a single language, and all mainstream commercial relational DBMSs support it with varying conformance. A database language may also configure the DBMS, compute over query results by counting, summing, averaging, sorting and grouping, and enforce constraints.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-038 -->

- **SQL: the declarative language of relational data**

  SQL had two advantages over older read-write APIs such as ISAM or VSAM. One command could access many records, and the programmer no longer had to specify how to reach a record, with or without an index. SQL is a domain-specific language used to manage data, especially in a relational database management system. It is set-based and declarative, not imperative like C or BASIC, though extensions add procedural features. It was among the first commercial languages to use Codd's relational model. It became an ANSI standard in 1986 and an ISO standard in 1987, and despite departing from the model it became the most widely used database language. Virtually no implementation adheres fully to the standard, so most SQL code needs changes to port between systems. Date and time syntax, string concatenation, NULLs and comparison case sensitivity vary from vendor to vendor. The Null marker means the absence of a value, distinct from 0 or an empty string, and it enforces three-valued logic: true, false and unknown.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-066 -->

- **SQL vs NoSQL: a trade-off, not a contest**

  Claiming that NoSQL is simply better, or that SQL is not scalable, reflects poorly in an interview, Singh warns. He treats the choice as a trade-off to settle by requirements, not as a contest with a single winner. The advice is to pick the technology that fits the requirements better.

  The two kinds differ in how they are built and what they store. Relational databases are structured with predefined schemas, while non-relational ones are unstructured, distributed and have a dynamic schema. In SQL each record has a fixed schema chosen before data entry and changed only through migrations. In NoSQL fields are added on the fly and a record need not have every field. SQL is a very powerful language for defining and manipulating data, whereas NoSQL queries are focused on a collection of documents and the syntax differs between databases.

  Scaling and reliability pull in different directions. SQL databases usually scale vertically, which can get very expensive, and scaling across servers is challenging. NoSQL databases scale horizontally on cheap commodity hardware, and many distribute data across servers automatically. The vast majority of relational databases are ACID compliant, so for data reliability and safe transactions SQL is still the better bet. Most NoSQL solutions sacrifice ACID compliance for performance and the ability to scale.

  Pick SQL for structured data with a strict schema, relational data, complex joins, transactions and very fast lookups by index. Pick NoSQL for a flexible schema, non-relational data, no need for complex joins, a very data-intensive workload and very high throughput for IOPS.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-064 -->

  *Figure: SQL and NoSQL databases side by side.*

  |  | SQL | NoSQL |
  |---|---|---|
  | Schema | Fixed before data entry | Dynamic, fields added on the fly |
  | Scaling | Usually vertical | Horizontal, on commodity hardware |
  | ACID | Vast majority comply | Most sacrifice it |
  | Pick it for | Strict schema, complex joins, transactions | Flexible schema, very high throughput |

- **Spatial database: points, lines and polygons**

  Does this city lie inside that country? In a spatial database that question is an SQL query, with a function such as ST_Contains comparing the shapes. A spatial database is a general-purpose database, usually relational, enhanced with spatial data that represents objects in a geometric space, along with tools for querying and analyzing it. Most represent points, lines and polygons, with data types mostly based on the OGC Simple Features specification. A spatial extension adds spatial datatypes that store spatial data as column values. Because locations need a spatial reference system, the database also tracks and transforms coordinate systems. Ordinary indexes sort values in a linear order, which is not optimal for queries in two or three dimensions, so a spatial index handles multi-dimensional ordering. The preferred spatial index is typically the R-tree: indexing places, rectangles and polygons, which groups objects by minimum bounding rectangle. Almost all current relational and object-relational DBMSs have spatial extensions. Web mapping applications need them for dynamic data that changes frequently.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-175 -->

- **MOLAP, ROLAP and HOLAP: three ways to store OLAP data**

  OLAP systems are traditionally grouped by how they store data: multidimensional (MOLAP), relational (ROLAP) and hybrid (HOLAP). Vendors disagree about the specifics of each type's benefits, so treat the comparisons below as general tendencies.

  MOLAP, the classic form, stores data in an optimized multi-dimensional array rather than a relational database, and often precomputes derived data such as consolidations into a data cube. It generally delivers better performance and needs less storage thanks to specialized indexing and compression. It can suffer database explosion from many dimensions, precomputed results and sparse data.

  ROLAP works directly with relational databases and needs no precomputation. Base and dimension tables are relational tables, new tables hold the aggregates, and it depends on a specialized schema design. It scales better to large volumes and very high-cardinality dimensions and works with any SQL reporting tool. But it is generally slower than MOLAP, and aggregate tables need custom ETL code.

  Most commercial OLAP tools now use hybrid OLAP. It lets the designer choose what sits where: aggregations in MOLAP and detail in ROLAP, or recent data in MOLAP and older data in ROLAP.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-169 -->

- **Querying and indexing in NoSQL databases**

  Ask a NoSQL database for a field it has not indexed and it may simply scan everything. Many run full scans for queries on non-indexed fields and apply filters after retrieving the data, though products behave differently here. Modern ones add optimizations. MongoDB supports compound indexes, Cassandra offers secondary indexes and materialized views, and Redis uses custom indexing. Elasticsearch uses Inverted index: from words to the documents that hold them for text search but can still scan non-indexed fields. These systems are designed to scale and to do key-based operations efficiently. They excel at basic CRUD and key lookups, while suitability for complex queries or joins varies.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-068 -->

- **Database constraints: rules the data must satisfy**

  The string "ABC" is not an integer but 123 is, and a database can enforce exactly that distinction. Constraints are rules that restrict the data that can be stored in the relations of a database. They are usually expressions that return true or false for whether the data satisfies them. A constraint can apply to a single attribute, a tuple (a row), or an entire relation (a table). A domain, the set of possible values for an attribute, is itself a constraint. It can be narrowed further, such as limiting an integer attribute to values between 1 and 10. SQL does this with check constraints.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-046 -->

- **Relational operations: selection, projection and join**

  Codd's original relational algebra had eight operators in two groups of four. Queries on a relational database are expressed in relational calculus or relational algebra. Four operators come from set theory: union, intersection, set difference, and the cartesian product, which matches every tuple of one relation with every tuple of the other. The other four are selection (SELECT with a WHERE clause), projection (extracting only specified attributes), join (connecting relations by their common attributes) and division. In SQL an INNER JOIN prevents a cartesian product, so a query over N tables needs N-1 inner joins.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-048 -->

- **Handling relational data in NoSQL without joins**

  Most NoSQL databases cannot join data in queries, so the schema generally needs to be designed differently. There are three main techniques for handling relational data.

  The first is multiple queries: instead of one query, run several. NoSQL queries are often faster than SQL queries, so the cost may be acceptable, but if too many are needed another approach is more appropriate.

  The second is non-normalized data. Instead of storing only foreign keys, store the actual foreign values with the data, such as a username in each blog comment, so no further lookup is needed. Copied values must be changed in many places when they change, so this approach works better when reads are much more common than writes.

  The third is nesting data. In document databases like MongoDB, put more data in fewer collections. Blog comments can sit inside the post document, so one retrieval returns all the data a task needs.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-067 -->

- **Stored procedure: code that lives in the database**

  Some of an application's logic can live inside the database itself. A stored procedure is executable code that is associated with, and generally stored in, the database. It collects and customizes common operations, such as inserting a tuple into a relation, gathering usage statistics, or encapsulating complex business logic and calculations. Procedures can greatly reduce the information transferred within and outside a system. Access can also be granted only to the procedures and not directly to the tables, for added security. They are not part of the relational model, but all commercial implementations include them, often with vendor-specific procedural extensions to SQL.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-047 -->

- **Views and materialized views: computed relations**

  A view stores no data at all. Relations that store data are called base relations, and in implementations they are tables. Derived relations are computed by applying relational operations to other relations, and in implementations they are called views or queries. A materialized view goes the other way: it is a pre-computed data set derived from a query and stored for later use. Querying it is faster than querying the base table, significantly so for frequent or complex queries. Materialized views also enable data subsetting, which reduces network loads, and are mostly used for performance and for keeping copies.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-050 -->

- **Vector database: finding what is similar**

  Traditional databases look up records by exact match. A vector database finds records that are semantically similar to an input. It stores and retrieves embeddings, which are machine-learned vectors with a few hundred to tens of thousands of dimensions. Semantically similar items, whether words, documents, images or audio, get vectors close to each other. It typically uses approximate nearest neighbor algorithms, and uses include semantic search and recommendation engines. In retrieval-augmented generation, the prompt's embedding queries the database for relevant documents, which are added to the language model's context window.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-174 -->

- **Choosing a database by workload**

  No database is best at everything, so pick the kind that matches the workload. OLTP databases suit transactional systems requiring strong consistency, and OLAP databases are optimized for complex queries and data analysis. Full-text search databases give fast, flexible text search. Document stores hold and query JSON-like documents, and key-value stores offer high-speed, simple data models. Graph databases manage highly connected data. Vector databases store and retrieve vector representations efficiently, and geospatial databases specialize in location-based data and queries. Singh advises weighing both the ACID and BASE models, and the application's own requirements, when choosing.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-053 -->

- **Polyglot persistence: several databases in one system**

  Force one database to meet every requirement and the result can be a non-performant jack-of-all-trades, master of none, because different databases solve different problems. Polyglot persistence means using multiple data storage technologies within a single system to meet varying storage needs. The idea mirrors polyglot programming. As the right language for each job may beat one language for everything, an application can talk to several databases and use each for what it does best. Joins enforce relationships in a relational database but become problematic as data grows. A graph database may handle relationships at scale but not transactions, which relational systems serve better, and a document database can hold the unstructured part. Martin Fowler expects any decent-sized enterprise to use varied storage technologies for different kinds of data. He would first ask how the data will be manipulated and only then choose the technology. The approach has two major drawbacks: a significant increase in operational complexity, and no support for keeping data consistent across the separate stores.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-164 -->

- **BASE consistency model: looser than ACID**

  ACID promises a lot, and some databases deliberately promise less. BASE is a looser alternative that NoSQL databases often adopt to gain scale and resilience. It is built on three ideas: basic availability, soft state and a delayed kind of consistency. Its properties are much looser than ACID guarantees, and there is no direct one-for-one mapping between the two models. Basic availability means the database appears to work most of the time. Soft state means stores need not be write-consistent, nor replicas mutually consistent, all the time. The third idea, covered in Eventual consistency: every reader agrees, but not yet, is that data may not be consistent immediately but eventually becomes consistent. In the meantime reads remain possible but may give an incorrect response. To scale and stay highly available, the logic moves from the database to separate servers, so the database becomes more independent and focused on storing data.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-056 -->

- **ACID vs BASE: choosing by requirements**

  Singh says there is no right answer between ACID and BASE. Both models were designed to satisfy different requirements, so choosing a database means weighing both against the application's needs.

  A fully ACID database is the perfect fit where data reliability and consistency are essential. It fails the whole transaction if any step errors. Databases built around traditional ACID guarantees, such as relational ones, choose consistency over availability. SQL databases such as MySQL and PostgreSQL are structured over the ACID model.

  BASE systems, common in NoSQL, choose availability over consistency, though MongoDB and Redis keep consistency and compromise availability when the network splits. A BASE database lets users read inconsistent data temporarily and reaches consistency later. DynamoDB and ElasticSearch use the BASE architecture. Developers must then be more rigorous about consistent data and know the chosen database's BASE behavior. Planning around BASE limitations can be a major disadvantage compared with the simplicity of ACID transactions. A database leans toward one side, though some NoSQL databases show certain ACID traits.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-057 -->

- **Time series database: built for timestamped data**

  Early time series databases were data historians recording sensor measurements. Today they also track the health of infrastructure and applications and serve IoT telemetry, smart energy grids and financial tick data. A time series database is optimized for data that forms a sequence of points indexed in chronological order. The data is uniform, timestamps mapped to metric values, and it grows rapidly. Entries rarely need cross-table relationships, so relational constraints are skipped, and workloads seldom need indefinite retention, which cuts storage and speeds queries. Specialized compression such as delta encoding or Gorilla compression, temporal indexing, and lifecycle management that drops whole old partitions in bulk exploit that uniformity.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-172 -->

- **Concurrency control: keeping simultaneous transactions correct**

  Running transactions at the same time is safe only if something keeps them from corrupting one another. Concurrency control is the set of mechanisms in a DBMS that handle isolation and guarantee the correctness of concurrent transactions. It constrains the timing of data access operations to orders that have the serializability and recoverability properties, which typically reduces performance. Serializability is often compromised for better performance when correctness allows, but recoverability cannot be, because that typically violates database integrity. The most common method, Two-phase locking: acquire everything, then release, works through locks. A transaction must first acquire a lock on an object, and that may be blocked while another transaction holds one.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-043 -->

- **ETL and ELT: two ways to fill a warehouse**

  Two workflows load a data warehouse, and they differ in where the transformation happens. In ETL, a staging layer holds raw data extracted from each source, and an integration layer transforms it, often into an operational data store. The integrated data then moves into the warehouse database, arranged into dimensions, facts and aggregate facts, and an access layer helps users retrieve it. ETL is inherently a batch process in most implementations. ELT drops the separate transformation tool. Data is extracted from heterogeneous sources and loaded straight into a staging area inside the warehouse, where all transformations run before landing in target tables.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-171 -->

  *Figure: ETL transforms the data before it is loaded into the warehouse.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[Extract from sources] --> B[Transform] --> C[Load into warehouse]
  ```

  *Figure: ELT loads the raw data first and transforms it inside the warehouse.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[Extract from sources] --> B[Load into warehouse] --> C[Transform inside warehouse]
  ```

- **Multi-model database: several models, one backend**

  Most DBMSs are organized around one data model. A multi-model database stores, indexes and queries data in more than one, such as document, graph, relational and key-value, against a single, integrated backend. It answers the weakness of polyglot persistence, whose several products bring operational complexity and no consistency across stores. Reported advantages include ingesting varied formats such as CSV and JSON without extra effort, and one query language, such as AQL or SQL/JSON, over related data. Architectures differ. Some engines support models such as documents and graphs natively, while others layer each model over an engine such as a key-value store.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-173 -->

- **NewSQL: SQL with the scale of NoSQL**

  Financial and order-processing systems outgrew conventional relational databases yet needed transactional guarantees that NoSQL could not give. NewSQL tries to reconcile the two. It is a class of relational database systems that seek the online scale of NoSQL while keeping ACID guarantees. The relational model and SQL remain the primary interface. Typical applications have heavy OLTP volumes of short-lived transactions that touch little data. Systems fall into three groups. Some are shared-nothing clusters, where each node manages a subset of the data. Some put optimized storage behind a SQL interface. Others shard transparently across nodes that agree through Consensus: getting machines to agree despite failures.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-163 -->

- **N+1 query problem: one query plus N more**

  One query fetches a list, and then N more fetch details that the first query could have returned. That is the N+1 query problem. The data access layer executes N additional SQL statements to fetch data that the primary query could have retrieved. The larger N is, the more queries run and the larger the performance impact. It is commonly seen in ORM tools and in GraphQL: asking for exactly the data you need. The fix is to optimize the SQL query, or to use a dataloader that batches consecutive requests into a single data request.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-063 -->

- **Transaction states: from active to terminated**

  A transaction starts in the active state, where it is being executed. When it executes its final operation it is partially committed, and when all operations succeed it is committed and its effects are permanently established. If any check by the recovery system fails, it is failed and cannot proceed. The recovery manager then rolls back all its writes, restoring the database to its earlier state, and the transaction is aborted. The recovery module can restart or kill it. After a commit, or with no rollback, the system is consistent and ready for a new transaction, and the old one is terminated.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-065 -->

  *Figure: A transaction either commits, or fails and is rolled back, and a killed one ends in termination too.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Active] --> B[Partially committed]
  B --> C[Committed]
  A -->|check fails| D[Failed]
  D -->|rollback| E[Aborted]
  E -->|if killed| F[Terminated]
  C --> F
  ```

- **Database schema: the shape of the data**

  A schema defines the shape of a data structure, specifying what kinds of data can go where. It can be strictly enforced across the entire database, loosely enforced on part of it, or not exist at all. A table has columns like a spreadsheet, from two to a hundred or more, each holding values of one type, with one value per row. A table can hold thousands or millions of rows. In SQL every record conforms to a fixed schema, chosen before data entry and changed only through migrations. In NoSQL the schema is dynamic and fields can be added on the fly.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-049 -->

- **Multiversion concurrency control: readers never wait for writers**

  Locks make readers wait for writers, which causes contention, especially between long read transactions and update transactions. Multiversion concurrency control avoids that by keeping multiple copies of each data item. An update creates a newer version instead of overwriting. Each user therefore sees a snapshot of the database at one instant, and a writer's changes stay invisible to others until it commits. The version a transaction sees depends on the isolation level, and the most common pairing is Snapshot isolation: a private snapshot for each transaction, where a transaction observes the data as of when it started. Readers pick the version by timestamp or transaction ID. Reads and writes are isolated without locks, so writers do not block readers, though some databases such as Oracle still use locks. Obsolete versions need cleanup. PostgreSQL's VACUUM FREEZE sweeps and rewrites the table periodically. Other systems keep the latest version plus an undo log, which can run out of space and abort transactions. The cost is storing multiple versions. The benefit is that reads are never blocked, which matters for read-heavy workloads.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-054 -->

- **Two-phase locking: acquire everything, then release**

  A transaction never acquires a lock after releasing one. That single rule is two-phase locking, a pessimistic concurrency control method that guarantees conflict-serializability by making each transaction acquire all its locks before releasing any. Locks are acquired in an expanding phase with none released, then released in a shrinking phase with none acquired, and schedules obeying this are serializable. The basic protocol uses shared (read) and exclusive (write) locks. Reading needs a read or write lock, writing needs a write lock, and several locks on one object may coexist only if none is a write lock. Because locks block, the protocol can deadlock when two or more transactions block each other. Strict 2PL releases write locks only after the transaction commits or aborts. Strong strict 2PL also holds read locks until the end, and most commercial database systems use it. Conservative 2PL takes every lock before execution, so a lock holder never blocks. It over-locks under light contention and needs declared read and write sets, so it is rarely used. Do not confuse any of this with Two-phase commit: asking everyone to vote before committing.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-165 -->

- **PostgreSQL isolation levels: four names, three behaviors**

  PostgreSQL accepts the four standard levels, covered in Isolation levels: trading protection for concurrency, but implements only three distinct ones, all built on Multiversion concurrency control: readers never wait for writers. Read Uncommitted behaves like Read Committed, the only sensible mapping onto its architecture.

  Read Committed is the default. A SELECT sees only data committed before the query began, so two successive SELECTs in one transaction can see different data if others commit between them.
