It is fine for simple cases such as transferring $100 between accounts. It is unsuitable for complex search conditions, where one command can see an inconsistent snapshot.

  Repeatable Read sees only data committed before the transaction began. That is stronger than the standard requires. It prevents every phenomenon, phantom reads included, except anomalies whose committed results match no one-at-a-time ordering of the transactions. A Repeatable Read transaction that tries to modify a row changed by a concurrent committed transaction is rolled back with an error. Applications must then retry the whole transaction. The view is stable but not necessarily consistent with a serial execution, so business rules may need explicit locks.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-177 -->

- **Snapshot isolation: a private snapshot for each transaction**

  Oracle, and PostgreSQL before 9.1, call snapshot isolation their serializable mode, even though it is not serializable. The naming is confusing, so users must know the difference to avoid anomalous behavior.

  Snapshot isolation guarantees that all reads in a transaction see a consistent snapshot of the database. The transaction commits only if its updates do not conflict with concurrent updates made since that snapshot. It works on a personal snapshot taken when it starts, and a write-write conflict aborts it if the values it updated have been changed externally since. It is usually implemented within multiversion concurrency control, so the transaction need only store its list of updates, which is scanned for conflicts before commit.

  Oracle, MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and MongoDB, among others, adopted it. It performs better than serializability while still avoiding most, but not all, of the anomalies serializability avoids. It shows none of the anomalies the ANSI SQL-92 standard prohibited, yet it permits others such as Write skew: the anomaly snapshot isolation allows. PostgreSQL implements Repeatable Read with it, so successive SELECTs see the same data.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-166 -->

- **Isolation levels: trading protection for concurrency**

  A database may run your transaction at a stronger level than the one you asked for, and the standard allows it. Isolation levels are settings that control how much locking a transaction does when selecting data, trading protection from concurrency effects against concurrency. Each is stronger than those below it, so a request for Read committed may be performed as Repeatable read.

  SERIALIZABLE guarantees the same effect as some serial execution, in which each transaction runs to completion before the next begins. Lock-based systems hold read and write locks to the end and take range locks for ranged SELECTs. Without locks, a serializable system detects write collisions among concurrent transactions and lets only one of them commit. REPEATABLE READ keeps read and write locks until the end of the transaction but manages no range locks. Phantom reads can therefore occur, and Write skew: the anomaly snapshot isolation allows is possible in some systems. READ COMMITTED guarantees that any data read was committed when read, but promises nothing if the read is repeated. READ UNCOMMITTED allows dirty reads, so one transaction may see not-yet-committed changes made by others.

  The default level varies quite widely between DBMSs, and most transactional databases let the user set any level. The ANSI definitions, based on three read phenomena, have been criticized as ambiguous and as not reflecting the isolation many databases actually provide.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-041 -->

  *Figure: Each level is stronger than the ones below it.* (layers; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Read phenomena: dirty, non-repeatable and phantom reads**

  The SQL-92 standard names three read phenomena that can occur when a transaction retrieves data another transaction might have updated. A dirty read occurs when a transaction retrieves a row that another transaction has updated but not yet committed. If that update is rolled back, the first transaction's view of the row is wrong. A non-repeatable read occurs when a transaction retrieves a row twice and another transaction commits an update to that row in between. A phantom read occurs when a transaction retrieves a set of rows twice and another transaction commits an insert or removal in that set in between.

  Each phenomenon belongs to particular levels. Dirty reads occur only at READ UNCOMMITTED, non-repeatable reads at READ UNCOMMITTED and READ COMMITTED, and phantom reads at every level except SERIALIZABLE.

  The standard only specifies which phenomena must not occur at each level, so a database may give stronger guarantees. PostgreSQL's Repeatable Read, for example, allows no phantom reads. Being free of all three is necessary but not sufficient for a serializable schedule. A fourth phenomenon shows why: a group of transactions whose committed result is inconsistent with every possible ordering of running them one at a time. Another is Write skew: the anomaly snapshot isolation allows, in which two writers who each read the same columns both update them, leaving data that mixes the two transactions.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-042 -->

  *Figure: Which read phenomena the SQL standard allows at each level.*

  | Level | Dirty | Non-repeatable | Phantom |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | READ UNCOMMITTED | Yes | Yes | Yes |
  | READ COMMITTED | No | Yes | Yes |
  | REPEATABLE READ | No | No | Yes |
  | SERIALIZABLE | No | No | No |

- **Write skew: the anomaly snapshot isolation allows**

  A bank lets either of two accounts run a deficit as long as their total stays at or above zero. Two concurrent $200 withdrawals each check against their own snapshot, both commit, and the total ends at -$200. That is write skew: two concurrent transactions read an overlapping data set, make disjoint updates and both commit, unaware of each other. Under serializability it is impossible, because one of the two transactions would have to occur first and be visible to the other. Snapshot isolation permits it.

  The fix is to force a write-write conflict. One way is a conflict table that both transactions update. Another is promoting a read to a write, such as Oracle's SELECT FOR UPDATE. The workarounds have costs. A table that materializes the constraint violates normal form, promotion is not always possible, and snapshot isolation leaves the user to maintain non-trivial constraints.

  Serializable Snapshot Isolation removes the workarounds. It detects and aborts dangerous triplets of concurrent transactions, as Cahill and colleagues showed in 2008, at the cost of more aborts. PostgreSQL 9.1 adopted it.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-167 -->

### Indexes, normalization and storage engines

A database is only as fast as the structure it uses to find a row, and only as trustworthy as the way its tables are laid out. This chapter covers both. Normalization structures a relational database to reduce redundancy and improve integrity, and the anomalies it prevents are the side effects of getting that wrong. An index is a data structure that finds rows quickly at the cost of extra writes and storage, and it comes in many shapes: hash tables, B-trees, inverted indexes and R-trees. Underneath sits the storage engine, the part of the database responsible for putting data into permanent storage, with a write-ahead log recording changes before they reach the data.

- **Normalization: storing each fact in one place**

  Store every fact in exactly one place, and a whole class of inconsistencies cannot happen. That is the promise of database normalization: structuring a relational database by formal rules, to cut down repeated data and improve the integrity of what is stored. Edgar F. Codd first proposed it as part of his relational model. The rules are applied in one of two ways, by synthesis, which creates a new database design, or by decomposition, which improves an existing one. The rules themselves form a ladder (see Normal forms: a ladder of stricter rules).

  Normalization organizes a database's columns and tables so that integrity constraints enforce their dependencies properly. The goal is that each elementary fact is recorded in only one place, so insertions, updates and deletions maintain consistency automatically. The benefits are concrete: less repeated data, more consistent data, a better data design and enforced referential integrity. A fully normalized database can also take new types of data with minimal changes to its structure, so the applications that use it are minimally affected.

  The costs are just as concrete: a more complex data design, more joins, slower performance and maintenance overhead. Some designs therefore give up part of normalization on purpose (see Denormalization: trading redundancy for read speed).

  <!-- sysd-blocks-093 -->

- **Database index: faster reads, slower writes**

  Without help, finding a row by one of its field values means testing rows one by one. That takes O(N) linear time on average, so the work grows in step with the size of the table. A database index is the help: a data structure that speeds up finding rows, at the cost of extra writes and storage to maintain it.

  An index is a copy of selected columns, much like a table of contents. It stores the column's values together with a key or pointer to the whole row, so the complete row can be retrieved efficiently. It can be built on one or more columns, which gives rapid random lookups and efficient ordered access. Many designs reach logarithmic O(log(N)) lookup, and some applications can reach flat O(1) lookup. Either way, the lookup is sub-linear.

  The bargain is write speed and storage in exchange for read speed. The index must be updated along with the data, so writes slow down, and designs balance lookup speed, index size and update cost. Indexes also create different views of the same data, so a large data set can offer different filters or sorting schemes without extra copies. Some databases index values transformed by a function or expression, such as upper(last_name), or build a partial index covering only records that meet a condition. Because many transactions access an index at once, it also needs concurrency control.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-084 -->

- **Hash table: jumping straight to the value**

  A hash table finds a value without searching for it. The key is hashed (see Hash function: any input, one fixed-size value), and the hash says where the value is stored. In a well-dimensioned table, the average lookup time does not depend on how many elements it holds. Search, insert and delete cost Θ(1) on average, against O(n) in the worst case. Hash tables implement associative arrays, in-memory tables, caches and sets, and Python dictionaries, Java HashMap and Go maps are built on them.

  Most hash functions are imperfect, so different keys can get the same index. Those collisions must be handled, typically by separate chaining or open addressing (see Hash collision resolution: chaining or probing). The load factor, the ratio of stored elements to slots, also matters. Performance deteriorates as it grows, so implementations keep it below a maximum and resize, or rehash, the table when it is reached. Rehashing is simple but expensive, so real-time systems may resize gradually. A hash table can also serve as a disk-based database index, although a tree-based index is more popular there (see B-tree: a search tree that grows wide, not tall).

  <!-- sysd-blocks-182 -->

- **B-tree: a search tree that grows wide, not tall**

  A B-tree is a search tree that grows wide instead of tall. It is a self-balancing tree that keeps data sorted and allows searches, sequential access, insertions and deletions in logarithmic time. It generalizes the binary search tree by letting nodes have more than two children, which lowers the tree's height and puts the data in fewer separate blocks. Fewer blocks matter most on disk, which has high latency and large blocks, so databases and file systems use B-trees.

  In Knuth's definition, a B-tree of order m has at most m children per node. Non-root internal nodes have at least m/2 (rounded up), and all leaves are on the same level. A non-leaf node with k children holds k-1 keys, which act as separation values dividing its subtrees. Search starts at the root and follows, at each level, the child whose key range contains the search value. Because child counts may vary within a range, a B-tree rebalances less often than other self-balancing trees. The price is some wasted space in nodes that are not full.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-103 -->

- **Write-ahead log: record the change before making it**

  Pull the plug in the middle of a transaction and the database still has to come back whole. Write-ahead logging is the family of techniques that makes this possible. Changes are first recorded in an append-only log on stable storage, and only then written to the database. It gives a database atomicity and keeps committed changes safe, two of the ACID guarantees (see ACID: four guarantees for every transaction).

  The central rule is that changes to data files may be written only after the log records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage. Because of that, data pages need not be flushed at every commit. After a crash, changes not yet applied to the data pages are redone from the log, which is roll-forward recovery, also called REDO. The log also cuts disk writes. Only the sequentially written log file must be flushed to commit a transaction, and one fsync of it may commit many concurrent small transactions. Archiving the log allows recovery to a chosen moment: restore an earlier physical copy, then replay the log to the desired time.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-185 -->

- **Storage engine: where the database meets permanent storage**

  When you save a row, something has to decide how its bytes reach permanent storage. That something is the storage engine, the part of the database engine responsible for putting data into permanent storage. It uses low-level storage structures to serialize the data model, so the data can be written to the chosen medium, and techniques such as indexing may improve performance. In storage, data sits in structures that look completely different from the conceptual level, arranged to make reconstructing it quick when users and programs need it.

  A DBMS usually reaches storage through the operating system and its file systems. Storage properties and settings are extremely important for efficient operation, so administrators maintain them closely. Conventional storage is row-oriented, but column-oriented databases also exist. For indexing, the B-tree is the most widely used structure in almost all relational databases. LSM-trees (see Log-structured merge-tree: built for a flood of writes) are widely used by NoSQL databases such as Cassandra, LevelDB and RocksDB.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-111 -->

- **Inverted index: from words to the documents that hold them**

  Reading every word of every document to answer one query is often not technically realistic. An inverted index avoids it: a database index that maps content, such as words, to its locations in a table or in a document or set of documents. It is the most popular data structure in document retrieval systems and a central component of search engines.

  Start with a forward index, which stores the list of words per document. Invert it and you get the list of documents per word. With that list, a query jumps to the word by random access, finds the matching documents quickly and then ranks them by relevance. The price is more processing whenever a document is added.

  A basic Boolean index records only whether a word occurs in a document, so it finds matches without ranking them. A word-level one also stores each word's positions, which supports phrase search at a cost in processing power and space. PostgreSQL's GIN indexes are inverted indexes with a separate entry for each component value, suited to values such as arrays.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-186 -->

- **R-tree: indexing places, rectangles and polygons**

  Finding every museum within 2 km of a location is the kind of question an R-tree answers. R-trees are tree data structures for spatial access methods, indexing multi-dimensional information such as geographical coordinates, rectangles or polygons, and spatial databases typically prefer them. The key idea is to group nearby objects and represent them by their minimum bounding rectangle one level up. A query that misses a bounding rectangle cannot hit any object inside it.

  So search compares each rectangle in a node with the query rectangle and descends only into overlapping children. Most nodes are never read, and at the leaves the stored objects are tested precisely. Like a B-tree, an R-tree is balanced, organizes data in pages and is designed for disk storage. Insertion descends into the subtree needing least enlargement of its bounding box, and a full node is split by a heuristic. The difficulty is a tree that stays balanced while its rectangles neither cover much empty space nor overlap much. R-trees give no worst-case guarantee, but they perform well on real-world data.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-187 -->

- **Anomalies: how an unnormalized table goes wrong**

  Hire a faculty member who has no course yet. A badly designed table may have no place to record them, unless the Course Code is set to null. That is an insertion anomaly, one of three undesirable side effects that can arise when a relation, the formal name for a table, has not been sufficiently normalized.

  An update anomaly appears when the same information sits on several rows. Change an address on some skill records only, and the relation is left inconsistent. A deletion anomaly appears when deleting data for one fact forces deleting a different fact. Remove a faculty member's last course record, and the faculty member is lost with it.

  Codd's objectives for normalization (see Normalization: storing each fact in one place) included freeing relations from these insertion, update and deletion dependencies and reducing the need to restructure as new data types are introduced. Most relations in third normal form (see Normal forms: a ladder of stricter rules) are free of all three anomalies.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-094 -->

- **B-trees and disk reads: why wide nodes win**

  At about 10 milliseconds per read, finding one record among a million takes 20 disk reads, or 0.2 seconds. A disk read costs far more than comparing keys, thanks to seek time and rotational delay. The fix is to index the index. An auxiliary index holds the first record of each disk block and is about 1% of the size of the original database. Searching it tells which one block to read. Index that index again and it has only 100 entries, small enough to fit in one disk block. Three block reads then replace 14, and the record takes 30 milliseconds instead of 150.

  This hierarchy of blocks, from a root block down to the leaf level, is the core idea behind the B-tree. Search cost falls from roughly log2 N disk reads to logb N, where b is the blocking factor: with 100 entries per block, log100 1,000,000 is 3 reads. When an index is searched often, its upper levels may sit in a disk cache and cost no disk read at all.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-104 -->

  *Figure: Disk reads to find one record in a million fall from 20 to 14 to 3 as the index is indexed again.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **B+ tree and B* tree: two refinements of the B-tree**

  Db2, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite all index their tables with a variant of the B-tree called the B+ tree. A B+ tree can be viewed as a B-tree whose nodes hold only keys, not key-value pairs, with an added bottom level of linked leaves.

  Internal nodes hold no record pointers, so every record pointer sits in a leaf. The result is a high fanout, meaning many children per node, typically 100 or more. That makes the tree shallow and cuts the I/O operations needed to find an element. Leaves are often linked in a list, which makes range queries and ordered iteration simpler and more efficient. A B-tree cannot build such a list, since not all its keys are in the leaves.

  The B* tree is a different refinement. It keeps non-root nodes at least 2/3 full instead of 1/2. It postpones costly node splits by sharing keys with a neighboring node, a spill that needs no new node.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-105 -->

- **Clustered and non-clustered indexes: where the rows live**

  A table's rows can sit on disk in only one order, so a table can have only one clustered index. A clustered index stores the rows in the order of the index key, while a non-clustered index is a separate sorted structure that points to rows stored elsewhere.

  Clustering helps mainly when data is read sequentially in index order or as a range, because neighboring rows are adjacent and fewer data block reads are needed. A non-clustered index keeps its keys in sorted order, and its leaf level points to each record, so the physical row order differs from the index order. A table can have many of them, usually on non-primary-key columns used in JOIN, WHERE and ORDER BY clauses. The difference shows in the leaf. In Microsoft SQL Server, the leaf node of a clustered index is the actual data, not a pointer to data stored elsewhere as in a non-clustered index.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-085 -->

- **Log-structured merge-tree: built for a flood of writes**

  Writing data sequentially is cheaper than scattering it in separate random access requests, and the log-structured merge-tree, or LSM tree, is built on that fact. It suits indexed access to files with a high insert volume, such as transactional log data. It keeps key-value pairs in two or more separate structures, each optimized for its storage medium.

  In a two-level LSM tree, a smaller component, C0, lives entirely in memory and C1 lives on disk. New records go into C0, and when it exceeds a size threshold, a contiguous segment of it is merged into C1. Sequential writing cuts total seek time on hard disks and latency on solid-state storage.

  LSM trees were designed for write-intensive workloads. When reads and writes mix, compaction, the merging of segments, invalidates cached data in buffer caches, and reads can see high latency and low throughput. Cassandra uses an LSM tree index to optimize write throughput, in contrast to the B-tree indexes most databases use.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-108 -->

- **Denormalization: trading redundancy for read speed**

  Normalizing a database spreads its facts across many tables, and reading them back takes joins. Across several relations stored as separate files, a join can be slow, even prohibitively so. Denormalization is the strategy applied to a previously normalized database to increase performance, by adding redundant copies of data or grouping data. It improves read performance at the expense of some write performance, often to cope with very large numbers of reads.

  There are two strategies. The DBMS can store and keep consistent the redundant copies, as with indexed or materialized views, or the designer can denormalize the logical design by hand. A hand-made design can match the query speed. But the designer must keep the copies consistent with constraints that slow writes, so under heavy write load it may perform worse than the normalized design. Denormalization should come only after a satisfactory level of normalization, such as third normal form. The gains are faster retrieval and easier queries; the costs are expensive inserts and updates and a greater chance of inconsistent data.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-107 -->

- **Hash collision resolution: chaining or probing**

  Two keys that hash to the same index must both still be found. Separate chaining builds a linked list of key-value pairs for each array index and traverses the list during a lookup. Open addressing stores every entry in the bucket array itself. It probes from the hashed-to slot, by linear probing, quadratic probing or double hashing, until it finds an empty slot. Open addressing degrades sharply as its load factor nears 1, with a maximum of about 0.6 to 0.75. Chaining degrades gradually, with the best maximum typically between 1 and 3. Cuckoo hashing guarantees O(1) worst-case lookup.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-183 -->

- **B-tree versus LSM-tree: faster reads or faster writes**

  The biggest difference between a B-tree and an LSM-tree can be said in one line: a B-tree enables faster reads, while an LSM-tree enables fast writes. The B-tree is the most widely used indexing data structure in almost all relational databases, and its basic unit of storage is usually called a page. A lookup traces down the range of keys until it finds the actual value. LSM-trees are widely used by NoSQL databases such as Cassandra, LevelDB and RocksDB. An LSM-tree keeps key-value pairs and persists them to disk in a Sorted Strings Table (SSTable) with sorted keys. Level 0 segments are periodically merged into level 1 by compaction.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-099 -->

  *Figure: The two index structures side by side: what each is good at, how it stores data and who uses it.*

  |  | B-tree | LSM-tree |
  |---|---|---|
  | Strength | Faster reads | Fast writes |
  | Stored as | Pages | Sorted Strings Tables |
  | Used by | Almost all relational databases | Cassandra, LevelDB, RocksDB |

- **Index data structures: no single best choice**

  A database index can be built on several data structures, and the best choice depends on the workload. The format that fits depends on whether data is indexed in memory or on disk, on the data formats, and on whether the system is write-heavy or read-heavy.

  A few structures recur. A skiplist (see Skip list: a linked list with shortcuts) is a common in-memory index type. A hash index is a common implementation of a map, and an SSTable is an immutable on-disk map. Two of the designs built from them differ sharply. An LSM tree combines a skiplist with SSTables for high write throughput, while a B-tree is a disk-based structure with consistent read and write performance. Other structures serve narrower questions. An inverted index serves document indexing, a suffix tree serves string pattern search, and an R-tree serves multi-dimensional search such as finding the nearest neighbor. Among the popular implementations are balanced trees, B+ trees and hashes.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-090 -->

  *Figure: Each index structure is matched with the job the facts name for it.*

  | Structure | What it serves |
  |---|---|
  | Skiplist | In-memory index |
  | Hash index | Implementing a map |
  | SSTable | Immutable on-disk map |
  | LSM tree | High write throughput |
  | B-tree | Consistent reads and writes on disk |
  | Inverted index | Document indexing |
  | Suffix tree | String pattern search |
  | R-tree | Multi-dimensional search, such as nearest neighbor |

- **PostgreSQL index types and what each is for**

  CREATE INDEX makes a B-tree by default, which fits the most common situations. The USING keyword picks another of PostgreSQL's types: Hash, GiST, SP-GiST, GIN and BRIN, plus the bloom extension. B-trees handle equality and range queries on sortable data and serve prefix patterns such as LIKE 'foo%', but not LIKE '%bar'. Hash indexes handle only equality. GiST covers geometric types and nearest-neighbor searches, and SP-GiST supports non-balanced structures such as quadtrees and tries. GIN indexes are inverted indexes for values with several components, such as arrays. BRIN indexes summarize block ranges by minimum and maximum, so they suit columns that correlate with physical row order.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-188 -->

- **Skip list: a linked list with shortcuts**

  A skip list gives O(log n) average search and insertion in an ordered sequence of n elements. It is a probabilistic data structure built as a linked hierarchy of subsequences, each skipping fewer elements than the one above. The bottom layer is an ordinary ordered list; each element appears one layer up with a fixed probability p. A search starts in the top list and moves right until the current element is greater than or equal to the target, then drops a level. Unlucky coin flips can unbalance it, so there is no absolute worst-case guarantee. Redis uses them for ordered sets, and RocksDB for its default memtable.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-184 -->

- **LSM-tree writes and compaction: buffer, flush, merge**

  An LSM tree does not edit data on disk. Every write lands first in an in-memory component, often a skip list or B+ tree. When that buffer is full, it is flushed sequentially to disk as an immutable sorted component, which avoids costly random writes. To keep data safe across a crash, the system may record every incoming write in a write-ahead log before adding it to the buffer.

  As data accumulates on disk, a merge process, much like merge sort, consolidates entries across levels. Moving level 0 segments into level 1 is called compaction. Since components are immutable, an update is treated as a new write, and a delete is marked with a tombstone entry. Obsolete entries and tombstones are removed later, during merging.

  How often to merge is a policy choice. Leveling keeps one component per level and merges often, which gives fewer components but more write amplification, meaning data is rewritten more often. Tiering allows several components per level and merges less often, which lowers write amplification but raises read costs.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-109 -->

  *Figure: A write is buffered in memory, flushed to disk as a sorted component and later merged by compaction.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Incoming write] --> C[In-memory buffer]
  A -.->|may log first| B[Write-ahead log]
  C -->|buffer full: flush| D[Immutable sorted component]
  D -->|merge: compaction| E[Next level on disk]
  ```

- **B-tree insertion and deletion: split and merge**

  A B-tree grows from the top: when a split reaches the root, the tree gets taller. Inserting starts with a search for the right leaf. If the leaf has fewer than the maximum number of elements, the key goes in, in order. Otherwise the node splits into two around a median key, and the median moves up to the parent as a separation value. The parent may split in turn. In deletion, a node left below the minimum takes an element from a sibling that can spare one, which is called a rotation. Otherwise it merges with a sibling, and merging can continue up to the root.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-106 -->

- **Bitmap index: bit arrays for values that repeat**

  Common indexes such as B+ trees work best when the indexed values do not repeat, or repeat only a few times. A bitmap index is built for the opposite case: values that repeat very frequently, such as a field with at most three distinct values. It stores most of its data as bit arrays and answers queries by performing bitwise logical operations on them. For such variables, it can have a significant performance advantage over the commonly used trees.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-091 -->

- **Covering index: answering from the index alone**

  An index normally only points the way, and the database still has to read the row it points to. A covering index removes that last step: it contains all the fields a query needs, so the query is answered without reading the table record. To find the Name for ID 13, an index on (ID) still requires reading the record, but an index on (ID, Name) does not. The speedup can be dramatic, but the extra keys make the index large and slow down inserts and updates. Some systems, with an INCLUDE clause, keep non-key fields only at the leaf level for a smaller covering index.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-087 -->

- **Dense and sparse indexes: every row or some rows**

  Should an index have an entry for every row, or only for some? A dense index holds the search key and a pointer to the actual record for every row. It needs more write-time maintenance and more memory than a sparse one, but values are found with a binary search and the data need not be ordered. A sparse index has entries for only some records, such as one per data block. It needs less maintenance, makes inserts, updates and deletes faster and uses less memory. Finding data through it is slower, because a scan across the page typically follows the binary search.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-100 -->

- **Indexes and database constraints: rules enforced by indexes**

  Many of a database's rules are enforced by indexes. Databases use them for constraints such as UNIQUE, EXCLUSION, PRIMARY KEY and FOREIGN KEY. Declaring an index UNIQUE creates an implicit constraint on the underlying table. Databases usually create an index implicitly on columns declared PRIMARY KEY, and some can reuse an existing index to enforce that constraint. Many require both the referencing and the referenced columns of a FOREIGN KEY to be indexed, which improves inserts, updates and deletes on the tables involved. An EXCLUSION constraint ensures that a predicate holds for no other record; it can implement UNIQUE or rules such as no overlapping time ranges.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-089 -->

- **Types of database indexes beyond trees and hashes**

  Beyond the main tree and hash designs, databases use many other index types. A dense index holds a key-pointer pair for every record of the sorted data file, while a sparse index holds one only for every block. A reverse-key index reverses the key before entering it, so 24538 becomes 83542, which suits sequence numbers whose new values increase monotonically. A primary index holds the table's key fields with a pointer to the non-key fields and is created automatically with the table. A secondary index covers fields that are neither ordering nor key fields.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-092 -->

- **Pessimistic and optimistic locking: assume the worst or the best**

  Locks keep data consistent in a multi-user environment by preventing simultaneous modifications. Pessimistic locking assumes conflicts will occur, so it locks the data before any change and blocks other users until the lock is released. Optimistic locking assumes conflicts are rare. It lets multiple users access data at once, checks for conflicts when changes are committed and rolls the operation back if one is detected. Pessimistic locking is safer for the data but can hurt performance, while optimistic locking is better for efficiency. Good practice is to hold locks for the minimum time, lock rows rather than whole tables, and retry transactions that fail due to conflicts.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-098 -->

- **LSM-tree lookups and range queries: checking newest first**

  A point lookup in an LSM tree checks the in-memory component first, then the disk levels in order. Newer levels come before older ones because they hold the latest updates and deletions. It stops as soon as it finds the key. A Bloom filter kept for each on-disk component can show that a key is definitely absent, so the component is skipped unread. Without Bloom filters a point lookup costs O(L), because each level must be searched; with them, a lookup of an existing key costs O(1). A range query scans each component and merges the results in a priority queue to reconcile duplicates, updates and deletes.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-110 -->

- **Database keys: primary, candidate, foreign and surrogate**

  A key is a column or group of columns that identifies rows of a table. A primary key uniquely identifies every row, and a composite key is a primary key made up of multiple columns. A candidate key is a set of attributes that identifies rows uniquely. A super key is the set of all keys that can do so. Keys that are not the primary key are alternate keys. A foreign key is a reference to the primary key of another table. A surrogate key is a system-generated value that identifies each entry when no other column could hold the properties of a primary key.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-101 -->

- **Composite index column order: why it matters**

  Think of a phone book ordered by city, then last name, then first name. Listing one city's numbers is easy, but finding every entry for one last name is tedious. An index on several columns behaves the same way. Row identifiers can be retrieved using only the first indexed column. On most databases, it is not possible or efficient to use only the second or a later column. With an index on (city, last_name, first_name), a search on city and first_name uses only city, then checks first_name sequentially. To improve performance, create the index with its columns in the order of the search columns.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-086 -->

- **Full table scans and the limits of indexes**

  Without an index, a query on last_name must look at that column on every row, which is a full table scan. With an index, the database follows the index structure, which is much cheaper. But a leading wildcard such as LIKE '%@wikipedia.org' cannot use the index, which assumes words go from left to right, so the database performs a full index scan. An extra index on reverse(email_address), queried with the reversed pattern, puts the wildcard at the right-most part, where the index works. With wildcards on both sides, a sequential search takes O(N) time; trigrams, three-letter fragments of text, in a GIN index lower lookup to about O(logN).

  <!-- sysd-blocks-088 -->

- **Functional dependencies: which columns determine which**

  Which columns depend on which? A functional dependency is a relationship between two attributes, typically between the primary key and a non-key attribute within a table. Second normal form requires that every non-candidate-key attribute depend on the whole candidate key, not just part of it, so the table must have no partial dependency. A transitive functional dependency occurs when a non-key attribute determines another attribute, such as Author Nationality depending on Author, which in turn depends on Title. Third normal form does not permit it. Both rules are part of a longer ladder (see Normal forms: a ladder of stricter rules).

  <!-- sysd-blocks-102 -->

- **Normal forms: a ladder of stricter rules**

  Normal forms are a ladder of increasingly strict rules for relations, from first normal form to sixth normal form. From least to most normalized they run UNF (unnormalized), 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, EKNF, BCNF, 4NF, ETNF, 5NF, DKNF and 6NF. Informally, a relation is called normalized if it meets third normal form. Normal forms beyond 4NF are mainly of academic interest, because the problems they solve rarely appear in practice.

  1NF requires scalar columns that cannot hold relations or composite values. 2NF requires every non-prime attribute, one that belongs to no candidate key, to depend on the whole of every candidate key. 3NF requires every non-trivial functional dependency to begin with a superkey, a set of columns that identifies rows uniquely, or to end with a prime attribute. BCNF is a slightly stronger version of 3NF, sometimes called 3.5NF. It addresses anomalies that 3NF as originally defined does not handle. It requires 3NF and that every functional dependency X to Y has a superkey X.

  Real-world designs cannot always comply perfectly. Singh advises that if one of the first three rules is violated, the application must anticipate problems such as redundant data and inconsistent dependencies. The history is short: Codd introduced 1NF in 1970, 2NF and 3NF in 1971, and, with Boyce, the Boyce-Codd normal form in 1974. Fagin added 4NF in 1977 and 5NF in 1979.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-095 -->

  *Figure: The normal forms were introduced one after another between 1970 and 1979.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Normalizing a table to third normal form, step by step**

  Normalization is climbing a ladder, one rung at a time. A higher normal form cannot be reached until the previous levels are satisfied, although some steps can be skipped when the data is already partly normalized. The example follows a table of books.

  First normal form needs each field to hold a single value, so a Subject field holding a set of values is extracted into a separate Title-Subject table. Second normal form needs every non-candidate-key attribute to depend on the whole candidate key. Price depended on Format as well as Title, so Price moves to its own table keyed by Title and Format. Third normal form removes transitive dependencies: Author Nationality depends on Author, which depends on Title, so nationality, publisher country and genre name each move into their own tables. For fourth normal form, suppose every book is offered in each location. Title is then not bound to a Location, so the Franchisee-Book-Location table is split into Franchisee-Book and Franchisee-Location. Fixing a violation of one normal form often also fixes a violation of a higher one.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-096 -->

  *Figure: Each step splits out the data that breaks one normal form.*

  | Form | What breaks it | Fix |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1NF | Subject holds a set of values | Separate Title-Subject table |
  | 2NF | Price depends on Format as well as Title | Price table keyed by Title and Format |
  | 3NF | Nationality depends on Author, which depends on Title | Nationality, publisher country and genre name get their own tables |
  | 4NF | Title is not bound to a Location | Franchisee-Book and Franchisee-Location tables |

- **Sixth normal form and columnar stores**

  In sixth normal form, every row holds just the primary key and at most one other attribute. Its drawback is a proliferation of tables. A 5NF table with one key column and N attributes needs N tables, and multi-field updates, inserts and deletes touch several tables. So 6NF should not be used for online transaction processing. Data warehouses, which do not permit interactive updates, use an internal 6NF representation in some DBMSs, known as a columnar data store. Column-oriented storage can save significant space through compression when a column has far fewer unique values than the table has rows, and it speeds up range queries.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-097 -->

### Storage systems

Every system you design eventually answers two questions: where does the data live, and what happens when the power goes out? The answer starts with a split in memory itself, because volatile memory needs power to keep its contents while non-volatile memory retains them after power is removed. The storage hierarchy ranks storage from primary memory, which the CPU reads directly, down through slower and cheaper secondary, tertiary and offline storage. Two kinds of drive hold data for the long term: hard disk drives, which store it magnetically on rapidly rotating platters, and solid-state drives, which use integrated circuits, typically NAND flash. This chapter follows both, shows how they fail and connect, and sees how a database builds the ACID guarantee of {{ref:sysd-blocks-210}} on them before it moves up to block storage and the layers built on it.

- **Memory versus storage: how a computer keeps its bits**

  Every text, number, image and sound a computer holds is a string of bits. Computer data storage is the retention of digital data using computer components and recording media, and its most common unit is the byte, equal to 8 bits. Two words are easy to confuse. Faster, volatile components are generally called memory, while slower, persistent ones are called storage. In current usage, storage means devices the CPU cannot reach directly, and memory means semiconductor read-write storage, typically DRAM. Keeping data brings choices. Compression uses a shorter bit string and takes tens of percent less storage for many kinds of data, but it costs more computation and may delay access. Encryption keeps chunks of stored snapshots from being rebuilt without permission. Check data and extra copies let a computer detect a random bit flip and correct it, through disk mirroring or RAID: many drives acting as one safer drive. Every medium also fails in its own way: head crashes on mechanical hard drives and electronic faults in flash can cause instant total loss.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-139 -->

- **Hard disk drives: waiting for the platter to come around**

  At 7,200 rpm, a hard disk waits 4.16 ms on average for the right sector to spin under the head; at 5,400 rpm the wait is 5.55 ms. A hard disk drive (HDD) is an electro-mechanical device that stores digital data magnetically on rapidly rotating platters. Magnetic heads on a moving actuator arm read and write them, in any order, and the data persists when power is off. Mechanics limit access time: seek time to move the head to the right track, rotational latency, and the time to transfer the data. Access time has not kept up with throughput, which has not kept up with the growth in bit density and capacity. HDDs cost much less per bit than the drives of Solid-state drives: no moving parts, new ways to fail, which cost four to nine times more, and HDDs still dominate the volume of server storage produced. Each block carries error-correcting bits, so a typical 1 TB disk with 512-byte sectors spends about 93 GB on them. Because single drives fail, storage providers rely on redundant HDD arrays and replace failed drives continually.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-199 -->

- **Volatile memory: fast, and forgetful without power**

  Cut the power and volatile memory forgets everything, quickly. It needs power to keep its contents, and most general-purpose random-access memory (RAM) is volatile. It serves as primary storage, a role The storage hierarchy: from nanoseconds to robot arms explains. It is usually faster than mass storage such as a hard disk drive, and its forgetfulness has a use: sensitive information becomes unavailable on power-down. There are two kinds, and both need continuous electrical current. Dynamic RAM (DRAM) keeps each bit in a capacitor and needs only one capacitor and one transistor per bit, so it is space-efficient, inexpensive and very popular. Static RAM (SRAM) is much faster and needs no refreshes, but each bit takes a cell of six transistors, so it cannot reach DRAM's capacity. SRAM is commonly used as CPU cache, for processor registers and in networking devices.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-192 -->

- **Non-volatile memory: data that outlives the power**

  Pull the plug and some memory still remembers. Non-volatile memory retains stored information even after power is removed, which is why it is typically used for secondary storage or long-term persistent storage. Most forms are unsuitable as primary storage, because compared with volatile RAM they typically cost more, perform worse or have a limited lifetime.

  The family splits by how a location is reached. Electrically addressed memory, such as Flash memory: NOR for random reads, NAND for bulk and read-only memory, is generally expensive and limited in capacity but fast. Mechanically addressed memory, such as hard disks, optical discs, magnetic tape and holographic memory, costs less per bit but is slower. These use a recording head: tape is sequential, since it must pass the head, while hard disks and optical discs give random access.

  Read-only memory comes in grades. Mask ROMs are programmed only at the factory, and PROM can be written once. EPROM is erasable by ultraviolet light but clears the whole device at once. EEPROM erases with voltage, but slowly. Newer electrically addressed technologies include ferroelectric RAM, magnetoresistive RAM, phase-change memory and ReRAM. ReRAM was seen as a flash replacement, but its cost and performance benefits have not persuaded companies to switch. Non-volatile main memory, NVDIMM being one example, is primary storage with non-volatile attributes, and it presents security challenges.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-193 -->

  *Figure: Non-volatile memory splits by how a location is reached.* (tree; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Durability: a commit that survives the crash**

  A database says the transaction is committed, and then the machine crashes. Durability is the ACID guarantee that the effects of committed transactions survive permanently, even through failures and catastrophic events. A durable system must survive three kinds of failure. Transaction failures interrupt a transaction. System failures lose volatile storage in a crash. Media failures lose stable storage, typically a disk. Whatever happens, the changes of incomplete transactions are reverted. To survive the loss of volatile memory, the database flushes an immutable sequential log of transactions to non-volatile storage before acknowledging a commit. This is the write-ahead log. Because changes are logged before they modify database state, committed transactions can be redone from it after a crash, and incomplete ones undone. Against media failure, stable memory is built from copying and robust writing protocols such as disk mirroring. Offline copies, checkpoints, incremental dumps and differential files save space and time compared with replaying every log file from the start. In a distributed database all nodes must coordinate before a commit is acknowledged, usually by Two-phase commit: asking everyone to vote before committing.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-210 -->

- **The storage hierarchy: from nanoseconds to robot arms**

  Some data a computer reaches in nanoseconds. Other data takes 5 to 60 seconds, because a robot has to fetch it. The storage hierarchy ranks storage from primary memory, which the CPU reads directly, down through slower and cheaper secondary, tertiary and offline storage.

  Primary storage, or main memory, holds the instructions the CPU continuously reads and the data it is actively using. Secondary storage is not directly accessible by the CPU, so input/output channels transfer the desired data into primary storage. It is non-volatile and usually an HDD or SSD, with access time per byte in milliseconds against nanoseconds for primary storage. It is less expensive, so modern systems typically have two orders of magnitude more of it. It is addressable by block and moved in large contiguous blocks to reduce seek time and rotational latency. Using several disks in parallel, as in RAID: many drives acting as one safer drive, increases the bandwidth between primary and secondary memory and eases the I/O bottleneck.

  Tertiary storage uses a robotic arm to mount removable media. It suits archiving rarely accessed data in extraordinarily large stores, but it is much slower than secondary storage: 5 to 60 seconds against 1 to 10 milliseconds. Offline storage sits on media that are removed or disconnected, and unlike tertiary storage it cannot be accessed without human interaction.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-140 -->

  *Figure: Each layer down from the CPU is slower and cheaper than the one above.* (layers; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Flash memory: NOR for random reads, NAND for bulk**

  Flash memory is a solid-state chip that maintains stored data without any external power source. It is a close relative of EEPROM, but erase operations must be done on a block basis and its capacity is substantially larger. Two designs dominate. NOR flash gives high-speed random access, reading and writing specific locations, and can retrieve as little as a single byte. NAND flash reads and writes sequentially at high speed in blocks and reads faster than it writes, though it is slower at reading than NOR. At high densities NAND costs less and offers more capacity for the same silicon. NAND cells are classed by bits per cell. Single-level cells hold 1 bit and give the best performance and endurance, at higher cost. MLC, TLC and QLC cells hold 2, 3 and 4 bits, cost less, and perform and endure less. Many drives, such as those in Solid-state drives: no moving parts, new ways to fail, use 3D NAND, with cells stacked vertically, which raises density while improving performance and reducing costs.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-194 -->

- **Solid-state drives: no moving parts, new ways to fail**

  A random read on a consumer NAND solid-state drive typically takes 0.05 to 0.2 ms. On a high-end hard disk it takes 2.9 ms, and on a laptop one 12 ms. A solid-state drive (SSD) uses integrated circuits, typically NAND flash, to store data persistently. With no moving parts it offers lower latency, resistance to physical shock, lower power consumption and silent operation. The price: SSDs are generally more expensive per gigabyte and have a finite number of write cycles, while hard disks offer far more capacity for the money. Every SSD has a controller, an embedded processor running firmware that manages data flow between the NAND and the host. It does bad block mapping, ECC, garbage collection, wear leveling, caching and encryption. SSDs also fail differently: sudden power loss can leave incomplete writes, and one failed chip can lose all data on it. Studies find lower failure rates than HDDs but more uncorrectable errors, and firmware bugs are a major cause of data loss.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-195 -->

  *Figure: On a log scale, the random access times of consumer NAND SSDs and hard disks sit far apart.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **How hard disks fail, and how drives hide it**

  The dramatic failure is the head crash: the head scrapes the platter and grinds away its magnetic film. Quieter faults the drive hides itself, remapping a failing sector's data to a spare while error correction can still recover it. S.M.A.R.T. counts those fixes but warns only of mechanical issues. Uncorrected bit read errors are specified at one in 10^16 bits for 2013 enterprise drives and one in 10^14 for 2018 consumer drives. Silent corruption is the worst kind. Drive grade does not predict failure rate, failure rates rise steadily with age, and in an array one drive's failure significantly raises the short-term risk of a second.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-200 -->

- **How drives connect: SATA, SAS, PCIe and NVMe**

  A fast drive on a slow connection is still slow. Hard drives connect over parallel ATA, Serial ATA (SATA), SCSI, Serial Attached SCSI (SAS) or Fibre Channel: lossless delivery for storage networks. SAS is a serial protocol that still uses SCSI commands. It is compatible with SATA: a SAS controller can drive SATA drives, but a SATA controller cannot drive SAS drives. SSDs use SATA 3.0 at up to 6.0 Gbit/s, SAS 3.0 at 12.0 Gbit/s or PCIe 3.0 x4 at 31.5 Gbit/s. NVMe, built for SSDs, offers much lower latency and higher throughput than AHCI.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-201 -->

- **Telling storage technologies apart**

  Two storage devices can look alike and behave nothing alike. Technologies are told apart by volatility, mutability, accessibility, addressability, capacity and density, and performance. Accessibility comes in two modes. In random access, any location is reached in about the same time. In sequential access, pieces are read in serial order, so access time depends on which piece was read last. Storage can also be location accessible, selected by numerical memory address, file addressable, or content-addressable. Performance is measured by latency, throughput, granularity and reliability.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-141 -->

- **Block storage: raw blocks owned by one server**

  A database would rather have the raw disk than a tidy folder tree. Block storage gives it that. It divides data into blocks and stores them as separate pieces, each with a unique identifier, and presents the raw blocks to the server as a volume. A volume is a fixed amount of storage on a disk or tape. The server can format it as a file system or hand control of the blocks to an application. That makes block storage the most flexible and versatile form, and databases manage blocks directly to squeeze out the most performance. The identifiers let the system place pieces wherever is most convenient and reassemble them on request. Disks attached to a server, hard or solid-state, are all block storage. It can also be reached over a high-speed network, through protocols such as Fibre Channel: lossless delivery for storage networks and iSCSI: disk commands carried over ordinary IP networks. Even then it presents raw blocks and is fully owned by one server, not a shared resource. In the cloud it emulates a physical block device such as a hard drive; Amazon EBS is an example.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-143 -->

- **RAID: many drives acting as one safer drive**

  Add drives to a machine and failures grow more frequent. Yet an array of drives can be far more reliable than any single high-capacity drive, and RAID is how. RAID (Redundant Array of Independent Disks) stores the same data on several hard disks or SSDs, so data survives a drive failure. Not every RAID level aims at that. RAID coordinates two or more drives into a disk array and distributes written data across it. The configurations are called RAID levels: trading capacity for safety. They differ in how much extra data they keep, how many drives they need, how fast they run, and how many failures they survive. The defining techniques are data striping, to improve read and write efficiency, and disk mirroring or parity drives, for data recovery. Using several disks in parallel also increases the bandwidth between primary and secondary memory and eases the I/O bottleneck. RAID guards against physical drive failure only. Operator error, software, hardware and virus destruction still threaten the data, and fire can take the whole array, so extra copies can be stored off site.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-149 -->

- **iSCSI: disk commands carried over ordinary IP networks**

  iSCSI lets a database server believe a remote disk is plugged in next to it. It is an IP-based storage networking standard that provides block-level access to storage devices by carrying SCSI commands over a TCP/IP network. Clients, called initiators, send commands to storage devices, called targets, on remote servers. A LUN (logical unit number) is an individually addressable logical SCSI device within a target, essentially a numbered disk. Initiators treat LUNs like raw disks. Rather than mounting remote directories as with Network File System: remote files that act local, the host formats and manages a file system on the LUN. It needs no dedicated cabling and runs over existing IP infrastructure, so it is seen as a low-cost alternative to Fibre Channel: lossless delivery for storage networks. The catch is competition for a fixed amount of bandwidth. A storage network can be severely degraded if it does not run on a dedicated network or VLAN. It mostly sends cleartext over TCP, so administrators usually isolate it on logically separate networks and authenticate initiators and targets with CHAP. It also serves storage consolidation: a server gets a new disk volume without cabling changes.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-206 -->

- **Data scrubbing: finding bad blocks before you need them**

  A block nobody reads can go bad unnoticed. Data scrubbing, also called patrol read, has the RAID controller periodically read and check every block in an array. That includes blocks not otherwise accessed, so bad blocks are detected before use. It uses the array's extra data to recover a bad block on a single drive and reassigns the recovered data to spare blocks elsewhere on the drive. Run as a background process, scrubbing finds and recovers from unrecoverable read errors, which reduces the risk of them causing double-drive failures during a rebuild.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-155 -->

- **Hardware or software: where RAID logic lives**

  Somebody has to decide which drive gets which piece of data. That job can sit in dedicated hardware. It can also sit in software, in the operating system or in the firmware and drivers of a standard drive controller. Hardware RAID controllers are expensive and proprietary, and each manufacturer's tooling for each operating system ensures vendor lock-in. Many modern operating systems provide software RAID. It may be a device-abstraction layer such as Linux md, a logical volume manager such as LVM, or a file system component such as ZFS or Btrfs. Cheaper firmware- and driver-based controllers may not work when the host operating system lacks driver support.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-156 -->

- **File storage: the folder tree everyone knows**

  To find a file in file storage, you need its complete path. File storage stores data as files and presents them to users as a hierarchical directory structure. It is built on top of Block storage: raw blocks owned by one server and gives a higher-level abstraction that makes files and directories easier to handle. A file system format provides that abstraction on secondary storage, organizing data into files and directories with metadata such as owner, access time and access permissions. It is the most common general-purpose storage solution: user-friendly, economical and easily structured. It appears the same to the user as it does on the hard drive. Many servers can reach file storage through file-level network protocols such as Server Message Block: from chatty to lean and Network File System: remote files that act local, without managing blocks or formatting volumes. That suits sharing many files and folders within an organization. Examples are Amazon EFS, Azure Files and Google Cloud Filestore.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-144 -->

- **Object storage: flat, huge and cheap**

  Object storage gives up the folder tree on purpose. It breaks data files into pieces called objects and stores them in a single repository that can be spread across multiple networked systems. The structure is flat, with no hierarchical directory, unlike file storage's hierarchy or block storage's equal-size blocks. Each object carries a globally unique identifier and metadata. File systems have fixed metadata, but object storage allows full custom object-level metadata for indexing, data-management policies and centralized management. An object can be addressed by its identifier within a bucket or across the whole system. Administrators need not build logical volumes or configure RAID.

  The trade is deliberate. Object storage gives up performance for high durability, vast scale and low cost, and it is relatively slow next to other types. It targets relatively cold data and is mainly used for archiving and for safekeeping copies of other data. It retains massive amounts of unstructured data that is written once and read once or many times. It is not for transactional data, because it lacks the locking and sharing mechanisms that keep a single, accurately updated version of a file. Applications use programmatic, mostly REST-based interfaces with basic create, read, update and delete functions. Some implementations add versioning, life-cycle management and movement of objects between storage tiers. The vast majority of Cloud storage: three kinds, billed by the meter leverages this architecture, as in Amazon S3: object storage at enormous scale and Microsoft Azure Blob Storage.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-145 -->

- **Cloud storage: three kinds, billed by the meter**

  Stop a cloud instance and one kind of its storage vanishes. Cloud storage is storage built on highly virtualized infrastructure, offered with cloud-native interfaces and elastic scaling. As a subset of cloud computing, it also brings multi-tenancy and metered resources. It can be used from an off-premises service or deployed on-premises. It comes in the three types you have met: Object storage: flat, huge and cheap, File storage: the folder tree everyone knows and Block storage: raw blocks owned by one server. The vanishing kind is the instance store. It is cloud-hosted block-level storage provided as part of a cloud instance, and unlike other block storage, its data is lost when the instance is stopped.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-147 -->

- **Amazon S3: object storage at enormous scale**

  As of 2025, Amazon S3 stores 500 trillion objects, hundreds of exabytes of data, and serves 200 million requests per second. At its peak it moves about 1 petabyte per second. Amazon Simple Storage Service (S3) is an AWS service that provides object storage through a web service interface. It aims to scale, stay available and keep latency low, with high durability, for archives, copies kept for recovery and analytics data lakes. Objects are the basic units, organized into buckets, and each is identified by a unique, user-assigned key. An object can be between 0 bytes and 5 TB. A single upload allows at most 5 GB, so larger objects must go through the multipart upload API. S3 has nine storage classes. Standard is the default for frequently accessed data, while Express One Zone gives single-digit millisecond latency but keeps data in one availability zone. A bucket can be mounted as a file system with FUSE-based tools, but S3 semantics are not those of a POSIX file system. The S3 API's broad adoption has produced S3-compatible storage from other providers.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-208 -->

- **Direct-attached, network-attached and SAN storage**

  Primary storage never goes over a network, but secondary or tertiary storage may. Direct-attached storage (DAS) is traditional mass storage that uses no network. Network-attached storage (NAS) is mass storage that another computer can access at file level over a local or wide area network or the Internet, commonly using Network File System: remote files that act local and Server Message Block: from chatty to lean. A NAS is flexible, since more storage can be added to what exists. A storage area network (SAN) is a specialized network that provides storage capacity to other computers, commonly associated with Fibre Channel: lossless delivery for storage networks. SANs once provided block-level storage and NAS file-level storage, a split that cloud services have shifted.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-142 -->

  *Figure: The three kinds differ in how the computer reaches its mass storage.*

  | Kind | How it connects |
  |---|---|
  | DAS | Uses no network |
  | NAS | Local or wide area network, or the Internet; file level |
  | SAN | Specialized network; once block level |

- **Fibre Channel: lossless delivery for storage networks**

  Two promises define Fibre Channel: data arrives in order, and nothing is lost. It is a high-speed protocol that delivers raw block data in order and without loss, and it achieves the lossless part with a credit mechanism. It is used mainly to connect servers to storage in storage area networks in commercial data centers. Fibre Channel Protocol (FCP) carries SCSI commands. There are three topologies: point-to-point, arbitrated loop and switched fabric. An arbitrated loop is a ring where only one pair of ports communicates at a time and one device failure breaks the loop. It was rarely used after 2010. In a switched fabric every device connects to switches that route with Fabric Shortest Path First. It scales to tens of thousands of ports, many port pairs talk at once, and a port failure stays isolated to its link. SANs are often designed with dual fabrics, two completely separate ones, so if the primary fails the second becomes primary. Data rates range from 1 to 128 gigabit per second.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-207 -->

- **Network File System: remote files that act local**

  In its second version, NFS could read only the first 2 GB of a file. Network File System (NFS) is a distributed file system protocol that lets a client computer access files over a network much like local storage. It builds on ONC's version of Remote procedure call: making a far-away function feel local, and every version after the first experimental one is defined in RFCs, so anyone can implement it. NFSv2 ran only over UDP, and its designers meant the server side to be stateless, with locking implemented outside the core protocol. NFSv3 added 64-bit file sizes and offsets, asynchronous server writes and READDIRPLUS, which returns attributes with directory listings. It also brought TCP support. That made NFS over a WAN more feasible and allowed transfer sizes beyond the 8 KB limit UDP imposes. NFSv4, influenced by AFS and SMB, adds performance improvements, mandates strong security and is stateful. It needs only one port, 2049, which simplifies use across firewalls. NFSv4.1 supports clustered servers, as Parallel NFS: metadata in one place, data in many describes, and NFSv4.2 adds server-side clone and copy and sparse files.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-202 -->

  *Figure: Each NFS version added something that earlier ones lacked.*

  | Version | What it brought |
  |---|---|
  | NFSv2 (RFC 1094) | UDP only; reads the first 2 GB of a file |
  | NFSv3 | 64-bit sizes, asynchronous writes, TCP |
  | NFSv4 (RFC 3010) | Stateful, strong security, port 2049 |
  | NFSv4.1 (RFC 5661) | Parallel access to clustered servers |
  | NFSv4.2 (RFC 7862) | Server-side clone and copy, sparse files |

- **Server Message Block: from chatty to lean**

  SMB 1.0 was chatty, and over slow links it showed. Server Message Block (SMB) is a communication protocol used to share files, printers, serial ports and other communications between nodes on a network. It relies on TCP and IP, with the server on TCP port 445, so it works across interconnected networks, including the Internet. SMB 1.0 performs poorly over high-latency links because it is chatty, block-level rather than streaming, limited to a 64K block size and not tuned for WAN links. SMB2 cut the chatter by reducing commands from over a hundred to nineteen. It also pipelines requests before earlier responses arrive and compounds multiple actions into one request to save round trips. SMB 3.0 added SMB Direct, SMB Multichannel and encryption, aimed at virtualized data centers. SMB over QUIC, introduced in Windows Server 2022, tunnels SMB in TLS 1.3 over UDP port 443 as a secure alternative to a VPN. In 1996 Microsoft published SMB 1.0 as CIFS, a name since dropped.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-204 -->

- **An SSD in front of slower disks**

  Put an SSD in front of hard-disk storage and it takes the hits. In a distributed environment, an SSD layer can absorb the large volume of user requests to slower HDD-based storage. The result is much higher bandwidth and lower latency than the storage system alone. On supercomputers such a layer is called a burst buffer. On one machine an SSD can cache a hard disk. It can be a separate drive, as with bcache, dm-cache and Apple's Fusion Drive, or flash built into a hybrid drive (SSHD). In ZFS an SSD can hold the intent log (SLOG) or serve as the level 2 read cache (L2ARC).

  <!-- sysd-blocks-198 -->

- **SSD endurance: how much writing a drive can take**

  A drive's datasheet says how much writing it can take. SSD endurance is listed as drive writes per day (DWPD), the number of full-capacity writes allowed daily within the warranty period. It is also listed as terabytes written (TBW), the total in that period. NAND lifespan is set by program-erase (P/E) cycles. TBW is the product of the P/E cycle resource and the capacity, so a 1 TB drive with TBW = 600 TB has 600 P/E cycles. Past its rated TBW, an SSD may lose data after three months (enterprise) or one year (consumer) without power. SSDs are therefore not suited to long-term archival storage.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-197 -->

- **Wear leveling and TRIM: sharing out the wear**

  Write to the same flash block again and again and it dies early. Wear leveling spreads write and erase operations evenly across all blocks of an SSD's flash memory. Without it, specific blocks would wear out early from repeated use, shortening the life of the whole drive. The controller moves rarely changed (cold) data off heavily used blocks so frequently changing (hot) data can be written there. The extra writes are called write amplification and must be balanced against performance and durability. File systems that support SSDs generally support TRIM, which lets the SSD recycle discarded data and reduces garbage collection.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-196 -->

- **Parallel NFS: metadata in one place, data in many**

  A traditional NFS server holds file names and their data together. Parallel NFS (pNFS), part of NFSv4.1, separates file metadata from file data, so a client can move data directly to and from a set of data servers. The data is striped among those servers. A pNFS server is a set of components controlled by a metadata server. The client contacts one metadata server to traverse the namespace, but may interact directly with the data servers when moving data. The client can thus take part in locating file data and avoid funnelling all transfers through one NFS server.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-203 -->

- **Opportunistic locks: caching that is not a lock**

  An SMB opportunistic lock (OpLock) lets a client cache a network file locally to improve performance, yet it is not a true lock and gives no mutual exclusion. When a client opens a file that no one else has open, the server grants an exclusive OpLock. The client may then cache all changes locally and needs fewer round trips. When another client opens the file, the server sends a break to revoke the OpLock. The first client flushes its changes and acknowledges, and only then does the server answer the second client consistently.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-205 -->

- **Object stores versus key-value stores**

  Object stores and key-value stores look alike from a distance, and the border between them is blurred. Both accept an arbitrary string as the identifier. It is an object identifier or URL in one case and a key of arbitrary bytes in the other. Both also accept data of arbitrary size. They differ in three ways. An object store associates a limited set of attributes, its metadata, with each piece of data. It is optimized for hundreds of megabytes or even gigabytes. It usually offers weaker consistency such as Eventual consistency: every reader agrees, but not yet, whereas key-value stores expect small values, in kilobytes, and offer strong consistency.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-152 -->

- **Where object storage earns its keep**

  Object stores suit six jobs. They hold archives, such as old data kept for auditing or client statements, in a cost-effective layer outside the core systems. They store unstructured data such as music, video and text documents. That beats the old, quite inefficient practice of keeping them as blobs in a relational database. Cloud-native applications get flexible, scalable storage through easy API access. A data lake gives business lines a place to dump data for later analytics, machine learning, ETL or a data warehouse. IoT sensor time series fit there too, as do copies of databases and file systems that load fast for recovery.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-146 -->

- **HDFS: very large files on cheap machines**

  The Hadoop Distributed File System (HDFS) is built to run on cheap machines and keep going when they fail. It is a distributed file system designed to run on commodity hardware. It is highly fault-tolerant, designed for low-cost hardware, and provides high throughput access to application data, which suits large data sets. It stores very large files reliably across the machines of a large cluster. HDFS stores each file as a sequence of blocks, all the same size except the last. It replicates the blocks of a file, which is how it tolerates failures.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-148 -->

- **Reed-Solomon codes: repairing data with polynomials**

  A common Reed-Solomon code carries 223 data symbols plus 32 parity symbols in each block and corrects up to 16 symbol errors. Reed-Solomon codes were introduced by Irving Reed and Gustave Solomon in 1960. They treat a block of data as symbols of a finite field and add check symbols. In the original view, the message symbols are the coefficients of a polynomial of degree less than k. The codeword is that polynomial's values at n distinct points. An RS(n, k) code adds t = n - k check symbols. It can detect up to t erroneous symbols, or locate and correct up to floor(t/2) of them at unknown locations. As an erasure code it corrects up to t erasures at known locations. In the Cauchy and Vandermonde forms, any K of the N codewords received are enough to reconstruct all N. A symbol counts as one error however many of its bits are wrong, so the codes suit burst errors. Storage systems use Reed-Solomon codes to correct the burst errors from media defects, and RAID 6 uses them too.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-209 -->

- **RAID levels: trading capacity for safety**

  RAID levels trade capacity, speed and safety against each other, and the clearest way to see it is to meet them one at a time. RAID 0, also known as striping, splits data evenly across all the drives in the array. It uses 100% of capacity and multiplies read and write throughput by the number of drives. But it survives no drive failure: any one drive failing makes the whole volume inaccessible, so it is a poor choice when data reliability matters. RAID 1, also known as mirroring, keeps an exact copy of a set of data on at least two drives. If a drive fails, the others still work. Any read can be served by any drive in the mirror, but write throughput is always slower because every drive must be updated. Capacity utilization is 50%.

  RAID 5 is striping with parity, a check value computed from the data. It needs at least 3 drives, spreads the parity across the drives as well as striping the data, and uses 67% to 94% of capacity. RAID 6 is like RAID 5 but writes parity to two drives, so it tolerates a two-drive failure, at 50% to 80% of capacity. RAID 10 combines striping with mirroring: all data is mirrored on secondary drives and striped across each set of drives to speed transfers. It tolerates up to one disk failure in each sub-array, at 50% of capacity. It survives multiple drive losses if no mirror loses all its drives. RAID 0+1 mirrors two stripes instead and is riskier to rebuild, since all drives of the surviving stripe are read.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-150 -->

  *Figure: Compare how much of the raw capacity each level leaves for data.*

  | Level | Method | Capacity used |
  |---|---|---|
  | RAID 0 | Striping | 100% |
  | RAID 1 | Mirroring | 50% |
  | RAID 5 | Striping with parity | 67%-94% |
  | RAID 6 | Parity on two drives | 50%-80% |
  | RAID 10 | Striping across mirrors | 50% |

- **Erasure coding: durability without three full copies**

  Keeping three copies of everything costs 200% extra storage. Erasure coding gets durability for far less. It chunks data into smaller pieces placed on different servers and creates parities, so after failures the chunks and parities rebuild the data. In 4 + 2 erasure coding, data is split into four even-sized chunks and a formula calculates two parities. Every two chunks need one parity block, so the overhead is 50%. Assuming a node has a 0.81% annual failure rate, Backblaze's calculation gives 11 nines of durability, against 6 nines for three copies. In RS(10, 4), 10 MB of data becomes ten 1 MB blocks plus four 1 MB parity blocks. It tolerates up to 4 concurrent failures at a storage overhead of 14/10 = 1.4×, against 50/10 = 5.0× for full copies. Large systems in data centers increasingly use erasure-coded storage, most commonly Reed-Solomon codes. RAID is generally applied to an array on one host. If that host fails, the array goes with it. Erasure coding generally spans several hosts, so operations continue when any one host stops.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-151 -->

  *Figure: A 4 + 2 erasure code adds far less storage overhead than three full copies.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Parity check: one extra value repairs one loss**

  One extra number can repair any single loss. A parity check appends one checksum value, computed from k source values, to those values. If any one of the values is erased, it is easily recovered by summing the remaining variables. In erasure-coding terms, it is the special case of an optimal erasure code where n = k + 1.
