RAID 5 is a widely used application of the parity check using XOR. It gives the same single-drive failure protection as RAID 1 with fewer hard drives.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-153 -->

- **How a RAID array still gets lost**

  RAID protects against a failing drive, yet arrays still get lost. Failures are correlated, since drives in an array are often the same age and environment. In a study of about 100,000 drives, two failures within one hour were four times more likely than an exponential distribution predicts. Large drives may take hours if not days to rebuild. With one redundant drive, a second failure loses the array. A large RAID 5 array is likely to hit an unrecoverable read error on a surviving drive. A crash during a write can leave parity inconsistent with data, the write hole, so parity cannot rebuild a failed disk.

  <!-- sysd-blocks-154 -->

## Scaling and consistency

The more people use a system, the more work it has to do. Scalability is the property of a system to handle a growing amount of work, and this part of the course begins with it. Beside it stands high availability, which aims to keep a system performing at an agreed level, usually uptime, for longer than normal. The tools range from adding nodes, or adding resources to a single node, to duplicating critical components as redundancy, to letting servers come and go automatically with the load. Each tool has limits, because a formula such as Amdahl's law caps how far a task can speed up as resources are added.

### Scalability and availability

Two questions run through this chapter: how does a system grow, and how does it stay up? The answers start with two definitions. Scalability is the capacity to handle a growing amount of work, and high availability aims to ensure an agreed level of operational performance for a higher than normal period. From there the chapter covers the strategies for scaling, the limits that Amdahl's law and the Universal Scalability Law place on them, and the redundancy that keeps a system running when parts fail. It also shows how to measure reliability, starting with the mean time between failures, the predicted average time between inherent failures of a repairable system during normal operation.

- **Scalability: taking on more work without losing performance**

  A package delivery system scales by adding vehicles. But if every package must pass through a single warehouse for sorting, that warehouse limits how far the system can scale.

  Scalability is the property of a system to handle a growing amount of work. A system is scalable when it can take on more work, typically by adding resources, without losing performance. A search engine is a computing example: it must support growing numbers of users and growing numbers of indexed topics. Marc Brooker offers a precise test. A system is scalable in the range where the marginal cost of additional workload is nearly constant.

  Design decides which side of that line a system lands on. Early Gnutella flooded every query to all nodes, so each peer's load grew with the number of peers. BitTorrent scales well because each peer's demand is independent of the number of peers. Strategy matters too. A system must keep applying a cost-effective way of scaling, and past the point where that strategy stops being financially viable, it is hard to scale further. A scalable database can be upgraded with more processors, devices and storage to process more transactions, easily and without shutting down.

  <!-- sysd-scale-059 -->

- **High availability: staying up when parts fail**

  Ask whether a system is available and the user's test is simple: can I reach it to submit, update or retrieve my work? If not, the system is unavailable from the user's perspective. High availability is a characteristic of a system that aims to ensure an agreed level of operational performance, usually uptime, for a higher than normal period.

  Reliability engineering offers three design principles: eliminate single points of failure, provide reliable crossover, and detect failures as they occur. Single point of failure: the part with no spare takes up the first. Eliminating them means building in Redundancy: spare parts that raise availability, so the failure of one component does not mean the failure of the entire system. Yet the crossover, where work passes from a failed part to its spare, tends to become the one part whose failure stops everything. So it must itself be reliable.

  More parts are not automatically better. Complex systems have more potential failure points, which can undermine availability. But one simple machine must be taken down entirely for patching and operating system upgrades. Advanced designs use load balancing and Failover: when a standby takes over instead. The most common cause of outages is human error, so a highly available complex system must need less human intervention to restore operation.

  A reliable system is available, but an available system is not necessarily reliable. A fault-tolerant system goes further. It has no service interruption, at a significantly higher cost. It needs a full duplicate of the hardware, so a second system takes over with no loss in uptime. A highly available system has minimal interruption instead.

  <!-- sysd-scale-068 -->

- **Redundancy: spare parts that raise availability**

  Ten hosts that are each up only half the time can together reach 99.9023% availability. That is the promise of redundancy. It is the intentional duplication of critical components or functions of a system to raise its reliability, usually as a standby or fail-safe. For N parallel components of availability X, combined availability is 1 - (1 - X)^N, so redundancy raises it exponentially. Passive redundancy uses excess capacity to reduce the impact of failures, accepting some performance decline. Active redundancy runs multiple items of the same kind and monitors them. Voting logic reconfigures around a failed item automatically, so performance does not decline. With an odd number of three or more devices doing identical work, the majority overrides any device that disagrees. The formula holds only if failures are independent and can be detected: two power supplies on one socket fail together. Redundancy also adds complexity, so Marc Brooker advises ensuring a net-positive gain.

  <!-- sysd-scale-073 -->

- **Mean time between failures: an average that misleads**

  Most engineers assume a system has a 50% chance of surviving to its mean time between failures. It does not. The real chance is about 37%, and the misreading can lead to bad design decisions. Mean time between failures (MTBF) is the predicted average time between inherent failures of a repairable system during normal operation. For a non-repairable system the equivalent is mean time to failure. Three identical systems that fail after 100, 120 and 130 hours have an MTBF of 116.667 hours, the average of the three. The 37% follows from assuming a constant failure rate, of which MTBF is the reciprocal. Parts in series fail the system if any one fails, so adding them lowers the MTBF. Parts in parallel fail it only if the second fails during repair of the first, so faster repair shrinks the vulnerability window. For disk drives, the annualized failure rate is usually more relevant, because MTBF is only a mean lifetime.

  <!-- sysd-scale-133 -->

- **Scaling up or scaling out: one big machine or many**

  Large social networks exceed the capacity of even the largest supercomputer, so no single machine can carry them. That is one reason systems can grow in two directions. Scaling horizontally, or out, means adding nodes, such as going from one web server to three. Scaling vertically, or up, means adding resources such as CPUs, memory or storage to a single node. The reverse moves are scaling in and scaling down.

  Vertical scaling adds power to an existing machine. It is simple to implement, easier to manage and data consistent. It also avoids the harder programming, and the throughput, latency and synchronization issues, of spreading work across nodes. The risks are high downtime, harder upgrades, and a single machine whose failure stops everything, as Single point of failure: the part with no spare explains. Some applications do not scale horizontally at all.

  Horizontal scaling adds more instances to the pool, so load is distributed more evenly. It brings more redundancy, better tolerance of faults, flexibility, efficiency and easier upgrades. It also lets high-performance computing do tasks that once needed expensive supercomputers. The costs are increased complexity, data inconsistency and increased load on downstream services, plus software for efficient resource management and maintenance.

  <!-- sysd-scale-061 -->

  *Figure: Compare what each direction of growth adds, gains and costs.*

  |  | Scale up (vertical) | Scale out (horizontal) |
  |---|---|---|
  | What it adds | Resources to one node | More instances to the pool |
  | Gains | Simple, easier to manage, data consistent | Redundancy, flexibility, easier upgrades |
  | Costs | High downtime, harder to upgrade, single point of failure | Complexity, data inconsistency, downstream load |

- **Stateless and stateful: does the server remember you?**

  An HTTP server understands each request on its own, as if it had never met you before. That is what makes a protocol stateless: the receiver keeps no session state from earlier requests, while a stateful protocol may retain it. IP and HTTP are stateless. TCP and FTP are stateful, and an FTP server keeps the user's login, working directory and transfer mode. Stateless designs buy visibility, reliability and scalability. Observing an exchange needs only one request, recovery from failures such as packet loss is easier, and the server can quickly free resources. The cost is performance, because repetitive data travels with every request. HTTP servers add state back with a session identifier in a cookie that refers to session state stored on the server. Stateless web servers can be autoscaled, as Autoscaling: letting the load add and remove servers describes. On Kubernetes: a cluster that steers itself toward the state you declare, scaling a stateless application only means adding pods, but stateful workloads are harder because their state must survive a pod restart.

  <!-- sysd-scale-138 -->

- **Amdahl's law: why more processors give less**

  Speed up a part of a program that takes 10% of its running time by a factor of 10,000, and the whole program runs only 11% faster. That is Amdahl's law, a formula that limits the speedup of a task as resources are added to the system executing it. The overall gain is capped by the fraction of time the improved part is used. In parallel computing, the work that cannot run in parallel sets the limit, such as building a file list before threads process the files. Optimize a section that takes 99% of the time by a factor of 100 and the overall speedup is only 50. Half the potential gain is lost to the remaining 1%. So improve the part that takes most time. Take parts of 3 s and 1 s. Making the 3 s part twice as fast gives 1.60 overall, but making the 1 s part five times faster gives only 1.25. In a fixed-size computation, each added processor adds less usable power than the last.

  <!-- sysd-scale-136 -->

  *Figure: Speeding up the part that takes most time gives the bigger overall gain.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Autoscaling: letting the load add and remove servers**

  Cloud providers charge for usage, not peak capacity, so a farm that always matches its load can lower its bills. Autoscaling is a cloud computing method that automatically adjusts the number of active servers in a server farm to match the load on the farm. It launches servers when activity is high and removes them when it is low. Because it follows actual usage instead of a fixed schedule, it handles unexpected spikes better. An autoscaling group is the set of instances under its control, with a desired capacity never below the minimum size or above the maximum. A scaling policy changes that capacity when a metric such as CPU utilization crosses a threshold. A cooldown period then blocks further scaling right after an action. Autoscaling is reactive by default. Scheduled scaling changes limits at set times for known, sudden changes. Netflix found that aggressive scaling up with delayed, cautious scaling down served uptime and responsiveness best.

  <!-- sysd-q-067 -->

  *Figure: A metric crossing its threshold sets off a chain that ends in a cooldown.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Metric crosses a threshold] --> B[Scaling policy changes desired capacity]
  B --> C[Group launches or removes instances]
  C --> D[Cooldown blocks further scaling]
  ```

- **Dimensions of scalability: growth in six directions**

  Growth is not one thing. Scalability can be measured along several dimensions, and each asks a different question. Administrative scalability is the ability of a growing number of organizations or users to access a system. Geographic scalability is staying effective while expanding from a local area to a larger region. Functional scalability adds new functionality without disrupting existing activities. Load scalability lets a distributed system expand and contract for heavier or lighter loads. Generation scalability means adopting new generations of components, and heterogeneous scalability means adopting components from different vendors.

  <!-- sysd-scale-060 -->

- **Diminishing returns: why doubling hardware falls short**

  Doubling a machine's processors sounds like doubling its speed. Suppose 70% of a program can be parallelized and the computing power doubles from 4 processors to 8. The program speeds up by only roughly one-fifth, while a fully parallelizable problem would speed up twofold. Amdahl's law bounds the maximum speedup from P processors using α, the sequential fraction of a calculation, because only the remaining 1−α can be parallelized. Designers are often advised to favor hardware scalability over per-node capacity, since adding a node is typically cheaper than performance tuning. Even so, adding more hardware is not necessarily the optimal approach, because it has diminishing returns.

  <!-- sysd-scale-065 -->

- **The Universal Scalability Law and the limit of capacity**

  At what point does adding capacity stop helping? Neil J. Gunther coined the Universal Scalability Law to answer that by calculation. It models the scalability of a distributed system using contention, the delay from waiting or queueing for shared resources, and coherency, the delay for data to become consistent. High contention indicates sequential processing that could be parallelized. High coherency suggests excessive dependencies among processes, so interactions should be minimized. The law lets you calculate in advance the maximum effective capacity of a system, and scaling up beyond that point is a waste.

  <!-- sysd-scale-066 -->

- **Eight strategies for scaling a system**

  Engineers reach for eight common strategies when a system must scale. Stateless services do not rely on server-specific data, so they are easier to scale. Horizontal scaling adds more servers so the workload can be shared, and a load balancer spreads incoming requests evenly across them. Auto scaling policies adjust resources based on real-time traffic. Caching reduces the load on the database and handles repetitive requests at scale. Copying data across multiple nodes, taken up in Replication: keeping several copies in step, scales reads while improving redundancy. Sharding, taken up in Database sharding: spreading one database across many servers, distributes data across multiple instances to scale writes as well as reads. Async processing moves time-consuming, resource-intensive tasks to background workers, and event-driven processing handles long-running tasks asynchronously, so the system can accept new requests.

  <!-- sysd-scale-062 -->

- **Scaling a database: indexes, caches, replicas and shards**

  A slow database has more fixes than a bigger server. Check the application's query patterns and create the right indexes, then pre-compute complex query results in materialized views to read them faster. Denormalization reduces complex joins to improve query performance. Caching frequently accessed data in a faster storage layer reduces database load. Database scalability is the ability of a database system to perform additional work when given greater hardware resources, such as more servers, processors, memory and storage. Vertical scaling boosts the database server with more CPU, RAM or storage. Replicas of the primary database on other servers scale reads. Sharding splits tables into smaller pieces spread across servers and scales writes as well as reads. Algorithmic innovations include row-level locking and table and index partitioning. Architectural ones include shared-nothing and shared-everything designs for multi-server configurations.

  <!-- sysd-scale-064 -->

- **Computer clusters: many machines acting as one**

  Ideally a cluster functions as a single system that users cannot tell from one machine. A computer cluster is a group of two or more computers, or nodes, that run in parallel to achieve a common goal. It distributes the workloads of many parallelizable tasks among its nodes, so they use the combined memory and processing power of every computer. A network connects the nodes, and software joins them into a cluster that may have shared storage, local storage on each node, or both. Typically at least one node is the leader node and entry point. It delegates incoming work to other nodes and, if needed, aggregates results into a response for the user. Clusters come in three types: highly available or fail-over, load balancing, and high-performance computing. The price is complexity. Every node needs the operating system, application and dependencies installed and updated, and shared storage and distributed data must be kept safe and in sync.

  <!-- sysd-scale-075 -->

- **Scale-out storage: how big a cluster can stay consistent**

  How large can a cluster grow before its copies of the data disagree? In scale-out storage, scalability is the largest cluster size that still guarantees full consistency, meaning only one valid version of the stored data in the whole cluster. Clusters that update copies asynchronously give "lazy" redundancy and are called eventually consistent. Their writes invalidate other copies without always waiting for acknowledgements, and reads typically do not check every copy, so a read can miss the preceding write. This model, taken up in Eventual consistency: every reader agrees, but not yet, suits designs that rate availability above consistency, such as web caches. It should be avoided for classical transaction-oriented applications.

  <!-- sysd-scale-067 -->

- **Scheduled downtime is still downtime**

  A site can claim very high availability simply by not counting its maintenance. Many do exactly that, excluding scheduled downtime from their availability calculations. But downtime, any period when a system is unavailable, is downtime whether or not it is scheduled. Scheduled downtime typically comes from disruptive maintenance, such as patches or configuration changes that need a reboot. Unscheduled downtime typically arises from a physical event such as a hardware or software failure, power outage, over-temperature shutdown or severed network connection. Truly continuous availability is rare and costly.

  <!-- sysd-scale-071 -->

- **Availability and the nines: a yearly budget of downtime**

  Five nines sounds like a boast. It is really a budget of about 5.3 minutes of downtime in a whole year. Availability is the percentage of time a system is up, usually measured over a year and often quoted in nines. It equals uptime divided by the sum of uptime and downtime. 90% is one nine, 99% is two nines and 99.9% is three, and each added nine makes the target exponentially more stringent. Per year, 99.9% allows about 9 hours of downtime and 99.99% about 53 minutes. A mnemonic says five nines allows approximately 5 minutes. Multiply or divide by 10 for other levels: four nines is 50 minutes and six nines is 0.5 minutes. Service level agreements often state monthly downtime or availability, so service credits can match monthly billing cycles. Uptime and availability are not always the same, because a system can be up while its service is not available, as in a network outage.

  <!-- sysd-scale-069 -->

  *Figure: Each added nine cuts the yearly downtime budget sharply.*

  | Availability | Nines | Downtime per year |
  |---|---|---|
  | 99.9% | Three nines | About 9 hours |
  | 99.99% | Four nines | About 53 minutes |
  | 99.999% | Five nines | About 5.3 minutes |

- **Mean time to repair versus time to recovery**

  A 24-hour repair promise with 6 days of added delays is no better than a 7-day recovery promise. The gap lies in what each clock measures. Mean time to repair (MTTR) is the average time needed to repair a failed component or device, a basic measure of how maintainable a repairable item is. It runs only from when repairs begin, and it generally excludes lead time for parts. Mean time to recovery runs from discovering a failure to resuming operation. With equal MTBF, a 24-hour MTTR gives higher operational availability than a 7-day one.

  <!-- sysd-scale-134 -->

- **Measuring availability: what users see versus what the admin reports**

  A system can be up all year and still be hit by a 9-hour network failure at peak usage. Users see it as unavailable, while the administrator claims 100% uptime. By the true definition, that system is approximately 99.9% available, or three nines: 8751 hours of available time out of 8760 hours. Measured availability depends on interpretation. Users often deem a system with performance problems partly or wholly unavailable even while it functions, and unavailable application functions may go unnoticed by administrators. A true measure is therefore holistic, and it needs comprehensive tools for watching the system that are themselves highly available.

  <!-- sysd-scale-070 -->

- **Recovery time and recovery point: how long and how much**

  Some outages end in minutes. Others never end: recovery time can be infinite, for example when a fire or flood destroys a data center and no secondary data center exists to recover to. Recovery time, also called Recovery time objective: how long you can stay down (RTO) or estimated time of repair, is the time for a planned outage or for full recovery from an unplanned one. It is closely related to availability. A second target, the Recovery point objective: how much recent data you can lose, sets the acceptable data loss for various failure events, a concern separate from data availability. Some users can tolerate service interruptions but not data loss, and a service level agreement formalizes an organization's availability objectives and requirements.

  <!-- sysd-scale-072 -->

- **Active-active and active-passive clusters**

  A cluster with two nodes can use them in two ways. The two most common high availability clustering configurations are active-active and active-passive. An active-active cluster has at least two nodes, all running the same kind of service at the same time. Its main purpose is load balancing: a load balancer spreads the work so that no node is overloaded. Because more nodes are available to serve, throughput and response times improve. An active-passive cluster also has at least two nodes, but not all of them are active. With two nodes, if the first is active, the second must be passive or on standby.

  <!-- sysd-scale-076 -->

- **Sequence versus parallel: how availability adds up**

  Chain two components that are each up 99.9% of the time, and the service is up less often than either. A service made of failure-prone components has an overall availability that depends on whether they sit in sequence or in parallel. In sequence, total availability is the product of the components' availabilities, so it decreases: two components at 99.9% each give 99.8%. In parallel, total availability is 1 minus the product of the components' unavailabilities, so it increases: the same two components at 99.9% each give 99.9999%. This is the arithmetic behind redundancy. A part added in series costs availability, and a copy added in parallel buys it.

  <!-- sysd-scale-074 -->

  *Figure: The same two 99.9% components give a lower or a higher total depending on layout.*

  | Layout | How totals combine | Two parts at 99.9% each |
  |---|---|---|
  | In sequence | Product of availabilities, so it decreases | 99.8% |
  | In parallel | 1 minus product of unavailabilities, so it increases | 99.9999% |

- **Forms of redundancy: hardware, information, time and software**

  Computing has four major forms of redundancy: hardware (dual or triple modular) and information (error detection and correction). The others are time (repeating an operation or sending several copies of data) and software (N-version programming). Dissimilar redundancy uses different things instead of copies of the same thing, because they are unlikely to share identical flaws. It is common for software, since identical software contains identical flaws. Geographic redundancy separates spare devices so power outages, floods, fires or storms are less likely to disable most or all of the system. Cloud providers use separations from over 621 miles (999 km) down to buildings over 300 feet (91 m) apart.

  <!-- sysd-scale-135 -->

- **Capacity planning: matching resources to demand**

  Too little capacity loses users, and too much sits idle. Capacity planning is the process of determining the capacity needed to meet changing demand. In IT it estimates the storage, hardware, software and connection resources required over a future period. A mismatch leaves resources under-utilized or demand unmet, and planning aims to minimize that gap. Four strategies exist: lead adds capacity as demand grows, lag adds only at full capacity, match adds small amounts as demand changes, and adjustment. Lead is risky when demand is unpredictable, and lag can lose users.

  <!-- sysd-scale-137 -->

- **Three bottlenecks that stop a system from growing**

  A system can stall on three kinds of weak spot. A scalability bottleneck is a part of the design, such as a centralized, slow or tightly coupled component, that stops a system from growing. A centralized component is the first, and it can also become a part whose failure stops everything, as Single point of failure: the part with no spare describes. High-latency components, which perform time-consuming operations, are the second. Tight coupling is the third, because it makes components difficult to scale. To build a scalable system, follow the principles of statelessness, Loose coupling: changing one part without breaking the rest and asynchronous processing.

  <!-- sysd-scale-063 -->

- **Clustering versus load balancing: servers that know each other**

  Servers in a cluster are aware of each other. Servers behind a load balancer are not, and they simply react to the requests it sends them. That awareness is the line between the two ideas. Clustering links servers that work together toward a common purpose, and it provides redundancy and boosts capacity and availability. Load balancing shares traits with clustering but is a different process, since it spreads requests across servers. The two combine well. Load balancing can be used together with clustering, and also with independent servers that share a purpose such as running a website, business application or web service.

  <!-- sysd-scale-077 -->

### Replication

Anything that exists only once can stop the whole system when it breaks. Replication answers that by maintaining multiple copies of data, processes or resources so that redundant components stay consistent. When one copy fails, failover lets a standby or replica take over so the system keeps operating. The hard part is writes: in single-leader replication one instance handles them all, while in multi-master replication any member can update, so conflicting changes must be prevented or resolved. Synchronous replication waits for the remote copy to acknowledge a write, asynchronous replication does not, and a quorum is the minimum number of votes needed before an operation may proceed.

- **Replication: keeping several copies in step**

  Keep a second copy of your data and one question follows at once: what happens when the copies disagree? Replication means maintaining multiple copies of data, processes or resources so that redundant components stay consistent. It is a fundamental technique across databases, file systems and distributed systems. It improves availability, accessibility and performance, and in databases it improves durability too.

  Replication does three jobs. Systems keep operating when components fail, through Failover: when a standby takes over. They serve requests from geographically distributed locations. And they balance load across machines. Copying data across multiple nodes also scales read operations while improving redundancy. Data replication stores the same data on multiple storage devices. Computation replication runs the same task many times, either on separate devices, in space, or repeatedly on one device, in time.

  Ideally users never notice. Access to a replicated entity is typically uniform with access to a single one. The switch to a replica after a failure should be hidden as much as possible. The challenge is keeping replicas consistent while managing the trade-offs between consistency, availability and partition tolerance, constraints known as the The CAP theorem: why no store can have everything. Do not confuse replication with Backup: a copy kept somewhere else. That copy stays unchanged for a long period, while replicas are updated frequently and quickly lose any historical state.

  <!-- sysd-scale-043 -->

- **Single point of failure: the part with no spare**

  One part failing alone can stop everything. That is a single point of failure: a part of a system that would stop the entire system from working if it failed. No spare or redundant option exists to keep the system functioning without it, and its interruption is substantially more disruptive than an error elsewhere. So it is undesirable in any system aiming at high availability or reliability. Systems are made robust by adding redundancy at every such point, found by identifying the critical components whose malfunction would cause total failure. At the system level, one normally deploys a load balancer for a server cluster, with spare servers ready to take over. At the site level, the whole cluster may be replicated elsewhere, because a data center can itself be a single point of failure. Scholars have argued that outsourcing that duplication to cloud providers only moves the single point of failure. The Internet avoids the problem: multiple paths let packets route around the failure of any one path or node.

  <!-- sysd-scale-056 -->

- **Failover: when a standby takes over**

  Failover is switching to a redundant or standby computer server, system, hardware component or network when the previously active one fails or terminates abnormally. The system keeps operating, and users should notice as little as possible. How it works depends on the replication scheme.

  In failover clustering, passive replica servers copy the master's data to prepare for takeover, while the master is the only server active for client interaction. In a primary-backup scheme, taken up in Primary-backup replication: one server orders every write, a standby process takes over if the primary fails. In master-slave replication, a slave is promoted to master or a new master is provisioned. In master-master replication, failover is simple, automatic and quick, because both masters already serve reads and writes.

  Tools make this concrete. In PostgreSQL a standby leaves standby mode and becomes the primary when pg_ctl promote is run. A warm standby is typically only moments from full availability once activated.

  Automatic failover can also be dangerous. If a primary cannot tell whether its secondary is healthy, one SRE design has it make itself unavailable and call a human, to avoid Split-brain: two nodes that both think they are in charge. That protects data but hurts availability and scales poorly.

  <!-- sysd-scale-058 -->

- **Gossip protocols: spreading news like an epidemic**

  In a network of 25,000 machines, a search string can reach every one of them in about 15 rounds of gossip. A gossip or epidemic protocol is a procedure of peer-to-peer communication based on the way epidemics spread. Each node periodically picks another node at random and shares what it knows. A rumor roughly doubles its reach each round, and the doubling keeps the protocol robust even when some messages are lost. That is why information reaches all nodes in time logarithmic in system size. Dissemination protocols flood information through the network with bounded worst-case load. Aggregation protocols compute network-wide values, such as the largest or smallest, with fixed-size pairwise exchanges. Gossip keeps distributed databases consistent, counts nodes, spreads news, builds overlay networks and elects leaders, and Dynamo uses a gossip-based protocol for membership and failure detection. The SRE book warns that heartbeats and gossip will always have reliability problems for master election and group membership, which are problems of Consensus: getting machines to agree despite failures.

  <!-- sysd-scale-128 -->

- **Single-leader replication: one node takes every write**

  In this design every write has exactly one destination. In single-leader replication, one database instance is the leader that handles all writes and propagates them to replica nodes. The leader logs its updates, and each replica acknowledges receipt. Replicas primarily serve reads, but they may serve stale data because of replication lag, the delay in propagating changes from the leader. In the familiar master-slave form, the master serves reads and writes and replicates writes to one or more slaves, which serve only reads. If the master goes offline, the system keeps operating in read-only mode until a slave is promoted to master or a new master is provisioned. The benefits are clear. Copying the whole database for safekeeping barely affects the master. Applications can read from slaves without loading it, and slaves can go offline and be synced back without downtime. The costs are also clear: more hardware and complexity, and downtime and possible data loss when the master fails. All writes still go to the master, and more read slaves mean more replication lag.

  <!-- sysd-scale-044 -->

- **Log shipping: a standby that replays the primary's log**

  If the primary dies, the transactions it has not yet shipped die with it. That is the bargain of log shipping, a high-availability setup. A standby server continuously replays the primary's write-ahead log (WAL) and is ready to take over if the primary fails. The primary runs in continuous archiving mode and each standby in continuous recovery mode, reading the WAL files, so the two servers are only loosely coupled. It needs no changes to database tables, so it has low administration overhead and a relatively low performance impact on the primary. File-based shipping sends WAL one 16MB segment at a time, cheaply over any distance. Record-based shipping streams WAL changes incrementally over a network connection. Because log shipping is asynchronous, archive_timeout can shrink the loss window to a few seconds at the cost of bandwidth, and streaming replication allows a much smaller one. A standby is typically moments from full availability once activated, which makes it a warm standby. Primary and standby should be as similar as possible, in hardware architecture and major PostgreSQL version.

  <!-- sysd-scale-131 -->

- **Leader election: choosing one organizer**

  Every node in a network must agree on a single organizer, and none may dispute it. Leader election is the process of designating a single process as the organizer of a task distributed among several nodes. A valid algorithm must terminate in finite time, ensure uniqueness (exactly one process considers itself leader) and ensure agreement (all other processes know who the leader is). The nodes must break the symmetry among them. With unique, comparable identities, they can choose the highest. No deterministic algorithm can elect a leader in an anonymous ring, where all processes are identical, because symmetry cannot be broken. In the Chang and Roberts ring algorithm each processor sends its ID clockwise, passing on bigger IDs and discarding smaller ones, so the highest ID wins. Leader election is equivalent to distributed Consensus: getting machines to agree despite failures, so the SRE book recommends formally proven systems wherever you see leader election, critical shared state or distributed locking. In Raft: consensus built to be understood, a follower that hears no heartbeat becomes a candidate and starts an election.

  <!-- sysd-scale-124 -->

- **Multi-master replication: every member can write**

  What if every copy of the data could accept writes? In multi-master replication, a group of computers stores the data and any member can update it. All members respond to client queries, and the system propagates each member's changes to the other members and resolves conflicts between concurrent changes. Unlike failover clustering, where passive replicas prepare for takeover and only the master serves clients, every master is active. In master-slave replication, a single master per data item makes consistency easier to achieve but is less flexible. The main purposes are increased availability and faster server response time. If one master fails the others keep updating, and masters can sit in several physical sites, enabling local write processing across data centers. The drawbacks are real. Most systems are only loosely consistent, lazy and asynchronous. Eager replication is complex and adds latency, and conflict resolution can become intractable as nodes and latency grow. Jim Gray argued that unless data splits naturally into disjoint sub-databases, concurrency control conflicts seriously degrade performance, with slowdown possibly scaling as O(n³) in the number of replicas.

  <!-- sysd-scale-045 -->

- **When two leaders disagree: resolving replication conflicts**

  If one record changes on two leader nodes at once, which change wins? The most common challenge in multi-master replication is exactly this. When concurrent modifications land on different leader nodes, a replicated database must either prevent the transactional conflict or resolve it afterwards. Most synchronous (eager) replication solutions prevent conflicts, while asynchronous (lazy) solutions have to resolve them. An eager system detects the conflict before confirming the commit and aborts one transaction. A lazy system lets both commit and resolves the conflict during re-synchronization. Conflict resolution methods include last-write-wins, application-specific logic and merging concurrent updates.

  <!-- sysd-scale-046 -->

- **CRDTs: data structures that merge themselves**

  League of Legends runs in-game chat for 7.5 million concurrent users, at 11,000 messages per second, on the Riak implementation of a conflict-free replicated data type. A conflict-free replicated data type (CRDT) is a data structure replicated across computers. Any replica can update it independently and concurrently, and a built-in algorithm resolves inconsistencies so replicas converge. Uncoordinated concurrent updates can leave replicas inconsistent in ways that may not be resolvable. Optimistic replication lets all updates through and merges later, and CRDTs are the data structures for which that merge always works. They are a common way to obtain Strong eventual consistency: same updates, same state, in two variants, state-based and operation-based. Their development was motivated by collaborative text editing and mobile computing, and they have also been used in online chat. Redis, Riak and Cosmos DB have CRDT data types. A sequence CRDT can build a collaborative real-time editor as an alternative to Operational transformation.

  <!-- sysd-scale-125 -->

- **Synchronous and asynchronous replication: wait or don't wait**

  For a 10 km distance the fastest possible round trip takes 67 μs, whereas an entire local cached write completes in about 10–20 μs. That gap is the heart of a choice every replicated system makes: does a write wait for the remote copy?

  Synchronous replication waits. A write is not complete until both local and remote storage acknowledge it, so it guarantees zero data loss with atomic write operations. In a synchronous database, a transaction is not committed until all servers have committed it, so failover loses nothing. The price is performance. Most applications wait for the write to complete, so overall performance falls considerably. It drops in proportion to distance, since minimum latency is set by the speed of light. Latency decides how far apart sites can be.

  Asynchronous replication does not wait. A write is complete as soon as local storage acknowledges it, and remote storage updates with a small lag. It can be near-real-time but more commonly runs on a schedule, and it is more cost-effective. Performance is much higher. But the most recent data may be lost if local storage fails, transactions might be lost in a failover, and replicas may return slightly stale results.

  Semi-synchronous replication sits between the two. A write counts as complete when local storage acknowledges it and the remote server receives or logs it. The remote write itself is asynchronous, so durability is not guaranteed on local failure.

  <!-- sysd-scale-047 -->

  *Figure: Waiting for the remote copy buys safety and costs speed.*

  |  | Synchronous | Asynchronous |
  |---|---|---|
  | Write completes when | Local and remote storage both acknowledge | Local storage acknowledges |
  | After a failover | Nothing is lost | Recent transactions may be lost |
  | Performance | Lower, and drops with distance | Much higher |
  | Replica state | Always in step | Slightly stale |

- **Quorum: how many votes are enough**

  Two groups cut off from each other cannot both hold a majority. That is the idea behind a quorum: the minimum number of votes a Distributed transactions: one commit across many databases must obtain before it may perform an operation in a distributed system. Quorum-based techniques enforce consistent operation, both as a replica control method and as a commit method that keeps transactions atomic despite network partitioning. In replica control each copy holds a vote, and an operation needs a read quorum Vr or a write quorum Vw. The rule Vr + Vw > V, where V is the total votes, makes every read quorum include the newest version. A second rule ensures two write operations on the same item cannot happen concurrently, and together the two rules maintain one-copy serializability. In commit protocols a transaction runs only if a majority of sites vote for it, so it cannot commit and abort at once. In a partitioned cluster, the sub-partition holding a majority of the votes stays available while the others fall into an auto-fencing mode.

  <!-- sysd-scale-122 -->

- **Leaderless replication: the Dynamo approach**

  In this design no node is special. In leaderless replication any replica accepts writes, as in Dynamo, a set of techniques for a highly available key-value store with no distinguished node. DynamoDB, built on Dynamo's principles, uses single-leader replication instead. Dynamo's principles are symmetry, with the same responsibilities on every node, and decentralization, peer-to-peer over central control. They also include incremental scalability, adding one node at a time, and heterogeneity, with work proportional to server capability. It partitions data with Consistent hashing: adding a server without reshuffling everything. For highly available writes it uses Vector clocks: a counter per process to detect causality and reconciles conflicting versions during reads. For temporary failures, a sloppy quorum and hinted handoff keep availability and durability when some replicas are unavailable. For permanent failures, anti-entropy with Merkle trees finds differences between replica owners so divergent replicas can be synchronized proactively. Membership and failure detection use a gossip-based protocol, which avoids a central registry and preserves symmetry. Cassandra, Project Voldemort and Riak were inspired by the Dynamo paper.

  <!-- sysd-scale-129 -->

- **The read replica pattern: writes to one, reads from many**

  Viewing an order history changes nothing, so it does not need to touch the primary. In the read replica pattern, all data-modifying commands go to the primary database and reads go to read replicas. Inserts, deletes and updates are sent to the primary and replicated to the read replicas, which serve reads such as viewing order details or order history. There are two common ways to implement it: embed the routing logic in the application code, or use database middleware. Middleware provides transparent routing between the application and the database servers, with rules customizable by user, schema, statement and so on. It acts as a proxy using the standard MySQL network protocol. It simplifies application code, since the application need not know the database topology, and any MySQL-compatible client can connect, which makes database migration easier. The cost is complexity and network latency. Because all queries go through it, middleware usually needs a high-availability setup to avoid becoming a single point of failure.

  <!-- sysd-scale-049 -->

  *Figure: Writes go to the primary, which replicates them to the replicas that serve reads.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  W[Inserts, deletes, updates] -->|sent to| P[(Primary database)]
  P -->|replicates to| R[(Read replicas)]
  R -->|serve| Q[Reads, such as order history]
  ```

- **Performance bottleneck: the slowest part sets the pace**

  A system moves at the speed of its slowest part. A bottleneck occurs when the capacity of an application or computer system is limited by a single component. It is the part with the lowest throughput of all parts of the transaction path. A common example is code that could use parallel processing but runs several independent processes sequentially instead of simultaneously. Tracking down bottlenecks, or hot spots, is called performance analysis. It is done with specialized profilers, with the objective of making those sections of code as fast as possible. Bottlenecks, like series circuits, are design structures that create single points of failure.

  <!-- sysd-scale-057 -->

- **Replication lag: reading your own writes**

  You place an order, check your order list a moment later, and the order is missing. The likely culprit is replication lag, the delay in propagating changes from the leader to its replicas, which can leave replicas serving stale data. Under network delay or server overload, replica data might be seconds or even minutes behind the primary. A user who checks an order right after placing it may hit a lagging replica and not see the order at all, so the setup needs read-after-write consistency. One mitigation is to send latency-sensitive reads, and reads that immediately follow writes, to the primary database. Another is to check whether a replica has caught up with the primary, which a relational database generally supports. Query the replica if it is up to date. Otherwise fail the read or read from the primary.

  <!-- sysd-scale-048 -->

- **Active and passive replication: who does the work?**

  When a request arrives, who does the work: every replica, or just one? In the active form, every replica processes the same request. In the passive form, one replica processes each request and transfers the result to the others. In a primary-backup or primary-replica scheme, one leader replica chosen by leader election processes all requests, a design predominant in high-availability clusters. In a multi-primary or multi-master scheme, any replica can process a request and distribute the new state. That calls for some form of distributed concurrency control, such as a Distributed locks: only one worker at a time manager. State machine replication: identical copies from ordered commands is sometimes mistakenly used as a synonym of Active replication: every replica applies every operation in order.

  <!-- sysd-scale-050 -->

- **Chain replication: writes that travel down a line**

  In chain replication, a write must pass through several nodes one after another. It is a family of multi-primary protocols that arrange replicas in a chain for writes to get high throughput and strong consistency. Modern multi-primary replication protocols optimize for the common failure-free operation, and chain replication is a popular family of them. It enables local reads on all replica nodes but has high latency for writes, which must traverse several nodes sequentially. The Hermes protocol takes another route. It combines invalidations and logical timestamps for strong consistency with local reads and high-performance writes from all replicas, committing after one multicast round trip.

  <!-- sysd-scale-052 -->

- **Three ways to ship changes to a replica**

  A leader can describe its changes to replicas in three ways. Statement-based replication logs write requests such as SQL statements and sends them to replicas for execution, which is problematic with non-deterministic functions or statements with side effects. Write-ahead log shipping replicates the storage engine's low-level log, which keeps data structures identical across nodes. Logical (row-based) replication describes changes at the row level in a dedicated log format, giving more flexibility and independence from storage engine internals.

  <!-- sysd-scale-053 -->

- **Logical replication: publishing changes row by row**

  Not every copy has to be a byte-for-byte clone. Logical replication replicates data objects and their changes based on their replication identity, usually a primary key, rather than copying physical blocks. Physical replication, which PostgreSQL also supports, uses exact block addresses and byte-by-byte copying. Logical replication uses a publish and subscribe model. Subscribers pull data from the publications they subscribe to on a publisher node, and may re-publish it to allow cascading or more complex setups. Replication of a table starts with a snapshot copy to the subscriber. Changes made since the copy are then sent continually and applied in the publisher's order, so transactional consistency holds within one subscription. Use cases include sending a subset of a database's changes, consolidating databases for analytics, replicating between major versions or platforms, and sharing a subset of data. A read-only subscriber causes no conflicts from a single subscription, but other writes to the same tables can cause conflicts.

  <!-- sysd-scale-132 -->

- **Three models of replication**

  Three models of data replication are widely cited. Transactional replication, used for replicating transactional data such as a database, follows one-copy serializability: valid outcomes on replicated data accord with ACID. The second model, State machine replication: identical copies from ordered commands, assumes a deterministic finite automaton and Atomic broadcast: everyone sees the same messages in the same order of every event. It is based on Consensus: getting machines to agree despite failures and is usually implemented as a replicated log of Paxos: agreement among unreliable processors rounds. In virtual synchrony, processes form a group, and a joining process receives a checkpoint of the replicated state. Multicasts reach all members in identical order, with membership changes delivered as a new membership view.

  <!-- sysd-scale-051 -->

- **Storage replication: copying disks, not files**

  Copy the disk and everything on it is copied too. Storage replication copies block-device updates to several physical disks, so any file system on top is replicated without modification. It is implemented in a disk array controller or in a device driver. Disk mirroring is the most basic method, but replication can also cross a network to distant disks. The purpose is to prevent damage from failures or disasters at one location or to improve the ability to recover data. Point-in-time replication copies periodic snapshots of only the changed data, so it can use cheaper links such as iSCSI or T1 instead of fiberoptic lines.

  <!-- sysd-scale-054 -->

- **Choosing a replication solution**

  No single replication solution fits every workload. Database servers can work together in two ways. For high availability, a second server takes over if the primary fails. For load balancing, several computers serve the same data. Read-only servers combine easily, but read/write servers are hard, because a write to any server must reach all servers so later reads stay consistent. This synchronization problem is the fundamental difficulty, and each solution minimizes it for a specific workload. Some let only one server modify data: a warm standby cannot be connected to until promoted, while a hot standby accepts read-only queries. Functionality is traded against performance.

  <!-- sysd-scale-130 -->

- **File-based replication: copying files, not blocks**

  Instead of a whole 4,096-byte disk block, file-level replication can transmit just the 100 bytes an application wrote. File-based replication copies data at the logical level of individual files rather than at the storage block level. It relies almost exclusively on software. A kernel filter driver can intercept file system calls such as open, write and delete and send them to another machine, which mimics them. It can skip data of no business value, such as temporary files. Batch replication compares source and destination and makes the destination match. It is generally free or inexpensive, such as rsync, but system-intensive, so it generally runs infrequently.

  <!-- sysd-scale-055 -->

- **Split-brain: two nodes that both think they are in charge**

  High-availability clusters watch node health over a private heartbeat link. If all those links fail while the nodes keep running, each node believes it is the only one running. That is split-brain: a state of data or availability inconsistency caused by two separate data sets with overlapping scope. It typically arises when servers stop communicating and synchronizing, as in a Network partitions: the cluster splits but every node keeps running. Each side then serves clients from its own data set with no coordination, which can corrupt data. The SRE book's diagnosis is that such a system solves a leader election problem with simple timeouts. But leader election is a form of distributed Consensus: getting machines to agree despite failures and cannot be solved correctly using heartbeats. Optimistic approaches let partitioned nodes keep working, gaining availability at the cost of correctness. Pessimistic approaches give up availability for consistency by limiting access to sub-partitions. The typical pessimistic approach is a quorum vote: the sub-partition with a majority of the votes stays available and the others fence themselves off. A two-node cluster without a witness cannot tell which member should be active when the heartbeat fails.

  <!-- sysd-scale-123 -->

  *Figure: Follow the arrows from lost heartbeat links to two data sets that disagree.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Heartbeat links fail] --> B[Each node thinks it is alone]
  B --> C[Each side serves clients separately]
  C --> D[Data corrupted or inconsistent]
  ```

- **Sending state or sending operations: two kinds of CRDT**

  State-based CRDTs replicate by sending full state to be merged, while operation-based CRDTs replicate by sending the update operations. State-based ones (CvRDTs) send their full local state, and the merge must be commutative, associative and idempotent, so reordering and duplicated messages do no harm. They are simpler to design and need only a gossip protocol, but the whole state must eventually reach every replica. Operation-based ones (CmRDTs) send operations such as +10 or -20, which must be commutative and associative. They use less bandwidth when transactions are few compared with the state size, but need middleware that never drops or duplicates operations and delivers them in causal order.

  <!-- sysd-scale-126 -->

  *Figure: The two kinds of CRDT trade bandwidth against what the network must guarantee.*

  |  | State-based | Operation-based |
  |---|---|---|
  | Sends | Full local state | Update operations |
  | Rule | Merge is commutative, associative, idempotent | Operations commutative and associative |
  | Needs | Only a gossip protocol | Middleware that never drops or duplicates |
  | Cost | Whole state must reach every replica | Less bandwidth when transactions are few |

- **Counters and sets built as CRDTs**

  A counter that many machines update at once needs a slot per machine. A G-Counter gives each node an array slot to increment. Replicas merge by taking the maximum of every slot, and the value is the sum of the slots. A PN-Counter combines two G-Counters, one for increments and one for decrements, and its value is the increment total minus the decrement total. A G-Set only allows adds and merges by union, and a 2P-Set adds a tombstone set so elements can be removed, though a removed element can never return. An OR-Set tags each add uniquely and removes only the tags it has observed.

  <!-- sysd-scale-127 -->

### Sharding and partitioning

Which piece of the data lives where? That one question drives this chapter. A partition is a division of a logical database into distinct, independent parts, and a shard is a horizontal partition that may sit on its own database server. The rules for assigning data range from key ranges, like the volumes of an encyclopedia, to hash functions that turn skewed data into a uniform distribution, with refinements such as consistent hashing and rendezvous hashing. Sharding also has a price: skew and hot spots, and more complexity in the infrastructure and the application code.

- **Database partitioning: cutting a big database into independent pieces**

  A query that touches only one partition runs on that partition's node and nowhere else, so throughput grows linearly as nodes are added. That is the promise of database partitioning: deliberately breaking a large database into smaller, independent parts. Each record, row or document belongs to exactly one partition, so each partition is effectively a small database of its own. It is normally done for manageability, performance, availability or load balancing. More complex queries can be parallelized across nodes, with extra challenges. Partitioning is often combined with replication: a record belongs to one partition but exists on several nodes, and a node can lead some partitions while following others. Systems name the pieces differently: shard in MongoDB, region in HBase, vnode in Cassandra, tablet in Bigtable: Google's structured storage at petabyte scale. None of this is a Network partitions: the cluster splits but every node keeps running, which is a fault in the network between nodes.

  <!-- sysd-scale-080 -->

- **How a database decides which partition holds a row**

  Every row needs an address, and the partitioning key supplies it. A relational database takes that key and applies a criterion: range, list, composite, round-robin or Hash partitioning: trading range queries for an even load. In Range partitioning: one volume of keys per partition, continuous ranges of the key go to each partition. List partitioning gives each partition a list of values. Iceland, Norway, Sweden, Finland and Denmark, for example, can form a partition for the Nordic countries. Composite partitioning combines schemes, such as range first and then hash. Round-robin partitioning sends the ith tuple in insertion order to partition (i mod n). That gives uniform distribution and parallel sequential access, but reaching tuples by a predicate means accessing the entire relation.

  Sharded systems add a few names for the same ideas. The sharding key is a column of the table, and the sharding algorithm uses it to decide which shard stores each row. Choosing the right key and algorithm is crucial for even distribution and performance. Directory-based sharding keeps a lookup table, the directory, that maps keys to shard locations, and routes data by consulting it. Hash-based sharding has an extension in Consistent hashing: adding a server without reshuffling everything, which moves less data when shards change. It can be seen as a composite of hash and list partitioning. Virtual bucket sharding maps data to virtual buckets and buckets to physical shards. That eases rebalancing without much data movement. When shards follow a real-world segmentation, such as European versus American customers, the right shard is easy to infer and only that shard is queried.

  <!-- sysd-scale-082 -->

  *Figure: Each rule maps a row's key to a partition or shard in a different way.*

  | Rule | How a row finds its partition |
  |---|---|
  | List | Its key is in the partition's list of values |
  | Composite | Schemes are combined, such as range then hash |
  | Round-robin | The ith tuple goes to partition i mod n |
  | Directory-based | A lookup table maps keys to shard locations |
  | Virtual bucket | Keys map to buckets, buckets to physical shards |

- **Range partitioning: one volume of keys per partition**

  Because the range boundaries are known, a request can be routed straight to the partition that holds its key. That is the appeal of range partitioning, which assigns continuous ranges of the partitioning key to partitions, like the volumes of an encyclopedia. A typical example is a partition for all rows whose zipcode column has a value between 70000 and 79999. Ranges must be contiguous but not overlapping, and key values at or above a range's upper bound go to the next partition. It works on ordered columns such as integers, longs or timestamps. Examples are customers by the alphabetical order of last name, transactions by date range, or user IDs 1 to 1000 in shard 1. Boundaries can be set manually or automatically so that the data is balanced across partitions. Range scans are efficient, but some access patterns, such as writing time-ordered keys, pile load onto one partition, a problem named in Skew and hot spots: one partition carries the load.

  <!-- sysd-scale-083 -->

- **Horizontal partitioning: same columns, fewer rows per table**

  Customers with ZIP codes below 50000 go in a table called CustomersEast, and those at 50000 or above in CustomersWest. That is horizontal partitioning: different rows of a table go into different tables. A view with a union over both tables gives the complete picture of all customers. Holding fewer rows in each table reduces index size, which generally improves search performance. It pays off when there is an obvious, robust and implicit way to tell which partition holds a row without searching the index, as a ZIP code does. Many guides treat the term as a synonym for sharding.

  <!-- sysd-scale-085 -->

  *Figure: Rows are routed by ZIP code, and a view with a union puts the two tables back together.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Customers] --> B{ZIP below 50000?}
  B -->|yes| C[CustomersEast]
  B -->|50000 or above| D[CustomersWest]
  C --> E[View: union of both tables]
  D --> E
  ```

- **Database sharding: spreading one database across many servers**

  Each shard is the single source for its subset of the data. A database shard is a horizontal partition of the data in a database or search engine. Each may be held on a separate database server instance. Every shard has the same schema and columns but holds a unique, independent subset of the data, and all the shards together contain all of it. Placing them on separate hardware spreads a database across many machines, which can significantly improve performance.

  Splitting tables over servers reduces the rows per table and the index size, which generally improves search. The search load then spreads over multiple servers, rather than only over several indexes on one server. That separates sharding from plain Horizontal partitioning: same columns, fewer rows per table, which stays within one schema instance and server. Sharding partitions the table the same way across potentially multiple instances of the schema. Large partitionable tables are distributed across servers, while smaller tables are replicated in full on each server. A mechanism is then needed to keep the replicated tables synchronized.

  Sharding relates to Shared nothing: every request served by a single node, since each shard can sit in its own schema instance, server, data center or region, and it aims to minimize cross-shard access. The sharding logic can live in the application, in a middleware layer between the application and the database, or in the database system itself. Shards also give logical independence. Each can be managed on its own for availability, and sensitive and non-sensitive data can be kept in different partitions for better manageability and security.

  <!-- sysd-scale-087 -->

- **Shared nothing: every request served by a single node**

  In a shared-nothing system, no two nodes compete for the same memory or storage. A shared-nothing architecture is a distributed computing architecture in which each update request is satisfied by a single node in a cluster. A node here is a processor, memory and storage unit. The intent is to eliminate contention among nodes. Shared everything, by contrast, satisfies requests with arbitrary combinations of nodes and so risks contention when several nodes update the same data at once. Shared-nothing removes single points of failure, so the system keeps running despite node failures, and nodes can upgrade hardware or software without a system-wide shutdown. It scales simply by adding nodes, because no central resource is a bottleneck. Data is typically partitioned among many nodes, and in a database the part on one node is a shard. Commonly used but rarely modified data can be replicated across nodes so more requests resolve on a single node. The weak point is any request that needs data from multiple nodes, which can dramatically reduce throughput.

  <!-- sysd-scale-141 -->

- **Skew and hot spots: one partition carries the load**

  With ideal distribution, ten nodes process ten times the data and throughput of one node. Skew eats into that. It is the uneven distribution of data or load across partitions, and a partition that receives excessive load is called a hot spot. A sensor network keyed by timestamp shows how it happens: writes concentrate in the partition for the current time period. Prefixing the timestamp with the sensor identifier in a compound key spreads that load. Other remedies are assigning records to nodes at random, at the cost of harder retrieval, key-range partitioning with optimized boundaries, or hash-based partitioning for even load.

  <!-- sysd-scale-081 -->

- **What sharding costs: harder queries and more to go wrong**

  Sharding buys scale with complexity, in the database infrastructure and in the application code. Developers may need to write more complex SQL queries to handle the sharding logic. Joins that span several shards are often not feasible or not efficient, because the data must be retrieved from multiple servers, and transactions across shards may need Distributed transactions: one commit across many databases. The ORDER BY operation gets more complicated: data is usually fetched from different shards and sorted in the application's code. The software that partitions, balances, coordinates and keeps the data correct can itself fail or introduce errors. Corruption or failure of one shard can affect the integrity of the entire dataset, and fail-over servers must maintain copies of all shards. Backing up the individual shards must be coordinated, and adding indexes, modifying columns or altering the schema all become harder. Uneven distribution, also called a hotspot, forces rebalancing, and changing the sharding scheme after the database is sharded is complex and time-consuming.

  <!-- sysd-scale-088 -->

- **Hash partitioning: trading range queries for an even load**

  Run a key through a hash function and its neighbors scatter. That is both the strength and the cost of hash partitioning, which turns skewed data into a uniform distribution so that load spreads evenly across partitions. It effectively prevents hot spots, but it sacrifices range query efficiency, because adjacent keys land on different partitions. A shard key such as a customer ID or transaction ID is hashed, which tends to spread data more evenly than range-based sharding. A proper hash function is needed to avoid collisions. Cassandra and MongoDB commonly use MD5. Cassandra also combines both approaches with compound primary keys: the first component is hashed to pick the partition, while the remaining components keep sort order within it. The simplest form is shard_id = hash(user_id) % num_shards, but adding or removing database servers then becomes expensive. That is the problem Consistent hashing: adding a server without reshuffling everything solves.

  <!-- sysd-scale-084 -->

- **Consistent hashing: adding a server without reshuffling everything**

  Add one server to a pool, and an ordinary hash table remaps nearly all of its keys. The key-to-slot mapping is a modulo operation, so changing the number of slots, here the servers, reshuffles almost everything, and reassigning everything is expensive. Consistent hashing is the fix. It is a technique that lets a hash table be resized while remapping only about n/m keys on average. Here n is the number of keys and m the number of slots.

  It hashes both the keys and the servers onto a circle, and assigns each key to the next server found clockwise from it. When a server fails or is added, only the keys next to it on the circle move. Adding the nth server relocates only a 1/n fraction of the keys. Karger and colleagues introduced it in 1997 as the basis of caching protocols that relieve hot spots on very large networks such as the Internet. A consistent hash function changes minimally as its range changes. Those protocols therefore need no current, or even consistent, view of the whole network and scale gracefully as it grows.

  In practice it spreads cache keys evenly across shards even if some fail. DynamoDB and Cassandra use it to minimize data movement during rebalancing, and CDNs use it to spread content over edge servers. To stay available and durable, it replicates each data item on N nodes, where N is the replication factor. In eventually consistent systems, the subject of Eventual consistency: every reader agrees, but not yet, the copies are made asynchronously. It is not perfect. In theory it spreads load evenly, but in practice load is often uneven and one server can become a hotspot. It also adds complexity, risks one failure triggering others in a chain, and makes key management costly when nodes transiently fail.

  <!-- sysd-scale-078 -->

  *Figure: Adding a server moves nearly every key in an ordinary hash table and only a fraction on the circle.*

  | Question | Ordinary hash table | Consistent hashing |
  |---|---|---|
  | A key goes to | A slot, by modulo | The next server clockwise on a circle |
  | After a server is added | Nearly all keys remap | Only a 1/n fraction of keys move |

- **Distributed hash tables: a lookup service with no center**

  In a distributed hash table, any node can find the value for any key, and no central coordinator is needed. A distributed hash table (DHT) is a distributed system that provides a lookup service similar to a hash table, with key-value pairs stored across the participating nodes. Most DHTs map keys to nodes with Consistent hashing: adding a server without reshuffling everything or Rendezvous hashing: every client picks the same server alone. Adding or removing a node then changes only the keys of adjacent IDs, whereas a traditional hash table remaps nearly the whole keyspace. A DHT has three parts. An abstract keyspace, such as 160-bit strings, comes first. A scheme then splits ownership of it among nodes, and an overlay network lets nodes find the owner of any key. Each node links to a few others, and a lookup is forwarded greedily to the closest neighbor, called key-based routing. A common design has O(log n) neighbors and O(log n) route length, as in Chord: finding the node that stores a key, Kademlia and Pastry. DHTs underpin distributed file systems and peer-to-peer file sharing, as in BitTorrent's distributed tracker and IPFS.

  <!-- sysd-scale-139 -->

- **Rendezvous hashing: every client picks the same server alone**

  Many clients, no coordinator, one answer: that is the point of rendezvous hashing, also called highest random weight (HRW) hashing, designed in 1996. It lets clients reach distributed agreement on a set of k options out of a possible set of n options. A typical use is agreeing on which sites, meaning servers or proxies, an object is assigned to. Each client chooses independently, yet all must pick the same sites, and the standard case is k = 1. All clients share a hash function h. For an object O, each computes the weight h(O, S) for every site S and picks the site with the highest weight. When a site fails, only its objects move, to the next largest weight, while a plain table of n sites would remap every object. Compared with Consistent hashing: adding a server without reshuffling everything, it is much simpler, needs no precomputed or stored tokens, and handles any k < n. It is now preferred over consistent hashing in many applications, such as the GitHub load balancer, Apache Ignite, Apache Kafka: a log that keeps messages after they are read and the Twitter EventBus pub/sub platform.

  <!-- sysd-scale-079 -->

- **Virtual nodes: giving each server many places on the ring**

  Servers are not spread uniformly around a hash ring, so some own more of it than others, which causes skew among nodes. A virtual node, or vnode, is an existing physical node mapped multiple times across the ring. Its share of the key space is then made of several small ranges. The number of duplicate labels a server gets is its weight. Without them, a failed server's keys all move to the next server clockwise, potentially doubling its load. With several positions, its keys go to different servers and spread more evenly. Virtual nodes also speed up rebalancing and lower the probability of hotspots.

  <!-- sysd-scale-089 -->

- **Chord: finding the node that stores a key**

  Chord supports one operation: given a key, it maps the key onto a node. This distributed lookup protocol lets peer-to-peer applications locate the node storing a data item. Data location is built on top, by storing each key and item at the node the key maps to. Chord uses consistent hashing: nodes are points on a circle, and the keyspace is split into contiguous segments whose endpoints are node identifiers. It adapts efficiently as nodes join and leave, and it answers queries even as the system keeps changing. Theory, simulation and experiments show that its communication cost and per-node state both grow logarithmically with the number of nodes.

  <!-- sysd-scale-140 -->

- **Vertical partitioning: splitting a table by its columns**

  Horizontal partitioning splits a table by rows; vertical partitioning splits it by columns. It creates tables with fewer columns and stores the remaining columns in additional tables, which is why it is also called row splitting. It goes beyond normalization, splitting columns even in an already normalized table. Infrequently used or very wide columns can be moved to a different machine. A common form separates static from dynamic data, since the static part is faster to access. A view across the two tables restores the original table at a performance penalty. A columnar database can be seen as one vertically partitioned until each column has its own table.

  <!-- sysd-scale-086 -->

- **Federation: many databases that look like one**

  Federation, also called functional partitioning, splits up databases by function and then presents the pieces as a whole. A federation makes several distinct physical databases appear as one logical database to end users. Federated schemas tie them together, expressing the commonality of data and specifying what the components may share. The result is a cohesive, unified view of data from multiple sources, which can include databases and other structured and unstructured data. A federated database is transparent, so users need not know where data is stored. It copes with differing hardware, protocols and data models, and it leaves existing data sources and their interfaces unchanged. The advantages are flexible data sharing, autonomy among components, unified access to heterogeneous data, and no tight coupling of applications with legacy databases. The disadvantages are extra hardware and complexity, complex joins of data from two databases, dependence on autonomous data sources, and limits on query performance and scalability.

  <!-- sysd-scale-091 -->

- **When sharding is worth it, and when it is not**

  The first rule of sharding is to try everything else first. It is generally recommended only when other optimization strategies have proven insufficient, because sharding a table before optimizing it locally adds needless complexity. The costs are listed in What sharding costs: harder queries and more to go wrong. The case for it is a single server holding too much data, serving too many requests, or answering ever more slowly as data grows. After a certain point it is cheaper and more feasible to scale horizontally by adding machines than vertically by buying more powerful servers. Singh adds using existing hardware instead of high-end machines, and scaling quickly by adding shards.

  <!-- sysd-scale-090 -->

### The CAP theorem and consistency

A consistency model is a contract between the programmer and a system: follow the rules for operations, and reads, writes and updates behave predictably. This chapter asks how strong that contract can be when the network divides into relatively independent subnets, which is what a network partition is. The CAP theorem, also called Brewer's theorem, says a distributed data store can provide at most two of three guarantees: consistency, availability and partition tolerance. From there the chapter covers eventual consistency, PACELC, which adds latency to the choice, the CP, AP and CA labels for databases, and why the theorem is so often misunderstood. It ends with the replication protocols, primary-backup, active and quorum-based, that put these choices into practice.

- **Consistency models: the contract between programmer and store**
