  Row X is replicated on nodes M and N. Client A writes to M, and then client B reads from N. Will B see the write? A consistency model is the contract that answers. It is a contract between the programmer and the system: if the programmer follows the rules for operations, reads, writes and updates behave predictably. The model decides whether B will definitely see the write, definitely not, or cannot count on it. Models define rules for the apparent order and visibility of updates, and they sit on a continuum with trade-offs. One model is stronger than another if it requires all the other's conditions and more, and a model with fewer constraints is weaker. Strict consistency is the strongest: every write must be seen instantaneously by all processors. It is only a thought experiment, because instantaneous message exchange is impossible. Replicas keep a system reliable and fast, but copies can drift. Synchronous replication, covered in Synchronous and asynchronous replication: wait or don't wait, gives tight consistency, yet global synchronization is costly. Weakening the consistency restrictions decreases that cost and improves performance.

  <!-- sysd-scale-092 -->

- **Eventual consistency: every reader agrees, but not yet**

  Until an update converges, different queries for the same record may see different values. That is the bargain of eventual consistency, a model used in distributed computing to achieve high availability. If no new updates are made to a data item, eventually all reads of that item return the last updated value. The model is also called optimistic replication, and a system that has reached that state is said to have converged. It is a weak guarantee. It promises only liveness, that reads eventually return the same value, with no safety guarantee, so any intermediate value is allowed before convergence. Services built this way are often described as BASE (basically available, soft state, eventual consistency), in contrast to traditional ACID. Asynchronous replication helps achieve it, but it can also leave data inconsistent. Many NoSQL databases use it to offer availability and partition tolerance at the price of reduced data consistency. Critics say it adds complexity: wrong assumptions about consistency levels cause subtle bugs that only appear during network failures or high concurrency.

  <!-- sysd-scale-097 -->

- **Network partitions: the cluster splits but every node keeps running**

  Nodes A and B sit on one side of a switch, and nodes C and D on the other. The switch fails. A and B can no longer reach C and D, yet every node works as before. That is a network partition: a division of a computer network into relatively independent subnets, either by design or because network devices fail. Distributed software must be designed to be partition-tolerant, meaning it still works correctly after the network is partitioned. Partitions are inevitable. Cables get cut, packets are lost or delayed by congestion, hardware breaks and network components are misconfigured. When nodes cannot communicate, the system either stops serving some or all requests, reducing availability, or serves as usual and gives nodes inconsistent views of the data. An apparent full partition may really be a very slow network, some but not all messages being dropped, or throttling in one direction only. That makes failures hard to reason about. Do not confuse it with Database partitioning: cutting a big database into independent pieces, which deliberately splits a database for scalability.

  <!-- sysd-scale-142 -->

- **The CAP theorem: why no store can have everything**

  A distributed data store can provide at most two of three guarantees: consistency, availability and partition tolerance. That is the CAP theorem, also called Brewer's theorem, and the three are the properties commonly desired when designing distributed web services. Consistency means every read receives the most recent write or an error, so all clients see the same data at the same time, whichever node they connect to. Availability means every request received by a non-failing node gets a response, with no guarantee that the response holds the most recent version of the data. Partition tolerance means the system keeps operating despite an arbitrary number of messages being dropped or delayed by the network between nodes.

  The catch is that no distributed system is safe from network failures, so partitions generally have to be tolerated, as Network partitions: the cluster splits but every node keeps running explains. During a partition, one must choose between consistency and availability. Choosing consistency, the system returns an error or times out when it cannot guarantee fresh data. Choosing availability, it always answers with the most recent version it has, even if that may be stale. In the absence of a partition, both can be satisfied, and during normal operation a data store covers all three.

  Gilbert and Lynch proved Brewer's conjecture in 2002 for the asynchronous network model. They then discussed solutions to the dilemma in the partially synchronous model.

  <!-- sysd-scale-107 -->

- **Anti-entropy and reconciliation: how replicas converge**

  To converge, an eventually consistent system exchanges updates between servers and reconciles concurrent updates by choosing a final state. Replicas converge through anti-entropy, which exchanges versions or updates of data between servers, and through reconciliation, which chooses a final state when concurrent updates have occurred. The most appropriate way to reconcile depends on the application. A widespread approach is last writer wins, and some systems use first writer wins where last writer wins is unacceptable. Another approach is to invoke a user-specified conflict handler. Timestamps are often used to detect concurrency between updates, and so is the technique in Vector clocks: a counter per process to detect causality. Reconciliation must happen before the next read. Read repair fixes an inconsistency when a read finds it. Write repair fixes it during a write and slows that write. Asynchronous repair runs outside reads and writes. In a database that stays available during a partition, nodes are typically re-synced to repair all inconsistencies once the partition is resolved.

  <!-- sysd-scale-098 -->

- **PACELC: the trade-off CAP leaves out**

  By CAP's own wording, a database counts as available if a query returns after 30 days. No real application accepts that latency. It is one limit of the The CAP theorem: why no store can have everything, which PACELC extends. If there is a partition (P), the trade-off is between availability (A) and consistency (C). Else (E), even in normal operation, it is between latency (L) and consistency (C). Consistent operations need a full network round trip on reads and writes, while low-latency systems relax consistency to reduce delay. Ignoring that trade-off is a major oversight, because it is present at all times, while CAP matters only during a partition. The four configurations are PA/EL, PA/EC, PC/EL and PC/EC. PC/EC gives firm ACID-style consistency, and PA/EL gives high availability and low latency with a more complex consistency model. PA/EC and PC/EL give only conditional guarantees, so the developer must still write code for the cases where a guarantee is not upheld. PC does not mean fully consistent: the system does not lower consistency below its baseline during a partition, and reduces availability instead.

  <!-- sysd-scale-101 -->

  *Figure: PACELC asks one question during a partition and another in normal operation.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A{Is there a partition?}
  A -->|yes| B[Trade availability against consistency]
  A -->|no, else| C[Trade latency against consistency]
  ```

- **Strong eventual consistency: same updates, same state**

  Deliver the same updates to two nodes in different orders, and they still end up in the same state. That is the guarantee of strong eventual consistency. Plain eventual consistency is only a liveness guarantee: updates will be observed eventually, but nothing is promised about the values seen before convergence. Strong eventual consistency adds a safety guarantee. Any two nodes that have received the same set of updates, in any order, are in the same state. A common way to ensure it is CRDTs: data structures that merge themselves.

  <!-- sysd-scale-099 -->

- **CP, AP and CA: sorting databases by what they sacrifice**

  The physical network cannot be guaranteed stable, so a distributed database must choose partition tolerance. That leaves a trade-off between consistency and availability, and three labels follow from it. A database is classed as CP if it keeps consistency, AP if it keeps availability, and CA if it assumes no partitions.

  A CP database gives consistency and partition tolerance at the expense of availability. When a partition occurs, it shuts down the non-consistent node until the partition is resolved. MongoDB and Apache HBase: Bigtable on top of Hadoop are CP examples, and etcd: the cluster's memory, and why it picks consistency also favors consistency over availability during a network partition. An AP database gives availability and partition tolerance at the expense of consistency. All nodes stay available during a partition, but those on the wrong side may return an older version of the data. Once the partition is resolved, an AP database typically re-syncs the nodes to repair inconsistencies. Cassandra, CouchDB and ScyllaDB: a Cassandra-compatible rewrite in C++ are AP examples.

  A CA database gives consistency and availability across all nodes but cannot do so if any two nodes are partitioned, so it cannot tolerate faults. PostgreSQL and MariaDB are examples, and no NoSQL database is classed as CA. Databases built on ACID guarantees, such as relational ones, choose consistency over availability, while systems built on BASE, common in NoSQL, choose availability over consistency. Most modern distributed databases offer configuration options for both. The labels are not fixed, though: one source classifies MongoDB as a PA/EC system.

  <!-- sysd-scale-108 -->

  *Figure: The three classes differ in which guarantee they give up.*

  | Class | Keeps | Gives up | Examples |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | CP | Consistency and partition tolerance | Availability | MongoDB, Apache HBase, etcd |
  | AP | Availability and partition tolerance | Consistency | Cassandra, CouchDB, ScyllaDB |
  | CA | Consistency and availability | Partition tolerance | PostgreSQL, MariaDB |

- **Common misreadings of CAP: what the theorem does not say**

  The slogan of the CAP theorem, pick two of three, is useful, but as a simplification it misleads, and the theorem covers only a narrow case. Brewer's 2012 clarification says designers need to sacrifice consistency or availability only in the presence of partitions, and that partition management and recovery techniques exist. CAP prohibits only a tiny part of the design space: perfect availability and consistency in the presence of partitions, which are rare. The theorem is about 100% availability and consistency. A more realistic discussion weighs latency against consistency when there is no partition, as PACELC: the trade-off CAP leaves out does. Consistency in CAP is not consistency in ACID transactions, and availability in CAP is not the high availability of software architecture. Choosing a database purely on CAP is not enough. Companies do not pick Cassandra for chat just because it is an AP system, but for a list of other characteristics. The ByteByteGo guide still finds CAP useful because it opens a set of trade-off discussions, but says it is only part of the story.

  <!-- sysd-scale-103 -->

- **Primary-backup replication: one server orders every write**

  In the simplest primary-based protocol, every write goes to a single server, and reads can be local. Each data item has one primary that coordinates its writes, and the other replicas copy the updates. The primary sends each update to those replicas, waits for acknowledgements from all of them, and then acknowledges completion to the client. Because it orders all incoming writes, every process sees them in the same order. The price is that the client may wait long for the acknowledgement. A non-blocking variant updates locally first and asks the other replicas later. That is faster, but it does not guarantee the copies are consistent.

  <!-- sysd-scale-104 -->

  *Figure: The primary acknowledges the client only after every backup has acknowledged.*

  | Step | What happens |
  |---|---|
  | 1 | The write is forwarded to the primary |
  | 2 | The primary sends the update to the backups |
  | 3 | The primary waits for acknowledgements from all of them |
  | 4 | The primary acknowledges completion to the client |

- **Active replication: every replica applies every operation in order**

  In active replication, updates reach each replica as an operation to execute, and a process at each replica carries it out. Every replica must apply all updates in the same order. That requires a totally-ordered multicast, a way to deliver each operation to every replica in one agreed order. Implementing it in large distributed systems raises a scalability issue. An alternative sends each operation to a central coordinator, the sequencer, which assigns a sequence number and forwards the operation to all replicas. That does not solve the scalability problem either.

  <!-- sysd-scale-106 -->

- **Quorum-based replication: ask enough servers before you act**

  Before a client reads or writes replicated data in quorum-based replication, it must get permission from several servers. Unlike primary-based protocols, replicated-write protocols carry out all updates on all replicas, and voting is one way to do that. For a file replicated on N servers, an update needs agreement from at least N/2 + 1 servers. The change is then applied and a new version number is assigned. To read, a client asks N/2 + 1 servers for the file's version number. The read completes if all the version numbers it receives are the most recent version. See Quorum: how many votes are enough for the quorum idea itself.

  <!-- sysd-scale-105 -->

- **Sequential consistency: one order that everyone sees**

  A write need not be seen instantly, but writes by different processors must be seen in the same order by all processors. That is the heart of sequential consistency. It requires that the result of any execution is as if all operations ran in one sequential order, with each process's operations in its program order. It has no notion of time or of the most recent write, and it is weaker than strict consistency. Lamport proposed it in 1979. It can produce non-deterministic results, because the interleaving of operations between processors can differ from run to run.

  <!-- sysd-scale-093 -->

- **Linearizability: every operation appears to happen at one instant**

  A counter reads a value, adds one and writes it back. Two processes can both read 0 and both write 1, so one increment is lost. That counter is not linearizable. In a linearizable system, although operations overlap on a shared object, each operation appears to take place instantaneously. The property is also called atomic consistency. It is sequential consistency with a real-time constraint. Each operation has a begin and an end time, and can be placed at one point between them while the order still gives sequential consistency. Equivalently, every call has a linearization point between its invocation and response, where it appears to occur instantly. This lets a programmer reason about the system: if every operation preserves an invariant, the whole linearizable system does. The counter becomes linearizable with an atomic compare-and-swap retried on failure, an atomic fetch-and-increment, or a lock around the critical section. Locks can suffer significant contention overhead. The price is latency: in an atomically consistent store, the sum of the read delay and the write delay is at least the message delay.

  <!-- sysd-scale-094 -->

- **Causal consistency: only related writes need one order**

  Two writes are causally related when the processor making the second has just read the first. This holds whether the writes came from the same processor or from different ones. Causal consistency builds on that idea. Hutto and Ahamad defined it in 1990 as a weakening of sequential consistency that splits events into causally related ones and unrelated ones. If event b takes effect from an earlier event a, every process sees b after a. Potentially related writes must be seen by all processes in the same order. Concurrent writes may be seen in a different order on different machines.

  <!-- sysd-scale-095 -->

- **Session guarantees: four promises to a single client**

  Session guarantees are four consistency models proposed in a 1994 paper for the case of a single user or application making the data modifications. Client-centric models cope with inconsistencies at lower cost when no updates are simultaneous. Monotonic reads ensure that after a process reads x, its later reads return the same or a more recent value. Monotonic writes ensure that a process's write to x completes before its next write to x. Read-your-writes ensures that what a process wrote to x is available to its next read. Writes-follow-reads ensures that a write after a read of x applies to the same or a more recent value.

  <!-- sysd-scale-096 -->

- **Where real databases land on PACELC**

  The default versions of early Amazon Dynamo: a key-value store built for constant failure, Cassandra and Riak are PA/EL: they give up consistency for availability during a partition and for lower latency in normal operation. Fully ACID systems such as VoltDB/H-Store, Megastore, MySQL Cluster and PostgreSQL are PC/EC, and so are Bigtable: Google's structured storage at petabyte scale and HBase. MongoDB can be classified as PA/EC: in the baseline case the system guarantees reads and writes to be consistent. Amazon DynamoDB: Dynamo as a managed service follows a strong leader model with read-after-write consistency. Its SDKs read eventually consistently by default, while a consistent read returns a current view or an error. One source differs, saying MongoDB and Redis resolve network partitions by keeping consistency and compromising on availability.

  <!-- sysd-scale-102 -->

- **Four patterns for living with eventual consistency**

  Eventual consistency ensures that updates to a distributed database are eventually reflected across all nodes, and four patterns help applications achieve it. In the event-based pattern, services emit events and others listen to update their own databases. That keeps services loosely coupled but delays consistency. In background sync, a background job makes data across databases consistent, so consistency arrives more slowly because the job runs on a schedule. In a saga, described in The saga pattern: local transactions with undo steps, a sequence of local transactions each updates data in a single service. In CQRS, described in CQRS: splitting the writes from the reads, reads and writes go to separate, eventually consistent databases that can each be tuned.

  <!-- sysd-scale-100 -->

### Consensus, ordering and distributed transactions


A single database can promise that a transaction is all-or-nothing. Once the data lives on several machines, that promise has to be rebuilt from messages between them, and the machines can fail or disagree about the time. This chapter starts with the distributed transaction and the voting protocol that completes one. It then turns to how machines order events without a shared clock, how they notice that a peer has died, and how a group of them can agree on a single value even when some fail. That agreement problem is the foundation for distributed locks, leader election and replicated state machines.


- **Distributed transactions: one commit across many databases**

  One database can make a transaction all-or-nothing on its own. Spread that transaction over several databases and nobody owns the promise anymore. A distributed transaction is a transaction that runs across multiple nodes in a network, depending on where the data lives. It must still be atomic: it completes in its entirety or not at all, so all nodes commit or all abort and the whole transaction rolls back. The system has to coordinate that commit or rollback as one unit. Isolation is the hard property, because global serializability can be violated even if each database is serializable. The common algorithm for completing one correctly is the subject of Two-phase commit: asking everyone to vote before committing. It suits updates that commit within milliseconds to a couple of minutes. Booking a flight, a rental car and a hotel is too slow for it, since it would lock resources for as long as a day. Such long-lived transactions use undo steps instead; see Compensating transactions: undoing committed work.

  <!-- sysd-scale-001 -->

- **Two-phase commit: asking everyone to vote before committing**

  Several databases must all agree to commit a transaction, or none of them may. Two-phase commit is the distributed algorithm that makes every participant agree on whether to commit or abort. One node acts as the coordinator, and the protocol runs in two phases.

  In the voting phase, the coordinator asks all participants to commit. Each one runs the transaction to the commit point and writes undo and redo log entries. Then it votes Yes or No, and the coordinator collects the votes. In the commit phase, if every vote was Yes, the coordinator sends commit. Each participant completes the operation, releases its locks and resources, and acknowledges. If any participant votes No, or the coordinator's timeout expires, the coordinator sends rollback instead, and each participant undoes the transaction from its undo log.

  The protocol assumes every node has stable storage with a write-ahead log that survives a crash, so recovery can finish after a failure. Those log records are slow to generate.

  The weakness is blocking. A participant that has voted Yes must wait for commit or rollback, so if the coordinator fails permanently, some participants never resolve their transactions. It also cannot dependably recover when the coordinator and a participant both fail in the commit phase, because the failed participant may already have committed. It works through many temporary failures, but rare cases need manual intervention. It is not two-phase locking, which is a concurrency control protocol. In architectures built from many small independent services it is regarded as an anti-pattern, because it ties all participants more tightly together.

  <!-- sysd-scale-002 -->

  *Figure: Every Yes vote leads to commit; one No or a timeout leads to rollback.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Coordinator asks all to commit] --> B[Participants vote Yes or No]
  B --> C{Every vote Yes?}
  C -->|yes| D[Coordinator sends commit]
  C -->|no or timeout| E[Coordinator sends rollback]
  D --> F[Participants complete and acknowledge]
  E --> G[Participants undo and acknowledge]
  ```

- **Lamport timestamps: ordering events without a shared clock**

  Two machines never agree exactly on what time it is, so a timestamp from one clock cannot settle which event came first. A Lamport timestamp is a simple logical clock algorithm for ordering events anyway. Each process keeps a numeric counter that only has meaning relative to the messages moving between processes. It increments the counter before each local event and attaches it to every message it sends. On receiving a message, it sets its counter to the greater of its own value and the message's, then adds 1.

  The guarantee runs one way. If event a happened before event b, the counter for a is smaller than for b, but a smaller counter does not prove the order. Events in processes that never exchange messages are concurrent and cannot be ordered. Breaking ties with something like the process ID gives a total order, though an artificial one that implies no causality. The two-way guarantee needs other techniques; see Vector clocks: a counter per process to detect causality.

  <!-- sysd-scale-014 -->

- **Heartbeats: how a cluster notices a dead machine**

  A crashed machine does not announce itself. The other machines notice only because something they expected stopped arriving. Heartbeats are periodic signals that let a distributed system monitor the health and status of its components. In the push style, a node signals another node or a monitor at a regular interval, and silence beyond a set interval means failure. It is simple, but network congestion can cause false positives. In the pull style, a central monitor asks nodes for status, which reduces traffic but may slow detection.

  The interval is a trade-off: a short one costs overhead, while a long one makes everything wait. A false alarm that triggers failover can be highly undesirable, so the heartbeat transport must be reliable, often over more than one path. A cluster manager can track each node as Down, Init or Alive, and an Alive node that misses its acknowledgement timeout moves to Down. Protocols that make a group of machines agree also use heartbeats to maintain a quorum, a majority of nodes able to decide; see Paxos: agreement among unreliable processors.

  <!-- sysd-scale-006 -->

- **Happened-before: which events could have caused which**

  Not every pair of events in a distributed system can be put in order. The happened-before relation orders events by their potential causal relationship in a concurrent system, especially an asynchronous distributed one. Within one process, events follow the order they occurred in, and a message send precedes its receive. Events in processes that exchange no messages, directly or through third parties, are concurrent: neither came before the other. Processes cannot know the relation unless they use a logical clock, such as a Lamport clock or the one in Vector clocks: a counter per process to detect causality. If processes may behave arbitrarily, it cannot be detected, because they can forge the metadata.

  <!-- sysd-scale-112 -->

- **Vector clocks: a counter per process to detect causality**

  A single counter per process cannot tell an ordered pair of events from a concurrent one. A vector clock can. It is a data structure that determines the partial ordering of events in a distributed system and detects causality violations. For n processes it is an array of n logical clocks, one per process, and messages carry the sender's clock state, as in Lamport timestamps: ordering events without a shared clock.

  A process increments its own entry on an internal event or a send, and sends a copy of its vector with each message. On receipt it increments its own entry and takes the element-wise maximum with the received vector. One vector is less than another when every component is at most the other's and at least one is strictly smaller. If x happened before y, the vector for x is less than the vector for y. Lamport's 1978 clocks were scalars, and vector clocks generalize them. They reliably detect causality when processes only crash; when processes behave arbitrarily or maliciously, detection is fundamentally impossible. Cassandra uses them to ignore outdated state.

  <!-- sysd-scale-024 -->

- **Two-phase commit variants that send fewer messages**

  Plain two-phase commit is chatty, and its log writes are slow. Its variants keep its guarantees while cutting messages, log writes or completion time. In one common architecture each participant talks to a nearby transaction manager, and the managers run the protocol among themselves, with no central component. Presumed abort and presumed commit assume a default outcome so messages and log writes can be skipped, at the cost of extra work during recovery. Tree two-phase commit puts the coordinator at the root of a tree of participants. Dynamic two-phase commit has no predetermined coordinator: Yes votes race up the tree, and the node where they meet takes charge.

  <!-- sysd-scale-003 -->

- **Consensus: getting machines to agree despite failures**

  Getting a group of machines to agree on one value sounds easy until some of them fail. That is the consensus problem: a number of processes, some of which may fail, must agree on a single data value. The processes put forward candidate values, communicate with one another, and settle on one, even though some may be faulty or unreliable. The payoff is practical. Consensus is used to agree on which transactions to commit to a database and in what order, and it underlies the techniques in State machine replication: identical copies from ordered commands and Atomic broadcast: everyone sees the same messages in the same order.

  The obvious idea is to take the majority value, which needs at least one more than half of the votes. But faulty processes may skew the outcome, so that agreement is not reached or is reached wrongly. A real protocol must do better. The output must be the input of some process, since a protocol that always outputs 1 would be useless, and a process decides only once, irrevocably. With halting failures, a protocol must give three guarantees. Termination means every correct process eventually decides. Agreement means all correct processes decide the same value. Validity means that if all correct processes propose v, they decide v. A protocol that does this among n processes of which at most t fail is called t-resilient. Protocols are compared by running time in rounds of message exchange and by message complexity.

  The best-known protocols, described in Paxos: agreement among unreliable processors and Raft: consensus built to be understood, are used pervasively in distributed and cloud systems. They depend on an elected leader to make progress and tolerate only crashes, not arbitrary or malicious behavior.

  <!-- sysd-scale-008 -->

- **Distributed locks: only one worker at a time**

  When many machines share a job, something must make sure only one of them runs it. A distributed lock is a mechanism that ensures mutual exclusion across a distributed system. It lets only one node become the leader at a time and makes a scheduled task run on a single worker, which prevents duplicate execution. It also lets one process at a time use a shared resource such as a file system or network socket. Locks bring deadlock, where processes each hold a lock another needs; the lock manager reports it to one request, and that process must resolve it.

  The Google SRE book advises renewable leases with timeouts rather than indefinite locks, because a lease stops a crashed process from holding a lock forever. Chubby keeps lock information in small files in a replicated database on a fault-tolerant log run by the protocol in Paxos: agreement among unreliable processors. ZooKeeper and Redis, via the Redlock algorithm, can also provide locks. A lock is a low-level primitive to use with care; the SRE book says most applications should use a higher-level system instead.

  <!-- sysd-scale-007 -->

- **State machine replication: identical copies from ordered commands**

  Any deterministic program can be made a highly available replicated service by turning it into a replicated state machine. State machine replication is the technique for converting an algorithm into a fault-tolerant, distributed implementation. Its foundation is consensus: the copies agree on a global order for the operations, and each executes them in that order. Ad-hoc techniques may leave important failure cases unresolved, while the principled approach proposed by Lamport and others handles all cases safely.

  In a leader-based design, each client request is a command. The leader appends it to its log and applies it to its own state machine once it is committed, as described in Raft: consensus built to be understood. In the older family of protocols described in Paxos: agreement among unreliable processors, a continuous stream of agreed values acts as commands. Replicated state machines are the building block of data and configuration storage, locking and leader election. Because not every member of the group is in each quorum, a member may need to synchronize state from peers, for example with a sliding-window protocol.

  <!-- sysd-scale-020 -->

- **Single-value and multi-valued consensus**

  Do the machines agree once, or over and over? Single-value consensus agrees on one value, while multi-valued consensus agrees on a series of values over time. Single-value protocols, described in Paxos: agreement among unreliable processors, settle on one value, which can encode metadata such as a transaction committed to a database. Binary consensus restricts the value to a single binary digit, 0 or 1; it is a building block for general protocols, especially asynchronous ones. Multi-valued protocols, covered in Multi-Paxos: skipping the first phase with a stable leader and Raft: consensus built to be understood, agree on a series of values forming a growing history. Running single-value consensus repeatedly works, but dedicated protocols are more efficient.

  <!-- sysd-scale-012 -->

- **Synchronous and asynchronous systems: do messages move in rounds?**

  Does a system move in lockstep rounds, or does each message arrive whenever it arrives? In a synchronous system all communication proceeds in rounds. A process sends all the messages it needs in a round and receives all those from the others, so no message influences others sent in the same round. In an asynchronous system, messages have no such round structure. Real-world communication is often inherently asynchronous, but synchronous systems are easier to model. Consensus can be studied in either model. In a fully asynchronous system with a crash failure, the FLP result, described in The FLP impossibility result: a limit on agreement, rules out a deterministic algorithm.

  <!-- sysd-scale-011 -->

- **Three-phase commit: removing two-phase commit's blocking**

  Two-phase commit can leave participants stuck, waiting for a coordinator that never returns. Three-phase commit is a distributed algorithm that makes all nodes agree to commit or abort a transaction without that indefinite blocking. It splits the commit phase of two-phase commit in two. After the vote, the coordinator issues a pre-commit message that every participant must acknowledge, and only then does it send the final commit.

  The extra step removes the ambiguity. The coordinator sends doCommit only after all participants have acknowledged they are prepared, so no participant can have committed before all know the decision. Every phase can time out, so there are no indefinite waits. If the coordinator fails before sending preCommit, the participants agree the operation was aborted. A recovery coordinator queries the participants: if some are already in the commit phase it drives the protocol to commit, and if none received PrepareToCommit it safely aborts.

  The price is an assumption. The protocol needs bounded network delay and bounded node response times. With unbounded delays and process pauses it cannot guarantee atomicity, and it needs at least three round trips, which adds latency. In Skeen's original protocol a quorum can be connected yet unable to make progress; Keidar and Dolev's E3PC refines it so a quorum always can.

  <!-- sysd-scale-004 -->

  *Figure: The added pre-commit step must be acknowledged before the final commit is sent.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart LR
  A[Vote] --> B[Coordinator sends pre-commit]
  B --> C[Participants acknowledge]
  C --> D[Coordinator sends commit]
  ```

- **The Two Generals' Problem: why certainty is impossible**

  Two generals must attack at the same time, or the lone attacker dies. They can only communicate by messengers sent through enemy territory, and any messenger may be captured. This thought experiment, the Two Generals' Problem, illustrates the pitfalls of coordinating an action over an unreliable communication link. An acknowledgement can be lost as easily as the original message, so no number of confirmations leaves each general sure the other agreed. A potentially infinite series of messages would be needed.

  It was the first computer communication problem proven unsolvable: for any deterministic protocol, the sender of the last delivered message cannot tell whether it arrived. That is why TCP cannot guarantee state consistency between its endpoints. In practice, engineers accept the uncertainty and reduce it to an acceptable degree, for example by sending many messengers. No rule can be certain to prevent one general attacking without the other.

  <!-- sysd-scale-114 -->

- **Crash and Byzantine failures: stopping versus lying**

  A crashed machine at least has the decency to go quiet. A process can fail in two broad ways. It can crash, which means it abruptly stops and never resumes. Or it can fail in a Byzantine way, where no conditions are imposed on its behavior. A Byzantine process may come from a malicious adversary, may send contradictory or conflicting data to other processes, or may sleep and then resume after a lengthy delay.

  Byzantine failures are far more disruptive than crashes, so a protocol that tolerates them must be resilient to every possible error. Agreement among such processes also needs a stronger integrity rule: if a correct process decides v, then some correct process must have proposed v. The numbers are unforgiving. With n processors of which f are Byzantine, no algorithm solves consensus for n ≤ 3f when messages are oral. When messages are written, meaning signed, protocols exist that tolerate n = f + 1. Digital signatures let each receiver learn who originally created a message.

  The protocols in Paxos: agreement among unreliable processors and Raft: consensus built to be understood tolerate only crashes. PBFT is a Byzantine-tolerant protocol, listed with the threshold n > 3f.

  <!-- sysd-scale-009 -->

- **Atomic broadcast: everyone sees the same messages in the same order**

  Send the same messages to every replica in the same order and the replicas stay in step. Atomic broadcast, or total order broadcast, is a broadcast in which all correct processes receive the same set of messages in the same order. It is atomic because it either completes correctly at all participants or all abort without side effects. Total order is not FIFO or causal order: every participant simply receives messages in the same order, whatever the order of sending.

  Without failures it is easy: everyone follows a leader that decides the order. It is hard when computers fail, for example when the leader fails at the wrong time. With crash failures it is equivalent to consensus. Consensus reduces to it by proposing a value as a broadcast and deciding the first message received, and the reverse runs consensus on each next message. So the FLP result, described in The FLP impossibility result: a limit on agreement, applies to it too, though in practice it can be implemented by assuming less than FLP does about timings.

  <!-- sysd-scale-113 -->

- **ZooKeeper: a shared coordination service for cloud applications**

  ZooKeeper was the first open-source consensus system to gain traction, says the Google SRE book, because it was easy to use even for applications not designed for consensus. Apache ZooKeeper is an open-source server for highly reliable distributed coordination of cloud applications. It offers a hierarchical key-value store that serves as a configuration service, synchronization service and naming registry. Data lives in a tree of nodes, like a file system, that clients read and write to share configuration.

  The service is replicated over an ensemble of servers, each holding the whole data tree in memory plus a transaction log and snapshots on disk. Clients keep a TCP connection for requests, heartbeats and watch events. It can be viewed as an atomic broadcast system in which updates are totally ordered, and the ZooKeeper Atomic Broadcast (ZAB) protocol is its core. Typical uses are naming, configuration management, data synchronization, leader election and notification, as well as barriers and distributed locks. It is fast for read-dominant workloads, scales by adding nodes, and was modeled after Google's Chubby lock service.

  <!-- sysd-scale-111 -->

- **The FLP impossibility result: a limit on agreement**

  In 1985, three researchers proved something that sounds like a ban on distributed computing. Fischer, Lynch and Paterson showed that in a fully asynchronous message-passing system where even one process may crash, no deterministic consensus algorithm exists. The result has been mechanically verified, even under fairness assumptions. It does not say agreement can never be reached. It says only that, under the model's assumptions, no algorithm can always reach it in bounded time, and in practice the bad case is highly unlikely. Randomized consensus algorithms circumvent the result by achieving safety and liveness with overwhelming probability, even under worst-case scheduling.

  <!-- sysd-scale-010 -->

- **Paxos: agreement among unreliable processors**

  Google's Chubby lock service and Megastore run on Paxos, and so do the leader elections of DynamoDB. Paxos is a family of protocols for solving consensus in a network of unreliable or fallible processors. It is usually used where durability is required, such as replicating a file or a database whose durable state may be large. In most deployments each process plays three roles: Proposer, Acceptor and Learner. Merging the roles collapses the protocol into an efficient client-master-replica style deployment.

  Safety is always guaranteed: only proposed values can be chosen (validity), and no two learners can learn different values (agreement), whatever the pattern of failures. Termination is not guaranteed. That is consistent with the FLP result that no protocol can have safety, liveness and failure tolerance all at once. The conditions that stall progress are difficult to provoke. A group can make progress with n = 2F + 1 processors despite F simultaneous failures, because the non-faulty processes must outnumber the faulty ones. It also runs inside the database described in Spanner: a SQL database spread across the globe, while Cassandra uses it only for lightweight transactions.

  <!-- sysd-scale-015 -->

- **Byzantine fault tolerance: agreeing when some nodes lie**

  In the Byzantine generals allegory, the generals must agree on one plan, but traitors may vote selectively, telling some to attack and others to retreat. A Byzantine fault is a fault that presents different symptoms to different observers, including imperfect information on whether a component has failed. Byzantine fault tolerance (BFT) is resilience to such conditions. A fail-stop failure is only a crash that other nodes detect. A Byzantine node can emit arbitrary data, even looking healthy to some nodes, so it is the hardest failure class.

  Tolerating F Byzantine failures needs at least 3F+1 participants, 2F+1 independent communication paths and F+1 rounds of communication. Majority-quorum consensus that tolerates only crashes needs just 2f+1 replicas for f failures. With unforgeable digital signatures, one commander and two lieutenants can reach consensus despite a single traitor, who cannot impersonate others. BFT guarantees only that components receive the same value; it does not check the value. Blockchains use BFT-based consensus such as PBFT, Tendermint and Avalanche, and Boeing 777 flight control uses BFT too.

  <!-- sysd-scale-109 -->

- **Raft: consensus built to be understood**

  Raft was designed with an aim that is rare in this field: to be understandable. It is a consensus algorithm created as an alternative to the Paxos family, with its logic separated into parts, yet formally proven safe. It distributes a state machine across a cluster so that every node agrees on the same series of state transitions.

  Raft reaches agreement through one elected leader, which alone manages log replication and decides where new entries go without consulting the other servers. Each server is a leader or a follower, or a candidate during an election. Among its guarantees is election safety: one leader per term. In its base form Raft does not tolerate Byzantine failures: nodes trust the elected leader and assume all participants are trustworthy. The single-leader model also sends all reads, writes and log replication through one leader, a single point of failure and a bottleneck. Raft keeps the replicated log of the store described in etcd: the cluster's memory, and why it picks consistency, CockroachDB uses it in its replication layer, and MongoDB uses a variant in its replica sets.

  <!-- sysd-scale-021 -->

- **Consensus-based system patterns: where agreement gets used**

  Almost nobody runs a consensus algorithm bare. These algorithms only let nodes agree on a value once, so they live inside higher-level components such as datastores, configuration stores, queues, locks and leader election services. Using such components reduces complexity for designers and lets the underlying algorithm change. Many systems use consensus as clients of a service such as ZooKeeper, Google's Chubby or the one in Consul: from service discovery to service networking.

  Each pattern has its own cost. Replicated datastores apply replicated state machines and put consensus in the critical path, so performance, throughput and scale matter, and the read consistency on offer greatly affects scaling. A single leader gives coarse-grained mutual exclusion. A service written as a simple program can be made highly available by replicating it and electing one leader, which takes consensus off the critical path. A barrier blocks a group of processes until a condition is met, splitting a computation into phases. A large data-processing job, covered in MapReduce: two functions and a cluster that does the rest, uses one when it waits for its whole Map phase. A lone coordinator would be a single point of failure, so use a replicated state machine. Distributed queues should use leases rather than outright removal, so claimed tasks are processed. Queues and publish-subscribe systems often need good throughput but not very low latency, and atomic broadcast suits them well.

  <!-- sysd-scale-115 -->

- **Sizing a consensus group: why five replicas are common**

  Adding a sixth replica can make a group less available than it was with five. Consensus systems use majority quorums, so a group of 2f + 1 replicas tolerates f failures. The number of replicas is one of the most critical deployment decisions. Without Byzantine tolerance the minimum is three replicas, which tolerate one failure; with two, no failure can be tolerated. Byzantine tolerance needs 3f + 1 replicas for f failures.

  Most downtime is planned maintenance, which three replicas survive, but an unplanned failure during maintenance makes the group unavailable. Five replicas are therefore recommended, tolerating two failures. A typical ZooKeeper or Chubby deployment uses five replicas, needs three for quorum and survives two (40%) down. With six, four are needed and only 33% can be down. Each replica costs resources, and where every shard is a full consensus group the cost grows with the shard count. The number of replicas trades off reliability, frequency of planned maintenance and performance.

  <!-- sysd-scale-117 -->

  *Figure: Going from five replicas to six lowers the share that can be down.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Placing consensus replicas across failure domains**

  Keep every replica in one rack and a single rack failure ends the service. Spread them across the world and every write waits on a long round trip. Where to put a consensus group's processes trades off the failure domains the system should survive against its latency requirements. A failure domain is the set of components one failure can make unavailable, such as a machine, a rack, a datacenter or a region.

  As replicas move farther apart they survive bigger failures, but round-trip time and operation latency rise. If all clients sit in one domain, spreading further adds cost and latency for no benefit. Client-perceived latency is the key measure, so place replicas to minimize client round-trip time. Colocating replicas can hurt availability: with five datacenters and a sixth replica added in one, an outage there removes both spare replicas and cuts capacity by 33%. Sending every read to the nearest replica can cascade, as a load spike overwhelms it, then the next closest, and so on.

  <!-- sysd-scale-118 -->

- **Basic Paxos: prepare, promise, accept, accepted**

  Basic Paxos decides a single value in two phases, and each phase has two messages. It is the simplest Paxos protocol: each instance decides one output value over one or more rounds. In phase 1a, Prepare, a Proposer sends a Prepare message to at least a quorum of Acceptors, carrying a unique number n greater than any it used before. The number only identifies the message; it is not the proposed value. In phase 1b, Promise, an Acceptor that sees an n higher than any before replies with a promise. It will ignore proposals numbered n or lower, and it reports the highest-numbered proposal it has accepted, with its value.

  Once a quorum has promised, phase 2a, Accept, begins. The Proposer sends Accept(n, v), where v is the value of the highest-numbered accepted proposal reported, or its own value if none was reported. In phase 2b, Accepted, an Acceptor accepts (n, v) unless it has promised to consider only higher-numbered proposals, then tells the Proposer and the Learners. Learners learn the value after Accepted messages from a majority of Acceptors.

  Consensus is reached when a majority of Acceptors accept the same identifier number. Because each identifier carries one value, they accept the same value, and the chosen value is permanent and immutable. A round fails when Proposers send conflicting Prepares or no quorum answers, and a new round starts with a higher number. Losing one Acceptor while a quorum remains, or a redundant Learner, needs no recovery.

  <!-- sysd-scale-016 -->

  *Figure: The four messages of one Basic Paxos round, in order.*

  | Step | Message | Sent by to |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1a | Prepare(n) | Proposer to a quorum of Acceptors |
  | 1b | Promise | Acceptor to Proposer |
  | 2a | Accept(n, v) | Proposer to Acceptors |
  | 2b | Accepted | Acceptor to Proposer and Learners |

- **Multi-Paxos: skipping the first phase with a stable leader**

  A replicated state machine needs a continuous stream of agreed commands, and running a full Basic Paxos for each one would add a significant amount of overhead. Multi-Paxos runs a continuous series of Basic Paxos instances, with a stable leader, to agree on that stream. Clients send commands to the leader, which assigns each a new command number i and starts the ith instance of the algorithm with the acceptors. If the leader is stable, phase 1 (Prepare and Promise) can be skipped for later instances with the same leader. The round number I travels with each value. That cuts the failure-free message delay from proposal to learning from 4 delays to 2. A common deployment collapses Proposer, Acceptor and Learner into one Server role, leaving just Clients and Servers.

  <!-- sysd-scale-017 -->

- **Permissioned and permissionless consensus**

  If anyone can join a group, one attacker can pretend to be many members. Permissioned consensus runs among a fixed, known group of authenticated participants, while permissionless consensus lets anyone join dynamically. Without a closed group, a Sybil attack can defeat even a Byzantine-tolerant algorithm by creating enough virtual participants to overwhelm its threshold. Permissionless protocols counter it with an artificial cost of entry. Bitcoin's proof of work has participants compete to solve hash puzzles, earning the right to commit blocks in proportion to computational effort. Because proof of work is energy-hungry, later protocols use proof of stake, proof of space or proof of authority instead.

  <!-- sysd-scale-013 -->

- **Monitoring consensus systems: what to watch**

  A consensus group can look healthy while making no progress. Operators track how many members each group has and each one's status. A process may run yet be unable to progress, lag persistently, recover state from peers, be up to date, or lead. A leader-based system such as Multi-Paxos with no leader is totally unavailable, so the existence of a leader must be watched. Rapid leadership changes hurt performance. A term or view number marks each change: a fast increase signals a flapping leader, perhaps from network problems, and a decrease signals a serious bug. In a healthy system the consensus transaction number keeps rising.

  <!-- sysd-scale-119 -->

- **Cheap Paxos: tolerating failures with cheap spare machines**

  Some machines in a consensus group can be cheap. Cheap Paxos extends Basic Paxos to tolerate F failures with F + 1 main processors and F auxiliary processors, by dynamically reconfiguring after each failure. In stable periods the auxiliary processors take no part in the protocol, so they can be small, slow or cheap, or mainly devoted to other tasks. The saving costs liveness: if too many main processors fail in a short time, the system must halt until the auxiliary processors can reconfigure it. A third processor is needed because with only two, one cannot tell the failure of the other from failure of the communication medium.

  <!-- sysd-scale-019 -->

- **Fast Paxos: trading replicas for fewer message delays**

  Fast Paxos generalizes Basic Paxos to reduce end-to-end message delays. Basic Paxos takes 3 message delays from client request to learning; Fast Paxos allows 2. The price is more machines and more work for the client. It needs 3f + 1 acceptors to tolerate f faults, against 2f + 1 classically, and the client must send its request to multiple destinations. When proposals collide, recovery by the leader with a new round takes four message delays. If the leader specifies a recovery technique in advance, acceptors recover themselves in three delays, or two if all Learners are also Acceptors.

  <!-- sysd-scale-018 -->

- **Consensus performance: round trips and disk writes**

  Consensus has a reputation for being too slow for high throughput and low latency. The Google SRE book says this is untrue: implementations can be slow, but a number of techniques improve performance. Performance depends on the workload and on the deployment. Two physical limits matter most: network round-trip time and the time to write to persistent storage. Round trips take about a millisecond within a datacenter, a typical 45 milliseconds within the United States and 70 from New York to London.

  Acceptors must log commitments to disk so a restarted node honors them. A write takes one to several milliseconds, and if a small random write takes about 10 milliseconds, consensus is limited to roughly 100 operations per second. Batching several client operations into one proposal amortizes the fixed costs of disk logging and network latency. Pipelining keeps several proposals in flight without breaking global ordering. Stable-leader protocols, such as the one in Multi-Paxos: skipping the first phase with a stable leader, need only one round trip to a quorum, but every write goes through the leader, so distant clients pay latency.

  <!-- sysd-scale-116 -->

  *Figure: Round-trip time, one of the two physical limits on consensus, grows with distance.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Raft leader election: terms, timeouts and votes**

  Silence is how Raft detects a dead leader. The leader sends heartbeat messages, and each follower has a timeout, typically 150 to 300 ms, for hearing one. A follower that hears nothing for the election timeout becomes a candidate. It increases the term counter, votes for itself and requests votes from all other servers. Each server votes once per term, first come first served, and a majority of votes makes the candidate leader. A candidate that sees a larger term number steps down to follower. On a split vote a new term and election start, and a randomized election timeout makes repeated split votes unlikely.

  <!-- sysd-scale-022 -->

  *Figure: A follower that hears no heartbeat becomes a candidate; a majority of votes makes it leader, a split vote starts a new term.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Follower] -->|election timeout passes| B[Candidate]
  B -->|majority of votes| C[Leader]
  B -->|split vote| D[New term, new election]
  D --> B
  ```

- **Raft log replication: how followers catch up**

  In Raft the leader accepts client requests, appends them to its log and replicates them to the followers. It forwards each new entry as an AppendEntries message and retries indefinitely if a follower is unavailable. Once half or more of the followers confirm, the entry is committed, and so are all earlier entries. After a leader crash, logs may be inconsistent. The new leader finds the last entry where a follower's log agrees with its own, deletes the follower's later entries and replaces them with its own. A candidate cannot win an election unless its log contains all committed entries.

  <!-- sysd-scale-023 -->

- **The saga pattern: local transactions with undo steps**

  Distributed transactions are hard to scale and can hurt performance, so the saga pattern gives up the single big commit. A saga is a sequence of local transactions that together do the work of one distributed transaction. Each local transaction updates its own database and then publishes a message or event that triggers the next one. If one fails, for example by violating a business rule, the saga runs undo steps that reverse the changes made by the earlier local transactions; see Compensating transactions: undoing committed work.

  Sagas keep data consistent across services that each own their database. There are two ways to coordinate one. In choreography, each local transaction publishes domain events that trigger local transactions in other services. In orchestration, an orchestrator tells the participants which local transactions to run. The 1987 paper proposed sagas because long-lived transactions hold database resources for a long time, which significantly delays the shorter and more common ones. The costs are real: sagas are hard to debug and test, risk cyclic dependencies between participants, and lack of participant data isolation causes durability challenges.

  <!-- sysd-scale-005 -->

- **Compensating transactions: undoing committed work**

  Some mistakes cannot be rolled back. A compensating transaction is a transaction that reverses the effects of a previously committed transaction. It is needed when a business process fails after some steps have committed. Unlike a rollback, which discards uncommitted changes, it is a new transaction. It applies business logic to undo completed work, such as crediting $100 to undo a debit of $100. On failure, the compensations of completed steps run in reverse order. It is fundamental to the saga pattern. The limits: results are visible before they are compensated, a compensation can itself fail, and some effects, such as a sent email, cannot be undone.

  <!-- sysd-scale-110 -->

### How the big distributed data systems work


Google built a distributed file system for large clusters of commodity hardware, a storage system for structured data across thousands of commodity servers, and a SQL database that is synchronously replicated around the world. Amazon built a highly available key-value store to keep persistent state reliable while components fail all the time, and AWS now sells a managed NoSQL service. Open-source projects followed: Cassandra, which handles very large amounts of data across many commodity servers with no single point of failure, and Hadoop and HBase, built around HDFS or modeled after Google's storage system. This chapter opens each of them up. Each one is an answer to the same question: how do you keep working when machines fail?


- **Spanner: a SQL database spread across the globe**

  Spanner gives Google a SQL database spread across the globe that still answers with strong consistency. It is a scalable, multiversion, globally distributed and synchronously replicated SQL database, with automatic multi-site replication and failover. Its authors describe it as the first system to distribute data at global scale and support externally-consistent distributed transactions. Users can run arbitrary SQL queries on relational data, and transactions can span rows, columns, tables and databases within one Spanner universe. Data is versioned, so clients can read previous versions, subject to garbage collection windows.

  Underneath, Spanner uses the Paxos algorithm to shard data across up to hundreds of servers, spread over many Paxos state machines. The unusual ingredient is time. It leans on hardware-assisted clock synchronization with GPS and atomic clocks, and its TrueTime service gives monotonically increasing timestamps in data centers worldwide. The paper's time API exposes clock uncertainty, which is critical to external consistency, nonblocking reads in the past, lock-free snapshot transactions and atomic schema changes.

  <!-- sysd-scale-026 -->

- **Amazon Dynamo: a key-value store built for constant failure**

  On a platform that runs on tens of thousands of servers and network components in many datacenters around the world, something is always failing. Reliability at that scale is one of Amazon's biggest challenges, because even the slightest outage has significant financial consequences and impacts customer trust. How persistent state is managed in the face of these failures drives the reliability and scalability of the software.

  Many Amazon services mostly read data by primary key and put speed first, and joining the pieces of data that traditional databases split apart was extremely taxing. Amazon's response was Dynamo, a highly available key-value store built for internal use, which accepted a compromise in storage efficiency. Adoption lagged, because engineers avoided the overhead of provisioning and managing partitions and nodes; the later service in Amazon DynamoDB: Dynamo as a managed service automated those operations. Cassandra incorporates Dynamo's distributed storage and replication techniques.

  <!-- sysd-scale-042 -->

- **Amazon DynamoDB: Dynamo as a managed service**

  Engineers at Amazon avoided Dynamo because running it meant provisioning and managing partitions and nodes. DynamoDB, a managed NoSQL database service from AWS, automated those operations. It supports key-value and document data. DynamoDB hashes the partition key to pick a partition. Each partition stores up to 10 GB and by default handles 1,000 write capacity units and 3,000 read capacity units. One read capacity unit is one strongly consistent read per second for an item up to 4 KB. One write capacity unit is one write per second for an item up to 1 KB.

  Each partition has three nodes holding copies, with one leader chosen by Paxos. The leader sends a heartbeat every 1.5 seconds, and a node that stops hearing it can start a new election. A write goes to the leader, then a second node, then returns success while propagation continues to the third. A consistent read visits the leader, while an eventually consistent read picks a random node, trading consistency for availability so reads do not overload one node.

  <!-- sysd-scale-027 -->

- **DynamoDB partition and sort keys: choosing where items live**

  Every DynamoDB table needs a primary key, one or two attributes that uniquely identify each item and decide where it is stored. A key of one attribute is a partition key, which determines the physical location of the item. A key of two attributes is a partition key plus a sort key. The partition key picks the location and the sort key orders items inside it; items may share a partition key but not a sort key. A local secondary index keeps the table's partition key with a different sort key, while a global secondary index uses a different partition key.

  <!-- sysd-scale-028 -->

- **DynamoDB data modeling patterns: laying data out for access**

  In DynamoDB the layout of the data follows the questions it will be asked. Data modeling patterns are ways to lay data out, chosen to match a workload's access patterns. Single Table Design keeps related data together under one partition key, within the 400KB item size limit, to cut access latency. Multiple Table Design isolates data into purpose-specific tables by access pattern, and Hybrid Design blends the two. A layout that stores data changes as immutable events lets past state be rebuilt; see Event sourcing: keep the history, derive the present. Materialized Views pre-aggregate data. Time-Series Design suits logging and metrics: the partition key identifies the entity and the sort key holds the timestamp.

  <!-- sysd-scale-029 -->

- **Google File System: reliable storage on cheap, failing machines**

  Google's search engine generates enormous amounts of data that must be retained, and Google chose to keep it on clusters of cheap commodity computers. The Google File System was built for that job: a proprietary distributed file system that gives efficient, reliable access to data on large clusters of commodity hardware. Cheap machines fail often, so the design must guard against the high failure rate of individual nodes and the data loss that follows. Its other decisions favor high data throughput, even when that costs latency.

  Files are split into fixed-size chunks of 64 megabytes. They are usually appended to or read, and only extremely rarely overwritten or shrunk. A cluster has one master node and many chunkservers. The master gives each chunk a globally unique 64-bit label when it creates it and keeps the mapping from files to chunks. It stores metadata rather than chunks, including where each chunk's copies live, and stays current through periodic heartbeat messages from every chunkserver. Each chunk is replicated across the network, three times by default but configurable, and files in high demand may get a higher replication factor.

  A read shows why this scales. A client asks the master where a chunk lives, then reads the data directly from a chunkserver, so the master stays out of the data path. Because the master is not involved in reads, read rate grows with the number of chunkservers, reaching 583 MB/s for 342 nodes.

  Writes are controlled by time-limited leases. The master lets one process modify a chunk for a finite period, and no other process gets permission during it. The primary chunk holder pushes each change to the other chunkservers holding copies. The change is not saved until all of them acknowledge, which makes the operation atomic. Record Append lets many clients append to the same file at once, with atomicity guaranteed. GFS does not provide a POSIX interface. The lesson in the numbers: the master holds only metadata and stays off the data path, so adding chunkservers adds read capacity.

  <!-- sysd-scale-025 -->

  *Figure: The client asks the master where a chunk lives, then reads from a chunkserver directly.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  C[Client] -->|1. ask for location| M[Master: metadata only]
  C -->|2. read the data| S[Chunkserver]
  S -.->|3 copies by default| R[Other chunkservers]
  ```

- **Bigtable: Google's structured storage at petabyte scale**

  As of April 2024, Bigtable manages over 10 Exabytes of data and serves more than 7 billion requests per second. It is a distributed storage system for structured data, designed to scale to petabytes across thousands of commodity servers. Many Google projects store data in it, such as web indexing, Google Earth and Google Finance. Their demands run from URLs to satellite imagery in size and from bulk processing to real-time serving in latency. Google built its own database for scalability and better control of performance.

  Bigtable is built on Colossus, the Google File System, together with the Chubby lock service and SSTable log-structured storage. Tables are split into tablets of a few hundred megabytes or a few gigabytes, and hundreds to thousands of servers serve thousands to hundreds of thousands of tablets. Tablet locations live in META1 tablets, found via the single META0 tablet, which is not a bottleneck because lookups are cheap and clients aggressively cache locations. HBase and Cassandra are the best-known open source projects modeled after it.

  <!-- sysd-scale-038 -->

- **Apache Cassandra: a database with no special node**

  Cassandra has no head node. All nodes perform identical functions, so there is no single point of failure. It is an open-source distributed database that handles very large amounts of data across many commodity servers. It was designed to run on cheap commodity hardware and to handle high write throughput without sacrificing read efficiency. It aims to run on hundreds of nodes, possibly across data centers, where components fail continuously. The recipe combines Amazon's Dynamo storage and replication techniques with Google's Bigtable data storage engine model.

  Replication is asynchronous and masterless, and a cluster can span multiple data centers. Cassandra scales linearly: adding nodes raises read and write throughput while service continues. It is classed as an AP system, favoring availability and partition tolerance over consistency. Consistency levels are tunable for reads and writes, though strict consistency suits it poorly. It offers a simple wide-column model rather than a full relational one and suits well-defined access patterns that can be built into the schema. It has no multi-table JOINs, ad hoc aggregations or complex queries.

  <!-- sysd-scale-031 -->

- **MapReduce: two functions and a cluster that does the rest**

  A large server farm can use MapReduce to sort a petabyte of data in only a few hours. It is a programming model and implementation for processing large data sets on a cluster. The user writes a map function, which filters and sorts, and a reduce function, which summarizes. The runtime parallelizes the work across the cluster, handles machine failures and schedules communication. The paper's key contribution is not the two functions but the scalability and resilience to failure they bring a variety of applications.

  In the map step each worker applies the function to its local data. Shuffle redistributes data by output key so one key's data sits on one worker, and reduce processes each key's group in parallel. If a node falls silent, the master marks it dead and gives its work to other nodes. The paper reports more than ten thousand distinct programs at Google over four years. There are limits: it is usually not effective for quick jobs whose data fits in one machine's memory, and iterative algorithms such as graph processing are difficult.

  <!-- sysd-scale-040 -->

- **Apache Hadoop: shipping the code to the data**

  Hadoop's central trick is to ship the program to the data instead of the data to the program. It is a collection of open-source software utilities for reliable, scalable, distributed computing, built around HDFS storage and MapReduce processing. Both were inspired by Google's papers on MapReduce and the Google File System. Hadoop splits files into large blocks spread across the cluster. It then sends packaged code to the nodes so they process in parallel the data they hold, which is data locality. That lets a dataset be processed faster than on a conventional supercomputer architecture that moves data over high-speed networking.

  The base framework has Hadoop Common, HDFS, YARN (introduced in 2012) for cluster resources and scheduling, and MapReduce. Hadoop 3 allows multiple name nodes, which removes the single point of failure of Hadoop 2's one namenode, and uses erasure coding to decrease storage overhead. Hadoop suits batch-oriented, very data-intensive work; it is not for real-time work. Yahoo's Search Webmap, running on a Linux cluster of more than 10,000 cores, produced data used in every Yahoo web search query.

  <!-- sysd-scale-035 -->

- **HDFS architecture: one NameNode, many DataNodes**

  HDFS declares a storage machine dead after 2 minutes of silence, then starts copying its blocks elsewhere. It is Hadoop's distributed, scalable file system, storing large files across many machines. One NameNode tracks the files and holds the metadata, such as the number of blocks, which DataNodes store them and where replicas live. DataNodes store the blocks, and each sends a heartbeat to the NameNode every 3 seconds. Reliability comes from replicating data across hosts. With the default replication value of 3, two copies sit on one rack and one on a different rack. That keeps data available if a rack loses power or a switch fails.

  The secondary namenode is not a standby for failover: it checkpoints the primary's directory information so a failed primary can restart without replaying the whole journal. The single NameNode can become a bottleneck with many small files, and HDFS Federation allows multiple namespaces served by separate namenodes. HDFS gives up full POSIX compliance for higher data throughput, and it suits mostly immutable files rather than concurrent writes.

  <!-- sysd-scale-036 -->

- **Apache HBase: Bigtable on top of Hadoop**

  Google's Bigtable has an open-source cousin that runs on Hadoop. HBase is a non-relational distributed database modeled after Bigtable and written in Java. It runs on top of HDFS, a fault-tolerant way to store large quantities of sparse data with fast reads and writes at high throughput. It is a wide-column store with compression, in-memory operation and Bloom filters per column. It is not a direct replacement for a classic SQL database and has no SQL of its own, though Apache Phoenix adds a SQL layer. In CAP terms HBase is a CP system, and like Bigtable it is rated PC/EC under PACELC.

  <!-- sysd-scale-120 -->

- **The Cassandra data model: keyspaces, tables and partition keys**

  A Cassandra table is not as rigid as a relational one: rows in the same table can have different columns. Data is organized as keyspace, table, then row. A keyspace is like a database and sets the replication strategy. Each row is identified by a primary key whose first component is the partition key, and rows within a partition are clustered by the remaining key columns. Tables can be created, dropped or altered at run-time without blocking updates and queries. Each column carries timestamp metadata used to resolve write conflicts by last write wins, and the model is denormalized rather than joined.

  <!-- sysd-scale-032 -->

- **Cassandra gossip and failure handling: every node judges its peers**

  No node in a Cassandra cluster is in charge of knowing who is alive. Nodes routinely gossip cluster state, such as node bootstrap times and logical clock values, and use the clock values to ignore outdated state. A few seed nodes are guaranteed gossip contact points, which removes single points of failure. Each node judges the availability of the others with the Phi Accrual Failure Detector. A node that fails to respond is convicted and removed from writes, but can rejoin when heartbeats resume. With hinted handoff, the coordinator stores a write meant for an offline node as a hint and forwards it when the node returns.

  <!-- sysd-scale-034 -->

- **Cassandra's write and read path: commit log, Memtable, SSTable**

  Cassandra never overwrites data in place. It uses a log-structured merge tree index to optimize write throughput, unlike the B-tree indexes most databases use. A write goes to the commit log, a write-ahead log that ensures durability, and to the Memtable, an in-memory structure sorted by primary key. When the Memtable reaches size or time thresholds it flushes to an SSTable, an immutable file. Reads check the Memtable, then search SSTables from newest to oldest using bloom filters. Every change adds a new entry, and deletes use tombstones, which can slow delete-heavy workloads. Compaction merges SSTables to cut storage, drop tombstoned rows and speed reads.

  <!-- sysd-scale-033 -->

- **ScyllaDB: a Cassandra-compatible rewrite in C++**

  ScyllaDB's authors claim up to 2 million requests per second on one machine, and a cluster that matches a Cassandra cluster 10 times its size. Independent tests sometimes measured only about 2x. It is a source-available distributed wide-column data store designed to be compatible with Apache Cassandra, with significantly higher throughput and lower latency. It speaks Cassandra's CQL protocol and the DynamoDB API, but it is a complete rewrite in C++20 on the Seastar asynchronous library. Each node is sharded per CPU core: cores share nothing and communicate explicitly. Like Cassandra it is an AP database, with Paxos for lightweight transactions and Raft for schema and topology changes.

  <!-- sysd-scale-121 -->

- **The Bigtable data model: a sorted map with timestamps**

  Bigtable is a sparse, distributed, multi-dimensional sorted map. It maps two arbitrary strings, a row key and a column key, plus a timestamp, to an arbitrary byte array. It is not a relational database but a prototypical wide-column store, and it gives clients dynamic control over data layout and format. Each cell can hold zero or more timestamped versions of its data, and the timestamps allow both versioning and garbage collection of expired data. Google's copy of the web fits in one table. The row key is a domain-reversed URL, columns describe page properties, and the page column keeps versions stamped by fetch time.

  <!-- sysd-scale-039 -->

- **Hadoop job scheduling and YARN: from JobTracker to resource manager**

  In first-generation Hadoop, one JobTracker handed out all the MapReduce work. It pushes work to available TaskTracker nodes, keeping work as close to the data as possible. With a rack-aware file system, work that cannot run on the node holding the data goes to a node in the same rack. That reduces traffic on the main backbone network. By default Hadoop schedules by FIFO with 5 priorities. The fair scheduler gives pools a guaranteed minimum share, and the capacity scheduler gives queues a fraction of total capacity. YARN, the biggest change in Hadoop 2, replaced this engine with a resource manager and a master for each application.

  <!-- sysd-scale-037 -->

- **MapReduce dataflow: from input splits to the shuffle**

  The shuffle in a MapReduce job can take longer than the computation it feeds. A job flows through an input reader, map, partition, shuffle, sort, reduce and output writer. The input reader cuts input from stable storage into splits of 64 MB to 128 MB, one per Map call. A partition function sends each map output to a reducer, typically by hashing the key modulo the number of reducers. It should spread data roughly uniformly, or the job waits on slow reducers. A Combiner function can shrink the data sent over the network. In word count, map emits each word with a count and reduce sums them.

  <!-- sysd-scale-041 -->

  *Figure: A MapReduce job passes through seven stages from input to output.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Input reader] --> B[Map]
  B --> C[Partition]
  C --> D[Shuffle]
  D --> E[Sort]
  E --> F[Reduce]
  F --> G[Output writer]
  ```
