- **Discord message storage: from MongoDB to Cassandra to ScyllaDB**

  Discord's first version stored messages on a single MongoDB replica, and the story since is one of outgrowing each system in turn. Around November 2015 MongoDB held 100 million messages. RAM could no longer hold the data and index, latency became unpredictable, and storage had to move. Discord chose Cassandra. In 2017 it ran 12 Cassandra nodes with billions of messages; at the start of 2022 it ran 177 nodes with trillions.

  By then Cassandra had become a burden. Its latency was unpredictable, and maintenance operations had become too expensive to run. Cassandra's LSM tree makes reads more expensive than writes, and many concurrent reads on a server with hundreds of users create hotspots. Cluster maintenance such as compacting SSTables hurts performance, and garbage collection pauses cause significant latency spikes.

  The answer was ScyllaDB, a Cassandra-compatible database written in C++. Discord redesigned its architecture around a monolithic API, a data service written in Rust, and ScyllaDB-based storage. The payoff shows in the tail. The p99 read latency is 15ms on ScyllaDB against 40-125ms on Cassandra, and the p99 write latency is 5ms against 5-70ms. The thread through the story is predictability: each system was left when its latency stopped being predictable.

  <!-- sysd-scale-030 -->

  *Figure: The p99 latencies Discord reports for ScyllaDB and for Cassandra.*

  | p99 latency | ScyllaDB | Cassandra |
  |---|---|---|
  | Read | 15 ms | 40-125 ms |
  | Write | 5 ms | 5-70 ms |

## Messaging, APIs and architecture

Ask a web server for a page and you wait for the reply. That is synchronous communication, as with an HTTP request; in asynchronous communication the sender carries on without waiting. This part begins with the second kind. A queue holds messages until the receiver takes them, and an intermediary program translates, stores, routes and delivers them between systems. With such a buffer between producers and consumers, a system can scale, decouple its components, respond faster and survive failures.

### Message queues and brokers

A queue is a widely used data structure: it takes new elements at one end and gives them back from the other. Turn it into a software component between programs and it becomes a place where messages wait until the receiver is ready. This chapter follows that idea from the common variants of the queue to the intermediary programs, open protocols and open-source software built around it. One question keeps returning along the way: how many times does a message reach its consumer, at most once, at least once, or exactly once?

- **Waiting for a reply versus carrying on**

  Ask a web server for a page and you wait until it answers. That is synchronous communication, the way HTTP works: the sender waits for a reply. In asynchronous communication the sender carries on without waiting. Waiting is not always the right choice. An application may only need to tell another that an event occurred, and a sender should not stall because a recipient has crashed. Most applications mix the two: an interactive one can answer part of a request at once and queue other parts, such as billing, to be done later. A subsystem that performs message queuing, or broadcast messaging, can improve the whole system's behavior in these situations, and Message queues: leave it with the queue and move on shows how. It can even be layered over a synchronous request-response protocol, as some queue services do over HTTP. The underlying protocol then limits what they can offer.

  <!-- sysd-msg-047 -->

- **Four kinds of queue, from plain to double-ended**

  A queue takes new elements at one end and gives them back at the other. The simple kind is FIFO. A new element goes in at the tail and the oldest leaves from the head, so emails for payment responses go out in the same order. A circular queue, also called a ring buffer, links its last element to its first; LMAX's low-latency ring buffer runs in memory. In a priority queue, the element with the highest or lowest predefined priority is taken first. A deque, or double-ended queue, allows insertion and deletion at both ends, so it supports FIFO and LIFO.

  <!-- sysd-msg-056 -->

- **Message queues: leave it with the queue and move on**

  A message queue lets two programs talk without ever being busy at the same moment. The sender drops a message in and moves on, and the queue holds it until the receiver takes it. It is a software component, typically used for communication between processes or threads. It is the working form of the asynchronous idea in Waiting for a reply versus carrying on, because neither party needs to touch the queue at the same time as the other. The paradigm is a sibling of the publisher/subscriber pattern and is typically one part of a larger system of messaging middleware, described in Middleware that carries messages between systems.

  In practice an administrator configures the queue-manager or broker software and defines a named queue. An application registers a routine that listens for messages, and other applications connect and put messages onto the queue. The queue manager stores the messages until a receiving application connects, then calls the registered routine, and the application processes the message. Queues have implicit or explicit limits on the size of a single message and on how many may remain outstanding. Queuing systems that connect different computer systems typically add resilience so that messages do not get lost when a system fails. The software can be proprietary, open source or a mix, and it runs on private servers or as an external cloud service.

  <!-- sysd-msg-046 -->

- **Middleware that carries messages between systems**

  Call a procedure on another machine and you wait until it returns. Message-oriented middleware offers a looser deal. It is software or hardware infrastructure that supports sending and receiving messages between distributed systems. It insulates developers from the details of operating systems and network interfaces, so independently developed components on different platforms can interact. Middleware built on remote calls ties components tightly, because the caller waits; the message-oriented kind lets them stay loosely coupled. The sender hands a message to the provider and carries on, confident the provider keeps it until a receiver retrieves it. If the receiver fails, senders continue unaffected while messages accumulate until it restarts. The provider can also store, route or transform messages in transit. The cost is an extra component in the middle, the broker of The broker that sits between sender and receiver, which can reduce performance and reliability and make the system harder and costlier to maintain. A sender can also keep piling work on a recipient until it fails, so message flow must be monitored and adjusted.

  <!-- sysd-msg-138 -->

- **At most once, at least once, exactly once**

  How many times should a message reach its consumer? Once sounds right, yet it is the hardest answer to build. Delivery semantics name three choices: at most once, at least once, or exactly once. At-most-once means a message is delivered not more than once, so messages may be lost but are never redelivered. That suits use cases such as metrics gathered to monitor a system, where a small amount of data loss is acceptable. At-least-once loses no message but may deliver the same one several times. That is usually good enough when duplication is not a big issue. It is also fine when the consumer can deduplicate, for example by rejecting a duplicate write on a message's unique key. Most brokers offer at-least-once delivery, so consumers will eventually see duplicates. Exactly-once is the most difficult semantic to implement. It is friendly to users but costs a lot in performance and complexity. It matters for financial use cases such as payment, trading and accounting, especially when duplication is unacceptable and the downstream service does not support Idempotency: making a repeated request safe.

  <!-- sysd-msg-050 -->

  *Figure: The three guarantees side by side: what each allows and where it fits.*

  | Guarantee | What it means | Where it fits |
  |---|---|---|
  | At most once | Messages may be lost, never redelivered | Monitoring metrics |
  | At least once | No message lost, but duplicates possible | Duplicates are no big issue, or the consumer can deduplicate |
  | Exactly once | Hardest to build; costs performance and complexity | Payment, trading, accounting |

- **What a buffer between producers and consumers buys**

  In a small system a write is predictably fast. In a large distributed one, the same write can take an almost non-deterministic amount of time. Queues are used to manage requests under that uncertainty, and putting a buffer between producers and consumers buys four things. The first is scalability: at peak load, multiple instances of an application can add requests to the queue without risk of collision, a theme from Scalability: taking on more work without losing performance. The second is decoupling, since queues remove dependencies between components and simplify decoupled applications. The third is performance: endpoints interact with the queue, not each other, so producers can add requests without waiting for them to be processed. The fourth is reliability, because queues make data persistent and reduce the errors that happen when parts of the system go offline.

  <!-- sysd-msg-067 -->

- **From closed vendor protocols to open standards**

  Message queuing began on closed, proprietary protocols. Sun's JMS specification offered only a Java-only abstraction of a client API. Three open standards now serve open source queues. The first is AMQP, feature-rich and approved as ISO/IEC 19464 since April 2014; AMQP, the protocol that standardizes the bytes goes deeper. The second is STOMP, a simple, text-oriented protocol. The third, MQTT: publish-subscribe for tiny devices, is lightweight and aimed especially at embedded devices. AMQP and STOMP operate at the same level as HTTP, while the lightweight one operates at the level of TCP/IP. Some proprietary implementations, such as Amazon's SQS, use HTTP itself, but they stay constrained by that protocol.

  <!-- sysd-msg-049 -->

- **The broker that sits between sender and receiver**

  A sender should not have to know where its receiver is, whether it is running, or how many receivers there are. A message broker takes on that knowledge. It is an intermediary program that translates messages between the messaging protocols of sender and receiver and validates, stores, routes and delivers them. Because it translates from the sender's formal protocol to the receiver's, services written in different languages or on different platforms can talk to each other. Because it stands in the middle, it decouples processes and services. A broker may manage a workload queue or message queue for several receivers, with reliable storage, guaranteed delivery and perhaps transaction management. It offers two basic distribution patterns: point-to-point messaging, as in queues, and publish-subscribe messaging, where producers publish to topics that consumers subscribe to. Brokers are generally built on one of two architectures: hub-and-spoke, where a central server provides integration services, or a message bus acting as a communication backbone.

  <!-- sysd-msg-051 -->

- **AMQP, the protocol that standardizes the bytes**

  Most messaging standards describe an API. AMQP describes bytes. It is an open standard application layer protocol for message-oriented middleware. Because it is wire-level, any compliant tool can interoperate with any other regardless of language, unlike API-level standards such as JMS. It is a binary protocol that assumes a reliable transport such as TCP. It offers flow-controlled messaging with at-most-once, at-least-once and exactly-once guarantees, plus encryption and identity checks based on SASL and TLS. Messages travel one way over a link in transfer frames, and credit-based flow control keeps a receiver from being overwhelmed. Every transferred message must eventually be settled, so sender and receiver agree on its state; that settlement is how the guarantees are enforced. The bare message stays immutable in transit, so end-to-end signing, encryption and integrity checks stay valid. Version 1.0 focuses on the core features Internet-scale interoperability needs, with less explicit routing than earlier versions. Implementations include Apache Qpid, ActiveMQ, Solace and the 4.0 release of RabbitMQ: an Erlang broker that learned many protocols.

  <!-- sysd-msg-136 -->

- **RabbitMQ: an Erlang broker that learned many protocols**

  RabbitMQ began as an implementation of one protocol and now speaks several. It is an open-source message broker that originally implemented AMQP and has been extended through a plug-in architecture to support STOMP and other protocols. The server is written in Erlang and built on the Open Telecom Platform framework for clustering and failover. Client libraries exist for all major programming languages. Plug-ins add more: Shovel moves or copies messages from one broker to another, Federation shares messages between brokers, and Management monitors and controls brokers and clusters. RabbitMQ uses Raft to implement durable, replicated FIFO queues. System designs often place jobs on a queue such as Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ, for example for notifications, video processing and extracting transactions from accounts.

  <!-- sysd-msg-072 -->

- **ActiveMQ: a Java broker that speaks many protocols**

  ActiveMQ is a Java broker that does not leave everyone else out. It is an open source message broker written in Java with a full Java Message Service client; Java applications use JMS 1.1 and other languages use cross-language clients. It supports several transport protocols, among them OpenWire, STOMP and AMQP. ActiveMQ Classic gets high availability from file-system or database row-level locking, a shared persistence store, or replication using ZooKeeper, and it scales horizontally with a Network of Brokers. Artemis, based on the HornetQ code base, is the next-generation broker under the ActiveMQ umbrella: multi-protocol, embeddable, clustered and asynchronous.

  <!-- sysd-msg-139 -->

- **Choosing a queue's semantics: durability, expiry, filtering**

  A queue is a menu of choices, and several of them affect reliability and efficiency. Durability decides where messages live: in memory, on disk, or even in a database. Queues or messages may have a time to live (see Time to live: giving every cache entry an expiry date), and some systems filter data so a subscriber sees only messages matching pre-specified criteria. Delivery policies decide whether a message must arrive at least once or no more than once, as At most once, at least once, exactly once explains. Routing policies decide which servers receive a message when there are many queue servers. Batching policies and receipt notification for publishers also have substantial effects on transaction semantics, reliability and efficiency.

  <!-- sysd-msg-048 -->

- **Queues that live inside the operating system**

  Not every queue crosses a network. Many implementations work only inside an operating system or an application, for that system's purposes alone. UNIX has two common ones: one in the SYS V API and a later, similar one in POSIX. In SYS V, a blocking receive puts the caller to sleep until a message of the requested type is posted. A non-blocking receive returns at once to report that it failed. Graphical user interfaces use the same idea. A message queue, also called an event queue, passes mouse, keyboard and timer events to the application, which removes them one at a time in an event loop.

  <!-- sysd-msg-058 -->

- **Amazon SQS: queuing over HTTP**

  In Amazon's Simple Queue Service, neither the number of queues nor the message traffic has a limit, yet a single message body may not pass 256KB. SQS is a distributed queuing service, and messages can be of any type. It queues over HTTP: asynchronous behavior can always be layered over request-response semantics, but such a service is constrained by the underlying protocol. Its FIFO queues guarantee ordering within a message group, though not necessarily across retries or failures. A larger message can be split into segments, or stored in Amazon S3 or DynamoDB with only a pointer sent in the SQS message.

  <!-- sysd-msg-135 -->

- **Dead letter queues for messages that will not go through**

  One message that can never be processed can clog a queue. A dead letter queue is where a messaging system stores messages it cannot or should not deliver. Depending on the implementation, a message lands there if its queue does not exist or its time to live expires. It also lands there if another exchange rejects it, or if it was read and rejected too many times. Setting them aside lets the main queue keep moving. They can be inspected later, without blocking processing or wasting CPU cycles on a message that may never succeed. Studying them reveals common fault patterns and software problems. A consumer that finds a message invalid can forward it to an Invalid Message Channel, separating application-level faults from delivery failures. Managing these queues means watching them, raising alerts, and adding handlers for automated or manual remediation. In an SQS FIFO queue, later messages in a group wait until the preceding one is processed or moved to the dead-letter queue. There it is no longer retried, leaving a gap while the others continue in order.

  <!-- sysd-msg-134 -->

- **Seven features most message queues offer**

  Open the feature list of almost any queue and the same items turn up. Message queues commonly offer delayed delivery, delivery guarantees, dead-letter queues, ordering, poison pills, identity checks and task queues. Many queues let a message carry a specific delivery time, and a delay queue gives all messages a common delay. Queues may store multiple copies for redundancy and resend messages after failures to deliver at least once, while FIFO queues filter out duplicates automatically to deliver exactly once. A dead-letter queue receives messages other queues cannot process, as Dead letter queues for messages that will not go through describes. Most queues give best-effort ordering: messages are generally delivered in the order sent and at least once. In a FIFO queue the oldest entry, the head, is processed first. Poison pills are special messages that can be received but not processed. They signal a consumer to end its work, much like closing a socket in a client/server model. Queues check the identity of applications that try to access them, which allows messages to be encrypted over the network and in the queue itself. Task queues receive tasks and their data, run them and deliver the results, can support scheduling, and can run computationally intensive jobs in the background.

  <!-- sysd-msg-069 -->

- **How to choose a message queue**

  Picking a queue starts with a list of things to compare. They include speed and scalability, reliability (messages are not lost) and durability (messages kept safe over time). They also include ease of setup and management, ecosystem tools, integration with other software, and the protocols and languages supported. Decide the pattern first. Queues give one-to-one delivery and pub/sub lets many consumers subscribe to a topic. Brokers can offer both, while event streaming platforms offer only pub/sub. Those platforms scale more and suit high volumes, but they cannot guarantee delivery or track which consumers received a message. Then match the delivery guarantee to the need: most brokers offer at-least-once, so consumers see duplicates, and exactly-once costs performance and complexity. Most queues give best-effort ordering, while SQS FIFO orders only within a message group. Protocol matters too. JMS is an API, so systems from different vendors are not interoperable, while AMQP is wire-level, so compliant software interoperates. Finally, look at limits and failure handling: a dead-letter queue sets unprocessable messages aside, and SQS caps message bodies at 256KB.

  <!-- sysd-msg-059 -->

- **The enterprise service bus, and why it fell out of favor**

  One hub that every application talks through sounds tidy. An enterprise service bus is a pattern in which a centralized software component performs integrations between applications. It transforms data models, routes messages and converts communication protocols. In theory this standardizes communication and lets components scale independently and fail without affecting others. In many organizations, though, the bus came to be seen as a bottleneck. A single point of failure can bring down all communications, and a change to one integration can destabilize others. Message brokers are a lightweight alternative at lower cost, as ESBs have fallen out of favor.

  <!-- sysd-msg-053 -->

- **Locks, waiting and non-blocking queues**

  What happens when two threads want the same queue at once? A blocking algorithm uses locks. If Thread A is suspended while holding the lock, Thread B may wait for arbitrarily long periods and can starve. In the non-blocking alternative, Thread B is told that access is rejected instead of being made to wait, though other threads may still starve through rejections. Wait-free is stronger: all threads complete their tasks within a finite number of steps, which makes it non-blocking plus starvation-free. A non-blocking queue can be built with compare and swap (CAS). With no thread suspension and no lock waiting, latency drops and deadlock cannot occur.

  <!-- sysd-msg-057 -->

- **A job's trip through a queue**

  Follow one job through a queue and the steps are short. A producer publishes the job to the queue, then notifies the user of the job's status. A consumer later picks the job up, processes it, and signals that it is complete. Until then the message sits in the queue, stored until it has been processed and deleted. Each message is processed only once, by a single consumer.

  <!-- sysd-msg-068 -->

  *Figure: A job goes from producer to queue to consumer, and the user is told its status.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Producer] -->|publishes job| B[(Queue)]
  B -->|consumer picks it up| C[Consumer]
  C -->|signals complete| D[Job done]
  A -.->|notifies status| E[User]
  ```

- **Backpressure: stop a backlog from slowing everything**

  A queue that grows beyond memory slows down just when it is busiest: the result is cache misses, disk reads and even slower performance. Backpressure prevents this by limiting the size of the queue, which maintains a high throughput rate and good response times for the jobs already in it. Once the queue fills up, clients get a server-busy or HTTP 503 status code, which tells them to try again later. They can retry the request at a later time, perhaps with a backoff strategy (see Exponential backoff: waiting twice as long each time).

  <!-- sysd-msg-071 -->

- **Push or pull: who starts the delivery**

  Who starts the hand-off, the queue or the consumer? Most message queues provide both options. Pull means continuously querying the queue for new messages. Push means the consumer is notified when a message is available. Long-polling, described in Long polling: holding the request open until there is news, allows pulls to wait a specified amount of time for new messages to arrive. Pub/sub topics push their notices out instantly, which removes the need for consumers to poll for new information.

  <!-- sysd-msg-070 -->

- **Competing consumers share one queue**

  Several workers can drain one queue at once. The competing consumers pattern enables multiple concurrent consumers to process messages on the same message queue. There is no need to configure complex coordination between them. Each message is still processed only once, by a single consumer, as A job's trip through a queue describes. The price is order: the pattern cannot guarantee message ordering.

  <!-- sysd-msg-055 -->

- **Six named designs for services that exchange messages**

  Services that exchange messages can draw on named designs, and six are worth knowing. Asynchronous request-reply decouples backend processing from clients for long-running tasks, with the API answering HTTP 202 (Accepted) to acknowledge the request. Publisher-subscriber decouples senders from consumers and avoids blocking the sender to wait for a response; Publish–subscribe: speak to a topic, not to a person treats it in full. Claim check handles large messages by storing the whole payload in a database and transmitting only a reference, which is later used to retrieve the payload. Priority queue lets requests with a higher priority be received and processed more quickly than those with a lower priority. Saga, from The saga pattern: local transactions with undo steps, manages data consistency across services that each own a database, without distributed transactions, which are difficult to scale and can hurt performance. Competing consumers, from Competing consumers share one queue, lets multiple concurrent consumers process messages from the same channel without complex coordination, but cannot guarantee message ordering.

  <!-- sysd-msg-054 -->

- **Publish–subscribe: speak to a topic, not to a person**

  In publish–subscribe, a sender does not know who will read its message, and a reader does not know who wrote it. Publishers sort messages into classes, called topics, and send them without needing to know which components will receive them. Subscribers express interest in one or more classes and receive only messages in those classes, without needing to know who the publishers are. The pattern decouples the components that produce messages from those that consume them, and it supports asynchronous, many-to-many communication. A message published to a topic is pushed immediately to all subscribers, which often perform different functions and can each act on it in parallel. This contrasts with queue-based and point-to-point messaging, where producers send directly to consumers; JMS, for one, supports both models. The gain is greater network scalability and more dynamic topologies. The cost is that it can become harder to modify the publisher's logic or the structure of the published data. Compared with synchronous patterns such as RPC, pub/sub gives the highest decoupling. But it can lead to semantic or format coupling that makes systems entangled or brittle over time. Today it is told apart from its in-process cousin, described in The observer pattern, publish–subscribe's in-process cousin, by its emphasis on decoupling, asynchronous messaging and broker-mediated communication across a distributed system.

  <!-- sysd-msg-060 -->

  *Figure: One message published to a topic is pushed to every subscriber.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Publisher] -->|publishes| T[Topic]
  T -->|pushed| S1[Subscriber A]
  T -->|pushed| S2[Subscriber B]
  T -->|pushed| S3[Subscriber C]
  ```

- **MQTT: publish-subscribe for tiny devices**

  Despite its name, MQTT has no queues. It is a lightweight publish-subscribe network protocol for machine-to-machine messaging, suited to devices with limited resources or network bandwidth, such as Internet of things sensors. It runs over an ordered, lossless transport, typically TCP/IP. Clients connect to a broker, which receives messages from publishers and routes them to subscribers by topic, so devices and server applications stay decoupled. A broker discards a message with no current subscribers unless it is flagged retained. It keeps one retained message per topic and delivers it to each new subscriber immediately. A publisher can register a default message at connect time, which the broker sends to subscribers if it detects an unexpected disconnect. Each connection chooses a quality of service, in increasing order of overhead: at most once, at least once, or exactly once. That guarantee applies between MQTT sender and receiver, not to TCP. Ordering holds only within one client session on one topic, so messages from independent clients can arrive out of order.

  <!-- sysd-msg-137 -->

- **Why publish–subscribe scales and stays flexible**

  In publish–subscribe the topic is the only thing both sides share. Publishers are loosely coupled to subscribers and need not know they exist, so each side stays ignorant of system topology and works independently. Many systems also decouple the two in time, unlike client-server, where neither side can post or receive while the other is not running. Push delivery through topics removes the need to poll for updates, which brings faster response time and lower delivery latency; Push or pull: who starts the delivery compares push with pull. A publisher simply posts to a topic instead of keeping a roster of peers, so subscribers can change, upgrade, multiply or disappear while the system adjusts dynamically. Pub/sub can scale better than client-server through parallel operation, message caching and tree-based or network-based routing. Redundant subscribers can assure delivery with minimal added complexity: an exact duplicate of a logging subscriber can be added without any impact on other equipment. RSS and Atom syndication show pub/sub scaling beyond a single data center. They accept higher latency and no delivery guarantees, so a low-end web server can reach millions of subscribers.

  <!-- sysd-msg-064 -->

- **The observer pattern, publish–subscribe's in-process cousin**

  The observer pattern is a close relative of publish–subscribe. A subject keeps a list of observers and automatically notifies them of state changes, typically by calling one of their methods. It sets up a one-to-many dependency without tight coupling: observers register and unregister themselves, and the subject only needs to know they implement an update operation. Subject and observers hold direct references with no broker, and notification is typically synchronous, so the pattern suits in-process uses such as GUI toolkits. Publish-subscribe adds a broker, scales to distributed systems, filters by topic and isolates failures, whereas observer failures can affect the subject.

  <!-- sysd-msg-141 -->

- **NATS: a plain pub/sub server that can add persistence**

  NATS starts as a plain publish-subscribe server and adds persistence only when you ask for it. It is an open-source messaging system under the stewardship of the Cloud Native Computing Foundation. The server is written in Go, with client libraries for dozens of languages, and its core design principles are performance, scalability and ease of use. Core NATS is the publish-subscribe server. JetStream is an optional built-in persistence layer that adds streaming, queues, at-least-once and exactly-once delivery, replay, flow control and a key/value store. It replaced the older STAN (NATS Streaming) approach and uses the Raft consensus algorithm for cluster management and data replication.

  <!-- sysd-msg-140 -->

- **Where publish–subscribe hurts**

  Publish–subscribe's worst problems are a side effect of decoupling. A broker that stops delivering after a specified time cannot guarantee delivery, so assured delivery needs tighter coupling, such as receipt messages from subscribers. A publisher may assume a subscriber is listening when it is not, and may not be told if a subscriber such as a logger fails. It scales well for small networks with low message volume. As nodes and messages grow, instabilities such as load surges and slowdowns limit the maximum scalability. Brokers can be overloaded tracking subscriptions or fooled into notifying the wrong client, and encryption cannot stop authorized publishers from introducing damaging messages.

  <!-- sysd-msg-065 -->

- **Filtering: how a subscriber gets only what it wants**

  A subscriber rarely wants every message. In publish–subscribe systems subscribers typically receive only a subset, and the process of selecting the relevant ones is called filtering. Topic-based filtering publishes messages to named topics or channels, and subscribers who register for a topic receive all messages published to it. Content-based filtering lets subscribers define constraints on message attributes or content, and a message is delivered only if it matches. Hybrid systems categorize messages by topic and let subscribers apply content-based filters to the messages within those topics.

  <!-- sysd-msg-062 -->

- **With or without a broker in the middle**

  Who sits between the publisher and the subscriber? In most publish–subscribe systems, a central intermediary such as a message broker or event bus. Subscribers can be registered at build time, with handlers hardcoded as in GUI event handlers. They can be registered at initialization time, with subscriptions in XML configuration or metadata, or added and removed dynamically at runtime. Brokerless systems skip the intermediary: publishers and subscribers discover each other and exchange messages directly. The Data Distribution Service middleware, for one, uses IP multicast and metadata sharing to set up the communication paths.

  <!-- sysd-msg-063 -->

- **Message broker or event streaming platform**

  A message broker and an event streaming platform can look alike, but they make different trades. Brokers can support two or more messaging patterns, including message queues and pub/sub, while event streaming platforms only offer pub/sub-style distribution. Streaming platforms are designed for high volumes of messages, are readily scalable, and order streams of records into topics stored for a predetermined amount of time. In exchange, they cannot guarantee message delivery or track which consumers have received the messages. They also offer fewer fault-tolerance features such as message resending, and more limited routing and queueing capabilities.

  <!-- sysd-msg-052 -->

- **What publish–subscribe services add on top**

  Publish–subscribe services usually do more than relay messages. Topics can typically connect to many types of endpoints, such as message queues, serverless functions and HTTP servers. Fanout happens when a message sent to a topic is replicated and pushed to multiple endpoints, which gives asynchronous event notifications that allow parallel processing. These services often provide very high durability and at-least-once delivery by storing copies of the same message on multiple servers. Topics also authenticate applications that try to publish, which allows encrypted endpoints and encryption of messages in transit over the network.

  <!-- sysd-msg-066 -->

- **One consumer or every subscriber**

  A queue hands each message to one consumer. A topic hands it to everyone who subscribed. Queues hold messages until they are retrieved, whereas topics transfer messages with little or no queuing and push them out immediately. With a queue the sender often knows the destination it sends to. In pub/sub the publisher need not know who uses its information, and subscribers need not know where it comes from. Most messaging systems support both models in their API, for example the Java Message Service.

  <!-- sysd-msg-061 -->

  *Figure: A queue serves one consumer per message; a topic serves every subscriber.*

  |  | Message queue | Publish–subscribe |
  |---|---|---|
  | Who gets a message | One consumer | Every subscriber of the topic |
  | Holding | Held until retrieved | Pushed out at once, little or no queuing |
  | What the sender knows | Often the destination | Need not know who uses it |

### Event streaming and Kafka

Some messaging systems keep every message instead of discarding it after delivery. Apache Kafka does this: it stores messages in a durable log, so many consumers can read them. This chapter starts with jobs that run in an automated and unattended way, then moves to treating streams of events as the central input and output of computation. Along the way it looks at how Kafka organizes its data and how it can still lose messages, at engines that process streams, and at ways of copying database changes into other systems.

- **Apache Kafka: a log that keeps messages after they are read**

  Most queues hand a message over and forget it. Kafka keeps it. Apache Kafka is an open-source distributed platform, written in Java and Scala, for storing events and processing streams of them. Unlike queue-based systems, it retains messages in a durable, append-only log until they expire. So multiple consumers can read at different offsets, which are positions in the log, and pull at their own pace. The project aims to provide a unified, high-throughput, low-latency platform for handling real-time data feeds. Kafka can handle multiple producers and consumers, with disk-based data retention and high scalability. Ordering is guaranteed within each partition, one of the parts a topic is split into, but not across the entire topic. Kafka Connect moves data in and out of external systems, and the libraries of Kafka Streams: stream processing as a Java library support stream-processing applications. Kafka was originally built for massive log processing. It is used for log analysis, data streaming such as recommendations, watching systems and raising alerts, and carrying database changes elsewhere, a job that Change data capture: copying database changes elsewhere describes. Kafka Raft (KRaft) uses the Raft algorithm for metadata management.

  <!-- sysd-msg-036 -->

- **Batch processing: jobs that run unattended**

  Some work is best done with nobody at the keyboard. Batch processing is the running of a software job in an automated and unattended way. A user schedules a job, and a processing system runs it, typically at a configured time of day, when an event occurs or when computer resources are available. It collects data and processes it all at once, as in daily billing. The alternative handles data in real time, as in fraud detection, and Stream processing, where the data never ends takes it up. Batch applications stay critical because many business processes suit them and online systems are not optimized for high-volume repetitive tasks. They update information at day's end, generate reports and print documents by business deadlines. If a job needs only one input at a time, flow processing lowers latency per input. If it needs totals over all records, the whole batch must finish before any result is usable. A batch window is a period of less-intensive online activity in which batch jobs can run without interfering with interactive systems. It shrank as demands for online uptime grew.

  <!-- sysd-msg-133 -->

- **Stream processing, where the data never ends**

  A batch job, as in Batch processing: jobs that run unattended, knows where its data ends. A stream does not. Stream processing, also called event stream processing, is a programming paradigm. It treats streams, or sequences of events in time, as the central input and output objects of computation. It encompasses dataflow programming, reactive programming and distributed data processing. The data is an unbounded, continuous sequence of elements rather than a static dataset. A series of operations called kernel functions is applied to each element, and uniform streaming, where one kernel function applies to all elements, is typical. The program defines a dataflow sequence, and the execution environment applies the kernel automatically as new elements arrive. Kernels can also do aggregation windows or stateful modifications. Applying the same function to every record lets many records be processed at once. The paradigm sacrifices some flexibility for easier, faster and more efficient execution. It works well for data-centric workloads but less well for general-purpose processing with random data access, such as databases.

  <!-- sysd-msg-043 -->

- **Apache Spark: analytics without the trips to disk**

  Spark exists because MapReduce kept going back to disk. Apache Spark is an open-source unified analytics engine for large-scale data processing. MapReduce, from MapReduce: two functions and a cluster that does the rest, forces a linear dataflow that reads from disk and writes results to disk. Spark's foundation is the resilient distributed dataset, or RDD, a read-only multiset spread over a cluster. RDDs are immutable, their operations are lazy, and lost data is rebuilt from each RDD's lineage. They suit iterative algorithms and interactive analysis, cutting latency by orders of magnitude versus Hadoop MapReduce. Spark manages the workflow as a directed acyclic graph in which nodes are RDDs and edges are the operations on them. Its streaming ingests data in micro-batches, so batch code can be reused for streaming. The cost is a latency penalty equal to the micro-batch duration, while Storm and Flink process event by event. Libraries on Spark Core include MLlib for distributed machine learning and GraphX for graph processing, though GraphX is unsuitable for graphs that must be updated.

  <!-- sysd-msg-132 -->

- **Topics, partitions, brokers and consumer groups**

  Kafka's design comes down to a few moving parts. The message is the basic unit of data, like a record in a table, consisting of headers, a key and a value. Every message goes to a topic, which is like a folder on a computer, and topics have multiple partitions. Producers create new messages, batch them, send them to a topic and balance them across the partitions. Consumers work together as a consumer group to read messages from the broker. A Kafka cluster consists of several brokers, and each partition is replicated across multiple brokers to ensure high availability and redundancy. Partitions also give fault isolation and parallel processing: a consumer that delays committing an offset stalls only its own partition while the others remain unaffected. In 2025 Kafka added share groups as an alternative to consumer groups. They give queue-like semantics with individual acknowledgment and allow more consumers than partitions, where consumer groups assign each partition exclusively.

  <!-- sysd-msg-037 -->

  *Figure: Producers write to a topic whose partitions live on brokers, and a consumer group reads them.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Producers] -->|send to a topic| B[Topic split into partitions]
  B -->|replicated across| C[Cluster of brokers]
  C -->|read by| D[Consumer group]
  ```

- **How Kafka can still lose a message**

  Many developers believe Kafka by design guarantees no message loss. Its architecture and configuration decide how and when it might lose messages, and there are three places to look: the producer, the broker and the consumer. On the producer side, producer.send() does not send directly to the broker. The application thread puts the message in a record accumulator. A separate sender thread then sends it, so proper acks and retries settings are needed to make sure messages arrive. On the broker side, a healthy cluster should not lose messages. But they are usually flushed to disk asynchronously for higher I/O throughput, so an instance that goes down before the flush loses them. Replicas, covered in Replication: keeping several copies in step, must be properly configured to hold a valid copy of the data. On the consumer side, auto-committing might acknowledge records before they are processed, so a consumer that goes down mid-processing can leave some records never processed. A good practice combines asynchronous commits in the processing loop for throughput with synchronous commits in exception handling, so the last offset is always committed.

  <!-- sysd-msg-038 -->

- **Kafka Streams: stream processing as a Java library**

  Kafka Streams is a library written in Java for stateful stream-processing applications that are scalable, elastic and fault-tolerant. Its main API is a domain-specific language with high-level operators such as filter, map, grouping, windowing, aggregation, joins and tables. A lower-level Processor API implements custom operators and can be mixed with it. For stateful processing it keeps local operator state in RocksDB, which can write to disk, so the state can be larger than main memory. To survive failures, every update to the local state stores is also written to a topic in the Kafka cluster. The state can then be recreated by reading those topics back into RocksDB.

  <!-- sysd-msg-040 -->

- **Complex event processing: spotting the pattern in the events**

  Three small events, blowOutTire, zeroSpeed and driverLeftSeat, in a short time signal an accident, though no single measurement shows it. That is complex event processing: techniques for extracting information from event streams as they arrive, to identify meaningful events such as opportunities or threats. A complex or composite event is inferred from simpler constituent events, as bells, a tuxedo, a gown and rice signal a wedding. The techniques include detecting causality, membership or timing relationships between events. They also include continuous SQL queries over timestamps and windows, such as joining stock orders to trades matched within one second. Typical uses are stock trading and credit-card fraud detection.

  <!-- sysd-msg-045 -->

- **Change data capture: copying database changes elsewhere**

  Databases drift out of sync. Constant data changes leave databases, data lakes and data warehouses disagreeing, and change data capture, or CDC, replicates and syncs data across systems to overcome this. It is a set of design patterns for determining and tracking data that changed. The source is the system with data believed to have changed, and the target is the system that needs to act on the changed data. A CDC tool monitors the database transaction logs through a source connector to capture inserts, updates and deletes. The changes are transformed, published to a message queue and propagated to targets such as data warehouses, analytics platforms and distributed caches like Redis. There a sink connector consumes the log and updates the targets in real time. A popular solution uses Debezium with Kafka Connect to stream changes from source to target, with Kafka as the broker. In the push model the source creates a snapshot of changes and delivers rows downstream. In the pull model the downstream target requests the data from the source.

  <!-- sysd-msg-041 -->

  *Figure: A CDC tool reads the transaction log and ships changes through a queue to the targets.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[(Source database)] -->|transaction log| B[Source connector]
  B -->|changes published| C[Message queue]
  C --> D[Sink connector]
  D -->|updates in real time| E[(Targets)]
  ```

- **Three ways to detect that a row has changed**

  Three families of methods notice that data has changed. The first uses extra columns. With a timestamp column, any row stamped more recently than the last capture is considered changed. With version numbers, changed rows are marked with a version. At capture all data with the latest version is considered changed, and the reference table then gets a new version number. A status column can mark a row as changed. It can also complement the other methods by showing that a row with a new version or later date should not yet be updated on the target. Using time, version and status together is a particularly powerful mechanism, because the three elements are not redundant. The second family uses triggers. Events on the transactional table are logged into a queue table that can later be played back to replicate the data to a target. The third reads the database transaction log. That has minimal impact on the database, needs no application changes, and can replay the original transactions in the order they were committed. It is hard, though. No standard exists for the log format, most databases do not document it, and uncommitted changes later rolled back must be eliminated.

  <!-- sysd-msg-042 -->

- **Three execution models for stream engines**

  Stream engines differ mainly in how they run. Distributed stream processing engines are grouped by execution model into native continuous engines, micro-batch engines and distributed logging fabrics. Native continuous engines process elements individually as they arrive, optimizing for sub-second, real-time latencies; Apache Storm, Flink (see Apache Flink: one engine for batches and streams) and Apache Samza belong here. Micro-batch engines collect incoming elements into small time windows to achieve high-throughput stream semantics, as Apache Spark Streaming does with live data in small discrete chunks. Distributed logging fabrics, such as Apache Kafka, serve as the persistent, append-only transport layer. Managed services such as AWS Kinesis and Google Cloud Dataflow run streams in the cloud.

  <!-- sysd-msg-044 -->

  *Figure: The three execution models and an example of each.*

  | Model | How it works | Examples |
  |---|---|---|
  | Native continuous | Processes elements individually as they arrive | Apache Storm, Flink, Apache Samza |
  | Micro-batch | Collects elements into small time windows | Apache Spark Streaming |
  | Distributed logging fabric | Persistent, append-only transport layer | Apache Kafka |

- **Apache Flink: one engine for batches and streams**

  Flink runs batch and stream programs on the same engine. Apache Flink is an open-source, unified stream-processing and batch-processing framework. Its core is a distributed streaming dataflow engine, and its pipelined runtime executes both kinds of program, processing events one at a time on finite and infinite datasets. A dataflow starts at sources such as a message queue or file system, applies any number of transformations, and ends at sinks. The streams form a directed acyclic graph that can branch and merge. Checkpoints are automatic asynchronous snapshots of application state and source stream position. After a failure Flink resumes from the last completed checkpoint, which gives exactly-once state semantics within an application. Savepoints are manually triggered checkpoints. A user can stop a program and resume it from the same state and stream position. That allows updates without losing state and, since Flink 1.2, a change of parallelism. Flink has no storage system of its own, so it provides source and sink connectors to systems such as Apache Kafka, Amazon Kinesis, HDFS, Apache Cassandra and Elasticsearch.

  <!-- sysd-msg-131 -->

  *Figure: A Flink dataflow runs from sources through transformations to sinks, with checkpoints of its state.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Sources] --> B[Transformations]
  B --> C[Sinks]
  B -.->|snapshots state| D[Checkpoint]
  ```

- **Why Kafka is fast: sequential writes and zero copy**

  Kafka turns a bursty stream of random message writes into linear ones. Its message-set abstraction groups messages, which leads to larger network packets and larger sequential disk operations. That reliance on sequential I/O is one of two design decisions that carry the most weight in Kafka's performance; the other is the zero-copy principle. Without zero copy, data is loaded from disk to the OS cache, copied to the Kafka application, copied to the socket buffer, then copied to the network card. With zero copy, the OS cache copies the data directly to the network card via the sendfile() command, saving multiple copies between the application and kernel contexts.

  <!-- sysd-msg-039 -->

### Event-driven architecture, event sourcing and CQRS

Instead of one part of a system calling another and waiting for an answer, parts can announce that something happened and let others react. That is event-driven architecture: components communicate by producing and reacting to events, usually through a message broker that publishes and delivers them asynchronously. This chapter follows the idea outward. It covers storing the full series of actions as the source of truth, and splitting commands that change state from queries that only read it. It also looks at how to wire such a system with or without one orchestrator, what an event carries, and how consumers and events fail.

- **Event-driven architecture: parts that announce, not command**

  A car goes from for sale to sold. That is an event: a data point, a significant change in state. It announces the change and says nothing about what should happen next.

  Event-driven architecture builds whole systems from announcements like this. Producers publish events to a router, the router filters them and pushes them to consumers, and the consumers use them to reflect the change in the system. Usually the events travel through a The broker that sits between sender and receiver, which publishes and delivers them asynchronously. The publisher is unaware of who consumes an event, and the consumers are unaware of each other.

  That ignorance is the point. It keeps services loosely coupled, decouples producers from consumers and makes it easy to add a new consumer. Systems built on events are highly scalable and distributed, horizontal scaling gets simpler, and the whole is more resilient to failure. Typical uses are metadata and metrics, server and security logs, integrating heterogeneous systems, and fanout and parallel processing. Widely used technologies include Apache Kafka: a log that keeps messages after they are read, Amazon EventBridge, Amazon SNS and Google PubSub.

  The price is real. Guaranteed delivery, error handling and exactly-once, in-order processing are all hard. Such systems are complex in general and inherently hard to test.

  <!-- sysd-msg-020 -->

  *Figure: A producer publishes to a router, which filters events and pushes them to consumers.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  P[Producer] -->|publishes| R[Router]
  R -->|pushes| C1[Consumer]
  R -->|pushes| C2[Another consumer]
  ```

- **Domain-driven design: code that speaks the business's language**

  A loan system might have loan applications, customers and a method called accept offer. That is domain-driven design in miniature. The structure and language of the code, down to class and method names, match the business domain, modeled with input from the domain's experts. Experts, users and developers share one ubiquitous language, used both in the model and in describing requirements.

  The approach rejects a single unified model. It divides a large system into separate areas, each with its own model, an idea developed in Bounded context: where one model holds. An aggregate binds objects under a root entity: outside objects may reference only the root, which checks that changes stay consistent. Combined with CQRS: splitting the writes from the reads and Event sourcing: keep the history, derive the present, aggregate roots take a command as input and output one or more events.

  Before any of that, event storming helps. In this workshop, stakeholders, domain experts and developers map the domain's events to discover subdomains, boundaries and aggregates. Critics say the approach demands much isolation and encapsulation, and Microsoft recommends it only for complex domains where the model clearly helps.

  <!-- sysd-msg-127 -->

- **Event store: a database of nothing but events**

  In an event store, the events are the only real facts. Everything else is derived from them. An entity's state at any point in its history is rebuilt by replaying its events in order. Objects that aggregate the recorded data are not stored. Runtime code builds them on the fly by traversing the history, then discards them.

  Stored events never change, even erroneous ones. The only way to correct one is to add a new event with the new values. Backdated events, which take effect before earlier ones, are easier to handle this way. Only the new event is stored, and the code redetermines the objects from the new facts, with no rollback. The disadvantage is that code may need to re-instantiate every object in memory each time a service call arrives for a given dossier or policy.

  One newspaper website keeps every article, image and byline in an event store. It denormalizes the raw data into views fed to ElasticSearch nodes for website searches. Apache Kafka: a log that keeps messages after they are read is also a distributed event store and stream-processing platform.

  <!-- sysd-msg-022 -->

- **Event sourcing: keep the history, derive the present**

  Storing only the current state forgets how things got there. Event sourcing keeps the whole series of actions instead. It changes the programming paradigm from persisting states to persisting events, recorded in an append-only Event store: a database of nothing but events. That store acts as the system of record and can be used to materialize the domain objects.

  Do not confuse it with Event-driven architecture: parts that announce, not command, as people constantly do. Event sourcing uses events as state, a different approach to storing data. Event-driven architecture uses events to communicate between service boundaries. Event sourcing is one of several patterns for implementing an event-driven architecture.

  Keeping the full history pays off. It gives audit trails that can enable compensating actions, lets data be reconstituted from the event store after a failure, and suits real-time reporting and high-compliance audit logs. The costs are an extremely efficient network infrastructure and a reliable way to control message formats, such as a schema registry, because different events carry different payloads.

  In a microservice system, a service such as the shopping cart emits events to a Kafka broker acting as the event store. Other services consume them, each determining its own domain model. A stream can also be fed by Change data capture: copying database changes elsewhere. There, a connector pulls data from tables and transforms it into events, which are pushed to Kafka for other sinks to consume.

  <!-- sysd-msg-021 -->

- **The fallacies of distributed computing**

  Programmers new to distributed applications invariably make the same false assumptions. L. Peter Deutsch and others at Sun Microsystems listed them as the fallacies of distributed computing. The original list begins with four: the network is reliable, latency is zero, bandwidth is infinite and the network is secure. It continues: topology doesn't change, there is one administrator, transport cost is zero and the network is homogeneous.

  Each false belief has a price. Assume the network is reliable, and applications get little error handling. They stall or wait forever during an outage, and may fail to retry stalled operations when the network returns. Ignore latency and the packet loss it causes, and developers allow unbounded traffic that drops more packets and wastes bandwidth. Ignore bandwidth limits, and bottlenecks appear.

  Later additions include a ninth fallacy, that the party you communicate with is trustworthy. Richards and Ford added three more: versioning is simple, compensating updates always work, and Observability: asking questions you did not plan for is optional.

  <!-- sysd-msg-128 -->

- **Broker or mediator: two ways to wire an event system**

  Who is in charge when events flow? Event-driven architecture has two primary topologies, broker and mediator, and the two can be combined in a hybrid model.

  In the broker topology there is no orchestrator. Components broadcast events to the entire system, and the reward is higher performance and scalability. In the mediator topology a central orchestrator controls the workflow of events, and the reward is better control and error handling.

  Put plainly, the choice trades the speed and scale of the first against the control and error handling of the second.

  <!-- sysd-msg-026 -->

  *Figure: The two topologies differ in who coordinates and in what each one gives.*

  |  | Broker topology | Mediator topology |
  |---|---|---|
  | Coordinator | None, components broadcast events | A central orchestrator |
  | Gives | Higher performance and scalability | Better control and error handling |

- **When consumers fail and events vanish**

  A consumer chokes on an event. What now? One answer is a separate error-handler processor. The failing consumer sends the erroneous event to it asynchronously and moves on. The processor tries to fix the event and sends it back to the original channel. If it fails, it sends the event to an administrator for inspection. The catch is that events resubmitted this way are processed out of sequence.

  Data loss is the other danger. A component crashes before it has processed an event and handed it to the next component, so the event is dropped and never reaches its destination. To minimize this, persist events while they are in transit and dequeue them only after the next component acknowledges receipt. These features are known as client acknowledge mode and last participant support.

  Event-driven systems are also susceptible to The fallacies of distributed computing, misconceptions that can cause significant problems in development and deployment.

  <!-- sysd-msg-030 -->

- **Simple, stream and complex event processing**

  A mature event-driven architecture often uses all three general styles of event processing together: simple, stream and complex.

  In simple event processing, a notable event tied to a specific, measurable change of condition initiates downstream actions. It drives the real-time flow of work and reduces lag time and cost. In event stream processing, ordinary events such as orders or RFID transmissions are screened for notability and streamed to subscribers. This drives the real-time flow of information and in-time decisions.

  Complex event processing looks at patterns of simple and ordinary events to infer that a complex event has occurred, and then takes action. The events may cross event types and span a long period, and their correlation may be causal, temporal or spatial. It needs sophisticated event interpreters, pattern definition and matching, and correlation techniques. It is commonly used to detect business anomalies, threats and opportunities.

  A fourth approach, online event processing, uses asynchronous distributed event logs to process complex events and manage persistent data. It reliably composes related events across heterogeneous systems and allows very flexible distribution patterns with high scalability and strong consistency. What it cannot do is guarantee upper bounds on processing time.

  <!-- sysd-msg-029 -->

- **Inside an event: header, payload and how much to carry**

  An event is made of a header and a body, also called the payload. The header may hold the event name, a time stamp and the event type. The payload provides the details of the detected state change, and it should not be confused with the logic applied in reaction to the event.

  The design question is how much to put in the payload. Put in all the necessary attributes, and speed and scalability improve. The risks are data consistency problems from multiple systems of record, stamp coupling and bandwidth issues at scale. Put in only keys or IDs, and consumers fetch the data from sources such as databases. That minimizes bandwidth and coupling, but it is less scalable and slower because of the queries.

  These two methods are ends of a spectrum, not a binary choice. Architects must size payloads to the needs of the event consumers.

  <!-- sysd-msg-028 -->

- **Command–query separation: asking should not change the answer**

  Asking a question should not change the answer. Bertrand Meyer built command–query separation on that idea. Every method should be either a command that performs an action or a query that returns data, but not both. A method returns a value only if it has no side effects.

  Queries never change state, so any query can be called anywhere, such as in assertions, without fear of side effects. It has limits. A combined method such as a stack's pop can be more convenient. In multithreaded code, separate increment and value calls leave a race condition that a locked increment-and-return avoids. The pattern in CQRS: splitting the writes from the reads generalizes the principle to services.

  <!-- sysd-msg-129 -->

- **CQRS: splitting the writes from the reads**

  A command is an instruction to perform a task that changes the system, and it returns only success or failure. A query requests information without changing state or causing side effects. Command Query Responsibility Segregation, or CQRS, extends Command–query separation: asking should not change the answer to the level of services, with separate interfaces for sending commands and queries. The two play different roles, so each can be optimized as needed.

  Many systems push the split into the data. Read models process queries and write models process commands, usually tailored to their tasks and often held in physically separate stores. CQRS is often combined with event sourcing. Then the store of events is the write model and the official source of information, and the read model offers materialized, highly denormalized views.

  The benefits are independent scaling of read and write workloads, easier optimization, clear boundaries and no complex joins when querying. The drawbacks are a more complex design, possible message failures or duplicate messages, the challenge of Eventual consistency: every reader agrees, but not yet, and more maintenance effort.

  <!-- sysd-msg-024 -->

  *Figure: Commands and queries get separate interfaces, models and, with event sourcing, different stores.*

  |  | Command side | Query side |
  |---|---|---|
  | Does | Changes state | Only reads |
  | Returns | Success or failure | Information |
  | Model | Write model | Read model |
  | With event sourcing | Store of events, the official source | Materialized, denormalized views |

- **Domain events and integration events**

  Some events stay home, and some travel. Domain events signify important occurrences within one business domain. They are restricted to one area with its own model (see Bounded context: where one model holds), and they are vital for preserving business logic. Their payloads are typically lighter, with only the information needed for processing. Integration events communicate changes across different such areas and are crucial for keeping data consistent across the entire system. Their payloads tend to be more complex, with additional attributes, because the needs of their potential listeners differ significantly.

  <!-- sysd-msg-027 -->

- **The four layers an event passes through**

  An event passes through four logical layers: the producer, the channel, the processing engine and downstream activity. The producer senses a fact and represents it as an event message. Converting data from sources as diverse as email clients and sensors into one standard form is a significant task.

  The channel carries events from the producer to the engine. Several channels can be open at once and are read asynchronously, with events queued for later processing. The engine selects and executes the reaction, such as ordering a product and notifying personnel when stock is low. The downstream layer shows the consequences, such as an email.

  <!-- sysd-msg-033 -->

  *Figure: An event moves through four logical layers, from the producer to the consequences downstream.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Event producer] --> B[Event channel]
  B --> C[Processing engine]
  C --> D[Downstream activity]
  ```

- **Event granularity: how many events, how much detail**

  How many events should a system publish, and how much should each say? Finding the right number is difficult. Too many detailed events can overwhelm the system and make the event flow hard to analyze, a problem worse when rollbacks are required. Overly consolidated events make consumers do unnecessary processing and send unnecessary responses.

  Mark Richards recommends considering the impact of each event and whether consumers need to read the payload to decide their actions. In a compliance check, publishing only compliant and non-compliant events can suffice. Each event is then processed only by relevant consumers, and unnecessary workload falls.

  <!-- sysd-msg-031 -->

- **Getting a synchronous answer from an event-driven system**

  Sometimes the caller needs an answer now, even in a system built on events. Synchronous transactions in an event-driven architecture can be built on the request-response paradigm, implemented in two ways. One uses two separate queues, one for requests and one for replies, and the event producer must wait until it receives the response. The other uses one dedicated ephemeral queue, a short-lived one, for each request.

  <!-- sysd-msg-034 -->

- **The timeout antipattern: too short, too long**

  How long should a caller wait? Both answers hurt. A short timeout may fail legitimate requests prematurely and lead to complex workarounds. A long timeout gives slow error responses and a poor user experience. This difficulty of setting timeout values in distributed systems is the timeout antipattern.

  The pattern in Circuit breaker: stop calling a service that is failing can address it. It watches service health through heartbeats, synthetic transactions or real-time usage, which enables faster failure detection.

  <!-- sysd-msg-035 -->

- **Fixing events by adding events: the double timeline**

  In an event store you cannot edit history, so how do you fix a mistake? Give each event two dates: the valid date, when it became valid, and the transaction date, when it was entered into the database. A correcting event carries the new values, keeps the event date of the event it corrects, and has a different transaction date. This ensures reproducibility at every moment in time, even in the period before the correction took place. It also allows situations that were based on erroneous events to be reproduced, if required.

  <!-- sysd-msg-023 -->

- **Apache Avro: compact binary data that carries its schema**

  Avro is a row-oriented framework, developed within Apache's Hadoop project, for two jobs: turning data into bytes, covered in Serialization: turning data into bytes and back, and making remote calls, covered in Remote procedure call: making a far-away function feel local. Hadoop uses it both as a format for persistent data and as a wire format between its nodes and from client programs to its services. Schemas are defined in JSON and data is serialized in a compact binary format. Data can be stored with its schema, so a serialized item can be read without knowing the schema ahead of time. Unlike Thrift and Protocol buffers: schemas that skip the field names, Avro needs no code-generation step when a schema changes, and its binary encoding is smaller and faster.

  <!-- sysd-msg-130 -->

- **Event schema evolution: changing events without breaking consumers**

  Event-driven systems look loosely coupled in space, time and synchronization, yet they stay tightly coupled, through subscriptions and patterns, to the semantics of the event schema and values. That is why changing events is hard. Schemas can become inconsistent across services, and compatibility must hold while the system is updated gradually.

  Strategies include versioning events, such as semantic versioning or schema evolution, to maintain backward and forward compatibility. Adapters can translate events between old and new formats, so processing stays consistent across components. One format that needs no code-generation step when a schema changes is Apache Avro: compact binary data that carries its schema.

  <!-- sysd-msg-032 -->

- **McDonald's event platform: a registry, a gateway, regional clusters**

  McDonald's platform is a tour of this chapter's problems, with an answer to each.

  The first problem is keeping events consistent. An event registry defines a standardized schema, and custom SDKs (software development kits) process events and handle errors. That ties together the shape of an event (Inside an event: header, payload and how much to carry), the way that shape changes over time (Event schema evolution: changing events without breaking consumers) and the failures a consumer can hit (When consumers fail and events vanish).

  The second is control. An event gateway verifies who is calling and what each caller may do. Utilities and tools fix events, keep the cluster healthy and perform administrative tasks.

  The third is scale. A regional architecture on AWS provides global availability. Within a region, producers shard events by domain, the sharding idea behind Database sharding: spreading one database across many servers, and each domain is processed by its own MSK cluster. Each cluster auto-scales on MSK metrics such as CPU usage, using a workflow built on step-functions and re-assignment tasks.

  The thing to remember: the platform splits events by domain, with a cluster for each. A registry and its SDKs keep every producer speaking one standard schema.

  <!-- sysd-msg-025 -->

### Monoliths, microservices and service discovery

An application can be one self-contained unit that performs every step of a business function, or a collection of small, loosely coupled services that can be deployed and scaled independently. This chapter walks that range, from the monolith and the layers of an N-tier design to microservices and the older service-oriented architecture. Splitting an application creates new problems. Clients must find service instances whose locations change, a proxy paired with each service can handle their communication, and a distributed trace can track one request through all the services that fulfil it. The chapter also covers how services collaborate, through shared rules for exchanging messages or through a central coordinator.

- **Loose coupling: changing one part without breaking the rest**

  A change in one component should disturb the others as little as possible. That is the promise of loose coupling. A loosely coupled system is one whose components make little or no use of knowledge of the definitions of other components. A loosely coupled component can be replaced by another implementation of the same service.

  In code, a class that depends only on an interface can be served by any implementing class. A new class replaces the old without changing the dependent one. In distributed systems, loose coupling comes from transactions, queues in message-oriented middleware and interoperability standards. Publish–subscribe gives the highest level of decoupling. Synchronous patterns such as RPC, a call that runs a function on another machine, create tightly coupled components. Services stay loosely coupled when they pass only key data. A letter-sending service takes a customer identifier and looks up the address itself.

  Loose coupling has a price. Decoupling in time makes transactional integrity hard and needs extra coordination protocols. Replication creates consistency issues. An asynchronous caller can overload the recipient until it fails.

  <!-- sysd-msg-143 -->

- **Monolithic application: one unit that does everything**

  A monolith is built as a single unit and handles every step needed to satisfy a business need, not one particular task. For a small team with little complexity, it is still a good choice. It is relatively simple and low cost. Development and debugging are simple, communication is fast and reliable, testing is easy, and ACID transactions are supported.

  The trouble grows with the codebase. Maintenance gets harder, the application is tightly coupled and hard to extend, and it commits the team to a particular technology stack. The whole application is redeployed on each update, and a single bug can bring down the entire system. Monoliths lack elasticity, scalability and the ability to survive faults. Once one becomes too complex, it can be refactored into Microservices: small services that scale on their own or a distributed application.

  Even on a single machine, a monolith may be performant enough for the current workload. Yet it is less available, durable, changeable and scalable than a well-designed distributed system. Common architectural patterns for monoliths, each with trade-offs, are layered architecture, the Modular monolith: one deployment, independent modules and microkernel architecture.

  <!-- sysd-msg-091 -->

- **Microservices: small services that scale on their own**

  A monolith that supports three functions must be scaled in its entirety, even if only one function is under strain. Microservices avoid that. The architecture organizes an application into a collection of small, loosely coupled services that communicate through lightweight protocols. Teams can develop, deploy and scale each service independently, so only the strained function's service is scaled out.

  There is no universally agreed definition. Each service is generally designed around one business capability, inside the boundary of one domain model (see Bounded context: where one model holds), with its own codebase managed by a small team. Small is a matter of responsibility, not size. Each service also persists its own data, a database per service, unlike the traditional model where a separate data layer handles persistence.

  The benefits follow from independence. Services deploy independently, give multiple teams agility, improve tolerance of faults and data isolation, and remove any long-term commitment to a particular technology stack. The costs are just as real. They are the complexity of a distributed system, harder testing, expensive maintenance, challenging communication between services, problems keeping data correct and consistent, and network latency and congestion.

  The complexity of a monolith does not disappear when it is split into services. Some of it becomes operational complexity, so teams need decentralized delivery (see Continuous delivery: always ready to release) and DevOps, with holistic watching of every service.

  <!-- sysd-msg-083 -->

- **Service-oriented architecture: building from services that already exist**

  The aim is to build applications purely from existing services. Service-oriented architecture, or SOA, focuses on discrete services instead of a monolithic design (see Monolithic application: one unit that does everything). It is intended to be independent of vendors, products and technologies, and is a good choice for system integration. One definition gives a service four properties. It represents a repeatable business activity with a specified outcome, is self-contained, is a black box to its consumers, and may be composed of other services.

  SOA promotes reuse at the macro, service level rather than the class level. A service treated as a project separate from its consumers can be delivered quickly and independently. That also encourages good design, because the service is designed without knowing who its consumers are.

  SOA can be implemented with web services or microservices. It has costs. Without compact, binary ways of calling a service remotely, applications could run more slowly and need more processing power. Stateful services reduce the provider's scalability if it must keep each consumer's context, and they increase coupling. Testing is hard, because there is no uniform testing framework.

  <!-- sysd-msg-094 -->

- **Service discovery: finding services that keep moving**
