  In a monolith, parts call each other with ordinary method or procedure calls. Microservices have no such luxury. They run in virtualized or containerized environments. There the number and location of service instances change dynamically, so clients need a way to reach a changing set of ephemeral instances.

  Service discovery is the answer. It automatically detects devices and services on a network, which reduces the manual configuration effort required from users and administrators. A service discovery protocol is a network protocol that helps accomplish it. It needs a common language, so software agents can use one another's services without continuous user intervention. Many protocols exist, including DNS Service Discovery and Simple Service Discovery Protocol. Another example is Kubernetes: a cluster that steers itself toward the state you declare, which provides two modes of service discovery, using environment variables or its own DNS.

  <!-- sysd-msg-092 -->

- **Service mesh: a proxy beside every service**

  As the number of services grows, routing the calls between them becomes increasingly complex. A service mesh makes it managed, observable and secure. It is a dedicated infrastructure layer for service-to-service communication, and it gives visibility into communications, secure connections, and automated retries and backoff for failed requests.

  It has two parts. Network proxies paired with each service form the data plane, and a set of management processes forms the control plane. The data plane intercepts and processes calls between services. The control plane coordinates the proxies and provides APIs to manipulate and observe the whole network.

  Each service instance is paired with a Reverse proxy: a front door for servers called a sidecar, which shares its container and is managed by an orchestration tool such as Kubernetes: a cluster that steers itself toward the state you declare. The sidecars can support service discovery, load balancing and secure communications, including checks on who a caller is and what it may do. Istio, Cilium, Linkerd and Consul: from service discovery to service networking implement the architecture, and many meshes use the Envoy proxy on the data plane.

  <!-- sysd-msg-093 -->

- **Distributed tracing: following one request through many services**

  When one user request passes through many services, finding the slow or failing one is hard. A distributed trace helps. It is an interrelated series of discrete events, called spans, that track the progression of a single request through the services that fulfil it. A trace shows the causal and temporal relationships between the services.

  Spans carry unique identifiers that let a tracing backend build parent-child relationships between them, and span information is typically passed in the HTTP headers of outbound requests. Instrumenting an application means sending span information to the backend, which correlates the spans into traces. The main way to view a trace is a swimlane view, as in Jaeger.

  Tracing is mainly used for anomaly detection, fault analysis, debugging and diagnosis. It has overhead, so in production there is a trade-off between how fine-grained the tracing is and its cost. It can also generate a large volume of messages, so it must often be possible to switch it off, at compile time or at run time. OpenTelemetry is a CNCF open source project that supports it.

  <!-- sysd-msg-145 -->

- **N-tier architecture: layers in the code, tiers on the machines**

  Layers and tiers sound alike, but one is a design and the other is a place. Layers divide an application logically, each with a specific responsibility. They manage dependencies: a higher layer can use services in a lower layer but not the other way around. Tiers are physically separated and run on separate machines. A tier can call another directly or use asynchronous messaging, and several layers may share one tier. Separating tiers physically improves scalability and resiliency but adds latency from the extra network communication.

  Layers can be closed or open. In a closed layer architecture a layer can call only the next layer down, which limits dependencies but may create unnecessary network traffic. In an open one it can call any layer below.

  The widely used 3-tier design has three layers. A presentation layer handles user interactions, a business logic layer validates data, and a data access layer operates on the database. In 2-tier, the presentation layer runs on the client and talks to a data store, with no business logic layer. In single-tier, everything runs on one application or server.

  The advantages are improved availability, firewall-like layers for security, independent scaling of tiers and easier maintenance by different people. The disadvantages are added complexity, network latency that grows with the number of tiers, a hardware cost per tier, and harder network security.

  <!-- sysd-msg-080 -->

  *Figure: The widely used 3-tier design stacks a presentation layer, a business logic layer and a data access layer.* (layers; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Orchestration versus choreography: who decides the order**

  Two services must cooperate on one job. Who decides the order? In choreography, nobody does. Service choreography describes the exchange of messages and the rules by which the microservices interact, with point-to-point communication between them. In orchestration, a central orchestrator acts as the center of authority. It is responsible for invoking and combining the services, and it describes the interactions between all participating services. The orchestration pattern also includes transaction management among different services.

  Each style wins somewhere. Orchestration is more reliable because it has built-in transaction management and error handling, while choreography's point-to-point communication makes scenarios where services fail much more complicated. Orchestration also scales more easily in one respect. Adding a service means only the orchestrator changes its interaction rules, whereas in choreography all the interacting services must change.

  Orchestration pays for this. It adds latency, because all services talk through the central orchestrator, and throughput is bound to the orchestrator's capacity. The orchestrator is also a single point of failure: if it goes down, no services can talk to each other, so it must be highly available. Netflix Conductor is a real-world microservice orchestrator.

  <!-- sysd-msg-078 -->

  *Figure: The two styles differ in who controls the interaction and in how they handle failures and growth.*

  |  | Choreography | Orchestration |
  |---|---|---|
  | Control | Shared rules, point-to-point messages | A central orchestrator |
  | Failures | Much more complicated scenarios | Built-in transaction management and error handling |
  | Adding a service | All interacting services must change | Only the orchestrator changes |

- **Microservices versus SOA: a question of scope**

  Microservices and SOA are sometimes used interchangeably, but they differ, and the main distinction comes down to scope. SOA defines how to make software components reusable through service interfaces and common communication standards. Microservices are many smallest independent service units, aimed at team autonomy and decoupling. Another view calls microservices a modern interpretation of SOA, a new implementation approach popular since 2014 that stresses continuous deployment and agile practices. Among their characteristics the literature lists fine-grained interfaces, business-driven development and lightweight container deployment.

  <!-- sysd-msg-097 -->

- **Service provider, broker and consumer**

  Each SOA building block can play any of three roles: service provider, service broker or service requester, which is the consumer. The broker is also called a registry or repository. The provider creates a web service and gives its information to the service registry. The broker makes information about the service available to any potential requester. Public brokers are available everywhere, while private brokers reach a limited public. A consumer locates entries in the broker's registry with find operations. It then binds to the provider to invoke its web services, under a standardized service contract with business, functional and technical parts.

  <!-- sysd-msg-096 -->

- **Service-oriented design principles**

  No industry standard fixes the exact composition of a service-oriented architecture, but many sources have published their own principles. Services adhere to a standardized service contract. They stay loosely coupled through reference autonomy, where services only know of each other's existence. They also use location transparency, where a service can be called from anywhere in the network. Services act as black boxes that hide their inner logic. They are autonomous over the functionality they encapsulate, and stateless, returning a value or an exception to minimize resource use. They should be long lived, composable into other services, discoverable through communicative metadata, and divided to promote reuse of code.

  <!-- sysd-msg-095 -->

- **Service registry and registration: the address book of instances**

  If service instances come and go, someone must keep the address book. That is the service registry: a database containing the network locations of service instances that clients can reach. It must be highly available (see High availability: staying up when parts fail) and up to date. Instances get into it in one of two ways. With self-registration, an instance registers and de-registers itself, and may send heartbeat requests to keep its registration alive. With third-party registration, the registry tracks running instances by repeatedly checking the deployment environment or subscribing to events. It records newly available instances and de-registers terminated ones.

  <!-- sysd-msg-082 -->

- **Components of a microservice architecture**

  A set of microservices usually sits among a handful of supporting components. A load balancer distributes incoming traffic across multiple backend services. A CDN, a group of geographically distributed servers holding static content, is checked first by clients before they reach the backend.

  The API gateway handles incoming requests and routes them to the relevant services. It talks to service discovery and to a component that confirms who users are and what they may do (see Identity provider). Services register themselves in the service registry and discovery component, which the gateway searches to find the services it needs to talk to. A management component monitors the services. Microservices are designed and deployed in different domains, and each domain has its own database.

  <!-- sysd-msg-079 -->

  *Figure: Each supporting component has one job around the domain services.*

  | Component | Job |
  |---|---|
  | Load balancer | Spreads incoming traffic across backend services |
  | CDN | Servers holding static content, checked first by clients |
  | API gateway | Routes incoming requests to the relevant services |
  | Identity provider | Authenticates and authorizes users |
  | Service registry | Where services register; the gateway searches it |
  | Management component | Monitors the services |
  | Domain services | Each domain has its own database |

- **Client-side and server-side discovery**

  Once instances have registered their locations, a client has two ways to find one. In client-side discovery, the client obtains a service's location by querying a service registry that manages and stores the network locations of all services. In server-side discovery, the client sends its request to an intermediate component, such as a load balancer, which forwards it to an available service instance. The difference is who does the lookup: the client, or something in between. Tools used to implement service discovery include Eureka, Apache ZooKeeper, Consul: from service discovery to service networking and Kubernetes services: one stable address for a changing set of pods.

  <!-- sysd-msg-081 -->

  *Figure: The two patterns differ in who finds the instance and where the request goes first.*

  |  | Client-side discovery | Server-side discovery |
  |---|---|---|
  | Request goes first to | The service registry, which the client queries | An intermediate component such as a load balancer |
  | Who finds the instance | The client | The load balancer, which forwards the request |

- **Microservices best practices**

  Most rules for good microservices come down to one: keep them independent. Model services around the business domain (see Domain-driven design: code that speaks the business's language), with loose coupling and high functional cohesion, and make each do one thing well. Each service owns and manages its own data, kept private to it, so coupling falls and services can evolve independently. Shared database schemas are a cause of coupling. Services should communicate only through well-designed APIs, avoid leaking implementation details and keep API changes backward compatible. Services should talk over lightweight protocols, and the options include REST: the architectural style behind most web APIs, gRPC: fast, typed calls between services or message brokers.

  Design for failure at infrastructure, database and service levels, with bulkheads, Circuit breaker: stop calling a service that is failing or Graceful degradation: doing less instead of stopping, and fail fast so failures do not cascade. Retry policies and caching improve availability. A large attack surface calls for security at every level of the communication path, and with many services centralized logging becomes critical for finding issues. Containerization deploys microservices in isolation and simplifies their scaling and deployment.

  <!-- sysd-msg-074 -->

- **Monolith versus microservices: start simple, or split early?**

  Should a new system begin as a monolith or as microservices? Plainly, it depends on team size, business maturity and latency needs. Singh's guide advises starting with a monolith when building a new system, while accepting that each approach has its own advantages and disadvantages.

  Microservices are not a silver bullet. They solve an organizational problem, and adopting them is about organizational priorities and team structure as much as technology. Questions to ask before moving include whether the team is too large for a shared codebase and whether teams are blocked on other teams. Others are whether microservices bring clear business value, whether the business is mature enough, and whether the current architecture limits the team through communication overhead. Not every application must be broken up. Microservices are solutions to complex concerns, and a business without such concerns does not need them.

  Latency can settle the matter outright. Latency-sensitive applications such as real-time gaming, at millisecond latency, and low-latency trading, at microsecond latency, avoid microservices because network latency between separate processes is unbearable. Microservices are usually stateless, with state kept in a database, but gaming and trading keep state in memory for quick updates. These applications also talk to the server at high frequency and must reach the same running instance, so they need web socket connections and sticky routing.

  <!-- sysd-msg-073 -->

- **Bounded context: where one model holds**

  Inside a bounded context, one domain model is consistent and valid. It is a core idea of domain-driven design, and it defines an area that ensures clarity and separation of concerns. A bounded context often maps to a microservice, and a one-to-one mapping is typically ideal, because it keeps clear boundaries, reduces coupling and enables independent deployment and scaling. One context may be split into several microservices for varying scalability needs, or several contexts consolidated into one microservice for simplicity or lower operational overhead. The choice should balance domain-driven design principles with business goals, technical constraints and operational requirements.

  <!-- sysd-msg-085 -->

- **Cell-based architecture: limiting the blast radius**

  Cell-based architecture organizes computational resources into self-contained cells. Each cell operates independently on a subset of requests, while the design keeps scalability, fault isolation and availability. A cell typically holds multiple microservices and acts as an autonomous unit. Entire sets of microservices may be replicated across cells, so requests can be rerouted to another working cell on failure, which limits the impact of localized failures. The pattern in Circuit breaker: stop calling a service that is failing works at two levels here. Inside a cell it stops failures spreading among microservices, and between cells it isolates a failing cell and redirects traffic to the remaining ones.

  <!-- sysd-msg-086 -->

- **Code sharing between microservices**

  Ideally, microservices follow a share-nothing architecture. In practice, code must often be shared across services. Common approaches are separate shared libraries for reusable components such as a security library, replicating stable modules with minimal changes across services, or consolidating several microservices into one. Each approach has its own advantages and trade-offs, depending on context and requirements.

  <!-- sysd-msg-089 -->

- **Microservice granularity: how small is small enough**

  How big should a service be? The right granularity is found through iterative collaboration between architects and developers, and it is ultimately set by business drivers. Neal Ford's integrator factors, such as shared transactions or tightly coupled processes, favor combining services. His disintegrator factors, such as surviving faults or independent scalability, favor splitting them.

  Very fine-grained services are easier to test and deploy independently. They tend to have lower performance and reliability, because of more communication between services and more complex choreography. Coarse-grained services are more robust and reliable, thanks to less communication overhead, but harder to test and deploy, because a change affects a wider scope.

  <!-- sysd-msg-084 -->

- **Reach-in reporting antipattern**

  A reporting service needs data that lives inside other services, and pulling it out directly causes trouble. Retrieving the data can break the bounded contexts of microservices, reduce the timeliness of the data, or both. This holds whether the data is pulled directly from databases, retrieved via HTTP or collected in batches. The pattern is called the reach-in reporting antipattern.

  The alternative is for the databases to push the needed data to the reporting service asynchronously. Pushing needs a separate contract between the microservices and the reporting service, and it can be complex. But it preserves bounded contexts while keeping data timely.

  <!-- sysd-msg-088 -->

- **Testing and observing microservices**

  Many independently deployed services must stay testable and visible. Sam Newman suggests keeping microservice interfaces stable and making backward-compatible changes as they evolve, so deployments need not be coordinated across services. He proposes consumer-driven contract testing as a better alternative to traditional end-to-end testing. To keep the system visible, he suggests log aggregation, metrics aggregation and Distributed tracing: following one request through many services. Richards and Ford propose that each microservice have its own architectural characteristics, rather than uniform ones for the whole distributed system.

  <!-- sysd-msg-090 -->

- **Consul: from service discovery to service networking**

  Consul is a service networking platform developed by HashiCorp, and it was first released as a service discovery platform. Registered services and nodes can be queried through either a DNS interface or an HTTP interface. It also provides a service mesh for secure service segmentation across any cloud or runtime, and distributed key-value storage for application configuration. The Envoy proxy provides security, visibility and resilience for all application traffic. Consul can also be used to perform distributed locks.

  <!-- sysd-msg-144 -->

- **Distributed monolith: microservices in name only**

  A system can look like microservices and still behave like a monolith. A distributed monolith resembles the microservices architecture but is tightly coupled within itself, like a monolithic application. Signs are a need for low-latency communication, services that do not scale easily, dependencies between services, shared resources such as databases, and tightly coupled systems. Scalability is a primary reason to adopt microservices, yet a distributed monolith makes most components depend on one another, which increases design complexity.

  <!-- sysd-msg-076 -->

- **Microservices pitfalls**

  Microservices fail to deliver in familiar ways. Service boundaries not drawn around the business domain, a lack of business alignment and a lack of clear ownership are common pitfalls. Teams underestimate how hard it is to build a distributed system, and a lack of design for faults can let failures cascade. A shared database or common dependencies between services undermine their independence, the kind of coupling that marks a Distributed monolith: microservices in name only. A lack of Idempotency: making a repeated request safe and trying to do everything ACID instead of BASE are further pitfalls.

  <!-- sysd-msg-075 -->

- **Modular monolith: one deployment, independent modules**

  A modular monolith is still one application, built and deployed as a single unit. Its code, though, is broken into independent modules, one for each feature. Reducing each module's dependencies lets a module be enhanced or changed without affecting the others. Done right, this reduces the complexity of maintaining a monolith as the system grows, which pays off in the long term.

  <!-- sysd-msg-077 -->

- **Strangler fig pattern: replacing old code section by section**

  The strangler fig pattern wraps old code with the intent of redirecting it to newer code, or of logging uses of the old code. In a rewrite, the code is divided into many small sections. Each is wrapped, then swapped out for new code before the next section is tackled. This is less risky and more incremental than swapping out the entire piece of software at once, and it can migrate a monolithic application to a microservices architecture. Logging shows how often old code runs in production, which decides whether to delete it or rewrite it.

  <!-- sysd-msg-142 -->

- **Incremental migration to microservices: code first, data later**

  Microservices are considered a viable way to modernize an existing monolith, and modernization of legacy applications is done incrementally. The iterative approach migrates application code first, with the new microservices temporarily relying on the existing monolithic database. As the system becomes better understood, the data is decoupled and restructured so each microservice has its own database. That simplifies migration and reduces data migration errors. The trap is the data-driven migration antipattern: prioritizing data migration during the move from a monolith. Replacing code section by section is the idea behind the Strangler fig pattern: replacing old code section by section.

  <!-- sysd-msg-087 -->

### APIs: REST, GraphQL and gRPC

An API is the doorway through which one piece of software offers a service to another. REST draws its constraints from the architecture of the Web, GraphQL gives clients exactly the data they request and no more, and gRPC lets a program call a procedure on another computer as if it were local. Under all three lies serialization, which turns a data structure into a format that can be stored or sent and rebuilt later. The chapter also covers SOAP and the craft of documenting, versioning and changing an API without breaking the clients that depend on it.

- **API: the contract between two pieces of software**

  You almost never see an API, because it was not built for you. API stands for Application Programming Interface: a set of definitions and protocols for building and integrating application software. It is a software interface through which one piece of software offers a service to other pieces of software. Unlike a user interface, it works under the hood, for machine-to-machine communication. An API is sometimes called a contract: the provider sets out what it must supply, and the consumer what it must send. The calls go by several names, including subroutines, methods, requests and endpoints. A main purpose is to hide internal details and expose only the useful parts, kept consistent even if the inside later changes. Choosing the right API technology, such as REST: the architectural style behind most web APIs, GraphQL: asking for exactly the data you need or gRPC: fast, typed calls between services, is a crucial part of any system.

  <!-- sysd-msg-001 -->

- **REST: the architectural style behind most web APIs**

  REST is the default way to design an API, and the word has wandered a long way from its meaning. It stands for Representational State Transfer, first introduced by Roy Fielding in 2000. It is a software architectural style, created to describe and guide the design of the Web's architecture. Its constraints say how a distributed, Internet-scale hypermedia system should behave. A REST API, also called a RESTful API, conforms to those constraints, which The six constraints that make an API RESTful lists.

  In a REST API the fundamental unit is a resource, and HTTP request methods say what to do with it. GET requests a representation of a resource. POST submits an entity and often changes state. PUT replaces the resource with the payload, PATCH applies a partial change, and DELETE removes it. A users resource shows the pattern. GET on /users lists all users, and POST on /users adds one. GET, PATCH and DELETE on /users/{id} read, update or delete a single user.

  REST emphasizes uniform interfaces, independent deployment of components, scalable interactions and a layered architecture. That layering promotes caching, which reduces the latency users perceive, enforces security and encapsulates legacy systems. The style is simple, flexible, portable, cache-friendly and decoupled, but it can over-fetch data and need multiple round trips. A warning on vocabulary: RESTful properly means following the constraints. The term now mostly means HTTP API design and verb practices, which have little to do with REST as originally formulated.

  <!-- sysd-msg-002 -->

- **Remote procedure call: making a far-away function feel local**

  Calling a function on another computer can look exactly like calling one in your own program. That is a remote procedure call, or RPC. The program causes a procedure to run in a different address space, commonly on another computer. The call is written as if it were a normal local call. The programmer writes essentially the same code either way. Typically it is request-response. The client sends a message with parameters, the server responds, and the client is blocked meanwhile unless it sent an asynchronous request. The illusion has limits. Remote calls are usually orders of magnitude slower and less reliable than local ones, so telling them apart matters. A caller often cannot know whether a failed remote procedure ran, though idempotent procedures are easily handled. Many incompatible technologies implement RPC, including XML-RPC, JSON-RPC and SOAP: XML envelopes for web services. Modern frameworks such as gRPC: fast, typed calls between services add efficient binary Serialization: turning data into bytes and back, HTTP/2 multiplexing, streaming and error handling.

  <!-- sysd-msg-018 -->

- **GraphQL: asking for exactly the data you need**

  A REST endpoint hands you whatever it was built to return. GraphQL lets the client ask for less. It is a query language and server-side runtime for APIs that gives clients exactly the data they request and no more. Through a single endpoint, the client names the exact fields it wants, nested ones included, and the server returns just those. A schema describes what clients can do. A query is a request made of fields and arguments, a mutation modifies server-side data, and a resolver is the handler that generates the response. The advantages are no over-fetching, a strongly defined schema, code generation support and optimized payloads. The costs are that complexity shifts to the server side, caching becomes hard, versioning is ambiguous and the N+1 problem appears. One source puts the complexity on the client side and warns of abusive queries if not safeguarded. GraphQL is not a full graph query language such as SPARQL: it cannot return all of an individual's ancestors in a single query.

  <!-- sysd-msg-004 -->

- **Serialization: turning data into bytes and back**

  Copying a data structure's memory straight onto the wire does not work reliably. Byte ordering, memory layout and each language's own data representation differ across architectures, so the format must not depend on the machine. Serialization translates a data structure or object state into such a format, one that can be stored or transmitted and reconstructed later, possibly on another computer. Rereading the bits creates a semantically identical clone of the original. This is called marshalling, and the reverse is deserialization or unmarshalling. Systems use it to send messages over networks, store data in databases and on disk, and make remote procedure calls. It has costs. The encoding is serial, so extracting one part means reconstructing the whole object. Some language serializers are also unsafe with untrusted input. Python's pickle is not secure against erroneous or malicious data, and PHP's unserialize() is often dangerous on completely untrusted data.

  <!-- sysd-msg-125 -->

- **The six constraints that make an API RESTful**

  REST comes down to six guiding constraints, and one of them is optional. They are uniform interface, client-server, stateless, cacheable, layered system and, optionally, code on demand. A system that applies them can be called RESTful.

  Client-server separates clients from servers by a well-defined interface, with the interaction managed through HTTP. The uniform interface constraint gives one uniform way of interacting with a given server. Stateless means no client context is stored on the server between requests, so a client at rest consumes no server storage. Cacheable means every response states whether it can be cached and for how long the client may keep it. A layered system is built from several layers. A client cannot ordinarily tell whether it is connected directly to the end server or to an intermediary. Code on demand is the optional one. Servers can temporarily extend or customize a client by sending executable logic that runs in a standard Virtual machine: a whole computer made of software.

  The payoff is a set of desirable properties: performance, scalability, simplicity, modifiability, visibility, portability and reliability. Fielding also named practices that break the rules. Embedding session information in URIs violates REST because it can hurt shared caching and server scalability. HTTP cookies violate it too, because they can fall out of sync with the browser's application state. The sources differ on one point: one says an API must conform to all the constraints, code on demand included, to be RESTful.

  <!-- sysd-msg-003 -->

  *Figure: Six constraints define REST; only code on demand is optional.*

  | Constraint | What it means |
  |---|---|
  | Uniform interface | One uniform way to interact with a given server |
  | Client-server | Clients and servers separated by a well-defined interface |
  | Stateless | No client context kept on the server between requests |
  | Cacheable | Each response says whether and how long it can be cached |
  | Layered system | A client cannot tell the end server from an intermediary |
  | Code on demand | Optional: servers extend a client with executable logic |

- **The uniform interface: one way to talk to every resource**

  In a fully RESTful system a client needs to know only one address. The uniform interface is fundamental to any RESTful system. It gives every part one uniform way to interact, which simplifies and decouples the architecture so each part can evolve independently. It has four pieces. Resources are identified by URIs. A resource is conceptually separate from the representation returned, which could be HTML, XML or JSON rather than the server's internal form. A client holding a representation, with its metadata, has enough information to modify or delete the resource's state. Each message is self-descriptive, carrying enough information to say how to process it, such as a media type that names which parser to invoke. The fourth piece is HATEOAS: letting the server say what you can do next: after the initial URI, the client follows server-provided links, with no hard-coded knowledge of the server's structure. Because only the first identifier must be known, identifiers can change without warning, so client and server must be loosely coupled.

  <!-- sysd-msg-017 -->

- **HATEOAS: letting the server say what you can do next**

  An overdrawn account offers one link: deposit. That small detail is HATEOAS at work. Hypermedia as the engine of application state is a REST constraint. Under it, a client discovers what it can do next from the hypermedia links the server returns. In the account example, a response offers links to deposit, withdraw, transfer or close. Once the account is overdrawn, only the deposit link remains, so the available actions vary with the resource's state. The client enters through one entry point URL, and every later request is discovered inside a response. It needs little prior knowledge of the server beyond a generic understanding of hypermedia. HTML is itself hypermedia, and formats such as HAL, JSON-LD, Siren and Collection+JSON add links to JSON or XML. The constraint decouples client and server and lets server functionality evolve independently. Fielding says the strictness of REST aims at software design on the scale of decades, and that many constraints oppose short-term efficiency.

  <!-- sysd-msg-123 -->

- **Serialization formats from compact binary to readable text**

  Serialization formats run along a line from compact binary to human-readable text. At the compact end is Sun's External Data Representation, XDR, published in 1987: an open binary format standardized as RFC 4506. XML went the other way. It gave a human-readable text encoding, useful for objects that people read or that other systems consume regardless of language. It lost the compact byte stream, which mattered less once storage and transmission capacity grew. JSON is a lightweight plain-text alternative to XML. It is commonly used for client-server communication in web applications, is independent of JavaScript and is standardized as RFC 8259. YAML is a strict superset of JSON that adds data type tags, cyclic data structures, indentation-sensitive syntax and several forms of scalar quoting. Large scientific datasets have binary standards of their own: HDF, netCDF and GRIB. Avro, from Hadoop, serves as a format for persistent data and as a wire format, with binary and JSON encodings. Unlike Protocol buffers: schemas that skip the field names, it needs no code generation when a schema changes.

  <!-- sysd-msg-126 -->

- **Protocol buffers: schemas that skip the field names**

  Protocol buffers save space by never sending a field's name. Protocol Buffers is an open-source, cross-platform data format and interface definition language for serializing structured data in a compact, forward- and backward-compatible way. It was designed to be smaller and faster than XML or JSON. Schemas and services are described in a .proto file and compiled with protoc into native language bindings. A sender or recipient invokes that generated code to produce or parse the data. A schema identifies each field by an integer, and the data carries only those numbers, which saves bandwidth and storage. The compact binary wire format is not self-describing. The text format is self-describing but loses compatibility, so it suits only human editing and debugging. gRPC: fast, typed calls between services uses protocol buffers as its interface definition language and to encode data. The format suits small chunks of data, not exceeding a few megabytes, so it is not streamable, and it has no built-in compression.

  <!-- sysd-msg-006 -->

- **gRPC: fast, typed calls between services**

  gRPC is said to be 5X faster than JSON, and its design explains why. It is a high-performance, open-source Remote Procedure Call framework that can run in any environment. It defines a service and the methods that can be called remotely, with their parameters and return types, using protocol buffers as the interface definition language. The client encodes a call in binary and sends it over HTTP/2. The server decodes it, invokes the application and returns an encoded result. Binary encoding and network optimizations are behind the speed. Around that core sit bidirectional streaming and flow control, cancellation and timeouts. Load balancing, tracing and health checking are pluggable. gRPC suits efficient communication between microservices, low latency and high throughput, and polyglot environments. Its disadvantages are limited browser support, a steeper learning curve, payloads that are not human readable, and being relatively new compared with REST and GraphQL. Because gRPC relies on HTTP trailers, a browser cannot be a gRPC client without a proxy.

  <!-- sysd-msg-005 -->

- **SOAP: XML envelopes for web services**

  In financial messaging, SOAP produced messages 2-4 times larger than FIX and CDR. That weight explains much of its story. SOAP is an XML-based messaging protocol specification for exchanging structured information in web services, usually carried over HTTP. A message is an ordinary XML document with a required Envelope and Body, an optional Header, and an optional Fault element that reports processing errors. It travels from its originator through intermediary nodes, which process the header blocks aimed at them, to the ultimate receiver. HTTP won as transport because it works well with firewalls, which normally filter distributed protocols such as GIOP/IIOP or DCOM. XML's lengthy syntax eases error detection and avoids byte-order problems but slows processing. And because SOAP is protocol-agnostic, it cannot use REST's uniform interface or caching and must reimplement them. Verbosity, slow XML parsing and no standard interaction model led services to use HTTP more directly, as REST does.

  <!-- sysd-msg-122 -->

- **API documentation: telling clients what they need to know**

  A parameter cannot be null. A function is not thread safe. Details like these are what API documentation records. It describes what services an API offers and how to use them, and it is crucial for developing and maintaining the applications that use the API. It may include classes and methods, usage scenarios, code snippets, design rationales and contracts, but it usually omits implementation details. The catch is that it tends to be comprehensive. Writers find it hard to keep updated, and users find it hard to read carefully, which can yield bugs.

  <!-- sysd-msg-014 -->

- **API release policies: private, partner and public**

  Not every API is meant for the whole world. A company can release one in three ways. A private API is for internal company use only. A partner API is open only to specific business partners, which lets the company exercise quality control by curating which apps have access. A public API is available for use by the public. Public does not always mean open to everybody, though: access is granted either by API tokens or by customer status validations.

  <!-- sysd-msg-012 -->

- **Web API: an API reached over HTTP**

  A shipping company's API can be added to an eCommerce site. The site can then order shipping and show current rates, without the developer typing in the shipper's rate table. That is a web API at work. It is typically a set of specifications, such as HTTP request messages. Along with them comes a definition of the structure of the response messages, usually in XML or JSON. The term API is often used to mean web APIs, which allow communication between computers joined by the internet. The trend has run from SOAP-based web services and service-oriented architecture towards REST-style web resources and resource-oriented architecture.

  <!-- sysd-msg-011 -->

- **API versioning and deprecation: changing without breaking clients**

  Adding a new parameter to a function call can break compatibility with the clients that make it. Once an API is public, its interface stability matters, so parts subject to change should be documented as unstable. A public API can also declare parts deprecated, making them candidates for removal or backward-incompatible change. Designing the version number in advance simplifies upgrades. GraphQL mostly avoids the problem, because it returns only the data explicitly requested. New types or fields can be added without a breaking change, and @deprecated marks parts being retired. Common practice is a versionless API, though Singh lists its versioning as ambiguous.

  <!-- sysd-msg-013 -->

- **API pagination: six ways to return a big list in pieces**

  There are six common ways to hand back a large dataset in pieces, and they trade simplicity against speed. Offset-based pagination passes an offset and a limit, as in GET /orders?offset=0&limit=3. It is simple but inefficient for large offsets, because rows must be scanned and skipped. Page-based pagination gives a page number and a page size, as in GET /items?page=2&size=3, and has the same problem for large page numbers. Cursor-based pagination marks a position with a cursor, typically an encoded string that points to a specific record. Skipped records are not scanned, so it is efficient for large datasets, if slightly more complex. Keyset-based pagination filters by a key, as in GET /items?after_id=102&limit=3, and needs a unique, indexed key. Time-based pagination uses a timestamp or date range and misses no records when new ones are added, but needs a reliable timestamp. Hybrid pagination combines techniques, such as cursor with time-based, for the best performance and flexibility, at the price of careful design.

  <!-- sysd-msg-009 -->

  *Figure: Each pagination method trades one strength against one catch.*

  | Method | Strength | Catch |
  |---|---|---|
  | Offset-based | Simple | Inefficient for large offsets |
  | Page-based | Easy to use | Same problem for large page numbers |
  | Cursor-based | Efficient for large datasets | Slightly more complex |
  | Keyset-based | Efficient | Needs a unique, indexed key |
  | Time-based | Misses no new records | Needs a reliable timestamp |
  | Hybrid | Best performance and flexibility | Needs careful design |

- **API design best practices beyond the URL path**

  API design is more than choosing URL paths. It means choosing resource names, identifiers and path patterns, plus HTTP header fields and rate-limiting rules within the API gateway. For a RESTful API the path structure can follow the domain model. Semantic paths make the API easier to understand, so users find the right call in the documentation. Defining only a few basic HTTP methods simplifies the design; PATCH, for example, can often be a problem for teams. Designing for idempotence in advance makes an API more robust: GET is idempotent, but POST has to be designed properly to be idempotent. Limiting the status codes in use to a defined few simplifies application development, and designing the version number in advance simplifies upgrades. For batch operations, use batch or bulk as a keyword and put it at the end of the path. A set of query rules such as pagination, sorting and filtering makes an API more flexible.

  <!-- sysd-msg-008 -->

- **RPC call sequence: from caller to server and back**

  A remote call looks like a local one, but a lot happens in between. The caller makes a local procedure call, with parameters pushed on the stack as usual. The client stub packs the parameters into a message (marshalling) and makes a system call to send it. It is the code that stands in for the remote procedure on the caller's side. The client's operating system sends the message to the server machine, whose operating system passes the incoming packets to the server stub. The server stub unpacks the parameters (unmarshalling) and calls the server procedure. The reply traces the same steps in reverse.

  <!-- sysd-msg-019 -->

  *Figure: A remote call passes through two stubs and two operating systems, and the reply comes back the same way.*

  | Step | Who | What happens |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 | Caller | Makes a local call, parameters on the stack |
  | 2 | Client stub | Packs the parameters (marshalling), makes a system call |
  | 3 | Client OS | Sends the message to the server machine |
  | 4 | Server OS | Passes the incoming packets to the server stub |
  | 5 | Server stub | Unpacks the parameters, calls the server procedure |
  | 6 | Reply | Retraces the same steps in reverse |

- **Choosing between REST, GraphQL and gRPC**

  Ask which of REST, GraphQL and gRPC is best, and the sources answer that none is. There is no silver bullet, and the right choice depends on the application's requirements and the team. The comparison runs on eight criteria: tight coupling, chattiness, performance, integration complexity, caching, built-in tooling and code generation, discoverability, and ease of versioning. Chattiness means how many separate API calls it takes to get the information needed.

  REST rates low on coupling, high on chattiness and good on performance. It rates medium on complexity, great on caching, bad on code generation, good on discoverability and easy on versioning. GraphQL rates medium on coupling, low on chattiness and good on performance. It rates high on complexity, custom on caching and good on code generation. The ratings for gRPC are high on coupling, medium on chattiness and great on performance. Its complexity is low, its caching custom, its code generation great, its discoverability bad and its versioning hard.

  In practice, REST suits simple, uniform interfaces between separate services and straightforward caching, though assembling related data from separate endpoints may take multiple round trips. GraphQL is good at aggregating data from several sources for rapidly evolving frontends. It can allow abusive queries if not safeguarded, and its caching is more complicated than REST's. The advice is to focus on the domain and the requirements, not the technology.

  <!-- sysd-msg-007 -->

  *Figure: The three technologies rated on the same eight criteria.*

  | Criterion | REST | GraphQL | gRPC |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Coupling | Low | Medium | High |
  | Chattiness | High | Low | Medium |
  | Performance | Good | Good | Great |
  | Complexity | Medium | High | Low |
  | Caching | Great | Custom | Custom |
  | Code generation | Bad | Good | Great |
  | Discoverability | Good | not rated | Bad |
  | Versioning | Easy | not rated | Hard |

- **GraphQL schema and type system**

  A GraphQL service begins as a list of types. Types with fields make up the schema definition, and functions called resolvers retrieve and map the data for each field. The type system describes what data can be queried, so clients can send queries that return predictable results. The root type, Query by default, holds all queryable fields. Fields are nullable by default, a trailing exclamation mark makes a field required, and square brackets make it a list. A query is validated against the schema before the server executes it, and the result mirrors the shape of the query, typically as JSON.

  <!-- sysd-msg-015 -->

- **GraphQL operations: queries, mutations and subscriptions**

  GraphQL does three things with data: it reads it, changes it and watches it. A query defines the exact shape of the data the client needs, and the data comes back in the same shape. A mutation creates, updates or deletes data. It generally takes variables that pass data from client to server, and it defines the shape of the data returned afterwards. A subscription sends live updates from server to client. The client defines the shape of the data it needs, and when a mutation updates the field, data goes to all subscribed clients. Real-time updates are commonly implemented using WebSocket: one persistent channel, open both ways.

  <!-- sysd-msg-016 -->

- **OpenAPI Specification: writing the contract first**

  What if the contract existed before the code? In contract-first development the API contract is agreed before any code is written. Downstream developers can then mock the server and start testing right away, a shift-left testing practice. The OpenAPI Specification is a machine-readable interface definition language for describing, producing, consuming and visualizing web services. An OpenAPI Description is a formal description of an API that tools can use to generate code, documentation, test cases and more. Generated documentation keeps documentation, client libraries and source code in sync. The specification is language-agnostic and declarative, so clients can consume a service without knowing its implementation.

  <!-- sysd-msg-124 -->

- **API performance optimization: five cheap wins**

  Five habits make an API respond faster. Pagination streams large result sets back in pieces, which improves responsiveness. Asynchronous logging sends logs to a lock-free buffer and returns at once instead of touching the disk on every call. The logs are flushed to disk periodically, which significantly reduces I/O overhead. Data caching stores frequently accessed data, so callers check the cache before querying the database, and in-memory stores such as Redis are quicker. Compressing requests and responses, for example with gzip, shortens transmission time. A connection pool reuses open database connections, avoiding the cost of opening and closing one each time.

  <!-- sysd-msg-010 -->

### Real-time communication

A client that wants fresh information has several options. Polling means repeatedly checking a service for its status, and long polling has the server hold the request open until new information is available or a timeout is reached. Push technology turns the exchange around, so the server rather than the client starts it, as in push notifications and in web push, which delivers real-time events such as incoming calls or messages over HTTP/2. Or the browser and server can cooperate over WebSocket, a bidirectional channel over a single TCP connection that begins with an HTTP Upgrade request and a 101 response, then exchanges frames and closes with its own handshake. A notification system adds the machinery to validate, schedule and deliver messages through channels such as in-app messages, email, SMS and social media pushes.

- **Polling: asking again and again whether anything is new**

  Polling is like constantly asking whether there is anything new, even when there may be no update. It means repeatedly checking an external device or service for its status, a synchronous activity driven by the client, to retrieve updated information. That makes it resource-intensive and inefficient. The client gets updates only when it asks, so it can miss real-time information, though developers gain more control over when and how data is fetched. With short polling the browser keeps retrying until it gets the latest data. It is a solid option when an infrastructure limitation prevents the use of Webhooks: letting the other service call you. Polling fails to scale when there are too many devices to check, because the time needed to poll them can exceed the time available to service them. The alternative is interrupts, signals from devices that say they need attention. In many situations they cut processor spinning and bandwidth use.

  <!-- sysd-msg-101 -->

- **Push technology: the server speaks first**

  In push technology, also called server push, the server rather than the client starts the exchange. That differs from the pull method, where the client initiates it. Clients usually say which information they want through the publish-subscribe model. A client subscribes to channels on a server, and the server pushes new content to subscribed clients automatically. Chat and synchronous conferencing are push services, because messages are pushed to the user as soon as the messaging service receives them. Push-enabled web applications include software updates, stock tickers, webchat, auctions, online betting and gaming, and sport results. Email is only partly push. SMTP is a push protocol. But the last step, from mail server to desktop, usually uses a pull protocol such as POP3 or IMAP, which clients poll frequently. IMAP's IDLE command lets the server tell the client when new messages arrive. Push is not always available. When restrictive security policies block incoming HTTP requests, push is sometimes simulated by polling, in which the client periodically checks the server for new information.

  <!-- sysd-msg-098 -->

- **Long polling: holding the request open until there is news**

  A server that is asked whether anything is new can decline to answer until there is. That is long polling. If the server has nothing new when the poll arrives, it holds the request open instead of sending an empty response. It replies only when information is available or a timeout threshold is reached. The reply completes the open request, and the client immediately, or after a defined interval, issues another to re-establish a pending connection. Unlike normal polling, this removes the response latency between information becoming available and the client's next request. It is not true push, though. It emulates server push where real push is not possible, such as sites whose security policies reject incoming HTTP requests. It is easy to implement, nearly universally supported and good for small-scale projects. But it is usually not scalable, because every response needs a new connection, which is intensive on the server. Reliable message ordering can also be an issue across multiple requests.

  <!-- sysd-msg-100 -->

- **Push notification: a message from the server to your screen**

  A push notification can show a short message, set a badge on the app icon, light the notification LED or play an alert sound. It is a message pushed from a back-end server or application to a user interface such as a mobile or desktop application. Typical content is chat messages, vendor special offers, event reminders and changes to subscribed topics such as the weather. Notifications are either local or remote. For a local one, the application schedules the notification with the device's OS. For a remote one, a server sends it. The client application registers on the server with a unique key, such as a UUID or Apple Device Token. The server then sends the message against that key over a protocol such as HTTP or XMPP: federated chat protocol with presence. Real-time push notifications can raise privacy issues, since they can be used to link social network pseudonyms to the real identities of smartphone owners.

  <!-- sysd-msg-105 -->

- **Web push: one connection for every event**

  Radio use is a major drain on mobile devices, and separate persistent connections, each with its keep-alive traffic, waste it. Web push consolidates all events into one session through a single service that distributes them as they arrive. It is the set of web standards that deliver real-time events such as incoming calls or messages to a user, based on a simple protocol over HTTP/2. The model has three actors: a user agent, a push service and an application server. A subscription is two resources. A private subscription resource lets the user agent receive messages and delete the subscription. A public push resource is shared with the application server to send messages. The user agent POSTs to the push service to subscribe and gets 201 Created. The application server POSTs the message body to the push resource. For at-least-once delivery, the user agent must acknowledge each message with an HTTP DELETE. Chrome, Firefox and Edge implement the W3C Push API fully, and Safari partly, as of February 2023.

  <!-- sysd-msg-107 -->

- **Techniques for real-time updates over HTTP**

  An HTTP server cannot automatically initiate a connection to a browser, so the browser has to start things. Web applications were built around a client-server model in which the client always starts a transaction. That left the server no way to push data without first receiving a request. Two families of technique work around it. In the first, the browser does the heavy lifting by polling. With short polling the browser keeps retrying until it gets the latest data. With long polling the server does not return a result until new data has arrived. In the second, the browser and server cooperate through WebSocket: one persistent channel, open both ways or Server-sent events: a one-way stream over plain HTTP. Once the connection is established, the server can send the latest data straight to the browser. The two differ in direction. SSE is uni-directional, so the browser cannot send a new request to the server, while its rival is full-duplex, so the browser can keep sending new requests.

  <!-- sysd-msg-099 -->

  *Figure: Two families give four techniques: the browser polls, or browser and server cooperate.*

  | Technique | Who does the work | How updates arrive |
  |---|---|---|
  | Short polling | Browser | Keeps retrying until it gets the latest data |
  | Long polling | Browser | Server holds its result until new data arrives |
  | WebSocket | Browser and server | Full-duplex: the browser can keep sending requests |
  | Server-sent events | Browser and server | One-way: the browser cannot send new requests |

- **WebSocket: one persistent channel, open both ways**

  Before WebSocket, a two-way web app had to fake it. It polled over several HTTP connections and sent upstream messages as separate calls. That meant multiple TCP connections per client, an HTTP header on every message and client-side tracking of replies. WebSocket is a communications protocol that gives a bidirectional channel over a single TCP connection. The channel is persistent, so client and server can each send data at any time, independently of the other.

  That gives full-duplex interaction with lower overhead than half-duplex alternatives such as HTTP polling, because the server can send content without being asked first. RFC 6455 describes an independent TCP-based protocol: a thin layer that adds an origin-based security model, naming, framing and a closing handshake. HTTP servers see only its handshake, as an Upgrade request. TCP alone deals with streams of bytes with no inherent notion of a message. WebSocket enables streams of messages on top of it.

  It suits games, stock tickers, multiuser applications with simultaneous editing, and user interfaces that expose server-side services in real time. Its advantages are full-duplex asynchronous messaging, a better origin-based security model, and light weight for both client and server. Its limits are that terminated connections are not automatically recovered and older browsers lack support, though modern major browsers support the standardized protocol.

  <!-- sysd-msg-108 -->

- **WebSocket opening handshake: an HTTP request that switches protocols**

  A WebSocket begins life as an ordinary HTTP request. The client sends a GET Upgrade request, with HTTP version at least 1.1, so one port can serve both HTTP clients and WebSocket clients. The request carries Host, Upgrade: websocket, Connection: Upgrade, a Sec-WebSocket-Key of 16 random bytes base64-encoded, Sec-WebSocket-Version 13, and an Origin header from browser clients.

  The server must prove it received the handshake, so that it does not accept connections that are not WebSocket connections, such as crafted XMLHttpRequest or form submissions. To prove it, the server appends a fixed GUID to the Sec-WebSocket-Key value, takes the SHA-1 hash, base64-encodes it and returns it in Sec-WebSocket-Accept. Another source says these headers are meant to stop a caching proxy from re-sending a previous WebSocket conversation. It adds that they give no way to check who is connecting, no privacy and no integrity.

  The server then replies 101 (Switching Protocols). Any other status means the handshake has not completed and HTTP semantics still apply. The client sends no frames if the Sec-WebSocket-Accept value is missing or wrong. A server that rejects the handshake must return an HTTP error. Examples are 403 Forbidden for an unwanted origin, 426 Upgrade Required, with its supported versions, for a wrong version, and 404 Not Found for an unavailable service. After the 101 response HTTP is no longer used, and both sides can send data in either direction over a binary frame-based protocol. A WebSocket can also be established over HTTP/2 with the extended CONNECT method of RFC 8441. That carries it in one stream, so other streams keep carrying HTTP traffic. RFC 9220 adapts this for HTTP/3.

  <!-- sysd-msg-109 -->

  *Figure: The server proves it saw the handshake, then both sides leave HTTP behind.*

  | Step | Who | What happens |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 | Client | Sends an HTTP GET Upgrade request with a Sec-WebSocket-Key |
  | 2 | Server | Appends a fixed GUID to the key, takes the SHA-1 hash, base64-encodes it |
  | 3 | Server | Returns it in Sec-WebSocket-Accept with a 101 response |
  | 4 | Client | Sends no frames if the Accept value is missing or wrong |
  | 5 | Both | Switch to the binary frame-based protocol, sending in either direction |

- **WebSocket frames and messages**

  After the opening handshake, either side may send data messages (text or binary) and control messages (Close, Ping, Pong) at any time. The protocol is frame-based rather than stream-based, with minimal framing. A message is one frame if unfragmented and two or more if fragmented. Intermediaries may split or coalesce frames, so endpoints must not depend on frame boundaries. Fragmentation lets a sender start a message of unknown length without buffering it. Fragments must arrive in order and must not interleave with another message's fragments unless an extension allows it. Control frames may be injected between fragments, so a ping is not stuck behind a large message, but they are never fragmented. A frame header holds a FIN bit, set on the last frame of a message, and three reserved bits. It also holds a 4-bit opcode, a mask bit, a payload length and, if the mask bit is 1, a 32-bit masking key. Opcodes are 0 continuation, 1 text, 2 binary, 8 Close, 9 Ping and 10 Pong.

  <!-- sysd-msg-110 -->

  *Figure: Six opcodes name the frame types; Close, Ping and Pong are control frames.*

  | Opcode | Frame type |
  |---|---|
  | 0 | Continuation |
  | 1 | Text |
  | 2 | Binary |
  | 8 | Close (control) |
  | 9 | Ping (control) |
  | 10 | Pong (control) |

- **WebSocket through proxies and load balancers**

  WebSocket is unaware of proxies and firewalls, yet its handshake is HTTP-compatible, so it can pass through HTTP infrastructure. HTTP servers can share ports 80 and 443 with a WebSocket gateway or server. Behind a configured proxy, the client sets up a persistent tunnel with HTTP CONNECT. Some proxies are transparent and work with WebSocket. Others make the connection fail, and unencrypted traffic through a proxy without WebSocket support will likely fail. Encrypted WebSocket Secure connections succeed more often, and connections on port 443 are significantly more likely to succeed than on port 80. Load balancers add their own demands. They must support persistent connections, so a server can keep a WebSocket open with a client. Dedicated hosts for WebSocket connections, separate from the HTTP servers, are probably easier to manage. Interactive messaging traffic can induce unusual loads on some components. Nginx has acted as reverse proxy and load balancer for WebSocket applications since 2013.

  <!-- sysd-msg-115 -->

- **WebSocket closing handshake: ending a connection cleanly**

  A WebSocket ends with a polite exchange. Either peer can start by sending a Close control frame, opcode 8. The other replies with a Close frame if it has not already sent one, and both peers may safely start it at the same time. After sending a Close frame a peer sends no more data frames, and after receiving one it discards further data. Once an endpoint has both sent and received Close, it must close the TCP connection. The server does so immediately, and the client ideally waits for the server to do it.

  It complements the TCP closing handshake, which is not always reliable end to end with intercepting proxies. It also avoids cases where data is lost unnecessarily. Servers may close the connection whenever they want, but clients should not close it arbitrarily. Either way, closure begins with the closing handshake.

  A Close frame may carry a 2-byte status code followed by a UTF-8 reason of at most 123 bytes, which clients must not show to end users. Defined codes include 1000 normal closure, 1001 going away, 1002 protocol error and 1003 unsupported data. Others are 1007 invalid payload data, 1008 policy violated, 1009 message too big and 1011 internal server error. Codes 1005, 1006 and 1015 are reserved and must not be sent in a Close frame. The range 1000 to 2999 belongs to the protocol, 3000 to 3999 to libraries and frameworks registered with IANA, and 4000 to 4999 to private use.

  <!-- sysd-msg-113 -->

  *Figure: Close status codes are split into three ranges by who may define them.* (scale; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Notification system architecture: from business service to your inbox**

  A notification system takes notifications from business services, validates and schedules them, and delivers them through channels such as in-app messages, email, SMS and social media pushes. It covers in-app notifications, email notifications, SMS and OTP notifications, and social media pushes. The path has stages. Business services send notifications to a notification gateway, which can take one at a time or batches of them. The gateway forwards them to a distribution service that validates, formats and schedules them according to settings. Two repositories feed it: a template repository pre-defines message formats, and a channel preference repository pre-defines preferred delivery channels. Notifications then go to routers, normally message queues, and channel services pass them to the internal and external delivery channels. Last, a tracking and analytics service captures delivery metrics, so the operations team can view reports and improve the user experience.

  <!-- sysd-msg-106 -->

  *Figure: A notification travels from a business service through gateway, distribution and routers to a delivery channel; dashed lines show the repositories that pre-define message formats and preferred channels.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Business services] --> B[Notification gateway]
  B --> C[Distribution service]
  C -.-> T[(Template repository)]
  C -.-> P[(Channel preference repository)]
  C --> R[Routers: message queues]
  R --> S[Channel services]
  S --> D[Delivery channels]
  ```

- **Webhooks: letting the other service call you**

  Why keep asking when the other service can simply tell you? Instead of continuously asking a payment processor or a shipping vendor for information, you create an endpoint in your application server and give it as a callback. That endpoint is a webhook. Every time something interesting happens, the external service calls it and provides the information. Data is pushed to the application as soon as it is available, which makes webhooks ideal for real-time updates. Because they use HTTP, they fit into web services without new infrastructure. They need care, though. Network issues can cause missed notifications, so webhooks need proper retry mechanisms. The receiver should authenticate each incoming POST against spoofing and check its timestamp against replay. Options include an HMAC signature in a header, a shared secret, mutual TLS, or a sender IP list that is not sufficient alone. And because a sender lets users set an arbitrary destination URL, OWASP names webhooks a common vector for server-side request forgery. The mitigation is to re-check the resolved IP before each delivery, not only at registration.

  <!-- sysd-msg-102 -->

- **WebSocket API: opening and using a socket from a browser**

  A browser opens a WebSocket with one constructor, new WebSocket(url [, protocols]), which starts the opening handshake. The URL scheme must be ws, wss, http or https, with no fragment. The send(data) call takes a string, Blob, ArrayBuffer or ArrayBufferView, and if the buffer is full the connection is closed and an error event fires. The API raises open, message, close and error events, and the close event reports a code, a reason and whether the closing handshake completed. The readyState is CONNECTING (0), OPEN (1), CLOSING (2) or CLOSED (3).

  <!-- sysd-msg-116 -->

- **HTTP streaming: a response that never ends**

  The simplest way for a server to keep talking is never to finish the response. HTTP server push, also called HTTP streaming, sends unsolicited asynchronous data from a web server to a web browser. The server does not close the connection after serving the response, so an event can go out at once instead of waiting for the client's next request. It can use chunked transfer encoding or the multipart/x-mixed-replace content type from 1995. Browsers treat it as a document that changes with each push. Pushlets send snippets of JavaScript, but the server cannot control browser timeouts, and a timeout forces a page refresh.

  <!-- sysd-msg-104 -->

- **Server-sent events: a one-way stream over plain HTTP**

  With server-sent events, or SSE, the client makes one request and the connection stays open. The server then sends events whenever new data is available. SSE is a server push technology in which a client receives automatic updates over an HTTP connection. The client requests a URL through the JavaScript EventSource API to receive an event stream, whose media type is text/event-stream. The mechanism was first specified in 2004, and the W3C published it as a recommendation on February 3, 2015. SSE is simple to implement for both client and server, supported by most browsers and causes no trouble with firewalls. Its limits are that it is unidirectional, so the client can only receive once its request is sent. The number of open connections is capped, and binary data is not supported. When sending high-frequency data, the server must manage backpressure to avoid saturating clients, with client-side buffering, adaptive limits on the event rate, or event batching. Real-time messaging and live location tracking can use either WebSockets or SSE.

  <!-- sysd-msg-103 -->

- **Presence information: who is free, busy or away**

  The small icon beside a contact that says free for chat, busy, away or do not disturb is presence information. It is a status indicator that conveys the ability and willingness of a potential communication partner to communicate. A client publishes a presence state to a presence service, which stores it as the user's availability record, the presentity, and distributes it to interested users, called watchers. Presence from several devices can be aggregated and inferred from observation, such as marking a user Away when the keyboard is idle. Because presence is highly sensitive, a presentity may limit what each watcher sees, for example by blocking selected watchers.

  <!-- sysd-msg-149 -->

- **XMPP: federated chat protocol with presence**

  Anyone can run an XMPP server, and there is no central master. XMPP is an open, XML-based communication protocol for real-time chat, presence information and contact list maintenance, with near-real-time exchange of structured data. The network is federated like email, and users on any server interoperate through a Jabber ID. It looks like an email address, username@domain, and an optional /resource suffix names one of the user's clients. A client sends a message to its own server, which delivers it instantly if the recipient is online and otherwise holds it. For a user on another server, it connects to that server. Clients connect over a TLS-encrypted TCP stream on port 5222, and servers talk to each other on port 5269. The native transport is long-lived TCP, with BOSH over HTTP for web clients and firewalled users, and XMPP can also use WebSockets. Extensions called XEPs add features such as multi-user chat and OMEMO encryption, which the server operator cannot decrypt. XML is text, so XMPP has higher network overhead than binary protocols, and large files are best sent out-of-band.

  <!-- sysd-msg-148 -->

- **Push message delivery controls: TTL, urgency and topic**

  A web push message can be told how long to live, how urgent it is and which older message it replaces. The TTL header, in seconds, says how long the push service keeps the message for an intermittently connected device. After that the service must not deliver it. With a zero TTL the message goes out at once if the user agent is available and otherwise expires. The Urgency header, from very-low to high, helps battery-powered devices stay dormant. A Topic header of up to 32 characters makes a message replace any outstanding one with the same topic, so an offline device receives no outdated messages.

  <!-- sysd-msg-150 -->

- **Reconnecting a WebSocket with backoff**

  After an abnormal closure, a client that reconnects at once can do harm. The closure may be transient, so reconnecting can work. If it is nontransient, clients that all reconnect immediately and persistently amount to a denial-of-service attack that can keep the service from recovering. So clients should back off. The first attempt should be delayed by a random time, and a value chosen randomly between 0 and 5 seconds is a reasonable initial delay. If it fails, later attempts should wait increasingly longer, as in Truncated exponential backoff: putting a ceiling on the wait. Terminated WebSocket connections are not automatically recovered, so the client has to do this itself.

  <!-- sysd-msg-119 -->

- **WebSocket URIs: ws and wss**

  WebSocket defines two URI schemes: ws for unencrypted connections and wss for connections protected by TLS. A wss URI is called secure, and its traffic gets TLS's usual confidentiality, integrity and checking of who the endpoint is. The port is optional, with a default of 80 for ws and 443 for wss. The handshake requests a resource name, the path plus any query, or "/" when the path is empty. That lets one host and port serve several services. Fragment identifiers are meaningless in WebSocket URIs and must not be used.

  <!-- sysd-msg-121 -->

- **WebSocket security: origin checks, TLS and validation**

  WebSocket requests are not restricted by the same-origin policy that limits regular cross-domain HTTP requests. So security rests on the browser's Origin header, TLS and whatever client check the server chooses. The Origin header tells the server which script origin made the request. A server meant only for certain sites should verify the origin and answer an unacceptable one with HTTP 403 Forbidden. Without that check, cross-site WebSocket hijacking, similar to Cross-site request forgery: abusing a site's trust in your browser, is possible when the connection is authenticated with cookies or HTTP credentials. The check stops trusted browsers running malicious JavaScript from faking a handshake, but not non-browser clients, which can send any Origin. The protocol prescribes no way to check a client. The options, such as cookies or tokens, are the subject of Authentication: proving who you are, and tokens are better when sensitive data is sent. Confidentiality and integrity come from TLS, through wss URIs. Both sides must validate incoming data, and implementations should cap frame and message sizes, since one huge frame or a long stream of small fragments can exhaust memory.

  <!-- sysd-msg-114 -->

- **WebSocket extensions: optional features negotiated up front**

  A WebSocket can gain abilities such as compression, but only if both sides agree during the opening handshake. The base specification defines no extension. The client offers extensions in Sec-WebSocket-Extensions, in order of preference. The server accepts some or all by listing them in its response, and never lists one the client did not request. Order matters: operations are applied in the server's order, so "foo, bar" makes bar(foo(data)). Extensions can use the three reserved RSV bits and the extension data field. One example, permessage-deflate, compresses data messages with DEFLATE and sets RSV1 on the first frame.

  <!-- sysd-msg-118 -->

- **WebSocket masking: stopping scripts from forging HTTP on the wire**

  In an experiment, attackers poisoned caching proxies by sending data on an upgraded connection that looked like an HTTP GET. Masking is the defense. A client XORs every frame it sends to the server with a random 32-bit key, so a script cannot control how its data looks on the wire. It does so whether or not TLS is used, with a fresh key for every frame. Each payload byte is XORed with the key byte at index i modulo 4, so the same algorithm masks and unmasks. A server must not mask its frames, and it must close the connection on receiving an unmasked one.

  <!-- sysd-msg-111 -->

- **WebSocket ping and pong: checking the other end is alive**

  Ping and Pong are WebSocket control frames used as keepalive and heartbeat, to check that the other endpoint is still responsive. Either side may send a Ping at any time while the connection is open. It can serve as a keepalive, a latency measurement or a check on the remote endpoint. An endpoint that receives a Ping must answer with a Pong as soon as practical, carrying the same application data, unless it already received a Close frame. A Pong may also be sent unsolicited as a one-way heartbeat. No response is expected, and a Pong with no prior Ping is ignored.

  <!-- sysd-msg-112 -->

- **WebSocket subprotocols: agreeing what the messages mean**

  WebSocket carries messages, and a subprotocol says what they mean. It is an application-level protocol layered over WebSocket messages, which client and server agree on in the opening handshake. The client lists the subprotocols it accepts in Sec-WebSocket-Protocol. The server selects one of those values and echoes it, and must not reply with a value the client did not offer. Names should be registered and should contain the ASCII domain name of the originator to avoid collisions, such as "chat.example.com". A backward-incompatible change is versioned by renaming the subprotocol, for example to "v2.bookings.example.net", which clients treat as completely separate.
