  | Primary-secondary | The secondary can serve reads to balance load | Replication latency can make its reads inconsistent |
  | Primary-primary | Both nodes handle reads and writes and replicate to each other | The same product updated on both can end up in an unpredictable state |

- **Observability: asking questions you did not plan for**

  Observability is the ability to ask arbitrary questions about a system without knowing ahead of time what to ask. Its three pillars are logging, tracing and metrics. Logging records discrete events, such as an incoming request or a visit to a database, and has the highest volume of the three. Teams define a standardized logging format so keywords can be searched across massive logs. Tracing is request-scoped. It follows one user request through the API gateway, load balancer, services and database, which helps identify bottlenecks. Metrics are aggregatable measurements such as service QPS, API responsiveness and latency, with raw data recorded in time-series databases like InfluxDB. Prometheus pulls the metrics, Grafana displays them, and the alert manager sends email, SMS or Slack notifications. OpenTelemetry unifies the three pillars in a single framework. Monitoring watches predefined sets of telemetry, whereas observability explores properties and patterns that were not defined in advance. Metrics and logs must be instrumented up front, so an unforeseen issue can require shipping new code.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-098 -->

- **Site reliability engineering: software engineering applied to operations**

  Site reliability engineering, or SRE, is a discipline that applies software engineering to IT infrastructure and operations. It aims to monitor and improve the availability and performance of deployed software systems. SREs are responsible for a combination of availability, latency, performance, efficiency, change management, monitoring, emergency response and capacity planning. The discipline focuses on automation, system design and improved resilience, typically with an Infrastructure as code: servers described in files, not set up by hand methodology. It is considered a specific implementation of DevOps that concentrates on building reliable systems, while DevOps covers a broader scope of operations. Common practices include automating repetitive tasks and defining reliability goals to prevent endless effort. Toil management is a principle: toil is manual, repetitive, automatable operational work. Reliability goals are defined and measured with SLIs, SLOs and error budgets. Other principles are defining, testing and running a process for managing incidents, and change and release management including CI/CD.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-104 -->

- **The 3-2-1 backup rule**

  Keep at least 3 copies of the data, on 2 different types of storage media, with one copy offsite in a remote location. That is the 3-2-1 rule. Different media avoid losses with similar causes: optical discs may survive being underwater while LTO tapes may not, and SSDs cannot suffer head crashes. An offsite copy, which can be cloud storage, protects against fire and natural disasters. No storage is perfect, so many experts also keep a second local physical copy. Ransomware can overwrite a backup drive that stays plugged in, so at least one backup medium should be disconnected when not in use.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-191 -->

- **Tiered backups: fast restores nearby, long memory far away**

  Backups do not matter, recovery does. The scenarios you must recover from should dictate the backup method, how often you take restore points, where you store backups and how long you keep them. The less recent data you can lose, the more serious an incremental strategy should be. The faster users must be rescued, the more local backups should be. A tiered strategy follows from both: frequent, quickly restored backups near the live datastores, and fewer, longer-retained backups on more remote, more independent storage. The first tier holds many frequent backups, retained hours to single-digit days and restored in minutes. It protects against most software bugs and developer error. The second tier holds fewer backups for single-digit or low double-digit days on local distributed filesystems, restoring in hours. Later tiers use nearline tape libraries and offsite media against site-level issues, and they are taken less often but retained longer. Reaching back further helps with low-grade corruption bugs found months later, but old backups may be unusable after code and schema changes. Google drew the line between 30 and 90 days.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-209 -->

  *Figure: Read down the tiers: restores get slower while retention gets longer and the storage more remote.*

  | Tier | Where backups live | Kept for | Restored in |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | First | Near the live data | Hours to single-digit days | Minutes |
  | Second | Local distributed filesystems | Single-digit or low double-digit days | Hours |
  | Later | Nearline tape libraries and offsite media | Taken less often, kept longer |  |

- **Backing up live data: freeze it, then copy**

  Files being actively updated are hard to back up consistently. One way is to quiesce them, take a snapshot, resume live operations and back up the snapshot. A snapshot is an instantaneous filesystem function that presents a copy as if frozen at one point in time, often through a copy-on-write mechanism. Snapshotting a file while it changes yields a corrupted file, as does doing so across interrelated files such as a database. A database hot backup combines a snapshot of the data files with a snapshotted log of changes made during the backup. A restore applies the log to bring the copy up to when the backup ended.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-192 -->

- **Disaster recovery strategies: choosing the measures**

  The right recovery measure depends on the cost of downtime compared with the cost of implementing it. A disaster recovery strategy is the set of measures chosen to restore systems and data after a disaster. It derives from the business continuity plan, and a cost-benefit analysis picks the measures. Common strategies are backups to tape sent off-site, backups to disk on-site and copied off-site, and replication off-site. Cloud options include replicating metadata to a private cloud, hybrid cloud replication for instant fail-over, and disaster recovery as a service from a third-party vendor. Precautions include local mirrors, surge protectors, backup generators and fire prevention systems.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-094 -->

- **Disaster recovery practices: controls, tests and permissions**

  Every $1 spent on hazard mitigation, such as a disaster recovery plan, saves society $4 in response and recovery costs. Disaster recovery practices are the controls, tests and procedures that keep a plan working when a disaster happens. Controls are preventive, detective or corrective, and the plan records them. DR tests exercise them regularly, verify the plan and expose weaknesses or gaps. A cloud recovery strategy should be flexible enough for partial failures, such as recovering specific files, as well as full environment failures. Define who may execute the plan, and separate those permissions from access to backup data to limit unauthorized actions.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-096 -->

- **Testing data recovery before you need it**

  Components that are not continually exercised fail when you need them most. Recovery dependencies, mostly backups, can be latently broken without anyone knowing until recovery is attempted. So recovery must be tested continuously. Finding a broken restore process before you need it lets you take another backup, provision more resources or change the SLO. You only know you can recover your recent state if you actually do so. Manual staged tests become drudgery, so automate them and run them as part of normal operations. Alert when a recovery process stops sending a heartbeat of success. Only a full end-to-end test is proof enough. Check that backups are valid and not empty, and that resources suffice for setup, restore and post-processing. Check that recovery finishes in reasonable time and that progress is observable. Make sure no critical dependency lies outside your control.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-214 -->

- **Backups versus archives: built to be restored**

  People do not want backups, they want restores. The most important difference between backups and archives is that backups can be loaded back into an application while archives cannot. A backup effort should therefore focus on data recovery. Archives safekeep data for long periods to meet auditing, discovery and compliance needs. They need not recover within service uptime limits, and a week to retrieve logs for a month-long audit may be acceptable. Real backups must be recovered quickly, or users lose useful access from the onset of the problem until recovery completes. Teams define SLOs for data availability across failure modes and practice demonstrating they can meet them.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-208 -->

- **Data loss failure modes: 24 types to plan for**

  Data loss comes in 24 distinct types, and a restore plan must handle them in any combination. Losses may come from user action, operator error, application bugs, infrastructure defects, faulty hardware or site catastrophes. A loss may be big bang, such as 1 million rows replaced by 10 in a minute. It may be creeping, such as 10 rows deleted every minute for weeks. A study of 19 Google recovery efforts found that software bugs causing deletion or lost referential integrity were the most common user-visible loss. The hardest were low-grade corruption found weeks or months later.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-212 -->

- **Out-of-band validation: trust storage, but verify**

  Trust storage systems, but verify. Even consensus-based storage is not infallible in practice, so applications cannot know all their data is good until they check. Out-of-band data validation is a system of checks and balances within and between an application's datastores. It detects low-grade corruption or loss before it becomes unrecoverable. Speed matters because bad data propagates, with references to missing or corrupt data copied and links fanning out. The sooner a loss is known, the easier and more complete recovery is. Validation pipelines are often map-reduce or Hadoop jobs. They slow engineering in the short term but give developers courage to move faster later, much as unit tests do. Validators must be balanced: too strict and engineers abandon them, too lax and corruption slips through. Validate only invariants whose failure devastates users, such as file contents matching folder listings. At scale validators cost compute and lower cache hit rates, so tier them. Daily validators catch the most disastrous scenarios within 24 hours, and more rigorous validation runs less often.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-213 -->

- **Point-in-time recovery: time travel for data**

  Point-in-time recovery restores each affected artifact to its own unique point in time, possibly for millions of users across days, weeks or months. Google calls it time-travel. A solution that offers it across ACID and BASE datastores, while meeting strict uptime, latency, scale, velocity and cost goals, is a chimera today. Building it yourself costs velocity. Many projects compromise with a tiered backup strategy, such as days of costly local snapshots plus full and incremental copies every two days. Gradual losses may take days to notice, so recovery needs snapshots from further back. Merging restored data with the current state significantly complicates the restore.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-211 -->

- **Least-loaded round robin: send work where requests are fewest**

  In least-loaded round robin, each client tracks its active requests to every backend in its subset and round robins among the backends with the fewest. Loaded tasks tend to be slower, so the policy moves load away from them. An unhealthy task may fast-fail with 100% errors and attract traffic because it looks lightly loaded; counting recent errors as active requests fixes this. The active-request count is also a poor proxy for capability, since a backend twice as fast may look equally loaded. Each client sees only its own requests, and in practice large services see the most loaded backend using twice the CPU of the least loaded.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-225 -->

- **Weighted round robin: backends report how they are doing**

  What if backends told clients how busy they are? In weighted round robin, they do. Each client keeps a capability score per backend and distributes requests round robin in proportion to those scores. Backends include their observed queries per second, errors per second and utilization in each response, health-check replies included. Clients adjust the scores from each backend's successful requests and utilization cost, with a penalty for failures. In practice it worked very well, drastically narrowing the spread between the most and least loaded tasks after clients switched from least-loaded round robin. The difficulty is that clients decide in real time with only partial or stale backend state.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-226 -->

- **Packet forwarding in network load balancers**

  A network load balancer can hand a packet to its chosen backend in three ways. Network address translation needs a tracking-table entry for every connection, so it precludes a completely stateless fallback. Changing the destination MAC address lets the backend reply directly to the sender (Direct Server Response), which saves a great deal when replies are large. But every balancer and backend must then sit in one broadcast domain, which stops working at scale. Encapsulation wraps the packet in a GRE-encapsulated IP packet. Balancer and backend can then be on separate continents, at the price of 24 bytes of overhead that may exceed the MTU.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-221 -->

  *Figure: Three ways to forward a packet, and what each one costs.*

  | Method | What happens | The catch |
  |---|---|---|
  | Network address translation | The balancer rewrites addresses | A tracking-table entry per connection; no stateless fallback |
  | Change the MAC address | The backend sees the original IPs and replies directly | All balancers and backends in one broadcast domain |
  | Encapsulation | The packet is wrapped in a GRE-encapsulated IP packet | 24 bytes of overhead that may exceed the MTU |

- **Managing expectations with SLOs**

  Publishing SLOs sets expectations for system behavior, so users can tell whether a service fits their use case. A team building a photo-sharing site might avoid a service promising strong durability and low cost for slightly lower availability, though it could suit an archival records system. Keeping an internal SLO tighter than the advertised one leaves room to respond to chronic problems before users see them. Do not overachieve either. Users build on what a service actually delivers, so performing far above its SLO breeds over-dependence. Remedies include planned outages, throttling some requests, or designs that are not faster under light load.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-195 -->

- **Request-based availability: counting requests instead of minutes**

  A system serving 2.5M requests a day with a 99.99% daily target can serve up to 250 errors and still meet it. That is request-based availability: the proportion of requests that succeed over a rolling window, instead of the proportion of time a system is up. Time-based availability counts uptime, and a 99.99% target allows up to 52.56 minutes of downtime a year. But for globally distributed services some traffic is almost always served somewhere, so uptime is rarely meaningful. The success rate over all requests approximates unplanned downtime as the end user sees it. Batch systems can count records processed successfully and unsuccessfully instead of requests.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-198 -->

- **Setting an availability target: what is one more nine worth?**

  One more nine of availability is worth what it adds in revenue. Raising a $1M-revenue service from 99.9% to 99.99% is worth $900, so ask whether that offsets the cost, which is often the key factor. A target also depends on what users expect, whether the service is paid or free, what competitors offer, and whether it serves consumers or enterprises. A fast-growing consumer product can take a lower target because feature speed matters more. Without a revenue translation, a yardstick is the background error rate of ISPs, between 0.01% and 1%. Errors driven below that fall within the noise of a user's Internet connection.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-199 -->

- **Multiple service levels for shared infrastructure**

  Clients of a shared storage system can want opposite things. Low-latency users want empty request queues, while offline-analysis users want queues never empty, so the system never idles. A cost-effective answer is to partition the infrastructure and offer it at multiple independent levels of service. Low-latency clusters carry substantial slack capacity for short queues and isolation. Throughput clusters run hot with less redundancy, perhaps at as little as 10-50% of the cost. Explicit levels expose the cost of each, so clients pick the cheapest that meets their needs. The classes can run on identical hardware and software, varying resource quantities, redundancy, geographic provisioning and configuration.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-200 -->

- **Borg: a cluster operating system that restarts failed tasks**

  Hardware failures are frequent: thousands of machines and thousands of disks fail in a typical cluster-year. Borg, a distributed cluster operating system, abstracts these failures away from users and service teams. It runs users' jobs, either long-running servers or batch processes, as sets of identical tasks on a cluster's machines. Borg finds machines for a job's tasks, monitors them, and kills and restarts a malfunctioning task, possibly on a different machine. Each job declares its resource needs, and Borg bin-packs tasks onto machines. Because tasks move, clients reach them through a naming service that resolves a name and task index to an IP address and port.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-217 -->

- **Life of a request through a large serving stack**

  A request to a large serving stack crosses many layers before the reply is assembled. It passes through DNS, a global load balancer and a reverse-proxy frontend, then application frontend and backend servers, and finally a storage layer such as Bigtable. The whole trip takes a few hundred milliseconds. GSLB, the global load balancer, steers the request at three points: the IP address returned to the user, the service frontend, and an unloaded backend. Many moving parts mean many potential points of failure, and a failing GSLB would wreak havoc. Rigorous testing, careful rollout and graceful degradation keep the service reliable.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-219 -->

  *Figure: Follow the numbered steps from the DNS lookup to the assembled page.*

  | Step | Where | What happens |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 | DNS | Google's DNS server consults GSLB, which picks the frontend IP address returned to the user |
  | 2 | Google Frontend | A reverse proxy terminates the TCP connection and looks up the service |
  | 3 | GSLB | It finds an available service frontend, which receives an RPC with the HTTP request |
  | 4 | Service frontend | It builds a protobuf request and asks GSLB for an unloaded backend |
  | 5 | Backend | It reads Bigtable, and the reply travels back |
  | 6 | Service frontend | It assembles the HTML |

- **N+2 capacity planning: spare tasks for updates and failures**

  Sizing a service divides expected peak load by what one task can handle, then adds spare tasks so peak load is still served during updates and machine failures. With about 100 QPS per task and an expected peak of about 3,470 QPS, at least 35 tasks are needed. N+2 raises this to 37, since an update plus a machine failure could otherwise leave only 35. Backends are placed per region, for example 17 tasks in the USA, 16 in Europe and 6 in Asia. South America uses 4 at N+1, saving 20% of hardware for a small risk of higher latency.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-218 -->

  *Figure: Backend tasks per region: three regions run N+2 and South America runs N+1.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **What a well-defined SLA contains**

  A well-defined SLA names the type of service and the performance level it expects, especially reliability and responsiveness. It describes how performance is monitored: which statistics are gathered, how often, and how customers can access them. It gives contact details and the order for reporting a problem. The response time frame is when the provider starts investigating, and the resolution time frame is when the issue is fixed. Finally, it states the repercussions. If the provider misses its commitments, the customer may have the right to terminate the contract or ask for a refund for losses from the service failure.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-101 -->

- **Cloud service level agreements**

  Because cloud resources are shared, a cloud SLA spans the cloud itself. Providers offer it as a service-based agreement rather than a customer-based one. Performance is measured and reported from the end user's ability to consume resources. Cloud SLAs focus on data center characteristics and, more recently, network characteristics to support end-to-end SLAs. The downside is that the complex environment makes the root cause of service interruptions hard to determine. Yet applications moved there must reach the same or more demanding service levels. Any SLA management strategy has two phases: negotiating the contract and monitoring its fulfillment in real time.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-102 -->

- **Black-box and white-box monitoring**

  Black-box monitoring tests externally visible behavior as a user would see it. White-box monitoring uses metrics exposed by the system's internals, such as logs or an HTTP handler emitting statistics. Black-box monitoring is symptom-oriented and catches active problems, so it suits paging: it only bothers a human when a problem is already causing real symptoms. White-box monitoring can detect imminent problems and failures masked by retries, and it is essential for debugging. In a multilayered system one person's symptom is another's cause. Slow database reads are a symptom for the database SRE but a cause for the frontend SRE watching a slow website.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-203 -->

- **Alerting and paging: wake a human only when it matters**

  Paging a human is expensive, because it interrupts work or sleep. When pages are too frequent, people skim or ignore them, even a real one masked by noise, and outages can be prolonged. Good alerting therefore pages a human only for an urgent, actionable condition that is actively or imminently user-visible. Every page should be actionable, need intelligence rather than a robotic response, and concern a novel problem. People can react with urgency only a few times a day before becoming fatigued. Monitoring should answer what is broken (the symptom) and why (a possibly intermediate cause), and keeping the two apart is key. Put effort into catching symptoms rather than causes. Email alerts are of very limited value and quickly overrun with noise, so favor a dashboard of ongoing subcritical problems. Pages with rote responses are a red flag: remove the root cause or fully automate the response. In one over-alerting case, the team eased an SLO dominated by a long tail of mean latency to 75th percentile latency and disabled email alerts.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-204 -->

- **Incident management: from detection to post-incident review**

  Left unmanaged, an incident can escalate into an emergency, crisis or disaster. Incident management is the process of limiting the disruption an incident could cause to operations, services or functions, followed by a return to business as usual. It identifies, analyzes and corrects hazards to prevent recurrence. An incident response or incident management team, designated beforehand or during the event, is put in control to restore normal functions, and an incident commander leads the response. Frameworks follow a lifecycle of detection, classification, response coordination, containment, recovery and post-incident review. In IT service management the first goal is restoring normal service operation as quickly as possible while minimizing business impact. Normal operation here means service within the SLA.

  Afterward, post-incident analysis determines why the incident happened despite precautions. Its findings feed back into policy and its practical implementation. Root cause analysis should assess human factors. An active failure has immediate effects, while latent failures come from high-level decisions and lie dormant until a triggering event combines with them. Typical challenges are growing alert and event noise, a lengthy problem resolution process, and inability to predict and prevent service degradations or outages. For computer security incidents, a computer security incident response team analyzes the situation, determines how far an intrusion reached and takes corrective action.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-187 -->

  *Figure: Incident frameworks follow these six stages in order.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Detection] --> B[Classification]
  B --> C[Response coordination]
  C --> D[Containment]
  D --> E[Recovery]
  E --> F[Post-incident review]
  ```

- **SRE team models: five ways to organize**

  SRE teams are organized in several models: kitchen sink, infrastructure, product or application, embedded and consulting. A kitchen sink team oversees an expansive, often unbounded scope, including performance optimization, incident management and automation. Infrastructure teams keep the systems that support other teams' workflows up, fast and efficient, while platform teams develop the software and systems used across the organization. Product or application teams are dedicated to specific products, and large companies typically have several. In the embedded model, individual SREs or pairs join software engineering teams to apply automation, monitoring and incident response. Consulting teams instead advise organizations on adopting SRE practices.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-105 -->

- **Business impact analysis: what a disruption would cost**

  A business impact analysis identifies and evaluates the effects of disruptions on operations and determines the recovery priorities and strategies the organization needs. It identifies critical activities and their dependencies, and assesses the financial, operational, reputational and legal impact of disruption. For each function it assigns two objectives. The recovery point objective is the acceptable data loss, such as whether losing 2 days of data is acceptable. The recovery time objective is the acceptable time to restore the function. The longest that key services can be unavailable before stakeholders see unacceptable consequences is the maximum tolerable period of disruption.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-185 -->

- **Disaster recovery tiers: from no off-site data to automation**

  Disaster recovery tiers grade recovery solutions from no off-site data up to highly automated recovery. SHARE defined seven tiers in 1992, and IBM updated them to eight in 2012. Tier 0 has no off-site data or recovery plan, so recovery may be impossible. Higher tiers keep data fresher and recover faster. Tier 2 adds a hot site to restore tape backups. Tier 4 uses disk-based point-in-time copies. Tier 7 adds automated application recovery, which restores systems faster and more reliably than manual procedures.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-186 -->

  *Figure: Each tier up the table keeps data fresher and automates more of recovery.*

  | Tier | What it adds |
  |---|---|
  | 0 | No off-site data or recovery plan, so recovery may be impossible |
  | 1 | Off-site backups but no systems to restore them on; days to weeks of data lost |
  | 2 | A hot site to restore tape backups; hours to days of data recreated |
  | 3 | Electronic vaulting of mission-critical data, more current than shipped tapes |
  | 4 | Disk-based point-in-time copies for fresher data and faster recovery |
  | 5 | Data kept consistent between production and recovery data centers |
  | 6 | Data kept current with little or no loss, without relying on applications |
  | 7 | Automated application recovery, faster and more reliable than manual procedures |

- **Gmail restores user data from tape**

  Gmail lost a significant amount of user data despite many safeguards, internal checks and redundancies. The loss went beyond what its internal recovery means could restore, so the team turned to GTape, Gmail's global offline tape backup. It was the first large-scale use of GTape to restore live customer data, though similar restores had been simulated many times.

  Those simulations paid off. The team estimated how long the restore would take. It restored all accounts within several hours of the estimate, and recovered 99%+ of the data before the estimated completion time. The smooth recovery relied on a central plan, the product of regular dress rehearsals and dry runs, with many teams, even unrelated ones, pitching in.

  The case shows Defense in depth: layers against data loss at work. Backing up an online system gives defense in depth at two layers. One guards against failure of internal redundancy and backup subsystems. The other guards against a wide failure or zero-day in a device driver or filesystem under the disks. Large disk and network resources for replication did not remove the need for a tape layer, as Replication is not backup: it copies your mistakes too explains. Multiple layers guard against breakdown or compromise of any single protection mechanism. Failures are treated as inevitable, so planning covers foreseeable failures and some amount of random, undifferentiated breakage as well.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-215 -->

- **Runaway deletion at Google Music**

  A redesigned, more efficient data deletion pipeline wrongly removed about 600,000 audio references, affecting 21,000 users. The damage was found over a month after the pipeline's first run. The team disabled the pipeline, then split up. SREs recovered data from offsite tape while developers hunted the root cause, since recovery would be in vain until the bug was fixed.

  The timing helped. The recovery came weeks after the annual disaster recovery testing exercise, so the tape team knew its subsystems' limits and had a tool tested in that exercise. Recovering the tracks meant recalling over 5,000 tapes, split into 5,475 restore jobs. SRE requested them programmatically, since a person typing one restore a minute would need over three days. The 1.5 petabyte first wave ran past its two-day estimate, with 17 bad tapes and 1,862 tapes a vendor omitted. Redundant encoding let the team recall redundancy tapes, and users had the tracks back in just short of 7 days.

  About 161,000 tracks were deleted before being backed up. Store-bought and promotional ones were reinstated from original copies, while user-uploaded files were re-uploaded by clients over more than a week.

  The root cause was a race condition. Stages designed to run in strict succession slowed as data grew, the timing assumption failed for more data, and wrong data was deleted nondeterministically. The pipeline was redesigned to remove the race. Monitoring was enhanced to catch runaway deletion bugs before users notice. One example is alerting when the global deletion rate crosses an extreme threshold such as 10x the 95th percentile.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-216 -->

### Containers, orchestration and deployment

A container packages an application with its dependencies so that it runs the same in any environment, and much of this chapter grows from that idea. First come the Linux kernel features that isolate containers, from chroot to namespaces and cgroups, which control what a process can see and how much of the system it can use. Next come Docker, with its images and registries, and Kubernetes, which orchestrates containers so that one that goes down is replaced by another without downtime. Along the way you will meet nodes, Pods and the probes the kubelet runs to learn whether a container is healthy.

- **Chroot: changing what a program thinks the root is**

  A program can be fooled about where the file system begins. Chroot, a Unix command and system call, changes the apparent root directory for a process. In this chroot jail a program cannot name, and normally cannot reach, files outside the tree. Engineers use it to build and test software against only its expected dependencies, and to run legacy software whose libraries would clash with the host's. It is a weak jail: a privileged program can often chroot again to break out, and it limits no I/O, bandwidth, disk space or CPU time. The isolation of Containers: an application and everything it needs, isolated can be seen as an advanced form of it.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-146 -->

- **Kubernetes: a cluster that steers itself toward the state you declare**

  A cluster of machines is a lot to keep in order by hand. Kubernetes, also known as K8s, is an open-source system that does it for you: it automates deploying, scaling and managing software. It assembles computers, virtual or bare metal, into a cluster (see Computer clusters: many machines acting as one) that runs workloads packaged in Containers: an application and everything it needs, isolated. The software has two halves, a control plane and the nodes on which applications run.

  Everything speaks one language. Kubernetes defines compute and storage as objects that can be managed as such. Its internal components, its extensions and the workloads on it all rely on the Kubernetes API. Its building blocks, called primitives, deploy, maintain and scale applications based on CPU, memory or custom metrics.

  Kubernetes is not mere orchestration, which executes a defined workflow of first A, then B, then C. It is a set of independent, composable control processes that continuously drive the current state toward the desired state. Its design is greatly influenced by Google's internal system Borg.

  In production the control plane usually runs across multiple computers and a cluster runs multiple nodes, which gives fault tolerance and high availability. Kubernetes is commonly used to host microservice-based systems, because it and its ecosystem of tools provide the capabilities those architectures need.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-050 -->

- **Containers: an application and everything it needs, isolated**

  The promise of a container is that an application runs the same everywhere. A container is an isolated user-space instance that the operating system kernel allows alongside others, packaging an application with its dependencies. Programs inside can see only the container's contents and the devices assigned to it, and each container gets a subset of the computer's resources. The package holds the code and all its dependencies, such as specific runtime and library versions. The application therefore runs quickly and reliably from one computing environment to another. That decoupling lets container-based applications be deployed easily and consistently, and gives developers and operations teams a clear separation of responsibility between application logic and deployment.

  Containers cost less than full virtualization. Their programs use the operating system's normal system call interface, so nothing is emulated and no intermediate machine layer sits in between. They are lightweight and use just the resources they need. Linux containers rely on Linux namespaces and Cgroups: the kernel's budget for a group of processes, and the kernel often adds resource management so that one container's activity has limited impact on others.

  The trade-off is flexibility. A container cannot host a guest operating system different from the host's, or a different guest kernel. On Linux, other distributions are fine, but Windows cannot be hosted. Typical uses are securely allocating finite hardware resources among many mutually distrusting users, and consolidating server hardware by moving services from separate hosts into containers on one server.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-063 -->

- **Cgroups: the kernel's budget for a group of processes**

  How does Linux stop one runaway process from eating the whole machine? Cgroups, short for control groups, is a Linux kernel feature that limits, accounts for and isolates the resource usage of a collection of processes. The resources include CPU, memory and disk I/O. A control group is a set of processes bound by the same criteria and tied to a set of limits. Groups are hierarchical, each inheriting limits from its parent. A group can be capped at a memory limit (including file system cache), I/O bandwidth, CPU quota, CPU set or open files. Some groups can get a larger share of CPU or disk I/O. Cgroups also measure usage, for billing for example. Cgroup v2 has a single process hierarchy and works on processes rather than threads, whereas v1 allowed multiple hierarchies; the first kernel supporting v2 was Linux 4.5. LXC, systemd and Kubernetes all use cgroups. Since Linux 4.19, the out-of-memory killer can kill a whole cgroup as a single unit to keep the workload intact.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-145 -->

- **Namespaces and cgroups: what a process sees and what it may use**

  Two kernel features let a process believe it owns a machine while keeping it from taking more than its share. Namespaces control what a process can see, and cgroups control how much of the system's resources it can use. Together they underpin Kubernetes, LXC and Podman. A namespace partitions kernel resources, so one set of processes sees one set of resources and another set sees a different one. Each gets the illusion of being the sole user of the system. As of Linux 5.6 there are eight kinds: mount, process ID, network, inter-process communication, UTS, user, cgroup and time. In a PID namespace the first process is PID 1, and its exit makes the kernel kill all others in that namespace. A network namespace has its own IP addresses, routing table and firewall rules. User namespaces map IDs between container and host, so a process can be root inside the container yet an unprivileged ID on the host.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-064 -->

- **Pod lifecycle: from Pending to Succeeded or Failed**

  A Pod is disposable by design, and its lifecycle shows how. A Pod, the unit Kubernetes runs on a node, is created with a unique UID. It is scheduled to a node only once and stays there until it terminates or is deleted.

  Its phase is a high-level summary, not a state machine. A Pod starts in Pending, which means it is accepted but its containers are not yet set up: it may be waiting to be scheduled or downloading images. It moves to Running once it is bound to a node and at least one primary container starts. It ends in Succeeded or Failed. Succeeded means all containers terminated in success and will not be restarted. Failed means all terminated and at least one failed, by a non-zero exit or a system kill. Unknown means the state could not be obtained, typically a node communication error.

  Each container is Waiting, Running or Terminated, and a preStop hook runs before it terminates. The kubelet also records conditions, such as Initialized, ContainersReady and Ready. Ready means the Pod can serve requests and joins the load balancing pools of all matching Services. Readiness gates add custom conditions: the Pod is Ready only when its containers are ready and every gate is True.

  The kubelet may restart a failed container, but a Pod that fails unrecoverably, sits on a failed node or is evicted is deleted. A Pod is never rescheduled. A near-identical replacement with a new UID takes over, maybe on another node, and anything tied to the old Pod's lifetime, such as a volume, is recreated.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-227 -->

  *Figure: A Pod moves from Pending to Running and ends in Succeeded or Failed.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Pending] -->|a container starts| B[Running]
  B -->|all succeed| C[Succeeded]
  B -->|one failed| D[Failed]
  ```

- **Container probes: how Kubernetes decides a container is healthy**

  A container can be running and still be of no use: it may be deadlocked, or still warming its caches. Kubernetes finds out with probes, periodic checks (see Health checks: noticing which servers are down) that the kubelet runs on a container, either by running code inside it or by making a network request. An exec probe treats exit code 0 as healthy. A TCP probe is healthy only if a connection to the port opens. An HTTP probe counts any status from 200 up to but not including 400 as success. A gRPC probe uses the gRPC Health Checking Protocol. Liveness probes decide when to restart a container, for example one that is deadlocked. Readiness probes decide when it can accept traffic, covering slow startup work such as warming caches. A startup probe runs only at startup, and until it succeeds no liveness or readiness probes run. For a slow-starting application, give it a failureThreshold times periodSeconds long enough for the worst-case startup, such as 30 * 10 = 300s.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-161 -->

  *Figure: Each probe asks a different question and has a different consequence when it fails.*

  | Probe | Question it asks | If it fails |
  |---|---|---|
  | Liveness | Is the container stuck? | The kubelet restarts it |
  | Readiness | Can it accept traffic? | Pod IP leaves the Service's EndpointSlices |
  | Startup | Has the application started? | The kubelet kills it and applies the restart policy |

- **Docker: containers that share one kernel**

  Every container on a Docker host shares one operating system kernel. That is why a server can run several at once and use fewer resources than machines that each boot their own system. Docker is a platform that packages software into containers using operating system-level virtualization. The containers are isolated from one another, bundle their own software, libraries and configuration files, and can communicate through well-defined channels. On Linux, Docker uses kernel isolation features such as cgroups and namespaces, plus a union-capable file system such as OverlayFS. Namespaces mostly isolate an application's view of its environment, including process trees, network, user IDs and mounted file systems, while cgroups limit memory and CPU. The Docker daemon, dockerd, is a persistent process that manages containers and listens for Docker Engine API requests, and the docker command-line client lets users talk to it. On macOS, Docker runs its containers inside a Linux guest system (see Virtual machine: a whole computer made of software).

  <!-- sysd-reliab-045 -->

- **Container images and registries: how an application is shipped**

  A container starts from an image. A Docker image is a read-only template used to build containers, and images are how applications are stored and shipped. A Dockerfile, a text file, commonly specifies the Linux distribution of an image, the installation commands for the language runtime and the application source code. Images live in a registry, a repository that stores and serves them. Clients connect to it to download, or pull, images for use, and to upload, or push, images they have built. Docker Hub is the default registry where Docker looks for images, and it is a public registry that anyone can use. Registries can also create notifications based on events.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-046 -->

- **Container orchestration: replacing what fails, without downtime**

  In production, the containers running applications must be managed so that nothing goes down. Container orchestration automates that: it deploys, scales and manages containers so that one that fails is replaced by another without downtime. Kubernetes does this in several ways. It exposes a container by DNS name or IP address and load balances traffic when it is high. With automated rollouts and rollbacks, you describe the desired state and Kubernetes changes the actual state to match at a controlled rate. With automatic bin packing, you say how much CPU and memory each container needs and it fits them onto your nodes to make the best use of resources. Self-healing restarts and replaces failed containers, kills those that fail a user-defined health check, and does not advertise them to clients until they are ready to serve. Kubernetes is not an all-inclusive platform as a service, though: it works at the container level, does not build applications and has no built-in databases or message buses.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-148 -->

- **Container runtime: the software that starts and stops containers**

  Something has to actually start a container. That is the container runtime, the software responsible for the lifecycle of containers, including launching, reconciling and killing them. Every Kubernetes node must run one, and the kubelet, the agent on each node, talks to it through the Container Runtime Interface (CRI). The CRI decouples maintaining core Kubernetes from any one runtime. containerd and CRI-O are widely used CRI-compliant runtimes. Kubernetes was originally tightly coupled to Docker and dropped official Docker support as a runtime with v1.24 in May 2022. Docker Engine itself has been built on containerd and runc since version 1.11.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-049 -->

- **Kubernetes nodes: the machines that run the pods**

  Every few seconds, each node in a Kubernetes cluster reports its status to the API server in a heartbeat message. A node, also called a worker or minion, is a machine where containers are deployed. Every cluster has at least one, and it hosts the pods that make up the application workload. It runs a container runtime plus components that connect its containers to the network. The kubelet is an agent on each node that makes sure its pods' containers are running and healthy, starting, stopping and maintaining them as the control plane directs. When the control plane detects a node failure, a higher-level controller is expected to launch the pods on another healthy node. On each node, kube-proxy acts as a network proxy and load balancer, routing traffic to the appropriate container by the IP and port of the incoming request.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-054 -->

- **Kubernetes pods: the smallest thing Kubernetes runs**

  The smallest unit Kubernetes administers is not a container. It is a pod, the basic deployable unit, made of one or more containers co-located on the same node. In the most common case each pod has a single container. Each pod has a unique IP address within the cluster, shared by every container inside it, so applications can use ports without the risk of conflict. Containers in a pod reach each other on localhost, while containers in different pods have distinct IP addresses and talk over IP networking. A pod can also declare shared storage volumes, which let its data survive a container restart. Pods are ephemeral and disposable, so they are rarely created directly. A workload resource such as a Deployment creates them, replicates them for scale and replaces them when a node fails.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-055 -->

- **Pod restart policy: when a container that exits comes back**

  When a container exits, should Kubernetes start it again? The restartPolicy in a Pod spec answers that: Always, OnFailure or Never, with Always the default. Always restarts a container after any termination, OnFailure only if it exits with an error (a non-zero exit status), and Never not at all. Individual containers can override the Pod's policy with their own restartPolicy and ordered restartPolicyRules that compare the exit code with listed values; the first match applies. Sidecar containers ignore the Pod-level policy, since a sidecar is an init container whose own restartPolicy is Always. The RestartAllContainers action restarts the whole Pod in place. Containers stop without honoring the grace period or preStop hooks, init containers re-run, and the Pod keeps its UID, IP address and volumes. That suits workloads where rescheduling is costly, such as batch jobs or AI/ML training. The Kubernetes project advises designing for unannounced restarts either way.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-228 -->

- **CrashLoopBackOff: a container that keeps failing and waiting**

  The first time a container crashes, Kubernetes restarts it immediately. After repeated crashes it waits, using an exponential backoff (see Exponential backoff: waiting twice as long each time), so a faulty container cannot swamp the system with failed starts. That cycle of failing, restarting and waiting is CrashLoopBackOff. Delays start at 10s and double each time up to a default cap of 300s, and running successfully for a duration such as 10 minutes resets them. Typical causes are application errors, bad configuration such as wrong environment variables or missing files, too little memory or CPU, and slow-starting applications failing health checks. Investigate with kubectl logs and kubectl describe pod.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-229 -->

- **Graceful pod termination: TERM first, KILL only after the grace period**

  A deleted Pod is not killed at once. Pods are processes, so they should terminate gracefully rather than be stopped abruptly with a KILL signal. When you request deletion, the cluster records the intended grace period. The kubelet then has the container runtime send a TERM signal to each container's main process so it can clean up. After the grace period, KILL goes to any remaining processes and the Pod is deleted from the API server. A preStop hook runs before a container enters the Terminated state, whereas an in-place Pod restart skips the grace period and preStop hooks.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-230 -->

- **Container persistent storage: data that outlives a container**

  In Kubernetes, a container's filesystem is wiped when the container restarts, which is limiting for anything but trivial applications. Data that must outlive a container needs a volume. A volume provides persistent storage and shared disk space for the containers in a pod, and the same volume can be mounted at different points by different containers. A Docker volume likewise lets data persist independently, remaining after a container is deleted or re-created. Kubernetes was historically suited only to stateless services (see Stateless and stateful: does the server remember you?), but databases need persistence. The Container Storage Interface separated the code for external storage systems from the core Kubernetes code base.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-061 -->

- **Sidecar and init containers: helpers that share a Pod**

  Most Pods hold one container, but a Pod can hold several that cooperate. These containers are co-located, co-scheduled and share resources, and Kubernetes manages the Pod rather than the container. In a typical multi-container Pod, one container serves files from a shared volume to the public while a separate sidecar container refreshes those files from a remote source. Sidecar containers provide auxiliary services to the main application, such as a service mesh. Init containers by default run to completion before the application containers start. An init container with restartPolicy Always is a sidecar: it starts before the application and runs until the Pod shuts down.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-159 -->

- **Labels and selectors: how Kubernetes finds the right objects**

  Kubernetes tags its objects, and everything else finds them by tag. Labels are keys that clients attach to any API object, such as pods and nodes, and label selectors are queries that resolve to the matching objects. A service's label selector chooses the pod instances that its router or load balancer sends traffic to. Changing pod labels or a service's selector therefore controls which pods receive traffic, which supports deployment patterns such as Blue-green deployment: swap environments, roll back by swapping again or A/B testing. This dynamic control over which resources implement a service gives the infrastructure loose coupling.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-060 -->

- **Kubernetes services: one stable address for a changing set of pods**

  Pods are ephemeral, and the set of healthy ones changes from moment to moment, so a frontend cannot keep track of backend IP addresses. A Kubernetes service solves this. It is a set of pods that work together, such as one tier of a multi-tier application, and it gives that group one stable endpoint. A label selector defines which pods belong to it. Service discovery gives the service a stable IP address and DNS name. It load balances traffic round-robin across the matching pods, even as failures move pods from machine to machine. Kubernetes offers two modes of service discovery: environment variables or Kubernetes DNS. On each node, kube-proxy forwards requests to the correct containers. By default a service is exposed inside the cluster, for example back-end pods balancing requests from front-end pods, but it can also be exposed outside it.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-058 -->

- **Kubernetes Service types: ClusterIP, NodePort, LoadBalancer and ExternalName**

  Not every service should be reachable from everywhere, so Kubernetes lets you choose how each one is exposed. The type field is nested functionality, each level adding to the previous one, and several types build on ClusterIP as a foundation.

  ClusterIP, the default, exposes the Service on a cluster-internal IP, so it is reachable only from within the cluster. A Gateway can expose it to the public internet, and so can the object described in Kubernetes Ingress: HTTP routes into the cluster. NodePort exposes the Service on each node's IP at a static port. The control plane allocates it from a range, by default 30000-32767, and every node proxies that same port into the Service.

  LoadBalancer exposes the Service externally through a load balancer. Kubernetes offers no load balancing component itself, so you provide one or integrate with a cloud provider. A LoadBalancer Service typically starts as a NodePort Service, and the cloud-controller-manager then configures the external load balancer to forward traffic to that node port.

  ExternalName maps the Service to a DNS name by returning a CNAME record for the external hostname, with no proxying of any kind. A headless Service sets the cluster IP to None, so no cluster IP is allocated and kube-proxy ignores it. DNS returns individual Pod IPs instead, so a client can connect to whichever Pod it prefers.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-151 -->

  *Figure: Each Service type exposes the Service differently, and several build on ClusterIP.*

  | Type | Exposes the Service | Detail |
  |---|---|---|
  | ClusterIP (default) | Inside the cluster only | A cluster-internal IP |
  | NodePort | On each node's IP | Static port, default 30000-32767 |
  | LoadBalancer | Outside, through a load balancer | Starts as a NodePort Service |
  | ExternalName | As a DNS name | A CNAME record, no proxying |
  | Headless | As individual Pod IPs | Cluster IP None; kube-proxy ignores it |

- **Kubernetes Ingress: HTTP routes into the cluster**

  Write an Ingress and nothing happens until a controller picks it up. An Ingress is a Kubernetes API object that exposes HTTP and HTTPS routes from outside the cluster to services inside it, using rules defined on the Ingress resource. An Ingress controller fulfils it, usually with a load balancer. It can give Services externally reachable URLs, load balance traffic, terminate SSL/TLS and offer name-based virtual hosting. Each rule has an optional host and a list of paths, each with a backend naming a Service and port. Both host and path must match before traffic is sent there. A fanout setup routes traffic from a single IP address to more than one Service based on the requested URI. That keeps the number of load balancers to a minimum. TLS ends at the ingress point, so traffic onward to Services and Pods is plaintext. An Ingress does not expose arbitrary ports or protocols; anything other than HTTP and HTTPS is usually exposed with a Service of type NodePort or LoadBalancer.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-152 -->

- **Ingress path and host matching: which backend gets the request**

  Which Service should answer a request for /foo/bar/baz? Ingress rules decide by matching the request's host and URL path. Every path needs a pathType, Exact, Prefix or ImplementationSpecific, or it fails validation. Exact matches the URL path exactly and case-sensitively, while Prefix matches element by element on the path split by slashes, so Prefix /foo/bar matches /foo/bar/baz but not /foo/barbaz. When several paths match, the longest wins, and between equal matches an Exact path beats a Prefix path. A host can be exact, such as foo.bar.com, or a wildcard such as *.foo.com, which covers a single DNS label. Anything unmatched goes to the default backend.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-153 -->

- **Docker run workflow: from docker run to a running container**

  What actually happens when you type docker run? Docker has three components: a client that talks to the daemon, a host whose daemon listens for API requests, and a registry that stores images. The daemon manages Docker objects such as images, containers, networks and volumes. When docker run executes, Docker pulls the image from the registry, creates a new container and allocates a read-write filesystem to it. It then creates a network interface that connects the container to the default network, and starts the container.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-042 -->

- **Docker Compose: a multi-container application from one command**

  Docker Compose is a tool for defining and running multi-container Docker applications, and it creates and starts all the containers with a single command. It uses YAML files to configure the application's services. The docker-compose.yml file defines those services and their configuration options, such as the path of the Dockerfile used to build one. The docker compose command-line utility then runs commands on several containers at once, for example building images, scaling containers or restarting stopped ones.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-047 -->

- **Docker Swarm: several Docker engines acting as one**

  Docker Swarm provides native clustering for Docker containers, turning a group of Docker engines into a single virtual Docker engine. A Docker service lets containers be scaled across multiple Docker daemons. The resulting set of cooperating daemons, communicating through the Docker API, is a swarm, integrated into Docker Engine since Docker 1.12. Swarm is managed with the Raft consensus algorithm (see Raft: consensus built to be understood), so a majority of Swarm nodes must agree before an update is performed. The docker stack tool manages Swarm services with a configuration file very like docker-compose.yml, and can manage a Swarm cluster across multiple machines.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-048 -->

- **Virtual machine: a whole computer made of software**

  Most deployments use only a small part of a server's physical resources, which is the opening that virtual machines fill. A virtual machine is the virtualization or emulation of a computer system that provides the functionality of a physical computer. It runs as a virtual computer with its own CPU, memory, network interface and storage, created on a physical hardware system. The physical hardware is the host and the emulated machine is the guest; one host can emulate several guests, each running a different operating system. Server consolidation is a top reason for using them: many virtual servers can be placed on each physical server to improve utilization. Because a VM is isolated, what runs inside cannot interfere with the host, which suits testing new applications, setting up production environments and isolating applications for security. System virtual machines substitute for a real machine and can execute entire operating systems. A process virtual machine instead runs a single program in a platform-independent environment, and the Java virtual machine is a well-known example.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-065 -->

- **Hypervisor: the software that creates and runs virtual machines**

  One machine can run several operating systems at once, and if one crashes the others keep working. A hypervisor, or virtual machine monitor, is the software, firmware or hardware that makes this possible by creating and running virtual machines. The machine it runs on is the host and each virtual machine is a guest. The hypervisor presents guest operating systems with a virtual platform and treats CPU, memory and storage as a pool that can be reallocated between guests. Unlike an emulator, the guest executes most instructions on native hardware. Type-1, or bare-metal, hypervisors run directly on the host's hardware, as Hyper-V, Xen and VMware ESXi do. Type-2 hypervisors run on a conventional operating system like any other program, as VirtualBox and VMware Workstation do. Modern hypervisors use hardware-assisted virtualization, and Intel and AMD released their first x86 processors with it in 2005.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-044 -->

- **Virtualization versus containerization: a guest OS or a shared kernel**

  A virtual machine brings its own operating system along. A container borrows the host's. In traditional virtualization a hypervisor virtualizes the physical hardware. Each virtual machine then holds a guest operating system, a virtual copy of the hardware it needs, and the application with its libraries and dependencies. Containers virtualize the operating system instead of the hardware, so each contains only the application and its dependencies. That is why containers are much more lightweight: they share the OS kernel and use a fraction of the memory VMs require. They use just the computing resources they need, whereas VMs raise hardware utilization by placing many virtual servers on one physical server.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-043 -->

  *Figure: A virtual machine carries a whole guest system, while a container shares the host's kernel.*

  | Property | Virtual machine | Container |
  |---|---|---|
  | Virtualizes | The hardware | The operating system |
  | Each instance carries | A guest OS, virtual hardware and the app | Only the app and its dependencies |
  | Memory use | Much more | A fraction of a VM's |

- **Virtual machine snapshots and migration: an undo button for a whole machine**

  Restoring a virtual machine snapshot undoes every change made since. A snapshot is the state of a virtual machine at an exact point in time, which makes it a useful backup technique before a risky operation. Each snapshot creates a new file used as an overlay for its predecessors. New data goes to the topmost overlay, and reads scan the hierarchy for the most recent version. A snapshot can also move to another host machine with its own hypervisor. Stopping the VM, snapshotting, moving and resuming it there is known as migration. Failover (Failover: when a standby takes over) is similar and lets the VM keep operating if its host fails.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-066 -->

- **Physical, virtual and container deployment: three eras of running applications**

  On physical servers, an application's resources could not be bounded, so one application could take most of them and leave others underperforming. One application per server did not scale either, because resources were underused and servers were costly. Virtualization runs several virtual machines on one server's CPU, isolating applications and improving utilization, but each VM is a full machine with its own operating system. Containers relax the isolation to share the operating system, so they are lightweight. Each has its own filesystem, share of CPU, memory and process space, and is portable across clouds and OS distributions. They also give faster image creation than VM images.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-149 -->

- **Continuous delivery: always ready to release**

  Continuous delivery bets that releasing often is safer than releasing rarely. It is a software engineering approach in which teams produce software in short cycles, ensuring that it can be reliably released at any time. Every commit is built and packaged by a build server and tested by several techniques before it can be marked releasable. The deployment pipeline is the set of validations a change must pass on its way to release. Its purpose is visibility, feedback and continually deploying any version to any environment through full automation. The approach brings the pain forward: tough tasks are tackled early, which fosters automation and swift issue detection. Frequent releases carry fewer changes each, so problems are easier to find and fix and their impact lasts a shorter time. Code not yet ready for users can be committed early (see Feature toggle: shipping unfinished code hidden behind a switch), because long-lived branches become impractical. Obstacles include a lack of test automation, differences between development, test and production environments, tests that need a human oracle, and regulated domains needing customer-side or on-site testing.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-143 -->

- **CI/CD pipeline: from a merged change to a deployed one**

  CI/CD combines continuous integration with continuous delivery or, less often, continuous deployment. A CI/CD pipeline is three processes in order. First comes frequent merging of small changes into a main branch. Then software is produced in short cycles so it can be released at any time. Last comes automatic rollout of new functionality. The services compile the incremental code changes, then link and package them into deliverables. Automated tests verify the functionality and automated deployment services deliver it to end users. The aim is early defect discovery, higher productivity and faster release cycles. Traditional methods instead integrated a collection of updates into one large batch before deploying. Small teams can be more productive with one repository and one pipeline, whereas larger organizations may have separate ones for each team or even each service. Least privilege is hard to apply to pipeline permissions because the architecture is dynamic. Administrators may allow more permissive permissions while adding compensating security controls to limit the blast radius.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-144 -->

  *Figure: A change flows from merge to end users through automated stages.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Merge small changes] --> B[Compile, link, package]
  B --> C[Automated tests]
  C --> D[Automated deployment]
  D --> E[End users]
  ```

- **Release engineering: making releases repeatable rather than unique**

  Reliable services need reliable release processes, and that means no unique snowflakes. Release engineering is the discipline of building and delivering software, defining every step from source storage and build rules to testing, packaging and deployment. Binaries and configurations are built reproducibly and automatically, so releases are repeatable and changes to the release process are intentional. In the self-service model, product teams run their own release processes and decide how often to release, with releases automated until problems need an engineer. High velocity rests on the view that frequent releases mean fewer changes between versions, which makes testing and troubleshooting easier. Some teams build hourly and pick the build to deploy from test results. Several layers of access control gate who can approve source changes, create a release, approve cherry picks, deploy a release or change build configuration. Almost all changes need code review. Teams should budget for release engineering at the start, since good practice put in early is cheaper than retrofitting it.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-162 -->

- **Infrastructure as code: servers described in files, not set up by hand**

  Instead of building a server's configuration by hand, you apply a pre-set one. That is infrastructure as code: managing and provisioning data center resources through machine-readable definition files rather than physical hardware configuration or interactive configuration tools. The infrastructure covers bare-metal servers, virtual machines and their configuration. Definitions live in version control, so infrastructure is treated like software, reviewed and deployed automatically, which reduces manual errors and lets teams reproduce environments reliably. The declarative approach defines the desired state and the system works out what to do. The imperative approach lists the commands to run in order. IaC more often uses declarative definitions. In the push method the controlling system sends instructions directly to the server, and in the pull method the server retrieves its own. Tools include CFEngine, Puppet, Chef, SaltStack, Ansible and Terraform. The templates themselves need security review: a 2020 cloud threat report identified around 200,000 potential vulnerabilities in infrastructure-as-code templates.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-147 -->

- **Twelve-factor app: principles for an application that scales and behaves**

  Twelve principles describe an application that is reliable, scalable and manageable. Keep all code in one place under version control such as Git, and list every dependency so the app is easy to install. Keep settings such as database credentials separate from code, so they can change without rewriting it. Treat other services, such as databases or payment processors, as separate components the app connects to. Separate the stages of preparing the app, releasing it and running it in production. Design processes so that no part relies on a specific computer or its memory. Expose the app through a network port, without storing critical information on a single machine. Handle more work by adding more copies of the same process, and make each process start quickly and shut down gracefully. Keep development very similar to production to avoid surprises, record what the app does in logs, and run special administrative tasks separately from the app.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-041 -->

- **ConfigMaps and Secrets: configuration that changes without a rebuild**

  Kubernetes Secrets are not encrypted at rest by default. They are designed for confidential data such as certificates, registry credentials, passwords and ssh keys, so they need extra setup to be fully secured. With ConfigMaps they form two closely related mechanisms for storing configuration, so that changes need no rebuild of the application. A pod receives the data as environment variables or as files in a mounted volume, and volume mounts reload automatically without a container restart. A ConfigMap or Secret goes to a node only if a pod there requires it, is held only in memory, and is deleted with that pod.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-059 -->

- **Hermetic builds: the same revision, the same result, on any machine**

  Build the same product at the same source revision on different machines, and the results should be identical. A hermetic build is insensitive to the software installed on the build machine. It depends on known versions of build tools such as compilers and of dependencies such as libraries, and relies on no services external to the build environment. Build tools are themselves versioned by source revision. A project built last month therefore does not use this month's compiler when a cherry pick forces a rebuild, since that compiler may have incompatible features. Every binary can display its build date, revision number and build identifier.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-165 -->

- **Release branching and cherry-picking: fixing a release without moving it**

  Most major projects do not release from the mainline. All code is checked into it, but releases come from a branch cut at a specific revision, and changes are never merged from the branch back. Bug fixes go to the mainline first and are then cherry picked into the release branch. That avoids picking up unrelated changes and means the exact contents of each release are known. To fix a bug in an older release, rebuild at the same revision as the original build and include the specific later changes. This tactic is called cherry picking. Each cherry pick request is approved or rejected individually.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-164 -->

- **Release pipeline: how a revision becomes a signed, canaried package**

  How does a source revision become something deployable? A release pipeline turns a tested revision into a deployable package by branching, building, testing, packaging and canarying, and it logs each step. It starts with a continuous test system that runs unit tests on the mainline at every submitted change. Releases are cut at the revision of the last continuous test build that passed all tests, so release-time builds are less likely to fail.

  The pipeline creates a release branch from the requested integration revision, then compiles the binaries and runs unit tests, often in parallel, in environments dedicated to those tasks. Unit tests are re-run on the release branch with an audit trail, because cherry picks can leave a branch with code that exists nowhere on the mainline.

  Packages are named, versioned with a unique hash and signed. Labels such as dev, canary and production mark a package's place in the release, and reapplying a label moves it to the newest package. Build artifacts then go to system testing and canary deployments; a typical canary starts a few jobs in production after system tests finish. Each step's result is logged, and a report of all changes since the last release is created.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-163 -->

  *Figure: A revision passes through branching, building, packaging and testing before its canary deployment.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Mainline passes tests] --> B[Release branch cut]
  B --> C[Build and unit tests]
  C --> D[Package named, hashed, signed]
  D --> E[System tests]
  E --> F[Canary deployment]
  ```

- **Horizontal Pod Autoscaler: adding Pods when load rises**

  When load rises, the HorizontalPodAutoscaler adds Pods, and when it falls, it takes them away. It automatically updates a workload resource such as a Deployment or StatefulSet to scale capacity to match demand, which is the idea of Autoscaling: letting the load add and remove servers applied to Pods. Horizontal scaling responds to increased load by deploying more Pods, unlike vertical scaling, which would give the running Pods more memory or CPU. The autoscaler is an API resource plus a controller in the control plane, running a control loop intermittently, by default every 15 seconds. Each period it reads metrics, and a utilization target is a percentage of the Pod's resource request. The core calculation is desiredReplicas = ceil(currentReplicas x currentMetricValue / desiredMetricValue): a current value of 200m against a desired 100m doubles the replicas, and 50m halves them. The control plane skips scaling when the ratio is close enough to 1.0, within a tolerance that defaults to 0.1. With several metrics, each is evaluated and the largest desired replica count is used, up to the configured maximum.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-155 -->

- **Autoscaler flapping controls: stopping the replica count from swinging**

  Replica counts can fluctuate frequently as the evaluated metrics change, which is called thrashing or flapping. On scale-down the autoscaler uses the highest desired count from a stabilization window, a rolling maximum. That way it does not remove Pods only to recreate them moments later. The default window is 300 seconds. Scaling policies cap the rate of change as a number of Pods or a percentage per period. By default scale-up adds at most 4 Pods or 100% of the running replicas every 15 seconds. A tolerance of 10% makes the autoscaler ignore changes inside the threshold.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-156 -->

- **Scaling to zero: no replicas while a workload is idle**

  Some workloads sit idle for long periods and are expensive to keep running, such as consumers of an occasionally used queue or jobs needing dedicated hardware like GPUs. Scaling to zero lets an autoscaler reduce such a workload to no replicas and bring it back when a metric shows demand. It works with custom (object) or external metrics, where minReplicas can be set to 0. It is not available for resource metrics such as CPU or memory, which can only be measured on running Pods. While a workload is held at zero, the autoscaler sets a ScaledToZero condition, which tells it apart from one deactivated manually.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-157 -->

- **Pod requests and limits: what a container asks for and may use**

  A container can tell Kubernetes how much CPU and memory it needs and how much it may use, and those declarations drive scheduling and enforcement. The kube-scheduler uses the resource requests of a Pod's containers to decide which node to place the Pod on. The kubelet enforces limits so a running container cannot use more than its limit. CPU limits work by throttling, where the kernel restricts CPU access, and memory limits by out-of-memory kills. Autoscaling measures utilization as current usage divided by the Pod's requested resources, so requests must be set. Without one, CPU utilization is undefined and the autoscaler takes no action. A Pod's CPU and memory can also change after creation. In-place resize updates the desired state through the /resize subresource, and the kubelet applies it to running containers. Only CPU and memory can be resized, and resizePolicy says whether a restart is needed. Resizing by replacement works on any Kubernetes version and can change any Pod specification, but it replaces Pods, so the workload must tolerate planned disruptions.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-160 -->

- **Rolling update: replacing a version one instance at a time**

  A rolling update swaps old instances for new ones one by one, so the application stays available throughout. A Deployment's strategy type is RollingUpdate, the default, or Recreate. A rolling update gradually scales down the old ReplicaSets and scales up the new one, and it suits periodic releases. Recreate kills all existing Pods before creating new ones, which suits non-critical applications or early development. Two settings set the pace. The first, maxUnavailable, caps the Pods that may be unavailable during the update. The second, maxSurge, caps the Pods created above the desired number. Each is a number or a percentage, and each defaults to 25%: a percentage is rounded down for maxUnavailable and up for maxSurge. With maxUnavailable at 30%, at least 70% of desired Pods stay available, and with maxSurge at 30% the total never exceeds 130% of desired. They cannot both be 0, so at least one must allow change. The minReadySeconds setting is how long a new Pod must be ready without a crash before it counts as available, and it defaults to 0.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-150 -->

  *Figure: Three settings control the pace of a rolling update.*

  | Setting | What it caps or sets | Default |
  |---|---|---|
  | maxUnavailable | Pods unavailable during the update | 25%, rounded down |
  | maxSurge | Pods created above the desired number | 25%, rounded up |
  | minReadySeconds | How long a new Pod must be ready to count as available | 0 |

- **Deployments and ReplicaSets: the right number of Pods, and undo**

  A bad rollout can be undone because Kubernetes keeps the old version around. A ReplicaSet keeps a stable set of replica pods running at any given time, and uses a selector to identify the pods associated with it. A Deployment is the higher-level mechanism that manages ReplicaSets, usually for a workload that keeps no state.
