You declare the desired state, and the Deployment controller changes the actual state to match it at a controlled rate. The ReplicaSet controller manages the scale, while the Deployment controller manages what happens to the ReplicaSet, such as whether an update is rolled out or rolled back. Updating the Pod template (see Pod templates: the blueprint a controller copies from) creates a new ReplicaSet that is scaled up as the old one is scaled down. A Deployment's revision history is kept in its old ReplicaSets, 10 by default; once an old one is deleted, that revision can no longer be rolled back to. A Deployment is progressing, complete or failed to progress, and progressDeadlineSeconds (default 600) sets how long to wait before reporting failure.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-056 -->

- **StatefulSets: giving each instance an identity and an order**

  Scaling a stateless application only means adding more pods. Stateful workloads are harder, because state must be preserved when a pod restarts and may need to be redistributed when scaling. A StatefulSet is a Kubernetes controller that enforces uniqueness and ordering among the instances of a pod so that such applications can run. Both properties matter. Databases are stateful, and in high-availability mode many have a primary and secondary instances, so the ordering of instances matters. Applications such as Apache Kafka distribute data among their brokers, so one broker is not the same as another and instance uniqueness matters.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-057 -->

- **Kubernetes control plane: the brain behind the API**

  Every operation on pods goes through one door: the API server. The Kubernetes control plane manages the cluster's workload and its worker nodes and directs communication across the system. In production it usually runs across multiple computers for fault tolerance and high availability. The API server serves the Kubernetes API using JSON over HTTPS as both the internal and external interface. It processes and validates REST requests (see REST: the architectural style behind most web APIs) and updates the state of API objects in the key-value store that backs all cluster data (see etcd: the cluster's memory, and why it picks consistency). The scheduler selects the node an unscheduled pod runs on, based on resource availability and other constraints. It tracks allocation so workload is not scheduled beyond a node's available resources. The controller manager runs the controllers, including the node, job, EndpointSlice and ServiceAccount controllers, as a single process. Kubernetes follows a primary/replica architecture, with components divided between those that manage an individual node and those that form the control plane.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-051 -->

  *Figure: The control plane's main components each have one job.*

  | Component | What it does |
  |---|---|
  | API server | Serves the Kubernetes API; every operation on pods goes through it |
  | etcd | Backing store for all cluster data |
  | Scheduler | Picks the node for an unscheduled pod |
  | Controller manager | Runs the controllers as a single process |

- **Kubernetes controllers: loops that keep reality matching the declaration**

  Declare three instances of a pod, and a controller notices when only two are running. A Kubernetes controller is a reconciliation loop that drives the actual cluster state toward the desired state by creating, updating and deleting the resources it manages. Objects record the desired state in a spec field, while the controller of the resource keeps a status field describing the current state up to date. In the example, the Deployment controller finds two running and schedules the creation of another. The ReplicaSet controller runs a specified number of copies of a pod across the cluster and creates replacement pods if the underlying node fails. The DaemonSet controller ensures a pod runs on every node, which suits workloads tied to the host such as log collection and storage services. The Job controller runs pods to completion, as in a batch job. Label selectors often specify the set of pods a controller manages. The controller manager is one process managing several core controllers, and custom controllers can be installed to extend Kubernetes together with custom resources.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-053 -->

- **Pod templates: the blueprint a controller copies from**

  Change a pod template and nothing happens to the Pods already running. A pod template is the specification a workload controller uses to create the Pods it manages. Controllers for workload resources such as Deployments, Jobs and DaemonSets create Pods from a template included in the workload object. The template is part of the workload's desired state. Changing it has no direct effect on existing Pods. The controller creates replacement Pods from the new template instead of patching the old ones, until all old Pods are replaced. A running Pod can be edited in place only a little, since most metadata is immutable.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-158 -->

- **Kubernetes operators: a human operator's knowledge, automated**

  Some applications need a human who knows how to run them. A Kubernetes Operator captures that knowledge and automates it, for example taking and restoring backups or handling upgrades together with schema or configuration changes. It is the combination of custom resources and custom controllers. The Kubernetes API can be extended with Custom Resources, declared through Custom Resource Definitions that can be registered and unregistered without restarting a running cluster. Custom controllers observe those resources and reconcile the cluster toward the declared desired state, giving users a declarative API.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-062 -->

- **etcd: the cluster's memory, and why it picks consistency**

  During a network partition, etcd favors consistency over availability, because consistency is crucial for correctly scheduling and operating services. That is the CAP trade-off (The CAP theorem: why no store can have everything) made on purpose. etcd is a persistent, lightweight, distributed key-value data store, originally developed as part of CoreOS. In Kubernetes it is the backing store for all cluster data. It reliably holds the cluster's configuration, and so represents the overall state of the cluster at any given point in time. The API server uses its watch API to monitor the cluster and roll out critical configuration changes. It also restores any divergence back to the desired state declared there.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-052 -->

- **Ingress controllers and classes: who carries out the rules**

  Ingress controllers should all fit the reference specification, but in reality they operate slightly differently. An Ingress controller carries out the Ingress rules, and one must be running to satisfy an Ingress. Ingresses can be implemented by different controllers, so each should name an IngressClass. That resource carries extra configuration, including the name of the controller that implements the class. An IngressClass can reference a parameters resource, cluster-scoped by default or namespaced. Namespaced parameters let the cluster operator delegate control of settings such as load balancer configuration to a workload's team.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-154 -->

- **Feature toggle: shipping unfinished code hidden behind a switch**

  A feature toggle lets unfinished code ship hidden. It is a condition in the code that enables or disables a feature at runtime, as an alternative to maintaining multiple feature branches. Toggles are also called feature flags, switches or gates. An unfinished feature can be merged into the main branch and hidden behind a toggle. It can then be switched on in a test environment, or in production on demand for some or all users. That shortens integration cycles and allows many small incremental versions, so releasing often becomes easier. Toggles come as release, experiment, ops and permissioning types, which differ by how long they should live. An ops toggle can act as a kill switch that disables a feature at runtime during an incident. Toggle debt arises when a feature is toggled on permanently and dead code remains, so toggles need lifecycle management. Martin Fowler says a release toggle should be your last choice; it is better to break the feature into smaller parts that can each be released safely.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-141 -->

- **Configuration distribution models: four ways to get settings to a running service**

  Configuration changes are a potential source of instability, so every distribution scheme stores configuration in the main source repository and enforces strict code review. The schemes differ in how they trade flexibility, simplicity and drift between the stored and the running version.

  Mainline: changes to configuration files at the head of the main branch are reviewed and then applied to the running system. This decouples binary releases from configuration, but the running version can skew from the checked-in one. Same package: shipping configuration files in the binary's package binds the two tightly and limits flexibility, but simplifies deployment because only one package is installed.

  Separate configuration packages: snapshotting configuration alongside its binary lets each change independently. A wrong feature flag value can then be fixed by cherry picking, rebuilding the configuration package and deploying, without a new binary. External store: configuration that must change often or while the binary is running can be read from an external store such as Chubby, Bigtable or a source-based filesystem. Project owners weigh these options and choose case by case.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-166 -->

- **Blue-green deployment: swap environments, roll back by swapping again**

  Blue-green deployment makes a release a switch, and a rollback the same switch in reverse. Two servers or environments are kept, one blue and one green. Only one handles requests at a time, for example the one DNS (see DNS: the phone book of the Internet) points to, while the other is a staging server on a private network. Changes are installed on the non-live environment and tested through the private network; once verified, it is swapped with the live one and the changes go live. Because requests move instantly from one environment to the other, ideally no request goes unfulfilled, so downtime is reduced. Rollback is quick: traffic is simply routed back to the previous live environment, which never received the deployed changes. The cost is running two environments at once, and duplicate infrastructure, even temporarily, can be prohibitive for smaller organizations. Complex database migrations are harder, since blue and green must hold consistent data; migration tools that keep both environments backward compatible are a common solution. Blue-green is often contrasted with Canary release: trying a new version on a small slice of users and suits high-stake updates.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-039 -->

- **Deployment strategies: recreate, rolling, blue-green, canary, shadow and A/B**

  There is more than one way to replace a running version of an application with a new one, and each manages the update differently. Recreate terminates all existing instances at once and then creates new ones with the updated version; it suits non-critical applications or early development. A rolling update replaces instances one by one, keeping availability high during the process, and suits periodic releases. Blue-green keeps two identical environments, one with the current version and one with the updated version, and switches traffic from blue to the prepared green environment. A canary sends the new version to a subset of users or servers for testing before broader deployment, to validate its impact on that subset. Shadow deployment redirects a copy of live traffic to the new version so it can be tested without affecting production users. It is the most complex strategy, because it needs mock services that interact with the new version. A/B testing runs several versions at once on different users to compare performance or user experience, so it aims at optimizing user experience. Another list of the most-used strategies names big bang, rolling, blue-green, canary and feature toggle deployment.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-040 -->

  *Figure: Each strategy replaces a running version in a different way.*

  | Strategy | How it works | Note |
  |---|---|---|
  | Recreate | Terminates all instances, then creates new ones | Non-critical apps, early development |
  | Rolling update | Replaces instances one by one | Periodic releases |
  | Blue-green | Switches traffic from blue to the prepared green | Two identical environments |
  | Canary | New version goes to a subset of users or servers | Validates impact first |
  | Shadow | Copies live traffic to the new version | Most complex: needs mock services |
  | A/B testing | Runs several versions at once on different users | Optimizes user experience |

- **Canary release: trying a new version on a small slice of users**

  Turn a feature on for 1% of users and leave everyone else off: that is a canary release. It exposes a new version or feature to a small set of users first, so it can be tested incrementally before a wider rollout. The canary validates the version's impact, and if the feature's performance is not satisfactory it can be rolled back without adverse effects. Blue-green deployment is often contrasted with it. Feature flags are an alternative way to run canary launches and allow targeting by geographic location or by user attributes. The SRE book calls it a best practice to test a new release on a small subset of a typical workload. The open questions are how long to wait and how big the canary should be. In Google's release process, a typical canary deployment starts a few jobs in the production environment after system tests complete. In Kubernetes a canary is done with multiple Deployments, one per release, and a release_track label with values such as canary and production tells pods apart.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-142 -->

- **Risk-based rollouts: pushing as carefully as the service demands**

  A rollout should be as careful as the service is sensitive. A risk-based rollout fits how fast and how widely a release is pushed to the risk profile of the service. In development or pre-production, builds can run hourly and be pushed automatically when all tests pass. For large user-facing services, a push starts in one cluster and expands exponentially until all clusters are updated. For sensitive infrastructure, the rollout may stretch over several days, interleaving instances in different geographic regions. Automation can update all jobs at once or roll a new binary out to successive clusters over hours.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-167 -->

### Authentication and security

Every request that reaches a system raises two questions: who is asking, and what may they do. This chapter takes both in turn. It starts with authentication, the act of proving an assertion such as a user's identity, and the three kinds of evidence behind it: something the user knows, has or is. It then turns to authorization, which specifies rights to access resources, and to OAuth 2.0, which lets a user grant an application consented access to another site without sharing credentials. Along the way come the attacks that shape the defenses, such as cross-site scripting, and the details that matter, such as the random data called a salt that goes into password hashing.

- **Authentication: proving who you are**

  A password does not prove who you are. Like a key card, it implies authenticity without guaranteeing it. Authentication is the act of proving an assertion, such as the identity of a computer system user.

  Two ideas are easy to blur. Identification only indicates who a person or thing is, while authentication is the process of verifying that claim. In computing, a user's identity often has to be verified before confidential data or systems can be reached.

  Authentication is also distinct from permission checking, which Authorization: deciding what you may do covers. Authentication verifies that you are who you say you are. Permission checking verifies that you are allowed to do what you are trying to do. It often follows authentication but does not presuppose it, because an anonymous agent could be authorized for a limited set of actions.

  Trust has to come from somewhere. Most secure internet communication relies on centralized trust. In HTTPS, public certificate authorities vouch for the authenticity of websites, and OpenID Connect: login built on OAuth rests on the same model, with companies such as Google authenticating users for other applications. The alternative is decentralized, peer-based trust. In a web of trust, as in PGP, individuals personally verify and sign each other's cryptographic keys, with no central authority.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-015 -->

- **Cross-site scripting: when a page runs an attacker's code**

  A browser trusts a page because of where it came from, and cross-site scripting exploits exactly that. Cross-site scripting (XSS) is a web-application vulnerability that lets attackers inject client-side scripts into pages viewed by other users. Under the same-origin policy, content from URLs with the same scheme, host name and port gets the same permissions, as HTTP origins: why the browser checks the certificate matches explains. The injected script arrives from the trusted site, so it runs with that site's permissions and can reach session cookies.

  The kinds differ in where the script hides. In reflected XSS, a server uses client data, usually query parameters, to build a page without sanitizing it, as when a search page echoes the query. Stored XSS is more devastating: the server saves the attacker's data and shows it to other users, as on a message board that lets users post HTML. In DOM-based XSS the data never touches the server, because the page's own JavaScript reflects it into the page. It is a case of code injection, grouped under Injection in the 2021 and 2025 editions of the OWASP Top 10.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-127 -->

- **Authentication factors: know, have, are**

  Every way of proving who you are draws on one of three kinds of evidence. Authentication factors are the three categories of evidence used to verify identity: something the user knows, something the user has, and something the user is. Each factor covers a range of elements used to verify a person's identity before granting access, approving a transaction, or signing a document.

  Knowledge factors are things the user knows, such as a password, passphrase, PIN, challenge-response or security question. Ownership factors are things the user has: an ID card, a security token, or a cell phone holding a software token. Inherence factors are what the user is or does, such as a fingerprint, retinal pattern, face, voice, signature or other biometric identifier.

  Security research has determined that a positive authentication should verify elements from at least two factors, and preferably all three. Even the strongest-sounding factor can disappoint. Fingerprints were historically the most authoritative method, but court cases in the US and elsewhere have raised fundamental doubts about their reliability.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-016 -->

  *Figure: Each factor is a different kind of evidence, with examples from each.*

  | Factor | What it is | Examples |
  |---|---|---|
  | Knowledge | Something the user knows | Password, PIN, security question |
  | Ownership | Something the user has | ID card, security token, cell phone |
  | Inherence | Something the user is | Fingerprint, face, voice |

- **Salt: why identical passwords should not look identical**

  Two users pick the same password, and anyone reading an unsalted password database can see it, because identical passwords give identical hashes. A salt is random data fed as an additional input to a one-way function that hashes a password or passphrase, as Hash function: any input, one fixed-size value explains. The system concatenates salt and password, hashes the result, and stores the hash with the salt. The salt needs no encryption, since knowing it would not help the attacker.

  A fresh salt for each password gives different hashes for the same password. It also forces an attacker to hash each guess separately against every entry. And it defeats the precomputed tables described in Rainbow tables: cracking hashes by lookup, since building a table for every unique salt is not viable. A salt of 16 bytes (128 bits) or more is generally sufficient. Reusing one salt is dangerous: a table that accounts for it becomes viable, and cracking one hash exposes others with the same password.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-120 -->

- **Authorization: deciding what you may do**

  Knowing who someone is settles nothing until the system decides what that person may do. Authorization is the function of specifying rights to access resources, usually through an access policy, and then deciding whether a particular subject may access a particular resource. Subjects can be human users, software or hardware. Resources can be files, data, programs, devices or application functions.

  Access control enforces the policy by approving or rejecting access requests from authenticated consumers. Identity and access management runs in two phases. A configuration phase creates the user account and defines its access policy. In the usage phase, authentication comes first and access control follows. Consumers should get only what they need to do their jobs, an idea covered in Least privilege: only what the job needs.

  Maintaining this data is not trivial. It often costs as much administration as managing credentials, because changing a user's authorization means changing or deleting the matching access rules. Broken authorization is often listed as the number one risk in web applications.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-030 -->

- **OAuth 2.0: access without sharing your password**

  You can give an application a narrow view of your account without ever handing over your password. That is the promise of OAuth 2.0. It is an open standard for access delegation that lets a user grant an application consented access to resources on another site without sharing credentials. An app holding an OAuth token can reach only the parts of the user's profile that the user allowed.

  OAuth 2.0 is an authorization protocol, not an authentication protocol. It is designed primarily to grant access to a set of resources such as remote APIs or a user's data. Four roles take part. The resource owner owns the protected resources, and the client needs access to them. The authorization server issues tokens, described in The access token: a key with limits, after authentication and consent. The resource server validates the tokens and returns resources. Scopes specify exactly why access may be granted, and the acceptable scope values depend on the resource server.

  OAuth 1 is specified in RFC 5849 and OAuth 2 in RFC 6749. The newer version has critics. Singh lists three common disadvantages: it lacks built-in security features, has no standard implementation, and has no common set of scopes. Eran Hammer, a former lead author, argued that OAuth 2.0 became more complex, less interoperable and less secure than 1.0. He blamed the removal of protocol-level signatures and cryptography, and the many items left for implementations to decide.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-022 -->

- **Least privilege: only what the job needs**

  An account that only creates backups may run backup applications, and it cannot install software. That is the principle of least privilege in miniature. Every module, such as a process, user or program, should be able to access only the information and resources necessary for its legitimate purpose.

  The payoff comes in three ways. Limiting what code can do system-wide means a vulnerability in one application cannot be used to exploit the rest of the machine. Code with limited scope is easier to test for its possible actions and interactions. And the fewer privileges an application requires, the easier it is to deploy.

  Jerome Saltzer's original formulation says every program and every privileged user should operate with the least amount of privilege necessary to complete the job. The idea is associated with privilege bracketing: assume privileges at the last possible moment and dismiss them as soon as they are unnecessary. True least privilege is hard, though. Practice removes the privileges judged unnecessary, which leaves more than the true minimum.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-126 -->

- **Multi-factor authentication: more than one proof**

  A stolen password opens every account that asks for nothing else. Multi-factor authentication (MFA) closes that gap. It grants a user access only after they present two or more distinct types of evidence, or factors, to an authentication mechanism. The premise is that an unauthorized actor is unlikely to supply every factor. If one is missing or wrong, access stays blocked. Accounts with MFA enabled are significantly less likely to be compromised.

  Two-factor authentication is the special case of exactly two factors, such as a bank card together with a PIN. Stacking checks of one kind adds nothing: a fingerprint, a face and a PIN with a day code is still two-factor. Single-factor authentication, the weakest level, offers little protection from misuse.

  Rules have caught up with the practice. PCI DSS requirement 8.3 requires MFA for remote access into a card data environment. The second Payment Services Directive has required strong customer authentication on most electronic payments in the European Economic Area since 14 September 2019.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-017 -->

- **Why OAuth is not a login system**

  A valet key gives access without saying who is holding it, and an OAuth token works the same way. That is why using OAuth on its own as a login method, called pseudo-authentication, is a trap. OAuth says nothing about who the user is.

  The client asked for a token, got one and used it, without knowing who authorized it or whether a user was there at all. Much of the point of OAuth is delegated access where the user is not present. That is bad for authentication, where the point is to find out who is there.

  The temptation is understandable, because the issuing service usually authenticates the user along the way. OAuth was not designed for login, though, and the assumption can cause major security flaws. A stolen valet key lets an attacker impersonate its user to any application relying on OAuth2 for pseudo-authentication against the same authorization server. The approach in OpenID: sign in through a third-party provider avoids this, because its response is an assertion of identity and cryptographic verification prevents the theft. The fix built on OAuth itself is OpenID Connect: login built on OAuth.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-034 -->

- **Continuous authentication: checking all session long**

  Most computer systems check who you are once, at log-in, and trust you from then on. That can be a critical security flaw. Continuous authentication keeps monitoring and verifying a user throughout a session, based on biometric traits, instead of only at the initial log-in. Smartphone sensors can extract behavioral attributes such as touch dynamics, keystroke dynamics and gait recognition, which verify users implicitly and continuously. Systems built on these behavioral traits are known as active or continuous authentication systems.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-018 -->

- **Digital authentication: proving identity over a network**

  Digital authentication, also called electronic authentication, is a group of processes that establish and present confidence in user identities to an information system by electronic methods. It is technically challenging, because users are authenticated remotely over a network. In NIST's generic model, an applicant proves their identity to a credential service provider (CSP) and becomes a subscriber. The subscriber receives an authenticator, such as a token, plus credentials such as a user name. The subscriber then proves possession of the authenticator to a relying party, the service being used, in a session. A man-in-the-middle can pose as both parties, so extra identity factors may be required.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-019 -->

- **Access control models: how a policy is written**

  A rule about who may do what has to be written down somehow, and the way it is written decides how it is checked. Access control models are the ways an authorization policy is expressed and checked, such as lists, roles, attributes and relationships.

  Authorizations are expressed as access policies, for example as a capability or as the kind of list described in Access control lists: a permission list on every resource. In the role-based model, subjects get one or more roles, and access is allowed when the resource has been assigned at least one of them Role-based access control: permissions through roles covers it. A model based on relationships is gaining prominence with the rise of social media, and Relationship-based access control: permission through relationships covers that one.

  A policy language can go further. One framework is policy-based and attribute-based, so it can weigh attributes of the user, action, resource and context. It supplies the policy language that OAuth lacks, while OAuth handles consent and access delegation. That framework is XACML: a policy language, not an engine.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-031 -->

- **A security checklist for system design**

  Security is easier to build in than to bolt on, so one guide lists what a design should cover by default. Secure design protects sensitive information and keeps the infrastructure stable. The guide's key design points are authentication, authorization, encryption, vulnerability, network security, terminal security, container security, API security, audit and compliance, emergency responses, third-party vendors and disaster recovery.

  A few points show how the pieces fit. Multiple factors work because an unauthorized actor is unlikely to supply them all. The standard in WebAuthn: logging in with a key pair instead of a password verifies identity with digital signatures rather than shared passwords. Passwords are stored as salted hashes, with a unique salt per password. Authorization follows least privilege.

  Under vulnerability, XSS lets attackers inject scripts into pages other users view, and contextual output encoding counters it. Forged requests, the subject of Cross-site request forgery: abusing a site's trust in your browser, are countered by embedding extra authentication data, such as unique tokens, in requests. Zero trust does not trust users and devices by default, even on a corporate LAN. In transit, OAuth forbids sending tokens or passwords in the clear and requires TLS on its endpoints.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-028 -->

- **Sessions, tokens and other ways to stay logged in**

  After you log in once, a website has to recognize you on every later request, and it has six common ways to manage a logged-in user's identity.

  With a session, the server stores the user's identity and gives the browser a session ID cookie, which lets the server track login state. Cookies do not work well across devices. With a token, the identity is encoded into a token that the browser sends on later requests. The server needs no session storage, though tokens need encryption and decryption. A standard format for such tokens uses digital signatures for trust; JSON Web Tokens: identity that carries its own proof explains it. The signature travels inside the token, so no server session is needed.

  The other three methods involve a second party or device. A central authentication service can make one login work across multiple sites, which Single sign-on: log in once, reach everything covers. OAuth 2.0 lets one site get limited access to your data on another site without being given your passwords. QR-code login encodes a random token into a QR code, and scanning it logs the user in on mobile without typing a password.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-021 -->

- **Cross-site request forgery: abusing a site's trust in your browser**

  Your browser will vouch for you to any site that holds your cookie, even when you did not ask it to. Cross-site request forgery (CSRF) is an exploit in which a web application receives unauthorized commands from a user that it trusts. An innocent user is tricked into submitting a request they did not intend, through image tags, hidden forms or JavaScript, which changes session state or the user's account.

  It works because browsers automatically and invisibly include a domain's cookies in any request to that domain. A forged request from another page therefore looks genuine. Unlike XSS, which exploits the trust a user has in a site, CSRF exploits the trust a site has in a user's browser.

  An attack needs a site without CSRF protection, a state-changing action, input values the attacker can determine, and a victim who is logged in. GET is meant to be safe, yet a GET can be forged with an IMG tag. Applications that use GET to change state should switch to POST or add anti-CSRF protection.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-129 -->

- **The access token: a key with limits**

  Every request in an OAuth exchange rides on one small string. An access token is a credential, usually an opaque string, representing an authorization issued to the client for accessing protected resources. It represents specific scopes and durations of access, granted by the resource owner and enforced by the resource server and authorization server. A token may be an identifier used to look up the authorization information, or it may carry that information itself, as data plus a signature.

  The token replaces a username and password with a single credential the resource server understands. It can be more restrictive than the grant that produced it, which spares the resource server many authentication methods. The client should request the minimal scope necessary. The server may issue less, and it must say what scope it granted.

  The client presents the token to the resource server to reach protected resources. Tokens must not be forgeable or guessable, so the chance of guessing one should stay at or below 2^(-128). They must stay confidential and travel only over TLS.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-134 -->

- **Refresh tokens: short-lived access that renews**

  An access token should expire quickly, and the refresh token is what makes that bearable. A refresh token is a credential the authorization server issues to the client for obtaining new access tokens. When the current token expires or becomes invalid, the client uses it to get a new one. That lets access tokens be short-lived and carry fewer permissions than the owner authorized.

  Issuing a refresh token is optional. Unlike access tokens, refresh tokens are intended only for authorization servers and are never sent to resource servers. When the access token expires, the client authenticates with the authorization server and presents the refresh token. The server validates it and issues a new access token and, optionally, a new refresh token. The requested scope must not exceed the original grant, and the token is bound to the client it was issued to.

  Rotation reveals theft. The server issues a new refresh token with each refresh and invalidates the old one, so the attacker or the legitimate client will eventually present an invalidated token. Refresh tokens must be kept confidential.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-135 -->

- **JSON Web Tokens: identity that carries its own proof**

  A JSON Web Token carries its own proof inside it. A JSON Web Token (JWT) is an Internet standard for creating data, optionally signed and optionally encrypted, whose JSON payload asserts a number of claims. It is a Proposed Standard, RFC 7519, and relies on the JSON Web Signature and JSON Web Encryption standards.

  A JWT has three parts: a header naming the signing algorithm, a payload containing a set of claims, and a signature that validates the token. Each part is Base64url-encoded and the parts are joined with periods. The signature is computed over the encoded header and payload, typically with HMAC using SHA-256 (HS256) or an RSA signature with SHA-256 (RS256). One party, usually the server, signs with its private key. Anyone holding the matching public key can verify the token.

  Tokens are compact and URL-safe. The client sends the JWT in the Authorization header with the Bearer schema. User state is never kept in server memory and the token is self-contained, so this is stateless and avoids repeated database queries.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-032 -->

  *Figure: A JWT is three Base64url-encoded parts joined with periods.* (layers; drawn in the EPUB)

- **OpenID Connect: login built on OAuth**

  OAuth 2.0 can tell an application what it may reach, but not who is knocking. OpenID Connect fills that gap. It is a thin authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that adds login and profile information about the person who is logged in. Clients can verify an end user's identity from the authorization server's authentication and fetch basic profile information.

  It specifies a RESTful HTTP API with JSON as the data format, so web, mobile and JavaScript clients can ask about authenticated sessions and end users. The current application is the relying party. The provider gives it a one-time code, which the token endpoint exchanges for an access code valid for an hour. The token arrives in the format of JSON Web Tokens: identity that carries its own proof. The relying party then calls the UserInfo endpoint with a secure token to learn about the end user.

  Because it sits on top of OAuth, it has a built-in permission layer that asks the user to agree to what the service provider may access. The older standard in SAML: identity assertions in XML achieves consent only by developer hard-coding.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-024 -->

- **JWT claims: the statements inside a token**

  A token is only as useful as what it says. The claims of a JWT are the name/value members of the JSON object, called the JWT Claims Set, that the token conveys. Claim names fall into three classes: registered, public and private. Private names are agreed between producer and consumer and can collide, so they need caution. The registered claims are a starting point, not a mandatory set, and each application defines which it uses.

  The common ones tell a service who issued the token and for whom. The iss claim names the issuer, sub names the subject, and iat records when the token was issued. The aud claim lists the intended recipients. If it is present and the processor is not named, the JWT must be rejected. A token must not be accepted on or after its exp time, nor before its nbf time. Implementers may allow a few minutes of leeway for clock skew. The jti claim gives the token a unique identifier, which can prevent replay.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-138 -->

- **Creating and validating a JWT, step by step**

  Making a JWT is a short recipe, and checking one is the same recipe run backward, with a rejection at every step. Creating a JWT builds a claims set and then signs or encrypts it. Validating one reverses those steps and rejects the token if any step fails.

  To create one, build the Claims Set, take its UTF-8 octets (bytes) as the message, and build a JOSE header. Then sign the message as a JWS payload (a JSON Web Signature) or encrypt it as JWE plaintext (a JSON Web Encryption). No canonicalization is needed. For nested signing or encryption, the resulting JWS or JWE becomes the new message and the steps repeat with a cty header value of JWT. Otherwise that JWS or JWE is the finished JWT.

  Validation starts by checking that the JWT contains at least one period. The part before the first period is base64url-decoded into a JOSE header, which must be valid JSON and contain only parameters the implementation understands and supports. The validator then decides whether the JWT is a JWS or a JWE, and validates the signature or decrypts accordingly. If the header's cty value is JWT, the message is itself a nested JWT and validation starts again on it. Otherwise the message is base64url-decoded and must be valid JSON, which becomes the Claims Set.

  If any step fails, the JWT must be rejected as invalid input. Even a JWT that validates should be rejected unless its algorithms are acceptable, because which algorithms may be used is an application decision.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-139 -->

- **Stopping CSRF: tokens, cookies and headers**

  A forged request can carry the victim's cookies, but it cannot carry a secret the attacker never sees. Most CSRF defenses build on that. They embed extra authentication data in requests so the application can spot requests from unauthorized locations.

  The synchronizer token pattern embeds a secret, unique token in every HTML form and verifies it on the server. The attacker cannot put a correct token in forged requests. In the cookie-to-header technique, the server sets a random token cookie, and JavaScript copies it into a custom HTTP header. The server validates the token. A double submit cookie sets the token as a cookie and as a hidden form field, then checks that they match. The server stores no token, but a site with cookie-setting functionality can bypass the scheme.

  Two defenses lean on the browser. The SameSite cookie attribute set to strict makes the browser send the cookie only on same-site requests, which defeats CSRF if the browser implements it correctly. Checking the Origin or Referer header is another approach, and a request omitting Referer must count as unauthorized.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-130 -->

- **Rainbow tables: cracking hashes by lookup**

  A rainbow table is a bargain struck between storage and processing time. It is a precomputed table of cryptographic hash outputs, usually used to recover passwords from stolen hashes. It needs less processing time and more storage than brute force, and more processing time and less storage than a table holding the hash of every possible password. It stores only the ends of long chains built by alternating the hash function with reduction functions. A table fits one hash function and fails against large salts, which would need a table per salt value. Use declined as of 2020, as salting spread and GPU brute force became practical.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-121 -->

- **Salted password hashing: how to store a password**

  Store a password as plain text, and anyone with internal access can read it. Store a bare hash, and precomputation attacks such as rainbow tables can undo it. The safer practice is to store each password as a hash of the password plus a unique random salt, never as plain text or a bare hash.

  According to OWASP, a salt is a unique, randomly generated string added to each password as part of the hashing process. It is not meant to be secret and can be stored in plain text in the database. What it does is make the hash result unique to each password. The database stores the hash of the password plus the salt.

  To validate a login, the system fetches the user's salt, appends it to the entered password, hashes the result, and compares it with the stored hash. If they match, the password is valid.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-020 -->

  *Figure: A login is checked by hashing the entered password with the stored salt and comparing hashes.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[User enters password] --> B[Fetch the user's salt]
  B --> C[Append salt, then hash]
  C --> D{Hashes match?}
  D -->|yes| E[Password is valid]
  D -->|no| F[Password is not valid]
  ```

- **OAuth 2.0 clients and endpoints**

  Before OAuth does anything, the client has to introduce itself. It registers with the authorization server, giving its client type and redirection URIs, and the server issues a unique client identifier. That identifier is not a secret and must not alone authenticate the client. A confidential client can keep its credentials secret, for example on a secure server. A public client cannot, as with an installed native application or a browser-based one. Three endpoints do the work. The authorization endpoint obtains authorization by redirecting the user-agent (the browser), the token endpoint exchanges a grant for an access token, and the client's redirection endpoint receives responses.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-136 -->

- **The OAuth 2.0 flow, from request to resource**

  The whole of OAuth 2.0 comes down to one exchange: the client asks for a token, and the resource server accepts it. In this flow a client obtains an access token from the authorization server, with the resource owner's consent, and uses it to request resources from the resource server.

  First the client requests authorization from the authorization server. It supplies its client id and secret as identification, the scopes it wants, and an endpoint URI to receive the access token or authorization code. The authorization server authenticates the client and verifies that the requested scopes are permitted, and the resource owner interacts with it to grant access. The server then redirects back to the client with an authorization code or an access token, depending on the grant type. It may also return a refresh token.

  With the access token the client asks the resource server for the resource. The resource server accepts and validates the token and returns the appropriate resources. The way the token is obtained is called an authorization grant, or authorization flow. The framework specifies several grant types for different use cases, such as Resource Owner Password Credentials (ROPC), which OAuth 2.0 grant types compared compares.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-023 -->

  *Figure: The flow runs from the client's request to the resource server's reply, in five steps.*

  | Step | Who acts | What happens |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 | Client | Asks the authorization server for authorization, naming the scopes it wants |
  | 2 | Authorization server | Authenticates the client; the resource owner grants access |
  | 3 | Authorization server | Redirects back with an authorization code or an access token |
  | 4 | Client | Presents the access token to the resource server |
  | 5 | Resource server | Validates the token and returns the resources |

- **OAuth 2.0 grant types compared**

  A grant is how a client proves it has permission to ask for a token. An authorization grant is a credential representing the resource owner's authorization that the client uses to obtain an access token. RFC 6749 defines four grant types and a way to add more.

  The first type sends the resource owner to the authorization server, which authenticates them and returns an authorization code. The owner's credentials are never shared with the client. The code lets the server authenticate the client and delivers the access token directly to the client, without passing through the user-agent, where it could be exposed. This grant is optimized for confidential clients, and The authorization code grant, step by step walks through it.

  The implicit grant, for in-browser JavaScript clients, issues an access token directly, with no intermediate code, and saves round trips. But it does not authenticate the client, it exposes the token to the user-agent, and it issues no refresh token.

  The resource owner password credentials grant exchanges the user's own username and password for a token. Use it only where the client is highly trusted, such as the device operating system, and no other grant is available. It carries higher risk because it keeps the password anti-pattern the protocol avoids: the client could abuse or leak the password. In the client credentials grant, the client authenticates with only its own credentials, when acting on its own behalf or on access previously arranged. Only confidential clients may use it, and it should not include a refresh token. Extension grants use an absolute URI, defined by the authorization server, as the grant_type value.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-132 -->

  *Figure: Each grant type suits a different kind of client and carries its own trade-off.*

  | Grant | Who it suits | Key point |
  |---|---|---|
  | Authorization code | Confidential clients | The owner's credentials never reach the client |
  | Implicit | In-browser JavaScript clients | Exposes the token; no refresh token |
  | Resource owner password | Highly trusted clients, such as the device OS | Keeps the password anti-pattern |
  | Client credentials | Confidential clients acting for themselves | No refresh token should be included |

- **The authorization code grant, step by step**

  The authorization code grant is a redirection-based flow that obtains access and refresh tokens via the user-agent and is optimized for confidential clients. Its trick is a two-step exchange: the browser carries only a short-lived code, and the real token goes straight to the client.

  The client directs the user-agent to the authorization endpoint with its client identifier, requested scope, local state and a redirection URI. The server authenticates the resource owner and establishes whether they grant or deny access. If access is granted, the server redirects the user-agent to the redirection URI with an authorization code and any state the client provided. The client then makes a POST to the token endpoint with grant_type authorization_code, authenticating and repeating the redirection URI. The server authenticates the client, validates the code, checks that the URI matches, and returns an access token and optionally a refresh token.

  Several safeguards surround the code. It must expire shortly after it is issued, with a maximum lifetime of 10 minutes recommended, and the client must not use it more than once. If a code is used twice, the server must deny the request and should revoke tokens previously issued from it. The code is bound to the client identifier and redirection URI. The recommended state parameter, which the server returns unchanged, helps prevent cross-site request forgery. If the redirection URI is missing, invalid or mismatching, the server must not automatically redirect the user-agent to it.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-133 -->

- **Attacks on OAuth 2.0 and their defenses**

  OAuth moves secrets through browsers and redirects, and attackers have found the weak spots. If an attacker alters redirect_uri, the authorization code can reach a URI they control. The server must check that the URI used to get the code matches the one used to redeem it. An open redirector forwards a user-agent to any location named in a parameter. It can leak a code or token if clients may register only part of a redirection URI. CSRF against a client's redirection URI lets an attacker inject their own code, so the client needs a non-guessable state parameter.

  In clickjacking, an attacker loads the authorization page in a transparent iframe over dummy buttons, and servers can send an x-frame-options header of deny or sameorigin. Secrets must never travel in the clear, so the server must require TLS on its endpoints. A formal analysis also found the AS Mix-Up Attack, in which a client forwards secrets to a malicious one of several authorization servers. The draft of OAuth 2.1 recommends PKCE for all types of client; PKCE: a one-time secret for the authorization code explains it.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-035 -->

- **PKCE: a one-time secret for the authorization code**

  On a phone, a malicious app can register as a handler for the legitimate app's custom URI scheme and receive its authorization code. A secret built into the client would not stop it. Proof Key for Code Exchange (PKCE) is an OAuth 2.0 extension that binds the code to a one-time secret only the real client holds.

  For each authorization request the client creates a random secret, the code verifier, and sends a code challenge derived from it. Later it sends the code with the verifier, and the server transforms the verifier, compares it with the stored challenge, and denies access if they differ. The verifier never crossed a channel the attacker can observe, so an intercepted code is useless.

  The verifier is a high-entropy random string of 43 to 128 characters. The challenge is either the verifier itself, called plain, which an eavesdropper can see, or S256, the base64url encoding of the SHA-256 hash of the verifier. A client that can use S256 must, and it must never downgrade to plain afterward.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-137 -->

- **Preventing XSS: encode, sanitize, restrict**

  Stopping XSS starts with how output is written. Contextual output encoding escapes untrusted strings for where they land in the document: HTML entity, JavaScript, CSS or URL escaping. Apps that need no rich input can largely eliminate XSS this way. When users may submit HTML, encoding is not enough, because the browser must render it. A sanitization engine then lets safe elements through and escapes dangerous ones such as script tags. Session cookies are a target because client-side scripts can read them. An HttpOnly flag makes a cookie unavailable to scripts, and SameSite=Strict strips it from cross-origin requests, though neither fully prevents XSS.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-128 -->

- **WebAuthn: logging in with a key pair instead of a password**

  Passwords fail in familiar ways: people reuse them across services, choose weak ones, and sites store them badly. WebAuthn is a W3C web standard defining an API that websites use to authenticate users with public-key credentials, commonly called passkeys. It verifies identity with digital signatures instead of shared passwords. An authenticator, a device or program, proves to the website that the user possesses it. At registration, its signed attestation statement carries the public key the website later uses to verify its signed assertions.

  Platform authenticators are built into the operating system, such as Windows Hello and Apple Keychain. Roaming ones connect over USB, Bluetooth Low Energy or NFC. The scheme resists some phishing, the luring of users to fake sites, because the authenticator only offers credentials registered on the same website. A roaming hardware authenticator resists malware, because its keys sit on a separate device. WebAuthn grew from U2F, which improved on TOTP and SMS codes that left users open to phishing. Although touted as a password replacement, most sites implementing it still use passwords in some capacity.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-124 -->

- **API security practices**

  Securing an API comes down to a short list. One guide's tips are to use OAuth2, WebAuthn and leveled API keys. Then add authorization, rate limiting, whitelisting, an API gateway, error handling, input validation and API versioning, and check the OWASP API security risks.

  Several of these build on earlier entries. With OAuth 2.0, an access token replaces the user's password. The resource server understands it, and it can carry fewer rights than the grant that produced it. Tokens go only over TLS, never in the clear. WebAuthn verifies identity with digital signatures. Authorization should follow least privilege, so every module, user or program can access only what its legitimate purpose needs.

  Two tips guard against abuse. Input validation guards against code injection, where unsanitized input modifies application logic. Rate limiting matters for credentials. Without it, an attacker can try an arbitrary number of codes until one works. A limit tied to a session ID can be reset by creating new sessions.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-029 -->

- **Zero trust: no one is trusted by default**

  Sitting inside the corporate network is not reason enough to be trusted. Zero trust is a security strategy in which users and devices are not trusted by default. That holds even on a privileged network such as a corporate LAN, and even for users and devices verified before. Trust based on a perimeter or a VPN is commonly not enough for networks of many zones, cloud services, remote and mobile environments and IoT devices.

  Instead, zero trust establishes identity verification, validates device compliance before granting access, and ensures least privilege access to only explicitly authorized resources. It advocates mutual authentication that checks the identity and integrity of users and devices regardless of location. NIST SP 800-207 defines it as concepts that reduce the uncertainty of enforcing accurate per-request access decisions when the network is viewed as compromised. A full solution includes enhanced identity governance with policy-based access controls, micro-segmentation, and overlay networks or software-defined perimeters.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-131 -->

- **Signed, encrypted and nested JWTs**

  A JWT can be signed, encrypted, both, or neither. It is carried either as a signed JWS or an encrypted JWE, may nest one inside the other, and can also be left unsecured. In a JWS the claims are digitally signed and form the payload. In a JWE they are the encrypted plaintext. When both are needed, producers should normally sign first and then encrypt, which prevents stripping the signature and gives the signer privacy. An unsecured JWT is a JWS with the alg value none and an empty signature. A conforming implementation must support only HS256 and none, while RS256 and ES256 are recommended.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-140 -->

- **JWT security pitfalls**

  The worst JWT mistake is letting the token say how it should be checked. Some JWT libraries validated tokens wrongly based on the alg field, most commonly by accepting alg=none. Developers should never let the JWT header alone drive verification. Even a token that validates should be rejected unless its algorithms are acceptable, which is an application decision. A token's contents also cannot be trusted unless they are cryptographically secured and the signing key is verifiably under the issuer's control.

  Storage and privacy matter too. A JWT should reach the client by a secure mechanism such as an HTTP-only cookie, because client-side JavaScript can read local or session storage. A JWT may carry privacy-sensitive information, so encrypt it or send it only over TLS.

  The deepest trade-off is statelessness. If a service must invalidate a session before the token expires, it can no longer trust the token alone and must check a data store. That removes the main advantage of JWTs. Some have argued that JWTs are hard to use securely because the standard offers many algorithms and options.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-033 -->

- **Argon2: a password hash that costs memory**

  Argon2 is a key derivation function that won the 2015 Password Hashing Competition. It makes brute-force attacks expensive by using a large, fixed-size memory region. All three modes are tuned by execution time, memory required and degree of parallelism. Argon2d maximizes resistance to GPU cracking but risks side-channel attacks, Argon2i resists those, and Argon2id is a hybrid. RFC 9106 recommends Argon2id if you do not know the difference or if side-channel attacks are a viable threat. Its default for all environments is 2 GiB of memory, 1 iteration and parallelism 4. Where memory is constrained, it suggests 64 MiB, 3 iterations and parallelism 4.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-123 -->

- **bcrypt: a hash that can be made slower**

  bcrypt is a password-hashing function, based on the Blowfish cipher, designed by Niels Provos and David Mazières. It incorporates a salt against rainbow table attacks. It is also adaptive: the iteration count can be raised over time, so it stays resistant to brute-force search as computing power grows. Its key setup repeats a configurable number of rekeying rounds, which can make hashing arbitrarily slow. Inputs are a password of up to 72 bytes, a cost and a 16-byte salt. The cost is log2 of the iterations, so 12 means 4,096. Passwords are cut at 72 bytes, only 18 characters in the worst case of 4-byte UTF-8.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-122 -->

- **How attackers get around MFA**

  MFA raises the bar, but it can still be bypassed through phishing, SIM swapping, fatigue attacks and implementation flaws. Many approaches remain vulnerable to phishing, man-in-the-browser and man-in-the-middle attacks, so users should not share verification codes with anyone. SMS codes are weak. Phones can be cloned, and maintenance personnel can read texts. SS7 vulnerabilities let messages be redirected to attackers, and SIM swap attacks hand duplicate SIM cards to criminals. An MFA fatigue attack floods a user with push login requests until one is accepted by mistake. Number matching is an interim mitigation, and phishing-resistant MFA is advised instead of push notifications.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-119 -->

- **Identity provider**

  Somebody has to keep the list of who the users are. An identity provider is a centralized trusted system that stores and manages user identities and authenticates users on behalf of other applications. It authenticates a user either by validating a username and password or by validating an assertion from a separate identity provider. Service providers rely on it to assert who a user is. A service provider may still keep a local account for the user, holding attributes unique to its own service. An identity broker connects many service providers with different identity providers, so one login works with any application, whatever protocol it follows.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-026 -->

- **Single sign-on: log in once, reach everything**

  Single sign-on is an authentication scheme in which a user logs in once, with a single set of credentials, to reach several related but independent applications. It removes the need to log in separately to each application, and true single sign-on lets the user access services without re-entering authentication factors. It works because credentials and identity information are kept in one place, by the central trusted system that Identity provider describes.

  In the flow, the user requests a resource and the application redirects them to the identity provider. The user signs in, the identity provider sends a single sign-on response to the application, and the application grants access. Same sign-on is different: every application still asks for authentication but reuses credentials from a directory server, where true single sign-on passes one authentication token. Because applications support different authentication mechanisms, it must store the credentials used at first sign-in and translate them for each system. The converse, single log-out, ends access to several systems with one action.

  Benefits include one set of credentials to remember, less password fatigue and lower IT support cost.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-025 -->

  *Figure: In single sign-on the application sends the user to the identity provider and waits for its response.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[User requests a resource] --> B[Application redirects to identity provider]
  B --> C[User signs in]
  C --> D[Identity provider sends SSO response]
  D --> E[Application grants access]
  ```

- **Kerberos: tickets instead of passwords on the wire**

  On a network where anyone can listen, Kerberos never sends your password. It is a ticket-based protocol for proving identity on a non-secure network, with mutual authentication: user and server each verify the other. It builds on symmetric-key cryptography and needs a trusted third party, the key distribution center (KDC), whose authentication server (AS) and ticket-granting service (TGS) issue the tickets.

  At logon the client authenticates to the AS, which returns a time-stamped ticket-granting ticket (TGT) encrypted with the TGS's secret key. To use a service, the client sends the TGT to the TGS, which issues a service ticket and session keys. The client presents that ticket to the service, which decrypts it with its own secret key and checks the client's authenticator. It replies with the timestamp encrypted under the session key, which lets the client trust the server.

  Tickets have a lifetime, so clocks must be synchronized within configured limits, five minutes by default in MIT's setup, or authentication fails. A central KDC is also a weak point: compromising it lets an attacker impersonate any user.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-125 -->

  *Figure: Kerberos trades tickets in four steps, and the password is never sent.*

  | Step | Between | What happens |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 | Client and AS | The client authenticates and gets a ticket-granting ticket (TGT) |
  | 2 | Client and TGS | The client sends the TGT and gets a service ticket and session keys |
  | 3 | Client and service | The client presents the service ticket with its request |
  | 4 | Service and client | The service replies with the timestamp encrypted under the session key |

- **OpenID: sign in through a third-party provider**

  OpenID is an open, decentralized authentication protocol that lets users sign in to many sites through a third-party identity provider. A site, the relying party, uses that provider to authenticate users. It needs no login system of its own, and users need no separate password for each site. The provider gives each user a unique identifier, an OpenID, and prompts them to authenticate when a supporting site redirects them there. The design has weak spots. A malicious relying party can send users to a bogus provider page to steal credentials, and the provider's log of every OpenID login makes cross-site tracking easier.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-036 -->

- **The risks of single sign-on**

  Single sign-on trades convenience for a bigger target. Because one login unlocks many resources, stolen credentials do more damage, and a compromised main SSO password exposes every supported application. It should ideally be paired with strong methods such as smart cards and one-time password tokens. It also increases dependence on highly available authentication systems. Losing them can deny access to every system unified under it, though session failover can keep operation going. Where access must be guaranteed at all times, as in security or plant-floor systems, that risk may make single sign-on undesirable.

  Authentication is also slower, because every application must ask the SSO provider to verify. The SSO token cannot be protected with the HttpOnly cookie flag. An XSS flaw on the logged-out website can let an attacker steal it and hijack the session. A stolen SSO session reaches every site using the system. Kerberos and the XML-based scheme in SAML: identity assertions in XML originally gave users no choice about releasing personal information. As federated services spread and privacy rules such as the GDPR tighten, OpenID Connect: login built on OAuth has become more attractive.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-037 -->

- **SAML: identity assertions in XML**

  Security Assertion Markup Language (SAML) is an open XML-based standard for sharing identity, authentication and permission information between systems, such as an identity provider and a service provider. It enables identity federation: identity providers securely pass authenticated identities and their attributes to service providers. In single sign-on, the user requests a resource at a service provider. It sends an authentication request to the identity provider through the user's browser and trusts the identity information it gets back. SAML is geared to enterprise security but can be complex to install and maintain. OAuth and OIDC use JSON and RESTful communication that suit mobile and modern web applications.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-027 -->

- **Single sign-on configurations**

  Single sign-on can ride on different mechanisms. In the Kerberos setup, the initial sign-on gets a ticket-granting ticket. Other applications, such as email clients, wikis and revision-control systems, use it to acquire service tickets without another prompt. In the smart-card setup, the initial sign-on prompts for the card, and other applications use it too, with certificates or passwords stored on it. Mobile devices can log users onto many systems using OpenID Connect or SAML with an X.509 certificate identifying the device, which counts as something you have.

  <!-- sysd-reliab-038 -->

## Design interview questions

The rest of the course is a set of design questions, the kind an interviewer asks and a good answer takes apart piece by piece. The first is a URL shortener, which must create a unique short alias for a URL, redirect visitors to the original, and stay available with minimal latency. A pastebin stores plain text such as source code snippets or error logs and shares it by link, which makes it a close cousin. After that comes instant messaging, which sends messages in real time between two or more parties, and which can be built so that only the sender and the intended recipients can read them. Each question gathers the ideas it needs before it walks through a full answer.

### Design a URL shortener

A short link does one job: it makes a long URL substantially shorter while it still leads to the same page, through a redirect. That convenience has costs, because short URLs add a layer of complexity to retrieving pages and bring abuse, linkrot (links that stop working) and privacy risks. This chapter looks at how a shortening service ties each long URL to a unique key built from letters and digits, and at Base62, which writes numbers with 62 symbols. It also covers why some providers let links expire after a set time, on a certain date, or after a number of uses. It ends with a full design that must create unique aliases, redirect visitors and stay highly available with minimal latency.

- **URL shortening: a short address that redirects**

  Long links are easy to mistype and hard to fit in a message that limits length. URL shortening fixes both. It makes a long URL substantially shorter, yet it still leads to the same page, because a redirect points to the page with the long URL. The browser asks for the short address and gets back a redirect instruction. It carries an HTTP status code such as 301 (moved permanently), 302 (found), 307 (temporary redirect) or 308 (permanent redirect). HTTP redirects: the 3xx codes and where they send you covers those codes.

  A short URL saves space when sharing, and it lets links be tracked individually across devices. It helps messaging technologies such as SMS, reduces typing when copying from print, is easier to remember, and can serve as a permalink. Shortening services also give detailed click statistics, which can be simpler than setting up an equally powerful server-side analytics engine and need no access to the server. For security, they typically do not support data: and javascript: URLs, to combat attacks like cross-site scripting and session hijacking.

  <!-- sysd-q-030 -->

- **What short links cost**

  Every short link adds a hop. Short URLs add a layer of complexity to retrieving pages and bring abuse, linkrot and privacy risks. Each access needs at least one more DNS lookup, possibly cached, and one more HTTP or HTTPS request. That adds latency, and a risk of failure if the service becomes unavailable. Linkrot follows from the same dependence: if the service stops working, all URLs it issued become broken. A short URL also hides the target address, so it can redirect to unexpected or malicious sites and bypass site blocklists. Browsers do not resend POST bodies on a redirect, an operational limit of shortening services.

  <!-- sysd-q-032 -->

- **Short link expiration**

  A link that lives forever is not necessarily a good thing. Some providers let a shortened URL expire after a set time, on a certain date, or after a number of uses. Obsolete short URLs stay in circulation long after they stop pointing to a relevant destination, which has security implications. A short-lived URL suits a one-off access or file download that is no longer needed within a couple of minutes. A Microsoft Security Brief recommends short-lived URLs, for security rather than convenience. Providers claiming that short URLs never expire may still discontinue the service. Expiry is a time to live, an idea from Time to live: giving every cache entry an expiry date.

  <!-- sysd-q-033 -->

- **Base62: seven characters, trillions of keys**

  Each character added to a short link multiplies the number of possible links by 62. Base62 writes numbers with 62 symbols: the capital letters A-Z, the lower case letters a-z and the digits 0-9. A key of N Base62 characters can name 62^N different URLs. The alphabet suits URLs because the output [a-zA-Z0-9] needs no special characters escaped, while Base64: carrying binary data as plain text adds + and / characters that cause issues for URLs. Base62 is also deterministic, with no randomness: one input number or hash always gives the same encoded string.

  <!-- sysd-q-034 -->

- **Short URL key generation**

  Once a service has a long URL, it needs a key to pair with it. A shortening service ties each long URL to a unique key, the part after the domain name, that it builds from letters and digits. Keys can be written in base 36, which is 26 letters and 10 numbers, or in base 62 when upper and lower case differ, as Base62: seven characters, trillions of keys describes. Keys are case-sensitive most of the time, so using the wrong case may lead to a different destination URL. A hash function can form the key, or a random number can make the key sequence unpredictable. Users may also propose custom keys.

  <!-- sysd-q-031 -->

- **Designing a URL shortener**

  The interview question asks for a service that turns a long URL into a short alias and sends visitors back to the original. The service must create a unique short alias for a URL, redirect visitors to the original URL, and expire links after a default timespan. It needs high availability and minimal latency. Preventing abuse and recording analytics are extended requirements.

  Start by checking scale assumptions with the interviewer. Assume a read-heavy 100:1 read/write ratio and 100 million links generated per month. That is about 40 URLs per second written and 4000 redirections per second. Taking each request and each stored record as about 500 bytes, incoming bandwidth is 20 KB/second and outgoing is about 2 MB/second. Keeping 12 billion records for 10 years needs around 6 TB. By the 80/20 rule, caching 20% of the 350M redirection requests per day needs around 35GB of memory per day. This is the style of reasoning in Back-of-the-envelope estimation: sizing a system roughly.

  Two tables suffice at first: users (name, email, createdAt) and URLs (expiration, hash, originalURL and the creator's userID), with the hash column indexed. Data that is not strongly relational suits NoSQL such as DynamoDB, Cassandra or MongoDB. The API has three calls. Create URL takes an API key, the original URL and an optional expiration, and returns the short URL. Get URL maps a short URL back to the original. Delete URL returns a boolean result. The API key prevents abuse: it lets the service limit each user to a certain number of requests per second or minute, a standard practice for developer APIs.

  The hard part is making the key, as Short URL key generation describes. Base62 (A-Z, a-z, 0-9) gives about 3.5 trillion 7-character keys (62^7), and MD5 hashing the URL yields 32 hex digits to make one. Both risk duplicates and collisions, and recomputing hashes adds overhead. A counter encoded in base62 is a single point of failure, and several counters collide. ZooKeeper can hand each server a range such as 1 to 1,000,000, which guarantees non-duplicate keys, and it can itself run in several instances. The alternative is a standalone Key Generation Service that creates unique keys ahead of time in a separate database. Used keys move to another table under locking, so concurrent servers never share one, and some keys are kept in memory.

  To create a URL, the API server gets a unique key from the Key Generation Service, which marks it used. The server writes the entry to the database and cache and returns HTTP 201 (Created). To access a URL, the API server checks the cache first and falls back to the database. It then issues an HTTP 301 (Redirect) to the original URL, or sends HTTP 404 (Not found) if the key is missing. The redirect works as HTTP redirects: the 3xx codes and where they send you explains.

  To scale out the database, partition it horizontally by hash, list, range or composite schemes, as Database sharding: spreading one database across many servers describes. These can still distribute data and load unevenly, and consistent hashing fixes that; see Consistent hashing: adding a server without reshuffling everything. Redis or Memcached servers beside the API server cache 20% of daily traffic, as Caching: answering from a copy instead of the source describes. They use Least Recently Used eviction, which discards the least recently used key first. On a cache miss they read the database and update the cache. Expired links can be removed in two ways. Active cleanup is a lightweight cron-like service that periodically deletes them from storage and cache. Passive cleanup is a lazy removal when a user accesses an expired link.

  To remove single points of failure, run multiple instances of the servers and the Key Generation Service. Put load balancers between components, add read replicas for the database, a standby replica for the key database, and a replicated cache. The thing to remember is the shape. It is a read-heavy lookup, where a cache serves the hot links and a Key Generation Service makes sure no two links share a key.

  <!-- sysd-q-029 -->

  *Figure: The API server reads the cache and the database, and takes each new key from the Key Generation Service.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  V[Visitor] --> L[Load balancer]
  L --> A[API server]
  A -->|checks first| C[(Cache)]
  A -->|on a miss| D[(URL database)]
  A -->|gets a key| K[Key Generation Service]
  K --> E[(Key database)]
  ```

### Design Pastebin

A pastebin is an online content-hosting service where users store plain text, such as source code snippets or error logs, and share it by link. In the design question, a user enters text and gets a random link, then views the paste by its URL. Pastes do not expire by default but may have a timed expiration, and the service tracks monthly visits, deletes expired pastes and stays available. A reader who has just met the URL shortener will find the problem familiar.

- **Pastebin**

  Chatrooms gave pastebins their purpose. Sending large blocks of computer data there disrupts closely interleaved conversation, so users are told to paste elsewhere and share the link. A pastebin is an online content-hosting service where users store plain text, such as source code snippets or error logs, and share it by link. Each stored text entry is commonly called a paste, and account holders can typically edit or delete their pastes at any time. Accounts let users manage and organize their content, and many platforms let users set a paste as public or private. Pastebins may add features such as commenting, rendering markup like Markdown or ReStructuredText, or version control. Designing one is like designing a URL shortener, as Short URL key generation sets it up, except that the service stores the paste contents instead of the original unshortened URL.

  <!-- sysd-q-063 -->

- **Designing Pastebin**
