  The interview question asks for a service where a user enters text and gets a random link, then views the paste by its URL. Pastes do not expire by default but may have a timed expiration. The service tracks monthly visits, deletes expired pastes and stays available. Out of scope are registering an account, verifying email, logging in, editing the document, setting visibility and letting the user choose the shortlink.

  Traffic is not evenly distributed, pastes are text only and analytics need not be realtime. Assume 10 million paste writes and 100 million reads per month, a 10:1 ratio, which is 4 writes and 40 reads per second on average. Each paste is about 1.27 KB: 1 KB of content, a 7-byte shortlink, a 4-byte expiration, a 5-byte created_at and a 255-byte paste_path. That means 12.7 GB of new content per month and about 450 GB in 3 years.

  A relational database can act as a large hash table that maps the generated url to a file server and path. Instead of a file server, use a managed object store such as Amazon S3, or a NoSQL document store. Object storage: flat, huge and cheap covers object stores. A NoSQL key-value store is another alternative to the relational hash table, and a good answer discusses the trade-offs between SQL and NoSQL. In the pastes table, a primary key on the shortlink column creates an index that enforces uniqueness. An extra index on created_at speeds lookups to log time instead of a full table scan, as Database index: faster reads, slower writes explains.

  To generate the unique url, take the MD5 hash of the user's ip_address plus timestamp, or of random data. Base 62 encode it and keep the first 7 characters. The 62^7 values suffice for 360 million shortlinks in 3 years. Base 62 encodes to [a-zA-Z0-9], which suits urls without escaping special characters, and it is deterministic. Base 64 is another popular encoding, but its additional + and / characters cause issues for urls.

  To create a paste, the Web Server, a reverse proxy, forwards the request to the Write API server. That server generates a unique url, regenerates on a duplicate, saves to the SQL pastes table and the Object Store, and returns the url. To view a paste, the Web Server forwards the request to the Read API server. It checks the SQL Database for the url, fetches the contents from the Object Store if found, and otherwise returns an error message. Clients use a public REST API, and internal communications could use Remote Procedure Calls.

  Because realtime analytics are not required, MapReduce the Web Server logs to get hit counts. The Analytics Database could be a data warehouse such as Amazon Redshift or Google BigQuery. To delete expired pastes, scan the SQL Database for entries whose expiration timestamp is older than the current timestamp. Delete them or mark them as expired, as Short link expiration discusses.

  Do not jump straight to the final design. State that scaling is iterative: benchmark and load test, profile for bottlenecks, address them while weighing alternatives and trade-offs, and repeat. In the scaled design, an object store like S3 handles 12.7 GB of new content per month. A memory cache serves popular content for the 40 average reads per second and traffic spikes. SQL read replicas handle the cache misses. See Caching: answering from a copy instead of the source and The read replica pattern: writes to one, reads from many.

  <!-- sysd-q-062 -->

  *Figure: Writes and reads take separate paths through the Web Server, and the logs feed analytics.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  C[Client] --> W[Web Server]
  W -->|create| WA[Write API server]
  W -->|view| RA[Read API server]
  WA --> S[(SQL Database)]
  WA --> O[(Object Store)]
  RA --> S
  RA --> O
  W -.->|logs, MapReduce| A[(Analytics Database)]
  ```

### Design a chat service like WhatsApp

A chat message looks simple: you type, someone else reads. Underneath, the service must deliver it in real time, hold it when the recipient cannot be reached, and keep it private from everyone except the two ends. This chapter starts with instant messaging itself, then covers store and forward, end-to-end encryption and the Signal Protocol, and the argument over who should be able to read messages. It ends with two designs: a worked answer to the WhatsApp interview question, and a look at how WhatsApp itself delivers messages.

- **Instant messaging**

  Email conversations are not real time. Instant messaging is. It is synchronous communication that sends messages in real time between two or more parties over the Internet or another computer network. A reply can arrive at once. It covers private messaging between two users and chat rooms or groups. Modern apps go beyond text to multimedia, emojis, file transfer, voice calling and video chat, and they connect known users through a contact list or chat rooms. Most services run as centralized networks on the operator's servers, unlike peer-to-peer protocols such as XMPP. Most protocols are proprietary, so users cannot reach people on other networks. Storing messages in the cloud carries a risk that the provider holds the decryption keys and can read them. Encryption is the main way apps protect privacy, and End-to-end encryption can be on by default.

  <!-- sysd-q-003 -->

- **End-to-end encryption**

  Encrypting a chat does not help much if the company running it can still read the chat. End-to-end encryption closes that gap. It is a way of building a secure communication system in which only the sender and the intended recipients can read the messages. The sender's device encrypts each message so that no third party, including the provider, can decrypt it, and recipients decrypt it on their own devices. Encryption in transit alone is not enough, because providers can read messages that pass through their intermediaries and storage. Server-side disk encryption is not enough either, since the provider holds the keys. Around 2014, when WhatsApp encrypted part of its network, the term came to require that neither the provider nor an attacker in transit can decrypt. The protection stops at the endpoints, though. A hacked device can leak the key or the decrypted messages, and a backdoor, a secret way of bypassing normal encryption, can undo the design.

  <!-- sysd-q-070 -->

- **Store and forward**

  A text sent through SMS: the text message that may never arrive to a phone that cannot be reached does not vanish. It waits at a service center until the phone is reachable again. That is store and forward. Data goes to an intermediate station that keeps it in storage and sends it on later, to its destination or to another intermediate station. The station verifies the integrity of the message before forwarding it. A switching center accepts a message from the sender, holds it, and forwards it according to the priority the sender set and the availability of an outgoing channel. If the destination is unreachable, the center keeps the message and retries later, which raises the chance of delivery. If the destination is available, the message goes at once. Email over SMTP works the same way. The technique suits networks with intermittent connectivity, high mobility, long delays, high error rates or no direct end-to-end connection. Its limit is speed: delay-tolerant store-and-forward networks offer no real-time services.

  <!-- sysd-q-069 -->

  *Figure: A message waits in the station and is retried until the destination can be reached.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Sender] --> B[Station stores message]
  B --> C[Check integrity]
  C --> D{Reachable now?}
  D -->|yes| E[Send at once]
  D -->|no| F[Keep it and retry later]
  F -.-> D
  ```

- **Signal Protocol**

  WhatsApp built the Signal Protocol into its clients after a November 2014 partnership, and by April 2016 every form of communication on WhatsApp was end-to-end encrypted. The protocol is a non-federated cryptographic protocol, formerly called the TextSecure Protocol, that provides End-to-end encryption for voice and instant messaging conversations. It combines the Double Ratchet Algorithm, prekeys and a key agreement protocol. Prekeys are one-time ephemeral public keys uploaded in advance to a central server. The ratchet pairs an ephemeral key exchange with a symmetric-key ratchet, and it added offline messages and better resilience to out-of-order messages. It is called self-healing because after an attacker compromises a session key it automatically blocks access to the cleartext of later messages. The protocol gives confidentiality, integrity, authentication, forward secrecy and post-compromise security, but not anonymity, and it needs servers to relay messages and store public key material. Group chats combine a pairwise double ratchet with multicast encryption. Users can compare public key fingerprints through an outside channel to avoid a man-in-the-middle attack.

  <!-- sysd-q-072 -->

- **End-to-end encryption versus provider access**

  Should the company that runs a chat service be able to read your messages? Without end-to-end encryption, a provider can easily offer search and scan for illegal content. But anyone with access to the stored data, by design or through a backdoor, can read it too. With the encryption, the provider cannot hand over decrypted messages on government request. Governments, law enforcement agencies and child protection groups worry about criminal investigations. Security experts and privacy advocates defend the encryption. Some governments have passed laws targeting it, while the UK's Information Commissioner's Office and the US's CISA argue for its use.

  <!-- sysd-q-071 -->

- **Messaging metadata and sealed sender**

  Encrypt every word of a message and a server can still see who talks to whom, and when. The Signal Protocol does not stop a provider from keeping that metadata. Signal says it keeps recipient identifiers only as long as needed to send each message. The closest thing to metadata it stores is each user's last connection time, with precision reduced to the day. Sealed sender hides the sender from the server: the sender's identity travels inside each message, encrypted with a key the server lacks. A simultaneous wiretap of the device or servers can still show that its IP address contacted a server at certain times.

  <!-- sysd-q-073 -->

- **Chat application on Redis pub/sub**

  Redis can play two roles in a simple chat app: it stores the messages and it announces them. The server publishes each chat message to a topic that subscribers pick up. A web socket connects client and server. The pub-sub server opens several connections to Redis: one updates the data models and publishes, the others subscribe and listen. On connecting, the client gets the member list and history from Redis. A new member is announced on the member_add topic. A new message goes into a Redis sorted set with zadd, ordered by arrival time. It is published to the messages topic, so the recipient's client receives it.

  <!-- sysd-q-004 -->

- **Designing a chat service like WhatsApp**

  A chat service like WhatsApp has to support one-on-one chat, group chats of at most 100 people and file sharing. It must be highly available with minimal latency. The extended requirements are sent, delivered and read receipts, last seen time and push notifications. Start with scale. Assume 50 million daily active users, each sending at least 10 messages to 4 different people a day. That is 2 billion messages a day, or 24K requests per second, and 5 percent of the messages are media files. At 100 bytes per message, text needs about 200 GB a day. The 100 KB media files need 10 TB a day, about 38 PB over 10 years. The 10.2 TB of daily ingress works out to around 120 MB per second.

  The data model is small. Tables hold users (name, phoneNumber), messages (type, content, timestamps and a chat or group ID), chats and groups, plus two many-to-many tables, users_chats and users_groups. Each service owns its tables, in PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store like Cassandra. The API has four calls. Get all chats or groups takes a user ID. Get messages takes a user ID and channel ID. Send message takes a user ID, channel ID and message, and returns a boolean result. Join or leave a channel completes the set. The system is built from microservices, which scale horizontally and decouple. Five services do the work: user (HTTP and authentication), chat, notification, presence for last seen, and media for uploads. Each owns its data, and they talk over REST or the lighter gRPC.

  How does a message reach the other phone? Pulling by periodic HTTP requests or long polling does not scale, since most responses are empty. Push over WebSockets delivers data without delay and is full-duplex, unlike one-way Server-Sent Events, and a cache of active connections shows who is online. The sender's chat service has the sequencing service give the message a unique ID, persists it and queues it for sync. If the recipient is online, the message is pushed over their web socket. Otherwise it goes via the push server. The chat service queues an event with device-platform metadata, and the notification service forwards it to Firebase Cloud Messaging and the registration token or Apple Push Notification service: reaching Apple devices. The queues give best-effort ordering and at-least-once delivery.

  Receipts and last seen ride on the same connection. On login the client opens a web socket, and the presence service updates the user's status and notifies friends. For last seen, the client sends a heartbeat ping and the last active timestamp is kept in a Redis or Memcached cache. A client acknowledgment (ACK) shows a message was delivered and sets its deliveredAt field. The message is marked seen, setting seenAt, once the user opens the chat.

  Storage grows fastest in media. Partition the database horizontally by hash, list, range or composite schemes, with consistent hashing against uneven load, as in Database sharding: spreading one database across many servers. Cache older messages with LRU eviction, and paginate group history so users with limited bandwidth load old messages only on request. The media service keeps files in object storage such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage or Google Cloud Storage, or in HDFS or GlusterFS. Static files are served from a CDN such as CloudFront or Cloudflare. Multimedia is sent by uploading the image, audio or video to an HTTP server, then sending a link to the content with its Base64 encoded thumbnail where applicable.

  To remove single points of failure, run multiple service instances, load balancers, read replicas and a replicated cache. Keep a standby API Gateway too, the one entry point for HTTP, WebSocket and TCP/IP. Kafka or NATS make notifications robust. WhatsApp itself uses Store and forward. Its server stores a message, tries to forward it to the addressee and repeatedly requests acknowledgement of receipt. It deletes the message once acknowledged or, if undelivered, after 30 days. The thing to remember: when the recipient is online the message is pushed, and when not it waits in a queue until it can be delivered.

  <!-- sysd-q-002 -->

  *Figure: Follow one message from the sender's chat service to an online or an offline recipient.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Sender's chat service] --> B[Sequencing service adds ID]
  B --> C[Persist, queue for sync]
  C --> D{Recipient online?}
  D -->|yes| E[Push over web socket]
  D -->|no| F[Queue push event]
  F --> G[Notification service]
  G --> H[FCM or APNS]
  ```

- **How WhatsApp delivers messages**

  In April 2012 WhatsApp handled two billion messages a day. By August of that year it was ten billion. The protocol under that traffic is a customized version of the open standard XMPP, the Extensible messaging and presence protocol. A 2019 US Department of Justice document calls it FunXMPP. An account uses the phone number as its username. The app compares the numbers in the address book with the central database of users and adds contacts to the contact list automatically.

  Delivery is store and forward. A message is stored on a server, which tries to forward it and repeatedly requests acknowledgement. Once acknowledged it is deleted, and if it is still undelivered after 30 days it is deleted too. A multimedia message is uploaded to an HTTP server, and only a link to the content, plus a Base64 encoded thumbnail where applicable, travels in the message.

  Messages are encrypted with the Signal Protocol, and end-to-end encryption was completed for every form of communication in April 2016. Users can verify each other's keys, and calls use SRTP. A user can link up to four devices to one account. They sync with the primary phone, which originally had to stay online for them to work, until multi-device support removed that requirement.

  <!-- sysd-q-005 -->

### Design a social feed like Twitter

A social feed has one job: out of everything posted, show each reader the posts worth reading, and show them fast. That takes two decisions. The first is how a new post reaches its followers' feeds, by push, by pull or by a mix of both, and the second is how the posts in a feed are scored so the most relevant appear first. The chapter begins with two building blocks, the Apache Lucene search library and the fan-out pattern, then covers feed models, ranking, EdgeRank and trending topics. It closes with the worked Twitter design, Twitter's technology stack and a pipeline that narrows 500 million tweets to a ranked, filtered and mixed set.

- **Apache Lucene**

  Apache Solr, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, CrateDB, MongoDB Atlas Search and Netflix's search all rest on the same core, Apache Lucene. Lucene is a free and open-source search engine software library, originally written in Java, and a widely used foundation for production search. It suits any application that needs full-text indexing and searching. It is only a library, with no crawling or HTML parsing, so projects such as Apache Nutch extend it with both. It also offers fuzzy search based on edit distance, and its MoreLikeThis class recommends similar documents by term-vector similarity.

  <!-- sysd-q-093 -->

- **Fan-out**

  One message, many destinations. In messaging middleware, fan-out is the pattern that delivers one message to one or several destinations, possibly in parallel, without halting the sender to wait for any response. AMQP can be used with routing schemes such as point-to-point, fan-out, publish/subscribe and request-response, which version 1.0 of the standard leaves to the implementation or the network protocol. The pattern also appears inside a system. A single incoming request can trigger a long transitive chain of dependent requests to several systems, with high fan-out at various points.

  <!-- sysd-q-092 -->

- **Feed fan-out models**

  Fanning out 60 thousand tweets delivered per second would overload a traditional relational database. Building a feed is intensive, especially for users who follow many accounts. Publishing a post to every follower's feed is heavy when the author has millions of followers.

  Push, or fan-out on write, sends a new tweet to all followers' feeds immediately. The system need not scan a user's followers list for updates, but database writes increase. In the primer's design a push places the tweet in each follower's home timeline in a memory cache, an O(n) operation: 1,000 followers mean 1,000 lookups and inserts. So the feed store needs fast writes, such as a NoSQL database or memory cache.

  Pull, or fan-out on load, builds the feed and holds it in memory only when a follower reloads it. That cuts writes, but recent tweets appear only on request and server reads increase.

  The hybrid combines both: users with fewer followers use push, while users with many followers, such as celebrities, use pull. Fan-out for users with millions of followers can take several minutes. So the primer suggests not fanning them out, and merging their tweets from search into the home timeline at serve time.

  <!-- sysd-q-021 -->

  *Figure: Push and pull trade writes against reads, and the hybrid splits users by follower count.*

  | Model | Feed built | Effect |
  |---|---|---|
  | Push (fan-out on write) | Immediately, when a tweet is posted | More database writes |
  | Pull (fan-out on load) | When a follower reloads | Fewer writes, more reads |
  | Hybrid | Push for few followers, pull for many | Combines both |

- **Feed ranking**

  Facebook's early feed ranking multiplied three numbers, while modern models weigh thousands of factors. Feed ranking scores each item in a feed by how relevant it is to a specific user, so the most relevant appear first. It can use parameters such as relevance, time and engagement. EdgeRank scored each item as Affinity × Weight × Decay. Affinity is the closeness of the user to the creator, higher when the user often likes, comments on or messages them. Weight is a value per kind of interaction, so a comment can count more than a like. Decay lowers the rank of older interactions.

  <!-- sysd-q-022 -->

- **EdgeRank**

  By 2013 the algorithm that replaced EdgeRank weighed more than 100,000 factors. EdgeRank is the name commonly given to the algorithm Facebook used to decide which posts to show in a user's News Feed. The simplified 2010 version scored posts on three parts: user affinity, content weight and a time-based decay parameter. Newer posts tend to hold a higher place than older ones. As of 2011 Facebook stopped using EdgeRank and moved to a machine learning algorithm. Such ranking shapes what users see out of what they follow, and it can produce a filter bubble when updates confirm their opinions.

  <!-- sysd-q-091 -->

- **Trending topics**

  Trending topics look like a feature of their own, but the functionality is built on top of search. It shows the queries, hashtags and topics searched most often in a recent window. The system caches the most frequently searched queries, hashtags and topics from the last N seconds. A batch job refreshes them every M seconds. The ranking algorithm can also weight trending topics and personalize them for the user.

  <!-- sysd-q-026 -->

- **Designing a social feed like Twitter**

  A social feed like Twitter lets users post tweets of text, image or video and follow other users. They read a newsfeed of tweets from the people they follow, and they search tweets. The service must be highly available with minimal latency, and it must scale. The extended requirements are metrics and analytics, retweets and favorites. The system design primer scopes out the Twitter Firehose, filtering by visibility settings, hiding @replies to people the user does not follow, and the hide-retweets setting.

  Two sets of assumptions size it. One author, Singh, assumes a read-heavy system with 1 billion total users, 200 million daily active users and 5 tweets per user per day. That gives 1 billion tweets a day and about 12K requests per second. At 100 bytes per message, text is about 100 GB a day. Media is in 10 percent of tweets at 50 KB each. That adds 5 TB a day, about 19 PB over 10 years, and about 60 MB per second of bandwidth. The primer instead assumes 100 million active users and 500 million tweets per day. It assumes an average fanout of 10 deliveries per tweet, 60 thousand tweets delivered on fanout per second and 100 thousand read requests per second.

  The tables hold users, tweets (type, content, userID), favorites, followers (an N:M relation), feeds and feeds_tweets. Each service owns its tables, on PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store such as Cassandra. Posting a tweet takes a user ID, content and an optional media URL. Following or unfollowing takes a follower ID and a followee ID. Getting the newsfeed takes a user ID and returns the tweets to show. A microservices architecture scales horizontally. Each service owns its data: user, newsfeed, tweet, search, media, notification and analytics. They talk over REST or the lighter gRPC, with service discovery.

  The heart of the design is the feed. Building one retrieves the accounts a user follows, fetches their tweets, ranks them by relevance, time and engagement, and returns pages. Because that is intensive, feeds are pre-generated in the cache and refreshed periodically. The choice is among the models of Feed fan-out models. Pull builds the feed when a follower reloads, with fewer writes and more reads. Push writes each tweet into followers' feeds at once, with more writes. The hybrid pushes for users with fewer followers and pulls for celebrities. In the primer's design, posting stores the tweet in the author's SQL timeline. The fan-out service finds the followers, inserts the tweet into each home timeline in a memory cache (1,000 followers mean 1,000 inserts) and queues notifications. To read the home timeline, the timeline service gets tweet ids and user ids from the memory cache in O(1). It then fetches tweet details and user details in bulk from the tweet info and user info services in O(n).

  Search uses Elasticsearch, built on Apache Lucene. The search service tokenizes the query, normalizes capitalization and converts it to boolean operations. It then scatter-gathers across the cluster, asking every node and merging the answers, and ranks and sorts the results.

  The fan-out service is the bottleneck. Fan-out for users with millions of followers can take several minutes, racing with @replies. So re-order at serve time, skip fanning out highly followed users, and merge their tweets in at read time. Keep only several hundred tweets per home timeline and only active users in the cache, rebuilding from SQL after 30 inactive days. Read replicas cannot absorb cache misses, so add federation, denormalization, SQL tuning and NoSQL. Cache the top 20% of tweets with LRU eviction, and paginate. Keep media in object storage behind a CDN. For resilience, run multiple service instances, load balancers and read replicas. The thing to remember: fan-out is the heart of a feed, and celebrities break the simple version of it.

  <!-- sysd-q-020 -->

- **Twitter's technology stack**

  Twitter's stack can be read layer by layer, from the phone in a user's hand down to the database. On the client side, the mobile apps use Swift and Kotlin, with a PWA, a progressive web app built to behave like an installed app. The web client uses JavaScript, React and Redux. Behind the clients, the services run on Mesos with Finagle. Below the services sit the stores. Caching, the layer that keeps frequently used data close at hand so it need not be fetched again, uses Pelikan Cache and Redis. The databases, which keep the data itself, are Manhattan, MySQL and PostgreSQL. That makes four layers: client, services, cache and database. The feed design in Designing a social feed like Twitter relies on the last two working together.

  <!-- sysd-q-024 -->

- **Twitter's tweet recommendation pipeline**

  A day's tweets are far too many to rank one by one. Twitter's recommendation pipeline narrows 500 million tweets to a ranked, filtered and mixed set in five stages: candidate sourcing, global filtering, scoring and ranking, filtering, and mixing. Candidate sourcing starts with the 500 million tweets, and global filtering cuts them down to 1500 candidates. Scoring and ranking then works on those candidates with a neural network of 48M parameters. A further filtering stage achieves author and content diversity, so the timeline does not rest on one author or one kind of content. The final mixing stage blends the tweets with ads recommendations and Who to Follow. The shape is a funnel: the big cut comes first, and the relevance scoring that Feed ranking describes comes after it.

  <!-- sysd-q-023 -->

  *Figure: The five stages run in order, and the first big cut is from 500 million tweets to 1500 candidates.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Candidate sourcing: 500 million tweets] --> B[Global filtering: 1500 candidates]
  B --> C[Scoring and ranking]
  C --> D[Filtering for diversity]
  D --> E[Mixing with ads and Who to Follow]
  ```

### Design a video streaming service like Netflix

A video service sends a stream of packets that plays as it arrives, to viewers on very different devices and connections. This chapter follows a video from upload to screen. It starts with streaming itself and the codecs that compress video, then covers transcoding, adaptive bitrate streaming and its two main protocols, HTTP Live Streaming and MPEG-DASH. It also looks at the ways a stream reaches many viewers, from unicast copies to CDN servers, and adds recommendations and geo-blocking. It closes with a worked Netflix design and three case studies: Netflix's technology stack, YouTube's dedicated transcoding chip and Netflix Open Connect.

- **Streaming media**

  You can start watching a film before the file has finished arriving. That is streaming media. It is multimedia delivered over a network as a stream of packets and rendered in real time or near real time. A download is different: the user obtains the entire file first. Streams are compressed with video coding formats such as H.264 and HEVC, and assembled into a container such as MP4 or WebM. A streaming server delivers them by a transport protocol such as RTMP or RTP. In the 2010s, HTTP Live Streaming, Smooth Streaming, HDS and the non-proprietary MPEG-DASH emerged to give adaptive streaming over HTTP, as an alternative to proprietary transport protocols. A broadband speed of 2 Mbit/s or more is recommended for standard-definition video, 5 Mbit/s for high-definition and 25 Mbit/s for ultra-high-definition. UDP sends the stream as small packets, which is simple and efficient but gives no delivery guarantee. TCP guarantees delivery but stalls the stream on loss, which client buffering softens. Buffering delay is acceptable for Video on demand, but video conferencing loses fidelity if it exceeds 200 ms.

  <!-- sysd-q-045 -->

- **Recommender system**

  Netflix tracks how you scroll, not only what you watch. Its engine records profile information, browsing and scrolling behavior, the time and date of viewing, the device used, and the number of searches and search terms. Those records feed a machine learning model built on viewing history. That is a recommender system: an information filtering system that suggests the items most relevant to a particular user, such as what to watch next. It matters wherever users face many options. Collaborative filtering builds a model from a user's past behavior and similar decisions by other users. Content-based filtering uses pre-tagged characteristics of items to recommend others with similar properties. The first needs a lot of data about a user, which is the cold start problem. The second needs very little to start but recommends only items similar to the seed. Most systems are hybrids that combine approaches, which can be more accurate and ease cold start and sparsity. Netflix uses a hybrid of similar users' habits and titles resembling those a user rated highly.

  <!-- sysd-q-047 -->

- **Collaborative filtering**

  The whole idea of collaborative filtering fits in one assumption: people who agreed before will agree again. It predicts a user's interests from taste information collected from many users. The assumption is that two people who share opinions on one issue are likelier to agree on others than a random pairing. The prediction is specific to the user but uses information from many users, unlike giving every item one average score. User-based filtering finds users with rating patterns like the active user's and predicts from their ratings. Item-based filtering, 'users who bought x also bought y', builds an item-item matrix and matches the user's data against it. Instead of explicit ratings it can use implicit observations, such as what a user listened to or bought. Its key challenges are cold start, where new users or items lack data, sparsity of the huge user-item matrix, and scalability. Open rating systems invite shilling attacks, with positive ratings for one's own items and negative ones for competitors'. And because it recommends from past ratings, it favors popular products.

  <!-- sysd-q-101 -->

- **Video codec**

  Raw video needs too much storage and bandwidth to record, send or stream. A codec fixes that. It is software or hardware that compresses and decompresses digital video, an encoder and a decoder in one, usually following a standard video coding format. Compression is typically lossy, so decompressed video has lower quality than the original. The bit rate trades off against quality, algorithm complexity, sensitivity to errors, random access and latency. Encoding usually subsamples the less perceptually important color information, applies a transform (the 8x8 DCT is most popular), quantizes the output and entropy-encodes the values. Decoding inverts each stage as far as possible, but quantization cannot be inverted, so decoding only approximates. Standards specify only the decoding process, so video quality can vary dramatically between encoders that use the same standard. As of 2016 the most widely used format was H.264, with HEVC as its successor and the open, free VP8, VP9 and AV1 as alternatives.

  <!-- sysd-q-102 -->

- **Adaptive bitrate streaming**

  One video has to play well on a high-end connection and on a low-end one. Adaptive bitrate streaming does that: it encodes video at several bit rates and lets the player switch between them as bandwidth, CPU and device conditions change. An encoder encodes one source at multiple bit rates, and each stream is segmented into small multi-second parts. The client first downloads a manifest describing the segments and their bit rates. It starts with the lowest bit rate stream, requests a higher one when throughput exceeds the downloaded segment's bit rate, and a lower one when throughput deteriorates. The client's ABR algorithm decides which segments to download. Throughput-based algorithms use recent download throughput, buffer-based ones use only the buffer level, and hybrid ones combine both. Because it is built on HTTP, packets traverse firewalls and NAT, the server keeps no per-client session state, and existing HTTP caches and servers can be used. Delivered through content delivery networks, it scales to millions of concurrent viewers. The costs are extra encoding and storage, more complex operation than traditional streaming, and no single standard for digital rights management.

  <!-- sysd-q-042 -->

- **HTTP Live Streaming**

  In HTTP Live Streaming nobody downloads 'the video'. The player downloads a playlist, then the small segments it lists. HLS is an HTTP-based protocol from Apple for transferring unbounded streams of multimedia data, live or on demand. Version 7 is specified in RFC 8216. The receiver can adapt the bit rate to current network conditions to keep playback uninterrupted. A Media Playlist lists the Media Segments to play in sequence. A Master Playlist lists Variant Streams, each the same content at a particular bit rate, format and resolution. A segmenter, also called a packager, cuts the media into segments no longer than a constant target duration, typically 10 seconds, each with its own URI. Each segment has a unique Media Sequence Number, so clients can order and locate them. A live playlist is only appended to or trimmed from the front, and the server adds EXT-X-ENDLIST when the final segment is published. Because it is plain HTTP, it works with large-scale HTTP caching infrastructure, and segments can be encrypted.

  <!-- sysd-q-043 -->

- **Video on demand**

  Video on demand lets the viewer choose what to watch and when. It is a media distribution system that lets users access television shows, films and videos digitally on request. A selected video can begin playing immediately, which is streaming, or be downloaded for deferred viewing. Streaming has become the more popular way. The business models are subscription (SVOD, a regular fee for unlimited programs), transactional (TVOD, a fee per title) and advertising-based (AVOD, free to viewers). Near video on demand broadcasts copies of a programme at staggered intervals, typically every 10-20 minutes, which is bandwidth-intensive.

  <!-- sysd-q-104 -->

- **MPEG-DASH**

  Netflix and YouTube both support MPEG-DASH. It is Dynamic Adaptive Streaming over HTTP, an international-standard adaptive bitrate technique that streams media from conventional HTTP web servers. Content is split into small segments, each a short slice of playback time, and offered at several bit rates as alternative segments covering aligned intervals. During playback the client's adaptation algorithm picks the highest-bit-rate segment that can be downloaded in time to avoid stalls. The standard does not specify that logic. The reference client dash.js offers buffer-based (BOLA) and hybrid (DYNAMIC) algorithms. A media presentation description (MPD) describes each segment's timing, URL and media characteristics such as resolution and bit rate. DASH reuses existing HTTP web server infrastructure and is codec-agnostic. It is not a transport protocol. It was published as ISO/IEC 23009-1:2012 in April 2012. It is not directly supported in HTML5, so JavaScript players use the Media Source Extensions. Of the HTTP-based adaptive implementations, only DASH and HLS are still actively developed and used in 2026.

  <!-- sysd-q-044 -->

- **Video transcoding**

  A raw video is rarely the version a phone should receive. Video transcoding converts a video by decoding it to an intermediate uncompressed format, YUV for video, and re-encoding it into a target format and quality for different devices. It is needed when a target device does not support the format or has limited storage. The diversity of mobile devices makes it a must for mobile content adaptation. Raw video is transcoded into different compression rates and resolutions, such as mobile (720p), laptop (1080p) or high-resolution TV (4k), so the requested quality can be fetched. Transrating lowers the bitrate without changing the video format. Transsizing changes the picture size. The cost is quality. Transcoding to a lossy format loses detail, and the artifacts are cumulative, a loss called digital generation loss. So treat the original recording as the master copy and transcode each version only from it. Standalone tools such as FFmpeg or cloud services such as AWS Elemental MediaConvert can implement the step in a video pipeline.

  <!-- sysd-q-037 -->

- **Live streaming**

  A live stream has only a few seconds to get from camera to screen. Live streaming delivers video over the internet in real time, usually with a latency of just a few seconds. The camera and microphone capture raw video. It goes to the server side to be compressed and encoded to a standard such as H.264, making the data much smaller. The encoded data is divided into segments, usually seconds long, so it takes much less time to download or stream. The streaming server must support different devices and network conditions, so it produces multiple files at different bitrates and uses adaptive bitrate streaming. Live data is pushed to CDN edge servers, so millions of viewers can watch from a nearby edge server, which significantly lowers transmission latency. Viewers' devices decode and decompress the data and play it. For replay, the encoded data also goes to a storage server that viewers can request from later. The standard protocols are Real-Time Messaging Protocol, HLS and DASH, and HLS and DASH both support adaptive bitrate streaming. Video conferencing applications such as Skype use real-time communication protocols for lower latency.

  <!-- sysd-q-036 -->

- **Streaming delivery methods**

  If 1,000 people watch the same 300 kbit/s stream by unicast, the server needs 300 Mbit/s. With multicast it needs only 300 kbit/s. Unicast sends a separate copy to each recipient. It is the norm on the Internet but does not scale when many users want the same program. Multicast sends one stream to a group, cutting server and network load. It may not work on every network, and it loses video on demand functionality. Peer-to-peer protocols send prerecorded streams between computers so the server is not a bottleneck, but they raise technical, performance, security, quality and business issues. CDNs use intermediate servers to distribute the load.

  <!-- sysd-q-046 -->

- **Real-Time Messaging Protocol**

  RTMP keeps one TCP connection open and sends audio, video and control messages through it, interleaved. The Real-Time Messaging Protocol was built by Macromedia for Flash Player to stream audio, video and data over the Internet. It uses port 1935 by default, with persistent connections for low latency. After a handshake of three packets from each side, streams are split into fragments of dynamically negotiated size, by default 64 bytes for audio and 128 for video. Variants include RTMPS (over TLS), RTMPE (Adobe's encryption), RTMPT (tunneled in HTTP to pass firewalls) and RTMFP (over UDP). Enhanced RTMP widens its limited codec choice while staying compatible with existing infrastructure.

  <!-- sysd-q-103 -->

- **H.264**

  By December 2024, 79% of video industry developers used H.264, including streaming services such as Netflix, YouTube and Vimeo. Advanced Video Coding (AVC, H.264, MPEG-4 Part 10) is a block-oriented, motion-compensated video compression standard. It is by far the most commonly used video format. Savings of 50% or more in bit rate over MPEG-2 Part 2 are reported. The same digital satellite TV quality takes 1.5 Mbit/s with H.264 against around 3.5 Mbit/s with MPEG-2. High Profile is by far the most used of its profiles, the sets of capabilities for classes of applications. The format is patent-restricted, so commercial use requires royalties.

  <!-- sysd-q-105 -->

- **HEVC**

  HEVC compresses 25% to 50% better than H.264 at the same quality. High Efficiency Video Coding, or H.265, is a patent-encumbered standard published in 2013 as H.264's successor. For 4K at 30 frames per second it needs about 50 Mbps and 22.5 GB per hour, against 100 Mbps and 45 GB for older H.264 profiles. It uses coding tree units up to 64x64 samples instead of 16x16 macroblocks, which needs much more signal processing to compress. Licensing is the catch: combined patent fees are higher than for H.264, a main reason adoption on the web has been low.

  <!-- sysd-q-106 -->

- **AV1**

  In a 2020 study, AV1 encodes at 2160p took on average 590 times longer than AVC. AV1, AOMedia Video 1, is an open, royalty-free video coding format from the Alliance for Open Media, and the successor to VP9. Unlike H.264 and H.265, it is royalty-free, and its alliance was motivated by the high cost and uncertainty of HEVC patent licensing. The payoff is bandwidth: Netflix's 2017 tests found AV1 about 25% more efficient than VP9. The cost is compute. In the study VP9 took 5.2 times and HEVC 4.2 times as long as AVC. And 2017 decoding ran at about half the speed of VP9.

  <!-- sysd-q-107 -->

- **Geo-blocking**

  A film available in one country may be missing in the next. Geo-blocking is technology that restricts access to Internet content based on the user's geographical location. The location comes mainly from the IP address, mapped to a country or region with GeoIP databases. Netflix restricts content by region mainly because of legal distribution laws tied to deals with producers and distributors, while on YouTube the publisher chooses. Blocking can be network-level, filtering IP packets, or application-level, denying access after detecting the location. It is imperfect: IP-to-location mapping is inaccurate, and VPN or proxy services let users evade IP-based blocks.

  <!-- sysd-q-038 -->

- **Designing a video streaming service like Netflix**

  A video streaming service like Netflix lets users stream and share videos, search by title or tag and comment, while a content team uploads new videos. It needs high availability with minimal latency, high reliability so no upload is lost, and scalability. The extended requirements are geo-blocking of certain content, resuming playback from where the user left off, and recording video metrics and analytics. The estimate is read-heavy: 1 billion total users, 200 million daily active users and 5 videos watched a day. That is 1 billion videos a day, 5 million uploads a day at a 200:1 read/write ratio, and 12K requests per second. At 100 MB per video, about 500 TB of storage is needed every day, and about 1,825 PB over 10 years. The minimum ingress bandwidth is around 5.8 GB per second.

  The tables hold users, videos (title, streamURL, tags, userID), tags, views and comments. Each service owns its tables, on PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store such as Cassandra. Upload takes a title, description, byte stream and optional tags. Stream takes a video ID, codec, resolution and an optional offset in seconds. Search takes a query and an optional next-page token, and add comment takes a video ID and text. The system is built from microservices that each own their data model: user, stream, search, media for uploads and processing, and analytics. They communicate over REST or the lighter gRPC, with service discovery.

  The hard part is upload. Two-hour raw 8K footage can reach 4 TB, so uploads go into a message queue such as Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ. Processing is a long-running task, and the queue decouples it from uploading. A file chunker splits each video by scene, not by equal timestamps, so a requested chunk is less likely to be interrupted. A machine-learning content filter checks for copyright, piracy and NSFW material and sends problems to a dead-letter queue. Then Video transcoding takes over. A transcoder decodes to an intermediate format and re-encodes with different codecs, using FFmpeg or AWS Elemental MediaConvert. The quality conversion yields 4K, 1440p, 1080p and 720p, stored in HDFS, GlusterFS or an object store such as Amazon S3.

  Delivery is the other half. A CDN stops users from re-fetching the same content. Netflix's Open Connect partners with thousands of ISPs. It delivers around 95% of traffic over direct ISP connections from appliances in over 1000 locations, and fails over to Netflix servers. Adaptive bitrate protocols such as HLS adapt playback to network conditions, as Adaptive bitrate streaming explains. To resume playback, the offset stored in the views table retrieves the scene chunk at that timestamp.

  Search runs on Elasticsearch. Trending content comes from caching the most frequently searched queries of the last N seconds and refreshing them every M seconds with a batch job. Geo-blocking, driven by legal distribution rights, finds the user's location by IP or profile region and redirects blocked users to an error page. A machine-learning model predicts what to watch next from viewing history. Cache static media with Redis or Memcached using LRU eviction, falling back to the database on a miss. Shard horizontally, using consistent hashing against uneven distribution.

  To remove single points of failure, run multiple instances of each service. Place load balancers between clients, servers, databases and cache servers, and use read replicas and a replicated distributed cache. The thing to remember: most of the work happens before anyone presses play, in the queue, the chunker, the transcoder and the CDN.

  <!-- sysd-q-035 -->

  *Figure: An upload passes through a queue, a chunker, a filter and a transcoder before the CDN serves it.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Content team uploads video] --> B[Message queue]
  B --> C[File chunker splits by scene]
  C --> D[Content filter]
  D -->|problems| E[Dead-letter queue]
  D --> F[Transcoder]
  F --> G[(HDFS or object store)]
  G --> H[CDN]
  H --> I[Viewers]
  ```

- **Netflix's technology stack**

  Netflix's stack names a tool for each job, from the phone to the data warehouse. The native mobile apps are built in Swift and Kotlin and the web application in React, and GraphQL carries communication between the frontend and the server. Backend services rely on ZUUL, Eureka, the Spring Boot framework and other technologies. For data, the databases include EVCache, Cassandra and CockroachDB, and video is stored on S3 and served through Open Connect. Kafka and Flink handle messaging and streaming. Flink and Spark process data, which is visualized with Tableau, and Redshift holds structured data warehouse information. Delivering the software itself relies on CI/CD, the automated build and release pipeline, with tools such as Jenkins, Gradle, Spinnaker and Chaos Monkey.

  <!-- sysd-q-041 -->

- **YouTube's video transcoding unit**

  YouTube handles 500+ hours of uploaded video every minute on average. Every upload must be transcoded: raw video is converted into different compression rates for different viewing devices, such as mobile (720p), laptop (1080p) or high-resolution TV (4k). Software-based encoding became slow and costly, so YouTube built a dedicated chip. It is the VCU, the Video transCoding Unit, developed for warehouse-scale video processing in the way GPUs and TPUs serve graphics and machine learning. The design is clusters of VCU servers, with accelerator trays of cards that hold encoders and decoders.

  The VCU cluster generates the different resolutions and stores them in cloud storage. The design gave 20-33x improvements in computing efficiency over the previous optimized system. Transcoding, the step this unit serves, is described in Video transcoding.

  <!-- sysd-q-039 -->

- **Netflix Open Connect**

  Around 95% of Netflix's traffic globally is delivered over direct connections between Open Connect and the internet service providers (ISPs) that customers use to reach the internet. Open Connect is Netflix's purpose-built CDN, responsible for serving its video traffic, and it goes a step further than a traditional CDN. It places appliances at partner ISPs. Netflix partners with thousands of ISPs to localize its traffic and deliver content more efficiently. These Open Connect Appliances (OCAs) sit in over 1000 separate locations around the world. If an appliance has issues, it can fail over, and traffic is re-routed to Netflix servers. That makes it a private CDN: one company's own network, built to serve its own video traffic. For the general idea of a CDN and its edge servers, see Content delivery networks: serving users from nearby and Origin and edge servers: where a CDN's content lives.

  <!-- sysd-q-040 -->

### Design a ride-hailing service like Uber

Open a ride-hailing app and the screen shows nearby cabs, an ETA and a price. This chapter takes that screen apart. It starts with nearest neighbor search, the problem of finding the point closest to a query point, and the proximity service that applies it to places within a radius. It adds dynamic pricing, then ends with the worked Uber design and a look at Uber's technology stack.

- **Nearest neighbor search**

  In high-dimensional space, checking every point one by one can on average beat the clever indexes. Nearest neighbor search is the optimization problem of finding the point in a given set that is closest, or most similar, to a query point. Closeness is a dissimilarity function, most often a distance metric such as Euclidean or Manhattan distance over a d-dimensional vector space. A k-nearest neighbor search returns the k closest points instead of one. The simplest exact solution is linear search: compute the distance from the query to every point, in O(dN) time, with no structure to maintain. Space partitioning avoids the full scan. A k-d tree repeatedly bisects the search space, and queries walk from root to leaf in average O(log N) time for randomly distributed points. When tree indexes stop helping in high dimensions, approximate search may return a point within c times the distance to the true nearest. That trades guaranteed answers for speed or memory. Proximity graph methods such as HNSW are the current state of the art for it.

  <!-- sysd-q-090 -->

- **Proximity service**

  Storing each place's latitude and longitude and computing the distance to every place makes a nearby search very inefficient. A proximity service returns the places within a given radius of a location, such as nearby restaurants. Its design has two key services. A business service adds, deletes and updates place information and lets customers view details. A location-based service returns the places near a given location and radius. The geohash algorithm speeds up the search. It divides the planet into four quadrants along the prime meridian and equator, then keeps dividing each grid into four. A grid is named by alternating longitude and latitude bits. Nearby places in a grid are then found with a prefix match on the geohash column, for example geohash LIKE '01%'. Geohash has limits: one grid can hold very many places, such as downtown New York, and another none, such as the ocean. More complicated algorithms optimize the process.

  <!-- sysd-q-017 -->

- **Dynamic pricing**

  Uber has capped how high surge pricing can go in emergencies since 2015. Dynamic pricing, also called surge pricing, sets flexible prices from current market demand, rising at peak demand and falling at low demand. That encourages buying when demand is low and discourages it when demand is high. In some sectors economists see it as a more efficient allocation of limited resources. Algorithmic pricing does this automatically, to maximize the seller's profit. It is often criticized as price gouging, so operators add guardrails. Drivers, meanwhile, may hold off accepting rides until surge raises fares.

  <!-- sysd-q-089 -->

- **Designing a ride-hailing service like Uber**

  A ride-hailing service like Uber lets customers see nearby cabs with ETA and pricing, book a cab and see the driver's location. Drivers accept or deny rides, see the pickup location and mark the trip complete on reaching the destination. The system needs high availability with minimal latency, and it must scale. Trip ratings, payment processing, and metrics and analytics are extended requirements. Assume 100 million daily active users, 1 million drivers and 10 million rides daily, with 10 actions per user. That is 1 billion requests daily, or 12K requests per second. At 400 bytes per message, storage is about 400 GB a day and about 1.4 PB over 10 years. Minimum ingress bandwidth is around 5 MB per second.

  The tables hold customers, drivers, trips (source, destination, status), cabs (registration number, type), and ratings and payments by trip ID. Each service owns its tables, on PostgreSQL or a distributed NoSQL store such as Cassandra. Request a ride takes a customer ID, source and destination. Cancel takes a customer ID and an optional reason. Accept or deny takes a driver ID and ride ID, start or end uses a driver ID and trip ID, and rating takes a score. The services are microservices that own their data: customer, driver, ride (ride matching and quadtree aggregation), trip, payment, notification and analytics. They communicate over REST or the lighter gRPC, with service discovery.

  A customer requests a ride with source, destination, cab type and payment method. The ride service finds nearby drivers and the ETA and broadcasts the request. Once a driver accepts, the customer sees the driver's live location and ETA. Pulling location by periodic HTTP requests or long polling does not scale: it adds request overhead, and most responses are empty. A WebSocket push model delivers data without delay and is full-duplex, unlike unidirectional Server-Sent Events.

  Finding nearby drivers is the hard query, the one Proximity service describes. A radius query on PostgreSQL or MySQL is too slow at scale. Geohash encodes coordinates as hierarchical base-32 strings, so the customer's geohash is compared with drivers' geohashes, indexed in memory. A quadtree, whose internal nodes have four children, splits two-dimensional space to search points in a range efficiently. Split a node only past a threshold, update it on each driver location update, and cache the latest updates in Redis.

  Race conditions arise when many customers request rides at once, so the ride matching logic is wrapped in a mutex and every action is transactional. Nearby drivers are ranked by parameters such as average rating, relevance and past feedback, so the best are notified first. Under high demand, surge pricing temporarily raises prices in reaction to increased demand and limited supply, as Dynamic pricing describes. Payments go to a third-party processor such as Stripe or PayPal, with a webhook capturing payment data. Push notifications flow through a message queue or broker such as Kafka to Firebase Cloud Messaging and the registration token or Apple Push Notification service: reaching Apple devices.

  Shard by region, such as zip codes, with consistent hashing against uneven load. Cache recent customer and driver locations in Redis or Memcached with LRU eviction, refilling from the database on a miss. Remove single points of failure with multiple service instances, load balancers between clients, servers, databases and caches, read replicas and replicated caches. A dedicated broker such as Kafka or NATS makes notifications robust. The thing to remember: the heart of the design is the nearby-driver lookup, and the rest is keeping it fast and safe when many riders ask at once.

  <!-- sysd-q-016 -->

  *Figure: The ride service looks up nearby drivers in a location index, then broadcasts the request.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Customer requests ride] --> B[Ride service finds nearby drivers]
  B --> G[(Geohash and quadtree index)]
  B --> C[Broadcasts request]
  C --> D[Driver accepts]
  D --> E[Customer sees live location]
  ```

- **Uber's technology stack**

  Uber built its own React framework, Fusion.js, for its web frontend. It also uses visualization.js for geospatial visualization. The mobile apps use the RIB architecture with VIPER instead of MVC, in Swift for iOS and Java for Android. Uber Gateway is a dynamic configuration on top of NGINX. Client-server communication uses gRPC: fast, typed calls between services and QUIC, and APIs are defined with Apache Thrift.

  Backend services use Spring Boot for Java, uAct for event-driven architecture and Cadence for asynchronous workflow orchestration. Flipr, later UCDP, is a unified configuration store, and H3 is a location-index store library. The main OLTP store, the database for live transactions, is the strongly consistent DocStore, which employs MySQL and PostgreSQL with the RocksDB engine. Big data uses the Hadoop family with Hudi and Parquet file formats and Alluxio as cache. Time-series data is in Pinot and AresDB. Hive, Spark and Marmaray process data, and Apache Kafka: a log that keeps messages after they are read and Flink handle messaging and streaming. DevOps uses a monorepo with devpod environments and Spinnaker for continuous delivery, with uMetric for metrics, uMonitor for alarms and M3 as the observability database.

  <!-- sysd-q-018 -->

### Design a web crawler

A web crawler visits the Web page by page, following links from a list of starting addresses, so that a search engine has something to index. The web is too large to fetch in full, so a crawler needs rules for what to download, when to return and how to avoid overloading the sites it visits. This chapter covers those rules, the robots.txt standard that sites use to set limits, and what happens to the pages afterward: indexing, ranking with PageRank and measuring how similar two pages are. It closes with a worked design for a crawler and the search engine behind it.

- **Web crawler**

  One photo gallery can look like 48 different pages to a crawler. With four sort orders, three thumbnail sizes, two file formats and an option to hide user content, it serves the same content under 48 different URLs. A web crawler is an Internet bot that systematically browses the World Wide Web, usually run by search engines to index the pages it downloads. It starts from a list of seed URLs and fetches those pages. It finds their hyperlinks and adds them to the list of URLs still to visit, called the crawl frontier. Frontier URLs are visited recursively under policies for selection (Crawl selection policy), re-visit (Crawl re-visit policy), politeness (Crawl politeness policy) and parallelization. The web is so large that a crawler can download only a limited number of pages in a given time, so it must prioritize. A parallel crawler runs multiple processes, so it needs a policy for assigning newly found URLs: two processes can discover the same URL and download the page twice. Crawlers typically identify themselves in the User-agent field of the HTTP request.

  <!-- sysd-q-049 -->

- **Robots exclusion protocol**

  A polite crawler checks before it fetches. The robots exclusion protocol, usually called robots.txt, is the standard by which a website tells visiting web crawlers which portions of the site they may visit. A site owner puts a robots.txt file at the root of the site. A compliant robot fetches it before any other file, uses it to decide which links to follow, and assumes no limits if the file is missing. The protocol is purely advisory and relies on voluntary compliance. Malicious bots may ignore it or use it to find disallowed paths. Developed in 1994, it was published as a proposed standard, RFC 9309, in September 2022. The standard sets no visit interval, though that is the most effective way to avoid overload. The non-standard Crawl-delay is read differently: Yandex takes seconds between visits, Bing a window of 1 to 30 seconds, and Google ignores it. Robots meta tags and X-Robots-Tag headers act at finer grain, but only after the page loads, whereas robots.txt acts before the request.

  <!-- sysd-q-055 -->

- **Crawl politeness policy**

  The first proposed delay between requests to one site was 60 seconds. At that rate a site of more than 100,000 pages would take over 2 months to download. A crawl politeness policy is the set of rules a crawler follows to avoid overloading the websites it visits. Crawlers fetch data faster and deeper than human searchers, so one making many requests per second or downloading large files can cripple a site's performance. The costs include network bandwidth, server overload and poorly written crawlers that can crash servers or routers. The robots exclusion protocol only partly solves this. It says which parts of a server to avoid but suggests no interval between visits, the most effective way to avoid overload. Major search engines support an extra Crawl-delay parameter in robots.txt giving the seconds to wait between requests. Cho uses 10 seconds, WIRE 15 seconds and Dill et al. 1 second. The Mercator crawler is adaptive: if a download from a server took t seconds, it waits 10t seconds before fetching the next page from it.

  <!-- sysd-q-054 -->

  *Figure: Proposed waits between requests to one site range from 60 seconds down to 1 second.* (bar; drawn in the EPUB)

- **Crawl re-visit policy**

  A crawl of part of the web can take weeks or months, and the web does not wait. Creations, updates and deletions happen meanwhile, and the search engine pays a cost for holding an outdated copy. The crawl re-visit policy is the rule that decides when a crawler checks pages again for changes, to keep its stored copies from going stale. The usual cost functions are freshness, a binary measure of whether the local copy is accurate, and age, a measure of how outdated the copy is. A uniform policy re-visits all pages at the same frequency. A proportional policy re-visits pages that change more often more frequently, in proportion to their estimated change rate. The surprise is that uniform beats proportional on average freshness, because a proportional policy spends crawls on rapidly changing pages whose freshness lasts only briefly. The optimal policy is closer to uniform. To keep average freshness high, ignore pages that change too often. To keep average age low, raise access frequency sub-linearly with a page's rate of change.

  <!-- sysd-q-053 -->

- **Crawl selection policy**

  Even large search engines cover only part of the public web: a 2009 study showed they index no more than 40-70% of the indexable web. A crawl selection policy decides which pages a crawler downloads, ranking them by an importance metric because only a fraction of the web can be fetched. The downloaded fraction should hold the most relevant pages, not a random sample. So the policy needs an importance metric built from a page's intrinsic quality, its popularity in links or visits, and sometimes its URL. It must work with partial information, since the full set of pages is unknown while crawling. A breadth-first crawl captures pages with high PageRank early, because the most important pages have many links from numerous hosts. OPIC gives each page an initial sum of cash, split equally among the pages it links to. The crawler downloads the frontier pages holding the most cash first. Some crawlers skip any URL containing a "?" to avoid endless URL traps (see Spider trap), though this is unreliable when a site rewrites URLs.

  <!-- sysd-q-050 -->

- **How search engines work**

  When you search, you are not searching the web. You are searching an index the engine built earlier. Search engines work through three processes: crawling pages, indexing what was collected, and serving ranked results for queries. Crawlers start from a list of known pages, the seeds, and follow links to discover and download new pages. The collected information is analyzed and organized into a massive index. The engine extracts keywords, content type, freshness, language and other signals to learn what each page is about and how relevant it may be to queries. To serve a query, the engine first analyzes it for meaning and intent, identifying keywords, recognizing synonyms and interpreting context. It then retrieves pages from the index by matching the query's keywords with indexed content, and ranks the retrieved pages by relevance and other factors.

  <!-- sysd-q-056 -->

  *Figure: The three processes run in order: crawl, index, then serve ranked results.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Crawl: follow links from seeds] --> B[Index: analyze and organize]
  B --> C[Serve: analyze the query]
  C --> D[Retrieve from the index]
  D --> E[Rank by relevance]
  ```

- **Search engine indexing**

  Without an index, an engine would scan every document in the corpus. An index of 10,000 documents can be queried within milliseconds, while a sequential scan of 10,000 large documents could take hours. Search engine indexing is the collecting, parsing and storing of data so that information can be retrieved quickly and accurately. The index is paid for with extra storage and a considerably longer update time. Parsing breaks documents into tokens for the forward and inverted indices. With several languages, identifying each document's language comes first, because later steps such as stemming depend on it. Tokenizing is hard when words are not delineated by whitespace, as in Chinese or Japanese, so a parser is often built per language. Indexing is a producer-consumer chain: the crawler fills the corpus, the forward index consumes it, and the inverted index consumes the forward index. That lets indexers work asynchronously. Adding a document while the index keeps answering queries invites race conditions. A simple uncompressed index for 2 billion web pages would hold 500 billion word entries, about 2500 gigabytes at 5 bytes per word. Compression shrinks it at the cost of compression and decompression time.

  <!-- sysd-q-108 -->

- **PageRank**

  PageRank treats every link as a vote. It is a link analysis algorithm, used by Google Search, that gives each page in a hyperlinked set a numerical weight measuring its relative importance. A page linked from many high-PageRank pages gets a high rank itself, so the rank is defined recursively. The web is a graph, with pages as nodes and hyperlinks as edges. The output is a probability distribution: the chance that a person randomly clicking links lands on each page. Each page passes its PageRank equally to the pages it links to. The damping factor d, generally around 0.85, is the chance the surfer keeps following links; otherwise they jump to a random page. The values are computed iteratively until they stop changing, and the original paper reports 322 million links converging in 52 iterations. It favors older pages, since a new page has few links, and paid links and link farms can manipulate it.

  <!-- sysd-q-109 -->

- **Cosine similarity**

  Two documents of different lengths can still be about the same thing. Cosine similarity captures that. It is the cosine of the angle between two non-zero vectors, their dot product divided by the product of their lengths. It depends only on the angle, not the magnitudes, and lies in [-1, +1]: proportional vectors score +1, orthogonal ones 0, opposite ones -1. In text mining each word is a coordinate and a document is the vector of its word counts. The measure then shows how alike two documents are in subject matter, regardless of length. Its cost is low for sparse vectors, because only the non-zero coordinates count.

  <!-- sysd-q-111 -->

- **Sitemaps**

  A sitemap tells a crawler what to visit, where robots.txt tells it what to avoid. It is an XML protocol that lets a webmaster tell search engines which URLs on a site are available for crawling. That makes it a URL inclusion protocol, complementing robots.txt, a URL exclusion protocol. It guarantees neither indexing nor ranking, but it helps crawlers find isolated URLs. The file has a required loc for each URL and optional lastmod, changefreq and priority (0.0 to 1.0, default 0.5), which are only hints. One sitemap holds at most 50,000 URLs or 50MiB uncompressed, and a sitemap index file may list up to 50,000 sitemaps.

  <!-- sysd-q-112 -->

- **Deep web crawling**

  A vast number of pages sit in the deep or invisible web, where regular crawlers cannot find them. Deep web crawling is the effort to reach them. They are usually reachable only by submitting queries to a database, and no links point to them. Google's Sitemaps protocol and mod oai are intended to let such resources be discovered, though it also multiplies the number of links to crawl. Screen scraping software can be customized to query a web form repeatedly and aggregate the results. Pages built on AJAX cause problems for crawlers, and Google has proposed a format of AJAX calls its bot can recognize and index.

  <!-- sysd-q-057 -->

- **Focused crawler**

  A crawler does not have to want every page. A focused crawler, also called a topical crawler, tries to download only pages similar to a given query or topic. A page's importance can be expressed as its similarity to a query. The main problem is predicting a page's text similarity to the query before downloading it. One predictor is the anchor text of links, and another is the full content of pages already visited. Performance depends mostly on how rich in links the topic is, and a focused crawl usually relies on a general web search engine to supply starting points.

  <!-- sysd-q-052 -->

- **URL normalization**

  To a crawler, two different strings can name one page. URL normalization, also called URL canonicalization, modifies and standardizes a URL in a consistent way, so that one resource has one form. Crawlers usually normalize URLs to avoid crawling the same resource more than once. Typical normalizations convert URLs to lowercase, remove "." and ".." segments, and add trailing slashes to a non-empty path component.

  <!-- sysd-q-051 -->

- **Spider trap**

  A calendar whose pages keep linking to the next day, and the next, never ends. That is a spider trap: a set of web pages that makes a crawler issue an infinite number of requests or crash. Some traps are made on purpose, to catch spambots or crawlers that waste bandwidth; others are accidents. Typical forms are indefinitely deep directory structures, dynamic pages that produce an unbounded number of documents, and session ids that require cookies. A trap acts like an infinite loop and can crash a poorly written crawler. Sites with traps usually list them in robots.txt, so a polite bot that obeys it stays out.

  <!-- sysd-q-113 -->

- **Jaccard index**

  How alike are two sets? The Jaccard index answers with one number: the size of their intersection divided by the size of their union. It is a normalized measure of overlap, from 0 for sets with nothing in common to 1 for equal sets. The Jaccard distance is 1 minus it. Unlike the simple matching coefficient, it ignores attributes absent from both sets, so it suits sparse data. For documents, the resemblance of two documents is the Jaccard coefficient of their shingle sets, as W-shingling describes. MinHash and locality-sensitive hashing approximate it at scale from compact fixed-size signatures.

  <!-- sysd-q-110 -->

- **W-shingling**

  The phrase "a rose is a rose is a rose" has five runs of four words, but only three of them are different. A w-shingling is a set of unique shingles, each a run of w contiguous tokens (n-grams) from a document, used to measure how similar two documents are. Repeats collapse in the set, which is why the example gives three. The resemblance of two documents is the size of the intersection of their shinglings divided by the size of the union, from 0 to 1. That is the Jaccard index.

  <!-- sysd-q-114 -->

- **Designing a web crawler**

  A web crawler feeds a search engine. The service must crawl a list of URLs, build a reverse index of words to pages and generate static titles and snippets. A user enters a search term and sees matching pages with those titles and snippets. It must be highly available and produce search results fast. The crawler must not get stuck in an infinite loop, which happens if the link graph contains a cycle. Search analytics and personalized results are out of scope, and only anonymous users are supported. Search traffic is not evenly distributed: some searches are very popular, while others are executed only once.

  The assumptions are 1 billion links to crawl and a refresh rate of about once per week, more often for popular sites. They also include 4 billion links crawled each month, 500 KB average stored size per page and 100 billion searches per month. That makes 2 PB of stored page content per month, which is 500 KB per page times 4 billion links, and 72 PB in 3 years. The load is 1,600 write requests per second and 40,000 search requests per second.

  The data model is two tables. links_to_crawl is ranked initially by overall site popularity, and crawled_links stores processed links with their page signatures. Both could live in a key-value NoSQL database, with Redis sorted sets keeping the link ranking. If the initial list is not reasonable, the crawler can be seeded with popular sites that link to outside content, such as Yahoo or DMOZ.

  The Crawler Service runs in a loop. It takes the top ranked link and checks crawled_links for a similar page signature. If a similar page exists, it lowers the link's priority, which prevents a cycle. Otherwise it crawls the link and queues a job for the Reverse Index Service and one for the Document Service, which makes the static title and snippet. It generates the page signature, removes the link from links_to_crawl and inserts the link and signature into crawled_links.

  Duplicate URLs can be removed with sort and unique for small lists. With 1 billion links to crawl, MapReduce can output only the entries that have a frequency of 1. Detecting duplicate content is more complex. Generate a signature from each page's contents and compare signatures for similarity, using an algorithm such as the Jaccard index or Cosine similarity. Each crawl result carries a timestamp of the last crawl. After a default period, say one week, all pages are refreshed, and frequently updated or popular sites are refreshed sooner. A robots.txt file could give webmasters control of crawl frequency, as Crawl politeness policy explains.

  A search goes from the client to a reverse-proxy web server, then to the Query API server. That server parses the query, removes markup, splits it into terms, fixes typos, normalizes capitalization and converts it to boolean operations. It asks the Reverse Index Service for matching documents, ranks them and returns the top ones, and the Document Service returns titles and snippets. The public API is REST, and internal calls could use RPC.

  Popular queries can be served from a memory cache such as Redis or Memcached. That cuts response times, protects the Reverse Index Service and Document Service, and absorbs uneven traffic and spikes. Those two services will likely need heavy sharding and federation. The crawler itself can keep its own periodically refreshed DNS lookup and pool many open connections, and it needs enough bandwidth, since crawling is bandwidth intensive. The thing to remember: the crawler must never fetch what it has already seen, and the page signature check is what breaks the cycle.

  <!-- sysd-q-048 -->

  *Figure: The Crawler Service skips a link whose page looks like one it has already stored, which prevents a cycle.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[(links_to_crawl)] --> B[Crawler Service takes top link]
  B --> C{Similar signature?}
  C -->|yes| D[Lower link priority]
  D -.-> A
  C -->|no| E[Crawl the link]
  E --> F[Reverse Index job]
  E --> G[Document Service job]
  E --> H[(crawled_links)]
  ```

### Design a personal finance app like Mint

A personal finance app has four jobs: connect a financial account, extract its transactions, categorize them, and analyze monthly spending by category. Users can override a category by hand, but nothing is re-categorized automatically. Two building blocks come first in this chapter. A heap is a tree in which the highest- or lowest-priority element always sits at the root, and open banking lets banks share customer financial data with authorized third-party providers through APIs. Then the worked design builds the whole service.

- **Heap**

  A heap keeps its most urgent item exactly where you can reach it: at the root. It is a tree in which each parent's key is at least (max heap) or at most (min heap) its children's keys. That is only partial order, not sorting, since siblings and cousins have no order between them. A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored in an array. Links are implied by indices: from index 0, node i has children at 2i+1 and 2i+2, so no extra memory is needed. Insertion adds an element at the end and sifts it up until the rule holds again. Removing the root moves the last element to the root and sifts it down. This makes a heap an efficient way to build a priority queue, and it also drives heapsort and graph algorithms such as Dijkstra's algorithm.

  <!-- sysd-q-087 -->

- **Open banking**

  For years your bank's data stayed inside the bank. Open banking changes that: it lets banks share customer financial data with authorized third-party providers through application programming interfaces (see API: the contract between two pieces of software). With explicit customer consent, such a provider can read account information or initiate payments. Regulation drove the shift. The EU adopted PSD2 in October 2015, and in 2016 the UK required its nine biggest banks to give licensed startups transaction-level access.
