The openness has risks: hackers can target third-party apps, phishing can trick customers, and employees may hold excessive access privileges.

  <!-- sysd-q-088 -->

- **Designing a personal finance app**

  Build the backend of a personal finance app in the style of Mint. A user connects a financial account, the service extracts its transactions and categorizes them, and the user analyzes monthly spending by category. Users may override a category by hand, but nothing is re-categorized automatically. The service also recommends a budget that the user can set manually, and it sends notifications when spending approaches or exceeds the budget. It must be highly available, and extra logging and analytics are out of scope.

  The assumptions shape the design. Traffic is not evenly distributed, adding or removing accounts is rare, budget notifications need not be instant, and sellers determine a transaction's category. The automatic daily update covers only users active in the past 30 days. The scale is 10 million users with 30 million financial accounts and 50,000 sellers. They produce 5 billion transactions and 500 million read requests a month, a 10:1 write to read ratio. A transaction is about 50 bytes: user_id 8, created_at 5, seller 32 and amount 5. So 5 billion a month means 250 GB of new transaction content a month and 9 TB in 3 years. The average load is 2,000 transactions per second against 200 read requests per second. The system is write-heavy, because users make transactions daily but few visit the site daily.

  To connect an account, the client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Accounts API server. That server writes the account to the SQL accounts table, indexed on id, user_id and created_at. The API is public REST. Extraction runs when the user first links an account, on manual refresh, and daily for users active in the past 30 days. It takes a while, so the API server queues a job on Amazon SQS or RabbitMQ. The Transaction Extraction Service pulls from the queue and stores raw transaction logs in an object store. It then calls the Category and Budget Services, and the Budget Service alerts users through a Notification Service. Finally it updates the SQL transactions and monthly_spending tables.

  The Category Service seeds a seller-to-category dictionary with popular sellers: 50,000 sellers at under 255 bytes each take about 12 MB of memory. Sellers outside the seed are crowdsourced from user overrides, and a heap (Heap) gives the top override in O(1). Budgets start from a generic template that allocates category amounts by income tier, so the 100 million budget items need not be stored. Only a user's overrides go in a budget_overrides table. Monthly spending can come from SQL queries over transactions into monthly_spending, which has far fewer rows than 5 billion transactions. Alternatively, MapReduce jobs on the raw transaction files can categorize and aggregate, which reduces database load.

  For reads, a memory cache such as Redis or Memcached holds sessions, category stats and recent transactions. The Read API server returns hits and otherwise reads the SQL database and updates the cache, the cache-aside pattern. Static content comes from a CDN-cached object store. The cache should serve the 200 average read requests per second, which are higher at peak, and it also absorbs uneven traffic and spikes. SQL read replicas handle cache misses, unless they are bogged down replicating writes. Writes are the harder side, since 2,000 average writes per second might be tough for a single SQL write master-slave. The remedies are federation, denormalization and SQL tuning, and perhaps moving some data to NoSQL. Keep only a month of transactions in the database. The rest goes to a data warehouse or object store, which comfortably handles 250 GB of new content a month.

  Remember the shape of the load. The system is write-heavy, extraction is slow so a queue carries it, and the few reads are served from a cache.

  <!-- sysd-q-015 -->

  *Figure: Follow an account from the client to the queue, the extraction service and the stores it fills.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Client] --> B[Reverse proxy]
  B --> C[Accounts API server]
  C --> D[(SQL accounts table)]
  C -->|queues a job| E[Queue]
  E --> F[Transaction Extraction Service]
  F --> G[(Object store: raw logs)]
  F --> H[Category Service]
  F --> I[Budget Service]
  I --> J[Notification Service]
  F --> K[(SQL transactions)]
  ```

### Design a cache for the most recent search queries

What happens when a search request finds its answer already in the cache, and what happens when it does not? The service in this chapter must handle both, and it must stay highly available. The chapter first introduces a data structure, the doubly linked list, whose nodes each hold a data field plus links to the previous and the next node. Then it puts that structure to work in the design of a cache for recent search queries.

- **Doubly linked list**

  A doubly linked list lets you walk in either direction. It is a chain of nodes, each holding a data field plus links to the previous and the next node. The head and tail are directly accessible, and any node can start a new traversal. Adding or removing a node changes more links than in a singly linked list. It is still simpler and often more efficient, since a node already links to its predecessor and no traversal is needed to find it. Removing the first or last node needs care so the head and tail references are updated.

  <!-- sysd-q-068 -->

- **Designing a search query cache**

  Build a cache that remembers the results of recent search queries. The service handles a user's search request that hits the cache and one that misses it, and it must be highly available. The assumptions: traffic is not evenly distributed, and popular queries should almost always be in the cache. Serving from cache needs fast lookups, and latency between machines must be low. Memory is limited yet millions of queries must be cached, so the design must decide what to keep or remove and how to expire or refresh entries.

  The scale is 10 million users, 10 billion queries per month and 4,000 requests per second. A cache entry holds a 50-byte query, a 20-byte title and a 200-byte snippet, 270 bytes in total. Suppose all 10 billion queries were unique and all were stored. The data would be 2.7 TB per month: 270 bytes per search times 10 billion searches. That is why the cache cannot keep everything. A memory cache such as Redis or Memcached serves popular queries, cutting read latency and sparing the Reverse Index and Document Services. Reading 1 MB sequentially takes about 250 microseconds from memory, while SSD takes 4x and disk 80x longer.

  The client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Query API server. That server parses the query, removes markup, splits it into terms, fixes typos, normalizes capitalization, converts it to boolean operations and checks the cache. On a hit, the memory cache moves the entry to the front of the list and returns the cached contents. On a miss, the Query API gets ranked matching documents from the Reverse Index Service. It gets titles and snippets from the Document Service, then caches the entry at the front of the list.

  Since cache capacity is limited, a least recently used (LRU) approach expires the older entries. The cache is a doubly linked list plus a hash table. New items are added at the head, items to expire are removed from the tail, and the hash table gives fast lookup of each list node. The list itself is the subject of Doubly linked list. Entries must be updated when page contents change, a page is added or removed, or page rank changes. The simplest way is a maximum time an entry may stay cached, the time to live (TTL), and this approach is cache-aside.

  To handle the request load and the memory needed, scale the cache horizontally. Giving each machine its own cache is simple but likely gives a low hit rate, and giving each a full copy is simple but wastes memory. Sharding the cache across all machines in the cluster is more complex but likely the best option. A hash such as machine = hash(query) picks the machine, and consistent hashing is likely wanted. The thing to remember is the pairing: a doubly linked list plus a hash table gives fast lookup and cheap eviction. A hash of the query then spreads the cache over many machines.

  <!-- sysd-q-001 -->

### Design a sales rank by category

Which products sold best this past week, in each category? This service calculates the answer and lets users view it, with high availability. The general e-commerce site and anything beyond the sales rank calculation are out of scope. The chapter is a single worked design.

- **Designing a sales rank by category**

  Build a service that calculates the past week's most popular products by category and lets users view them, with high availability. The general e-commerce site and anything beyond the sales rank calculation are out of scope. The assumptions: traffic is uneven, an item can be in multiple categories but cannot change category, and there are no subcategories. Results must be updated hourly, though more popular products might need more frequent updates.

  The scale is 10 million products, 1 billion transactions per month and 100 billion read requests per month, a 100:1 read to write ratio. A transaction is about 40 bytes: created_at 5, product_id 8, category_id 4, seller_id 8, buyer_id 8, quantity 4 and total_price 5 bytes. That is 40 GB of new transaction content per month, which is 40 bytes times 1 billion transactions. Over 3 years it is 1.44 TB, assuming most are new transactions rather than updates. The average load is 400 transactions per second and 40,000 read requests per second.

  Raw Sales API server log files go to a managed object store such as Amazon S3, rather than a self-managed distributed file system. The Sales Rank Service runs MapReduce with those logs as input and writes the results to an aggregate table, sales_rank, in a SQL database. The MapReduce has several steps. First it transforms records to (category, product_id) with sum(quantity), then it performs a distributed sort. The sorted list is inserted into the sales_rank table. That table is indexed on id, category_id and product_id, for log-time lookups instead of scanning the whole table and to keep the data in memory.

  To view rankings, the client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Read API server, which reads the SQL sales_rank table. The public API is REST, with RPC for internal calls. The 40,000 average read requests per second, higher at peak, should be handled by a memory cache instead of the database, which also absorbs uneven traffic and spikes. With such a large volume of reads, SQL read replicas might not handle the cache misses, so additional SQL scaling patterns are probably needed.

  The 400 average writes per second, higher at peak, might be tough for a single SQL write master-slave. SQL scaling patterns include federation, denormalization and SQL tuning, and some data might also move to NoSQL. The analytics database could be a data warehouse such as Redshift or BigQuery. Keep a limited time period in the database and the rest in a warehouse or an object store, which handles 40 GB of new content per month. The thing to remember is the split: the rank is computed in batch by MapReduce from raw logs, and the heavy read traffic is answered from a cache.

  <!-- sysd-q-019 -->

### Design the data structures for a social network

A social network is a graph, and the interview question is how to search it. A social graph represents social relations between entities, and it can be stored as an adjacency matrix, whose elements show whether pairs of vertices are adjacent, or as an adjacency list that stores an unordered list of neighbors for each vertex. Breadth-first search explores it level by level, the shortest path problem asks for the path with the smallest total edge weight, and bidirectional search runs one search forward from the start and one backward from the goal. The folk idea of six degrees of separation says a chain of friend-of-a-friend links joins any two people. The worked design lets a user search for someone and see the shortest path to that person.

- **Social graph**

  A social network is a graph before it is anything else. A social graph represents social relations between entities, and it is a model of a social network. Relations can be mutual or one-way. On Twitter the relation between users is unidirectional, unlike classical networks such as Facebook, which makes information propagation closer to how information spreads in real life. In 2012, Twitter's social graph held 537 million accounts connected by 23.95 billion links. Such graphs are typically stored in graph databases, and Facebook uses TAO, a custom distributed system optimized for fast reads at massive scale.

  <!-- sysd-q-155 -->

- **Adjacency matrix**

  A graph can be stored as a table of ones and zeros. An adjacency matrix is a square matrix representing a finite graph, whose elements show whether pairs of vertices are adjacent. For a simple graph of n vertices it is an n-by-n matrix. Its element Aij is 1 if an edge runs from vertex i to vertex j, else 0, and its diagonal is 0 because simple graphs have no loops. An undirected graph gives a symmetric matrix, a directed graph's matrix can be asymmetric, and edge weights can be stored directly in the elements. The matrix tests in constant time whether two vertices are adjacent, but listing a vertex's neighbors means scanning a whole row, which takes O(|V|) time. Each entry needs one bit, so a directed graph fits in |V|²/8 bytes. For a large sparse graph, Adjacency list need less storage.

  <!-- sysd-q-159 -->

- **Adjacency list**

  What does this vertex connect to? An adjacency list answers by storing, for each vertex, an unordered list of its neighbors. Implementations vary. One is a hash table from each vertex to an array of neighbors, and another is an array indexed by vertex number pointing to linked lists. A third uses vertex and edge objects, which use more memory but can store data per edge. Listing a vertex's neighbors takes constant time per neighbor, so the total time is proportional to the vertex's degree. Testing whether an edge exists is slower. With unsorted neighbors it takes time proportional to the smaller degree of the two vertices. With a sorted array and binary search it is logarithmic in the degree. For a sparse graph the list is far more space-efficient than Adjacency matrix. Its space is proportional to the vertices plus edges, against the square of the vertices for a matrix.

  <!-- sysd-q-158 -->

- **Breadth-first search**

  Breadth-first search explores a graph level by level. It starts at a root and explores all nodes at the current depth before moving to the next depth level. It keeps a queue of nodes met but not yet explored, labels each vertex explored when it is enqueued, and stores a parent link on each vertex. The parent links trace the shortest path back to the root. BFS uses a first-in-first-out queue where depth-first search uses a last-in-first-out stack. It finds the path with the fewest edges between two nodes, an advantage over depth-first search. It is also complete: it reaches a goal if one exists, even in an infinite graph. Time is O(|V|+|E|), since every vertex and edge is explored in the worst case. On an unweighted graph, BFS is Dijkstra's algorithm with the priority queue degenerated into a plain queue.

  <!-- sysd-q-153 -->

- **Shortest path problem**

  A road map is a graph. Intersections are vertices, road segments are edges weighted by length, travel time or cost, and directed edges model one-way streets. The shortest path problem asks for a path between two vertices so that the sum of its edge weights is as small as possible. The right algorithm depends on the graph. For a single source with non-negative weights the choice is Dijkstra's algorithm. Bellman–Ford suits weights that may be negative, A* search algorithm handles a single pair using heuristics, and Floyd–Warshall handles all pairs. On an unweighted graph, Breadth-first search solves the single-source problem in O(E + V). Adding a constraint, such as keeping a second metric under a threshold, makes the problem NP-complete. Real roads are harder still: travel time varies with traffic, road work, weather and accidents, and there is no accepted definition of an optimal path under uncertainty.

  <!-- sysd-q-154 -->

- **Bidirectional search**

  Two searches that start at opposite ends and meet in the middle can beat one search that goes all the way. Bidirectional search finds a shortest path by running one search forward from the start and one backward from the goal, stopping when the two meet. With branching factor b and start-to-goal distance d, each of the two searches costs O(b^(d/2)), and their sum is much less than the O(b^d) of a single search. The backward search must be able to find, for any node, the parent nodes that have an edge into it. Termination needs care: Goldberg and others explained the correct conditions for bidirectional Dijkstra, and bidirectional A* needs a special stopping criterion. On single-pair queries, bidirectional Dijkstra often visits far fewer vertices than the one-directional version. Each search explores roughly half the space. Contraction hierarchies also answer queries with a bidirectional search.

  <!-- sysd-q-157 -->

- **Six degrees of separation**

  Any two people are supposedly six or fewer friend-of-a-friend links apart. The idea generalizes to an average social distance that is logarithmic in population size. With 30 contacts each, six rounds of handshakes would reach a population as large as the United States. Measurements come close: in a 2007 study the average among 240 million Microsoft Messenger users was 6, and on Twitter in 2010 it was 4.67. Detractors argue that Milgram's small-world experiment did not demonstrate the claim, and they call it an academic urban myth.

  <!-- sysd-q-156 -->

- **Designing a social network graph**

  Build a service where a user searches for another person and sees the shortest path to that person. It must be highly available. The assumptions: traffic is uneven, some searches are more popular than others, the graph data will not fit on a single machine, and graph edges are unweighted. The scale is 100 million users with 50 friends each on average, giving 5 billion friend relationships. There are 1 billion friend searches per month, or 400 search requests per second.

  The exercise avoids graph-specific solutions such as GraphQL or a graph database like Neo4j. Without that constraint, a graph database or graph query language could be used. Without millions of users (vertices) and billions of friend relationships (edges), a general breadth-first search (BFS) would solve this unweighted shortest path task. At this size users cannot all fit on one machine, so they are sharded across Person Servers, which are accessed through a Lookup Service.

  The client calls a reverse-proxy web server, which forwards to the Search API server, which forwards to the User Graph Service. The User Graph Service asks the Lookup Service for the Person Server holding the current user and retrieves that user's friend_ids. It then runs a BFS with the user as source and the friend_ids as adjacent nodes. For each adjacent node it must again ask the Lookup Service which Person Server stores that id, a step with potential for optimization. The public API is REST, and internal communication could use remote procedure calls.

  Person data can be served from a memory cache such as Redis or Memcached. That cuts response times and downstream traffic at 400 average read requests per second, higher at peak, especially for repeated searches and well-connected people. Complete or partial BFS traversals can be stored in the cache to speed later lookups, or computed offline in batch and stored in a NoSQL database. To reduce machine jumps, batch friend lookups hosted on the same Person Server, and shard Person Servers by location, since friends generally live closer to each other.

  Two more ideas shrink the search. Run two BFS searches at once, one from the source and one from the destination, then merge the two paths, which is the method of Bidirectional search. Start the BFS from people with many friends, since they more likely shorten the degrees of separation to the target. Set a time or hop limit before asking the user whether to keep searching. The thing to remember is that the sharded graph makes every hop a possible machine jump. Batching, location sharding and a two-way search all aim to cut the cost of each search.

  <!-- sysd-q-064 -->

### Scale a system to millions of users on AWS

A website that starts on one server has to grow without falling over. This chapter follows a simplified e-commerce site as it evolves from a monolith on one server to a service-oriented or microservice architecture. Scaling is iterative: benchmark or load test, profile for bottlenecks, address them while weighing alternatives and trade-offs, then repeat. The chapter also introduces the virtual private cloud, an on-demand, configurable pool of shared resources inside a public cloud that isolates one organization's resources from the others. AWS-specific details are not required, since the principles apply outside AWS too.

- **Scaling a website in stages**

  A website that starts on one server cannot stay there once the traffic arrives. This is how a simplified e-commerce site grows, from a monolith on one server to a service-oriented or microservice architecture. It has an inventory service for product descriptions and inventory, and a user service for registration, login and user information. As the user base grows, one application server cannot handle the traffic, so the application server and the database server move onto two separate servers. When one application server is still not enough, a cluster is deployed, and a load balancer routes incoming requests so each server gets an even load. If the database becomes the bottleneck, frequent read queries go to read replicas by separating reads from writes, which greatly increases database write throughput. When one database cannot carry both the inventory and user tables, there are three options. One is adding CPU and RAM, which has a hard limit. Another is partitioning horizontally across more database servers, and the third is adding a caching layer to offload reads. Finally the functions are modularized into separate services.

  <!-- sysd-q-066 -->

  *Figure: Each stage removes the bottleneck of the one before it.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Monolith on one server] -->|user base grows| B[Application and database servers split]
  B -->|one application server not enough| C[Cluster behind a load balancer]
  C -->|database bottleneck| D[Read replicas serve reads]
  D -->|one database cannot carry all| E[Partition or add a cache]
  E --> F[Separate services]
  ```

- **Virtual private cloud**

  A virtual private cloud gives one organization a private corner of a public cloud. It is an on-demand, configurable pool of shared resources that isolates that organization's resources from the others. Isolation normally comes from a private IP subnet and a virtual communication construct per user, such as a VLAN or a set of encrypted channels. A per-VPC virtual private network function secures remote access through authentication and encryption. Amazon's VPC lets EC2 instances be connected to legacy infrastructure over an IPsec VPN. On Google Cloud a VPC is a global resource and its subnets are regional.

  <!-- sysd-q-160 -->

- **Scaling a system to millions of users**

  Scale a service from a few users to millions on AWS, discussing general scaling patterns, since the principles apply outside AWS too. A user makes a read or write request, and the service processes it, stores user data and returns results. It must keep high availability as it grows. Scaling is iterative: benchmark or load test, profile for bottlenecks, address them while weighing alternatives and trade-offs, then repeat. The assumptions are uneven traffic and a need for relational data. The target is 10 million users, 1 billion writes and 100 billion reads per month, a 100:1 read to write ratio, at 1 KB per write. That is an estimated 1 TB of new content per month and 36 TB in 3 years. The average load is 400 writes per second and 40,000 reads per second.

  With one or two users, start with a single box for simplicity: a web server on EC2, storage for user data and a MySQL database. Start with SQL because relational data is needed. Scale vertically when needed, and monitor to find bottlenecks. Vertical scaling, a bigger box, can get very expensive and leaves no redundancy or failover, and the alternative is horizontal scaling. An Elastic IP gives a public endpoint that survives reboots and eases failover, and DNS such as Route 53 maps the domain to it. Open only the needed ports: 80, 443 and 22 for SSH from whitelisted IPs.

  As users grow, vertical scaling gets expensive and blocks scaling MySQL and the web server independently. So store static content in a managed object store such as S3, and move MySQL to a separate box, for example RDS. The split adds complexity, changes to the web server and new security needs. Secure it with encryption in transit and at rest. Put the web server in a public subnet and everything else in a private subnet, all inside a virtual private cloud (Virtual private cloud).

  When one web server bottlenecks at peak hours, scale horizontally behind a load balancer such as ELB or HAProxy, terminating SSL there. Use multiple web servers and MySQL in master-slave failover across multiple availability zones. Then separate the web servers, running as reverse proxy, from the application servers and scale each independently, for example read-API and write-API servers. Move static and some dynamic content to a CDN such as CloudFront.

  For a read-heavy 100:1 workload, move frequently accessed content and session data to a memory cache such as ElastiCache, which makes the web servers stateless. Add MySQL read replicas too, splitting reads and writes in the web server. Traffic spikes in business hours and drops afterward. Autoscaling groups for each web and application server type, across availability zones, keep up with the spikes and cut costs.

  Near the full constraints, keep a limited period of data in MySQL and the rest in a warehouse such as Redshift. Scale the memory cache for 40,000 reads per second, though read replicas may struggle with cache misses. The 400 writes per second may strain a single SQL write master-slave. Use federation, denormalization or SQL tuning, and consider moving suitable data to NoSQL such as DynamoDB. Work that need not be real-time goes to queues and workers. In a photo service, the application server queues a job, and a worker creates the thumbnail, updates the database and stores the thumbnail in the object store. The thing to remember is the loop: each fix removes one bottleneck and exposes the next, so benchmark, profile and fix again.

  <!-- sysd-q-065 -->

### Design Gmail

Sending an email looks like one act, but it is a relay race between programs. SMTP is the Internet standard protocol that mail servers and clients use to transmit electronic mail, and a message passes through user agents, submission agents, transfer agents and delivery agents, each with its own role. The message itself is a header section of fields followed by an optional body, and MIME extends the format to carry non-ASCII text and multimedia attachments. This chapter follows mail through the SMTP transaction, queues and retries, bounce messages and the MX record that names a domain's mail server. It ends with retrieval by POP and with spam, the unsolicited bulk mail that every mail design must handle.

- **Simple Mail Transfer Protocol**

  SMTP only pushes mail; it never pulls it. The Simple Mail Transfer Protocol is the Internet standard that mail servers and clients use to transmit electronic mail, and it is a delivery protocol only. Mail goes to the next-hop server as it arrives, routed by destination server rather than by individual user, while POP and IMAP handle retrieval. SMTP is connection-oriented and text-based: a sender issues command strings and a receiver replies, over a reliable ordered stream, typically a TCP connection. Replies are 2xx positive, 4xx transient or 5xx permanent. Servers talk to each other on TCP port 25, and clients submit mail on port 465 or 587 to a submission server that requires authentication. Original SMTP could not authenticate senders, so spoofing is possible. Modern servers add SPF, DKIM, DMARC, DNSBLs and greylisting to reject or quarantine suspicious mail.

  <!-- sysd-q-115 -->

- **Email message format**

  An email message is plain text, and one blank line splits it in two. It is a header section of fields followed by an optional body, in the syntax RFC 5322 specifies, and a blank line separates the two. A header field is a name, a colon and a field body. A long body can be folded onto several lines by inserting a line break before whitespace. A conformant message uses US-ASCII characters, with each line at most 998 characters and ideally at most 78. The header fields carry most of the semantic information, because the RFC 5322 body is only a series of uninterpreted lines of text. Non-ASCII header text uses the RFC 2047 encoded-word syntax, and non-ASCII bodies use the encodings of MIME. A header must include at least a From field and a Date field.

  <!-- sysd-q-136 -->

- **MIME**

  Email was designed for 7-bit ASCII, so how does a photo get through? MIME, the Multipurpose Internet Mail Extensions, extends the email format to carry non-ASCII text and multimedia attachments. It adds character set specifiers and two content transfer encodings: quoted printable for mostly 7-bit text, and base64 for arbitrary binary data. Attachments are widely sent as base64 because original SMTP transports only 7-bit ASCII, so the attachment is encoded before sending and decoded on receipt. A MIME message can hold several parts. The type multipart/mixed carries a cover letter and documents, multipart/alternative the same content in several formats, and multipart/related HTML with its images. Parts can nest, and the sender can mark a part as shown inline or as an attachment. The message forms a tree whose leaves are single-part content types and whose inner nodes are multipart types, which lets IMAP fetch one part without the rest.

  <!-- sysd-q-123 -->

- **Email spam**

  Most email is junk. Email spam is unsolicited messages sent in bulk by email. Because sending is cheap, it grew to an estimated 90% of global email traffic by 2014 and about 85% of email in 2021. Spam burdens recipients, who must manage, filter or delete it without compensation from the sender, which makes it a negative externality. Spammers need addresses, so they and list merchants gather huge lists, harvesting addresses without the owners' consent. They misspell filtered words or hide the message text in an image to defeat pattern-matching and text-based filters. They send through vulnerable third-party systems such as open mail relays, open proxies and networks of malware-infected PCs, called zombies. To resist, administrators pre-emptively block dynamic IP ranges, require forward-confirmed reverse DNS and impose strict requirements on delivering servers, which can burden small domestic mail servers. Many ISPs block outgoing port 25.

  <!-- sysd-q-128 -->

- **SMTP mail transaction**

  An SMTP conversation is strictly polite: one command at a time. A mail transaction hands one message to a server in three steps: MAIL, one or more RCPT, then DATA. A session starts when the client opens a connection and the server sends a greeting. The client then normally sends EHLO to identify itself, and the dialog stays lock-step unless pipelining is agreed. MAIL starts a transaction and resets the receiver's state. Its reverse-path is the source mailbox used to report errors, and a 250 reply accepts it. RCPT gives one forward-path per command and can be repeated. A recipient known to be undeliverable gets a 550 reply, and RCPT without a prior MAIL gets 503. After DATA the server replies 354 and treats the following lines as the message until a line holding only a period. The client must not send message data unless it gets 354. To let users send a line that is a single period, the client adds an extra leading period to any line starting with one. The server removes it. When the server finishes storing the data it sends 250, which confirms the transaction. By returning 2yz, the server accepts responsibility to deliver the message, retry transient failures and notify the sender of permanent ones. A 4yz after the end of data means the server must not deliver and the client keeps responsibility. A 5yz means the client should not retry to the same server without review. The client ends the connection with QUIT, to which the receiver must send 221 before closing.

  <!-- sysd-q-130 -->

  *Figure: Read the steps of one transaction from top to bottom.*

  | Step | Client sends | Server answers |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 | Opens a connection, then EHLO | Sends a greeting |
  | 2 | MAIL | 250 accepts the reverse-path |
  | 3 | RCPT, once per recipient | 550 if undeliverable; 503 without MAIL |
  | 4 | DATA | 354, then lines are the message |
  | 5 | Message lines, then a lone period | 250 confirms and takes responsibility |
  | 6 | QUIT | 221, then the channel closes |

- **SMTP envelope versus message header**

  A letter's address is written on the envelope, not on the page inside, and email works the same way. A mail object has an envelope that SMTP uses for delivery and content made of a header section and a body. The envelope holds the originator address to which errors are reported, one or more recipient addresses and optional extension data. The content, sent in DATA, has a header section and a body. Delivery follows the envelope, not the header. So the To field may be unrelated to the addresses the message is delivered to, and From may not be the actual sender. Bcc recipients are normally given only in the envelope and not listed in the header. Return-Path, added at final delivery, preserves the MAIL command's reverse-path, which can differ from the sender's mailbox when errors go to a special error-handling mailbox. The content is US-ASCII text, though extensions such as 8BITMIME can relax the restriction for the body.

  <!-- sysd-q-134 -->

- **Email header fields**

  Header fields come in six groups. Originator fields say who sent the message. From names the author, and Sender names the agent that actually transmitted it and must appear when From has several mailboxes. Reply-To suggests where replies go, or else they go to From. Destination fields name the recipients: To holds the primary recipients, Cc others who receive a copy, and Bcc recipients whose addresses are not revealed to the others. How Bcc is handled is implementation dependent. The line may be removed from every copy, or Bcc recipients may get a separate copy that carries it. Identification fields matter for conversations: every message should have a Message-ID, and replies should carry In-Reply-To and References. Informational fields are Subject, Comments and Keywords, optional and meant for humans, and Subject is the most common. Trace fields record the route. Each SMTP server prepends a Received line and must not change or delete earlier ones, and final delivery adds Return-Path, so the timestamps help find slow relays. Servers can also record authentication checks in fields such as Authentication-Results, Received-SPF and DKIM-Signature. Resent fields are added when a user reintroduces a message into the transport system; they are informational and must not drive normal reply handling.

  <!-- sysd-q-137 -->

  *Figure: Each group of header fields has its own job.*

  | Group | Fields | Job |
  |---|---|---|
  | Originator | From, Sender, Reply-To | Who wrote and sent it |
  | Destination | To, Cc, Bcc | Who receives it |
  | Identification | Message-ID, In-Reply-To, References | Names a message and its parent |
  | Informational | Subject, Comments, Keywords | Notes for humans |
  | Trace | Received, Return-Path | Records the route taken |
  | Resent | Resent fields | Added when a message is reintroduced |

- **SMTP queueing and retries**

  Email expects some deliveries to fail at first, so it keeps trying. Mail that cannot be transmitted immediately must be queued and periodically retried, and a queue entry holds the envelope information as well as the message. After a failed attempt the sender must delay retrying that destination. The retry interval should be at least 30 minutes, and the give-up time generally at least 4-5 days. Failures are typically transient. That favors two connection attempts in the first hour, then backing off to one every two or three hours, in the spirit of Exponential backoff: waiting twice as long each time. A client should keep a list of unreachable hosts with their timeouts rather than retry every queued item. Retrying many messages to a dead host wastes overhead and blocks the sender. When several recipients share a destination server, only one copy should be sent: one MAIL, a RCPT for each recipient, then one DATA. Retry parameters must be configurable, and every activity needs a per-command timeout.

  <!-- sysd-q-132 -->

- **Bounce messages**

  A server that accepts a message with 250 after DATA takes on responsibility for it. It must not lose the message for frivolous reasons such as a later host crash. A bounce message is the notice an SMTP server sends the originator when it accepted a message but cannot deliver it. The notice goes to the envelope return path, using a null reverse-path (<>) for the notice itself. Servers must not send notifications about problems with notifications, so no notice is sent when the return path is already null, and the null path prevents error-report loops. Some failures after acceptance cannot be avoided. A soft DNS error may block recipient validation, the target may be a mailing list, or the server may be a relay. Rejecting a message during the SMTP transaction is better than bouncing it afterwards. Backscatter happens when a misconfigured server bounces mail whose envelope sender was forged, so the bounce lands on an innocent party. Many ISPs disable non-delivery reports for this reason.

  <!-- sysd-q-133 -->

- **Mail agents and relays**

  A message crosses several programs between its sender and its reader. A mail user agent submits mail to a mail submission agent, which hands it to a mail transfer agent (MTA). The submission and transfer agents are often the same software started with different options. The boundary MTA looks up the recipient domain's mail server in DNS, using the record described in MX record, and connects to the target MTA. Transfer is one connection between two MTAs or a series of hops through intermediaries. A receiving server may be the final destination, a relay that stores and forwards, or a gateway that forwards using a protocol other than SMTP. A relay passes on the message data without modification except for adding trace information. A gateway may need to transform the message because the two transport environments differ. Counting the Received header fields is an effective way to detect mail loops, with a large rejection threshold, normally at least 100 entries. The final hop hands the message to a mail delivery agent, which saves it in the mailbox format or forwards it by SMTP or LMTP. Clients then retrieve mail with IMAP or POP. A relay returns 550 if policy forbids relaying.

  <!-- sysd-q-116 -->

- **MX record**

  How does a sending server know where to deliver mail for a domain? It asks DNS for an MX record, a DNS resource record naming the mail server responsible for accepting email on behalf of that domain. An MX record carries a preference value and the host name of a mail server, and a domain may have several of them. The sending MTA gets the list of servers with their preferences and tries the lowest preference number first. The preference is an unsigned 16-bit field, so valid values range from 0 to 65535. The named host must map to address records (A or AAAA) and must not point to a CNAME record. With no MX record, the sender treats the domain as having an implicit MX of preference 0 pointing at itself. A temporary DNS error means the message must be queued and retried later. Several MX records give load balancing and redundancy, and allow high-availability clusters of mail gateways for one domain. They cannot move mail service to another port or weight servers of unequal priority.

  <!-- sysd-q-126 -->

- **Post Office Protocol**

  POP is built to empty the mailbox. The Post Office Protocol is an application-layer Internet standard protocol that email clients use to retrieve email from a mail server. It gives a client access to a mailbox, called a maildrop, and supports list, retrieve and delete operations on messages. POP3 clients typically connect, retrieve all messages, store them on the client computer and delete them from the server. This suited users with only temporary dial-up connections who read mail offline. Clients may instead leave mail on the server and download only new messages, identified through the UIDL unique-id list command. Mail marked for deletion is removed from the maildrop only when the client ends the session. A POP3 server listens on TCP port 110, and encryption is requested with the STLS command or by connecting to POP3S on port 995. The original login was an unencrypted USER/PASS pair, and APOP adds a challenge-response using MD5.

  <!-- sysd-q-120 -->

- **Email delivery**

  Email travels from the sender's mail client to the recipient's mailbox in a handful of hops. The sender's mail user agent formats the message and sends it with the submission protocol, a profile of SMTP, to its local mail submission agent. That agent takes the destination from the SMTP envelope, not the message header. The part before the @ is the local part, and the part after is a domain name it resolves in DNS. DNS answers with the MX records listing the domain's mail exchange servers, which are MTAs, often run by the recipient's ISP. The sending server transfers the message by SMTP. The receiving MTA may forward it to other MTAs before the mail delivery agent places it in the recipient's mailbox. The recipient's client then collects it by POP3 or IMAP. Domains usually have several mail exchange servers so they can keep accepting mail when the primary is unavailable. Email favors reliability over speed to cope with unreliable links and busy servers. Mail can be queued and retried for up to five days before a permanent-failure notice. Accepting a message obliges an MTA to deliver it or send a bounce message back. Open relays that accepted mail for anyone were exploited by spammers, so they are now rare and many MTAs refuse mail from them.

  <!-- sysd-q-122 -->

- **Internet Message Access Protocol**

  IMAP makes a remote mailbox behave like a local folder. It is an Internet standard protocol that email clients use to retrieve and manage messages on a mail server over a TCP/IP connection. It was designed for complete management of a mailbox by multiple clients. Clients generally leave messages on the server until the user deletes them. The server holds the mailbox structure of content, folders and per-message state, and local copies are only a temporary cache. So IMAP needs far more server resources and cost per mailbox than POP. Flags such as read, replied to or deleted are stored on the server, so different clients see each other's changes. Clients can ask the server to search, and can fetch individual MIME parts such as the text without its attachments. IMAP IDLE lets the server notify connected clients of mailbox changes, but clients must keep a TCP connection open. An IMAP server listens on port 143, or 993 for IMAP over TLS, and RFC 9051 defines the current version.

  <!-- sysd-q-119 -->

- **POP versus IMAP**

  POP downloads, and IMAP shares. POP downloads mail to one device, whereas IMAP keeps the mailbox on the server so many clients can share it. POP3 moves messages from the server to the client and deletes them there, though it can leave them. POP gives a completely static view, so the client must reconnect and re-authenticate to see changes. IMAP gives a dynamic view and reports new mail and changes made by other connected clients. POP has no folders and no server-side message state, so two POP clients cannot sync read state. It has no IDLE either, so clients must reconnect periodically to check. POP is simpler and easier to implement. IMAP remedies many of its shortcomings, at the cost of far more server resources per mailbox. A POP UIDL is a visible ASCII string up to 70 characters, while an IMAP UID is a number local to a folder, paired with a UIDVALIDITY value. Webmail providers such as Gmail and Outlook.com support both.

  <!-- sysd-q-121 -->

  *Figure: POP and IMAP differ on where the mailbox lives.*

  |  | POP | IMAP |
  |---|---|---|
  | Messages | Downloaded to one device, then deleted | Stay on the server, shared by clients |
  | View of mailbox | Static | Dynamic |
  | Folders and read state | None on the server | Kept on the server |
  | New-mail alerts | None; reconnect to check | IDLE |
  | Server cost per mailbox | Lower | Far more |
  | Message identifier | UIDL, up to 70 characters | UID per folder, with UIDVALIDITY |

- **IMAP commands and responses**

  An IMAP session is a text dialogue in which the client sends tagged commands and the server returns data and a tagged completion result. IMAP assumes a reliable data stream such as TCP and listens on port 143, or 993 for implicit TLS. Each client command carries a tag. The server's completion response repeats it with OK, NO or BAD, a protocol error, so the tag shows which command finished when several are in progress. Server data and other status lines start with "*" as untagged responses and may be sent unilaterally. A client must therefore be ready to accept any response at any time. A client may pipeline commands without waiting for completion. If a command could affect another's results, the server must execute them in the order given. The server must send mailbox size updates automatically, and only EXPUNGE may reduce the message count, because EXISTS cannot. A connection is in one of four states: not authenticated, authenticated, selected or logout. A client must select a mailbox before commands that affect messages.

  <!-- sysd-q-143 -->

- **IMAP unique identifiers**

  How does an email client tell messages apart when it returns a week later? An IMAP unique identifier (UID) is a number that identifies a message in a mailbox, stable across sessions when paired with the mailbox's UIDVALIDITY. A message can also be addressed by its sequence number, its relative position from 1 to the number of messages in the mailbox. A UID is an unsigned non-zero 32-bit value assigned in strictly ascending order as messages are added, and it need not be contiguous, unlike a sequence number. A UID must not change during a session and should not change between sessions, so an offline client can resynchronize. UIDVALIDITY lets a client detect changed UIDs: if UIDs fail to persist, the new value must be greater than the old. UIDNEXT is the predicted UID of the next new message, so a client can tell whether mail arrived since it last checked. The mailbox name, UIDVALIDITY and UID together must refer to a single immutable message forever, and an expunged message's UID is never reused under the same UIDVALIDITY.

  <!-- sysd-q-140 -->

- **Email spoofing**

  Original SMTP could not check who a sender really was. Email spoofing is designing a message's header so it appears to come from a known or trusted source. Spam and phishing typically use it to mislead the recipient about the message's true origin. Even casual users can negotiate directly with receiving and relaying servers to build a misleading message. A sender's own software can set From freely. A domain owner can specify which servers may send for the domain, and servers can sign mail with SPF and DKIM, so spoofed addresses can be flagged. These techniques do not protect against misspelled lookalike domain names.

  <!-- sysd-q-125 -->

- **SMTP security**

  SMTP cannot authenticate mail or check integrity at the transport level, so its security is built around it. That means authenticating clients, encrypting server-to-server connections and declaring a domain's TLS policy. SMTP-AUTH makes the client log in to the mail server, which lets legitimate users relay mail and denies relay to spammers. It does not guarantee the authenticity of the envelope sender or the From header. Spoofing remains possible unless the server limits from-addresses to those the user may use. STARTTLS lets a server advertise TLS and a client upgrade the connection. It is opportunistic and resists only passive observation, because negotiation is in plain text and an active attacker can strip the commands, a downgrade known as STRIPTLS. MTA-STS lets a domain declare, in a policy file and DNS TXT record, that it supports secure channels. Senders cache it and never use insecure channels until it expires. DANE for SMTP publishes a hash of the TLS certificate in DNS secured by DNSSEC. Real mail security lies in end-to-end methods on the message body, such as digital signatures.

  <!-- sysd-q-118 -->

- **Spam filtering**

  Spam filtering is an escalating game against people who keep inventing new evasions. It combines techniques that detect and refuse unsolicited bulk mail. They include content-based filtering, DNS-based blackhole lists (DNSBL), greylisting, spamtraps, enforcing SMTP's technical requirements and checksumming to detect bulk mail. Another is costs on the sender, such as proof-of-work or micropayments. Each has strengths and weaknesses. Bayesian filters rely roughly on word probabilities: a message with many words used only in spam and few never used in spam is likely spam. Machine learning more broadly can also identify spam. Spammers adapt, for example by adding random words to weaken Bayesian filters, which is called Bayesian poisoning. Outbound protection applies the same techniques to mail leaving a provider's network and blocks the message or shuts off its source. Email authentication against forged From addresses became popular in the 2010s, with servers using SPF, DKIM and DMARC. Filtering has collateral damage. It uses server and network resources. Rejected legitimate mail forces senders to contact recipients out of channel, and mail sent to a spam folder gives the sender no notice. Silently dropping mail violates the expectation that mail is delivered or returned, so it should be considered only with very high confidence that a message is seriously fraudulent. IMAP defines $Junk and $NotJunk keywords so users or delivery agents can mark junk, and $Phishing for likely phishing mail.

  <!-- sysd-q-129 -->

- **Designing Gmail**

  Design the path that carries an email from one person to another. Alice sends from her client, and the Gmail server stores the mail and makes it available to Bob. SMTP's objective is to transfer mail reliably and efficiently, and email favors reliability over speed so it copes with unreliable network links and busy servers. RFC 5321 sets minimums: message content of at least 64K octets, 100 buffered recipients, local parts up to 64 octets and domains up to 255. Providers cap attachments, typically at 25MB or less in the early 2010s.

  SMTP is the protocol between client and server and between mail servers, but it only delivers. The recipient's client fetches mail from the mailbox with IMAP or POP. A mail object is an envelope, with the error-return address and recipients, plus content of header and body. Delivery follows the envelope, so To can differ from the delivery list, and Bcc lives only in the envelope. Every message has a globally unique Message-ID, and replies name the parent in In-Reply-To and References, which lets a client rebuild conversation threads. Headers follow RFC 5322, and non-ASCII text and attachments use MIME.

  The server keeps each mailbox: messages with strictly ascending UIDs and a UIDVALIDITY value, per-message flags such as \Seen and \Deleted, and folders. This server-held state costs far more per mailbox than POP.

  Alice's client submits the message by SMTP to her mail server, on port 587 or 465 with authentication, and that server hands it to its mail transfer agent. The sending MTA asks DNS for the MX records of the recipient's domain and tries the lowest preference first, randomizing among equals. For a Gmail address the answer is Gmail's SMTP server. The MTA connects to the receiving server on port 25 and runs MAIL, RCPT and DATA, sending one copy for all recipients there. After the final 250 the receiver owns the message and must deliver it or report failure. A mail delivery agent saves the accepted message in the recipient's mailbox format, so the Gmail server holds the mail until Bob's client asks for it.

  When Bob logs in, his client fetches new mail through the IMAP or POP server. IMAP leaves messages on the server so several clients share a mailbox, POP downloads and deletes, and IMAP IDLE pushes new-mail notices instead of polling. IMAP lets the server search so clients need not download every message, and fetch single MIME parts such as text without attachments. Searching massive mailboxes can overload the server unless storage, indexing and search are carefully built.

  About 85% of email was estimated to be spam in 2021, so incoming mail is filtered by content, DNS blocklists, greylisting, Bayesian or learned models and sender authentication. Mail sent to a spam folder gives the sender no notice. Attachments travel as MIME parts. Original SMTP carries only 7-bit ASCII, so binary files are base64-encoded into a multipart message. The size the transport sees can differ from what the user sees. Mail that cannot be sent is queued and retried, at least 30 minutes apart, for at least 4-5 days. Several MX servers keep a domain accepting mail if one fails, and undeliverable mail is bounced with a null return path. The thing to remember is that the job splits in two: servers push mail with SMTP, and clients pull it with IMAP or POP.

  <!-- sysd-q-058 -->

  *Figure: Mail is pushed by SMTP between servers and pulled by Bob's client.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Alice's client] -->|submits by SMTP| B[Alice's mail server]
  B -->|asks for MX records| C[DNS]
  B -->|SMTP, port 25| D[Gmail SMTP server]
  D --> E[Delivery agent]
  E --> F[(Recipient's mailbox)]
  F -->|IMAP or POP| G[Bob's client]
  ```

### Design Google Maps

As of March 2021 Google Maps had one billion daily active users and 99% coverage of the world. A simplified design breaks into 3 high-level components: location, map rendering and navigation. Navigation leans on shortest-path algorithms, from Dijkstra's algorithm and the A* search to contraction hierarchies, which precompute shortcuts so a query can skip unimportant vertices. Rendering rests on map tiles, a world map projected into one huge 2D image and cut into small blocks, in Web Mercator, the standard projection for web mapping. Geocoding, which turns an address into a latitude and longitude pair, connects the two.

- **Dijkstra's algorithm**

  Dijkstra's algorithm finds the shortest paths from a source node to every other node in a weighted graph, such as a road network. It starts with distance zero at the source and infinity elsewhere. It then repeatedly picks the unvisited vertex with the lowest distance, and updates each unvisited neighbor's distance if the route through that vertex is shorter. It can stop as soon as the shortest path to one chosen destination is known. A min-priority queue selects the closest vertex, and a binary heap (Heap) gives O((V+E) log V). Sparse networks such as road maps suit it. Modern routing systems pair it with preprocessing such as A* search algorithm or landmark heuristics. Preprocessing with Contraction hierarchies can be up to seven orders of magnitude faster. The algorithm gives incorrect results when edges have negative weights, because its greedy strategy finalizes a vertex's distance before a cheaper path through a negative edge is seen.

  <!-- sysd-q-148 -->

- **A* search algorithm**

  A* is Dijkstra's algorithm with a sense of direction. It is an informed, best-first search on a weighted graph that finds the cheapest path from a start node to a goal node. It keeps a tree of paths from the start and extends the one that minimizes f(n) = g(n) + h(n). Here g(n) is the cost from the start to n, and h(n) is a heuristic estimating the cheapest remaining path to the goal. On a road map the heuristic can be the straight-line distance to the goal, the physically smallest possible distance. A* returns an optimal path when the heuristic is admissible, meaning it never overestimates. Dijkstra's algorithm is the special case where h(x) = 0 for all nodes, and A* differs from greedy best-first search because it also counts the distance already travelled. A close estimate cuts node expansions and a poor one causes many. Its biggest practical drawback is that it keeps all generated nodes in memory, and in travel routing it is generally outperformed by algorithms that pre-process the graph.

  <!-- sysd-q-149 -->

- **Geocoding**

  Type an address into a map and it becomes a point on the globe. Geocoding turns a text description of a location, such as an address or place name, into geographic coordinates, usually a latitude and longitude pair. Reverse geocoding converts coordinates back to a place name or address. A geocoder combines an input dataset of descriptive text, a reference dataset of feature locations, and software that matches each input to a reference feature. Address interpolation uses street segments tagged with address ranges. The geocoder parses the address, matches a segment whose number range includes it, and estimates the position along that segment. Accuracy varies, from building centroids and interpolated street positions to postal code centroids. Misspelled or incomplete input and outdated reference data cause mismatches. Geocoders handle abbreviations such as E for East, and cleaning the input, called address scrubbing, improves accuracy. Asking for the city and region resolves ambiguity, such as the same street name in two towns. The grid-style geocode described in Geohash: a place as a short string encodes latitude and longitude into a short alphanumeric string.

  <!-- sysd-q-152 -->

- **Contraction hierarchies**

  Dijkstra's algorithm is impractical on road networks, which have tens of millions of vertices. Contraction hierarchies are a speed-up technique that precomputes shortcuts in the road graph, so a query can skip unimportant vertices. Road networks change rarely, so seconds to hours can be spent once on preprocessing, and queries are then answered in microseconds. The idea relies on roads being highly hierarchical: highway junctions rank above a junction into a dead end. A shortcut joins two non-adjacent vertices with the weight of their shortest path. Preprocessing contracts vertices one by one. It removes a vertex and adds a shortcut between two neighbors only if their shortest path goes through it. Choosing the best contraction order is NP-complete, so heuristics are used. A query runs a bidirectional search from the start and target over the graph plus shortcuts. Both searches follow only edges to more important vertices, which keeps the search space small. If edge weights change more often than the road topology, a customization phase can include current traffic or honor preferences such as avoiding ferries or highways.

  <!-- sysd-q-150 -->

- **Map tiles**

  A map of the whole world is cut into small pieces, and your device fetches only the pieces it needs. The world's map is projected into one huge 2D image and broken into small blocks called tiles, which the client joins seamlessly into the visible map. When the user pans, most tiles stay relevant and only new ones are fetched. Zoom level 0 shows the whole world in one tile. Each level doubles both dimensions, so one tile becomes 4, and about 22 levels suffice. Web Mercator (Web Mercator projection) is used, with latitude limits near 85 degrees. The OpenStreetMap XYZ convention serves tiles at URLs like .../Z/X/Y.png, with Z the zoom level. Tiles are static and rarely change, so a CDN backed by cloud storage such as S3 serves them from a nearby location. Most tiles are raster images such as PNG or JPEG. Vector tiles are rendered by the client, which can style them and keep text readable when rotating.

  <!-- sysd-q-061 -->

- **Web Mercator projection**

  Virtually every major online map provider draws the world in Web Mercator, including Google Maps, Mapbox, Bing Maps and OpenStreetMap. It is a variant of the Mercator map projection that applies spherical formulas to WGS 84 coordinates, and its identifier is EPSG:3857. The spherical form makes it slightly non-conformal, but it needs only a fraction of the computing resources of the ellipsoidal one. Mercator projects the poles at infinity, so Web Mercator cannot show them. Google Maps cuts off coverage at 85.051129° north and south, the latitude at which the full map becomes a square.

  <!-- sysd-q-151 -->

- **Designing Google Maps**

  Design a map service in the style of Google Maps, which as of March 2021 had one billion daily active users and 99% coverage of the world. A simplified design breaks into 3 high-level components: location, map rendering and navigation.

  The location service records user location updates, which clients send every few seconds. That data is used to detect new and recently closed roads, to improve the map's accuracy over time, and as an input for live traffic data. The road network is modeled as a graph: intersections are vertices, road sections are edges, and edge weights are the travel time along that section. Map data can live in a spatial database, which is needed for dynamic data or a huge amount of geographic data and supports spatial queries and geometry manipulation.

  For rendering, the world's map is projected into a huge 2D image and broken into tiles. Tiled web maps use Web Mercator, and Google Maps cuts coverage at 85.051129° north and south. Zoom level 0 shows the whole world in one tile and each level doubles both dimensions, so one tile becomes 4. About 22 zoom levels are sufficient for most practical purposes. Clients request tiles by URL such as .../Z/X/Y.png. On a pan most displayed tiles stay relevant and only new ones are fetched, which beats fetching one image for the whole viewport. Tiles are static and rarely change, so a CDN backed by cloud storage like S3 serves them, and users load the tiles they need from a nearby CDN. To support zooming and panning, pre-calculate the map blocks at different zoom levels and load the images when needed. Pre-computing individual tiles is easy to parallelize.

  The navigation service finds a reasonably fast route from point A to point B. It calls a Geocoding Service to resolve an address to a latitude and longitude pair, and a Route Planner Service to find the route. Geocoding matches an address to a street segment whose address range includes the house number and interpolates the position within that range. The Route Planner calculates the top-K shortest paths between A and B. It estimates the time of each path from current traffic and historical data, then ranks the paths by predicted time and user filtering.

  Plain Dijkstra's algorithm is impractical on networks with tens of millions of vertices. A* with a straight-line-distance heuristic helps, but it is generally outperformed by algorithms that pre-process the graph. Contraction hierarchies precompute shortcuts, spending seconds to hours once because roads change rarely. They then answer queries in microseconds with a bidirectional search that only climbs toward more important vertices. When live traffic changes edge weights more often than the road topology, a customization phase re-applies the stored contractions with new weights. It can also honor preferences such as avoiding ferries or highways. The thing to remember is the split: static tiles from a CDN draw the map, and a pre-processed graph answers the route.

  <!-- sysd-q-060 -->

  *Figure: The client reaches three services: location, a CDN for tiles, and navigation.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Client] -->|location updates| B[Location service]
  A -->|tile requests| C[CDN]
  C --> D[(Cloud storage)]
  A -->|route request| E[Navigation service]
  E --> F[Geocoding Service]
  E --> G[Route Planner Service]
  ```

### Design a stock exchange

A stock exchange records the interest of buyers and sellers in an order book, and a matching engine uses that book to decide which orders can be executed. Traders place orders of standard types such as market, limit and stop. The aim is microsecond latency, reached by doing less on the critical path: fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage. This chapter covers the parts, from FIX, the electronic protocol for the real-time exchange of information about securities transactions, and market data to processor affinity and non-blocking algorithms. Then it assembles them in one design.

- **Non-blocking algorithm**

  Locks make threads wait, and a waiting thread accomplishes nothing. An algorithm is non-blocking if the failure or suspension of any thread cannot cause the failure or suspension of another thread. It is lock-free if there is guaranteed system-wide progress and wait-free if there is also guaranteed per-thread progress, and obstruction-freedom is the weakest guarantee. Locks can cause deadlock, livelock and priority inversion, and they force a trade-off between coarse-grained locking, which limits parallelism, and error-prone fine-grained locking. Non-blocking algorithms use atomic read-modify-write primitives provided by the hardware, most notably compare-and-swap, in a carefully designed order of reads, read-modify-writes and writes. Compilers and many CPUs reorder operations unless told not to, so memory barriers are needed. A single-reader single-writer ring buffer FIFO can be implemented safely with only a memory barrier. Correct lock-free code is difficult to write, and without hard deadlines wait-free algorithms may not be worth their extra complexity.

  <!-- sysd-q-100 -->

- **Order types**

  Before an exchange can match anything, it must know what each trader asked for. Order types are the standard instructions a trader can place on a trading venue, such as market, limit and stop orders, each with its own execution rules. A market order executes immediately at the best available price and is filled as long as willing counterparties exist. It gives certainty of execution but no control over the price received, and in fast-moving markets its fill price can differ widely from the last quote. A buy limit order executes only at the limit price or lower, and a sell limit order only at the limit price or higher. The trader controls the price, but the order may never be filled. A limit order that the Order book can satisfy on arrival is marketable: it may be filled in part from the book, with the rest added to the book. Fill-or-kill orders are filled completely on the first attempt or cancelled. All-or-none orders must be filled in full or not at all. Immediate-or-cancel orders execute at once but allow partial fills. A day order lasts until the end of the day's trading session. A good-til-cancelled order persists until a cancelling order, although brokers may set limits such as 90 days. A conditional order executes only when a condition is met. A stop order becomes active when the price reaches the stop price, and a stop-limit order then becomes a limit order.

  <!-- sysd-q-095 -->

- **FIX protocol**

  Both sides of a trade speak the same protocol. FIX is an electronic communications protocol for the real-time exchange of information about securities transactions and markets. It is the standard for pre-trade communications and trade execution, used by the buy side and sell side, including mutual funds, investment banks, brokers and stock exchanges. Classic FIX tagvalue messages are ASCII text. Each field is a numeric tag plus a value separated by the SOH character, so messages are self-describing. A message has a header, a body and a trailer. The FIXT session layer is a point-to-point protocol usually run over TCP, and it guarantees delivery in both directions through sequence numbers and retransmission of missed messages. For speed, Simple Binary Encoding uses native binary types in fixed positions, giving much lower latency and more deterministic performance than tagvalue. The FIXP session layer lets peers negotiate delivery guarantees: recoverable (exactly-once, with retransmission), idempotent (at-most-once) or unsequenced. Retransmission delays are often undesirable in fast markets. FAST is a binary protocol used mostly for sending multicast price data over UDP.

  <!-- sysd-q-098 -->

- **Order book**

  A stock exchange is, at heart, two lists. The order book is the list of orders that a trading venue uses to record the interest of buyers and sellers in a financial instrument. It holds one list of buy orders and one of sell orders. Each entry keeps the number of securities, the price the buyer or seller bids or asks, and some means of identifying the party. Orders at the same price sit on one price level. A Matching engine uses the book to decide which orders can be executed. A bid equal to or higher than the lowest ask is filled at once and never joins the open book. If such crossing orders stay unmatched because of an error or a market condition, the book is said to be crossed. The highest bid and the lowest ask are the top of the book, and the difference between them is the bid-ask spread. Book depth is the number of price levels. A book can be kept to a fixed depth, with orders beyond it ignored or rejected, or hold unlimited levels.

  <!-- sysd-q-094 -->

- **Market data**

  Market data has to reach traders before the market changes. It is the price and other related data for a financial instrument, reported by a trading venue such as a stock exchange. A record carries the instrument identifier (ticker symbol and exchange code), the latest bid and ask price and the time of the last trade. Quote data and trade data are often generated over different feeds. Delivery is highly time-sensitive, so specialized ticker plants collect and push massive data streams. Distribution platforms use specially designed protocols to raise throughput or reduce latency. UDP multicast delivers data efficiently to many recipients at once, and the FAST protocol of FIX protocol exists for multicast market data. In a feed handler, sources connect to a server that redistributes data. It forwards a client's subscription to the sources if it has no cached data, then sends every update for an instrument to all subscribed clients. Reference data such as identifier codes and security terms does not change in real time and usually comes from the issuer, while prices come from the exchanges.

  <!-- sysd-q-097 -->

- **Matching engine**

  The matching engine decides who trades with whom. It is the component that uses the order book to determine which buy and sell orders can be fully or partially executed. Orders are matched as the interest of buyers and sellers can be satisfied. An order whose bid is equal to or higher than the lowest ask can be fulfilled immediately and does not become part of the open orders book. A limit order may be partially filled from the book, with the remainder added to the book. A market order may be split across several counterparties at different prices. Electronic markets give market orders the highest priority, then limit orders first-come-first-served. Conditional orders get priority by the time their condition is met, and special kinds such as iceberg and dark-pool orders get lower priority. In a low-latency exchange design the matching engine is single-threaded on the critical path and pinned to a CPU, so there is no context switch and no locks.

  <!-- sysd-q-096 -->

- **Processor affinity**

  Leaving a thread where it is can make it faster. Processor affinity, also called CPU pinning, binds a process or thread to a CPU or a range of CPUs so that it executes only on the designated processors. A thread that resumes on its old CPU may find data still in that CPU's cache and take fewer cache misses. But pinning forces it to wait for that CPU to become free. It suits CPU-intensive processes with few interrupts, while an ordinary program that is interrupted more often might be slowed down. On Linux it is set with the taskset program or the sched_setaffinity system call.

  <!-- sysd-q-099 -->

- **Low-latency critical path design**

  A modern stock exchange reaches microsecond latency with one principle: do less on the critical path. That means fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage. Non-critical tasks leave the path. The market data flow and the reporting flow are off it and have different latency requirements. Key components can be single-threaded, each pinned to a CPU as in Processor affinity, with no context switch and no locks. Each runs one task after another in a single loop. Components can talk through shared memory as an event bus instead of a hard disk, and run together on one giant server without containers.

  <!-- sysd-q-028 -->

- **Designing a stock exchange**

  Design a stock exchange, a system whose aim is microsecond latency. It gets there by doing less on the critical path: fewer tasks, less time on each task, fewer network hops and less disk usage. The trading flow is that critical path, with strict latency requirements. An order enters the order manager, passes mandatory risk checks and is matched, and the execution leaves through the order manager. The market data flow and the reporting flow are not on the critical path and have different latency requirements, so non-critical tasks are removed from the trading flow.

  Clients send orders, instructions to buy or sell, to a broker or directly to the exchange. FIX, the standard protocol for pre-trade communications and trade execution, carries them as numeric tag and value fields. FIX sessions use sequence numbers and retransmission on request, so delivery survives a disconnection. High-performance sessions can instead pick idempotent or unsequenced delivery, since retransmission delays are often undesirable in fast markets. Binary encodings such as Simple Binary Encoding cut latency, because no translation is needed to put data into a format computers can use. Fixed-length fields make performance more deterministic.

  A market order executes at once at the best available price, giving certainty of execution but no price control. A limit order executes only at its limit price or better and may never fill. Time-in-force and conditional instructions add rules. Day orders expire at the session close, good-til-cancelled orders persist, immediate-or-cancel allows partial fills, and a stop order activates at its stop price. The order book is the data model. It is a list of buy orders and a list of sell orders. Each entry holds the party, the number of securities and the price, and orders at one price are grouped into a price level. The top of the book is the highest bid and lowest ask, their gap is the bid-ask spread, and book depth is the number of price levels kept.

  The matching engine uses the book to decide which orders can be fully or partially executed. A bid at or above the lowest ask fills at once, and a partly filled limit order rests on the book. Matching priority favors market orders, then limit orders first-come-first-served, with conditional orders ranked by when their condition is met and iceberg or dark-pool orders lower. Market data, the latest bid, ask and last trade, is published off the critical path. Its delivery is highly time-sensitive, ticker plants handle the streams, and UDP multicast serves many recipients at once.

  All components run on a single giant server with no containers, and shared memory serves as the event bus with no hard disk. Other components listen on the bus and react, in the event-driven style of Event-driven architecture: parts that announce, not command. The order manager and matching engine are single-threaded on the critical path, and each is pinned to a CPU. There is no context switch and no locks, and the loop runs tasks one by one in sequence. Locks block threads and risk deadlock and priority inversion, so the design avoids them in shared structures. Lock-free data structures raise parallel performance, and a single-reader single-writer ring buffer needs only a memory barrier. The thing to remember is that speed here comes from removing work: fewer tasks, fewer hops and less disk on the critical path.

  <!-- sysd-q-027 -->

  *Figure: An order crosses the critical path in order, and the execution leaves through the order manager.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Client] -->|order| B[Order manager]
  B --> C[Mandatory risk checks]
  C --> D[Matching engine]
  D -->|matched| E[Order manager sends execution out]
  ```

### Design Google Docs

Two people can edit the same document at once, on different devices, and the system must merge their edits automatically and almost instantly. Real-time groupware needs fine-granularity sharing of data and fast response times. This chapter starts with collaborative real-time editing and the concurrency control that groupware needs. Then it turns to operational transformation, a technique for keeping replicated documents consistent under concurrent edits. The worked design puts these ideas into one service.

- **Collaborative real-time editing**

  Two people type into the same document at the same moment, and both must see the result. Collaborative real-time editing lets several users edit the same document at once on different devices, with their edits merged automatically and nearly instantly. It synchronizes the edits of all online users automatically and periodically, which avoids or minimizes edit conflicts. Asynchronous editing, delayed or offline, makes each user submit, update and merge manually, so several users can edit the same line and cause conflicts. The difficulty is communication latency. Users need their own edits incorporated instantly, yet instant incorporation means edits land in different versions of the document. If Bob turns Mary into Hary while Alice turns it into My, each receives edits made on versions that never existed locally. The most sophisticated solutions need no server and no locking, so all users edit all parts at once. A basic client-server design instead makes one editor the collaboration server, which is less powerful but cheap. A sequence CRDT can serve as an alternative to Operational transformation.

  <!-- sysd-q-146 -->

- **Groupware concurrency control**
