  Concurrency control for groupware has unusual demands. Groupware is a computer system that supports two or more users working on a common task through a shared environment. Such systems often require fine-granularity sharing of data and fast response times. A paper on the topic separates real-time groupware from other multi-user systems and sets out their requirements. It presents a concurrency control algorithm that is simple to use and responsive, because users operate directly on the data without obtaining locks. The paper applies it to group text editing and notes that the behavior wanted in many such systems is non-serializable.

  <!-- sysd-q-147 -->

- **Operational transformation**

  Operational transformation repairs edits that arrive out of context. It is a technique for keeping replicated documents consistent under concurrent edits by transforming each operation's parameters against the effects of concurrent operations already executed. Ellis and Gibbs pioneered it in 1989 for collaborative editing of plain text. In 2009 it was adopted as a core technique behind Google Wave and Google Docs. Each client holds its own copy and edits it without locking or blocking. Changes are propagated, and each receiver transforms them before executing. Take the text abc, with O1 = insert x at 0 and O2 = delete c at 2. Untransformed, O2 would delete b instead of c, so after O1 it must become delete at 3. The goals are causality preservation, which keeps operations in cause-effect order, and convergence, which makes all copies identical once all operations have run. The CCI model adds intention preservation. OT is hard to get right: formal proofs are complicated and error-prone, and a former Google Wave engineer found implementing it painful. Differential synchronization and sequence CRDTs are alternatives.

  <!-- sysd-q-145 -->

- **Designing Google Docs**

  Design a collaborative document editor in the style of Google Docs. The system must merge edits from different users on different devices automatically and almost instantly. Real-time groupware needs fine-granularity sharing of data and fast response times. The groupware concurrency algorithm of Ellis and colleagues is simple and responsive: users operate directly on the data without obtaining locks.

  Clients send document editing operations to a WebSocket server, which handles the real-time communication. Document operations are persisted in a message queue, and the file operation server consumes them and generates transformed operations using collaboration algorithms. Three types of data are stored: file metadata, file content and operations.

  One of the biggest challenges is real-time conflict resolution. Users need their own edits shown instantly, but because of network latency those edits are applied to different versions of the document. If Bob turns Mary into Hary while Alice turns it into My, each receives edits made against versions that never existed locally. Remote edits must still be applied despite conflicts with local ones.

  Common conflict-resolution algorithms are operational transformation (OT), differential synchronization (DS) and conflict-free replicated data types (CRDT). With OT each client holds its own replica and edits it without locks. It transforms changes received from others before executing them, which suits high-latency environments such as the web. OT adjusts an operation's parameters for concurrent operations already executed. Untransformed, deleting position 2 would delete b instead of c, so after inserting x at position 0 of abc it must become position 3. OT must keep causality, with operations executing in their cause-effect order, and convergence, with all copies identical once every operation has run. Intention preservation is a further goal.

  OT is hard to get right. Formal proofs are complicated and error-prone, a former Google Wave engineer found implementing it painful, and every change to the data must be captured. A sequence CRDT can build a collaborative real-time editor as an alternative, and differential synchronization is another. Google Docs is said to use OT, which was adopted in 2009 as a core technique behind Google Wave and Google Docs. CRDT remains an active research area. A basic alternative is a client-server model where one editor acts as the collaboration server, though changes may not show on a client until the server answers. It is less powerful but cheap, suiting limited processing resources. The thing to remember is that operations flow through a queue, and transformation is what keeps every copy of the document the same.

  <!-- sysd-q-059 -->

  *Figure: Editing operations pass through a queue before the file operation server transforms them.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A[Clients] -->|editing operations| B[WebSocket server]
  B --> C[Message queue]
  C --> D[File operation server]
  D --> E[(Metadata, content, operations)]
  ```

### Design a payment system

Double charging a customer is one of the most serious problems a payment system can have, so it must execute each payment order exactly once. This chapter builds toward that demand from the ground up. It starts with the bookkeeping method that keeps the books balanced and with the systems that settle financial transactions by transferring monetary value. It then follows a card payment through the third-party companies, the payment service provider and the gateway, that let businesses accept electronic payments. It ends with the process of comparing records in different systems to make sure the amounts match, and with a full design that ties it all together.

- **Double-entry bookkeeping: every debit has a credit**

  Every transaction in a company's books is written down twice. In double-entry bookkeeping, each one is recorded with equal and opposite entries: a debit in one ledger account and a credit in a second. Total debits then equal total credits, which is a partial check that the transaction was recorded correctly. The method rests on the accounting equation, and every recorded transaction keeps that equation in balance. A debit is a transfer of value to an account and a credit a transfer from it. A debit increases an asset, while a credit increases a liability. The purpose is accurate financial records in which errors or fraud can be detected. Daybooks, or journals, hold preliminary records that are totalled before posting to the nominal ledger, the main book of accounts. As volume grows, companies use accounting information systems to automate the tracking.

  <!-- sysd-q-077 -->

- **How money settles: batches, real time and instant**

  Settling a payment can take seconds, or it can wait for a batch. A payment system is any system used to settle financial transactions through the transfer of monetary value. An automated clearing house processes batches as a net settlement system, so settlement may be delayed, which poses settlement risk; it suits low-value, non-urgent transactions. Real-time gross settlement settles each transaction as soon as it is processed, one to one without netting. Its payments are final and irrevocable, and it suits high-value, urgent ones. Instant payment systems run 24x7x365 and complete a transfer, from debit of the payer's account to credit of the beneficiary's, within 10–15 seconds.

  <!-- sysd-q-081 -->

- **Payment service providers: accepting cards without a bank deal**

  A merchant that wants to accept different payment methods does not have to partner with one bank. A payment service provider, or PSP, makes that possible. This third-party company lets businesses accept electronic payments, such as credit card and debit card payments. It is an intermediary between the consumers who pay and the retailers who accept payment. It sets up the technical connections with acquiring banks, the merchants' banks, and with card networks, and it manages processing and those outside relationships. It often also acts as a gateway, the subject of Payment gateways: carrying payment details, never the money. Beyond processing, a PSP may offer risk management, digital wallets, reporting, currency exchange and fraud protection. Fees are typically a percentage of each transaction or a fixed cost per transaction. The merchant remains responsible for data protection, so compliance with PCI DSS matters. A PSP must follow one of four levels set by annual transaction volume, from Level 1 over 6 million to Level 4 under 20,000.

  <!-- sysd-q-078 -->

- **Payment gateways: carrying payment details, never the money**

  A payment gateway sits in the middle of a card payment, yet it is not directly involved in the money flow. It is a merchant service that authorizes credit card or direct payment processing for e-businesses, online retailers and traditional stores. Typically it is a web server to which the merchant's website or point of sale system is connected. It passes payment information between a payment portal, such as a website or mobile phone, and the front end processor or acquiring bank. One gateway often connects several acquiring banks and payment methods under one system. Some let transaction data go straight from the customer's browser to the gateway, bypassing the merchant's systems, using a redirect or an iframe. Many also screen orders for fraud before the authorization request goes to the processor. A bank or a specialised provider such as a PSP can supply one. White label gateways let PSPs, e-commerce platforms or acquiring banks brand the technology as their own.

  <!-- sysd-q-079 -->

- **Approved in seconds, funded in days: a card payment**

  A card payment is approved in about 2–3 seconds, yet from authorization to funding it typically takes 2-3 days. The two stages are separate, and each has its own trip through the banks.

  First comes authorization. The merchant forwards the transaction details to the gateway. The gateway converts the message from XML to ISO 8583 or a variant and passes it to the processor used by the merchant's acquiring bank. The processor forwards the details to the card association, such as Visa or Mastercard. The association may act as the issuing bank or route the transaction to the correct card issuing bank. The issuing bank approves or denies with a response code and a failure reason. The answer returns through the processor and gateway to the website, typically in 2–3 seconds, and the issuer holds an authorization for the approved amount.

  Then comes clearing and settlement. After the merchant fulfills the order, the process repeats to clear the authorization. That moves the issuing bank's auth-hold to a debit and prepares settlement with the acquiring bank. At the end of the day the merchant submits its approved authorizations as a batch to its acquiring bank via its processor. The acquiring bank then makes a batch settlement request of the card issuer. The issuer pays the acquiring bank, usually the next day, and the acquiring bank deposits the approved funds into the merchant's account the same or next day.

  <!-- sysd-q-080 -->

  *Figure: The table follows one card payment from the merchant's request to the deposit in the merchant's account.*

  | Step | Who | What happens |
  |---|---|---|
  | 1 | Merchant | Forwards the transaction details to the gateway |
  | 2 | Gateway | Converts the message to ISO 8583 and passes it to the processor |
  | 3 | Processor | Forwards the details to the card association |
  | 4 | Card association | Routes the transaction to the card issuing bank |
  | 5 | Issuing bank | Approves or denies and holds the authorization |
  | 6 | Merchant | Submits approved authorizations as a batch at day's end |
  | 7 | Issuer | Pays the acquiring bank, usually the next day |
  | 8 | Acquiring bank | Deposits the funds, the same or next day |

- **Payment reconciliation: the safety net behind exactly-once**

  Even a payment system that charges each customer exactly once still needs a second system to check its work. That system performs reconciliation: comparing records in different systems to make sure the amounts match each other. It is always necessary, even with the exactly-once semantics of Exactly-once execution: retry plus a duplicate check, because there are many places that can go wrong. It is a safety net.

  Take a $200 PayPal purchase. Under double-entry bookkeeping it appears in three places. The e-commerce site holds a $200 order, PayPal a $200 transaction, and the ledger a $200 debit for the buyer and a $200 credit for the seller. Reconciliation lines these records up. Formats are the first obstacle: one system writes the timestamp "2022/01/01" and another "Jan 1, 2022", so a layer transforms them into the same format. Volume is the second, and big data processing handles it. A streaming platform such as Flink serves near real-time reconciliation, as in Stream processing, where the data never ends. End-of-day batch processing such as Hadoop is the other route, as in Batch processing: jobs that run unattended.

  Timing is the third. Say the daily cut-off is 00:00:00. A record stamped 23:59:55 internally may be stamped 00:00:30 at PayPal, the next day, so it is missing from today's PayPal records and causes a discrepancy. Such a break is categorized as a temporary break and run later against the next day's PayPal records. If a match is found, the break is cleared and no more action is needed.

  <!-- sysd-q-008 -->

- **Designing a payment system that charges exactly once**

  The question is how to design the system that takes a customer's payment for an order and moves the money correctly. One requirement comes before all others. The system must execute each payment order exactly once, because double charging a customer is one of the most serious problems it can have.

  The flow starts when a user clicks the Buy button. A payment event is generated and sent to the payment service, which stores it in the database. One payment event may contain several payment orders, for example when products from multiple sellers are bought in one checkout. The payment service calls the payment executor for each payment order. The executor stores the order, then calls an external payment service provider, or PSP, to finish the credit card payment. A PSP is a third-party intermediary with connections to acquiring banks and card networks. The card payment goes through the processor and card association to the issuing bank, which approves or denies with a response code. The round trip typically takes 2–3 seconds.

  Once the payment succeeds, the payment service updates the wallet with how much the seller holds. It then calls the ledger service, which appends the new ledger information to the database. The ledger uses double-entry bookkeeping, explained in Double-entry bookkeeping: every debit has a credit: each transaction is recorded as equal and opposite debit and credit entries, so debits equal credits. This keeps records accurate and lets errors or fraud be detected. Take a $200 watch paid through PayPal. The site records a $200 purchase order, PayPal a $200 transaction, and the ledger a $200 debit for the buyer and a $200 credit for the seller.

  Exactly-once, the guarantee in Exactly-once execution: retry plus a duplicate check, becomes easier when split in two. At-least-once is implemented with retry, and at-most-once with an idempotency check. When the PSP call fails on a network error or timeout, the client retries the payment, which may succeed at a later attempt. The idempotency key, covered in Idempotency keys: how a server spots a repeated request, stops the retry from charging twice. It is usually a client-generated UUID that expires after a period, and it goes in an HTTP header such as idempotency-key. Checking and recording the key must be atomic, so that no other request can slip in between, for example with a unique constraint or Redis SET NX.

  Afterward the system checks itself. Every night the PSP or banks send settlement files holding the bank account balance and the day's transactions; for cards, authorization to funding typically takes 2-3 days. Reconciliation, described in Payment reconciliation: the safety net behind exactly-once, compares records in different systems to make sure the amounts match. A layer transforms different formats into one, and big data processing handles volume: Flink for near real-time, or end-of-day batch such as Hadoop. A record stamped 23:59:55 internally but 00:00:30 at PayPal falls on different days around a 00:00:00 cut-off. It is marked a temporary break and rerun against the next day's PayPal records, which clears it if it matches. Reconciliation is always necessary even with exactly-once semantics, because many places can go wrong; it is a safety net.

  One duty sits outside the flow of money. The PSP must follow PCI DSS at one of four compliance levels set by annual transaction volume, and gateways screen orders for fraud before authorization. To remember: retry freely, charge once, record both sides of every transaction, and check again afterward.

  <!-- sysd-q-007 -->

  *Figure: Follow one payment from the Buy button, through the payment executor and the PSP, to the wallet and the ledger.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A([Buy button]) -->|payment event| B[Payment service]
  B -->|each payment order| C[Payment executor]
  C -->|credit card payment| D[External PSP]
  B -->|on success| G[Ledger service]
  G -->|appends| DB[(Database)]
  B -->|on success| E[Wallet]
  ```

### Design a notification system

A notification system has to reach people on very different kinds of devices and networks. Firebase Cloud Messaging, or FCM, is a cross-platform Google messaging service that composes, sends, queues and routes push notifications between app servers and client apps. Apple's push notification service lets third-party application developers send notification data to applications installed on Apple devices, and the Short Message Service carries short text messages over cellular networks. At the center of the design sits a notification service that consumes events from a message queue, such as Kafka, and forwards each request to FCM or Apple's service according to the device platform.

- **SMS: the text message that may never arrive**

  Studies show that around 1% to 5% of text messages are lost entirely, even in normal operation. The Short Message Service, or SMS, is a mostly paid text messaging service of telephone and mobile systems that lets phones exchange short messages over cellular networks. Messages carry up to 160 characters, and the signaling protocol limits the payload to 140 bytes. Delivery is not guaranteed, and many implementations give the sender no way to learn whether a message arrived in time. Messages are treated as lower-priority traffic than voice, so some arrive long after they matter. SMS gateways let computers send messages over the Internet through a short message service center. Businesses such as banks, e-gaming, logistics and e-commerce use application-to-person messages to reach customers. The messages are not encrypted, so carriers and third parties can read them, phone-number metadata may leak, and senders can be spoofed.

  <!-- sysd-q-076 -->

- **Firebase Cloud Messaging and the registration token**

  Firebase Cloud Messaging finds an app on a device through a token issued at first start. The client app sends its credentials to FCM, which generates a registration token, the Instance ID, for that app instance. Notifications must include it. The client passes it to the app server, which caches it. Storing each token with a timestamp and pruning stale ones keeps the set manageable.

  FCM is a cross-platform Google messaging service that composes, sends, queues and routes push notifications. It superseded Google Cloud Messaging, adding iOS and web devices to Android behind a unified API. Messages are composed in the console or sent from the app server using the Firebase Admin SDK or HTTP. FCM queues messages in storage when the device is offline, as in Store and forward, then forwards them to a platform-level transport and routes them to the target devices. In a typical design, a notification service reads events from a message queue such as Kafka, and Message queues: leave it with the queue and move on covers queues. It then dispatches requests to FCM or to Apple's service, described in Apple Push Notification service: reaching Apple devices.

  <!-- sysd-q-074 -->

- **Apple Push Notification service: reaching Apple devices**

  Apple Push Notification service, or APNs, lets third-party application developers send notification data to applications installed on Apple devices. A notification can carry badges, sounds or custom text alerts. At launch Apple stated that push notifications conserve battery better than the background processes pull technology needs, such as Polling: asking again and again whether anything is new. In December 2015 it released an HTTP/2 provider API that replaced the legacy binary interface, shut down at the end of March 2021. The maximum payload is 4 kilobytes, up from 2 kilobytes. The API uses TCP port 443, and port 2197 is allowed when firewalls block outbound access to 443.

  <!-- sysd-q-075 -->

- **Designing a notification system for Android, iOS and the web**

  The task is to build a notification service that reaches users on Android, iOS and the web. At its center, a notification service consumes events from a message queue, such as Kafka. It forwards each request to Firebase Cloud Messaging (FCM) or Apple Push Notification service (APNs) according to the device platform.

  A messaging solution such as FCM is cross-platform, composes, sends, queues and routes notifications reliably, and provides a unified API between app servers and client apps. When the client app first starts, it sends credentials (Sender ID, API Key, App ID) to FCM. FCM generates a registration token, also called the Instance ID, that must be included in notifications. The client sends the token to the app server, which caches it. Tokens pile up, so the recommended practice is to store each with a timestamp and remove stale ones from time to time.

  For the web, the IETF Web Push protocol defines the exchange. The user agent, the client on the user's device, POSTs to the push service to subscribe. A 201 response returns the subscription URI and a push resource URI, which must be shared with the application server confidentially. The application server requests delivery by POSTing the message to the push resource. A 201 response there means the push service accepted it, not that it reached the device.

  The push service stores messages for intermittently connected devices, which improves delivery reliability. The sender must give a time to live in seconds; once it elapses the service must not deliver, and it may retain a message for less time. A message can carry an urgency of very-low, low, normal or high, defaulting to normal. The device may ask to receive only messages at or above a level, which saves battery because radio use is costly. A message with a topic of at most 32 characters replaces any outstanding message with the same topic. A device that was offline then gets only the latest update.

  The device acknowledges a message by an HTTP DELETE, and without one the service should retry until the advertised expiration. Delivery receipts tell the sender the outcome: 202 on acceptance, then 204 once acknowledged, or 410 Gone on failure. They matter for critical messages, since knowing a message arrived avoids retransmission, polling and state resynchronization. Transient messages, such as an incoming call, may not need reliability. A push service may expire a subscription at any time. It must answer 404 Not Found to a sender using an expired one, so servers and clients must be prepared for changes in subscription state.

  Apple's HTTP/2 provider API for APNs allows payloads up to 4 kilobytes and uses TCP port 443, or port 2197 when firewalls block outbound 443. The Short Message Service (SMS) is a further channel, carried over SMS gateways through a short message service center, with messages of up to 160 characters. Delivery is not guaranteed, though, and about 1% to 5% of messages are lost even in normal operation. At scale, a push service must hold very many open TCP connections and can redistribute load with 307 redirects. Stored messages take significant storage, so it may reject large bodies with 413 but must accept bodies of 4096 bytes or less.

  <!-- sysd-q-006 -->

  *Figure: The table lists the status codes in the Web Push exchange and what each tells the sender.*

  | Code | What it tells the sender |
  |---|---|
  | 201 | Subscription created, or message accepted by the push service |
  | 202 | Delivery receipt: accepted |
  | 204 | Delivery receipt: acknowledged by the device |
  | 410 Gone | Delivery receipt: failure |
  | 404 Not Found | The subscription has expired |
  | 307 | Redirect that redistributes load |
  | 413 | Message body too large |

### Design a permission system

A permission system answers one question: may this subject perform this operation on this resource? Authorization sits after authentication, which is assumed done, and it is itself a security mechanism that must not be easy to abuse to get around the protection it provides. The models in this chapter answer the question in different ways: a list of permissions attached to a resource, roles and privileges, the discretion of an object's owner, the evaluation of attributes, relationships between subjects and resources, or a policy set centrally. Around them sit the points that retrieve, evaluate and enforce a policy, the standards that describe them, and the requirement that two or more people must be involved in authorizing critical operations.

- **Access control lists: a permission list on every resource**

  Take a file with a short list attached: Alice may read and write, Bob may only read. That list is an access control list, or ACL. It is a list of permissions attached to a system resource, saying which users or system processes may access it and which operations they may perform. Each entry in a typical ACL names a subject, the user or process asking for access, and an operation. A filesystem ACL is a table of access-control entries giving individual users' or groups' rights to specific objects. On routers, switches and servers, an ACL applies rules to ports or IP addresses, with the hosts or networks allowed to use them, much like a firewall. ACLs are easy to understand but error-prone with a high maintenance cost. Maintaining authorization data often costs as much administration as managing authentication credentials. The minimal form of the model in Role-based access control: permissions through roles is equivalent to an ACL whose only entries are groups. Modern SQL-based ACLs manage groups and inheritance in a hierarchy, so they can express everything that model expresses.

  <!-- sysd-q-010 -->

- **Role-based access control: permissions through roles**

  When someone joins a company or changes departments, a role-based system needs only one change: assigning the right roles. Role-based access control, or RBAC, restricts system access to authorized users and is defined around roles and privileges rather than individual users. Roles are created for job functions and permissions are assigned to roles, so users get permissions only through their roles. The model has subjects, roles, permissions and sessions, with many-to-many assignments, and a subject may have several simultaneous sessions in different roles. Roles can form a hierarchy in which higher-level roles subsume the permissions of sub-roles, and constraints can enforce the rule explained in Separation of duties: two people for critical operations. RBAC eases administration in large organizations with hundreds of users and thousands of permissions, and Kubernetes offers it, with each role listing allowed actions. The costs are role explosion when finer granularity is needed, and extreme complexity across dozens of systems without hierarchical roles. An ACL grants or denies write access to a particular file, whereas an RBAC permission is an operation, such as creating a credit account in a financial application.

  <!-- sysd-q-014 -->

- **Discretionary access control: the owner decides**

  In discretionary access control, or DAC, whoever holds a permission may hand it on. It restricts access to objects by the identity of subjects or the groups they belong to. It is discretionary because a subject holding a permission can pass it, perhaps indirectly, to any other subject, unless restrained by Mandatory access control: a policy users cannot override. In the common owner-based implementation, each object has an owner who controls its permissions and can make policy decisions. DAC is built on ACLs, and the owner group's policy grants or restricts access. The Unix file mode is a straightforward example, with read, write and execute bits for User, Group and Others. Capability systems are a second implementation. Subjects can transfer access, but not to just any subject, since the passer must already have access to the receiver, in line with least privilege. DAC is easy and flexible, but permission control is scattered and the object's owner group has too much power.

  <!-- sysd-q-011 -->

- **Attribute-based access control: rules over attributes**

  A user can edit a document if they own it and it is in draft mode. A rule like that, built from attributes, is attribute-based access control, or ABAC, in miniature. ABAC is an access control paradigm in which a subject's authorization is decided by evaluating attributes of the subject, the object, the requested operation and sometimes the environment. Its policy rules are Boolean functions of those attributes, so the only limits are the policy language and the availability of attributes. The attributes fall into four categories: subject (age, clearance, department, role), action (read, delete, approve), object (type, department, classification, location) and contextual (time, location). Unlike Role-based access control: permissions through roles, ABAC expresses complex rule sets over many attributes and needs no explicit authorizations for individual subjects. It can protect API methods, such as allowing managers to approve transactions up to their approval limit. The recommended architecture divides the work among the points described in Policy decision and enforcement points: who asks, who decides. ABAC is flexible, but its rules can be complicated and the implementation hard, and more granular controls add performance overhead.

  <!-- sysd-q-013 -->

- **Policy decision and enforcement points: who asks, who decides**

  In an API, the business logic can run only after another component has said Permit. An interceptor asks a Policy Decision Point (PDP) whether the caller may perform an action. The PDP fetches the policy and attributes and returns Permit or Deny, and only on Permit is the business logic called. That is authorization split into points. Each independent policy must be retrieved, evaluated and enforced. A Policy Retrieval Point retrieves it from a policy repository, the PDP evaluates it, and a Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) enforces it. The PEP intercepts a user's request to a resource, asks the PDP whether access is approved or rejected, and acts on the answer. The PDP is the central, environment-independent point that makes the final decision: Permit, Deny, NotApplicable or Indeterminate. Policy Information Points hold the data that policy conditions are evaluated against, such as resource status, session state or time of day. The PDP queries them for attribute values when needed.

  <!-- sysd-q-085 -->

  *Figure: The enforcement point asks the decision point, which fetches the policy and the attributes before it answers Permit or Deny.*

  ```mermaid
  flowchart TD
  A([User request]) --> B[Policy Enforcement Point]
  B -->|asks| C[Policy Decision Point]
  R[(Policy repository)] --> P[Policy Retrieval Point]
  P -->|policy| C
  C -->|queries| I[Policy Information Points]
  C -->|decides| D([Permit or Deny])
  ```

- **XACML: a policy language, not an engine**

  XACML says how to write an access policy, but not how to build the engine that evaluates it. It is an XML-based standard markup language for specifying access control policies, published by OASIS. It defines a declarative, fine-grained, attribute-based policy language, an architecture and a processing model for evaluating access requests, and it can also implement role-based access control. In the architecture of Policy decision and enforcement points: who asks, who decides, the enforcement point converts the user's request into an XACML authorization request. The decision point evaluates it and returns Permit, Deny, NotApplicable or Indeterminate. When rules contradict each other, combining algorithms such as deny-unless-permit and permit-unless-deny merge their decisions into one. An obligation is a directive from the decision point to the enforcement point on what must happen before or after approval, such as logging. If the enforcement point cannot comply, access may not be realized, while advice may be ignored. Open Policy Agent is a general-purpose open-source decision point. XACML 3.0 added delegation, which lets an authority hand all or part of its authority to another user without modifying the root policy.

  <!-- sysd-q-082 -->

- **The AAA authorization framework: chained agreements**

  In the AAA authorization framework, a request succeeds only if two agreements are both honored: user to home organization, and home organization to service provider. It is a framework for understanding the authorization of Internet resources and services, assuming the parties are already authenticated. It names four entities: the user, the home organization, the provider's AAA server, and the service equipment that delivers the service. There are three sequences. In the agent sequence the AAA server applies policy and configures the equipment. In pull the equipment asks the AAA server. In push the user first gets a ticket from the AAA server and presents it to the equipment.

  <!-- sysd-q-086 -->

- **Mandatory access control: a policy users cannot override**

  In mandatory access control, or MAC, the policy is not the user's to change. A secured environment, such as an operating system or database, constrains a subject's ability to access or modify an object under a centrally set policy. Subjects and objects carry security attributes, which the kernel checks against the policy on every access. Users cannot override the policy or grant access to restricted files, unlike in DAC. Once tied to multilevel security and military systems, MAC now reaches mainstream systems through SELinux, AppArmor and Windows Mandatory Integrity Control. It is strict and straightforward but not flexible.

  <!-- sysd-q-012 -->

- **Relationship-based access control: permission through relationships**

  In a social network, users share posts with other specific users, so who may see a post depends on who is connected to whom. Relationship-based access control, or ReBAC, evolved from RBAC. In it, a subject's permission to access a resource is defined by the presence of relationships between subjects and resources. It allows fine-grained permissions of exactly that kind. ABAC attributes can be compared with one another to give relation-based control, and XACML conditions can implement relationship-based access control.

  <!-- sysd-q-083 -->

- **Separation of duties: two people for critical operations**

  The same person should not both create a login account and authorize its creation. That is separation of duties: two or more people must be involved in authorizing critical operations, so no individual can breach security through dual privilege. By extension, no person may hold a role that exercises audit, control or review authority over another role held at the same time. In RBAC, constraints that restrict permission inheritance from opposing roles achieve it, and RBAC is particularly well suited to it. XACML conditions can implement segregation-of-duty checks.

  <!-- sysd-q-084 -->

- **Designing a permission system, from ACLs to policy points**

  The task is to design the part of a system that decides what each user may do. Authorization sits after authentication, which is assumed done. It is itself a security mechanism, so it must not be easy to abuse to get around the protection it provides.

  The simplest model is an ACL, covered in Access control lists: a permission list on every resource: a list of rules granting or denying users access to a resource. It is easy to understand, but error-prone with a high maintenance cost. In DAC the owner decides, as Discretionary access control: the owner decides explains: an access policy set by the object's owner group grants or restricts access. It is easy and flexible, but permission control is scattered and the owner group has too much power. In MAC, covered in Mandatory access control: a policy users cannot override, a central policy and classification labels on owners and resources decide access, and users cannot override it. It is strict and straightforward but not flexible.

  The data model of RBAC, covered in Role-based access control: permissions through roles, is subjects, roles and permissions with many-to-many assignments. Permissions attach to roles, users acquire them only through roles, and a subject can hold several sessions in different roles. Roles can form a hierarchy in which higher roles subsume permissions of sub-roles. Constraints enforce separation of duties, such as not letting one person both create and authorize an account. RBAC is flexible in assigning roles and accepted as best practice within a single system, but it can suffer role explosion when finer granularity is needed.

  ABAC evaluates attributes of the subject, the action, the resource and the environment through Boolean policy rules; Attribute-based access control: rules over attributes describes it. It is flexible, but its rules can be complicated and the implementation is hard. Relationship-based control, in Relationship-based access control: permission through relationships, defines permission by the relationships between subjects and resources. This gives fine-grained permissions, for example in a social network where users share posts with specific other users. The models combine: RBAC can implement DAC or MAC policies, and ABAC and relationship-based access control build on RBAC.

  Whichever model is chosen, the check is split into points, as in Policy decision and enforcement points: who asks, who decides. A PEP intercepts the request and asks a PDP, which evaluates policies fetched through a retrieval point and gets attributes from information points. In an API, an interceptor asks the PDP whether Alice can approve transaction 123. The PDP retrieves the policy and attributes and returns Permit or Deny, and only Permit runs the business logic; otherwise access is denied. XACML supplies a policy language and request/response scheme, but its specification does not cover how a PDP is built. Open Policy Agent is a general-purpose open-source PDP. When rules contradict, combining algorithms such as deny-unless-permit or permit-unless-deny resolve the conflict into one final decision. An obligation tells the PEP what must happen around an approved access, such as logging; if the PEP cannot comply, the approved access may not be realized.

  Fine-grained checks cost performance. The more granular the controls, the higher the overhead. RFC 2904 says the fields for both authentication and authorization should travel in a single message set to reduce latency. To remember: the shape stays the same across models. A request is intercepted, a decision point answers Permit or Deny, and the answer is enforced.

  <!-- sysd-q-009 -->
